15666-the-american-missionary-volume-48-:
The American Missionary for October 1894, volume 48, number 10, came from the American Missionary Association at Bible House, New York, at fifty cents a year in advance. Merrill E. Gates presided, with vice-presidents from Illinois, New York, and Massachusetts. The number reports a missionary society's work across America and abroad.

Editorials cover the annual meeting, Lowell, a financial statement, capital and labor, and the Alaska mission, with deaths of Hon. A. C. Barstow and Rev. Geo. S. Smith. Southern pages report Waldenses at Valdese, mountain notes, and a visit to Uncle Tom's Cabin. Indian mission services at Two Kettle village, Chinese distress, and the Bureau of Woman's Work follow. The issue shows missionary work as schools, churches, and relief, reported month by month.
22811-the-staircase-at-the-heart-s-delig:
Police headquarters supplies the frame for The Staircase at the Heart's Delight, a detective story dated 1894. The narrator looks back on his younger self, a man full of ambition who refused to drop a case when his colleagues moved on. He kept watching and waiting, certain another victim would be reported.

His patience shapes the whole tale. Because he alone stays with the puzzle, he is ready when fresh word arrives, and the odd results he promises begin to unfold. The story belongs to the early years of modern detective fiction, when dogged legwork mattered more than clever gadgets. It suits readers who enjoy a murder inquiry told by the man who would not let it go.
23177-the-inmate-of-the-dungeon-1894:
W. C. Morrow published The Inmate of the Dungeon in 1894, a grim work of fiction about prison life. A guard brings a convict into view. The man shuffles with pain, holding up by a string the heavy iron ball chained to his ankles so it will not drag on the floor.

The prisoner is about forty-five years old and worn down to skin and bone. Yet his frame still shows that he was once a man of rare bodily strength. Morrow dwells on that contrast, giving readers a stark picture of what long confinement in a dungeon can do to a human body.
26195-the-american-missionary-volume-48-:
The American Missionary for July 1894, volume 48, number 7, is the monthly journal of the American Missionary Association, sold at fifty cents a year from Bible House in New York. Its editorial pages cover finance, school anniversaries, and vacation plans, with a note on Mr. Wharton the evangelist.

Southern reports give anniversary exercises at Tougaloo University, Ballard Normal School, Beach Institute, Allen Normal School, Burrell School, and Orange Park. Church work, a letter on Chinese missions from Rev. W. C. Pond, the Bureau of Woman's Work, and a receipts list follow. The issue shows a missionary network at work in schools and churches across the South and West.
29684-prefaces-to-terence-s-comedies-and:
Lawrence Echard wrote these prefaces to Terence's comedies and Plautus's comedies in 1694, reissued by the Augustan Reprint Society. Both prefaces appeared in italic print, with upright type marking emphasis, names, and quotations, a detail the reprint preserves with care. French words in the Latin-1 version keep their accents, while the plain ASCII version drops them.

Echard's prefaces introduce two Roman comic masters to English readers, judging their wit, plots, and morals. A later note cites Echard's translation of Terence, edited with a foreword by Robert Graves in 1963. Students of classical reception will find a key early modern gateway to Roman comedy.
46584-punch-or-the-london-charivari-vol-:
Punch, or the London Charivari, for 15 December 1894, is one issue of that famed comic paper. It forms part of volume 107 of the run. Sir Francis Burnand was the editor of the paper at that time. The issue opens with a captioned cartoon, a talk in dialect between two men on a singer at the North London Tivoli.

Next comes a piece called A Tree with Variegated Leaves. It is made of letters that have found their way into the editor's box at 85, Fleet Street. The letters are printed so that their writers may claim them, the head note says. Most of the names at their feet were hard to read, and so they have been held back to dodge error. The last letter is left as the sum and moral of the whole row.
4865-history-of-the-united-netherlands-1:
Philip II's shadow falls over France as well as the Netherlands in this 1592 to 1594 volume, and John Lothrop Motley weighs the king's claim to the French throne. The Duke of Mayenne leads the Catholic party, the Duke of Guise escapes from Tours, and plotters advance the marriage of the Infanta as a path to the crown.

Parma, maligned by Commander Moreo, justifies himself to Philip, while French politicians and soldiers divide over Spanish money and aims. Motley sets Philip's pretensions beside the heroism of the age, showing a contest for France fought with marriages, subsidies, and armies. Readers see how the Dutch war and the French wars of religion became one tangled struggle.
4866-history-of-the-united-netherlands-1:
Maurice's sieges of 1594 display the Dutch army at its most methodical, and John Lothrop Motley follows the campaign from Gertruydenberg to Groningen. New siege techniques give Maurice an edge at Gertruydenberg, where Count Philip of Nassau has a notable adventure before the town capitulates.

Spanish troops mutiny, Verdugo twice tries to retake Coeworden, and Maurice then assaults Groningen, narrowly escaping danger himself before the city surrenders. Motley also raises the question of religious toleration in conquered towns. The volume shows a republic winning ground steadily, town by town, through discipline rather than dramatic single battles.
a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-papers: John Adams of Braintree, Harvard man and Boston lawyer, fills this first volume part compiled by James Daniel Richardson. Descended from early Massachusetts settlers, Adams studied law, taught school, and rose to the presidency. The volume prints his proclamations and messages in full. It records the official voice of the second president.
a-residence-in-france-during-the-years-1: Charlotte Biggs continues her letters from France into 1794 in this third part, opening on the sixth of January with a confession of shrinking from her task. Events have grown too numerous and too complicated for occasional remarks, she writes, and a narrator of no great pretensions may shrink from matter that will perplex the historian's choice. Removed from the great scene of intrigues, she records suffering felt before its causes are fully known.
a-spirit-in-prison-pg2994:
Robert Hichens opens on a tiny islet in the bay of Naples. This text was prepared from the 1908 Harper edition. Young Vere sits in the sun there, facing Nisida and distant Ischia. A boy's voice sings Napoli Bella across the still water. Vere has lived her life on that islet, in a house shadowed by her dead father's crime and her mother's long grief.

Forty-two chapters widen the story to Naples society, a love that tests every loyalty, and the slow freeing of a spirit the title names. Hichens writes lush, sunlit prose and builds his tragedy from family secrets and duty. The novel asks what the innocent owe the guilty who raised them.
alchemy-and-chemistry-1894: Alchemy and Chemistry is an 1894 paper by Herbert McLeod, the English chemist. McLeod wrote when the new profession of chemistry was taking stock of its own past. His paper sets the old art of alchemy beside the modern science that grew out of it, comparing the discarded parent with the disciplined successor. It is a short Victorian period piece on that descent, written by a working chemist rather than a historian.
arxiv-2412-01794:
Khaled Abud, Sergey Lavrushkin, Alexey Kirillov, and Dmitriy Vatolin teach image generators to care about perceptual quality by wiring in image quality assessment models. Diffusion generators reach remarkable fidelity yet still produce duds, partly because nothing conditions them on quality. Quality assessors, meanwhile, know exactly how to grade an image.

Gradient guidance toward higher quality scores worked but generalized poorly. Their IQA-Adapter instead conditions generation on a target quality level, learning the relationship between images and scores. Asked for high quality, it shifts output toward a cleaner subdomain; asked for low quality, it acts as a degradation model. Under high-quality conditioning, objective metrics improved by up to ten percent, with user preference confirming the gain.
arxiv-2412-03094: Chetcuti and Healey settle a question about maps between operator algebras that preserve the size of a certain average: can every such map be stretched into a structure-preserving one? Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-four. Earlier work answered yes only for special averages and for the smaller class of C*-algebras. Here the answer covers every symmetric Kubo-Ando mean between the broader AW*-algebras.
arxiv-2412-03394:
Duchemin and Blase propose a new route to self consistent GW calculations in twenty twenty-four. The GW method predicts charged excitation energies in molecules and solids. Standard self consistent versions replace the full dynamic self energy with a static, symmetrized form. The authors avoid that approximation by a joint diagonalization trick.

They jointly diagonalize the one body Green functions taken at input quasiparticle energies. Tests on the GW100 molecular set match the conventional approach closely. Mean absolute error on ionization potentials was sixty-five milli electron volts. Building the density matrix from the full Green function shifts results toward coupled cluster reference values. The scheme sits between quasiparticle and fully self consistent variants. The authors present it as more faithful to the dynamics.
arxiv-2412-10494:
Yushu Wu and a large team at Snap shrink a cinematic video generator until it runs on a phone, in real time. Server models take minutes on big graphics cards for one clip. Writing in twenty twenty-four, the team starts from a compact image backbone and searches for temporal layer arrangements that suit mobile hardware. An adversarial fine-tuning recipe then cuts the denoising process to four steps. The finished model has well under a billion parameters.

On a current flagship phone it produces a five-second video in about five seconds. The authors claim quality on par with the server giants it outruns by orders of magnitude. The point is access: creators with only a handset gain a tool that recently needed a data center. The framework is presented as comprehensive, spanning architecture and training.
arxiv-2412-12194:
Yi Hao Puah and three co-authors attack model watermarking in a paper from twenty twenty-four. Neural networks are valuable intellectual property worth protecting. Backdoor watermarking is the best-established ownership scheme. A secret trigger set makes the model answer in a telltale way, proving ownership.

Such watermarks were thought hard to remove. The authors find a critical flaw in how verification behaves. It lies in the trigger samples themselves, the scheme's secret key. Their package, BlockDoor, wraps a model to block trigger samples of all three known kinds. Blocked triggers mean the watermark cannot be demonstrated. Readers in machine learning security get a warning that a popular protection can be neutralized without retraining.
arxiv-2412-16594:
Basak Demirok and Mucahid Kutlu build a data set for spotting AI-written code in a paper from twenty twenty-four. Language models now write code that students and job candidates can pass off as their own. That raises ethical problems in assignments and interviews. Telling machine code from human code has become a practical need.

Their data set, AIGCodeSet, pairs both kinds of Python code. It holds about twenty-eight hundred AI-generated and about forty-eight hundred human-written samples. The machine samples came from three models: CodeLlama, Codestral, and Gemini Flash. Baseline detection methods were run on the set. A Bayesian classifier beat the other detectors in their experiments. Readers get an annotated benchmark for a new academic integrity problem.
arxiv-2412-19594:
Jacek Miȩkisz asks when non-periodic structures, like quasicrystals, can be truly stable, in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. Quasicrystals show order with no repeating pattern, a trait that has puzzled physicists since their first find. The paper looks back at their past, with classical lattice-gas models of particles that act on each other.

The heart of the work is ground states, the lowest-energy forms of such models. Some non-periodic tilings and symbol sequences do show up as ground states. Miȩkisz argues they stand up to small changes in forces, and to heat noise, just if a homogeneity rule holds. He calls it the Strict Boundary Condition. With no such rule, their seeming stability is an artifact of the picks made.
arxiv-2412-19694:
Stefan Gieseke and six co-authors study non-perturbative effects in two collider processes at the Large Hadron Collider. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four. Precision tests set the strong force strength and the proton's inner make-up. To match data to theory, small effects that sit outside the main maths must be gauged and stripped out.

With Monte Carlo event tools, they gauge those effects for paired jets and for a Z boson with a jet, each split three ways. The size of the effect shifts a lot between the two, which breaks a hope that one fix fits all. They propose a fresh triple-split measure of the soft spray in the Z case to test this in real data.
arxiv-2412-19994:
Yang Han and four co-authors survey how large language models are being reshaped for chemistry work. Their survey appeared in twenty twenty-four. General models train on web text, which lacks the deep facts chemistry needs. Chemistry data also comes in mixed forms, like flat graphs, three-space builds, and light spectra, which text drills miss.

The survey lays out ways to feed field facts and mixed data forms into such models. It also treats the models as agents that can call chemistry tools to speed lab work. Known test sets for chemistry skill are summed up at the end. The authors close with open gaps and paths they see as most ripe for new work.
arxiv-2501-00994:
Xiao and colleagues wrote in twenty twenty-five about redesigning operating systems for chips with hundreds of cores. Existing systems do not scale well and ignore what applications need. Their NetworkedOS builds a layered network of dependencies among applications, kernel, and hardware. A compile-time analysis maps how instructions connect to system services. A partitioning scheme then finds clusters of work that can run in parallel. Those clusters are placed on cores at run time with care for affinity.

The goal is fewer messages crossing between cores. Tests compared their system against Linux and a research system called Barrelfish. NetworkedOS ran up to about seven times faster than Linux on a large core count. It also roughly doubled Barrelfish speed in their tests. The work argues operating systems should exploit application structure directly.
arxiv-2501-01294:
Christian Reiher and Bjarne Schülke pin down minimum degree in simplicial complexes in two thousand twenty-five. A simplicial complex is a family of sets closed under taking subsets. Its size can be weighed against its vertex count. They ask how small a vertex degree is forced by that ratio.

A threshold value sets the largest ratio that still forces a low degree vertex. Past results from several teams covered parts of the range. The pair prove an exact formula for a broad new range of degrees. Their values blend powers of two with a subtracted term. Like results came from a rival team on their own.
arxiv-2501-02094:
Ali Baheri and Peng Wei introduced a logic for requirements that span several time and abstraction scales in a 2025 paper. Cyber-physical systems, from drone fleets to smart grids, must satisfy rules like a fleet-level deadline and a vehicle-level safety gap at once. Their Stratified Metric Temporal Logic adds an operator that pins each temporal property to a chosen abstraction level, so multi-scale demands read naturally while links between levels stay formal.

They prove the new logic strictly contains the standard metric temporal logic and expresses properties it cannot. Simulations of agents under both logics show stratified specifications improving coordination and cutting collisions, without meaningful cost in compute time or path quality. Multi-agent verification gains an expressive, still usable language.
arxiv-2501-02594: The BESIII Collaboration reported in twenty twenty-five the observation of a new decay channel of the charmonium state psi three six eight six. In this channel the psi particle decays into a negative kaon, an excited lambda baryon known as lambda fifteen twenty, and an anti-xi baryon, together with the charge-conjugate process. The available record states the observation claim itself, made by the large BESIII detector collaboration working in Beijing.
arxiv-2501-04094:
Matthew Golden, Kaushik Satapathy, and Dimitrios Psaltis set out a way to learn the laws of a moving fluid from data alone, at a scale past work could not reach. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Sparse fits from a library of candidate terms can bare a system's rules from space-time data. But known ways cost too much for rich data. The team's frame cuts that cost. As a test, they feed it fake data from high-grade runs of a turbulent fluid laced with magnetic fields, with loss from thickness and from opposites to flow. From a library far larger than past work used, the frame recovers the full set of rules for that fluid.
arxiv-2501-06294:
Li, Liu, and Song used a muon beam dump experiment to constrain hypothetical new particles in twenty twenty-five. In beam dump setups, particles produced in a target are hunted through missing energy or distinctive energy deposits. The NA64mu experiment fires high-energy muons and is sensitive to particles that favor muons.

Three models were tested against the experiment's data: axions coupled to photons, axions coupled to muons, and a dark sector carried by a massless force boson distinguishing muon and tau flavors. The photon-coupled axion space was not yet newly probed, but muon-coupled axions were excluded over a fresh region of mass and coupling strength. For the dark sector, the limits beat existing ones by nearly an order of magnitude. The authors project stronger reach from newer and future runs.
arxiv-2501-08894:
Yankang Liu and three co-authors built a way to solve elastic networks on curved surfaces of any shape. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, tackles crystal growth on curved ground. Past work could handle only shapes with spin symmetry. The math of stretch on curves is hard to state in clean form. That kept most solutions to round, neat cases.

The team solves the stretch equations by number, with no need for symmetry. They show it on a net that holds one point defect placed at any spot, and find the least energy state. They find the shift from a clean net to one with a five or seven fold defect turns on the domain shape. Readers in soft matter get a tool for odd curved ground.
arxiv-2501-11994:
Kryszkiewicz optimises transmit power in mobile systems while accounting for amplifier distortion in twenty twenty-five. Phones use SC-FDMA on the uplink because its signal envelope fluctuates less than OFDM. Gentler signals let amplifiers run more efficiently. Quality is usually guarded by a transmitter side error limit.

His approach models the nonlinear amplifier directly in the optimisation. The goal becomes the best signal to noise and distortion ratio at the receiver. An analytic model covers OFDM, and a semi analytic one covers SC-FDMA. Simulations show better receiver quality for both schemes. SC-FDMA still wins overall. The author argues amplifier aware design can boost performance and sustainability in next generation networks.
arxiv-2501-13294:
M. Romanova and colleagues simulated the flickering of a young star in 2025 to explain its changing light. TW Hya is a nearby classical T Tauri star still pulling in gas from its disk. Space and ground telescopes record light curves that jump in a messy, semi-regular way, with rhythmic components from hours to days.

Three-dimensional magnetic simulations model the star as spinning with a slightly tilted dipole magnet. For many settings, gas falls in an unstable regime and lands in several hot spots, producing messy light curves much like the observed ones. Changing field strength and tilt reshapes the rhythm pattern, sometimes hiding the star's own spin period. Matching spectra between model and sky supports unstable infall as the cause.
arxiv-2501-13994:
Hy Nguyen and five co-authors build a team of cooperating agents, running on one device, that keeps a moving target in view, in a conference paper from twenty twenty-five. Active tracking differs from passive watching: the camera itself must move to follow the target through cluttered scenes. Single agents gather too little information and falter when targets dart or hide.

Their system trains several agents together with reinforcement learning under a mixture-of-experts design. Each agent takes a distinct role, and the team coordinates viewpoints without extra hardware. Tests on interactive maps with moving and fixed obstacles showed stronger resistance to occlusion and rapid motion, plus longer tracking runs. The design aims at cheaper, sturdier tracking for navigation, surveillance, and robots.
arxiv-2501-17494:
Bouhlal and four co-authors trapped electrons in graphene dots in this paper from twenty twenty-five. A graphene quantum dot can hold an electron in a tiny region. The team studied scattering through such dots under three influences at once: a magnetic field, an energy gap, and circularly polarized laser light. Floquet theory handled the time-varying light.

Matching wave solutions at the dot's edges yielded the scattering coefficients. The gap and the laser both deepened electron localization inside the dot. Trapped states therefore lived longer before leaking away. Light intensity and polarization gave knobs to tune the confinement. The authors frame the setup as a control scheme for graphene nanodevices.
arxiv-2501-19394:
Konrad Menzel sets out what can be learned about cause and effect when units in one fixed population sway each other's outcomes. The paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. In equilibrium models, one person's outcome settles jointly with everyone else's. That breaks the neat setups used for treatment spillovers, where effects fade with distance.

Menzel first defines targets that a single network experiment can identify under weak assumptions. These are average partial responses, which may shift with the overall assignment pattern. Under a design-based view, weighted estimators of those targets are unbiased and settle as the network grows. For smooth equilibrium models he recovers weighted averages of response slopes, in the spirit of local treatment effects. With stronger assumptions the same targets rebuild the model's own parameters. The causal reading survives even without them.
arxiv-2502-03294:
Max Engelstein, Cole Jeznach, and Yannick Sire gauge the bad sets of answers to elliptic equations near edges, even when the equations act badly. New work has made clear how fast answers can fade to zero. It has also sized their zero sets and bad sets. Those gains took smooth, even terms and a neat domain edge. This work drops both crutches.

The new case is high co-dimension. The edge is thin, like a sheet in a block. Terms there are not even in strength, nor smooth in the set sense. Still, like bounds on bad sets hold near the edge. The key step bends a known scheme that sorts points in layers. It swaps the scheme's flat planes for cones. Shapes that fit the thin edge do the work. The gains push a new theory into the rough case where much use lives.
arxiv-2502-05194:
Farooq, Zahoor, and Francis derive mass distributions for primordial black holes with Press-Schechter theory. Such holes can form in the radiation era from rare early density bumps. A bump re-enters the Hubble radius and then collapses under gravity. The theory is completed by an excursion-set first-crossing construction. A smoothed density contrast and its variance S set up the counting frame. The variance links to the early curvature spectrum through radiation-era transfer.

For Gaussian statistics and a collapse threshold, the formation share is a tail formula. That tail has a controlled rare-event approximation. For a sharp-k filter, the density path is a random walk in S. A diffusion equation with an absorbing barrier gives the first-crossing density. That density yields the formation share per unit log mass. The results then map to the present-day dark matter share per log mass.
arxiv-2502-09894:
Brianna Grado-White, Guglielmo Grimaldi, Matthew Headrick, and Veronika Hubeny wrote a theoretical physics paper in twenty twenty-five about how gravity theories encode information. They study a formula that links the area of certain surfaces inside a curved spacetime to the amount of entanglement in a matching quantum system. Their version first picks a slice that runs through time, finds the largest surface on it, and then chooses the best slice. Homology, the rule tying surfaces to regions, is applied to volumes of spacetime itself.

The authors prove that the smallest allowed region in their setup matches the region expected from earlier work. They also try to build a simple network model where shortest cuts would give the same answers for changing states. That model needs the time slices to cooperate in a certain way, which holds in some cases but may fail in others.
arxiv-2502-12094:
Karthikeyan K and eight co-authors study when search plus self-feedback actually helps language agents reason. Their paper from twenty twenty-five compares ground-truth feedback against the model's own judgments inside inference-time search. Search uses the feedback as values to steer which reasoning paths to explore or drop. Math reasoning is the first testbed, tool-calling the harder second.

Self-feedback alone generalizes poorly, the experiments show. Search works when true feedback is available, or when feedback is carefully shaped for the domain. Complex tasks needed bespoke designs rather than off-the-shelf loops. The authors map the boundary conditions honestly: inference search is powerful, but its compass must be trustworthy or tailor-made.
arxiv-2502-13394:
Yao Xie and Xiuyuan Cheng wrote a tutorial recasting flow-based generative models as methods walking through probability space in a 2025 paper. Flow models morph one spread into another along invertible paths governed by plain change-based math rules. Giving exact likelihoods and fast sampling for images, signals, and anomaly detection. The tutorial builds their mathematics from the ground up for signal processing and machine learning readers.

Key ideas include the Wasserstein distance between distributions, gradient flows that descend energy landscapes, and how densities evolve along the governing math rules. Those tools yield convergence pledges that connect the models' empirical success to theory. The authors aim to give practitioners enough rigor to apply flow methods deliberately rather than by recipe.
arxiv-2502-16494:
Tony Puthenpurakal studies how the sizes of Ext groups grow over complete intersection rings, and finds the growth eventually goes quiet in an informative way. For a module over such a ring and an ideal primary to the maximal ideal, the lengths of Ext groups against powers of the ideal follow polynomial-type functions. Their degrees, tracked separately for even and odd homological levels, become constant for all large levels.

The maximum of those two constants is an invariant tying the ideal, the ring, and the module's support variety together. When that invariant is at most zero, the regularity of associated graded modules of syzygies stays bounded across all steps. An application gives a syzygetic Artin-Rees property for the module. Examples illustrate the results' edges. Support varieties, imported from group representation theory, here govern commutative algebra asymptotics.
arxiv-2502-18394:
Jacob Fein-Ashley, Neelesh Gupta, Rajgopal Kannan, and Viktor Prasanna wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It swaps the costly self-attention of transformers for fast Fourier steps, so very long texts can be read on plain hardware.

Self-attention grows with the square of the length, which chokes long contexts. SPECTRE gives each head a real FFT, a gate that adapts to the content, and an inverse FFT. The cost per layer drops to near linear. A prefix cache keeps text generation fast, and a wavelet add-on sharpens local traits at small cost. On the longest tests it runs up to seven times faster than a top baseline. Scores on book and image tasks match or beat that baseline, with few added weights.
arxiv-2503-01894:
Rashid Mushkani and five colleagues bring in LIVS, a dataset for aligning image generators with the values of the people who live in a place, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Text-to-image models shape how planners picture public space that is open to all. The set asks whose tastes those models speak for.

Thirty groups from the community spent two years to set out what counts. The set holds 37,710 pairwise comparisons across 13,462 images. Six criteria frame the calls: accessibility, safety, comfort, invitingness, inclusivity, and diversity. They boil down 634 concepts set by the community itself. Fine-tuning Stable Diffusion XL with preference optimization made its output match the notes more well. The tastes in those notes varied by who the raters were. The team says data of this plural, cross-cut kind is a must for fair AI in space and place.
arxiv-2503-02994:
Ahmed Jellal, Rachid El Aitouni, Pablo Diaz, and David Laroze study electrons passing through graphene under a magnetic influence in a 2025 physics study. A nearby material imprints an exchange field on the graphene, and two barriers scatter the traveling fermions. Solving the Dirac equation across five regions gives transmission and reflection rates through the transfer matrix method.

Group delay time, found with a wave packet and stationary phase analysis, shows how long particles linger. Both transmission and delay depend on spin, with clear shifts between spin orientations, especially when thin boron nitride layers are present. Enhanced tunneling peaks also appear. Spin-sensitive timing could serve future graphene electronics.
arxiv-2503-03494:
Mihael Liskij, Xuhua Ding, Gene Tsudik, and David Basin wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It defines a new tool, the Oblivious Digital Token, which lets a check on a device stay secret from all onlookers.

Devices prove who they are by showing a trait or a secret, but the check itself is plain to see. The need arose with digital emblems, marks the Red Cross backs to shield digital goods in cyber war. With this token a verifier can test a device without any party, even the device, learning that the test ran. The team gives a build that meets the safety bar even if the device's software is fully owned by a foe. A working demo shows it runs well in practice.
arxiv-2503-04094:
Seth Karten, Andy Luu Nguyen, and Chi Jin present PokeChamp, an AI agent that plays Pokemon battles at expert level. Their twenty twenty-five paper builds on minimax search, the classic method for two-player games. A language model fills three roles in that search.

The model proposes the player's moves, guesses what the foe will do, and scores each board state. No extra training of the model is needed. In the Gen 9 OU format, the agent beat the best past language-model bot and the best rule-based bot by wide margins. It also reached a rating that puts it in the top slice of human players on the Pokemon Showdown ladder.
arxiv-2503-04394:
Sabine Körbel computes, from first principles, how excess electrons hop through bismuth ferrite, a material whose electric domains may conduct along their walls. The paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Extra electrons in this compound curl into small polarons, tight knots of charge and lattice strain. Their levels sit deep in the band gap, so current likely moves by hopping, not free flow.

Körbel maps the energy landscape for a hop in the bulk and inside a common domain wall. The barriers come out modest, much like those in kindred oxides. Three wall types were checked as traps for the polarons. The walls hold them with a depth of about twice room-temperature thermal energy. From these numbers she estimates mobility and diffusion at room temperature. Measured conductivity data are then weighed against the intrinsic picture.
arxiv-2503-05394:
Sujoy Roychowdhury and seven co-authors guide large language models with classic code checks to write unit tests for Java methods. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Past ways feed the model a sample use of the method, or the whole class it sits in. Sample uses are often not there for new code. Whole classes can be too big, and the test code then falls short. The team's path uses fixed checks of the code's shape to pick the facts the model needs. That keeps the prompt tight and on point. The aim is sound test code that scales to large, complex classes.
arxiv-2503-07194: Henning Krause, writing alone in two thousand twenty-five, shows a bridge between two great worlds of categories: those built on sets with sums, and those built on triangles. The note sits in deep algebra. He proves that a place-based cut of a triangle world yields a like cut of a sum world, when one passes to their sum forms. From that, a growth of the base world gives a case where a cut exists just in the big world.
arxiv-2503-07394:
Simon Grall and colleagues present QBIOL, web-based software to model bioelectrochemical processes. This field sits at the base of uses in synthetic biology, health care, and catalysis. Past model methods cannot catch both the random motion of molecules and electron transfer. They also fail across the full time span, from picoseconds to minutes.

QBIOL joins molecular dynamics, applied math, GPU programming, and quantum charge transport in one tool. It runs counts of stochastic electron transfer. The team shows it by matching models to lab data on current from DNA fixed to an electrode. The DNA is redox-labeled. They also test redox species held in tiny spaces, under varied waveforms. Such setups matter for biosensing and catalysis.
arxiv-2503-07694:
Fankhauser asks if paths in pilot-wave thought can be seen or not in tests. The thought gives grains set spots at all times by strict rules. Yet lone grain paths stay out of test reach in the main. Two bids claim to crack that wall in late work tales. Weak speed probes claim to trace paths with soft touches. Odd-path tests claim a clash twixt true spots and wave spots.

Fankhauser holds that none of the bids lands its claim. Each reads fine in stock quantum terms with no clash at all. Those reads sit well with what pilot-wave thought calls too. The rows spring, he holds, from a dim view of what tests mean. No proof for or past the thought comes from the bids.
arxiv-2503-10194:
Davide Pradovera, Ralf Hiptmair, and Ilaria Perugia build fast stand in models for acts that ring in wave spread tasks. Their goal trait is field growth, the size of the fix tool for spread, writ through rules on the edge as sums. They first prove finds that link growth to traits of the tool that sets the spread task in its range of waves.

Those finds back the use of split part close fits as the stand in drive. Some ways fit the tool straight, or a chance sketched form of it to save time. Mixed ways join split part root find with base role close fits. The plans need no counts at wave counts that are not real, and they fit their picks as they go. Count tests on spread things in two dims show two ways in the lead, one for truth and one for speed.
arxiv-2503-11294:
Martin Výboh and co-authors studied compact versions of power market curves in 2025. Supply and demand curves drive energy market study, but storing and modeling them at full size is unwieldy. Standard squeezing methods shrink the curves into a small latent space, yet their rebuilds often break a basic economic rule: the curves must move monotonically, never bending the wrong way.

The authors weighed four methods, two linear and two nonlinear, in two- and 3D latent spaces. After preprocessing a three-year hourly data set from the Iberian power market to unify form and tame outliers. The nonlinear method UMAP ranked first across several error measures. An optional isotonic regression step, which forces monotonicity back into the output, cut errors further and restored validity for several methods, making the squeezed curves safer for downstream modeling.
arxiv-2503-12894:
Anamika Singh, Abhay Kumar Singh, and Eitan Yaakobi extended function-correcting codes in twenty twenty-five to b-symbol read channels. Ordinary error correction protects the data. Function-correcting codes protect only a function's value computed from the data. That is enough for machine learning inference and archival storage, where the computation matters more than every bit. Earlier work covered binary symmetric and symbol-pair channels.

The current paper develops the theory over finite fields for channels that read overlapping blocks of b symbols. The authors introduce irregular b-symbol distance codes, prove performance bounds, and give a graphical construction approach. Applied to specific function classes, their codes achieve lower redundancy than classical b-symbol codes at the same reliability — the savings that justify protecting functions rather than data.
arxiv-2503-13394:
Jan Kyzioł and Andrzej Okniński study, in a 2025 preprint, how a one-to-two resonance is born in driven nonlinear oscillators. Such systems can lock into rhythms where one cycle of forcing drives two of response. The authors ask whether that lock grows out of the main one-to-one resonance by period doubling, or appears on its own. They work with the steady-state amplitude curve of an effective equation for coupled oscillators. That curve is given implicitly, so its shape must be read from the function's differential traits.

Their result ties the birth of the one-to-two resonance to singular, isolated points of that implicit curve. Where the curve pinches in that special way, the new resonance can form. Numerical examples show the mechanism at work. The paper gives a cleaner test for when a driven system will slip into the doubled rhythm.
arxiv-2503-15494:
Prudhvi Naayini and four co-authors review AI tools that help people with poor sight in two thousand twenty-five. The review covers how such tools are built, where they are used, and what good they do. Key areas are computer vision, language tools, and wearable gear. Smart glasses, phone apps, and travel aids all come up.

Tools can name objects, describe a scene, and read text aloud as speech. Deep learning, mixed inputs, and fast live processing have made them easier to use. Gains include travel on one's own, social life, school, and work. The authors also flag cost, ethics, and fit for new settings. They call for joint work across fields for fair access.
arxiv-2503-17794:
Ketan Suhaas Saichandran and three co-authors help image generators keep up with long, detailed prompts by feeding the description in gradually. Models often drop objects or scramble spatial relations when a prompt packs in a complex scene. Their method, SCoPE, needs no training and plugs into existing systems.

The full prompt is first split into sub-prompts that run from broad scene layout down to fine detail. During generation the model interpolates between these versions, so coarse structure settles before intricacies arrive. On the GenAI-Bench dataset, visual question answering scores measuring alignment rose by more than eight points on average over Stable Diffusion baselines. Gains appeared on most prompts tested.
arxiv-2503-18694:
Ugne Miniotaite and a large team of co-authors map the crystal and magnetic structures of two rhenium oxides made under high pressure. The oxides take a wolframite type crystal form with a slanted cell. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

Muon spin tests paired with computer work on muon stop sites narrow the spin layout to two candidate patterns for both compounds. In both, the spins tilt off the main axes in one crystal plane. The ordered spin size is small, which fits why neutron scans show no clear magnetic signal. Bond checks back a set charge state for rhenium, and the authors link the small spin to orbit effects and bond mixing.
arxiv-2503-23894:
Shubham Kala, Abhishek Negi, and Hemwati Nandan study ringing black holes in twenty twenty-five. A disturbed black hole vibrates at characteristic frequencies called quasinormal modes. Their black hole is dyonic, carrying both electric and magnetic charge. The theory is Einstein-Euler-Heisenberg, a model of nonlinear electrodynamics.

The authors compute the modes of a non-rotating dyonic hole in detail. They trace how dyonic charge shapes the oscillation properties. Results are compared with holes carrying only electric or only magnetic charge in the same theory. The comparison exposes signatures unique to the dyonic case. Readers in gravitational physics get a finer fingerprint for telling charged black holes apart by their ringdown.
arxiv-2503-24294:
Martin Horák, Michal Šmejkal, and Martin Kružík build mathematical models for soft solids whose surfaces carry their own energy, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Gels, rubbers, and biological tissues all feel surface tension-like effects, and those effects can dominate when the body is small or very soft.

The authors set up variational models that treat bulk and surface mechanics together. Their new class, surface-polyconvex models, bakes surface energy into the constitutive law while guaranteeing that energy minimizers actually exist, a nontrivial point in nonlinear elasticity. They implement the models in a finite element code. Benchmark tests include the liquid bridge problem and the Rayleigh-Plateau instability, where surface energy drives the behavior. The models capture these surface-driven phenomena accurately. The authors pitch them as tools for designing soft materials in engineering and biology.
arxiv-2504-03294:
Liuyuan Wen and colleagues compute how strong magnetic fields reshape charmonium, the bound states of a charm quark and its antiquark. Such fields arise in heavy ion collisions and in magnetized stars, and they can mix and split particle states. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team uses a relativistic light-front method that treats the pair at near light speed, solving for masses. Internal wave functions with confining forces and gluon exchange built in. Fields of increasing strength were applied to watch the spectrum move.

The two best-known charmonium states mix as the field grows, and their magnetic sublevels split in a Zeeman pattern. Wave functions deform: momentum spreads sideways while narrowing along the field, and excited states develop double-humped parton profiles. The authors stress that relativistic effects and center-of-mass coupling drive much of the behavior, so nonrelativistic shortcuts would miss it.
arxiv-2504-05194:
Sebastian Barbieri and Nicolas Bitar build a broad frame for symbolic dynamics in their twenty twenty-five paper. Symbolic dynamics studies systems as streams of symbols, often laid over groups. Many spaces of interest, like tilings, do not form groups, so the old tools fall short.

Their new structure, the blueprint, codes a family of graphs by states, generators, and relations. It can cover groups, monoids, categories, and tiling spaces alike. On blueprints they define dynamics and show key traits survive quasi-isometries, maps that bend space in a bounded way. Those traits include whether the domino problem can be decided. As a use case, tiling domino problems in two or more dimensions are shown undecidable.
arxiv-2504-10994:
Ismael dePedro-Embid and four co-authors showed polariton lasers in twenty twenty-five that hold narrow linewidths near room heat. Exciton-polaritons are part light, part matter. They condense in semiconductor microcavities and emit laser-like light. That light is prized for sensing and spectroscopy. Heat in most cases kills them fast, in tens of degrees. It does so as excitons split.

The team put the condensate in micrometer-sized traps in the cavity. That changed the picture in a big way. Trapped condensates lived to about two hundred kelvin. They kept decoherence rates under ten gigahertz. Their linewidths were an order of magnitude narrower than rival solid-state systems at such heat. The team works in the mature aluminum gallium arsenide platform. Such traps point to polariton devices that run at room heat, for use in on-chip photonics.
arxiv-2504-12394:
Harry Gully and a large team of co-authors study galaxies in clusters in twenty twenty-five. Galaxies that stop forming stars are called passive or quiescent. How surroundings drive that shutdown is a key question in galaxy evolution. The team looked at four clusters seen as they were when the universe was younger.

They measured how many passive red-sequence galaxies exist at each brightness and mass. Data came from deep observations with the Very Large Telescope, plus two surveys. In all four clusters, faint, low-mass passive galaxies were more common than in the field. The cluster mass function also had a shallower low-mass slope. Readers see clear signs that cluster life hastens the shutdown of small galaxies.
arxiv-2504-13694:
Yilin Xie classifies special subgroups inside Ree groups in a 2025 algebra study. A fixer is a subgroup in which every element leaves at least one point of the space unmoved. The question is which fixers can be as large as a point stabilizer. The subgroup fixing one chosen point, in each primitive action of an almost simple group built on a Ree group.

Xie characterizes those large fixers completely for the actions considered. Such classifications feed the broader study of how big subgroups of simple groups can be. They also test conjectures about whether fixers must be smaller than stabilizers except in known cases.
arxiv-2504-15594:
Tatsuhito Hasegawa and Shunsuke Sakai chase a training-free way to set the temperature of a classifier's softmax output. Temperature strongly shapes how confident predictions look and how well they perform, yet it is usually tuned by trial and error. Their theory ties the optimal value directly to the dimension of the feature representation.

In practice the optimum still wanders with model and dataset, so they fit adjustment coefficients on top of the theoretical relationship. A batch normalization layer placed just before the output stabilizes the feature space. Large-scale experiments produced an empirical formula, refined by class count and task complexity, that estimates the temperature without further training. The formula generalized across diverse tasks.
arxiv-2504-19294:
Philipp Straubinger and four co-authors ran a repeat study in twenty twenty-five on making software tests more fun. The tool is IntelliGame, a plugin for the IntelliJ IDEA coding app. It gives points and feedback to push coders to write and run more tests.

Past work hinted that such game-like rewards help, but proof was thin. This study used one hundred seventy-four people in two groups, one with the plugin and one without. It also moved to a new language, TypeScript, and a larger pool. The plugin group wrote more tests, ran them more often, and used test tools more. Their code came out better, and the team reads this as proof the effect is real.
arxiv-2504-19394:
Toby Simonds tested whether language models can design high-powered rockets in 2025. Models shine at writing code, but designing physical machines is a different test. A benchmark called RocketBench links models to detailed rocket simulators and sets two jobs: hit a target height, then land with precision.

Top models showed solid textbook knowledge at first try. Given simulator feedback, though, they improved poorly and stalled below skilled human designers. Extra training with rewards changed the story: a modest-sized tuned model beat both the big general models and human experts. The study suggests practice with feedback, not raw size, unlocks engineering skill.
arxiv-2504-20094:
Hui and colleagues present MATCHA in twenty twenty-five, a chat based system that suggests video games to players. Movie tools can rely on fixed lists and simple tastes. Games change fast, and taste depends on skill, play style, and gear. Open chat also brings a risk of unsafe replies.

MATCHA splits the work among a team of small agents that each do one job. Some read what the user wants, some fetch games, and some rank choices and check for risk. Tests on real user requests beat six older methods on eight scores. The system also cut bias toward hit games and blocked most trick prompts.
arxiv-2504-21194:
Vedika Srivastava, Hemant Kumar Singh, and Jaisal Singh built a benchmark for locating the Earth scenes in astronaut photographs, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Where the International Space Station was when a photo was taken is known precisely. The ground places actually pictured, though, are usually not georeferenced. Finding them by machine is therefore far from simple.

Their benchmark, ISS-Geo142, holds one hundred forty-two images. It adds metadata and places found by hand. Three pipelines are tested on it. One uses neural network features cross-correlated over map areas. Another matches scale-invariant features, at heavy cost in computing. A third system, TerraByte, reasons over image content and station coordinates together. It uses a model that can see. TerraByte proved strongest. It placed about ninety percent of the images in the right spot. It also gave geographic descriptions that people can read.
arxiv-2505-00194:
Li and three colleagues ask how much sharp star size measures can reveal about the cores of hybrid stars in twenty twenty-five. Hybrid stars pack normal matter outside and quark matter at the core. Future X ray and gravity wave tools may pin star sizes down to a tenth of a kilometer. The team fed fake data at varied sharpness into a stats model.

Sharp sizes, above all for heavy stars, tightened bounds on where quark matter starts. They also narrowed how much of a core is quark matter. Yet even the sharpest sizes said little about how stiff quark matter is. That blind spot held across all settings they tried. Sharper tools help, but with clear limits.
arxiv-2505-02194: Şaban Güvenç and Cihan Özgür wrote this mathematics paper, published in 2025, in differential geometry. It studies biharmonic curves, curves obeying a fourth-order bending condition, inside warped product manifolds, spaces built by stretching one factor over another. The space pairs an open interval with a space of constant curvature. A main theorem drives the analysis, and the authors work through four cases to expose the curves' curvature behavior, including slant curves. Two examples over the round two-sphere close the paper.
arxiv-2505-02794:
Nicolas Wijsen and five co-authors simulated the great solar storm of March twenty twenty-three in twenty twenty-five to explain how some solar particle events spread almost all the way around the Sun. Fast coronal mass ejections drive shocks that accelerate particles; how those particles reach such wide longitudes is debated. One idea: the shock's flanks break away and keep traveling on their own.

Using a three-dimensional heliospheric model with direct shock injection, the team modeled two eruptions whose shocks merged into one envelope spanning two hundred eighty degrees. The free flanks persisted beyond twice Earth's orbital distance, and the combined front became a nearly circumsolar wave. Modeled arrival times and plasma jumps matched spacecraft observations across distances and longitudes, supporting the decoupling picture.
arxiv-2505-03294:
Maximilian Hauck extends a comparison theorem in p-adic cohomology to cover general coefficient systems, in a mathematics paper from twenty twenty-five. Using a stacky approach developed recently by others, he generalizes a result of Colmez and Niziol. That result links the crystalline cohomology of a special fiber with the p-adic étale cohomology of the generic fiber of a formal scheme. The extension allows coefficients in an arbitrary crystalline local system.

Along the way, Hauck establishes a version of a known fiber square with coefficients in the proper case. He also proves a comparison between syntomic cohomology and p-adic étale cohomology with coefficients in an arbitrary gauge object. His methods further describe the isogeny category of perfect gauges over the p-adic integers.
arxiv-2505-07394:
Harrison LaBollita and Antia Botana compute a nickelate's electrons in twenty twenty-five. Nickel oxide compounds recently showed superconductivity under pressure. The newest family member alternates single layers and bilayers in one crystal. Its electronic structure decides where the interesting physics lives.

The authors combine density functional theory with dynamical mean-field theory, self-consistently. The alternating structure produces layer-selective behavior. The single layer sits near a Mott insulating instability. The bilayer contributes most of the low-energy physics, at both ambient and high pressure. Overall the compound resembles the known bilayer superconductor in the same family. That suggests universal features across these nickelates. Readers in condensed matter theory get a map of which layers matter in a hybrid superconductor.
arxiv-2505-09294:
Fan Xu, Wuyang Chen, and Wei Gao study a gap in decision tree learning in a twenty twenty-five paper. Trees and forests sort data into classes, but they assume every test class was seen in training. In real work a new, augmented class can show up only at test time.

Their method, LACForest, bakes the new class into the split rule itself. A new score, augmented Gini impurity, uses unlabeled test data to shape the splits. The forest is then split further with pseudo-labeled cases of the new class. A neural version uses the same score. The paper gives convergence theory and tests that back the design.
arxiv-2505-14194:
Robin Engel and Patrick Lömker introduce a software package called Poleval in this two thousand twenty-five paper. The package serves a technique called HAXPES, which probes materials with hard X-rays. A full measurement campaign produces many spectra that must be treated in a consistent way. Poleval lets researchers handle, analyze, and plot such data inside one Python notebook.

Data live in structured objects, so processing takes only a few lines of code. That speed helps during beamtime, when choices must be made while the experiment runs. The notebook style also records each step, making results easy to share and refine into figures. The toolbox covers cleaning steps, grouping of spectra, and quantitative fits. It aims to make photoelectron spectroscopy more reproducible and team-friendly.
arxiv-2505-14794:
Kedong Wang, Cody Covington, and Kalman Varga simulate how an ionized water pair sheds its extra energy across molecules. Their paper from twenty twenty-five uses real-time density functional theory with moving nuclei. The process, intermolecular Coulombic decay, follows the loss of an inner-valence electron. Treating electrons and nuclei together lets charge flow and atom motion unfold in one run.

The vacancy sits in a set orbital of the water dimer. When it opens in the proton donor molecule, decay proceeds as expected. A fresh pattern also shows up: the proton rocks back and forth first. From there, the pair may settle with no transfer, or the proton may cross for good. When the vacancy sits in the acceptor molecule, no transfer occurs. Decay is then the sole outlet.
arxiv-2505-17394:
Joseph Lopes and a large team of co-authors show that beads driven by actin can flock by fleeing their own chemical trail. Their paper from twenty twenty-five studies biomimetic colloids pushed by actin treadmilling. Filaments grow at one end and shrink at the other, which drives the beads. Rivalry for actin monomers turns out to run the whole show. The beads move away from actin-rich zones, a trait called anti-chemotaxis.

That flight builds lopsided actin gradients around each bead. The gradients sustain the motion that made them. Flocking then grows from flight plus local rivalry for monomers. Polymerization rate, monomer spread, and bead speed set where the flock phase starts. Short-range pulls between beads emerge from the mix. The authors pitch the setup as a lab for active matter that trains itself.
arxiv-2505-18094: John Patty and Elizabeth Maggie Penn wrote this economics paper, published in 2025, with a jarring claim. When you pay people to comply, designing the reward to be accurate usually conflicts with designing it to work. In a binary choice setting, a principal wants maximum effort. Accuracy instead means minimizing both kinds of classification error. The authors show the cost distributions where the two optimal schemes coincide form a vanishingly thin set. Almost always, the goals demand different incentives.
arxiv-2505-19494:
Jagadeeshan, Raj, and Goyal built a benchmark in twenty twenty-five for finding Sanskrit documents with English queries. Sanskrit scriptures hold deep philosophical value, but language barriers limit access. Their dataset, Anveshana, focuses on chapters of the Srimadbhagavatam, a major Sanskrit text.

The dataset holds three thousand four hundred English-Sanskrit query-document pairs. The team tested three strategies: direct matching in a shared embedding space, translating documents, and translating queries. They fine-tuned several leading retrieval models for Sanskrit's features and adapted summarization to aid question answering. Translating documents worked best of the three routes. The authors released the dataset publicly. They aim to preserve the scriptures and share their importance more widely through better search.
arxiv-2506-00194:
Stéphane Vinet and co-authors showed a flexible quantum network design in 2025 that can reach up to a satellite and back. Metropolitan quantum networks will need satellite links for distance, but a satellite is only overhead sometimes. Their design reconfigures itself around that fact: while a satellite is in range, all ground nodes connect to it in a multipoint-to-point layout using time multiplexing. Otherwise the same hardware reroutes into a pairwise ground-only network.

In a five-node test network the team exploited both time and rate links of their photon-pair source and raised the ratio of true coincidences to accidental ones with no extra resources. They projected how the setup would perform carrying quantum keys, and sketched a field-ready version built on integrated photonics that could serve dozens of users.
arxiv-2506-02294:
Niclas Popp and co-authors wrote this machine learning paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on shrinking big models into small ones without teaching them bad shortcuts. When training data is thin, the small student model may latch onto stray cues that fail on new data.

Their fix uses a diffusion image generator to make extra training pictures. The generator aims at the spots where the big teacher and the small student disagree most, which creates hard cases the student must learn from. Tests ran on face, bird, and bar-scene data sets, plus a set built to punish shortcut use. The method placed first or second on mean accuracy across the board. It also lifted worst-group scores, the mark of a model that serves rare cases fairly. The authors present disagreement-guided generation as a guard against hidden data shift.
arxiv-2506-02594:
Ruibo Duan and colleagues let language models evolve both solvers and test problems for routing tasks. Their twenty twenty-five paper presents a closed-loop framework called ACEvo. Language models can write heuristic programs for hard planning problems. Training them on fixed benchmarks can hide solver weaknesses, though.

In ACEvo, one program invents harder problem cases over time. Another program improves as a solver against those cases. The contest creates a rising curriculum for both sides. Tests covered travelling salesman and vehicle routing problems. Evolved cases exposed larger gaps than standard benchmarks did. Solvers trained this way also handled shifted problem patterns better. The framework doubles as a lab for studying automated algorithm design.
arxiv-2506-14894:
Uritsky and five co-authors presented a new image analysis method in twenty twenty-five for mapping the sun's open magnetic field. The corona, the sun's outer atmosphere, sends out the solar wind along field lines that stretch into space, and these shape the storms that can reach Earth.

Their method, called QRaFT, traces faint streaks in telescope images of the corona. Those streaks follow the local field, so the traced lines sketch the field's layout. Tests on computer-made images showed the traces matched the true field within about four to seven degrees. The team also ran the method on real images from a space telescope and a ground camera. Cleaner maps of the open field could sharpen models of the solar wind and improve space weather forecasts.
arxiv-2506-16994:
Farrukh and three colleagues present Prmpt2Adpt in twenty twenty-five, a light way to adapt vision models to new settings with text prompts alone. Drones and small devices lack the memory for big adaptation schemes. Past prompt methods needed huge models and full source data. Their design pairs a slim teacher with a compact student.

A distilled image text model sits frozen inside the teacher detector. A prompt names the target look, and a light normalization step steers source features toward it. The teacher then labels target images to train the student on the fly. Tests showed near top accuracy with far faster adaptation and inference. Few source images sufficed.
arxiv-2506-18694:
Cotter, Knook, and Hope-Collins solved a wave equation faster in this paper from twenty twenty-five. The Helmholtz equation governs waves in acoustics and electromagnetics, and its indefinite form resists standard solvers. Their method applies a splitting iteration, called HSS, to a shifted version of the problem. The shift makes each step friendly to multigrid solvers.

The authors prove the iteration holds up as frequency and mesh change, given enough steps. Each step costs in line with problem size and can spread across many processors. Tests in two and three dimensions matched the theory. Total time grew only in step with frequency in the scalable range. The method targets large computing systems head-on.
arxiv-2506-21894:
Rafael Oliveira, Xuesong Wang, Kian Ming Chai, and Edwin Bonilla extend a classic trial-and-error search method to problems whose answers are whole functions. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. In such problems, each test means running a costly simulator or a real trial. Judging a result once you have it, by contrast, is cheap.

Their method samples a stand-in model, then picks the best action under that sample. The stand-ins are neural operators, treated as rough draws from a known type of random model. That trick skips the need to spell out doubt in full. The team proves bounds on how much the method can lose over time. Tests on physics problems ruled by partial differential equations beat rival search methods. Their approach found good answers with fewer costly runs.
arxiv-2506-23594:
Rameshri Patel, Manan Shah, Smruti Patel, and Bhoomika Pandya compute the traits of heavy baryons in this two thousand twenty-five particle physics paper. Their targets are the heavy omega baryons, one holding a charm quark, one a bottom quark, each paired with two strange quarks. They work in an independent quark model for the three-body system, with a Martin-like potential mixing scalar and vector parts in shares, its terms fit to ground-state data.

The model gives mass spectra for radial and orbital excitations. The team puts forth spin-parity calls for five charm omega states and four excited bottom omega states. They also work out magnetic moments of ground and first excited states, radiative decay widths, and transition moments. Non-leptonic weak decay widths and branching ratios for the charm baryon are set off against tests. That checks the model's power to call what comes next.
arxiv-2507-00394:
Geng Zhang and four co-authors speed up training of very long-sequence AI models in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Transformer training is split across many processors in a pipeline. Long inputs make attention costly and leave pipeline stages idle in bubbles. Their system, HelixPipe, splits attention work itself across stages so micro-batches overlap better. A first-in-last-out schedule balances memory while hiding data transfers.

They also recompute cheap parts instead of storing them, and chop the feed-forward blocks to cut fragmentation. Gains grow as sequences lengthen, beating existing pipelines. Data centers training long-context models feel this cost daily. The paper serves machine learning systems engineers. It offers a design, not just a tweak.
arxiv-2507-02194:
Hunt, Talpey, and Polagye ran tests in twenty twenty-five on how to steer a pair of cross-flow turbines in a tight channel. Such turbines pack a channel more full than most kinds, which can raise their yield. They tried three steer plans at block rates from just over a third to just past half.

One plan held speed in sync, one let each rotor run free, and one waved speed in each turn. At high block the plans gave no clear gain in yield. The wave plan in fact cut yield in most runs. Plain steer may thus be best at high block, which keeps design more simple.
arxiv-2507-05094:
The Belle and Belle II Collaborations report the first observation of two rare decays of B mesons, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. In one decay, a charged B meson turns into a doubly charged Sigma-c baryon and an anti Xi-c baryon. In the other, a neutral B meson decays into matching neutral partners.

Both end states pair a Sigma-c(2455) baryon with an anti Xi-c baryon, particles that each carry a charm quark or its opposite. Such decays are hard to produce and hard to spot, which is why they had not been seen before. Seeing them gives physicists new ground truth on how B mesons break down into heavy baryons. The rates and patterns of these decays test the rules that govern quark change. Results like these sharpen the picture built up by the two experiments over many years of data.
arxiv-2507-07094:
Chan studies whole numbers that split into three close factor pairs in twenty twenty-five. The topic ties to lattice points near the center of a hyperbola. A past result in the area carried a mistake, which this paper corrects. Sharp lower bounds are set for the gap between those points and the center.

Good examples are built from polynomials and Pell equations in a systematic way. The distance used is the L one metric, a sum of coordinate gaps. The work tidies a niche of divisor geometry. It also shows how rich the near center pattern can be.
arxiv-2507-09394:
Nandan Kumar Jha and Brandon Reagen watch attention learn in twenty twenty-five. Multi-head latent attention compresses key and value memory in transformers. It is popular, but how it affects a model's capacity during pretraining was unclear. The authors use random matrix theory as their lens.

They track the spectrum of a key matrix product across training. A light set of diagnostics based on the Marchenko-Pastur law does the tracking. Three variants are compared: standard attention and two latent forms. Capacity bottlenecks appeared locally, as sharp early spikes in specific layers. Those spikes persisted and spread, and they coincided with rank collapse. Only one variant avoided the worst of the pattern. Readers see how memory savings can quietly cost capacity.
arxiv-2507-12094:
Yiding Feng and Wei Tang studied how to compare imperfect forecasters in 2025. In practice, a provider offers chance forecasts to many choice makers, each with varied goals. The provider may hold several models, none of them perfectly calibrated, and must pick one to deploy. Judging which miscalibrated model is more useful is the problem the authors formalize.

They define the informativeness gap between two clues as the largest normalized payoff edge one can give over the other, taken across all possible choice tasks. This single notion contains several earlier contrast tools as special cases, including measures that compare a model against its calibrated version. And it recovers the classic Blackwell informativeness ordering when both clues happen to be perfectly calibrated.
arxiv-2507-13894:
Alberto García Martín-Caro, Javier Olmedo, and Jose Sánchez Velázquez test analogue Hawking radiation in moving cavities in two thousand twenty-five. Dynamical Casimir systems mimic Hawking glow from black holes. A cavity with moving walls makes particles from the vacuum. The team asks when that glow looks truly thermal.

Numeric work spans growing, shrinking, and speeding cavity setups. Thermal marks show in some growth cases but hinge on band and pace. Fit forms gauge how far spectra stray from ideal heat. Gray body factors swing with how long the push lasts. Results sort which rigs can fake gravity effects with care.
arxiv-2507-14494:
Roxanne Ziman and others talk with biomedical imaging experts about a tempting failure mode of AI image tools: images that look gorgeous and are scientifically wrong. The tools make pretty biology easy, but their design cannot guarantee truth, yielding fake molecules and alien anatomy. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team spoke with 17 practitioners and researchers. They mapped where in daily workflows the tools appear, and sorted attitudes from enthusiastic adopters to skeptical avoiders.

Contrasting current practice with earlier predictions about AI in the pipeline, the authors refocus debate on present harms and benefits. Their closing reminder borrows medicine's oath: first, do no harm. Human judgment remains necessary for empathetic, accurate scientific images, notably while public trust in science is fragile. The title quotes one interviewee's verdict on the outputs.
arxiv-2507-18894:
Ahmad Jafar Arifi and Kei Suzuki study the build of heavy quarkonia in a strong magnetic field. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five; the pack row gives no title or year, so the text head is the source. Quarkonia are bound pairs of a heavy quark and its antiparticle. A strong field can warp their shape and mix their spins.

They solve a two-body equation in a quark model that adds spin mixing and the steps a charge takes in a field, called Landau levels. A spread method that fits the field's round symmetry does the sum. The crosswise shape of the pair spreads out, while the lengthwise shape shifts little at this level. Stirred states trade places near near-crossings, a sign of how touchy the build is.
arxiv-2507-19994:
Ali Pedram and Ozgur Mustecaplioglu wrote this quantum physics paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on how precisely small quantum devices can measure things. Standard theory assumes the device is weakly tied to its surroundings and huge in scale, which real devices are not.

The pair study a chain of spins used as a probe, tied strongly to a heat bath. They compute the quantum Fisher information, the measure that caps measurement precision, in two ways: from the full microscopic math and from a shortcut thermodynamics built for tiny systems. Finite size and strong coupling shift the precision bound a lot, even for modest chains. The shortcut method misses those shifts, they find. Worked cases cover measuring magnetic fields and temperature. The paper warns that textbook limits can badly mislead builders of real quantum sensors.
arxiv-2508-04994:
Wenjie Hu, Ye Zhou, and Hann Woei Ho split maze driving for robots into a planner and a driver. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Standard deep reinforcement learning flounders in mazes. Rewards are sparse, exploration wanders, and horizons stretch long. Success rates sag, sometimes to total failure. A hierarchy is their remedy.

The high-level policy picks intermediate subgoals from a long view. It works on a slower time scale. The low-level policy turns each subgoal into wheel-level actions. Both levels run an improved deterministic policy gradient method. Subgoals break one hard journey into many easy ones. Mobile robots gain a sturdier route through complex mazes.
arxiv-2508-06294:
Pol Julià Farré, Chris Aaron Schneider, and Christian Deppe propose a key-growing protocol that mixes quantum signals with a classical physical assumption. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Quantum key schemes trade secrecy for slow rates and fussy single-photon gear. Their hybrid design aims for practical hardware.

The protocol encodes bits in both photon number and time slots at once. That pairing doubles the bits carried per pulse. Built-in identity checks guard against forged senders. Prior knowledge of the channel lets the scheme fight noise actively. Simulations confirm the design behaves as expected. In clean regimes with low loss and low dephasing, the error rate drops. Eavesdropping and forgery attempts stay detectable. The authors see a path to faster secure links with today's parts.
arxiv-2508-06494:
Yehonathan Litman, Fernando De la Torre, and Shubham Tulsiani present LightSwitch, a tool to relight photos of an object. Their twenty twenty-five paper deals with three-dimensional scenes shot from many angles. The goal is to change the light on the object while keeping its true shape and look.

Past tools relight one image at a time and ignore what the object is made of. LightSwitch infers the material traits of the subject and feeds them into a tuned diffusion model. A design that scales lets it relight many views at once, in as little as two minutes. Tests on fake and real objects match or beat top past methods.
arxiv-2508-06594:
Kikuchi builds a way to tell when a local policy shock turns into a whole economy effect in twenty twenty-five. Spillovers across towns blur cause and effect in spatial studies. His framework pairs a diffusion model with boundary hunting from process theory. A jump process tracks how effects spread, and first passage times mark regime shifts.

Applied to AI uptake across Japanese prefectures, effects jumped at a scale of about thirty-five kilometers. Whole economy effects ran well above local only estimates. Simulations show that ignoring the boundary understates true effects by a wide range. The tool tells evaluators when broad equilibrium math is a must, he argues.
arxiv-2508-07594:
Kleshnina, Holden, Heneghan, and Helmstedt wrote in twenty twenty-five about bringing sustainability into college math courses. Students need tools to face climate and nature loss, but math classes can feel far from those problems. The authors share four case studies from Australian courses. Each one uses real ecological questions that students can act on and check.

Topics include how populations grow and change, and how to fish without emptying stocks. Other cases cover judging risk for rare species and modeling climate effects on sea life. The methods are core ones: calculus, statistics, and operations research. Each case is ready for teachers to use as is. The goal is skill with numbers plus care for the living world.
arxiv-2508-08394:
Fernández-Fernández, Matsumoto, Vandersypen, Platero, and Bosco wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five, with given names shown as initials in the byline. It shows how spin-orbit coupling, a foe when spin qubits are shuttled, can be turned to run any two-qubit gate in one move.

Two spin qubits in a double quantum dot are slid toward each other by gate voltages. By setting the slide speed and the waits, and riding the strong spin-orbit force, the pair takes on any sought two-qubit gate at high fidelity. Gates that need many steps on still dots land in one step here. The route cuts control load for scaled quantum machines.
arxiv-2508-09494:
Jessy Lin leads a team of six on this paper from two thousand twenty-five. It teaches language models to study a body of text the way a good student does, a frame the authors call Active Reading.

Models hold vast facts in memory, yet recall is shaky and rests on how often a fact showed up in training. Here the model builds its own study plans for the given texts, then trains on them. On expert sets the method soaks up far more than plain fine-tuning. An eight-billion model gains hugely on a Wikipedia test and a finance test. Scaled up, the team trains a WikiExpert model on a vast run of made tokens that beats far bigger models on fact questions.
arxiv-2508-09994:
Zheng Jie Wong and Bingquan Shen probe attacks that silence speech recognition systems. Their paper came out in two thousand twenty-five. Small crafted changes to audio can make a model output nothing. Such attacks raise real risks for voice tools. The authors check how robust these attacks are. They also ask whether the tampering can be made harder to hear.

Full suppression of the output turns out to be a strict demand. Easing the goal to partial suppression lets the attack hide better. The changed audio sounds closer to the original. The team then tests defenses against the trick. A simple low-pass filter looks promising as a shield. The paper maps both the threat and a first line of defense.
arxiv-2508-10994:
Charles Kilpatrick and nine colleagues report the supernova 2025pht and the first progenitor star detected with the James Webb Space Telescope, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. The explosion, in the galaxy NGC 1637, shows broad hydrogen lines of a type II supernova. Archival Hubble and Webb images covered the site for decades before discovery. A follow-up image let the team pinpoint the likely progenitor.

The star appears in several Hubble epochs and in Webb imaging out to long infrared wavelengths. Fitting red supergiant energy distributions suggests a luminous star heavily reddened by circumstellar dust. The Webb photometry favors graphite-rich dust over silicate-rich dust. Extinction by that dust is high. The authors discuss what a carbon-dust-enshrouded red supergiant means for type II progenitors. Webb, they argue, will transform the hunt for progenitor stars.
arxiv-2508-13594: Kalyan Banerjee proves a case of Bloch's conjecture in algebraic geometry in this two thousand twenty-five paper. It says smooth projective surfaces with vanishing geometric genus have trivial Chow groups of zero-cycles. Banerjee proves it for all such surfaces whose two basic invariants both vanish, while the canonical self-intersection equals nine. The abstract states the result with no more detail, so the claim is just this check for the class named.
arxiv-2508-15194:
Wen Shen proves a result on curved spaces built as products, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five.
