He starts with a closed, simply linked space that is the same at every point, in the sense of a group action. He takes a key claim about vector bundles over that space: each stable class holds a bundle that fits the group action.

Under that claim, take any smooth closed space with the same shape type as the first. Shen shows some product of it with a sphere of high enough size can bear a metric with no negative sectional curvature. Many such base spaces meet the claim, among them the classic rank-one symmetric spaces.
arxiv-2508-17394:
Nir Mazor and Tom Hope teach a retriever to fetch exactly what a vision-language model needs to diagnose well. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Retrieval can enrich medical image reading with literature and records. Generic retrievers fetch what looks similar, not what helps. The models involved are general-purpose, not medical specialists. Training stays deliberately light.

Their retriever learns awareness of the reading model's habits. It returns images and texts that steer predictions toward correct ones. Small data and light fine-tuning suffice for competitive results. Clinical classification and visual question answering both benefit. The authors also name a fresh error type: inconsistent retrieval predictions. Different top hits can push the model to different answers. That failure mode deserves tracking in clinics.
arxiv-2508-17794:
Nathanael Arkor and Andrew Slattery study idempotence for relative monads in two thousand twenty-five. Monads are structures that shape how computations compose. Relative monads tie that shape to a chosen base functor. Idempotence means a repeat act adds nothing new.

In the relative world that idea splits in two. The split notions merge for plain monads but part here. The pair work out what drives the gap. As a key case, they give full accounts of idempotence for monads in extension form. The paper is a short theory note in category theory.
arxiv-2508-19494:
A large Euclid Consortium team, led by L. Ulivi, uses machine learning to hunt for rare paired black holes in space data. Their twenty twenty-five paper seeks dual active galactic nuclei, two feeding black holes close in one galaxy, and lensed ones, whose light is bent by a nearer mass. The pairs sought are less than an arcsecond apart, a hair-thin gap.

Such close pairs are hard to split by eye in survey images. A learned search can scan the flood of Euclid data far faster than people can. Finds of this kind test how galaxies and their black holes grow and merge over time. The paper reports the search and its method on behalf of the consortium.
arxiv-2508-19894:
Tatsuaki Tsuruyama wrote this physics paper, published in 2025. It proposes a second law of thermodynamics for information itself: copying degrades fidelity in a way that can be measured, and the measure shrinks steadily like a ball rolling downhill.

Information thermodynamics has priced erasing and measuring information, following Landauer's principle, but copying was treated as free of intrinsic loss. Tsuruyama models replication as a Markov process blurred by Gaussian noise. At each step he tracks entropy, cross-entropy, and the Kullback-Leibler divergence between original and copy. That divergence falls monotonically, behaving like a potential guiding the system to a steady state. The framework extends to DNA copying, where the energy spent on proofreading and repair can be written in the same terms. The paper aims at one language for physics and biology.
arxiv-2509-00094:
Abdullah Abdelfattah, Mahmoud I. Khalil, and Hazem Abbas build deep learning tools in 2025 to detect and correct pronunciation errors in Quran recitation. Recitation follows strict rules called Tajweed, set down by scholars over centuries, which makes sound assessment feasible. The barrier is scarce high-quality labeled data.

Their pipeline is largely automated and gathers recitations from expert reciters. A fine-tuned wav2vec2-BERT model splits audio at pause points, and a novel Tasmeea algorithm verifies transcripts. The result is eight hundred forty-eight hours of audio with hundreds of thousands of labeled clips. A benchmark, qdat_bench, tests phonemes, diacritics, and three Tajweed rules on real learner errors. Such tools could give learners precise feedback anywhere.
arxiv-2509-00194:
Ibrahim Nonkane and Jean Kaboré study lowest-weight modules over a spherical subalgebra in 2025, within the theory of rational Cherednik algebras. Such algebras blend polynomial and reflection-group actions and arise in geometry and representation theory, which studies how algebras act on vector spaces. The spherical subalgebra is a smoothed corner of the full algebra tied to invariant parts.

For a generic parameter, a Lie subalgebra built from basic invariants is shown to generate the whole spherical subalgebra. Under a mild compatibility condition, checked in the rank-one case, modules inside the polynomial ring match modules over a Cartan-type ring built from that subalgebra. The ring also maps onto a more naive quotient, and the two agree in set cases.
arxiv-2509-00494:
Debraj Dutta, with two co-authors, Ritwick Sarkar and Urna Basu, studies an Ising model, a grid of interacting spins used to model magnetism, held out of equilibrium. Temperature switches at random between values just above and below the critical point, the temperature where order appears.

Dutta and his co-authors track magnetization, the net alignment, and energy as the switching rate varies, and both change in a non-monotonic way, rising and falling rather than moving one way. Slow switching is explained by a renewal approach, and fast switching looks Boltzmann-like, like equilibrium at an effective temperature. A steady energy flow from hot to cold still proves the state is truly out of equilibrium.
arxiv-2509-00794:
R N Kohle leads a team of four authors on the Monge-Ampere equation. This equation is nonlinear and degenerate in form. It finds use in optimal transport, geometric optics, and geometry. The team seeks a fast and robust way to solve it. Boundary values are fixed by Dirichlet conditions.

Their scheme linearizes the equation at each step. It then applies a fixed-point iteration, solving a Poisson problem each time. A weighted residual serves as the input to that problem. For a weight above the largest eigenvalue of the Hessian, they prove contraction. The proof covers both classical and generalised solutions. Tests show the scheme beats Newton's method. It wins on both speed and stability in those tests.
arxiv-2509-01094:
Juntao Du and Zuoling Liu study sums of two operators on Bergman spaces. Those are spaces of functions used in complex analysis. Each operator mixes composition, where one function is plugged into another, with weights and derivatives. The pair uses different symbols and orders. The question is when their sum stays bounded or compact, two key traits in this field.

By splitting the preimage of a disk under the symbols in a careful way, Du and Liu settle the matter. They show the traits of the sum are fixed by the traits of each part alone.
arxiv-2509-01194:
Miguel Garcia-Bravo, Toni Ikonen, and Zheng Zhu study metric measure spaces. In such spaces, distance and volume are defined, but smooth structure may be absent. They focus on spaces where each Newton-Sobolev function has a Lipschitz version. A Lipschitz map stretches distances by at most a fixed factor.

The team proves this trait matches a geometric condition called very infinity-thick quasiconvexity, up to a certain scale. In plain terms, point pairs can be joined by rich families of near-shortest curves. They apply the result in three ways. A Poincare inequality improves from local to global form. Infinity-harmonic functions can be extended from set boundary values. The role of the condition for Sobolev extension sets also becomes clear.
arxiv-2509-01394: Markus Linckelmann proves that a conjecture by Giannelli about character degrees holds for a special class of blocks. In representation theory, blocks group the characters of a finite group, and the conjecture concerns characters of height zero. The cases settled here are blocks whose defect group is cyclic, or the Klein four group.
arxiv-2509-01494:
Automated code review promises to catch bugs before humans do. But existing benchmarks rarely mirror real project work. Zhengran Zeng, with nine co-authors, introduces SWR-Bench. It holds one thousand pull requests from GitHub, each checked by hand. Each case keeps the full project context. Reviews are judged at the pull request level, not on small code fragments.

A scoring method based on a language model checks the reviews. It asks whether issues in a ground truth list are covered. It agrees with human judgment about ninety percent of the time. Tests of leading tools and models showed weak results, with tools better at functional errors. Merging several reviews lifted scores sharply. The F1 score rose by up to about forty-four points.
arxiv-2509-01694:
Quang Minh Nguyen and Eytan Modiano build a framework for sharing network capacity while keeping service promises. Networks that many groups share must still guarantee data speed and low delay for each user. Their framework gives tunable chance based promises, meaning the promise holds with a stated likelihood. A policy at its core balances drift and penalty terms to keep the system stable over time.

The authors map which promise levels can be met at all in such networks. They prove their policy keeps average rates stable and nears the best result as the promise window grows. Tests in simulation back the theory and show strong handling of mixed demands. The work suits shared wireless and cloud setups where many tenants compete.
arxiv-2509-02594:
Sandhanakrishnan Ravichandran and seven co-authors present a 2025 medical AI evaluation of their clinical assistant DR. INFO on HealthBench, a benchmark of open-ended health conversations graded by expert rubrics. Multiple-choice tests miss context handling and uncertainty, which matter in real care.

The assistant uses an agentic retrieval design, searching sources before answering. On the benchmark's hard subset of a thousand cases, it scored well above leading frontier models named in the paper, across accuracy, completeness, and instruction following. A smaller head-to-head test against two rival assistants kept the lead. Weak spots remained in context awareness and completeness. The authors argue that behaviour-level, rubric-based grading is the right way to judge clinical support systems.
arxiv-2509-02694:
A. S. Dmitriev, D. G. Levkov, A. G. Panin, and I. I. Tkachev wrote a 2025 theoretical physics paper on how a gas of gravitationally interacting bosons settles around a Bose-Einstein condensate droplet, called a Bose star. Such stars are candidates for dark matter structures.

The authors argue the gas's kinetic evolution approaches a self-similar attractor, a solution that keeps its shape while rescaling over time. When outside conditions break the underlying scale symmetry, the attractor survives in altered form: it stays roughly self-similar, but its scaling dimension drifts slowly. They call that regime adiabatic self-similarity. It may govern how dark matter Bose stars grow inside cosmological models. The result gives a simpler long-time picture of a complex kinetic system.
arxiv-2509-02994:
Ramya M Anche and 21 co-authors laid out a 2025 design for PUFFINS, a small satellite that will measure polarized ultraviolet light from bright stars. Polarization describes how light waves line up, and dust between the stars leaves a fingerprint in it. Those readings can reveal the size and makeup of interstellar dust grains.

The satellite pairs a simple all-reflective telescope with a device that splits light by polarization and color. Parts were chosen at high readiness levels, meaning they are close to flight proven. The design aims for very low self-made polarization, which would shorten calibration in orbit. Over a planned nine-month observing stretch, a carefully picked star list could test leading ideas about how dust grains align.
arxiv-2509-03394:
Amirhossein Shahbazinia and 3 co-authors built CloudFormer in 2025 to predict performance loss for virtual machines in public clouds. Cloud providers pack many customers' virtual machines onto shared servers, which saves money but breaks performance isolation. Contention for caches, memory bandwidth, and network links can slow a machine badly and unpredictably.

Prediction is hard because tenants cannot see inside their black-box machines and workloads shift constantly. CloudFormer is a dual-branch transformer model that tracks both time patterns and system-level interactions. It reads hundreds of system metrics at one-second resolution, a finer grain than earlier benchmarks, which the team also releases as a dataset. Across diverse, unseen workloads it beat leading baselines on several measures. Its average prediction error came out under eight percent.
arxiv-2509-03494:
Yahya Benmahane and one co-author propose a 2025 method for judging image quality without a clean reference picture. Their base is mPLUG-Owl2, a large multimodal model that handles both images and text. Instead of retraining that whole model, they keep it frozen and tune only a small visual prompt added at pixel level.

At most a few hundred thousand parameters are trained, a tiny fraction of the full model. During testing the prompt is added to each image, and the model answers a fixed question about technical quality. Trials cover synthetic damage, realistic damage, and damage in artificial intelligence generated images across three datasets. Scores compete well with fully retrained systems and with specialist quality models. Code is released publicly by the authors.
arxiv-2509-03594:
Thomas R. Harvey addresses a new family of optimisers for training neural networks in a 2025 research paper. An optimiser is the rule that nudges network weights downhill on the loss landscape, the surface mapping how wrong the model is. Harvey takes the geometry of that landscape seriously, using the metric it naturally carries when drawn in higher-dimensional space.

Optimisers built on that induced metric are compared with standard methods, including SGD, Adam, and Muon, across tasks and architectures. They perform very well on low-dimensional examples and slightly beat leading methods on network training. Their effective step size shrinks automatically where the landscape curves sharply, acting like a smoothed form of gradient clipping. One variant also yields a built-in learning-rate schedule. Computational cost stays comparable to Adam, and the idea can modify existing preconditioning methods.
arxiv-2509-03794:
Juhun Lee and one co-author focus on training image diffusion models with video datasets instead of still photographs in a 2025 research paper. Diffusion models learn to generate images by reversing a gradual noising process. Standard training samples each picture independently, throwing away the temporal links between frames of a video. That design makes training slower and narrows what the model learns.

Their strategy exploits the temporal inductive bias of continuous video frames, the natural smoothness between neighbouring moments, without changing the model architecture. It drops into standard diffusion training pipelines directly. Tests use HandCo, a dataset of hand-object interactions where small finger movements carry distinct meanings. Training converges more than twice as fast, and image quality scores improve on training and validation data alike. Generative diversity also rises, because the model learns meaningful temporal variation. An optimisation analysis explains the gain: their regularisation reduces gradient variance, steadying training.
arxiv-2509-03894:
In a 2025 research paper, Ali Pourmand and three co-authors test whether gravitational instability can form planets a second time, in discs orbiting post-AGB binary stars. Post-AGB stars are evolved systems whose binary interactions shed material into circumbinary discs. Those discs resemble planet-forming discs in structure, chemistry, and motion, raising the question of second-generation planet formation.

Disc instability, where a disc's own gravity fragments it into giant planets, is assessed with the Toomre criterion under reasoned assumptions about disc mass, size, and temperature. The framework is first benchmarked on well-studied young discs like HL Tauri, where several systems show likely unstable past phases. Applied to post-AGB discs, the same analysis finds them generally stable today, mainly for their low masses. Viscous theory says they were stable even in the past, at higher masses. Higher viscosity values also fit the discs' expected lifetimes better.
arxiv-2509-03994:
In a 2025 mathematics note, Keita Mori and one co-author examine dormant opers coming from generalised hypergeometric equations, working in prime characteristic. An oper is a special flat bundle on an algebraic curve, and dormant means a curvature quantity vanishes, a phenomenon of characteristic p. Hypergeometric equations form a classical, explicitly solvable family, here generalised to higher rank.

The opers obtained this way are proved rigid among dormant opers: no deformation that stays dormant can move them. Rigidity is powerful because discrete data can then pin an object down completely. Joining the result with earlier enumerative work on dormant opers yields a complete, explicit description of the two-dimensional topological field theories that count such opers of PGL type. The formulas cover every prime up to seven. Explicit counts at small primes give concrete data for the wider programme linking differential equations in characteristic p with field-theory invariants.
arxiv-2509-04294:
Nuno Freitas and one co-author, Diana Mocanu, classify local solutions on twisted modular curves in a 2025 mathematics paper. Starting from an elliptic curve, a basic object in number theory, a related curve called X_E^-(p) collects other curves whose p-torsion data match in a twisted way. The authors decide exactly when that curve has points over each local number system, for every prime. Two applications follow from the classification.

Some curves with complex multiplication turn out to break the Hasse principle, a hoped-for local-to-global rule, for infinitely many primes. Under a standard conjecture, most rational elliptic curves do so for half of all primes. A new elimination trick also settles cases of a three-term exponential equation.
arxiv-2509-04594:
Ethan Davis, writing alone, benchmarks five ways of multiplying large matrices in a 2025 research paper. Matrix multiplication underpins deep learning, scientific simulation, and graphics, and high-level languages like Python lean on optimized low-level libraries for it. Five implementations face off: CuBLAS and hand-written CUDA on graphics processors, standard BLAS, OpenMP, and C++ threads on central processors. Performance is measured in floating point operations per second on square matrices.

For matrices at least ten thousand rows wide, a clear ranking emerged with overwhelming statistical significance. GPU libraries led, with CuBLAS first and custom CUDA second, followed by BLAS, then the two threading approaches. Hardware choice dominates raw linear algebra speed, the results confirm.
arxiv-2509-05094:
Probability theory written with categories can be extended from total to partial processes. Areeb Shah Mohammed develops that extension in a solo 2025 category theory paper. Starting from a special class of Markov categories, he constructs a category of partial kernels. That generalises earlier models of partial morphisms to a non-deterministic setting.

All morphisms are quasi-total, and a natural ordering records when one morphism restricts another. Key properties of categorical probability survive. They include positivity, conditionals, and product constructions. The main example comes from standard Borel spaces with Markov kernels. Variants cover finitely supported distributions and multivalued maps. Each variant keeps the same partial flavour.
arxiv-2509-05294:
Keeping old particle physics data usable for decades is the job described by Nathan Grieser and five co-authors in a 2025 paper on the LHCb Stripping project. Stripping cuts the huge collision data from the Large Hadron Collider down to samples that analysts can actually work with.

The paper covers the project's Python-based setup, its links to LHCb computing systems, and how large reprocessing campaigns are run for the first two data-taking runs. Workflow tools, automated testing, and parallel processing have modernised the work. The authors also report organisational lessons and a road map. The aim is lasting, efficient access to legacy data sets that still hold physics value.
arxiv-2509-05794:
Moving a running stateful service between machines without losing its memory is the problem tackled by Hai Dinh-Tuan and Jialun Jiang in 2025. Stateless services migrate easily, but stateful ones carry live data that must survive the move. Kubernetes, the main container platform, offers no built-in live migration for them.

Their scheme joins the message-based MS2M migration framework with forensic container checkpointing, a Kubernetes feature that snapshots a container's state. Two additions matter most: support for StatefulSet-managed pods, the usual home of stateful services, and a threshold cutoff that copes with heavy incoming message traffic. In tests, single-pod migration cut downtime by nearly ninety-seven percent against cold migration, while the StatefulSet route gave operators more flexibility.
arxiv-2509-05994: Perspective Abelian groups, a newly defined class in group theory, are generalized in two directions in a 2025 paper by Andrey R. Chekhlov and two co-authors. The two new classes are called IC-groups and TP-groups. Each generalization is nontrivial, loosening the original definition along a different axis. The authors obtain many results along both directions, which they present as gains in handling the original class's rather tangled structures and properties.
arxiv-2509-06594:
A bright patch of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays toward the Centaurus region is tested against candidate sources by Teresa Bister in a solo 2025 astrophysics paper. The excess sits near several possible origins, most famously the radio galaxy Centaurus A. Competing stories range from Centaurus A supplying everything above a certain energy to the Sombrero galaxy sending strongly bent events.

New models of the Galactic magnetic field let Bister test each scenario against the excess's direction, strength, size, and energy trend. A subdominant source in the region needs light nuclei and a moderate extragalactic field. The Sombrero idea needs a dominant charge near that of carbon. Centaurus A or the galaxy M83 supplying all the highest-energy flux also remains possible, within a narrow field range and with mixed composition, though another source may be needed at lower energies.
arxiv-2509-06694:
Small neural networks shaped by geometry and topology are proposed by Victor Toscano-Duran and two co-authors in a 2025 machine learning paper. Standard networks can approximate any continuous function, but modern designs often use huge parameter counts at high computing cost. A leaner, more readable architecture is the goal here.

Their barycentric neural network is a shallow model built from fixed base points and their barycentric coordinates, which encode position by weighted averages. It can represent continuous piecewise linear functions exactly, and such functions can approximate any continuous function on a bounded domain. A new training loss based on length-weighted persistent entropy, a stable summary of a function's shape, tunes the base points instead of inner weights. Experiments beat standard losses and converge faster, offering a greener route to function approximation.
arxiv-2509-06794:
Programming chips where data streams between tasks, without drowning in low-level detail, is the aim of a 2025 computer architecture paper led by Shihan Fang, with six co-authors. Deep learning workloads now stall on moving data more than on arithmetic. Dataflow accelerators stream data on chip to help, but programming models either demand heavy manual control or hide the communication that optimizers need to see.

Their model, Dato, is embedded in Python and treats tasks as a graph. Data communication and sharding, the splitting of inputs across the chip, become explicit types in the language. Tasks are first placed virtually on the accelerator, then the compiler produces a physical mapping that respects hardware limits. On an AMD neural processing unit and an FPGA board, Dato reached high hardware utilization and beat leading commercial frameworks on key kernels.
arxiv-2509-07094:
A charged Higgs boson hiding in top-quark decays is hunted through an unexplored channel by Saiyad Ashanujjaman and three co-authors in a 2025 particle physics paper. LHC searches for light charged Higgs bosons covered decays into tau leptons and quark pairs. They did not cover decay into a W and a Z boson, even though that mode dominates in triplet models.

Top-quark pairs where one top decays to a charged Higgs plus a bottom quark, with the Higgs then decaying to W and Z, mimic a known signature with an extra Z. The authors recast existing analyses to set limits on the product of the two branching fractions. The limits reach below one part in a thousand. The data show a mild two-sigma preference for a nonzero signal. In the Georgi-Machacek model, the limits probe the triplet's vacuum value more strongly than earlier searches.
arxiv-2509-07294:
Yuezhu Xu and 2 co-authors learn a neural Koopman operator model with a safety property built in, in a 2025 paper. A Koopman operator rewrites a nonlinear system, one whose response is not proportional to its input, as a linear model in a lifted space. Dissipativity means the system steadily loses energy, a trait many real systems have and a learned model should respect.

The method works in two stages: first fit an unconstrained neural Koopman model closely to data, then nudge its parameters just enough to enforce strict dissipativity. The authors prove the learned model's dissipativity carries back to the true system, accounting for noisy data, truncation, and unseen cases. A Duffing oscillator, a classic vibrating system with a nonlinear spring, serves as the test case. Guaranteed energy behavior makes learned models safer to use inside controllers.
arxiv-2509-07894:
How close are today's language models to students at physics Olympiads? Fangchen Yu and 16 co-authors build a benchmark to answer that in a 2025 paper. Earlier physics tests lacked current competition material and never compared model scores directly with human contestants, leaving ability claims hard to judge.

Their benchmark, HiPhO, gathers thirteen recent Olympiad exams from 2024 and 2025, mixing international and regional contests and problems that include diagrams and other formats. Human-aligned scoring lets model results sit beside real student performance. A yardstick of this kind shows where models handle hard, multi-step physics and where they still fall short, guiding both developers and educators who follow these competitions.
arxiv-2509-08094:
Mahmood Mousavi and 4 co-authors review a new way to model clean burning in a 2025 engineering paper. Aircraft and power plants must burn fuel with far less carbon and soot. The old tools pair fluid flow codes with detailed chemistry. They are accurate but slow, and the mix of turbulence and chemistry is hard to capture.

The new tools are neural networks taught with physical laws built in. Heat and mass rules go straight into the training step. No mesh is needed, and the models respect the laws by design. The review maps where these networks help most in clean combustion work. Faster, trusted models would let engineers test low-emission burners in days, not months.
arxiv-2509-08194:
Choosing which decision policy to trust for each new situation is automated in a 2025 optimisation paper by Caio de Prospero Iglesias and 2 co-authors. In contextual stochastic optimisation, decisions must respect hard feasibility limits while conditions vary. Candidate policies from different modelling traditions each win in different regions of the context space, and none dominates everywhere.

Prescribe-then-Select first builds a library of feasible candidate policies, then learns a meta-policy that picks the best one for the covariates at hand, implemented with ensemble methods. Routing between policies beats marrying one: hospitals, supply chains, and energy systems all face shifting contexts where yesterday's best model is today's second choice.
arxiv-2509-08494:
Whether an AI assistant protects or erodes its user's agency can be benchmarked, propose Benjamin Sturgeon and 3 co-authors in a 2025 paper. Delegation to AI is growing, and simple feed algorithms already steer people into mindless scrolling, a warning of what stronger assistants could do to human control over individual and collective futures.

HumanAgencyBench builds the notion of agency from philosophical and scientific theories, then evaluates assistants at scale. Language models help simulate and validate user queries and judge responses, keeping the evaluation affordable. An agency yardstick gives developers and regulators a way to ask, before deployment, whether a helpful assistant is quietly training its users out of deciding for themselves.
arxiv-2509-08694:
Drawing the line between land and coastal water in satellite images sounds easy until tides, mud, and glare confuse the colors. Zhen Tian and 3 co-authors present a robust segmentation framework in a 2025 research paper. Standard red-green-blue approaches train unstably and generalize poorly across maritime settings. Their Robust U-Net supervises learning in HSV color space, which separates color from brightness.

Five components work together: color supervision, gradient-based coastline refinement, shape cleanup, sea area cleanup, and connectivity control. Careful ablation tests show the color supervision contributes the most. The full framework cut training variance dramatically and improved segmentation quality across metrics, while staying computationally light. Code and configurations are public. Reliable coastal maps feed flood planning, habitat monitoring, and navigation chart updates, so steadier training is a practical win.
arxiv-2509-08794:
Star trackers tell a spacecraft which way it faces, and a new camera type may do the job cheaper. Dennis Melamed, Connor Hashemi, and Scott McCloskey measure an event-based star tracker's accuracy in a 2025 research paper. Event cameras report only changes in brightness, unlike ordinary framing cameras. Ground truth for real sky data has been the field's headache.

The team used Earth itself as the reference: a fixed camera watching stars move only through Earth's rotation. They compared the tracker's orientation estimates against the official Earth rotation measurements. Errors came out at tens of arcseconds, respectable for the technology. Event cameras also bring sparse data, high dynamic range, low power, and fast updates. The results, with code and data released, suggest event-based tracking suits low-cost, low-latency spacecraft attitude systems.
arxiv-2509-08894:
Patryk Iwanek reviews the variable sky as seen by the OGLE survey in a 2025 paper. OGLE began as a search for dark matter through gravitational microlensing, where a passing mass briefly brightens a star. It grew into a cornerstone of time-domain astronomy.

Three decades of high cadence, two-band observations cover about two billion stars in the Milky Way and Magellanic System. The review covers pulsating, eclipsing, rotating, and eruptive variable stars found by OGLE. Its public Collection of Variable Stars is a basic resource for many fields. Links with other major surveys widen its reach further, from stellar evolution to exoplanets.
arxiv-2509-08994:
Xuan Ji and 1 co-author show snowball bistability vanishes at moderate orbital eccentricity in a 2025 paper. A snowball Earth is fully ice covered. Stable snowball episodes need two stable climates, one frozen and one partly open, under the same conditions.

In a global climate model of a water planet with a slab ocean, that two-state behavior disappears when eccentricity reaches a moderate range. Stronger seasonal swings melt the frozen state away, while the warm state survives due to ocean heat storage. A simple ice model explains the loss through ice self-insulation effects. The authors link the result to debates about how common complex life conditions may be.
arxiv-2509-09894:
Jiayun Wang and 12 co-authors teach a neural operator to rebuild three-dimensional images inside the body straight from raw sound sensor readings in a 2025 imaging paper. Photoacoustic tomography promises rich pictures, but today's systems need dense sensor arrays and long scans, which blocks routine clinical use. Older pipelines reconstruct an image first and clean it afterwards, paying for two imperfect steps.

Their operator, PANO, learns the inversion itself in one pass, carrying both physical law and learned priors inside. Special convolutions respect the hemispherical sensor layout, and a wave equation constraint keeps results physically sane. On simulated and real data, even with sparse sampling, images came out sharp, inference ran in real time, and a standard algorithm was beaten by a wide margin.
arxiv-2509-09994:
Dinesh Chandra Maurya and 1 co-author test a modified gravity cosmos in 2025 where matter and geometry couple through a nonlinear function. Their model works inside a flat expanding universe and mixes curvature, the trace of matter's stress, and the matter Lagrangian with four coupling constants. Solving the altered field equations gives the expansion history in terms of today's measured densities and those constants, ready to be confronted with sky data.

A Markov Chain Monte Carlo fit against cosmic chronometers and the Pantheon supernova sample pins the constants down. With those values the authors trace the universe's slowdown and speed-up, the dark energy behaviour, and the cosmic age. Standard health checks, the Om diagnostic, causality, and energy conditions, are then run to confirm the model stays physically respectable.
arxiv-2509-10094:
René Aïd and 2 co-authors model what happens when two electricity exchanges share one order book in a 2025 mathematical economics paper. Recent intraday market rules created such shared books to sharpen competition and deepen liquidity, yet a quote posted through one exchange can be struck by a trade arriving through the other. Each exchange directs its own market maker through an incentive contract, and everyone in the model dislikes risk, though not by the same amount.

The authors prove the resulting contest between exchanges settles at a single Nash equilibrium, compute the best contracts, and solve numerically for each exchange's certainty equivalent. Economically, one sharp lesson emerges: paying for incentives behaves like a public good. When one exchange motivates its market maker well, the rival quietly profits too, inviting free riding.
arxiv-2509-10194:
Faruk Alpay and Hamdi Alakkad revisit fixed point theory in L1 spaces in this 2025 mathematics paper. A fixed point is where a mapping leaves a point unchanged, and such points anchor many existence proofs. The space L1 is known to lack the fixed point property in general, which raises the question of what extra condition brings it back.

The authors give a complete, self-contained proof that measure-compactness of a convex set is enough. Their route makes each step plain, from compactness ideas to normal structure and Kirk's theorem. They also survey backup strategies, including ultraproducts and renormings, and argue the true obstacle is the geometry of particular sets, not the space itself.
arxiv-2509-10394:
Light branching like a river delta is Tongxun Zhao and four co-authors' subject in this 2025 optics paper. When light crosses a gently random medium it splits into bright filaments called branched flow. Earlier work showed self-focusing, the medium bending light toward bright regions, makes branches appear sooner and sharper.

The authors ask what happens when the medium's response is nonlocal, meaning each point answers to light across a neighborhood. That averaging effect pushes the first branching point farther away and widens the filaments. Push nonlocality far enough and the flow returns to how it behaves with no nonlinearity at all: the self-focusing effectively gets screened out. A semi-analytical formula captures the effect, and the finding suggests a dial for controlling how light fragments in disordered media.
arxiv-2509-10594:
Small businesses want AI's benefits without its risks, and Iqbal H. Sarker with three co-authors offer them a framework in this 2025 perspective paper. Adopting artificial intelligence and large language models raises trust, ethics, and technical problems that small and medium-sized enterprises are poorly staffed to handle alone.

Their framework, SME-TEAM, organizes adoption into phases resting on four pillars: data, algorithms, human oversight, and model architecture. The point is to translate ethical principles, which are easy to state, into operating practice a small firm can actually run. The authors present it as a roadmap that treats trust and ethics not as brakes but as engines of resilience and competitiveness, aiming at innovation a business can sustain.
arxiv-2509-10694:
Silent errors in giant AI training runs are the target here. Kahfi S. Zulkifli and five co-authors go after them in this 2025 systems paper. Modern frameworks parallelize and optimize models aggressively. Those changes can quietly alter what a model computes. Performance degrades, and no crash announces it. Existing checks are either improvised or too costly for production use.

Their framework, Scalify, verifies that computational graphs stay semantically equivalent. It uses equality saturation and Datalog-style reasoning. Several tricks keep it fast. Graphs are partitioned, rewrites run in parallel, and layer results are memoized. Rewrite templates get reused, too. When graphs disagree, Scalify points to the precise code sites at fault. It checked models as large as Llama-3.1-405B in minutes, on an ordinary machine. Along the way, it exposed five unknown bugs. They were hiding in Amazon's production machine learning frameworks.
arxiv-2509-10794:
Roberto Vila and Helton Saulo propose new closed-form estimators for McKay's bivariate gamma distribution in this 2025 statistics paper. Such estimators skip all iterative fitting. Plug the data into a formula, and the parameters come out. Their first family comes from monotone changes to the likelihood equations. It contains the estimators of Zhao and collaborators as a special case.

A second family builds on the stochastic links between gamma random variables. It likewise covers the earlier work of Nawa and Nadarajah. The authors prove strong consistency and asymptotic normality for their proposals. Monte Carlo tests show performance close to maximum likelihood, and better than the existing closed-form rivals. A real data set from hydrology shows the methods at work, where paired measurements like rainfall and flow arise in a natural way.
arxiv-2509-10994:
Henrik Garde, David Johansson, and Thanasis Zacharopoulos wrote this 2025 mathematics paper. It concerns the Calderón problem. That problem asks whether hidden regions inside an object can be mapped from the surface. The mapping uses electrical measurements taken at the surface. The team studies objects whose conductivity differs by direction.

They extend a reconstruction method based on monotonicity. The method now works for direction-dependent materials in any number of dimensions. It starts from measurements on only part of the surface. It then recovers regions where conductivity differs from a known background. The results also clarify a puzzle. Two different internal layouts can sometimes produce identical surface data. The method even allows regions that block current fully or carry it perfectly.
arxiv-2509-11694:
D. González Picos and five co-authors separate the atmospheres of two young brown dwarfs from the discs around them, in this 2025 astronomy paper. Young brown dwarfs are stand-ins for giant planets, and the JWST's NIRSpec instrument now records their near-infrared spectra with unprecedented sensitivity.

Running atmospheric retrievals together with disc modeling on medium-resolution spectra, the authors detected more than twenty chemical species, including water, carbon dioxide, silicon monoxide, and rare isotopic forms of carbon monoxide. The isotope ratios they measured sit near solar values, as do the atmospheric carbon-to-oxygen ratios. Both dwarfs also glow with excess infrared light, matched by warm blackbody rings around six hundred fifty kelvin, plus optically thin carbon monoxide gas far hotter. The joint fit shows how JWST can disentangle a young object's air from its disc.
arxiv-2509-11894:
Ainulnabilah Nasirudin and Philip Bull propose fixing the sky's most used radio map with help from experiments built for another purpose. This 2025 radio astronomy paper treats the Haslam map at four hundred eight megahertz. It is the standard template for diffuse galactic synchrotron glow. Recent studies suggest large uncorrected flux scale errors in it.

The authors build a Gibbs sampling scheme. It jointly infers the true sky brightness field, the map's scale factors, and synchrotron spectral indices. Some fifty thousand parameters are in play. Idealized simulated data pair a one-degree map with coarse global-signal measures. Scale factors return accurate to a couple of percent in most sky regions. The corrected map lands within a few kelvin of the truth. Real global-signal maps would let the method fix the actual Haslam map.
arxiv-2509-12094:
Two graph models can post the same headline score. Yet they may fail on completely different nodes. Tianqi Zhao and two co-authors build NodePro in 2025 to expose that gap. NodePro is a profiling tool. It grades single nodes, one by one.

Each node gets plain profile scores from two families of signals. Data-side signals cover how unlike its features are, how unsure its label is, and how muddy its local structure is. Model-side signals track confidence and steadiness during training. Lining conduct up against profiles shows gaps that headline scores erase. Profiles also carry to unseen nodes. That supports trust judgments with no labels at hand. The tool also proves itself in one more way. It sniffs out bad or corrupted entries inside a structured knowledge graph.
arxiv-2509-12294:
Chemists summarize a molecule's skeleton with graph numbers. One recent index is the diminished Sombor index. It blends the degrees of linked atoms into a single score. Abdulaziz Mutlaq Alotaibi and three co-authors settle an extremal question about it in 2025. Their setting is molecular graphs. In such graphs, no atom has more than four bonds.

The graphs carry a fixed count of vertices. They also carry a set cyclomatic number. That number counts the independent rings. The authors find every graph that minimizes the index in this family. The result answers a conjecture from a recent paper. It covers all ring counts from three upward, once the graph is large enough.
arxiv-2509-12894:
Leekyeung Han, Hyunji Min and three co-authors launch DialNav in 2025, a joint task where a mover and a far guide talk in turns to reach a goal. Unlike past tasks, the guide must guess where the mover is, so talk is key, not extra.

To back the task they share RAIN, a set of human talks paired with paths through photo-true scenes. A full test suite grades both moves and talk. Trials with varied mover and guide models show where the task still strains systems. Data, code, and tests are public so others can build on the task.
arxiv-2509-13194:
Sarath Prem, Olesia Dmytruk and Mircea Trif tell true Majorana states from fakes in 2025 with a microwave cavity test. Zero-bias peaks hint at Majoranas in hybrid wires, but trivial states mimic the same peak. A new probe must test non-local spread, not just energy.

Cavity uptake clarity is the probe. True pairs show signal only when both ends touch the cavity at once. Trivial states show peaks under local touch alone. Disorder does not erase the split. Twin-dot poor-man pairs obey the same rule in exact math. A parity set-up via the cavity is also shown.
arxiv-2509-13394:
S. A. K. Leeney and 3 co-authors present a Bayesian system that cleans up supernova data on its own, in a 2025 paper. Cosmology done precisely with Type Ia supernovae stands or falls on data quality. Today, bad readings are often thrown out by hand. Coming surveys, such as the Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey, will produce far too much data for that.

Their system folds the hunt for anomalies into the fitting of light curves itself. It works with any model, and the team shows it with the SALT3 model, running on graphics processors for speed. For every reading, the method estimates the chance that the reading is off. At the same time it works out the physical parameters of the supernova. The authors apply the system to the Hawaii Supernova Flows data set.
arxiv-2509-13694:
Hanchen Ye and Deming Chen present StreamTensor in a 2025 hardware design paper. StreamTensor is a compiler framework. It makes tensors stream inside dataflow chips for large language models. Streaming results directly between compute kernels avoids memory bottlenecks. But managing kernel links, external memory, and buffer sizes together has resisted automation.

StreamTensor introduces a step-wise tensor type system. It encodes stream layouts in full. That enables automatic kernel fusion, buffer allocation, and memory tuning. The framework then searches three design levels: tiling, fusion, and resource allocation. The search balances speed against memory use. On field-programmable gate arrays running language models, it matched or beat leading designs on latency. Its energy efficiency was notably better than graphics processors.
arxiv-2509-13994:
Giacomo Bastianel and three co-authors optimize power grid layout a day ahead in a 2025 power systems paper. Wind and solar forecasts are uncertain. Lines are congested, and reinforcing the grid takes years. Rewiring the existing grid can relieve crowding almost for free. Optimal transmission switching and busbar splitting do the rewiring, if tomorrow's renewable output cooperates.

Their model plans the layout under uncertainty. Cases built from real offshore wind data represent forecast errors, clustered into a typical set. Strategies compared include re-planning hourly, fixing one layout all day, and capping the number of switching actions. Each plan is checked with AC power flow. Redispatch is then simulated against the realized weather. On AC and hybrid test grids, layout tuning saved money on crowded, renewable-heavy days. Using enough cases beat trusting a single forecast.
arxiv-2509-14094:
Radu Mardare, Neil Ghani, and Eigil Rischel build proof systems for metric algebra in a 2025 logic paper. Quantitative equational theories let equations carry distances. Two terms are not just equal but equal up to a tolerance. That suits systems where approximate equality is the honest notion. Their operations, however, only accept finite arities.

Metric equational theories remove that limit. Operation arities are now countable metric spaces, an extension inspired by enriched Lawvere theories. A subtlety appears, since a term's validity can no longer be certified apart from the equations. The authors solve exactly that problem. Adapting the sound and complete proof system known for the quantitative theories, they deliver deduction rules for the metric setting. The rules are both trustworthy and complete, exploiting the special structure of metric spaces.
arxiv-2509-14294:
Hira Naveed and five co-authors review how machine learning systems are monitored in live use in 2025. Models in production face shifting data and new settings. Performance can quietly decay, harming users and trust if no one watches.

Their multivocal review covers both research papers and practitioner sources, following the Garousi guidelines for such reviews. Well over a hundred studies were analysed for motives, goals and settings. The authors sort what gets monitored, which techniques and tools are used, and what each approach claims to add. Gaps and open challenges are mapped at the end. For teams running live models, the review offers a single map of current monitoring practice and its weak spots.
arxiv-2509-14594:
Yidan Sun and eleven co-authors bring in SynBench in 2025, a shared bench for making synthetic text with differential privacy, a formal cap on what data can reveal about one person. Private synthetic sets could let bodies share touchy corpora safely. Tests so far used mismatched setups and unaudited claims.

SynBench fixes shared scores for utility and fidelity and adds privacy audits across nine curated data sets from more than one domain. Pretraining overlap, often skipped, is built into the design. Language model based makers are scored under one frame. Checked promises matter, since a synthetic set that leaks membership defeats its own point. A shared audit bench should split true privacy gains from test artefacts.
arxiv-2509-14794:
Suren A. Fldzhyan, Stanislav S. Straupe, and Mikhail Yu. Saygin look for cheaper ways to make entangled photon states in a 2025 quantum optics paper. Producing many-photon entanglement is a bottleneck for photonic quantum computing, because costs usually explode as the target state grows. Their work focuses on GHZ-like states, where the amount of entanglement can be tuned.

The authors present a theory framework, checked with numerical simulations, that builds such states step by step from simpler intermediate states. By adjusting those intermediate states and optimizing the interferometer layout, they cut the photon cost of generation. In some tasks, states with less than maximal entanglement beat fully entangled ones on efficiency. The results give quantum engineers a flexible tool, even if the method is not a universal fix.
arxiv-2509-15094:
Aiman Al-Eryani studies a newer form of the parquet method in a solo 2025 paper on strongly linked materials. Parquet methods sit at the heart of top tools for such materials, from mean-field extensions to the renormalization group. A newer split, called single-boson exchange, rewrites the same physics with screened forces and Hedin vertices.

Al-Eryani shows how the fermion diagrams for two kinds of response in that form can be read as boson diagrams, a step called bosonization. The study also touches critical points, where materials switch phases. It links to the Hohenberg-Mermin-Wagner theorem, which bans some ordered phases in low dimensions. The work makes clear what the boson form shows about fluctuations.
arxiv-2509-15794:
Jihun Kim and Javad Lavaei estimate a system's hidden parameters while an attacker corrupts the data. System identification builds a model of a machine from its inputs and outputs. Attacks that slip past detectors are a growing threat to that task. The pair target a matrix that captures how past inputs shape current output.

From a batch of past data, their estimator's error shrinks fast as the model order grows, even when attacks strike at a set rate. A streaming version updates the estimate as new data arrive, with its own error bound. Joining both lets them rebuild the full system matrix. A robust controller can then be built from the cleaned model.
arxiv-2509-16194:
Grouping points around a few centers usually discards stray points one by one, but real noise often comes in whole sets, like a faulty data source. Vaishali Surianarayanan, Neeraj Kumar, and Stavros Sintos define a clustering task where up to a set number of whole groups may be discarded at once. The goal is to cover what remains with few centers at low worst-case distance.

They give the first approximation methods for this task, in both general and geometric settings, with fast near-linear versions for the geometric case. A hardness result bounds what any method can hope for. The model also fits database joins with faulty rows.
arxiv-2509-16294:
Tax agencies in the United States are turning to AI to handle rising workloads on aging systems. Sohail Shaikh surveys how the Treasury Department and the revenue service use these tools, based on public sources. Uses span chatbots for taxpayer help, robotic handling of routine tasks, and learning models that pick cases and flag fraud.

The survey also covers the guardrails in place, from privacy shields to oversight steps and openness efforts. The picture that emerges is a push and pull between new power and public trust. The account gives readers a map of where AI now sits inside tax administration.
arxiv-2509-16394:
Do chat models argue like people when a dispute gets heated and a deal must be struck? Deuksin Kwon and four co-authors stage multi-turn conflict dialogues between humans and models given matched personality profiles. They score the talks on word style, emotional swings such as anger, and strategic moves.

One leading model came closest on style and emotion, while another led on strategy. Still, large gaps to human behavior remained in all cases. The study sets a benchmark for how well models mirror people in tense social talks, and it shows the limits of personality prompting alone.
arxiv-2509-16894:
Zhijie Qiao, Haowei Li, Zhong Cao, and Henry X. Liu train a small race car to drive itself in a 2025 paper. The F1Tenth platform is a tenth-scale car used in classes and contests worldwide. Their method learns driving end to end by copying human drivers. No separate planning stack sits in between.

Results beat prior learning methods by a clear margin. Rule-based baselines also fell behind. Code is shared in a public repository. End-to-end learning on a cheap platform lets students test autonomy ideas safely. Lessons from the track can feed into full-size vehicle research, where testing errors cost far more.
arxiv-2509-16994:
Ina Salaj and Arijit Biswas predict audio-visual quality with hybrid attention in a 2025 paper. Streaming services must judge how good a clip looks and sounds together. Their model draws features from top single-mode predictors. Audio features come from a learned listener model. Video features come from a standard fusion metric.

An attention design blends the two streams with care. A relevance estimator states how much each mode drove the score for a given clip. That estimate could guide bitrate choices per title. Tests show better accuracy and robustness across content types. Smarter quality scores help platforms spend bandwidth where viewers notice it most.
arxiv-2509-17094:
Elton Pan and a large team plan crystal synthesis with a generative model in a 2025 materials paper. Making zeolites and similar crystals means searching a vast space of recipes. One structure can arise from many recipes, which suits a generative approach. Their model, DiffSyn, trained on tens of thousands of recipes from fifty years of literature.

As a proof of concept, the team made a target material from model-proposed routes. Theory calculations backed the chosen routes. The product had a silicon-to-aluminum ratio higher than any prior record for that material. Higher ratios should improve heat stability. Learned recipe planning could cut years of trial and error in materials labs.
arxiv-2509-17394:
Denis S. Grebenkov and Michael J. Ward analyze diffusion toward small reactive patches on a wall. Their 2025 arXiv paper considers a bounded three-dimensional region with a smooth reflecting border. A few small patches on that border can react with a wandering particle, and the patches compete for it, with surface reaction rates in the lead role.

By matched asymptotic expansions, the pair study classic targets: the mean first-reaction time and the splitting odds among patches with a Robin condition. For a spherical region, they derive a three-term expansion in the small-patch limit. It holds for any reactivity and folds in where the patches sit. They then turn to mixed Steklov problems and give the first account of how their eigenvalues and eigenfunctions behave. The results serve models of cells and sensors alike.
arxiv-2509-17694:
Dongxu Lu, Johan Jeuring, and Albert Gatt compare model-written and human-written lines in role-play dialogues. Their 2025 arXiv paper works on long, knowledge-grounded training simulations, where a model must stay in character across many turns. Judging that skill has been a weak point for the field.

Human raters scored multi-turn dialogues, and an automated model-as-judge setup ran beside them. Across turns, model responses degraded in naturalness, context keeping, and overall quality, while human responses improved. Raters consistently preferred the human lines. The automated judge, a Gemini Flash model, tracked human taste well in both pairwise and rated modes. That match validates a hybrid grading frame for future tests. The benchmark the authors leave behind exposes a widening gap over long exchanges, a caution for training tools that lean on generated dialogue.
arxiv-2509-17894:
Siu Hang Ho and 3 co-authors test ways to make a diffusion model run faster and cheaper. Their 2025 bench study uses the fast-DiT model, which makes images step by step. Bigger models tend to score better but cost more time, memory, and compute.

The team tries pruning, low-bit packing, teaching a small copy, and leaner attention steps. They also try a mix-of-experts plan, where just part of the net runs per input. Each trick is checked for how much score it keeps as cost falls. The results map which cuts are safe and which hurt output.
arxiv-2509-18894:
Watching wildlife with one sensor type leaves blind spots; drones miss sound, and traps miss the wide view. Jenna Kline and nine co-authors present SmartWilds, a synchronized multi-sensor data set, in this 2025 paper. It was gathered over four days in summer 2025 at a safari park in Ohio. A 220-acre pasture hosts deer, takin, and wild horses, plus native species.

Drone imagery, camera trap photos and video, and sound recordings were captured in sync. The team compares what each mode does best. The modes complement each other across land use, species detection, behavior, and habitat checks. Standard protocols make the setup repeatable at other sites. Future releases will add GPS tracks from tagged animals, citizen science data, and more seasons. The authors offer the set as open fuel for conservation AI. It targets endangered species research and habitat management.
arxiv-2509-18994:
Gabriel Moldovan and twenty co-authors present an upgrade to AIFS, the machine-learned weather forecast model run by the European weather centre ECMWF. The model has been in full operational use since February 2025. The update adds layers that keep outputs within physical limits, a revised training schedule, and a wider set of forecast variables.

The physical limits improve rain and snow forecasts in particular. The new variables, the authors report, are forecast with a high level of skill. Scores for the upper air also improve over the prior version of the model. Together the changes mark a step in the shift toward learned models standing beside classic physics-based forecasting.
arxiv-2509-19094:
Answering a question in a way that fits one person's tastes is harder than answering it in general. Alireza Salemi and nine co-authors propose Pathways of Thoughts, a method that personalizes answers from any large language model without retraining it. The hard part is guessing a user's preferences from long, noisy background text. Their method treats thinking as a chain of choices among moves like reasoning, revising, personalizing, and asking for clarification.

Following many such paths yields several draft answers with different angles. The method then merges and reweights the drafts by the inferred preferences of the user. On the LaMP-QA benchmark it beat strong baselines by up to about a tenth in relative score. Human judges preferred its answers in about two thirds of cases, with ties in most of the rest.
arxiv-2509-19194:
Ryo Namba and Motoo Suzuki rebuild the theory of particle creation in changing backgrounds on an exact version of the WKB method. The classic WKB approximation, a workhorse for quantum problems, has real flaws: its series diverges, it cannot see global behavior, and its quantization misses higher orders. Particle production, where a time-dependent field turns one vacuum into another, sits exactly in that gap. Exact WKB analysis resums the series and tracks solutions globally.

The authors define vacua directly from the exact WKB solutions and use those solutions as the mode functions for quantization. A quantity called the Voros coefficient renormalizes the solutions to match the distant past and future. Ambiguities that appear with it cancel once physical quantization conditions are imposed. The result is a self-contained framework needing no special functions and no approximations.
arxiv-2509-19394:
Antiferroelectric materials show doubled hysteresis loops when their polarization is driven by an electric field, a trait prized for energy storage and artificial synapses. Yi Zhang and twenty-nine co-authors explain why some of these materials instead show loops that look ferroelectric. Their model stacks many slightly different antiferroelectric loops, each switching at its own field, with disorder spreading those fields out. Where the ranges overlap, the sum mimics a ferroelectric loop.

The team produced this effect on purpose in thin films of lead zirconate and lead hafnate, classic antiferroelectrics. Fine-tuning growth conditions added controlled defects and non-uniform disorder. The fake ferroelectric states lasted for hours before relaxing back to the stable antiferroelectric ground state. The results show disorder itself can be a design tool, tailoring a material's electrical response rather than merely degrading it.
arxiv-2509-19794:
Particle accelerator operators juggle thousands of devices through layers of control software. M. King and thirteen co-authors present CATAP, a Python middle layer that sits between users and low-level controls. It offers one structured interface, with device knowledge stored in configuration files rather than scattered code. Facility-specific packages are then generated from those files.

The design draws on lessons from earlier middle layers at two accelerator facilities, where CATAP now runs. Centralizing control logic cuts the code each user must write for a task. It also preserves know-how that usually lives in operators' heads. Modern Python tooling may draw new contributors into accelerator software. The paper documents the architecture so other facilities can adopt the same pattern.
arxiv-2509-19994:
Models that align images, sound, and text in one space can be attacked through any of those doors. Zhifang Zhang and six co-authors strengthen targeted attacks on such multimodal models. Existing attacks falter two ways: their fake inputs fail on near-miss targets, and simple anomaly detectors spot them. Their Proxy Targeted Attack optimizes through several stand-ins on both the source and target sides.

Proxies widen the set of targets the fake input fools. They also smooth the input so detectors find less to flag. Targeted attacks matter because they impersonate chosen content, not just cause errors. Shared embedding spaces underpin search and moderation tools. Showing their weak points, with a method that generalizes, pressures builders to harden the alignment itself.
arxiv-2509-20694:
A new gamma-ray telescope array is being built at the LHAASO site in China. Zhipeng Zhang and two co-authors assess its expected performance in a 2025 conference paper for the International Cosmic Ray Conference. The LACT array will have thirty-two Cherenkov telescopes, each with a six-meter mirror.

The authors generate instrument response functions from detailed Monte Carlo simulations of gamma-ray showers and detector behavior. They study an eight-telescope subarray tuned for large viewing angles and the full array tuned for lower energy thresholds. The response files give effective area, angular resolution, and energy resolution across energies and offsets. These results guide which ultra-high-energy sources the array can realistically observe.
arxiv-2509-20894:
Light can be trapped at the edge of leaking, guided by states that theory says should not bind. Sae Endo and seven co-authors design slow-light waveguides from such bound states in the continuum in a 2025 optics paper. Their guides work away from special symmetry points, widening their use.

Earlier versions of these etchless waveguides only worked at one high-symmetry point. The new design uses Friedrich-Wintgen bound states, which arise when two guided modes with the same radiation channel couple. Simulations show slow light at off-symmetry points along the guide. Slow light strengthens interactions between light and matter on a chip. The authors present the scheme as a step toward practical, low-loss photonic circuits that need no etching.
arxiv-2509-21294:
Instruction data grounded in local Wikipedia content may serve Indian languages better than translated English data. The paper is the work of Pranjal Chitale and 6 co-authors. Many Indian languages lack large, culturally grounded training data. Synthetic data, made by models, offers a path forward. Most past synthetic sets were translated from English, which can miss local context. The authors test a bottom up method instead.

Their set, UPDESH, was built from language specific Wikipedia content using large open models. It holds millions of examples across thirteen Indian languages and English. Tasks span reasoning and text generation. Human checks and auto scores confirmed high quality. Models trained on UPDESH beat rivals across many multilingual tests. The work supports AI that fits local culture and language.
arxiv-2509-21594:
Measuring fetal blood oxygen through the mother abdomen could transform fetal monitoring. Weitai Qian and 9 co-authors analyse that diffuse optics method in a 2025 paper. Non stop reading of fetal oxygen saturation is the goal. Their workflow estimates it from non invasively sensed diffuse light intensity. Theoretical derivation comes first, then model run and animal tests.

A trait called the exponential pulsation ratio is proposed as key. Machine learning models fuse information across multiple detectors. Pregnant sheep, the gold standard large animal model of pregnancy, supplied in vivo data. Estimation errors were a few percent, with strong correlations to true values. The analysis also elucidates foundational limits of transabdominal fetal oximetry.
arxiv-2509-21694:
Atomistic base models give near quantum hit rate but run too slowly for large model runs. Lingyu Kong and 3 co-authors accelerate them in a 2025 paper. Deep, setting rich designs capture wide chemical and form motifs at high memory cost. Extended time and space scales stay out of reach. Their workflow targets message passing designs, the backbone of many such potentials.

Removing low contribution message passing layers prunes the backbone effectively. Setting count drops sharply while hit rate and data efficiency are preserved. Graph partitioning then scales the pruned model across hardware. Molecular dynamics at larger scales becomes useful. The workflow is general, applying to base interatomic potentials with message passing form beyond the tested cases.
arxiv-2509-22094:
Tomás Lopes and six co-authors present a faster way to read speckle-based fiber sensors in this 2025 paper. Such sensors are highly sensitive, but cameras read them slowly and with limited range, which caps their speed. The team's answer is event-based vision: a camera style that reports only changes, pixel by pixel, with very low delay. Coupled with the fiber, it promises high throughput and wide frequency coverage.

Their framework decomposes the raw event stream with the help of multi-point calibration and machine learning tuning. That let it separate signals from four actuators pressing the fiber at once, at points from a few centimeters to most of a meter away, with little crosstalk between them. The team then coupled the fiber to two plastic enclosures as an acoustic test. It recovered separable audio from each, with minimal distortion of the waveforms.
arxiv-2509-22294:
Yingying Li and four co-authors present a new framework for splitting a hypergraph into balanced parts while cutting as few hyperedges as possible. Partitioning matters for circuit design and parallel computing, where hyperedges connect many vertices at once. Their 2025 approach works at multiple levels and pursues several objectives together, through a non-convex constrained relaxation of the problem. A modified accelerated proximal gradient method generates varied vertex features, which helps the search avoid poor local answers.

The coarsening step builds a minimum spanning tree of the vertices. For large data, a tree over representative vertices stands in for the whole, and the rest are assigned to it. Refinement passes then migrate and swap vertices, sometimes re-clustering with fresh trees. On public benchmarks, the method cut hyperedges by a few percent on average against the leading partitioner KaHyPar, with much larger gains on some instances.
arxiv-2509-22994:
Sparse autoencoders promise readable features inside neural networks, but their layout can be messy. Zachary Baker and Yuxiao Li test whether variational methods tidy that layout. Their variant, the vSAE, swaps hard gating for sampling from learned Gaussian curves. A penalty term pulls those curves toward a standard normal shape. The hope was that sampling pressure would spread features out and cut overlap.

On Pythia-70M activations, the variant lost to a standard sparse autoencoder on core scores. It did win on feature independence and ablation tests. The penalty killed too many features, leaving many dead units. Naive variational tweaks, they conclude, do not help feature organization.
arxiv-2509-23094:
Diffusion-based language models generate well but run slowly at inference time. Yuchu Jiang and 6 co-authors speed them up with a smarter cache. Such models use two-way attention, so the standard key-value cache does not apply. Their d2Cache framework caches most token states for reuse. A two-stage selection picks which tokens get fresh updates at each step.

The rest reuse stored states, refreshed adaptively. The scheme also allows a quasi left-to-right decoding mode. That mode curbs early overconfidence in late tokens. On two models, LLaDA and Dream, speed rose a lot. Generation quality improved at the same time. Code is public.
arxiv-2509-23294:
Stretching a laser focus far past its natural length can unlock new plasma acceleration tricks. P Blum and 9 co-authors shape high-intensity pulses with adaptive optics. Their method programs the focal region of a standard off-axis parabolic mirror. The bright zone extends well beyond the Rayleigh length. Its intensity profile along the axis is also controllable.

Theory, simulations, and lab measurements all line up. The team then ran the method on a working plasma accelerator with off-the-shelf parts. Uses include dephasingless wakefield acceleration and plasma waveguides. Multi-GeV acceleration and flying foci could gain as well.
arxiv-2509-23694:
Search agents that read the live web can be led astray by the very pages they fetch. Jianshuo Dong and 8 co-authors built SafeSearch, an automated red-teaming framework for these LLM-based agents. It runs sandboxed safety tests that are scalable and cheap. Three hundred test cases span five risk categories, from misinformation to prompt injection, drawn partly from real incidents the authors observed.

Seventeen models across three agent scaffolds were attacked. The worst attack success rate topped ninety percent for one model in a workflow setting. Common defenses like reminder prompts helped little. The authors offer the framework as a practical way to measure and harden search agents.
arxiv-2509-23794:
Cities filling with delivery drones need roads in the sky and rules for flying them. Zhouyu Qu and 2 co-authors supply both: a markup language for describing drone road systems, and a short-term guidance algorithm. In their description scheme, roads carry varying lane counts and join through connecting lanes. The guidance method is decentralized and greedy, deciding seconds ahead from position and speed beacons sent by nearby drones.

Each drone acts on its own, choosing to stop, change lanes, or adjust speed, with no central coordinator. Simulations vary wireless and algorithm settings and track collision rate, average speed, and throughput. The authors argue the pairing keeps dense drone traffic safe and efficient.
arxiv-2509-23994:
Rules written in policy documents do not enforce themselves on AI agents. Gauri Kholkar and Ratinder Ahuja turn governance into runtime guardrails with their Policy-as-Prompt framework. The system reads design artifacts such as product requirements, technical designs, and code, plus risk controls, and builds a source-linked policy tree. That tree compiles into light prompt-based classifiers that monitor agents in real time.

The design enforces least privilege and data minimization, with provenance, traceability, and audit logs for conformity checks, and humans stay in the review loop. Evaluations show less prompt-injection risk, blocked out-of-scope requests, and fewer toxic outputs, each with auditable rationales.
arxiv-2509-24094:
A robot that can tell where it is from what it sees can find its way back to known places. Vignesh Ramanathan and 2 co-authors built Flash, a place-recognition system for event cameras, which record brightness changes pixel by pixel with very fine timing. Past systems pooled many events into dense pictures and needed long slices of data.

Flash instead uses slices shorter than a millisecond. It codes which pixels fired into compact binary frames and compares them with fast bit operations. Scores are scaled by how active each frame was. Flash beat prior systems by a wide margin on indoor and city-scale test sets, and it cut the time a robot runs unsure of its place.
arxiv-2509-24294:
Grounded theory turns interviews and field notes into structured theory, but expert hand-coding makes it slow to scale. Xinyu Pi and 2 co-authors built LOGOS, a system that automates the full workflow with large language models. It codes raw text, clusters meanings, reasons over a graph, and refines its scheme in rounds to build reusable codebooks.

To compare fairly, the team adds a five-part metric and a train-test split protocol. Across five varied corpora, LOGOS beat strong baselines. On complex data sets it matched expert-built schemes to a striking degree on average. The authors see a path to wider, cheaper qualitative research that keeps theoretical nuance.
arxiv-2509-24494:
Hongcheng Wang and 4 co-authors ask why tree-style branching helps a popular reasoning training method. Group Relative Policy Optimization scores thoughts without a value model, and its thought-level advantage estimates swing wildly. Branching several continuations per thought is common practice, but its theory was missing.

Under a minimal tree setting, the team finds a sharp asymmetry. Adding more sampled thoughts leaves a strictly positive floor under the estimation variance. Adding more continuations per thought drives the leading variance term to zero. Branching is thus principled, not a mere heuristic, within this estimator family. Experiments back the claim with steadier training and better final scores across math and vision.
arxiv-2509-26294:
Lionel Blondé, Joao Candido Ramos, and Alexandros Kalousis teach imitation with few demos by a noise-guided transport plan. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five; the pack row gives no title or year, so the text head is the source. When expert demos are scarce, big pre-trained or fat models are hard to bring to bear, and each demo must count.

Their method casts copy work as an optimal transport task solved by a two-side training game. It needs no pretrain and no special build, and doubt reads come by design. Tests span hard control tasks, up to a full humanoid, with as few as twenty demo steps. Skill stays strong in that lean regime.
arxiv-2510-00194:
Prasanna Parthasarathi and four colleagues published this 2025 paper improving how language models learn from rewards. The popular GRPO method trains models on reasoning tasks with a single score per answer. That design cannot tell which tokens in a long answer earned the score. The team's GRPO-lambda extension restores fine-grained credit using ideas from eligibility traces.

Their method rebuilds a lambda-return from token-level log-probabilities after each answer is generated. A critic-free estimate of the prediction error guides how credit flows backward. Several weighting variants were tried, and every variant beat plain GRPO in training. Gains during training ran between thirty and forty percent on the reported curves. Final scores rose by more than three points on average across five math benchmarks. The largest model tested, at seven billion parameters, gained the most.
arxiv-2510-00394:
Zhouyang Liu and four colleagues published this 2025 paper on judging how similar two graphs are, quickly. Measures like maximum common subgraph and graph edit distance are exact but NP-hard to compute. Neural approximations either compare every node pair at great cost or lose the graph's structure and size. Their method, Graph2Region, embeds each node as a closed region in space.

A whole graph becomes a summary region whose shape encodes structure and whose volume encodes size. Overlap between two graph regions then approximates their maximum common subgraph score. The leftover disjoint parts serve as a proxy for edit distance, so both scores come out together. Across fifteen datasets, the method improved MCS similarity accuracy by up to about sixty percent over leading rivals. Training and inference both stayed efficient in their benchmarks.
arxiv-2510-00494:
Julian Coda-Forno and eight colleagues published this 2025 paper on whether language models reason better with a separate thinking partner. Psychologists split thought into a fast, fluent system and a slow, deliberate one. The authors test dual architectures where a fluent base model trades latent messages with a coprocessor. Two fixes are on trial: widening the channel, and training both models jointly.

Experiments on GPT-2 and a Qwen model used matched budgets of latent tokens. Joint fine-tuning won consistently, while extra channel capacity helped only modestly. A single-model baseline with soft embeddings nearly matched the best dual system. That parity suggests today's dual designs mostly add compute, not better reasoning. Raising the latent budget past small values failed to harden performance on stress tests. Latent spaces overlapped heavily, with little sign of clean specialization between the partners.
arxiv-2510-00594:
