Prior work often assumed too much or ignored the sensitive attribute's own role.

Applied on top of any trained linear model with no retraining, the method shows exactly how parity shifts each coefficient, for sensitive and ordinary features alike. That feature-level view lets auditors see where bias persists or migrates through correlated variables. Tests cover synthetic and real data.
arxiv-2511-11394:
Bruno Mera and Tomoki Ozawa propose a microscopic mechanism by which generic Chern bands relax toward ideal Chern bands when coupled to a bath. Chern bands are energy bands with a topological twist, and ideal ones have a special quantum geometry sought for building fractional Chern insulators. The bath here is an Ohmic bosonic reservoir of the Caldeira-Leggett kind, coupled weakly to interacting electrons.

Under a Born-Markov treatment, the authors show analytically that states of a Chern band evolve toward states of the matching ideal band. A simulation of a massive Dirac model with Hubbard interaction confirms the picture: Berry curvature and quantum metric co-evolve toward the ideal trace condition.
arxiv-2511-11594:
James McCammon introduces TimeStampEval, a benchmark for finding the exact moment a spoken quote occurs in a long transcript when the written quote does not match the transcript word for word. Official records and speech-to-text output differ in small ways that defeat ordinary fuzzy matching.

Given a sentence-timestamped transcript and a slightly drifted target quote, the task is to return precise start and end times in milliseconds. A simple two-stage method improves retrieval accuracy sharply while cutting inference costs by over ninety percent. The motivating project assembles Congressional Record clips into an automated long-form podcast, a use case where cheap, accurate quote location is essential.
arxiv-2511-11794:
Miguel Correia and three co-authors map the analytic structure of the black hole S-matrix. The S-matrix encodes how waves scatter off a Schwarzschild black hole. The map is drawn in the plane of complex frequency. Analyticity is where causality leaves its mark on scattering. So the map has physical meaning, not just math interest.

The gravitational potential is continued to complex values. The singularity behind the horizon plays a key role. In the lower half-plane, the partial-wave amplitudes are analytic, with two exceptions. They are quasinormal mode poles and a branch cut from late-time tails. Stokes effects give the elastic amplitude its own upper half-plane cut. Wave scattering near black holes gains a firmer causal base.
arxiv-2511-11894:
Lingxiao Li and three co-authors generate molecules from written descriptions in stages. A chemist should be able to name functional groups, scaffolds, and property limits in words. Structures that honor all of them should come back. One-shot conditioning encodes the whole prompt once. It routinely drops some of the stated requirements.

Their frame, Chain-of-Generation, applies the description step by step. Each part of the prompt guides its own phase of generation. Three failures of the one-shot style are named. They include poor clarity of generated parts and missing substructures. Stepwise conditioning gives better compliance with the prompt. It also gives a clearer view of which words built which part.
arxiv-2511-11994:
Paulo Henrique Foganholo Biazetto and three co-authors design an extremum-seeking controller for Schrödinger-type systems. The dynamics are governed by complex-valued partial differential equations. The goal is to maximize a measured output, where the map that defines the optimum is unknown. Actuation sits at one boundary.

The goal value is the squared norm of the complex state at the far, free boundary. A two-step backstepping boundary control offsets the actuation dynamics. A small-signal Hessian estimate powers a Newton-style seeking law. The complex state space is viewed as a two-dimensional real one to make this work. Model-free optimization enters genuinely infinite-dimensional territory here.
arxiv-2511-12094:
Víctor A. Vicente-Benítez constructs a tool for solving Schrödinger equations whose potential is rough, given as the derivative of a square-integrable function. Such equations model quantum particles, and a transmutation operator can turn simple solutions into solutions of the harder equation. Building that operator for rough potentials needs a new route.

The construction uses a regularization based on a factorization named for Pólya, tied to a solution that never vanishes on the interval. The author shows such a solution exists and can be computed. Related results cover the impedance form of the problem, a Darboux transform, and series forms for solutions that expand in powers of the spectral parameter.
arxiv-2511-12294:
Bodhisatwa Chatterjee and four co-authors present ProofWright, a system that formally verifies code for graphics processors written by large language models. Models can generate fast CUDA kernels quickly, but the code often holds subtle correctness bugs. Testing misses cases, and manual verification cannot keep pace with the rate of generation.

ProofWright pairs automated formal verification with the generation process to give end-to-end guarantees on memory safety, thread safety and semantic correctness. On a standard kernel benchmark it verifies safety for a large share of generated kernels, finds errors that testing missed, and proves equivalence for a class of simple kernels. The overhead reported is a few minutes per kernel.
arxiv-2511-12594:
Rongkun Zheng and five co-authors present Seg-VAR, a framework that rethinks image segmentation as generating a mask step by step, in the autoregressive style used for image generation. Segmentation needs precise, low-level spatial perception, and visual autoregressive methods had not been explored for it. Their design borrows the multi-scale spirit of leading mask models.

Three parts work together. An image encoder makes latent priors. A second encoder turns masks into discrete latent tokens. It uses a location-sensitive color mapping to separate instances. A decoder then rebuilds masks from those latents. Training proceeds in stages, first learning the mask representation jointly with images, then refining latent changes, then aligning the two latent sources.
arxiv-2511-12694:
Mohamed A. Mabrok and Yalda Zafari introduce X-VMamba, a framework for explaining how vision state space models make their decisions. Mamba-style models have become strong alternatives to transformers. But unlike attention-based models, they offer no built-in map of which image patches mattered. The authors borrow an idea from control theory, controllability, to measure how each patch influences the model's internal state as an image moves through it.

They give two methods: a Jacobian-based one that works for any state space model, and a faster Gramian-based one for diagonal models, both running in a single forward pass. Tests on three kinds of medical images show early layers spread influence over broad textures while deeper layers focus on clinically meaningful patterns. Scanning order also shapes the patterns. The tools aim to make this model family easier to audit.
arxiv-2511-12994:
Debjit Basu studies when a layer of relations among a variety's defining equations is forced to be empty. Syzygies are the relations among equations, and relations among relations, that make up a projective variety's minimal free resolution; Koszul cohomology sorts them by weight. Basu finds when the weight one Koszul cohomology vanishes. That vanishing is not an end in itself: as spin-offs of more general results, he obtains claims about property (M_q), which controls higher syzygies, for minimal surfaces and for larger projective varieties.

By weighing properties (M_q) and (N_p) together, the analysis sharpens what is known about the shape of minimal free resolutions. A vanishing theorem gives geometers a test: check the terms, and a whole stratum of the resolution is known to be absent before anyone computes.
arxiv-2511-13494:
Jae Joong Lee probes how steadily vision-language models match images and text when the wording changes. Models such as CLIP score well at zero-shot tasks, but their response to careful language tweaks was unclear. The new LGIP benchmark separates harmless rewording from edits that truly change meaning.

Using forty thousand COCO images with human captions, the study auto-generates paraphrases and rule-based flips of object, color, or count. Nine models are scored on paraphrase stability and on favoring true captions over flipped ones. Some large models balanced both well, while SigLIP versions often preferred flipped captions, a flaw that standard retrieval scores miss entirely.
arxiv-2511-13594:
Masaaki Nakamura and Masanori Yamanaka derive the condition for the integer quantum Hall effect in interacting lattice fermions using spiral boundary conditions. That wrapping turns the system into a single long chain, which lets force and response directions be controlled cleanly. Their argument blends Lieb-Schultz-Mattis and Laughlin style reasoning.

It ties magnetic flux, Chern number, and electron density into a single integer link. Earlier derivations with periodic boundaries reached the same link only by a roundabout path, with extra dependence on system size cluttering the proof. The spiral approach removes that clutter and gives the Hall result directly for lattice systems.
arxiv-2511-13694:
Jay Bartroff and Asmit Chakraborty extend the Push algorithm to compute the shortest fixed-width confidence intervals for a bounded parameter. A confidence interval trades width against coverage, and for a fixed width the shortest valid one is the best a data analyst can report. The earlier Push method handled only the binomial case.

Their version works for any discrete bounded value, and for continuous ones whose interval probabilities have a quasiconcave shape. The Push result is provably the shortest non-decreasing one at its level, and its absence proves no such interval exists. Demonstrations on binomial, hypergeometric, and normal cases beat standard intervals, and an application uses World Health Organization tobacco data.
arxiv-2511-13994:
Yilun Zhu, Nikhita Vedula, and Shervin Malmasi improve product search for queries built on superlatives like best or most popular. Answering such queries means comparing items across several traits at once, which takes language understanding and domain knowledge. The authors show large language models can extract the hidden intent as structured attribute-value hints.

Their framework generates those hints alongside retrieval and feeds them into the ranking pipeline. Because calling a big model to re-rank directly is too slow, they transfer the superlative interpretations into lightweight models for deployment. The method raised standard search quality scores by clear margins over baselines, and the study explains how superlative meaning can be passed between models.
arxiv-2511-14094:
Hien Phan-Thanh, Nguyen Nguyen-Duc, Thuy Le-Quang, and two co-authors built SPECTRUMMATE, a compact spectrometer for small telescopes. Small scopes are cheap, portable, and easy to set up, making them ideal for schools and amateur astronomers, and they can still do useful science on bright objects. The design adapts the Sol'EX spectrograph and uses optics on hand at a Hanoi university laboratory.

The instrument covers visible light from 4000 to 6600 angstroms, capturing a few hundred angstroms per image with resolving power above twenty-five hundred. The team selected and aligned a collimator, grating, and objective lens to keep dispersion low and the unit compact, aiming at detailed spectral analysis for low-budget observatories.
arxiv-2511-14294:
Morgane Dumont, Ahmed Alsaloum, Julian Ernst, and two co-authors ask what drives the doubt in spatial micro forecasts. These models project people and homes, with their traits, over maps and years. Each run is a guess, and the spread of guesses is rarely checked. The team ran a variance-based test on the jobs module of MikroSim, a model of Germany, and split direct from indirect effects.

The usual sources of doubt, the values of weights and inputs, turned out to matter less than plain choices about how to build the model. Short summary scores also failed to show the full spread of doubt. The authors urge builders to weigh such choices with care and to state the doubt plainly in their reports.
arxiv-2511-14494:
Guoliang Tang and Jiaqun Wei characterize a special class of modules over tensor rings. Tensor rings combine a base ring with a bimodule in a standard construction. The modules in question are Gorenstein flat modules with an added projective coresolution property. Such modules play a role in relative homological algebra.

The pair give a precise test for when a module over the tensor ring has the property. The test reduces to two checks on its structure map and quotient. They also describe a related class of Gorenstein flat modules in explicit form. Applications cover trivial ring extensions and Morita context rings, two common ring constructions.
arxiv-2511-14694:
Rui Zhu, Xiaopu Zhou, and three co-authors present FOCUS, a compression module that lets DNA language models read much longer sequences. Models trained on DNA from many species learn the grammar of the genome, but attention costs grow fast with length. Stores of past keys and values also swell during generation, forcing crude cutoffs that drop distant information.

FOCUS squeezes the context in stages while keeping the features that matter, and it plugs into already trained models. The authors report near-lossless quality with far longer reach than window tricks allow. Longer context means gene regulation and other far-apart genomic signals can finally be modeled together in one pass.
arxiv-2511-14994:
Yue Yu, Xiaobo Zheng, and Shaoming He design a trajectory planner for drone swarms that keeps working when radio links are poor. Splitting the planning across the swarm saves central computing, but dropped messages and tight bandwidth make coordination fragile. Their framework, CA-ADTO, is built in two tiers for exactly that setting.

Each drone refines its own path with a parameterized dynamic programming method, while swarm-level agreement is reached through an asynchronous multiplier method that tolerates late updates. The design cuts communication overhead sharply compared with lockstep schemes. Swarms that can plan through bad links are a step toward real missions in disaster zones and contested airspace.
arxiv-2511-15194:
Jian Deng, Yuandong Wang, and four co-authors present Eq.Bot, a wrapper that gives robot manipulation policies a proper sense of geometry. Learning-based robot hands often stumble when objects are rotated or shifted, because their training never guaranteed consistent behavior under such moves. Hand-built fixes inside each network are costly, complex, and hard to port.

Eq.Bot instead canonicalizes: it rotates and shifts each observation into a standard frame, runs whatever policy is already in use, then maps the chosen action back to the real frame. The scheme rests on symmetry theory for planar motions and is meant to wrap any existing policy unchanged. Inspired by how people normalize a scene mentally before acting, it promises steadier manipulation with no retraining.
arxiv-2511-15394:
The BESIII Collaboration reports a search for a forbidden decay that would break a sacred rule of particle physics: lepton number conservation. The target process turns a Xi-minus baryon into a Sigma-plus plus two electrons, with no neutrinos to balance the lepton count. Seeing it would prove leptons can be created from nothing, a clue to why the universe holds more matter than antimatter.

Working blind on about ten billion J/psi events recorded at the BEPCII collider, the team finds no signal above the expected background. They set an upper limit on how often the decay can occur, at ninety percent confidence. Each null search of this kind tightens the space where lepton number violation can hide.
arxiv-2511-15594:
Koen Scheres and Rodolphe Sepulchre ask whether a circuit built to mimic neurons can be described as a sequence of discrete events. Excitable neuromorphic circuits are physical devices whose smooth electrical paths naturally break into event-like steps, much as neurons fire in spikes. Turning a continuous physical model into a discrete-event model is the goal of their study.

A discrete description would let engineers analyze and design such circuits with tools made for event systems rather than full continuous simulation. The authors discuss how to extract that model from the physical one and weigh what the method could offer neuromorphic control systems. The work is a short conceptual study of modeling method, scope, and promise.
arxiv-2511-15694:
Medha Kumar, Zifei Xu, Xin Wang, and Tristan Webb test how quantization, the compression of model weights into fewer bits, affects reinforcement learning in large reasoning models. Strong reasoning can now be trained by large-scale reinforcement learning without supervised fine-tuning. Quantization after training and quantization during training are well studied for fine-tuning, but their effect on this kind of reinforcement learning was an open question.

Systematic experiments on math benchmarks found a significant reasoning gap. Models quantized after reinforcement learning kept far more performance than counterparts whose reinforcement learning was itself quantization-aware, which seemed to harm the learning process. Post-training quantization and a low-rank adapter method for quantized models both performed better in their tests.
arxiv-2511-15794:
Pouya Asadi, David Cyncynates, and Stefania Gori argue that a crowd of axion-like particles solves two problems at once for the QCD axion. Axions are hypothetical light particles proposed to explain a symmetry puzzle and to serve as dark matter. A mechanism called axiogenesis could also create the cosmic excess of matter over antimatter, but the minimal version makes too few baryons or too much dark matter and strains axion quality.

In the axiverse picture, the QCD axion is a blend of several axion-like fields. New dissipation channels prevent overclosure of the universe, and extra symmetries keep the axion high quality. A two-axion toy model illustrates the fix, and the framework predicts signals within reach of dark matter, astrophysics, and collider experiments.
arxiv-2511-15894:
Shuang Guan and Kasso A. Okoudjou study when a signal can be uniquely recovered from its short-time Fourier spectrogram without phase information. Phase retrieval matters because many sensors record only magnitudes, and uniqueness guarantees that no other signal could produce the same recording. Their setting uses window functions whose Fourier transforms decay faster than any exponential, a very strong smoothness condition.

For such windows, they derive sufficient conditions on discrete sampling sets that ensure unique phase retrieval for square-integrable signals. The result generalizes earlier uniqueness guarantees that were proven only for Gaussian windows, the classic bell-shaped case. Knowing which sampling patterns suffice helps design measurement schemes where reconstruction is provably unambiguous.
arxiv-2511-15994:
Deepthi Potluri and six co-authors study the gap between search and thinking in medical question answering with CARE-RAG. Giving a language model the right evidence does not guarantee correct thinking with it. That gap is dangerous in medical settings governed by structured protocols. Written exposure therapy guidelines serve as the testbed for curated, clinician vetted questions.

Errors persist even when authoritative passages are supplied to the model. The proposed framework measures accuracy, consistency, and fidelity of thinking separately. Search can constrain outputs, results show, but not ensure safe logic. Safe deployment therefore needs thinking assessed as rigorously as search itself. The study offers an evaluation template for other protocol driven medical tasks.
arxiv-2511-16194:
Antoniadis and three co-authors study online interval scheduling when an advance hint from a learned model is at hand. Slots arrive one by one. Each must be taken or rejected at once, and taken slots may not overlap. The aim is the largest total length of taken slots. Hints promise better results, but a method must stay safe when hints err. Good design balances doing well under good hints against safety under hostile inputs.

Their SemiTrust-and-Switch frame unifies hint-based and classic methods, for both fixed-rule and random cases. Lower bounds prove the frame is tight in some settings. One random method blends smoothly between trusting hints and falling back on safe behavior. It stays robust, and its results degrade in a smooth way as hint quality drops.
arxiv-2511-16394:
The CMS Collaboration reports a search for Higgsinos, the hypothetical partners of the Higgs boson, in proton-proton collision data collected at 13 TeV during 2016 to 2018. The target scenario has four nearly equal-mass states, so the heavier neutral particle decays to the lighter one plus a virtual Z boson, leaving very soft leptons.

The analysis hunts events with large missing momentum plus either two muons, or one lepton and an isolated track, which recovers cases where a soft lepton was missed. Multivariate discriminants suppress backgrounds from standard processes and fake tracks. Mass gaps between the two neutral states were probed down to about one and a half GeV for a 100 GeV Higgsino, and Higgsino masses up to 115 GeV were excluded.
arxiv-2511-16594:
Bradley E. Schaefer and six co-authors report an unusual nova, FQ Circini, whose companion star is a massive hot Be star of about thirteen solar masses. The nova itself was an ordinary fast helium-nitrogen event, but its eruption amplitude of about three magnitudes is the smallest known for a classical nova. The quiet counterpart is a flickering blue emission-line star.

Photometry from TESS and amateur observers shows a coherent period of about two days from the companion's ellipsoidal shape. The Be star's decretion disk feeds mass across the Roche lobe into an accretion disk around a white dwarf of about one and a quarter solar masses. It is a disk-to-disk transfer seen in no other system. The authors name this a new class, high-mass cataclysmic variables, and note the white dwarf can never grow into a Type Ia supernova.
arxiv-2511-16794:
Victor Sanchez and seven co-authors use hierarchical Bayesian model selection to study soft, tissue-like materials slammed at ultra-high strain rates, a regime key for injury biomechanics and protective design. Laser-induced microcavitation can probe such materials, but noisy bubble data and uncertain parameters make picking the right constitutive model hard.

Their method explores competing models' parameter spaces with informed priors that penalize needless complexity. It adds a redundancy prior, an information-criterion-motivated prior, and a noise model that measures uncertainty in how plausible each model is. Synthetic tests recover the true models and values. On gelatin, fibrin, polyacrylamide, and agarose data, the credible models' best fits match the experiments, and a comparison across institutions on gelatin selects the same model, a reassuring check.
arxiv-2511-16994:
Changyu Zhou carries out a close analysis of the Riccati hierarchy, a chain of related equations in maths that is studied through its series solutions. The focus is a classic test that probes how solutions behave near singular points, and the numbers that come out of that test. Zhou works out every case for this chain and sets down the full set of test numbers.

A rigid pattern turns up in how free values enter the series solutions, level by level. Zhou also finds a special flow that works alongside the whole chain and uses it to write all solutions through a single polynomial formula. Where poles of solutions collide, the formula shows lower cases emerging as limits, and negative test numbers gain a clear reading through series used on ring-shaped regions.
arxiv-2511-17094:
He Huang and four co-authors question an expensive habit in video anomaly detection: examining every frame. Their system, ReCoVAD, watches surveillance-style video for unusual events but reasons in depth about only a small share of frames. The design copies the human nervous system, which pairs a fast reflex pathway with a slower, conscious one.

A light module first scores frames quickly, consulting a memory of past frames and their scores. Only novel frames go to a vision-language model, which writes event descriptions and refined scores, while a large language model periodically reviews those descriptions to catch new anomaly types and fix mistakes. On two standard datasets the system matched the best training-free results while processing roughly a sixth to a quarter of the frames rivals used. Sparse reasoning, the authors argue, is enough.
arxiv-2511-17194:
Zhiyuan Xu and three co-authors demonstrate an attack on large language models that works by nudging their internal activations rather than their inputs. Decoder-only transformers contain attention sinks and compression valleys, regions where, the authors show, small perturbations can be amplified as generation proceeds. Their method, Sensitivity-Scaled Steering, anchors a perturbation at the first token and reinforces it at the most sensitive layers and positions.

Instead of forcing an abrupt change, the attack drifts the model's behavior gradually, so early outputs still look fluent and harmless. Across several open-weight models and four kinds of target behavior, it achieved high success rates with little damage to general capability. The authors argue these internal structures should be treated as genuine hidden-state weaknesses, especially where models pass through supply chains that others can tamper with.
arxiv-2511-17394:
Jean-Pierre Delmas surveys elliptically symmetric distributions, a broad family of laws for random vectors used throughout signal processing and machine learning. These distributions generalize the multivariate Gaussian and, at the same time, extend symmetric one-dimensional laws to many dimensions. Delmas covers both the real case and the complex versions, circular and noncircular, that engineers use for complex-valued signals.

The chapter defines the family in two matching ways, through characteristic functions and stochastic representations, showing how the laws arise from spherically symmetric distributions under affine maps. It collects results on moments, marginals, conditionals, and stability under summation, gives well-known examples with their properties. A final part discusses estimation of the center and scatter matrix, from simple sample estimators to robust M-estimators and Tyler's estimator. A closing section touches on the Slepian-Bangs formula, a workhorse for detection tasks.
arxiv-2511-17794:
Zhao Song, Ndidi Bianca Ogbo, Xinyu Wang, Chen Shen, Matjaz Perc, and The Anh Han ask how cooperation survives in evolution when players can talk before they act. Earlier models used only a hand picked subset of possible strategies, which may hide important paths.

Expanding to the complete set of eight strategies changes the outcome greatly. Cooperation becomes stronger and more varied, driven by a new cyclic pattern sparked by suspicious cooperation. A role once credited to strategic defection turns out to be fragile. Long term behavior can include up to seven strategies living together, showing why full models matter.
arxiv-2511-18194:
Faheem Nizar, Elias Lumer, Anmol Gulati, Pradeep Honaganahalli Basavaraju, and Vamse Kumar Subbiah improve how multi agent language systems find the right specialized agent and tools for a job. Existing retrieval matches a query against one agent description, hiding the fine grained abilities of its many tools and leading to poor selection.

Their method represents tools and their parent agents as nodes in a knowledge graph. Vector search first finds candidate tools and agents, a weighted fusion reranks them by type, and graph traversal returns the parent agents. On a live benchmark of protocol based tools, recall and ranking quality improve clearly over the best prior retrievers.
arxiv-2511-18294:
Mengchun Zhang, Kateryna Shapovalenko, Yucheng Shao, Eddie Guo, and Parusha Pradhan decode brain signals for people the model has never seen. Reading EEG, the scalp signal of brain activity, fails most when a new subject's patterns differ from the training group. Past fixes fake new subjects or pad data in plain ways, and neither scales well.

MultiDiffNet skips fake data growth. It learns a compact code space tuned for many goals at once, and decodes straight from that space. Scores top prior work across tasks when test subjects and sessions are held apart from training. The team also release a shared test suite of four EEG tasks, from steady visual response to imagined speech, with a clean split protocol.
arxiv-2511-18394:
Chinmay Karkar and Paras Chopra test how well large language models forecast real-world events, and find the skill unevenly spread. Models show partial competence on social, political, and economic questions, but performance swings sharply with the kind of question and how it is framed. The team uses questions about events that happened after each model's training cut-off, so answers cannot be recalled from memory.

They vary the context supplied, the question type, and the addition of factual news material, then watch accuracy and calibration shift. Adding news changes how models form beliefs and where they fail. The headline lesson is in their title's borrowed line: forecasting ability depends heavily on what is asked and how, so a single forecasting score for a model can mislead.
arxiv-2511-18494:
Furen Deng, Yidong Xu, Fengquan Wu, Yanping Cong, Bin Yue, and Xuelei Chen map the radio sky from lunar orbit. Below a set low band, Earth's air and human noise block ground dishes. A line of small satellites around the Moon, the DSL or Hongmeng mission, can listen in that quiet band by combining signals.

The sky map rebuild is in form a linear inversion: a beam matrix links sky pixels to the joint measures. The team probe two error sources: sub pixel noise from cutting the sky into finite cells, and bias from the smoothing used to tame the inversion. Both can warp the global map if left unchecked. Their checks guide how to build a sound map of the dark radio sky.
arxiv-2511-18594:
Ahmad A Aziz El-Banna and Octavia A Dobre propose a light autoencoder for predicting the best beam in millimetre-wave systems that sense and communicate at once. Such waves form narrow beams that must align precisely, and finding the right beam normally takes heavy training traffic. Knowing the user's position can shortcut that search, and the authors feed position into the prediction problem for sixth-generation network settings.

Their network squeezes its input through a narrow middle layer, which cuts the computation the trained model needs. In simulations it matches the beam prediction accuracy of a standard deep network baseline while cutting complexity by more than four fifths. For dense future networks, a cheaper predictor could save both energy and airtime on every alignment.
arxiv-2511-18794:
Zhongtao Wang and 10 co-authors rebuild places that change across photo sets taken years apart. Cities are rescanned, build sites revisited, and wild zones watched for change. Past rebuild tools assume one fixed geometry, or smooth motion, and both fail when change is long term and abrupt.

ChronoGS uses a time modulated Gaussian form set on one shared anchor scaffold. All periods rebuild in that single frame, while stable parts and changing parts are split apart. The split yields consistent builds across eras, where a wall may stand in one and fall in the next. A new benchmark set backs the work. Long term change mapping is the use.
arxiv-2511-18994:
Christian Haase and Zongpu Zhang compute multigraded Betti numbers for Veronese embeddings of projective spaces. A Veronese map re-embeds a projective space by all monomials of a set degree, and its Betti numbers grade the relations among those monomials. Hochster's formula turns those numbers into homology of set simplicial complexes.

By studying those complexes with Forman's discrete Morse theory, the pair prove where the numbers vanish and where they do not. Morse matchings collapse most of a complex, which exposes its true homology at low cost. A graded census of Veronese relations guides work on syzygies, the chains of relations among relations in algebra.
arxiv-2511-19194:
C. D. Leonard and colleagues, writing with the LSST Dark Energy Science Collaboration, assess a test of gravity planned for the Rubin Observatory's LSST survey. The statistic involved, called E G, mixes galaxy lensing and clustering measures to probe gravity with few assumptions about the dark universe. Lens galaxies would come from the DESI instrument.

The authors update the error framework for this pairing and show the test stays nearly model-free when only large scales are used, if galaxy bias is handled with care. A forecast method also folds in uncertainty about the present matter density. With existing microwave background priors, the full survey data should give the test real power.
arxiv-2511-19294:
Phurtivilai Patt, Leyang Huang, Yinqiang Zhang, and Yang Lei improve three-dimensional Gaussian splatting by densifying the scene before optimisation starts. Standard splatting grows its points adaptively during training, which can leave floating artefacts and waste resources on redundant blobs. Their method combines sparse LiDAR measurements with depth estimates from matching photos to build a dense starting cloud, using a sampling scheme that favours regions important in meaning or geometry.

Starting dense lets the optimisation skip adaptive density control entirely and focus on the other attributes of each blob, reducing overlap while raising visual quality. The authors report results comparable to leading techniques with significantly lower cost. For scanning teams with a LiDAR unit at hand, the approach promises cleaner scenes for less compute.
arxiv-2511-19394:
Rachit Saluja and five co-authors argue that medical image models fail on small lesions partly because of how they treat the background. Standard training lumps every non-lesion pixel into one background class, throwing away anatomy: the tissues and organs around a lesion carry useful context. Their fix is to split that background into finer labeled parts.

Called BackSplit, the scheme trains with those detailed labels while costing nothing extra when the model runs. A theory result shows the richer labels raise expected Fisher information, tightening error bounds and steadying training. The authors present background splitting as a cheap, general boost for lesion segmentation.
arxiv-2511-19694:
Chin-Chia Michael Yeh and seven co-authors build a foundation model that classifies time series without fine-tuning. Labeled time series are costly, so a model that learns new tasks from a few examples in context is valuable. Earlier large time series models mostly forecast rather than classify, leaving that gap open.

Their model, TiCT, is a transformer pretrained only on synthetic data. A bit-based label code and a special output attention let it handle any number of classes. A Mixup-inspired pretraining mix with augmentation builds robustness to noise. On the UCR Archive benchmark, TiCT competes strongly, showing synthetic pretraining can support general classification.
arxiv-2511-19794:
Wenzhang Du warns that small machine learning gains are often noise dressed as progress. Papers routinely claim one or two point improvements from a single run, yet scores swing with random seeds, data order, and minor code details. Under real budgets only a few runs are affordable, so the test must be strict.

The proposed protocol pairs runs across seeds, builds bias-corrected bootstrap confidence intervals, and adds a sign-flip permutation test on per-seed differences. On CIFAR and AG News scenarios, single runs and unpaired tests often bless phantom gains. The paired protocol, even with three seeds, never does, acting as a guardrail against over-claiming.
arxiv-2511-19894:
Sixtus Dakurah proposes a new way to average brain network patterns across a group of people. Researchers often summarize each person's brain network with a maximum spanning tree, a simple unbiased skeleton of its strongest links. Group trees, though, are usually built from the average network, which outliers can skew, or by bootstrapping, which is costly.

Dakurah introduces a spectral representation called the spanning tree basis, which lets the group average tree be computed directly. He shows this average tree keeps the global properties of all the individual trees in the group. It also overlaps with the union of the shortest paths in the functional brain networks, linking the summary back to the original data.
arxiv-2511-19994:
Tao-tao Qiu, Yifu Cai, Yang Liu, Si-Yu Li, Jarah Evslin, and Xinmin Zhang review quintom cosmology, a family of dark energy models with a striking trait. In quintom models, the equation of state of dark energy can cross the cosmological constant boundary, something plain models cannot do. New DESI data favoring changing dark energy give the topic fresh weight.

The review moves from quintom dark energy to the quintom bounce, in which the universe contracts and rebounds instead of starting from a singular bang. The authors give three worked examples of a quintom bounce. They also present one example of a cyclic universe built with quintom matter, letting readers compare the constructions side by side.
arxiv-2511-20194:
Chen, Yu, Miao, and Qiu rebuild transformer attention on sparse coding ideas. Their 2025 paper targets in-context compositional learning. Models must infer rules from examples given in context. Tasks combine basic parts through hidden compositional rules. Plain transformers lack the built-in structure for this.

Sparse coding writes data as few dictionary atoms combined. The team recasts attention as exactly that operation. An encoding dictionary turns inputs into sparse coefficients. Those coefficients mix a decoding dictionary into outputs. Sparsity forces the coefficients to expose real structure. Target answers get coefficients blended from context examples. Visual reasoning tests used the RAVEN benchmark family. S-RAVEN and RAVEN tasks measured compositional generalization. Their method held up where standard transformers failed. Unseen rule combinations were handled more gracefully. Learned structure transfers across tasks more cleanly here. Large pretrained models remain untested territory. The idea marries classic signal processing with attention.
arxiv-2511-20294:
Mandaokar and Rinner make radar tracking both nimble and safe on small platforms. Their 2025 paper proposes SAFE-IMM for maneuvering targets. Interacting multiple model filters run several motion models at once. Mixing their outputs smoothly can lag behind sudden turns. Winner-takes-all switching reacts fast but jumps harshly.

SAFE-IMM gates the winner switch with a safety check. Covariance math bounds how far the jump can drift. Only provably bounded switches are allowed through. Robust likelihoods harden the filter against clutter. An adaptive transition matrix tunes model switching rates. Simulations tested the design against standard rivals. Real evaluation used nuScenes front-radar recordings. Accuracy stayed high at real-time rates throughout. Identity switches dropped compared with baselines. Numerical stability held on resource-limited hardware. The method drops into existing trackers simply. Drones and vehicles share the same constraints. Bounded responsiveness is the practical sweet spot.
arxiv-2511-20594:
Fan, Ohn, Dunson, and Lin bag variational Bayes to fix its overconfident error bars. Their 2025 paper adds bagging to variational Bayes. These methods estimate posteriors fast but crudely. The popular mean-field version treats each parameter as separate. That habit understates uncertainty and misses correlations badly.

Bagging resamples the data and refits the approximation many times. Averaging those fits yields a bagged posterior. Theory backs the construction with strong guarantees. Shrinkage rates hold for general model classes. A Bernstein-von Mises theorem certifies the uncertainty as valid. Off-diagonal covariance structure comes back even with mean-field parts. Misspecified models still get matching covariance, a robustness win. Tests covered parametric models and finite mixtures. Deep networks and VAEs were included too. Honest uncertainty from cheap estimates is the prize.
arxiv-2511-20694:
Kevin Lee, Russell Spiewak, and James Walsh release in 2025 a benchmark testing whether language models can do heliophysics, not just recite it. Heliophysics is the physics of the Sun and its surroundings. Real problems there demand physical assumptions, consistent units, and answers in strict scientific formats. The team built questions from problem sets used at the NASA and UCAR Living With a Star summer school.

The finished benchmark holds 158 question-and-answer pairs written by heliophysicists. Of these, 38 need numeric answers in set units and 52 need a symbolic expression. The remaining 68 need a short scientific statement. An automatic grader checks replies using unit-aware number tolerances, symbolic matching, and format validation. Against a single-shot baseline, four multi-agent patterns that split the work into planned steps were tested. Splitting the workflow along systems-engineering lines beat direct prompting on deduction problems, though not on recall questions.
arxiv-2511-20794:
Tuan Pham and Alessandro Rinaldo offer in 2025 a note with a simple upgrade for concentration inequalities, the bounds that say a random quantity stays near its average. Their object is a product of random matrices, each built from an identity plus a small step times a random matrix. Such products drive Oja's algorithm, a streaming method for principal component analysis, whose analysis needs the product to concentrate.

Fixed-time bounds existed: they control the product at one length. What practitioners need is an any-time bound, valid at every length, so stopping anytime is safe. The note's argument normalises the product by its expectation, spots a martingale, a fair-game process, and applies Doob's maximal inequality over spaced time blocks. The outcome: a time-uniform bound shaped like the fixed-time one, up to constants. The authors present it as a clean step for analyses of such processes.
arxiv-2511-20894:
Vivek Pandey, Amirhossein Mollaei, and Nader Motee design in 2025 faster ways for a robot to choose which camera features are worth tracking. A robot localises itself by following point features across frames, but frames hold far more points than it can process in real time. Picking the most informative subset is itself expensive with existing methods. The team proposes two greedy algorithms built to cut both running time and memory.

One is a stochastic greedy scheme that samples candidates instead of scoring every feature, sharply lowering the cost per selection round. Greedy selection for such information measures carries near-optimal guarantees, and the authors aim to keep that quality while shedding the usual overhead. The result is a favourable trade-off between computational efficiency and localisation accuracy. The methods target robots that must evaluate feature utility on the fly, inside the control loop.
arxiv-2511-20994:
Yuxiao Xiang and colleagues build in 2025 a safety guard that reads a multimodal model's thinking, not just its answer. Reasoning models can produce a harmless final reply while the intermediate trace contains biased inferences or instructions that violate policy. Existing guards check only the question and final answer, or read text without the image. GuardTrace-VL audits the full question-thinking-answer pipeline jointly over image and text, catching harm as it emerges mid-reasoning.

Training data came from a purpose-built corpus of about 11,800 multimodal examples, with 9,862 for training and 2,000 for testing, refined by model and human voting. A three-stage progressive training scheme teaches graded, context-dependent safety judgements. On the test set, spanning in-domain and out-of-domain cases, GuardTrace-VL reached an F1 of 93.1 percent on unsafe-reasoning detection. That beat the previous strongest multimodal defence by 13.5 percent, a wide margin for a guard model.
arxiv-2511-21294:
Minling Li, Changzhen Sun, Chao Wang, Dongyi Wei, and Zhifei Zhang quantify how big a nudge a rotating flow can survive, in 2025. The flow is Couette flow, fluid sheared between moving boundaries, governed by the Navier-Stokes equations with Coriolis forces from rotation. The transition threshold problem, posed by Trefethen and coauthors in 1993, asks how the largest safe disturbance shrinks as the Reynolds number grows.

Li and her coauthors prove an improved threshold for the three-dimensional rotating system at high Reynolds numbers. Suppose the starting disturbance stays below a bound that scales like the Reynolds number to the power minus alpha. Then, with alpha above two-thirds in one geometry and at least five-sixths in another, the flow exists for all time and stays near Couette flow. Rotation's dispersion and mixing do the stabilizing work, handled through function spaces tailored to the flow's stubborn zero modes.
arxiv-2511-21594:
Alex Ning, Vainateya Rangaraju, and Yen-Ling Kuo map the hidden geometry inside language models, in 2025. A transformer's latent states, the high-dimensional vectors it thinks with, are hard to inspect directly. The team extracted layer-by-layer activations from GPT-2 and LLaMA and flattened them into viewable form with two dimensionality-reduction tools, principal component analysis and UMAP, capturing states at several points inside each block.

The maps reveal structure nobody had documented: outputs of the attention components and the feed-forward MLP components occupy clearly separated regions across intermediate layers, in both model families. The first token's latent state carries an unusually large norm, a quirk tied to how models park information. GPT-2's positional embeddings trace a helix, and states evolve along orderly layerwise paths. With code released, the study offers a reproducible atlas for comparing how different architectures organize information internally.
arxiv-2511-21694:
Meiyu Li, Wei Ai, and Naeemul Hassan survey what research knows about false and misleading content on video platforms, in 2025. YouTube, TikTok, and their peers are now central information hubs for billions of users, and video's mix of image, sound, and text makes misleading content unusually persuasive and memorable. Recommendation systems that prize engagement over accuracy can amplify it further into echo chambers.

The survey organizes the literature three ways: by types of information disorder, by the methods used to study it, and by platform features that shape its spread. For types, it adopts Wardle's seven-part typology, finer-grained than the catch-all label fake news that much earlier work relied on. Detection and mitigation research is mapped against those categories. The authors close with the field's open challenges, aiming the synthesis at interdisciplinary teams building better responses to a problem no single discipline owns.
arxiv-2511-21994:
Zheng and colleagues investigate why reactive notebooks, promising spreadsheet-like sync between code and results, break that promise. IPyflow, Marimo, and Observable each define reactivity differently, and simple edits defeat each, leaving misleading stale outputs.

To make the problem concrete and discussable they built Rex. A fine-grained test suite for reactivity: small, carefully designed notebook scenarios that probe exactly which cells re-execute after each kind of edit, and which silently keep stale values instead. Running Rex on the three existing systems let them classify the failures into recurring patterns rather than isolated bugs, aiming to help programmers and implementers alike. The aims are practical: help programmers recognize the edits that make their notebook lie to them, and give implementers a shared benchmark for improving their systems. Without a testable definition, users cannot build a reliable mental model.
arxiv-2511-22294:
Laguna, Agostini, Ryser, and colleagues at ETH Zurich turn the structure of a radiology exam into free supervision. A chest study is not one image but several views of the same patient plus a report, and most self-supervised methods waste that organization by treating views as unrelated pictures. Their Multiview Masked Autoencoder learns by reconstructing masked views while aligning representations across a study's projections, so clinical redundancy becomes the training signal, yielding view-invariant, disease-relevant features without any labels.

On disease classification across three large public datasets, MIMIC-CXR, CheXpert, and PadChest, the method consistently outperforms supervised and vision-language baselines. A variant, MVMAE-V2T, additionally trains with the radiology reports as an auxiliary text signal while keeping inference purely visual, and it adds further gains exactly in low-label regimes where annotations are scarcest. Structured and textual supervision, they argue, are complementary.
arxiv-2511-22394:
Mulvey, Jordan, and Misquitta ask whether a carbon atom inside graphene carries an electric quadrupole moment, a measure of how its charge spreads unevenly. Literature values for graphite-like materials range from about minus 1.14 to plus 0.79 atomic units, because an atom inside a molecule is not directly observable and definitions disagree. The authors propose a framework for making well-defined statements about such atoms-in-a-molecule properties anyway.

The authors use basis-space iterated Stockholder atoms, a method partitioning a molecule's electron density among its atoms in a principled way. They compute the out-of-plane quadrupole component for carbon in graphene. They find it zero, within numerical precision. They argue the experimental value for graphite, measured by Whitehouse and Buckingham, came almost entirely from dipoles at the sample's edges, not from the carbon atoms themselves. They propose a more realistic electrostatic model for finite graphene flakes.
arxiv-2511-22494:
Frenkel revisits a puzzling sentence in Gibbs's classic work on equilibrium that seems to break a basic rule. For a small crystal in equilibrium with a fluid, Gibbs implied the chemical potential inside the solid need not equal the fluid's. That holds when surface free-energy density differs from surface tension, generally true for crystals. Yet equilibrium normally means equal chemical potentials everywhere, hence the Second Gibbs Paradox.

Frenkel explains the resolution in atomic terms, following Gibbs and Mullins's account allowing for vacancies and interstitials, missing or extra atoms. Treating these defects consistently shows the chemical potential inside a critical nucleus does equal the fluid's value. A critical nucleus is a tiny crystal in unstable balance with its fluid. The interior potential is set at the surface. A bulk crystal squeezed to the nucleus's pressure would not share that potential, and a small population of vacancies makes the balance possible.
arxiv-2511-22694:
Chaubet and Divol determine the best possible accuracy for recovering a diffusion operator's spectrum from samples. Weighted Laplace operators arise as continuum limits of graph Laplacians and encode the geometry of a data distribution. Given n samples from an unknown density on a known compact manifold, the task is to estimate the operator's eigenvalues and eigenfunctions. The authors establish the exact minimax rates, the best worst-case errors any estimator can achieve.

Eigenfunctions and eigenvalues converge at two different rates, both governed by the density's smoothness: smoother densities are estimated faster, plug-in methods attaining the eigenfunction rate. In the smoother regime efficient eigenvalue estimators exist. The eigenvalue rate combines an approximation term and an unbeatable parametric term. Along the way, they build a general framework for estimating nonlinear functionals over Hölder-Zygmund spaces, expected to serve many statistical problems beyond spectral estimation.
arxiv-2511-23094:
Kreiss and colleagues study how to detect the period of a stationary time series, data whose statistical character stays constant over time. The cycle shows up only as a sharp peak in its spectrum. Their tool is simple: fit a second-order autoregressive model, AR(2), which predicts each value from the previous two, and read the cycle frequency off the fitted model.

They show that when the spectral peak is sharp enough, the AR(2) model that best approximates the process in mean square correctly identifies the true frequency. They analyze the estimator in a near-to-pole setup where the peak sharpens as the sample grows. In that regime the estimator converges faster than the usual parametric rate. Its rate can come arbitrarily close to the best this estimator can achieve, a guarantee for a method that needs no knowledge of the underlying process.
arxiv-2511-23194:
Kim and Kim develop a computational bridge between four-dimensional superconformal theories and two-dimensional vertex operator algebras, passing through three-dimensional topological theories in between. Starting from the BPS particle spectra on the Coulomb branch of (G, G′) Argyres-Douglas theories, a family of strongly interacting quantum field theories, they extract data. The data are about the algebras living on the boundary of the twisted three-dimensional theory.

Their method uses quiver mutations and wall-crossing invariants to obtain the ellipsoid partition functions of the three-dimensional theories efficiently, without case-by-case guesswork. From those partition functions they read off the modular data of the boundary vertex operator algebras, which connect back to the Schur sector of the original four-dimensional theory. This gives physicists a practical route from a BPS spectrum to algebraic data that was previously hard to reach for whole families of theories.
arxiv-2511-23394:
Sumaya-Martínez and colleagues generalize the classic double-slit diffraction problem to illumination by three coherent plane waves at once. One arriving straight on and two arriving symmetrically at equal and opposite angles. Textbook treatments use a single incident wave, but multi-wave illumination is increasingly used to shape light. And closed-form solutions in the Fresnel regime, the near-field region where diffraction patterns still evolve with distance, were largely missing.

By tuning the angles and phases so the total incident field vanishes at the aperture edges, an edge-zero condition. They obtain compact closed-form expressions built from the standard Fresnel integrals, and the construction extends to any number of incident waves and to partially coherent light. Numerical simulations confirm the formulas and map how patterns depend on slit geometry, wavelength, coherence, and beam width, pointing to uses in apodization, structured illumination, beam shaping, and multiplexed sensing.
arxiv-2512-00094:
Diffusion models are trained on huge image collections, sometimes including pictures used without permission. Kexin Li, Guozhen Ding, Ilya Grishchenko, and David Lie present HMark in a 2025 study from the University of Toronto. HMark is a watermarking method meant to expose unauthorized training.

The marks are radioactive, meaning they transfer into a trained model's outputs, where they can later be detected. A useful mark must also stay invisible, survive processing, and carry several bits of information. The work gives artists and dataset owners a technical tool for proving when their images were absorbed into a generative model. Ownership disputes over training data are now common in courtrooms as well as labs.
arxiv-2512-00394:
Graphene's promise for electronics depends on growing large sheets without grain boundaries or extra layers. Johanna Huhtasaari and a large team report wafer-scale single-crystalline monolayer graphene in 2025. Controlling growth kinetics to avoid those defects has remained challenging.

The team demonstrates single-crystalline graphene free from multilayer domains, made by one-step delamination of epitaxial graphene from silicon carbide. A clean wafer-scale sheet is key to realizing graphene's full potential in advanced applications, including twistronics. The result moves graphene production closer to the uniformity that chip manufacturing demands. Delamination avoids the transfer steps that usually wrinkle or contaminate graphene sheets. Silicon carbide is the standard substrate for epitaxial graphene growth. For labs that grow such sheets, the gain is a sheet that is one clean layer from edge to edge. It has no weak seams to fail in a chip.
arxiv-2512-00494:
Entanglement is a resource for sensing, letting correlated spins measure fields more finely than independent ones. Alexander and Mahesh demonstrate quantum sensing with large spin clusters in solid-state NMR in 2025. They create, manipulate, and detect clusters of correlated nuclear spins using multiple-quantum techniques.

The clusters sensitively detect jitter in the width of radio-frequency control pulses, at the level of tens of nanoseconds. The authors also identify the coherence order that works best for practical sensing. Their results show a tabletop NMR setup can act as a precise diagnostic for the control electronics used across quantum technologies. Pulse-width jitter is a practical nuisance in every pulsed quantum experiment.
arxiv-2512-00694:
Five authors, led by Mengzhu Xu, present a 2025 machine learning paper on continual learning for video and language models. Such models must keep learning as new data, domains, and question styles arrive over time. The hard part is knowing what should stay stable and what should change.

Many current methods blur that line, route tasks in fixed ways, or replay old videos, which strains memory and privacy. The team's affordance-first decomposition names the stable parts and the flexible parts up front. Giving stability a clear home could help models learn new video tasks without forgetting old ones or storing past footage.
arxiv-2512-00794:
Bo Guo, Sijia Wen, Yifan Zhao, Jia Li, and Zhiming Zheng improve 3D scene rebuilding in a 2025 computer vision paper. A method called 3D Gaussian Splatting builds scenes from many soft 3D blobs and has reached striking accuracy. It struggles, though, where light cues mislead, such as shiny or blank surfaces.

In those places, brightness alone cannot pin down the true shape. The team's method, PolarGS, adds polarimetric cues, information in how light waves are oriented after bouncing off a surface. Those cues help separate shape from shine. The payoff is cleaner geometry on the surfaces that fool other methods.
arxiv-2512-00894:
Leandro Lyra Braga Dognini revisits a puzzle in statistical physics in a 2025 paper. The Boltzmann-Gibbs distribution is the classic rule for how a system at a fixed temperature spreads over its states. It comes from maximizing a famous entropy formula under simple constraints.

Dognini generalizes that maximization using a nonadditive entropy with extra parameters. Nonadditive entropies do not simply add when systems combine, which suits some complex systems. The work connects this broader distribution to the electronic partition function paradox, a known tension in how electron states are counted. Fresh math on old paradoxes can clarify when classic formulas should bend.
arxiv-2512-00994:
Hang Wu, Qin Wu, Yue Liu, and Mengmeng Shi study inventory choices under two kinds of doubt in a 2025 paper. A newsvendor must order stock before knowing demand: order too much and goods spoil, too little and sales are lost. Online commerce has raised the stakes for pricing and stocking together.

The authors model a sequential game between two competing retailers. Each first sets prices in public, then chooses inventory in private, while demand stays uncertain. They back the theory with experimental evidence. The setup mirrors leading e-commerce platforms, where rivals watch prices but hide stock. Results show how strategic play changes classic ordering rules.
arxiv-2512-01394:
Hiroshi Noguchi studies patterns formed by active units on a grid. Each site on the grid holds a state that cycles in a loop. Past work gave each site just one loop. Real systems may host more than one loop at each site.

Noguchi asks what changes when loops compete at each site. He ran active Potts models on a square grid. Neighbor sites pull on each other in the usual way. The runs show how rival loops shift the patterns in space and time. The work helps link lab patterns to the rules that drive them.
arxiv-2512-01594:
Sina Abdollahi and co-authors build secure links between confidential virtual machines. Such machines shield work from even the host operator. Their split memory keeps data safe. It also makes sharing data between machines slow and clumsy.

On Arm CCA hardware, the team adds first-class sharing. Links are confidential, attestable, and fast at once. Each machine can prove what it runs before data flows. Fast safe sharing helps split sensitive work across machines in clouds without giving up the shield that made them useful. Attestation binds code identity to the link, so a peer machine knows both who it talks to and what software runs there.
arxiv-2512-01694:
Hui-Fa Liu, Qi Su, and Ding-fang Zeng compute quasinormal modes of charged AdS black holes. Those modes are the ringdown tones of a perturbed hole. Boundary rules at the AdS edge shape the tones a lot. Choice of rules is thus a physics choice, not just math.

The team sets rules from two principles. The boundary metric must not deform. Electromagnetic energy flux at the edge must vanish. Under those rules they find the mode spectrum. Ringdown spectra test gravity theory and holography links to field theory. Field-vanishing rules also keep the dual field theory clean, which matters for holography uses of these black hole spectra.
arxiv-2512-01794:
Jian Liang and Hua-Yang Wang find solutions to supercritical nonlinear Schrodinger equations on an annulus. They seek positive solutions with prescribed mass. The supercritical regime breaks standard variational tools. An annulus adds shape constraints that complicate the search.

Their Hopf reduction turns the task into a lower-dimensional one. Reduction via the Hopf fibration tames the geometry. Existence proofs in this regime extend nonlinear optics and condensate theory, where mass-fixed states on ring domains model real traps and fibers. Prescribed mass matches experiment, where atom number or beam power is fixed first and the state must form under that exact total.
arxiv-2512-01994:
Some crystals pair up two different magnetic atoms into tiny two-spin units, and squeezing such a crystal can rewrite its magnetic behavior. A 2025 paper by M. J. Coak and a large team studies one such material, a copper-vanadium compound, whose copper and vanadium spins form antiferromagnetic pairs linked weakly through hydrogen bonds.

The team places the material under hydrostatic pressure, squeezing it evenly from all sides, and watches how its properties respond. Weak links between the spin pairs make the system sensitive, so pressure can tip it between different magnetic states. Such experiments show how to tune quantum magnets by force rather than by chemistry.
arxiv-2512-02094:
Simulating how light travels through the cosmos is slow, so cosmologists often cheat by slowing light itself down in the calculation. Nickolay Gnedin's 2025 paper examines a flaw in that reduced speed of light approximation: in some regimes it makes photons quietly disappear.

Gnedin shows the missing photons can be counted exactly for certain numerical schemes, turning a hidden error into a measurable one. He then explains how to almost fix the problem, restoring conservation where it matters. Radiative transfer underlies simulations of galaxy formation and cosmic reionization, so photon bookkeeping errors can distort big conclusions.
arxiv-2512-02194:
Sparse autoencoders are popular tools for opening up neural networks, extracting human-readable features from their inner activity. Sophie Wang and co-authors note in 2025 that those features are unstable, changing with random seed and settings, and propose ordered sparse autoencoders to fix the wobble.

Their design extends Matryoshka autoencoders in two ways: it imposes a strict ordering on the latent features, and it uses every feature dimension deterministically instead of sampling approximations. Ordered features should mean the same concept lands in the same place across runs. Consistency like that is what interpretability research needs before its findings can be trusted and compared.
arxiv-2512-02394:
Radar that senses in four dimensions promises perception that survives fog and darkness, but radar semantic segmentation is starved of open data and labels. A 2025 paper reproduces and extends the RaDelft radar dataset work, adding camera assistance to produce the labels the original release lacked.

The original dataset was a landmark yet offered only LiDAR annotations and no public code to generate radar labels, limiting reproduction and downstream research. Camera-assisted labeling uses the camera's view to help assign meanings to radar returns. Open labels and code are the kind of infrastructure that lets a whole research direction move faster.
arxiv-2512-02494:
Zihao Zhao and four co-authors speed up a key building block for learning systems that must decide. Differentiable optimization layers let a model solve a small optimization problem as part of its own reasoning. Learning through such a layer usually needs a gradient found by implicit differentiation.

That gradient step solves a linear system with second order terms, which costs heavy compute and memory. The team's algorithm finds the gradient using only first order information instead. Cheaper gradients could let decision aware models run on larger problems and smaller machines, widening their use in planning and control. That gain grows as models take on more choice points in each task they face.
arxiv-2512-03094:
Quantum computers may one day beat classic ones at learning tasks. Tomás Villalba-Ferreiro, Eduardo Mosqueira-Rey, and Diego Alvarez-Estevez test that claim in this 2025 study. They compare two quantum methods with classic models for sorting data into groups.

One method uses quantum support vector ideas, the other uses quantum neural nets. They test all models on the Iris data set and a reduced form of MNIST. The authors report that quantum models tend to do better as tasks grow harder. That trend, if it holds, hints where quantum learning may first prove useful. For quantum computing teams, the pair of test data sets shows where gains first appear.
arxiv-2512-03594:
Chip routing is one of the slowest steps in design. Afsara Khan and Austin Rovinski present a routing method in this 2025 work. Detailed routing must place wires while obeying strict, shrinking design rules.

Prior routers use iterative pathfinding for each net, which converges slowly. The authors accelerate convergence through offline reinforcement learning. Learned guidance can steer the router away from dead ends sooner. Faster routing shortens chip design cycles for ever denser processors. Offline learning reuses past routing runs, so no costly live trials are needed, and the router improves from data it already owns.
arxiv-2512-03994:
Companies running language models on legal, financial, or medical work need the models to respect internal policies, not just generic safety rules. Oren Rachmil and a large team propose a detector for policy violations in a 2025 machine learning preprint. Their move is to treat a violation as an out-of-distribution event inside the model's own activation space.

The method needs no training: it reads hidden activations, normalises them with a whitening-inspired transform, and scores how far a response sits from policy-compliant behaviour. Only the policy text and a few example samples are required, keeping deployment light. Across several models and challenging policy benchmarks, the detector reached F1 scores up to eighty-six percent. It beat both fine-tuned classifiers and judge-style prompting while using far less computation. The authors release their code publicly, aiming at organisations that cannot afford heavyweight moderation pipelines.
arxiv-2512-04094:
Neurons in brains grow branching dendrites. Artificial neurons modelled on them are cheap to compute and quick at inference. Yet they were built for still images, not sequences. Dongjian Yang and colleagues extend the idea to time series with Memory-DD, presented in a 2025 neural computation preprint. Their neuron aims at temporal prediction: sensor streams, financial series, and traffic flows.

Memory-DD couples two groups of dendrite-inspired neurons. Neither group uses a nonlinear activation function, yet together they realise nonlinear mappings and extract logical relationships between features across a sequence. On eighteen temporal classification benchmarks, the model beat the standard LSTM network on accuracy. On nine regression datasets it matched LSTM while using half the parameters and fewer operations. The authors present the design as carrying the dendritic family's low-cost advantages into sequence modelling, for both classification and regression jobs.
arxiv-2512-04194:
A controller that keeps a robot or vehicle safe most of the time may not be safe enough. Matisse Teuwen, Mathijs Schuurmans, and Panagiotis Patrinos design safety filters with explicit probability guarantees in a 2025 control theory preprint. Their setting is a discrete-time system buffeted by disturbances whose distribution may be arbitrary, even learned from data.

Their filters rest on piecewise affine probabilistic control barrier functions. Checking such a filter exactly means solving a mixed-integer program, which can be slow. The authors replace that step with a heuristic search over a handful of small quadratic or nonlinear programs. Any data-driven quantile estimator can plug in to bound the chance of a safety violation. Extensive numerical experiments show gains in both conservatism and computation time over existing methods. The framework also handles complicated safety sets.
arxiv-2512-04294:
Mohsen Ben Abdallah and Marwa Ennaceur sort a family of maps on a special algebra. The algebra is a changed form of the Witt algebra. It has both even and odd parts. The maps in question are called Rota-Baxter operators. The pair study the odd ones at weight zero. Odd maps flip the even-odd grade of each element.

Their sorting shows these maps are tightly boxed in. In one case, one part can be free while the other must vanish. In the rest, the free part must take a rigid shape. An odd whole-number shift sets which shapes can occur. The authors also prove each operator splits into even and odd parts in just one way. They show all rate-of-change maps on the algebra come from inside it. They also show none of these maps can be undone.
arxiv-2512-04394:
Cesar Cuenca and Jiaming Xu settle an open question about when large particle ensembles settle into a predictable average pattern. The law of large numbers says averages tame randomness as the count grows. For interacting particle systems at fixed temperature, the exact conditions were unclear. The problem was posed by Benaych-Georges, Cuenca, and Gorin. Their 2025 arXiv paper gives conditions that are both needed and enough.

The test runs through the growth of special generating functions built from Bessel functions. One proof path uses the moment method with Dunkl operators. The other uses a formula for generating functions of endless constellations. As payoffs, the pair prove the law for theta-sums and theta-corners of random matrices, with limits given by free convolution and free projection. The result holds at every temperature value, and it also covers a slice of theta-Dyson Brownian motion.
arxiv-2512-04694:
Baris Yilmaz, Bevan Deniz Cilgin, and Erdem Akagündüz present TimesNet-Gen, a deep learning system that fabricates realistic earthquake shaking records for a chosen site. Quake risk work needs site-specific ground motion, since local soil shapes how shaking feels. Real records for a given station are scarce. Their 2025 arXiv paper trains a generative model on accelerometer records in the time domain.

The design draws new records by resampling a latent space tied to one station at a time, with no extra conditioning inputs. Pretraining on Turkey's AFAD dataset used self-supervised learning. The frozen model then produced station-matched records for the separate NGA-West2 set, with no fine-tuning at all. Generated and real records matched closely in their distributions. Synthetic shaking that respects local soil can fill gaps in hazard maps where instruments have short histories.
arxiv-2512-04794:
João Marcos Palheta, Octavio Rodrigues Filho, Mohammad Soleymanibrojeni, and co-authors teach a transformer network to judge the stability of thirteen-atom metal clusters the way a chemist would. Such nanoclusters sit between molecules and bulk metal, and mixing two metals opens vast design space. Which mixes hold together, and whether the guest atom hides in the core or sits on the surface, is hard to guess. Their 2025 arXiv paper maps that landscape with physics first, then learning.

Quantum calculations on hundreds of bimetallic clusters revealed the trends that govern the contest: binding energies, distortion costs, coordination, and electronic gaps. The team then pretrained a transformer on thousands of single-metal clusters from a public database, tuned by the physics results. The model learned to rank new mixes by stability. Fast, physics-guided prediction could speed the hunt for catalysts and magnetic materials built atom by atom.
arxiv-2512-04994:
Théo Marty opens a series of articles aimed at classifying partial sections of flows — surfaces that cut across a moving system's paths without covering the whole space. Such surfaces are basic tools for understanding how a flow behaves over time, since watching where paths pierce it turns continuous motion into something easier to track. This first installment handles the dynamical side of the question.

Marty works with a flow on a compact space and a chosen rank-one cohomology class, which singles out a layered covering of the space. He gives a criterion for when a Lyapunov map — a function that changes steadily along the flow, in step with the covering — exists there. A key role goes to a recurrence set that measures how often paths return near where they started, and the article describes how that set changes as the chosen class varies.
arxiv-2512-05094:
James Ni and seven co-authors, including Yann LeCun, Trevor Darrell, and Jitendra Malik, ask whether humanoid robots can learn actions from videos that were themselves generated by artificial intelligence. Video generators are getting good at imagining people doing tasks in new settings, which could make them high-level planners for robots. The catch: generated video is noisy, and bodies warp in ways that make direct imitation fail.

Their pipeline lifts the video into a four-dimensional model of the human, then reshapes that motion for the robot's body. A physics-aware learning policy, called GenMimic, then tracks the motion with weighted three-dimensional keypoints and a symmetry bonus for movement. The team built a benchmark of generated human motion across many actions and settings. GenMimic beats baselines in simulation and moves a Unitree G1 humanoid coherently with no fine-tuning — a step toward robots directed by imagined video.
arxiv-2512-05794:
Rebonto Haque and six co-authors open up antibody language models to see what they have learned inside. These models generate antibody sequences, and their internal features are opaque. The team applies sparse autoencoders, an interpretability tool that splits tangled activations into cleaner features. Two flavors are compared: TopK autoencoders, and Ordered ones, which force features into a hierarchy. The goal is understanding, and steering generation toward desired traits.

TopK features matched biological concepts well, which helps map what the model knows. But a strong match did not guarantee control over generation. Ordered autoencoders reversed the bargain. Their features steered output reliably, yet their activation patterns were more tangled and harder to read. The findings draw a practical line for protein model research. If the aim is a map of learned concepts, TopK suffices. If the aim is precise control, order is worth its interpretive price.
arxiv-2512-05994:
Rohan Sharma and six co-authors build speech technology for the users adult trained systems serve worst: children. Children's voices are higher, less steady, and still developing. KidSpeak is a speech enhanced language model built for them. Its training runs in two stages, folding phonetic knowledge into the speech encoder. Across four tasks it averages about eighty seven percent accuracy.

Annotating children's speech by hand does not scale. The team's Flexible and Automatic Speech Aligner builds high quality training data automatically, improving alignment quality more than thirteenfold over human annotation on a standard child language corpus. Together, model and aligner form what the authors describe as the first comprehensive solution aimed at children's speech and language therapy. Early screening catches disorders when intervention works best.
arxiv-2512-06094:
Jasbir Singh and twelve co-authors forecast what the next generation of gravitational wave observatories will hear from the universe's middleweight and heavyweight black holes. LISA will listen from space; LGWA, the Lunar Gravitational Wave Antenna, from the Moon. Both target mergers of intermediate and supermassive black holes. The team seeds each young galaxy with one light black hole in a cosmological model, then computes merger timescales.

Uncertain sinking times give bracketed rates. In the optimistic case, both observatories could detect more than fifteen intermediate mass mergers a year; in the pessimistic one, fewer than five across the detectors' whole lifetimes. Supermassive mergers run slightly lower. LGWA shines for loud intermediate mergers at high redshift, LISA for the most massive systems. The eventual counts will judge the seeding models.
arxiv-2512-06194:
Lim Siang and Daniel O'Connor tackle a puzzle from factory control rooms: why did the plant computer choose that setting? Large plants use a two step control scheme, where a linear program first picks low cost target values for dozens of plant settings and the measures they must hold. When the result looks odd, staff often cannot tell which setting drove which measure.

Their fix looks at shadow prices, the hidden cost each limit adds to the best plan.
