They split each such price into shares that come from single free settings, then match settings to measures one to one with a standard pairing method. Plant staff can then check whether the control scheme still matches its design, and find which limits are holding the plant back. The tool is meant for live use beside real plant systems.
arxiv-2512-06294:
Quentin Badolle leads a team with Arthur Theuer and with Zhou Fang, Ankit Gupta, and Mustafa Khammash. They present DeepSKA, a neural tool for random reaction networks. Such networks model systems where chance rules each step, from chemical mixes to disease spread and wild populations. Guessing their average behavior is key, yet exact math rarely works and brute force simulation gets costly fast.

Deep learning tools are quick but opaque, with no promise that their answers can be trusted. DeepSKA is built to give both clarity and a guarantee. Its inner form stays open to read and works across states, times, and outputs. A few true simulations are then mixed in to keep estimates unbiased and tight. Across nine test networks, some with up to ten species, it was accurate while cutting effort by a wide margin. That mix suits science that feeds real choices.
arxiv-2512-06394:
M Xu, J Li, C Xiao, and H Qiu explain why the fading glow of some gamma ray bursts brightens again partway through. These bursts can leave behind a newborn magnetar, a neutron star with a huge magnetic field that sheds spin energy into the jet. How fast it sheds that energy depends on the field's strength and on the tilt between the field and the spin axis.

Past work used a fixed tilt to explain a flat stretch in the afterglow, and a shrinking tilt for a double flat stretch. Xu and team study a growing tilt instead. As the tilt grows, energy flows faster into the jet, and their sums show the afterglow should flare again, briefly and mildly. Two real bursts with early mild flares fit the picture well. The work gives observers a fresh cause to weigh when an afterglow refuses to fade smoothly.
arxiv-2512-06594:
Norton Szabo, Krisztian Sarneczky, Laszlo Kiss, and a large team recount how a Hungarian mountain station caught three small asteroids just before they hit Earth. The Piszkesteto station of the Konkoly Observatory found the impactors of twenty twenty two, twenty twenty three, and twenty twenty four. They are a small share of its near Earth object finds, but a striking one. Meter sized rocks on a collision course give observers only hours to react.

The team describes its upgraded survey gear and the observing plan behind the catches. A tight loop between quick analysis and ongoing data collection proved key, since each fresh image sharpened the orbit and told the telescopes where to look next. Immediate follow up squeezed the most from the short warning. The authors close with plans to widen the survey's sensitivity and its coverage of the night, so fewer small impactors slip past unseen.
arxiv-2512-06794:
Dimitry Shaiderman studies a game of persuasion that unfolds over time, where one side knows more than the other. A sender watches a changing state, modeled as a Markov chain, as it moves step by step. The sender cannot act directly, but can send signals that shape what the receiver believes about the current state. The receiver then acts on that belief, and each action helps decide the sender's reward.

Shaiderman asks how the best possible result for the sender behaves as future rewards count for more and more. He shows that, from a steady starting spread of states, this value falls in a steady, one-way pattern as patience grows. Joined with an opposite pattern found by earlier researchers, that result bounds how fast the values settle down. The findings also carry over to a wider class of Markov chain games.
arxiv-2512-06894:
Yue Liu, Chushun Tian, and Dahai He take a fresh swing at an old open problem in physics. It asks how the orderly laws of heat arise from the messy motion of many particles. The question traces back to Hilbert's famous list of problems. It matters again as physicists shift attention from imaginary ensembles to one single isolated system.

Studying two very different models, the authors find a shared pattern: probability piles up sharply on a small part of the possible states. One model is a finite chain of springs, nearly orderly in its mixing. The other is an endless wave equation that strongly resists mixing. In both, the shape of the space of states protects the pattern. Strange results follow, from a spring chain mimicking an ideal gas to a wave system dodging a classic overheating paradox.
arxiv-2512-07094:
Christopher Cruz builds a supervisor for artificial intelligence agents, arguing that deployed agents are far more fragile than their demos suggest. Most agent frameworks chain model calls together with no way to watch themselves, diagnose their own failures, or improve without a human mechanic. His runtime, VIGIL, sits beside a working agent rather than inside it, and does maintenance instead of the task itself.

VIGIL reads the agent's behavior logs and scores each event into a structured emotional register, kept in a persistent memory bank with fading and context rules. From that record it produces a diagnosis sorted into strengths, opportunities, and failures. Repairs come in two guarded forms: prompt updates that must preserve the agent's core identity, and code proposals that are only read, never silently applied. The pipeline is state-gated, so illegal moves raise errors instead of improvisation.
arxiv-2512-07194:
Yuchen Tian and co-authors add a brain-inspired learning signal to spiking neural networks, the energy-sipping models whose neurons fire in brief pulses. Such networks are usually trained with a stand-in for backpropagation. While the local rules real synapses use are hard to scale: they need detailed spike timing logs and can fight the global goal. Their rule, gated by a dopamine-like signal, keys on synchrony, how much neurons fire together.

Spike patterns are compressed into one synchrony score per batch. A short warm-up checks whether that score tracks the task's loss, then sets a fixed gate that scales the local updates. When synchrony proves unrelated to the task, the gate settles at neutral and the rule shrinks to gentle two-factor adjustments added only in deeper layers. Storage stays tiny, just which neurons fired and when they first fired.
arxiv-2512-07294:
Thi-Hau Nguyen, Thi-Hong-Hai Do, and Van-Nham Phan map the group states of electrons and holes trapped with light in an optical microcavity. When the particles and the cavity photons couple strongly, they form polaritons. The twist here is mass imbalance. Electrons and holes of unlike heaviness tilt the contest among three kinds of condensate.

Working with an unrestricted Hartree-Fock method, the authors solve linked equations for two order settings. One setting tracks the excitonic side, and the other tracks the photonic side. The model treats the electron-hole pull and the light coupling on an equal footing. As the imbalance shrinks, the ground state marches through phases. First comes disorder, then excitonic-like and polariton states, and at last a photonic-like condensate. Each phase signs its name in measurable places, such as pair momentum patterns. Raising the excitation density widens the condensed range.
arxiv-2512-08294:
Yexin Liu, Manyuan Zhang, Yueze Wang, and a large team of computer vision researchers posted a dataset paper on arXiv in December 2025. Their corpus, OpenSubject, supports subject driven image generation, where a model must place a specific person or object into new scenes. Current models often drift from the reference identity, especially in busy scenes with several subjects.

OpenSubject is built from video, using agreement across frames as an identity signal. A four stage pipeline filters clips, mines and pairs subjects, synthesizes reference images through guided outpainting and inpainting, then verifies and captions every sample. The result holds millions of samples and images. The team also built a benchmark scoring identity fidelity, prompt fit, and background consistency with a vision language judge. Training on OpenSubject improved generation and editing results, with the clearest gains in complex multi subject scenes.
arxiv-2512-08394:
Llorenc Balada Gaggioli, Didier Henrion, and Milan Korda, researchers in optimization, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. They tackle global optimization of polynomials whose objective has a low rank structure, written as a short sum of simple pieces. Standard relaxation hierarchies grow with the number of variables, which quickly makes large problems hopeless.

Their hierarchy, called LRPOP, sizes its semidefinite blocks by the rank of that decomposition instead of the variable count. That single change lets it solve low rank problems with thousands of variables and total degree in the thousands, far beyond sparse methods. Writing the polynomials in a Bernstein basis keeps the numerics healthy at that scale. Under standard assumptions, the hierarchy climbs from below to the true global minimum. For engineers and scientists whose objectives are naturally low rank, the method turns formerly impossible global guarantees into routine computations.
arxiv-2512-08594:
Ferdinand Verhulst, a mathematician in the Netherlands, posted a modeling study on arXiv in December 2025. He builds a compact macroeconomic model where national output depends on two kinds of investment: physical capital, and education with innovation. The question is how much each lever matters for long run growth.

Inside the model, small changes in the quality of education turn out to have a considerable impact on growth, outweighing their modest size. He also lets capital investment swing wildly, as hype cycles or erratic policy might cause. Then he adds a control rule: education investment responds to consumption levels. In that three dimensional system a tipping point appears. Beyond it, rising consumption eats into education and innovation spending so much that growth declines instead of rising. The model makes a sharp point for policy: prosperity that starves education can flip an economy into decline.
arxiv-2512-08694:
Masoud Khalkhali and Nathan Pagliaroli survey a bootstrap approach to noncommutative geometry based on random Dirac operators. The work starts from finite spectral triples, which encode geometry in operator terms. A toy model for quantum gravity motivates replacing integrals over metrics with integrals over Dirac operators instead.

The survey explains multitrace and multimatrix random models built from spectral triples, studied in a large size limit. Positivity conditions on moment matrices turn the problem into finite programs whose feasible regions bound coupling values and moments. Links to spectral geometry, including Laplace eigenvalues, are also discussed. Readers get a unified view of how consistency alone, through classic bootstrap ideas, can yield rigorous bounds in both standard and noncommutative settings.
arxiv-2512-08794:
Yaoying Fu and coauthors extend two core tools of topological data analysis so they can handle labeled data sets. Many real data sets carry category labels, such as labeled images or segmented shapes. Standard distance and homology tools treat points as unlabeled, so they miss that structure.

The authors define a general framework for labeled metric spaces and build new versions of Gromov Hausdorff distance and persistent homology for that setting. Their main result proves stability: the new homology is stable under the new distance, extending a classic theorem. To support computation, they also introduce a labeled version of persistence landscapes. That landscape map is shown to be Lipschitz, which controls how much outputs can change with inputs. The work gives labeled data a principled geometric treatment, with guarantees that match the unlabeled theory.
arxiv-2512-08994: Neil Kolekar gives error bounds on the count of monic irreducible polynomials over a finite field whose coefficients lie in a fixed affine algebraic set. The polynomials have a set degree, with all lower coefficients free in the set and the leading coefficient fixed at one. The algebraic set is a fixed collection of points in a finite field space of matching dimension. The result quantifies how many such irreducible polynomials exist, with an explicit error term.
arxiv-2512-09094:
Pedro Gordaliza and coauthors present a causal method to explain why medical image segmentation models lose results when data distributions shift. Deep learning models for medical imaging often drop sharply under such shifts, but the processes behind the drop are poorly understood. Knowing whether acquisition or annotation changes are to blame would guide fixes.

Their method extends causal attribution to high dimensional segmentation tasks. The data generating process is modeled as a causal graph, and Shapley values fairly divide results changes among single processes. Special challenges include high dimensional outputs, limited samples, and interactions between processes. Validation uses multiple sclerosis lesion segmentation across several centers and annotators. Failure modes depend on context in a clear way. When the annotator changes, annotation protocol shifts dominate the loss. When the imaging center changes, acquisition shifts dominate instead. That process specific accounting lets practitioners prioritize the right intervention for each deployment setting.
arxiv-2512-09394:
Julie Kallini and Christopher Potts argue that language models can serve as laboratory tools for linguistics. A central question in the field is what separates a possible human language from an impossible one, a line that reveals the built-in biases guiding how humans learn language. Testing that line directly on people is slow and ethically limited.

Kallini and Potts outline a phased research program. Language model architectures would be refined step by step so they get better at telling possible languages from impossible ones. Each improvement in that discrimination would support a linking hypothesis about human cognition, suggesting which inductive biases people might share with the models. The paper is a program statement rather than an experimental report. It makes the case that models, used carefully, can probe questions about the nature of human language that were previously hard to approach.
arxiv-2512-09494:
Daniele Morotti, Marco Uguccioni, and Luca Dell'Anna study electrical and heat transport through a quantum dot. The dot is described by the spinful Sachdev-Ye-Kitaev model, a system of strongly interacting fermions famous for behaving unlike an ordinary metal. It is connected to leads on both sides. Earlier work treated systems in equilibrium; this study treats the junction as a conductor out of equilibrium.

Using Keldysh field theory and avoiding the replica trick, the authors start from the equations. They derive results for the tunneling and zero-temperature limits, then compute the linear-response behavior numerically. They map how conductance, the thermoelectric coefficient, and the Seebeck effect depend on particle-hole asymmetry and on how strongly the dot couples to its leads. The results show non-Fermi liquid signatures. They identify coupling regimes where thermoelectric effects grow, suggesting fingerprints of this exotic physics that experiments on devices could detect.
arxiv-2512-09694:
Zhe Hu and colleagues present CDIP, a method for coherent diffraction imaging that removes the constraints its results usually depend on. Coherent diffraction imaging is a lensless technique that can image samples at atomic resolution and follow their motion. Its reconstruction step, phase retrieval, is unstable and ill-posed, and algorithms lean on constraints chosen by hand, limiting wider use.

CDIP combines untrained neural fields, networks that represent the specimen rather than learning from data, with a physics-consistent forward model of imaging. Separate handling covers static samples and dynamic cases. On simulated and experimental data, for both still samples and moving processes, CDIP outperformed iterative methods and learning baselines in fidelity. The authors present the results as a shift for imaging, with a framework that should transfer to ptychography and holography across X-ray, electron, and optical probes.
arxiv-2512-09794:
Pablo Ochoa and Ariel Salort study a Hénon type equation on all of space. The equation is driven by a nonlinear operator that mixes a local term with a nonlocal one. Equations of this Hénon family were first proposed to model spherically symmetric clusters of stars. The authors ask when solutions exist. Under a suitable relation among the parameters of the problem, they prove there is a threshold value that separates the two regimes.

On one side of the threshold, solutions to the equation exist. On the other side, none do. Locating such a dividing line is the central question for this kind of nonlinear problem. The authors also establish regularity properties, which describe how smooth any solution must be. Results like these clarify how the local and nonlocal parts of the operator interact, and they add to the theory of mixed operators in nonlinear analysis.
arxiv-2512-10094:
Agostino Capponi and Brian Zhu show that auctioning time can calm wasteful speed races in markets. In high frequency trading, firms burn cash and effort to be microseconds faster, and rivals submit redundant orders chasing the same opportunity. The authors propose selling artificial time priority instead: traders pay for precedence rather than racing for it, sending spending into auction revenue. Blockchains make the waste measurable, since repeat submissions sit in open records. They study Timeboost, a time priority auction launched on Arbitrum, a network that batches transactions before settling on Ethereum.

The launch serves as a natural experiment. After Timeboost arrived, redundant transactions fell and platform revenue rose versus comparable networks. Both movements match the theory's predictions. The result reframes a familiar arms race: if speed priority is valuable, selling it can beat letting everyone build faster mousetraps. Older markets cannot easily copy the measurement, but the mechanism travels.
arxiv-2512-10294:
Luís Marques, Maani Ghaffari, and Dmitry Berenson give robots honest prediction sets for what an action will do. Safe control needs to know not just the expected outcome of a move, but a region that contains the true resulting configuration with a stated probability. Their method, CLAPS, builds such sets with conformal prediction, a statistical framework giving distribution free guarantees without assuming the error's shape. The catch they fix: robot configurations are not flat Euclidean points. A mobile robot's pose lives on a Lie group, combining position and rotation, and ignoring that geometry wastes volume or breaks coverage.

Their analysis extends conformal guarantees to the planar motion group. Experiments on simulated and real robots suggest the sets are smaller yet keep coverage. The guarantees hold despite the dynamics model being wrong in unknown ways, under both random and model uncertainty.
arxiv-2512-10394:
Weifan Guan and co-authors build plumbing for robots run by language model agents. Vision-language-action models can decide what a robot should do. But connecting an agent's tool calls to real robot software usually means hand-written wrappers that break whenever the model or serving setup changes, forcing the whole link to be rebuilt.

Their middle layer, RoboNeuron, bridges the Model Context Protocol used by agents with ROS2, the common robot middleware. It creates agent-ready tools straight from robot software schemas, supports both single commands and chained routines, and keeps backend changes behind one stable boundary. In simulation and on real hardware, across base driving, arm motion, and model-driven grasping, robots changed backends without rewiring the system, and the code is public.
arxiv-2512-10794:
Jaskirat Singh and co-authors ask what a generative model really borrows from its teacher. Representation alignment trains diffusion models by distilling features from a strong pretrained vision encoder, and the folk wisdom says the teacher's global semantic quality, its ImageNet accuracy, is what matters. The authors suspect the spatial structure of the representation, how patch tokens relate to each other, matters more.

They tested the question at scale across twenty-seven vision encoders and several model sizes. And the answer was surprising: spatial structure, not global performance, drives generation quality. Two small fixes follow. Swapping the projection layer for a simple convolution was one fix. Adding a spatial normalisation layer was the other. Together, under four lines of code, they produced iREPA. It consistently sped up training convergence across encoders, model sizes, and training variants. The authors urge a rethink of how alignment works.
arxiv-2512-10994:
Sharvaj Kubal and colleagues present STARK, a method for cleaning noisy images from spatial transcriptomics, a technique that maps gene activity across tissue. At very low reading depths the images are especially noisy, and cell identities can be lost. STARK can also fill in missing gene expression values between measured spots.

The method pairs kernel ridge regression with a graph based smoother that adapts as the image improves. Each round updates the image using the current graph, then rebuilds the graph from the cleaner image, making it more resistant to noise. The authors prove the process settles at a stable point and that such points approach the truth as readings grow. On real data, STARK improved cell label transfer over competing methods.
arxiv-2512-11394:
Abhijit Chaudhari, Marius Jürgensen, and Mikael Rechtsman show that disorder need not destroy the precise transport in a Thouless pump, provided the pump is nonlinear. A Thouless pump moves light or particles by a strictly quantised amount per cycle as a system is slowly modulated, a topological effect prized for robust devices. In linear systems, imperfections scramble that quantisation.

Working with optical waveguide arrays that carry solitons, self reinforcing light pulses, the team demonstrates quantised displacement surviving in disordered nonlinear pumps. Transport can be whole number or fractional per cycle, as in clean systems. Nonlinearity brings a second gift: the pump can be run faster, with less need for slow, adiabatic change. The authors propose this as a design principle for integrated non reciprocal devices, components that pass signals one way but not the other, built on temporal modulation.
arxiv-2512-12094:
Yanting Teng and co-authors speed up Pauli propagation, a classic way to simulate quantum circuits by tracking strings of Pauli operators. When a circuit has a symmetry, many strings evolve in lockstep copies, wasting work. Their symmetry merging method collapses each copy set into one representative.

The savings scale with the symmetry orbit sizes, proven for shift and swap symmetries. Tests on all to all Heisenberg dynamics show better stability, most of all when truncation or noise enters. Open source code ships with the paper. Group theory, the work shows, can cut real simulation cost for quantum dynamics on ordinary computers, a useful counterweight as quantum hardware grows.
arxiv-2512-12794:
Yichen Liu, Hongyu Wu, and Bo Liu present a rule aware prompt framework for numeric reasoning in smart grids in a 2025 paper. Power grids produce high dimensional numeric telemetry and run by explicit operating rules. Language models are candidates for decision support, but most deployments read text logs and alerts, not rule grounded reasoning over grid measurements, the authors note.

Their framework builds prompts from reusable modules: role, domain context, numeric normalization, rule aware reasoning, value block, and output schema. Separating rule specification from normalized numeric deviations keeps prompts concise. On anomaly detection in the IEEE 118-bus network, rule aware z-score value blocks and a hybrid model with deep learning improved rule consistency and detection while reducing token use.
arxiv-2512-12994:
Boyuan Ning and Yasutaka Shimizu link two models used for interest rates and other random financial quantities. The CKLS process allows a flexible power in its noise term. The CIR process, an older classic, uses a square-root noise term and is much better understood.

They build a smooth change of variables between the two and pair it with a change of probability measure. A close review found serious errors in an earlier study of this same link, which they correct. Under the new measure, the transformed process follows CIR dynamics for the financially relevant range. That yields formulas for densities, moments, and long-run behavior.
arxiv-2512-13294:
Sooryansh Asthana, Yeshma Ibrahim, Norman Koo, and Sai Vinjanampathy unify several quantum sensor designs under one operator algebra model. Quantum sensors promise precision past classical limits, but Ramsey, twist-untwist, and random designs were usually treated apart. A single frame makes their sensitivity scaling comparable.

Operator orbits tied to state preparation explain how sensitivity grows with the number of subsystems. Using that picture, the team designs a projected ensemble sensor that beats shot noise performance. They also show the Fisher information, a precision measure, scales favorably under decoherence and particle loss. The framework guides sensor design with algebra rather than trial and error.
arxiv-2512-13394:
Zhiyu Yin, H. Arnold, J. F. Drake, and M. Swisdak investigate what caps the energy that particles gain during magnetic reconnection, the explosive rejoining of magnetic field lines. Earlier work showed a strong guide field limits gain by stiffening the reconnected lines. Simulations also showed maximum energy grows with system size, for reasons not yet pinned down.

Running large simulations with the kglobal model across many system sizes, they find the cap is set by the number of magnetic island mergers. Flux ropes form early and merge repeatedly, and Fermi reflection during those mergers dominates the energy gain. Bigger systems make more ropes and thus more mergers, explaining the size trend.
arxiv-2512-13594:
Simon Jacobsson studies the geometry of sets of tensors with fixed low rank. A tensor is a multi-way array of numbers, and rank limits how simply it can be built. He looks at three rank types at once: CP rank, multilinear rank, and tensor-train rank.

Jacobsson derives when the smooth parts of these sets form smooth homogeneous manifolds, spaces that look the same at each point. For CP and tensor-train ranks, the key term is that the rank is low enough. He then uses these structures to build Riemannian metrics for the sets. The paths of shortest length under those metrics are both complete and cheap to compute, which helps later work with low-rank models.
arxiv-2512-14294:
Ersyzario Edo Yunata and six coauthors review spectroscopic ellipsometry for two dimensional materials in a 2025 paper. The method shines polarized light on a sample and reads the change to learn its optical traits, without damaging atomically thin layers.

The review covers experimental setups and optical modeling for graphene, transition metal dichalcogenides, and other van der Waals materials. Hard parts include very low thickness, direction dependent traits, and substrate effects. Mueller matrix methods can separate in plane and out of plane parts of the dielectric tensor. Recent finds include extreme optical anisotropy, hyperbolic dispersion, and tunable plasmonic responses. The authors present the method as essential for basic studies and photonic device design.
arxiv-2512-14694:
In-in correlators are the basic observables of cosmology, the quantities that connect theory to the sky. They are traditionally computed with the Schwinger-Keldysh formalism, and that machinery is revisited here for theories with spin.

The treatment covers photons, gluons, and gravitons coupled to scalars in four-dimensional de Sitter space, the geometry of an exponentially expanding universe. A novel part of the work is its handling of boundary gauge-fixing in the underlying path integral. Cleaner methods here feed into predictions for the early universe, the setting where in-in correlators do most of their work in cosmology.
arxiv-2512-14794:
F. Serdouk and three coauthors study how charge moves through amorphous selenium, a solid with no neat crystal order. They use time of flight measures, which time how fast charge crosses a sample after a flash of light. Their goal is to map the density of states, the set of energy levels open to charge, and to track how hole mobility shifts.

They read the current traces with a Laplace transform method joined to a model of repeated trapping. That lets them rebuild the density of states across a wide span of heat, and spot shallow and deep trap levels. Test currents from computer models then show how hole drift shifts with heat and field strength. The work supports a steady picture of charge flow in disordered solids.
arxiv-2512-15494:
Vadim Alekseev and Andreas Thom study when approximation and stability properties of groups pass to their quotients in a 2025 paper. Such properties say, roughly, that a group can be closely mimicked by finite or simpler structures, and that near homomorphisms are close to true ones. Knowing whether they survive dividing out a subgroup is often hard.

The authors give several cases where these properties are inherited by quotients by finitely generated normal subgroups, or more strongly by normal subgroups with Kazhdan property T. They then combine these findings with variations of the Rips construction due to Wise and to Belegradek and Osin. The applications produce new examples with controlled approximation behavior.
arxiv-2512-15694:
Orkun Furat and co authors train physics informed neural operators to predict 3D EM fields shaped by metasurfaces in a 2025 paper. Metasurfaces, arrays of nanopillars, bend light according to their geometry. Designing new ones means searching huge design spaces with slow full wave runs.

The team builds synthetic training data by solving Maxwell's equations for many 3D metasurface shapes. Their neural operators also cut residuals against Maxwell's equations, which penalizes unphysical fields. Fewer than 5,000 examples already give reasonable results. The trained stand in predicts diffraction scores with 3.9 percent error and runs 67 times faster than a standard run, aiding gradient based design.
arxiv-2512-16094:
Jacob Feinleib, Matthew Dew, and N G Holmes study teamwork in college physics labs in their 2025 paper on arXiv. Lab groups can share each task, rotate roles each session, or split roles so each student keeps one job all term. Earlier work hinted that sharing helps, but many strategies had never been tested at scale.

The team surveyed a large sample of students at two institutions, asking how they split their lab time among the three styles. Statistical modeling linked the styles to outcomes like critical thinking, self-belief, agency, belonging, and feeling recognized. Role style did not change critical thinking. Sharing tended to help attitudes, splitting hurt them, and rotating fell in between, though significance varied by outcome.
arxiv-2512-16394:
Suleiman Saka and Sanchari Das review smart home research in their arXiv paper, posted in 2025. Connected devices could help older adults live independently, but they also bring security, privacy, accessibility, and usability risks, a bundle the authors call SPAU. The review covers two decades of work, from 2004 to 2024.

Screening in five phases left 44 peer-reviewed studies. From them the authors built the SPAU-IoT framework: 27 criteria across the four dimensions, from secure defaults to consent and assistive technology support. More than 70 percent of studies used authentication and encryption, but fewer than half addressed accessibility or usability. A threat model maps devices, networks, and servers to attacks like phishing and caregiver exploitation, accounting for age-related vulnerabilities. The paper ends with standards-aligned design guidelines.
arxiv-2512-16894:
Nicolas Curien, William Fleurat, and Adrianus Twigt study growing self-similar Markov trees, random branching structures that record the family history of particles that split and grow by rules tied to their labels. The Brownian continuum tree is one famous case.

The question is whether nested growth can link trees of unlike mass, as in halving a tree of mass one to get one of mass one half. The team focuses on trees that can be coupled into one rising family of nested subtrees across all start values. For Brownian and stable trees, that coupling yields simple new dynamics matching the scaling limits of known leaf-growth algorithms by Luczak-Winkler and Caraceni-Stauffer.
arxiv-2512-17494:
Frank Kiwy and a large team, including the Backyard Worlds: Planet 9 collaboration, hunt the Euclid space telescope's first data release for brown dwarfs, failed stars too small to burn hydrogen. They sifted 38,845 sources by their infrared colors, the patch where the coldest dwarfs, class T, are known to sit.

Each hopeful source then faced low-resolution spectra from Euclid's NISP instrument, template matching, and a human eye check. Fifteen candidates survived, and eight of them are new to science. The team estimates their distances from brightness and sizes up Euclid's power for this hunt. Even this quick first release, they show, can dredge up substellar objects past the reach of ground surveys.
arxiv-2512-17594:
Tosin Ige and five co-authors build a malware detector that admits when it faces something new. Most detectors assume every sample comes from a family they trained on, so a fresh strain gets a confident, wrong label. Shape-shifting malware, which rewrites itself to dodge signatures, makes that closed-world habit dangerous.

Their framework, MAD-OOD, works in two stages. First it draws a spherical border around each known family's cluster in a learned feature space, flagging samples that land outside every border as out of distribution. A second network then blends cluster calls, refined features, and standard classifier output for the final verdict. On benchmark sets with 25 known families plus novel strains held back, the system reached detection scores up to 0.911 AUC on the unseen families.
arxiv-2512-18394:
Zetao Lin, Benjamin Kadoch, Sadruddin Benkadda, and Kai Schneider track heavy dirt inside a fusion plasma. Tungsten flecks flake off the walls of fusion machines and, if they gather at the core, they cool the fuel and spoil the burn. Past models treated such flecks as weightless tracers that simply drift and spread.

Their runs, using a standard model of drift wave turbulence, give the flecks real heft. With mass in play, the flecks stop spreading in the plain diffusive way for a range of charge states and instead pile toward the core. The shift names a clear risk for future reactors and a lever, particle inertia, that wall and fuel design must respect.
arxiv-2512-18594: Sanjib Basu and Navdeep Tamang revisit a theorem by Grzegorek and Labuda. The result sits in measure theory, the branch of math that formalizes size and measurability of sets. Their short paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, states its aim directly. It presents a generalized version of that theorem in the setting of category bases. It also works to establish a variant formulation in Marczewski structures. Both settings are abstract frames for deciding which sets count as small or negligible.
arxiv-2512-18794:
Andrea Gokus and Rebecca Phillipson read the flicker of blazars, galaxies whose jets point almost straight at Earth. Gamma-ray light curves from the Fermi-LAT telescope record that flicker over years, but the series are not stationary, which breaks many standard statistics. Their paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, applies recurrence plots, a method that flags when a system revisits earlier states.

They analyze two sources, the BL Lac object Mkn 421 and the quasar PKS 1424-41, testing significance with surrogate data. Mkn 421 shows more determinism than PKS 1424-41, and both may hide nonlinear dynamics. The authors caution that the second claim needs tougher surrogates that mimic nonstationarity. Next they plan to extend the method to about fifty bright sources, comparing jet behavior across blazar classes.
arxiv-2512-19794:
Gudrun Hiller and Dominik Suelmann point to a little-used hunting ground for invisible particles. The ground is the rare decays of charm hadrons. The quarry could be neutrinos, axion-like particles, or dark photons. Any of them could slip away unseen from a decaying D meson or Lambda-c baryon. In the Standard Model, the rates for these decays are clean null tests. Yet for some new-physics values they are barely fenced in at all.

The authors recast past searches to map how large the signals could still be. Rates could reach a thousandth for dark photons. For axion-like particles, a ten-thousandth is in reach in some models. Heavy new physics with kept chirality faces tighter caps. Each decay mode probes other couplings. The paper surveys what charm plants, from BESIII and Belle II to planned ones, could see.
arxiv-2512-19894:
Kostas Karagiannis and two co-authors study algebraic structures that carry a group action. Their stage is a smooth projective variety. A finite group acts on it. The group's order is coprime to the field's characteristic. Koszul cohomology packages the syzygies of the variety's equations. With the group in play, it becomes a complex of group modules, not just vector spaces.

The team uses equivariant tools to lift known dimension formulas. The lifts are identities between virtual representations. They track how each group decomposes under the action, not just its size. For canonical curves, they get explicit formulas. The parts are equivariant Euler characteristics, Riemann-Roch theorems, and generating functions for Schur functors. Group theory thereby sharpens classic sums about curves.
arxiv-2512-20594:
Angelina Sherman, Ke Fang, and Dan Hooper forecast what a balloon-borne observatory could learn about the universe's most energetic particles. PUEO, the Payload for Ultrahigh Energy Observations, will hunt neutrinos at energies from about one to a thousand exa-electronvolts, beyond any current instrument's reach. The authors assess its sensitivity before it flies.

Cosmogenic neutrinos, born when ultrahigh-energy cosmic rays strike background light, are the primary target. PUEO can constrain the proton fraction of cosmic rays in scenarios with strong source evolution and extreme acceleration. Exotic sources fare differently: decaying ultraheavy dark matter is usually better probed by gamma rays, except above the highest energies where PUEO leads. Some cosmic string models will face their strongest constraints from PUEO.
arxiv-2512-21194:
Brigitta Malagurski Tortei, Sanath Narayan, and six co-authors built a test to catch vision-language models faking sight. Models ace question answering and captioning, but how much of that success is genuine visual reasoning and how much is language priors guessing plausible answers? VisRes Bench removes the verbal scaffolding and sorts pure seeing into three levels over more than nineteen thousand controlled images. Level one is perceptual completion and matching under blur, texture change, occlusion, and rotation. Level two is rule inference over a single attribute such as color, count, or orientation. Level three is compositional reasoning combining several attributes at once.

The verdict is unflattering. State-of-the-art models fall to near-random performance under subtle perceptual perturbations, exposing pattern matching where abstraction should be. Because each level isolates a distinct ability, failures localize exactly, telling model builders whether perception, rules, or composition needs the next breakthrough.
arxiv-2512-21594:
Hanxiang Yang, Haixiao Deng, and their co-authors study how to undo laser-induced energy modulation in a seeded free-electron laser. In such machines, a laser imprints an energy pattern on a relativistic electron beam so the beam can emit coherent, ultrashort X-ray pulses. The side effect is a larger energy spread, hurting beam quality.

The team studies demodulation with two modulators and a tunable phase shifter. Analysis and simulations show a half-period phase delay can nearly reverse the interaction and largely erase the leftover modulation. They design diagnostics from coherent undulator radiation that can detect weak leftovers. A dedicated demodulation undulator supports controlled studies. Early experiments at the Shanghai soft X-ray facility showed the modulation suppressed. The work points toward fully coherent X-ray sources that run faster without sacrificing beam quality.
arxiv-2512-21794:
Qiushi Han, David Simchi-Levi, Renfei Tan, and Zishuo Zhao design a mechanism that buys truthful information from strategic agents without knowing what those agents believe. A principal must pay agents enough to report honestly. Doing this adaptively, while learning their beliefs from scratch, is the challenge.

Their mechanism, DRAM, pairs mechanism design with online learning. Each round, it estimates the agents' beliefs and updates a distributionally robust linear program whose ambiguity set shrinks as evidence accumulates. The update trims payments down while keeping truthful reporting worthwhile. The authors prove agents report truthfully with high probability and that cumulative regret grows like the square root of the number of rounds. A matching lower bound shows no feasible adaptive mechanism can do asymptotically better. The framework accepts plug-in estimators, structured priors, and delayed feedback.
arxiv-2512-21994:
Federico Gonzalez, Carmen Tachino, and H Fabio Busnengo model how carbon dioxide units break apart when striking a copper 110 surface. Density functional runs feed a potential energy surface fitted by neural networks, and quasi classic trajectories then predict molecular and dissociative sticking probabilities. Results are compared with supersonic molecular beam tests at normal incidence across impact levels and surface temperatures.

General trends with impact energy agree with test, and splitting proves insensitive to surface heat between fifty and four hundred kelvin where the probability is appreciable. At higher impact levels near room heat, splitting strongly distorts the surface, creating copper adatom vacancy pairs stimulated by adsorbed carbon monoxide and oxygen products.
arxiv-2512-22294:
Philip Xu introduces Uni4D, a single system for searching large 3D model collections with words and for generating controllable four-dimensional, time-varying assets. Both jobs depend on aligning three kinds of data: text descriptions, 3D models, and images. Uni4D builds that alignment in three levels on top of the Align3D 130 dataset.

A multi-head attention and search model first tightens text-to-3D retrieval. Multi-view alignment then links 3D models to their images, and image-to-text alignment supports generating temporally consistent 4D content. Tests show high-quality retrieval and controllable generation from the combined system. Xu presents Uni4D as a step toward practical dynamic multimodal understanding, where one alignment scheme serves both finding current assets and creating new animated ones.
arxiv-2512-22394:
Jean-Pierre Magnot lays foundations for orthogonal polynomials built from inner products that need not come from a measure. Classic theory fixes an inner product on polynomial spaces through an integral, but general pre-Hilbert forms allow much more freedom. To each such inner product, Magnot associates a canonical Laplacian defined from an abstract derivation, and studies the operator forms that follow.

His main contribution is a resolvent-based distance between these polynomial geometries, plus quantitative stability results. If two Laplacians are close in the norm-resolvent sense, their Gram-Schmidt bases stay close too. So do their orthogonal projectors and reproducing kernels, in every finite degree. Examples include orthogonal polynomials on the unit circle under both classic integral geometries and Sobolev-type regularizations, and the thin annulus problem read as a resolvent limit.
arxiv-2512-22494:
Thang Pang Ern, Malcolm Tan Jun Xi, and Loh Wei Xuan Ryan investigate a curious function built from greatest common divisors. For two positive integers, the function divides the gcd of the sum and the product by the gcd of the pair itself. The natural question is how often the result equals one, measured as a limiting density over all pairs.

The authors compute that density as an Euler product over all primes, landing near 0.88 as the pairs grow without bound. Unexpectedly, their product matches the quadratic class number constant from the theory of real quadratic fields. They also study a higher-order analogue of the function, where the problem collapses to plain coprimality and the density becomes the famous six over pi squared.
arxiv-2512-22694:
Ahmad Moradpouri explores a sharpened version of a conjecture about how long an expanding universe like ours can last. The starting point is the species scale, the energy where quantum corrections to Einstein's gravity become significant, often the string scale, far below the Planck scale at weak coupling. Moradpouri studies a refined Trans-Planckian Censorship Conjecture tied to that scale, asking whether stringy modes can stay stringy and never cross the Hubble horizon.

The refined conjecture predicts a shorter lifetime for de Sitter spacetime and bounds the cosmological constant. Evidence is assembled from cosmological solutions across different compactifications of various string theories. Moradpouri also argues both versions of the conjecture clash with a big-bang singularity, so if they hold, the singularity must go, as in string gas cosmology.
arxiv-2512-22894:
Phil Cuvin, Hao Zhu, and Diyi Yang show that the manipulative interface tricks known as dark patterns also fool AI web agents. Dark patterns, like disguised ads and forced sign-ups, push human users toward choices against their own goals. The team built DECEPTICON, a test environment of seven hundred web navigation tasks that isolates individual dark patterns, mixing generated tasks with real-world ones.

Across leading agents, dark patterns steered behavior toward the malicious outcome in more than seventy percent of tasks, while human users fell for the same patterns at roughly half that rate. Worryingly, bigger models with more test-time reasoning were easier to steer, not harder. Standard defenses, including warning prompts and guardrail models, did not reliably reduce the effect. The authors frame manipulative design as an unmitigated risk for agents browsing the real web and call for dedicated defenses.
arxiv-2512-23094: Hossien Hossieni proposes a quantum model for how a proton shifting inside the adenine-thymine base pair of DNA could trigger a genetic mutation. The core tool is a new potential function describing that proton transfer. Around it, Hossieni builds a non-adiabatic framework, meaning the proton is not assumed to adjust smoothly to its surroundings, and uses it to compute mutation probabilities. The results are reported as consistent with findings from other researchers working on the same picture of spontaneous mutation.
arxiv-2512-23494:
Eddy Truyen and Wouter Joosen ask when a microservice application's processor and memory settings should be tuned. Most research optimizes these resources while the system runs, through scheduling and autoscaling. They instead apply an existing offline optimization framework during the release phase of the DevOps cycle, before deployment, a stage they note is largely unexplored.

Using the TeaStore benchmark application, they statistically compare optimization algorithms by sampling cost and by distance from the best configuration found. An upfront screening step that shrinks the search space proved helpful when hunting the true optimum on a limited budget, and necessary when comparing algorithms fairly. When a near-optimal setting is good enough, though, Bayesian optimization without screening performed better.
arxiv-2512-23694:
Lars van der Laan and Nathan Kallus import an old statistical virtue, calibration, into offline reinforcement learning. Agents trained from logged data must predict long-horizon values, but fitted value methods mix bootstrapping, function approximation, and distribution shift, and their guarantees usually demand strong assumptions about the function class. The authors propose a weaker, checkable reliability standard called Bellman calibration.

Roughly, states given similar predicted values should have average Bellman targets that match those predictions. That condition defines a scalar calibration error, estimated from off-policy data with doubly robust methods. Their Iterated Bellman Calibration procedure then recalibrates any learned value predictor through a one-dimensional correction, with histogram and isotonic variants. Finite-sample guarantees hold at one-dimensional rates without assuming Bellman completeness or realizability, and the analysis separates exactly when calibration can and cannot help.
arxiv-2512-24194:
A C Khunt, K Yavuz Ekşi, and P C Vinodkumar ask how one-sided pressure reshapes neutron stars. Inside a real star, pressure may differ by direction. Physicists call that difference anisotropy. The study works within general relativity. A standard model supplies the effect. The SLy equation of state supplies the matter. A second model cross-checks selected results.

Uneven pressure changes the global picture. Mass and radius shift as the effect strengthens. The moment of inertia moves too. So do compactness and the tidal response. A moderate push in the right direction raises the top mass a star can bear. Compactness can grow by up to a fifth. The stars still fit current data from NICER and from gravitational-wave events. Curvature measures then probe the inner field. Measures tied to matter react strongly. The Weyl curvature barely responds, as befits the free part of the field.
arxiv-2512-24494:
Bai-Ling Wang writes a memorial review for two giants of mathematical physics. Rodney Baxter and Chen-Ning Yang both died in 2025. Yang introduced non-abelian gauge theory. He also found the consistency conditions behind the Yang-Baxter equation. Baxter turned those conditions into a systematic theory of exact solvability. Statistical mechanics and quantum integrable systems were transformed.

The article traces both legacies as one story. Gauge theory's Yang-Mills formulation comes first. Its mass obstruction and its resolution through symmetry breaking follow. Instantons, monopoles, and Donaldson-Floer theory grow from that frame. The Yang-Baxter line runs in parallel. Factorized scattering leads to solvable lattice models, quantum groups, and Chern-Simons theory. Wang presents the two as one coherence principle. Local consistency generates global structure in both.
arxiv-2512-24694:
Reza Jahani, Md Farhamdur Reza, Richeng Jin, and Huaiyu Dai examine how user movement can rescue decentralized federated learning in sparse wireless networks. In that setting, devices train a shared model without a central server, but weak links and varied local data hurt results. Moving users can act as relays and bridges between groups.

Convergence analysis shows even random movement by a fraction of users can improve information flow and learning. A data-driven approach builds on that finding. Readers get theoretical and practical reasons to treat mobility as a resource, not a nuisance, when designing next-generation decentralized learning systems.
arxiv-2512-24794:
Andrew Tinits and Stephen Mann improve Noise2Noise training for Monte Carlo image denoising, a method that learns from pairs of noisy images without clean targets. Nonlinear steps applied to noisy targets bias the result, because a nonlinear function changes the expected value away from the clean image. That bias limits preprocessing choices that renderers commonly need.

Certain nonlinear functions can be handled so the bias is corrected, widening what training pipelines may use. Readers in graphics get more efficient denoiser training for Monte Carlo rendering, where clean reference images are costly. The gain is practical: realistic preprocessing no longer has to be avoided during learning.
arxiv-2601-00094:
Ali Dasdan studies a hard problem from graph theory: finding the longest simple cycle in a directed graph, where no point is visited twice. Exact solutions are too slow in general, yet the problem matters for biology, scheduling, and network study. His 2026 paper uses average weights of cycles, values that can be computed fast, to bound and estimate the best cycle.

One computation yields both strict bounds and simple estimates based on averages of those cycle means. Tests on standard circuit benchmarks give mixed news. The strict lower bounds fall far below the true values. The estimates do much better, with the better average depending on whether weights are even or skewed.
arxiv-2601-00294:
Bo-Ting Chen, Yu-Ping Wang, and Biao Lian link two rival ways to detect a shattered quantum state space. Some quantum models split into huge numbers of sealed sectors. Dynamics inside one sector never reach the others. That split is called Hilbert space fragmentation. Two recent methods claim to find the true split. They do not always agree with each other.

One method reads the commutant algebra of the model. The other factors an integer characteristic polynomial. The authors prove a comparison theorem for rational models. When the algebra center has only rational eigenvalues, one split must refine the other. Most known fragmented models meet that test. The team checks the theorem across those cases. A few models still split differently by method. Those cases mark where a unified definition is missing. The bridge narrows a basic conceptual gap.
arxiv-2601-00394:
Vadim Bernshteyn, Nicholas S Conroy, and two hundred sixty-four other co-authors, including the Event Horizon Telescope Collaboration, study the glowing ring around the black hole M87 star. Telescope images show the ring is brighter on one side than the other. Their 2026 paper asks what that uneven brightness can reveal about how fast the black hole spins.

Simulations of gas falling toward the black hole predict that the brightness pattern should wander as the plasma churns. The team compares three rounds of real observations with simulations run at many spin values. For strongly magnetized models, the data mildly disfavor very slow spin. That fits a model in which spin powers the black hole's jet. The authors also show how future observations could sharpen the spin estimate.
arxiv-2601-00894:
Gihyeon Sim is the sole author of a 2026 paper on when AI code models should stop and think harder. Most models spend the same effort on every input, easy or hard. Sim's method, PonderTTT, lets a model take extra training steps at test time, but only when they seem worth it. The trigger is the model's own rebuild error: how poorly it can rebuild its input.

The trigger needs no trained judge and no labels. One threshold is set on plain data, then nudged over time to hold a steady trigger rate. Tests used GPT-2 models of several sizes on a big code corpus. The gate won back more than four-fifths of the gain an all-knowing gate would get. It cut loss most on code written in new languages. The work shows a cheap way to spend compute where it pays.
arxiv-2601-00994:
Michael Bao is the sole author of a 2026 paper that builds a fake social network to study how AI agents persuade. The stage, called ElecTwit, mimics a platform like Twitter during an election. Past studies of persuasion used narrow games, which miss real-world mess. Bao's agents post, reply, and campaign in a richer social flow.

Most models tested used all twenty-five tricks in his catalogue. That spread is wider than past work had reported. Models differed a lot in which tricks they favoured, and in how much they persuaded. Two odd patterns stood out. Some messages used a kernel of truth, a true scrap bent to mislead. In other runs, agents grew fixed on ink, all demanding written proof at once. The study gives a test bed for persuasive AI in near-real settings. It aims to spot risks before such agents meet real voters.
arxiv-2601-01194:
Ercetin and Chraiti tackle decoding for wireless links that pass through several relays at very high frequencies. Each relay that boosts and forwards a signal also forwards noise, so quality drops hop by hop. Normal best decoding is hard when the signal shape is unknown and relays lack full channel data.

The pair recast the relay chain as a cleaning process much like those used in image generation models. They prove only the final signal quality matters, not how noise was split across hops. A receiver-side cleaner built on that result lowers error rates in tests, mainly at mid-level signal strength and with larger signal sets.
arxiv-2601-01694:
When a material with a charge-density wave, a regular pattern of electron density, is suddenly disturbed, its order rings and fades in ways that echo superconductors. Lingyu Yang, Ho Jang, Sankha Subhra Bakshi, Yang Yang, and Gia-Wei Chern describe that ringing in the Holstein model, where electrons couple to lattice vibrations, using a pseudospin picture borrowed from magnetism.

Their simulations on a square lattice show three regimes after a quench: locked oscillations, damped ringing, and slow overdamped settling. Unlike purely electronic systems, the Holstein model's oscillations never fully die, because the lattice keeps feeding energy back. The authors trace the survivors to a disturbed electron distribution, sharpening the contrast between lattice-driven and electronic phase dynamics.
arxiv-2601-01794:
Gravitational waves from two compact objects on eccentric orbits carry extra structure from the tides each body raises on the other. Quentin Henry computes that structure within the post-Newtonian approximation, an expansion in orbital slowness, pushing the tidal part to the relative two-and-a-half order for binaries on quasi-elliptic paths.

Henry starts from the dynamics of a companion paper. He derives the radiated energy and angular momentum. Then he derives the slow evolution of the orbital elements. The resulting equations are solved numerically for several systems. Eccentric corrections to the tides shift the wave phase enough that detectors might notice in parts of the source population. Waveform amplitudes are given mode by mode, expanded to high order in eccentricity, with full results supplied in an accompanying file.
arxiv-2601-01994:
Semiconducting barrier discharges spread uniform ionization waves across a surface in open air, and light shone on them can change their behavior. Ayah Soundous Taihi and David Pai synchronize nanosecond light pulses, from green to near-infrared, with the discharge and watch the plasma respond with fast imaging, spectroscopy, and electrical measurements.

Light-born carriers in the silicon enhanced plasma emission. They also raised the reduced electric field. The electrical energy did not change. Thresholds and strength both depended on wavelength. The explanation follows the light's absorption length. Carriers born in the interface depletion region separate well. They amplify by impact ionization. Deeper carriers, by contrast, are wasted. Silicon's optoelectronics thus reach up through the surface to steer a plasma.
arxiv-2601-02094:
Comparing forecasting networks is usually reduced to error scores, with interpretability tricks tied to each architecture. Krupakar Hans and V. A. Kandappan introduce Horizon Activation Mapping, a visualization inspired by image heatmaps that instead shows which stretches of the forecast horizon drive a model's gradients, working across model families.

Causal and anti-causal versions average gradient norms over subseries. The authors study how the pictures change. Batch size, early stopping, and data splits all matter. Architecture and dropout matter too. Seven model families, from MLP-based designs to attention, state-space, and diffusion forecasters, were mapped on a standard electricity transformer dataset. The plots support fine-grained choices about models and validation sets. Several known behaviors of specific architectures show up as visible trends. Theory and picture agree.
arxiv-2601-02194:
How a holomorphic function behaves near the boundary of its disk is classical analysis. The approach may be radial or along tangential paths. The topic has modern operator-theoretic depth. Shuaibing Luo and Bartosz Malman work in de Branges-Rovnyak spaces. These are Hilbert spaces of analytic functions tied to a bounded analytic symbol. Sarason's version of the Carathéodory-Julia theorem links boundary behavior to angular derivatives there.

The authors extend recent results on model spaces. The extensions reach these H(b) spaces and higher-order derivatives. Approach regions more general than the standard non-tangential ones are allowed. A new self-contained proof carries the argument. A sharpness limit is shown too. In the classical theorem, the non-tangential region cannot be replaced by any essentially larger one. The classical statement is already best possible in that respect.
arxiv-2601-02294:
Aditya Barman and four co authors, including Jan M. L. Martin, refine how chemists compute the total atomization energy of a molecule, the sum of all its bond energies. Very accurate methods build the answer from many correction layers. The question here is whether two layers, correlation from inner shells and higher order correlation beyond the standard CCSD(T) method, simply add up or interact.

They find the two layers do interact, most strongly when several second row atoms sit next to each other, and in systems with strong static correlation. Recomputing molecular shapes with the inner shell layer included raises energies across the board. From the results they propose a first W5 theory protocol and give revised reference energies for several key molecules, matching the active thermochemical tables well.
arxiv-2601-02394:
Yuan-Jie Chen proposes hydrodynamic whispering, a way for underwater robot swarms to communicate silently over short distances using water pressure signals instead of sound or radio. The goal is covert coordination, where a message should reach nearby swarm members and no one else. The transmitter is modeled in potential flow theory as an oscillating dipole source.

Its pressure field fades very fast with distance, forming a small secure bubble that is hard for outsiders to intercept. The receiver uses a conformal array of twenty four sensors inspired by the lateral line organ of fish. With phase shift keying adapted to slow mechanical actuators and a joint space time processing method to fight noise. In simulation the array gains about fourteen decibels and keeps the bit error rate near zero inside its effective range.
arxiv-2601-02494:
Carlos Jurado and a large team investigate why the chemical makeup of stars varies around the Milky Way's disk at a given distance from the center. Recent studies found coherent patterns in metal content around the disk, and Gaia data separately revealed ridge like features in stellar velocities. The authors ask whether the chemical patterns and the velocity ridges share one dynamical origin.

In Gaia DR3 disk stars, metal variations line up with the kinematic ridges, which points to a shared cause. Test particle simulations of a Milky Way like galaxy then test three suspects, transient spiral arms, the central bar, and a passing dwarf galaxy like Sagittarius. Bar and spiral arm interactions consistently reproduce both the chemical and kinematic features and their alignment, while the dwarf encounter does not match as well.
arxiv-2601-02594:
Jyothi Rikhab Chand and Mathews Jacob speed up energy based models for restoring degraded images. A class of models whose clear energy landscape and composable structure suit inverse problems, but which have been slow to train and sample from. Their shortcut is distillation. A pre trained diffusion model transfers its strengths into a multiscale energy based model, which then samples efficiently while keeping the interpretability of an energy function.

On top of the distilled model they build an annealed Langevin sampling method for posterior inference. It can produce the most probable restoration, the average restoration that minimizes squared error, and uncertainty estimates, all within one framework. Unlike diffusion approaches that need complex guidance machinery for latent variables, the energy based formulation handles the posterior directly. The result narrows the speed gap that kept energy models out of practical imaging.
arxiv-2601-02694:
Eilaf MA Babai, Aalaa MA Babai, and Koji Okamura run a head to head evaluation of deep learning forecasters for predicting network traffic, a core task for automating network management. Traffic is a hard time series, spiky and variable across networks and time scales, and the field offers everything from elaborate transformer models to surprisingly strong simple linear ones. The practical question is which model a network operator should actually deploy.

Twelve advanced forecasting models, transformer based and traditional deep learning alike, are tested against three statistical baselines on four real traffic data sets, across several time scales and forecast horizons. Accuracy is only part of the scorecard. Robustness to anomalies, tolerance of gaps in the data, and the effect of external factors are assessed as well, so the study reads as deployment guidance rather than a single leaderboard.
arxiv-2601-03294:
Kaibo Huang and seven co-authors watermark the behavior of AI agents, not just their words. As agents plan and carry out multi-step tasks on their own, owners need ways to prove provenance and protect ideas. Content watermarking can tag generated text. But it cannot identify the high-level planning choices, such as which tools and subgoals an agent picks, that actually govern execution.

Their framework, AgentMark, embeds multi-bit identifiers into planning decisions while keeping the agent useful. It draws out an explicit behavior distribution from the agent. It then applies distribution-preserving conditional sampling, so decisions carry the mark without drifting in their statistics. The scheme works even through black-box APIs and can combine with ordinary content watermarking. Experiments span embodied, tool-use, and social environments.
arxiv-2601-03394:
Aditi Singh and five co-authors computationally design organic dyes for dye-sensitized solar cells, tuning them by swapping in heteroatoms. Predicting such dyes is tricky because their key excitations involve long-range charge transfer, which cheap methods describe poorly, while accurate methods are too slow for broad screening. The team uses a range-separated hybrid functional with time-dependent density functional theory, plus a simplified, physically motivated tuning protocol that keeps the calculations fast and reliable.

They build a library of twenty-seven prototypical dyes, with one, two, or three nitrogen, oxygen, or boron atoms worked into a carbazole-based donor-pi-acceptor design. Charge-transfer excitation energies and frontier orbital alignment, the properties that govern light absorption and electron injection into the cell, are analyzed across the library. The work shows how targeted doping steers those frontier orbitals.
arxiv-2601-03494:
Kaiyuan Cao and four co-authors show how to steer dynamical quantum phase transitions, sudden changes that appear as a quantum system evolves in time. Their tool is double-mode squeezing, a way of preparing the starting state of an XY chain, a standard model of interacting quantum spins. Whether squeezing helps depends on the system's symmetry and settings, they find.

When squeezing breaks particle-hole symmetry, transitions become highly tunable: they can be created inside one phase or suppressed. When symmetry is kept and squeezing reaches a special strength, a universal pattern appears for any quench path. All Fisher zeros line up on the real-time axis and entanglement between paired modes maxes out. The work turns state preparation into a control knob for quantum dynamics.
arxiv-2601-03594:
Zejian Chen and five co-authors survey jailbreak attacks on large language and vision-language models, plus the defenses against them. A jailbreak tricks a model into ignoring its safety rules. The authors argue these weaknesses are structural, growing out of incomplete training data, ambiguous language, and the uncertainty built into generation itself. They also separate jailbreaks from hallucinations by intent and trigger.

The survey organizes the field along three axes: attacks, defenses, and evaluation. Attacks range from template tricks and encoding games to adversarial training and image-level perturbations. Defenses include prompt obfuscation, output screening, and alignment work inside the model. Evaluation uses measures like attack success rate and toxicity scores. A shared map helps defenders compare claims and spot untested ground.
arxiv-2601-03794:
Gabin Taibi and Joerg Osterrieder propose an algorithmic framework for systematic literature reviews, the careful surveys scholars use to summarize a field. Done by hand, reviews are slow and their study selection is hard to reproduce or audit. Their method combines natural language processing, grouping algorithms, and clarity tools to automate and structure how papers are picked and studied.

They demonstrate the framework on financial narratives, an emerging topic about how shared stories of economic events move markets and asset prices, drawing on the Scopus database. The review found real progress in modeling such narratives with language techniques, but also fragmentation, with the concept often cut down to mere sentiment. A repeatable review pipeline could help many fields keep up with publication growth without lowering standards.
arxiv-2601-03894:
Iñigo Sáez-Casares and six co-authors test whether convolutional neural networks can read cosmological parameters directly from galaxy cluster surveys. Field-level learning could bypass traditional summary statistics, but only if simulated training sets are both realistic and huge. The team uses galaxy clusters as tracers of large-scale structure and a fast approximate gravity code to generate training data.

They produced nearly thirty-three thousand mock X-ray cluster catalogs, assigning X-ray luminosities to dark matter halos through an empirical mass-luminosity relation with realistic scatter. A three-dimensional convolutional network then learned to predict cosmological parameters from the cluster density field. The study probes how far this pipeline can be trusted. If it holds up, cluster surveys could yield tighter constraints on the universe's makeup with less analytic machinery.
arxiv-2601-04394:
Sharanya Dasgupta and three co-authors treat two of language models' worst habits as one disease in a 2026 arXiv paper. Hallucinated falsehoods and unsafe outputs, they argue, both grow from drift in the model's internal activation patterns. A misalignment in the space where meaning is represented, rather than from two distinct failures needing two distinct cures.

Their system, ARREST, trains an external network to watch those fluctuations and step in selectively, steering drifted features back. Correcting falsehoods into truthful answers and unsafe continuations into refusals, soft or hard as the case demands — without retraining the model itself. In their tests the regulator not only corrected misalignment but produced softer, more graded refusals than models aligned by the standard reinforcement approach, thanks to adversarial training. The code is released publicly.
arxiv-2601-04494:
Julian Knodt and Seung-Hwan Baek bend grids without ever folding them, in a 2026 arXiv paper. A uniform grid wastes resolution where detail is sparse and starves where detail is dense, but deforming one adaptively is hard to do without inverting cells. Their method deforms the grid while guaranteeing local injectivity, so space is compressed where it can be and stretched where it must, with no foldovers.

The trick is to treat grid vertices as differential elements and optimize those, which proves smoother than moving coordinates directly. A vertex colouring splits the coupled system into independent sets that can be optimized concurrently, with Adam among the usable optimizers. injectivity stays easy to check because each vertex's valid region is fixed by its neighbours' colour class. The method extends to UV meshes with convex boundaries and is demonstrated on isosurface extraction for inverse rendering, image compaction, and mesh parameterization.
arxiv-2601-04594:
Zheyu Wu and ten co-authors report direct evidence that an exotic superconductor refuses to stay inside its assigned borders, in a 2026 arXiv paper. The heavy-fermion compound UTe2 hosts several superconducting phases in high magnetic fields. one of them, called SC3, was suspected of spilling beyond the boundary of the spin-polarized state where it was thought to live. Earlier evidence was indirect and capped at lower fields.

Measuring a very clean crystal in fields up to forty-five tesla, with the field rotated in a new plane. The team watches resistance vanish at low temperatures at field strengths below the metamagnetic transition measured when warmer. Superconductivity persisting outside the polarized state it supposedly required. The observation fits a scenario in which SC3's pairing is fed by quantum critical fluctuations rather than by the polarized state itself, sharpening the question of what glues its Cooper pairs.
arxiv-2601-04694:
Zhilun Zhou and seven co-authors design LLM multi-agent systems to survive their own members failing, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Fleets of cooperating agents now solve hard tasks, but they run scattered across devices and environments where agents crash or get perturbed. Prior work mostly plays defence after an attack; this team instead asks what makes a system resilient by construction, and finds two levers matter: the communication topology and each agent's prompt.

ResMAS builds resilience in two stages. First, a reward model learned to predict a system's resilience score trains a topology generator, via reinforcement learning, that designs robust communication graphs for the task at hand. Second, a topology-aware prompt optimization refines each agent's instructions according to its connections and interactions. Experiments across tasks show substantially better survival under varied constraints, and the framework transfers to new tasks and new models.
arxiv-2601-05094:
How dark a black material truly is depends on the angle of light, not just its look under soft lighting. Jiri Filip and Radomir Vavra measure that behaviour in a 2026 paper. Black materials matter for image registration, camera calibration, stray light suppression, and visual design. Ultra-black coatings attenuate light exceptionally but are costly and mechanically fragile, motivating a search for robust, accessible alternatives that still perform.

Using a gonimetric measurement system, the authors capture how isotropic samples reflect and scatter light across viewing and lighting geometries. Their analysis compares materials that appear equally dark head-on but diverge at grazing angles. Reliable reflectance data helps engineers choose black coatings for instruments where a stray reflection can ruin a measurement.
arxiv-2601-05294:
Zhian Jia, Kavan Modi, and Dagomir Kaszlikowski stretch a tool for odd chance rules into the realm of time in a 2026 paper. The tool is the Kirkwood-Dirac spread, a way to grade a quantum state that can take values no plain chance rule would allow. Their aim is time: states that span more than one time, not just more than one place. Past work had built a host of such time-state frames, but how the frames link, and where they part, stayed murky.

The team set out left, right, and twin forms of the time spread, for paths with more than one time step. They also give ways to read the forms off a real set-up, bit by bit. One clear frame for time and space at once helps labs weigh tests on quantum paths that run through time, from chats to stores.
arxiv-2601-05394:
Yuang Shi and 3 co-authors present a 2026 method for shrinking 3D Gaussian Splatting models, which store scenes as many small fuzzy blobs for realistic rendering. Their system sorts those blobs by role. Some mark sharp edges and outlines, while others fill smooth, flat areas.

Inside, a clustering step groups blobs by density and then refines the groups by quality, with no need for outside line drawings. The outline group can be sent first during streaming, so a scene skeleton appears before fine detail arrives. Tests on indoor and outdoor scenes report clearer images at the same file size, and indoor scenes kept good quality at a tiny fraction of the original size.
arxiv-2601-05594:
Shvetaank Tripathi and Prashant Shukla present, in a 2026 paper, exact formulas for the energy distributions of cosmogenic particles reaching Earth. These particles begin as cosmic rays striking the atmosphere, creating secondaries such as muons and neutrinos. A compact formula with physically meaningful parameters helps compare data across sites and altitudes.

The authors assume a modified power law with terms for energy loss, decay, and a high-energy source contribution. They parametrize primary proton and helium momentum, plus muon behavior including decay. A zenith-angle distribution follows analytically from the energy index. The same form fits modeled atmospheric muon and electron-neutrino distributions at various sites, giving one description for many particle types. One formula thus covers many kinds of particles and many places on Earth.
arxiv-2601-05694:
Aifei Zhang and 13 co-authors measure quantized heat flow in a 2026 paper on the Hofstadter butterfly. That name denotes a fractal energy spectrum that appears when electrons on a lattice face a strong magnetic field. Its special ground states, called Chern insulators, should show electrical and thermal conductance fixed by topological invariants. That thermal quantization had not previously been tested.

Working with a graphene and boron nitride moire superlattice, the team probed heat transport across the butterfly's states. Quantized heat flow, set uniquely by the topological invariant, appeared in quantum Hall states, Chern insulators, and even interaction-driven symmetry-broken versions. The result establishes that heat quantization is universal and tightly linked to topology in this system. Heat here flows in fixed steps, set by the state's basic shape and not by small details of the sample.
arxiv-2601-05794:
Eilam Cohen and 3 co-authors compare in 2026 two ways of making language models simplify text: careful prompting versus fine-tuning.
