The paper's approach uses flow as an intermediate model while adding tools that preserve contact motion and resist overfitting to scene views. The policy transfers to scenarios seen only in human demonstrations, rather than merely replaying robot training tasks. The work lowers the data price of teaching robots new skills from the videos people already produce.
arxiv-2602-10794:
Benjy Friedmann and Nadav Dym replace edge denoising with point transport for the traveling salesman problem in a 2026 paper. Neural combinatorial tuning has leaned on spread models that generate a quadratic edge heatmap stochastically. Their system, CycFlow, learns an instance-conditioned vector field that transports input coordinates continuously to a canonical circular arrangement.

The optimal tour then emerges from that compact model by angular sorting, bypassing the quadratic bottleneck of edge scoring in favor of linear coordinate motion. Data-dependent flow matching trains the transport. The paper reports solving speeds up to three orders of magnitude faster than leading spread baselines. Optimality gaps stay competitive, marking a paradigm shift from generating edges to moving points.
arxiv-2602-10894:
Kazuki Ota and three co-authors revisit regularized policy tuning for board games in a 2026 paper. Two-player games have long benchmarked reward-based learning. The paper analyzes reverse Kullback-Leibler regularization combined with entropy regularization in two-player zero-sum settings, theoretically and empirically.

The authors study steadiness of the policy update rule in normal-form games and finite-length games. They provide novel settling promises verified through number tests on mock games. From the regularized tuning they derive a useful model-free recipe, checked for training speed across five board games. The work connects game-theoretic steadiness to a recipe that learns efficiently without a model.
arxiv-2602-11094:
Black hole jets rank among the most violent sights in space. Andre L. B. Ribeiro and Nathalia M. N. da Rocha survey how next-making observatories may finally pin down how jets launch, narrow, and shed energy. Accretion, relativistic magnetism, and galaxy-scale feedback all meet in these flows.

They look ahead to the Event Horizon Telescope, the Cherenkov Telescope Array, the Rubin Observatory, and the Whole Earth Blazar Telescope. Each adds a other lens: sharp images, time-domain surveys, and multi-wavelength coverage. Theory must keep pace, through magnetically arrested disks, plasma microphysics, and relativistic simulations. The authors expect the coming decade to reshape jet physics.
arxiv-2602-11594:
Many real optimization problems are both nonconvex and nonsmooth, mixing rough surfaces with sharp corners and even functions that take infinite values. Welington de Oliveira and one co-author build a unified framework that pairs global approximations with locally built models to tackle such composite problems. They show that near-stationary points of the approximating problems converge to true stationary points under suitable conditions.

From that theory they derive practical algorithms based on tractable convex master programs built from local models, organized as a double loop that sharpens global approximations while adapting local ones. The approach stays flexible and implementable across a wide class of problems. Beyond the algorithms themselves, the framework lays groundwork for new methods in composite optimization.
arxiv-2602-11794:
Learning how linear random partial differential equations act from data is hard when the driving noise and starting states are hidden. Most deep learning methods assume access to one or the other. Others use fixed stand-ins that miss true randomness. Sebastian Zeng and two co-authors propose a structured latent-variable setup that needs only observed outcomes to learn random-driven motion.

A spectral Galerkin projection plus a truncated Wiener chaos expansion separates fixed evolution from random forcing in a principled way. That step turns the huge system into a finite system of plain change equations for latent temporal motion. Latent motion and forcing are inferred jointly through variational fitting, getting random structure back without seeing or faking noise during training. Tests on made-up data show state-of-the-art performance under comparable assumptions.
arxiv-2602-11994:
Surface brightness-colour relations let researchers turn Cepheid pulses into distances, but metal effects must be pinned down. Bailleul and fourteen co-authors derive such laws for classical Cepheids in the Milky Way and the Magellanic Clouds from Gaia photometry, quantifying the metallicity effect. They select the best Gaia brightness data and parallaxes, compile period-radius laws from the literature, and add a new law from direct imaging data.

Joining Cepheid radii with ranges from Gaia distance measures and paired stars, they derive surface brightness and colour for about 1,700 Cepheids. Three laws, one per galaxy system, clearly show metal dependence in the Gaia-based relations. The authors also derive relations linking slopes, zero points, and metallicity across the three systems, yielding tools for the inverse Baade-Wesselink method on Gaia-observed Cepheids.
arxiv-2602-12494:
Iterative root-finding methods generate error terms whose structure can reveal how the method behaves near roots. Mario DeFranco works alone here, studying recurrence relations arising from NRS(2) applied to a cubic polynomial. The paper proves that leading coefficients of the error terms, for a starting point at minus a1 over a2 in both coordinates, are positive-coefficient rational functions in the zeros of the polynomial.

Those terms are expressed as a sum over combinatorial objects the author calls radius-value trees. The result gives a concrete combinatorial picture of error growth for this method on cubics, linking algebraic coefficients to tree-like structures. Readers get a precise, if narrow, advance: error terms are not arbitrary, but positive rational functions in the roots, organised by radius-value trees.
arxiv-2602-12594:
The Cabibbo-favoured decay of Lambda_c plus to neutron, anti-K0, and pion plus is a window on low-energy baryon physics. Meng-Yuan Li led this work with four co-authors, addressing a current clash. LHCb and Belle analyses suggest the proton-K minus isospin-0 part dominates in Lambda_c plus to proton, K minus, pion plus.

BESIII, by contrast, hints at significant isospin-0 and isospin-1 parts in the neutron anti-K0 system. Found branching fraction exceeds SU(3) symmetry forecasts by a factor of 3 to 4, signalling strong low-lying resonance parts. In a coupled-channel chiral unitary approach, N(1535) and Lambda(1670) are dynamically generated. Calculations show a narrow peak from N(1535) in the pion-plus neutron spectrum and a distinct dip from Lambda(1670) in the anti-K0 neutron spectrum. That dip supports a molecular reading of Lambda(1670). Future measurements are encouraged.
arxiv-2602-12694:
Elite racing shoes rely on feather-light foams that cushion each stride and return energy, yet how those foams actually behave has been hard to pin down. Jeremy McCulloch and two co-authors test two ultra-low-density foams used in top racing shoes, pulling, squeezing, and shearing them in the lab. Both foams stretch and squeeze very differently, barely bulge sideways, and lose little energy per cycle, which points to efficient energy return.

The foams match closely in squeeze stiffness, near 268 and 299 kilopascals, but one is almost twice as stiff in shear, giving better side-to-side stability at similar bounce, 83% versus 89%. Fed into neural models paired with sparse regression, the data yield short, readable equations that fit the tests almost exactly. Those models can feed shoe and gait simulations to study speed and injury risk for individual runners.
arxiv-2602-12994:
Taylor-Couette flow, fluid sheared between rotating cylinders, can settle into some long-lived patterns at the same speed, a puzzle for theory and experiment. Marvin Kriening and five co-authors simulate the flow with realistic no-slip walls at all surfaces, including top and bottom lids, rather than convenient periodic boundaries. Realistic end walls change the motion substantially.

Extending the angular-momentum-flux system to include axial transport lifts agreement with the Eckhardt-Grossmann-Lohse model markedly. Scanning Reynolds number and roll count reveals multiple states with other roll numbers at identical speeds, producing pronounced hysteresis. As speed rises, the flow moves from Taylor vortices through wavy and turbulent wavy states to axisymmetric turbulent vortices. Modal energy budgets spot the transition mechanisms and how each state's momentum flux depends on control settings.
arxiv-2602-13094:
Quantum computing may soon help forecast financial time series, and small quantum reservoirs are a promising near-term design. Wendy Otieno and four co-authors build a quantum reservoir computing system using at most six interacting qubits for non-linear forecasting. They predict daily closing trading volumes for 20 quantum-sector companies from April 2020 to April 2025, plus minute-level volumes outside market hours on July 7, 2025.

Optimal reservoir settings yield trend sorting closeness above 86%. The model is platform-agnostic, realisable on superconducting circuits, trapped ions, and other qubit implementations. The results showcase small quantum reservoirs handling complex time links in financial data, suggesting real forecasting uses on near-term quantum hardware, even before large fault-tolerant machines arrive.
arxiv-2602-13394:
A companion study to the ARCHITECTS simulations asks what telescopes would actually see. Three zoom-in runs of the same galaxy, differing only in subgrid feedback recipe, are compared through quasar absorption sightlines for hydrogen and three metal ions, each tracing different gas phases. Column densities and covering fractions emerge as sharp diagnostics, since the ions differ in spatial pattern and origin.

All runs roughly bracket observed column densities, but direct comparison is limited by scarce detections and wide scatter. Covering fractions of weak absorbers constrain best, and here every model misses hydrogen and magnesium fractions, while delayed cooling overproduces oxygen and mechanical feedback alone matches carbon well. Maxime Rey leads the work with five co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13494:
Integer linear programs model countless discrete optimization problems, yet they are NP-hard and hard to speed up quantumly, since classical methods for many-constraint cases are global while quantum speedups exploit local structure. This paper bridges the gap through Gomory's group relaxation, which drops nonnegativity on variables positive in the linear programming optimum while keeping integrality. A competitive feasibility-preserving classical local search is built for the relaxation, plus a quantum algorithm with super-quadratic speedup under reasonable conditions.

When a nondegeneracy condition stronger than linear programming nondegeneracy holds, the approach recovers the exact integer optimum. Otherwise it tightens bounds on the optimum and can improve branch-and-cut by shrinking the integrality gap, as numerical tests confirm. Brandon Augustino leads the work with seven co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13694:
Gravity from Entropy changes the vacuum field equations. This paper derives and solves them for static sphere-shaped symmetric black holes. The classical Schwarzschild geometry gains small corrections scaling as the inverse fourth power of radius. The framework remains in line with current strong-field astrophysical observations. Higher-order geometric stresses drive a matching mass-evolution profile for dynamical solutions.

In the large-mass limit, the theory predicts a constant background evaporation rate, an inherent entropic leakage of the vacuum. At intermediate scales it replicates the standard Hawking radiation mass-loss law, with mass loss proportional to the inverse square of mass, through a purely classical response of the modified background. Udaykrishna Thattarampilly leads the work with two co-authors.
arxiv-2602-14294:
Scarlet Elgueta and nine co-authors select a 2026 arXiv set of infrared atomic lines for stellar abundance work. New infrared spectrographs demand reliable line lists, yet infrared abundance work faces larger uncertainties than optical work, driven by atmospheric models and atomic data quality. The paper delivers a homogeneous, reproducible line set in the Y, J, and H bands.

The lines rest solely on laboratory atomic data, tested against CRIRES spectra of six Gaia FGK benchmark stars spanning wide temperature, gravity, and composition ranges. Synthetic spectra from benchmark parameters were compared with observations, judging each transition on depth, saturation, blending purity, and profile agreement. The resulting robust lines should sharpen infrared abundance determinations across stellar types.
arxiv-2602-14694:
Quantum chips drift when stray links and loss creep in, so their idle state must be mapped. Rune Thinggaard Birke, with seventeen co-authors, tests shadow-based Lindblad mapping on a transmon chip. Full mapping grows fast with qubit count and soon turns too big.

Shadow Lindblad tomography reuses random test setups to get the same Lindblad numbers with far fewer runs. On one- and three-qubit parts, it matched full mapping within error bars. The team checked the local rules behind the speed-up in real hardware. The method opens a workable path to map larger idle chips.
arxiv-2602-14894:
Emile Emery, Joseph Le Bihan, and Jose Halloy connect electrical grid length and material stock to population density, comparing a French-calibrated scaling against thirty-five electrified countries. Their model samples substation locations through a nonlinear relation with population density, then builds a proxy network with the Kruskal algorithm.

The streamlined approach yields a local-scale proxy grid and reasonable national-scale totals for network length, revealing a population-spread connection that persists at large scales. Planners gain a light model linking where people live to how much grid they need. Infrastructure material becomes a function of settlement pattern.
arxiv-2602-14994:
Khan and colleagues tackle actual causation in hybrid domains, where actions cause both discrete jumps and continuous change. Formal accounts of cause go back to Aristotle, but most recent work treats discrete change alone, leaving continuous change little studied. The team works in hybrid temporal situation calculus, a framework that joins both kinds of change in one action theory.

They propose two definitions of primary cause in that framework. One is foundational in character. The other defines cause through contributions, checked from a counterfactual angle with a modified but-for test. The paper proves the two definitions equivalent and shows they carry properties that match intuition about what causation should mean.
arxiv-2602-15194:
Howell and He extend resolvent analysis to periodic dynamical systems with a time-spectral operator. Standard analysis finds the most boosted input-output shapes in flows from a steady base state. Extending it to periodic base flows brings hurdles from quasi-periodic effects and costly linear fits around a changing base flow. The new method uses the time-spectral method and Fourier collocation, working directly in the time domain.

Rather than mapping between truncated Fourier coefficients, it maps forcing and response profiles on a discrete time grid. That enables direct Jacobian checks at grid points, with no Fourier numbers needed for the base flow. The method achieves spectral convergence and fits current lab computing tools. Tests cover the forced Mathieu oscillator, the van der Pol system, and the complex Ginzburg-Landau equation. The method accurately predicts maximum energy boost and optimal response mode under optimal quasi-periodic forcing.
arxiv-2602-15294:
Du and colleagues present Experiment Automation Agents, a vision-language-model-driven agent system running complex lab microscopy jobs. The system joins multi-mode thinking, tool-boosted action, and added long-term recall to support self-run steps and hands-on user-guided readings. Built on a loose task-manager design, it allows jobs from fully agent-driven work to logic-defined scripts holding local LLM asks.

It offers a modern toolkit with two-way fit for Model Context Protocol, allowing device tools to be used or served across apps. The team shows it at an imaging beamline at the Advanced Photon Source, including auto zone plate focus, natural language-described feature search, and hands-on data capture. These results show how vision-capable agents can speed beamline work, reduce daily burden, and lower the skill wall for users.
arxiv-2602-15394:
Chen and colleagues study well-posedness of the periodic edge case for the steady gas even-heat Navier-Stokes system under the van der Waals rule. The main hurdle is the slope of the pressure, which sparks liquid-vapor shifts and leads to real wobbles and oneness.

A shift happens when the mean set size lies in the gas-liquid mix zone set by Maxwell. Adding thickness, they build a near system. When the mean sits in the Maxwell zone, the answer settles, as thickness goes to zero, to balance forms given by Maxwell's build, with the edge closing to a break. If the mean lies outside this zone, the final answer stays out, so no shift happens. This shows pressure slope, with the mean in the Maxwell zone, can seed shifts. The model offers a smoothed setup for telling shifts and a definition of allowed answers.
arxiv-2602-15494:
Giordano and Blossey look at random processes that stretch geometric Brownian motion, a workhorse model in physics and finance. The focus falls on cases where the usual long-run measure, the fix point of the stationary Fokker-Planck equation, may not exist at all. Whether it exists turns on the shape of the drift and diffusion terms, and also on the scheme used to step the process in discrete time.

The authors draw drive from models of turbulence, where geometric Brownian motion has long served as a classic case. Where the standard measure fails, they turn to infinite ergodicity, a recent idea from statistical physics for drift-diffusion processes. The paper is a heuristic tour of that idea, and it will interest readers who work with long-run laws for noisy systems.
arxiv-2602-15694:
Silveira and colleagues compute fragmentation functions for charm and strange mesons, describing how a quark hadronises with final-state hadrons carrying fractions of its initial momentum. The cascade they follow runs through pions and kaons plus charmed D and D_s mesons, and it starts with one quark turning into one meson. They get that first step from the relevant cut diagram, using Bethe-Salpeter wave functions built to respect Poincaré covariance together with quark propagators.

From there they derive twenty-five coupled jet equations for the cascade of emitted mesons. Solving those equations yields full fragmentation functions that give a consistent picture across light and heavy sectors. The work offers a unified account of quark fragmentation from light pions and kaons through to charmed mesons.
arxiv-2602-16194:
Permanent citizens assemblies are ongoing deliberative bodies of randomly selected citizens, organized into panels that rotate over time. Yusuf Hakan Kalayci and Evi Micha formalize temporal sortition for such bodies. Unlike one-off panels, which capture a single snapshot, permanent bodies let different groups gain a voice across successive panels. Small groups that may not merit a seat in every panel can still gain a voice across a sequence.

The framework demands proportional voice both within each panel and across the panel sequence. Building on Ebadian and Micha, the authors place the population in a metric space and seek both proportional voice and individual fairness, meaning each person has an equal chance of selection. They extend representation to time by requiring every initial segment of the sequence, viewed cumulatively, to reflect population structure. Algorithms give varying pledges for both goals, within panels and across sequences, while preserving fairness over time.
arxiv-2602-16594:
Abhishek Goudar and Angela Schoellig tackle joint control of small flying robots with no central computer and no outside positioning. Central control scales poorly, and global fixes may be absent. Each robot thus gauges its own pose from onboard odometry plus range measures to peers. Each robot also works out its own inputs to fly as a team, for example holding shape while scanning an area.

Pose gauging uses block coordinate descent with no strict sync between robots. Shape control is cast as inference on factor graphs, taking gauge error into account and solving fast. The system is fully spread out, needs no special paths, and hits decimeter-level accuracy. Real indoor and outdoor shape flights show it works, giving drone teams a robust way to fly together.
arxiv-2602-16994:
Rahul Thomas and co-authors present dynamic delayed tree expansion for improved multi-path speculative decoding. Multi-path speculative decoding speeds lossless sampling from a model. It uses a cheaper draft model to make a draft tree of tokens, then a verification step that accepts a subset. Prior work proposed various verification methods for independent rollouts, but their relative performance under matched settings remained unclear.

The paper first evaluates verification strategies across model families, tasks, and sampling regimes. Traversal verification dominates consistently, with optimal-transport-based methods lagging far behind. Analysis uncovers why. Optimal-transport methods achieve high multi-token acceptance near the root of the draft tree. But multi-token gains matter most deeper in the tree, where draft and target distributions diverge. Delayed tree expansion drafts a partial single path, delaying the branching point, preserving the target distribution and improving on root-node rollouts.
arxiv-2602-17294:
Delia Garijo led a three-author paper proving that covering points with the fewest guillotine cuts is NP-complete. The proof proceeds in two steps. First, the authors give a new NP-completeness proof for covering points with disjoint line segments. Then they adapt that proof to guillotine cuts.

The result shows the guillotine restriction does not make the covering problem tractable: even with cuts constrained to the guillotine form, finding a minimum cover stays computationally hard. The two-step argument gives complexity theorists a clean route to the guillotine result via the segment-covering problem, rather than a from-scratch reduction.
arxiv-2602-17494:
Andreas Langer led a five-author team on functional analysis and parallel domain decomposition for the TV-Stokes model. TV-Stokes cleans images in two steps. First it gauges a divergence-free tangent field with total variation regularization. Then it rebuilds the image. Strong in practice, its maths and parallel scope had gone uncharted. This paper lays its strict functional-analytic base.

Both steps sit in infinite-dimensional function spaces, with duals derived and the coupled system checked. The team spots analytic flaws in the first form, mended by a rival model. They prove the orthogonal projection onto the divergence-free subspace exists continuously, matching its discrete twin. Overlapping Schwarz-type iterations on both steps' duals yield the first domain decomposition for TV-Stokes. The discrete projection being locally computable, the scheme runs fully in parallel, suiting large, tight-memory image jobs. Tests back its correctness and parallel use.
arxiv-2602-17694:
Hui Ma and team propose AsynDBT, an asynchronous distributed bilevel tuning algorithm for in-context learning with large language models. Cloud-based models hide their parameters and gradients, so users must tune prompts by hand or by costly heuristics. In-context learning adapts models via examples in the input, yet high-quality data is often sensitive and hard to share.

Federated learning offers collaborative training with privacy, but past federated in-context approaches suffered stragglers and heterogeneous non-identical data. AsynDBT tunes both in-context samples and prompt fragments from model feedback, in an asynchronous distributed design. It provides privacy protection and adapts to varied compute settings, with a theoretical analysis backing convergence. Tests on multiple benchmarks show gains in effectiveness and efficiency.
arxiv-2602-17794:
Neethan Ratnakumar and team test whether reinforcement-learning-based help cuts squat effort with a plug-in hip-knee exo. Squatting demands heavy muscle effort and timing, and easing it matters above all in plants with repeat build work. A neural net unit, trained via reinforcement learning in a physics-based mock run, made real-time hip and knee torques from recent joint-angle and velocity traces.

Five healthy adults performed three-minute metronome-guided squats under three setups: no exo, exo with zero torque, and exo with active help. Effort was gauged by indirect calorimetry and heart rate tracking alongside motion data. Active help cut net energy rate by about ten percent against the other setups, with minor heart rate dips. Assisted trials showed reduced squat depth with smaller hip and knee bend. The unit adapts torque patterns to each wearer, spurring further hardware and control tweaks.
arxiv-2602-17894:
Michael Harding and team study learning from biased and costly data sources, seeking minimax-optimal data collection under a budget. Data collection anchors modern machine learning pipelines, when data must come from multiple mixed sources to study a target population. Sources differ in sampling costs. Group composition varies among source populations and between sources and the target, as in medical or polling studies.

The paper focuses on estimation of population and group means under a budget. Naive strategies such as matching the target distribution, or standard estimators such as the sample mean, can prove suboptimal. Instead, the authors develop a plan maximizing sample size: total sample size divided by a chi-squared divergence term plus one. They pair it with a post-stratification estimator, bounding its risk. Matching lower bounds establish minimax optimal risk. Techniques extend to prediction problems, giving an approach to multi-source learning with costly data.
arxiv-2602-18094:
Ling Lin and colleagues present OODBench, a benchmark for testing large vision-language models on out-of-distribution data. Existing models train on massive datasets assuming independent and identically distributed data, but real-world data often break that assumption. Mishandling out-of-distribution objects can create safety risks in driving and medical assistance, yet no valid benchmark has comprehensively assessed model performance on such data.

OODBench offers a mostly automated method with minimal human verification for building benchmarks and evaluating how models handle out-of-distribution data. It contains forty thousand out-of-distribution instance-category pairs, and current models still degrade notably, even when image categories are common. A reliable automated metric uses Basic-to-Advanced Progression questions to measure how out-of-distribution data affect questions of varying difficulty. The authors summarize findings to guide future research on acquiring and evaluating out-of-distribution data.
arxiv-2602-18494:
Xiu Li argues that meaning in visual intelligence is not static. His 2026 paper challenges the dominant view of semantics as fixed features of latent representations, found through geometric closeness in high-dimensional embedding spaces. That view, he argues, is physically partial.

Li treats intelligence as a property of a physical agent limited to finite memory, compute, and energy, engaging a high-entropy environment. He frames that interaction as a fiber bundle of observation semantics, where raw sensory data projects onto a low-entropy causal semantic manifold. Landauer's Principle then caps internal state transitions at a strict limit, termed the Semantic Constant B. To model a combinatorial world within it, the semantic manifold must crystallize into a discrete, compositional form. Language and logic thus emerge not as cultural artifacts but as necessities of being, the solid state of information. Understanding becomes building a causal quotient making the world compressible and predictable.
arxiv-2602-18794:
Forecasting turbulence with generative models raises a stats question. When a sampler makes many possible futures, how far can its whole spread drift from the truth? Victor Armegioiu, writing alone in 2026, gives error bounds for generative solvers of chaotic partial differential equations. He works at the level of statistical solutions of the incompressible Euler equations.

The work uses a correlation-measure frame. It proves a stability bound whose growth tracks a distance-weighted mean strain. That is kinder than a worst-case Lipschitz constant. One-step error splits into a resolved mismatch and a high-frequency tail that cannot be avoided. Those parts then flow through multi-step rollouts by a discrete Grönwall recursion. With apt regularity, they yield convergence of measured quantities. Finite-grid diagnostics thus gain a principled reading as resolved observables.
arxiv-2602-18994:
What is the spacetime shape of Sagittarius A*, the black hole at our galaxy's centre? Parth Bambhaniya, with five co-authors, tests it in 2026 using the relativistic orbit of the S2 star. A broad class of compact object models is considered, including Schwarzschild, Reissner-Nordström, Bardeen, Hayward, and Simpson-Visser black holes, plus a naked singularity spacetime.

For each shape, timelike geodesic equations are integrated and projected onto astrometric and spectral observables, with Rømer delay and relativistic redshift included. Predictions are tested against Very Large Telescope observations of S2, with Event Horizon Telescope shadow size limits imposed at once. Several spacetimes overlap in shadow imaging, notably Schwarzschild, Reissner-Nordström, and Bardeen, and remain the same against present S2 data. Statistical model comparison and charge-like parameter limits point to specific shapes testable with future sharp astrometry. Stars can probe spacetime. S2 is the probe here.
arxiv-2602-19294:
Page objects are a standard pattern for keeping automated web tests maintainable: each page of an app gets a tidy object that hides its controls behind readable methods. Yet building and updating those objects by hand is slow, and automated tools have seen little practical use. Betül Karagöz and three colleagues test whether large language models can take over that chore, using two leading code-capable models.

Their empirical study generates page objects for a benchmark of five web applications and evaluates what comes out. The question is practical throughout: can model-generated objects match hand-built ones closely enough to save real effort, and where do they still fall short? By measuring the generated artifacts against the benchmark, the paper maps both the promise and the current limits of letting language models maintain test suites.
arxiv-2602-19394:
Some systems that change over time can be modeled by generalized Bratteli diagrams, layered graphs whose paths carry invariant measures. Sergey Bezuglyi and four co-authors study tail invariant measures on those path spaces, allowing vertex sets at each level to be countably endless. The focus is subdiagrams, smaller diagrams inside a larger one, and whether measures defined on them extend to the whole diagram.

The authors give exact conditions for such extensions to be finite, stated through incidence matrices and their stochastic counterparts. Simple, stationary, and bounded-size diagrams get detailed treatment, along with their subdiagrams. Step-by-step methods build extensions and approximate the measures by counterparts on suitable smaller diagrams, with clear cases where no probability tail invariant measure exists.
arxiv-2602-19594:
Ayush Nangia and three co-authors introduce ISO-Bench, a benchmark testing whether coding agents can optimize real-world inference workloads. Tasks come from vLLM and SGLang, two popular language model serving frameworks. Each task gives an agent a codebase and bottleneck description, requiring an optimization patch judged against expert human solutions. Fifty-four tasks were curated from merged pull requests with measurable improvements.

Runtime-based metrics alone can be gamed, passing tests without capturing the code change's actual intent. ISO-Bench therefore combines hard execution-based metrics with soft language-model-based metrics, showing both are necessary for complete evaluation. No single agent dominates across codebases, and agents often spot correct bottlenecks but fail to follow through.
arxiv-2602-20094:
Scores on reasoning benchmarks do not prove a language model reasons with causes. High accuracy can come from memorizing semantic patterns instead of analyzing causal structure. A 2026 arXiv paper by Yuzhe Wang and two co-authors introduces CausalFlip, a benchmark for language model judgment designed to look beyond meaning matching.

CausalFlip builds judgment questions over event triples that can form confounder, chain, and collider relations. For each triple the benchmark constructs pairs of questions that reuse the same events yet yield opposite answers. Models leaning on meaning matching are steadily pushed toward wrong predictions. A noisy-prefix evaluation prepends causally irrelevant text before middle reasoning steps without changing the causal relations or logic. The authors evaluate training approaches. Explicit chain-of-thought supervision can still fall for spurious semantic correlations. Reasoning steps held inside the model greatly improve causal grounding. Base models hold latent causal reasoning abilities worth drawing out.
arxiv-2602-20394:
Shiba Biswal and two co-authors improve autoregressive sampling by choosing a better variable order. Autoregressive models sample tractably from learned distributions, but their quality depends heavily on the ordering used to factorize the distribution, through the complexity of the resulting conditionals. The authors first learn the Markov random field behind the data, then use its graph structure to build optimized orderings.

On two-dimensional image-like models, a structure-aware ordering narrows the conditioning sets, cutting model complexity. Numerical tests on Ising models with discrete data show graph-informed orderings give higher-fidelity samples than naive orderings. The lesson is that ordering is not a minor implementation detail: it shapes the difficulty of every conditional the model must learn. Structure-aware ordering thus offers a principled way to boost sample quality without changing the model class.
arxiv-2602-20494:
Time series analysis increasingly demands decisions, not just numbers, and Haotian Si and eleven co-authors extend it toward meaning. They introduce the Semantic-Conditional Time Series Reasoning task, which adds context and meaning to usual number models. To strengthen thought on hard time series problems, they propose a two-round reinforcement learning setup: the first round sharpens sense of basic time units, while the second targets meaning-tied thought.

The model, KairosVL, performs well across made-up and real-world tasks. Tests and cutouts show the setup boosts scores, preserves built-in thought ability, and greatly lifts transfer to unseen cases. The work highlights the promise of joining meaning thought with time models for real-world time series intelligence.
arxiv-2602-20694:
Entanglement in thermal quantum states has a finite reach, and Samuel O. Scalet proves that reach is bounded for a broad class of systems. The paper considers the Gibbs state of any local Hamiltonian on a spin chain at any finite temperature. It proves a finite entanglement length for that state, a single scale that governs how far entanglement extends along the chain.

The key consequence is sharp. After removing an interval at least as large as the entanglement length, the remaining left and right half-chains sit in a separable state, with no entanglement left between them. The result holds at all temperatures, so even cold chains cannot sustain entanglement across arbitrarily long gaps. Readers gain a clean, general bound on thermal entanglement in one-dimensional spin systems, with the entanglement length as the controlling scale.
arxiv-2602-20994:
Radiology reports could spare radiologists from labeling every tumor voxel. Brain-tumor reports are messy, though: they mix global findings with modality-wise notes, describe only the largest lesion, and hedge with words like mild or possible. Yubin Ge, Yongsong Huang, and Xiaofeng Liu handle that mess in this 2026 arXiv paper using MS-RSuper, a unified report-supervised method for brain lesion segmentation with substructures.

The method parses global quantitative findings and modality-wise qualitative cues, aligning cues like enhancement and edema with matching substructures through existence and absence losses. One-sided lower bounds handle partial quantities, anatomical priors respect cohort differences, and certainty tokens scale penalties while missing cues count less. On over twelve hundred report-labeled scans, the method largely beats sparse supervision and naive report supervision.
arxiv-2602-21094:
Terahertz spectroscopy measures semiconductor doping without touching the sample, unlike probe or capacitance methods. Joshua Hennig and six co-authors clarify exactly which doping ranges it can reach in this 2026 arXiv paper. They introduce a sensitivity metric for reflection terahertz time-domain spectroscopy, built from numerical simulations over material, layer thickness, doping type, and doping level.

Sensitivity values for silicon carbide, silicon, and gallium nitride in stacks of up to three layers produce heat maps over thickness and carrier density. Mapping published and new measurements onto those maps validates the metric. Accessible carrier densities span roughly five orders of magnitude, with details depending on material, doping type, and thickness. The metric also judges what future antenna and system improvements could add.
arxiv-2602-21294:
Strong magnetic fields in neutron stars were once attributed to a chiral plasma instability, until finite electron mass was found to damp it out. Steven Harris and Srimoyee Sen revive the mechanism in this 2026 arXiv paper. They show abrupt density and temperature perturbations can push the system far enough from weak equilibrium for the instability to survive. Shock waves supply such perturbations in core collapse and neutron star mergers.

Under suitable density and temperature conditions, shock-driven chiral imbalance sustains the instability despite electron-mass damping. In an already magnetized medium, the shock-driven chiral magnetic effect can also generate substantial ohmic heating. Shock waves thus emerge as a source of both strong heating and chiral instability in stellar explosions and mergers.
arxiv-2602-21394:
Xuan Chen and five co-authors present MemoPhishAgent, a memory-augmented, multi-modal language-model agent for phishing URL detection. Older detectors lean on static heuristics or reference lists that lag fast-moving attacks, and recent language-model systems mostly run fixed prompt pipelines that underuse reasoning.

MemoPhishAgent instead orchestrates phishing-specific tools on the fly and recalls past reasoning trajectories from episodic memory to guide new decisions. It lifts recall by 13.6 percent on two public datasets and by 20 percent on real suspicious URLs crawled from five social media platforms, with episodic memory alone adding up to 27 percent recall. Now in production, it screens 60,000 high-risk URLs a week at 91.44 percent recall.
arxiv-2602-21594:
Miroslav Krstic alone authors a note on asymmetry in strict Lyapunov functions and feedbacks for predator-prey links. Taming groups is hard. States and controls must stay positive. Motion differs near die-out versus crowded states. Finding strict Lyapunov functions that avoid LaSalle proofs and gauge settling is harder.

Among two-group types, mutualism borders on trivial. Competition makes taming with positive culling ruled out. Predator-prey forms the spot for taming study. Even barely stable predator-prey resisted taming with Lyapunov functions, except via cautious Matrosov-like methods yielding scant insight. This note designs clean, majorization-free strict Lyapunov functions. They extend Volterra-style functions to non-split builds. As a bonus, it gives joint feedback and Lyapunov designs using forward and back steps. In these frames, predator-prey is both strict-feedforward and strict-feedback, with gaps from usual forms forced by keeping states and inputs positive.
arxiv-2602-21694:
R. Ammendola and a large team tested transition-edge sensors for low-energy electrons, a key step toward precise spectroscopy for the PTOLEMY experiment. Their sensor is a titanium-gold bilayer about 60 microns square, cooled to near 80 millikelvin and fed by electrons from carbon nanotubes inside a cryostat. For electrons near 92 to 99 electronvolts, fully absorbed events gave a resolution of about half an electronvolt.

That result improves on prior work by roughly half, mostly because the sensor area shrank. A second measure, the peak width, improved by over 21 times, mainly because a smaller emission area cut back-scattering near the sensor. The team calls the work a major milestone for low-energy electron spectroscopy.
arxiv-2602-21794:
As mobile networks move to 5G, robust security testing grows more urgent given complex design and wider attack surface. Older 5G testing relies on black-box fuzzing, which cannot observe internal program state or cover data. Yu Wang and three co-authors present MulCovFuzz, a coverage-guided greybox fuzzer for 5G network testing. Unlike tools that depend only on system response, MulCovFuzz tracks code cover across system parts of the 5G system design and scores test cases by mixing cover rewards with speed metrics.

Tested on the open-source 5G build OpenAirInterface, MulCovFuzz clearly beats older fuzzing. Gains reach about 6 percent in branch cover, about 7 percent in line cover, and 16 percent in unique crash finds during 24 hours of fuzzing. MulCovFuzz found three zero-day flaws, two of which no other fuzzing tool found. This work pushes security testing tools for next-gen mobile networks.
arxiv-2602-21894:
Starting from the Habiro ring introduced by Garoufalidis, Scholze, Wheeler, and Zagier, Tess Bouis and one co-author build a q-deformed version of a number field's p-adic regulator, naming it the cyclosyntomic regulator. At the heart of the construction sits a sharpened form of Sulyma's norm maps from prismatic cohomology, one that moves between ordinary powers and Frobenius maps as the prime varies.

The construction thus deforms a classical arithmetic invariant into a q-family, with the refined norm maps bridging ordinary powers and Frobenius actions across primes. They also evaluate the cyclosyntomic regulator on units written as one less than a root of unity. These computed values give concrete values for the new regulator, anchoring the abstract construction in explicit unit values.
arxiv-2602-21994:
Genome data can betray sensitive traits, and even the questions a researcher asks can leak private intent. Kimon Antonios Provatas and Ilias Georgakopoulos-Soares present BEDCrypt, a system for studying genome intervals that keeps both data and queries hidden from the server doing the work. It rests on homomorphic encryption, which lets a server compute on locked data and return locked answers that only the client can open.

The system supports core interval tasks: coverage summaries, overlaps between interval sets, nearby-window queries, and set-similarity scores, all without exposing plain intervals or query sites. It assumes an honest-but-curious server, one that follows the rules but peeks at anything it can see. BEDCrypt thus lets labs outsource genome analysis to outside machines without handing over the genome itself.
arxiv-2602-22394:
Vision transformers pretrained on large data give general visual features, but strange artifacts appear across supervision styles and tasks. Cheng Shi and two co-authors trace those artifacts to lazy aggregation: the model uses meaningless background patches as shortcuts for global meaning, driven by global attention and coarse-grained meaning training. The mechanism, they argue, was never properly explained.

Their fix hand-picks patch features for the classification token, reducing the pull of background-led shortcuts. The change improves performance in every case across a dozen benchmarks under label, text, and self-training. The paper offers a new view on transformer behavior: artifacts are not noise but shortcuts the design invites.
arxiv-2602-22894:
Jin-Song von Storch fuses climate science with chance mechanics in this essay on wobbling events. Starting points are the Langevin formula and the fluctuation-dissipation theorem. The former entered climate research through Klaus Hasselmann's random climate models. The latter, in linear-response form, enjoys wide use despite an unsettled deeper origin.

The essay goes further by seeking the cause of seeming chance rather than merely sketching it, and by tying a fluctuation-loss link straight to the ruling tiny-scale formulas. It posits a summed fluctuation-loss link living in sums of the forcings that drive tiny-scale paths. That link yields well-defined large-scale amounts like variance and spectra in moving balance. Its loss erases memory of starting states, making chance basic to forced-lossy systems.
arxiv-2602-22994:
Hiroki Kanda and two co-authors study the entanglement phase flip of pseudo entropy in CFTs. Pseudo entropy generalizes entanglement entropy to cases where the in-state and out-state differ, here two edge states linked by edge-condition-changing operators. Using edge CFT methods, they compute the pseudo entropy and find a phase flip.

The flip turns on the conformal weight of the edge-condition-changing operators, the number that sets how each operator scales. For holographic CFTs, the field-theory results match the values computed in Anti-de Sitter space. This ties the edge calculation to its gravitational dual and sharpens the picture of pseudo entropy across the flip.
arxiv-2602-23094:
V. V. Braguta and three co-authors find a new in-space uneven phase in a spinning gluon plasma. Using first-basics number runs, the team discovers a mixed phase holding both locking and unlocking states in thermal balance. The edge spot between the two phases follows the local key heat.

The key heat of the local change is worked out as a function of spin speed and radius for a spinning system and within a local heat-settling guess. The two methods match closely. Math carry-over to real spin rates hints locking sits at the rim while unlocking appears near the spin axis. Uneven gluon action in the curved co-spinning background explains in numbers the striking quirk that the structure of this uneven phase breaks a plain Tolman-Ehrenfest picture. A first grid run of spinning two-flavour QCD backs a similar picture with moving quarks.
arxiv-2602-23194:
Kieran O'Grady surveys recent advances in the theory of moduli spaces of stable sheaves on hyperkähler manifolds of dimension greater than two. Moduli spaces collect the geometric objects of a given type into a single space of their own. The higher-dimensional hyperkähler case has seen rapid progress that this survey gathers and organizes.

The account starts from the well-known two-dimensional theory, the case of K3 surfaces, where the main ideas and tools are clearest. It stresses the techniques from that setting that carry over to higher dimensions. Readers get a route from the classical surface theory into the newer results for manifolds of dimension four and above.
arxiv-2602-23494:
Tamalika Samanta and 17 co-authors show strain patterning of flexomagnetism, the link of spin order to strain gradients. Flexomagnetism promises symmetry-broken spin phases out of reach with uniform strain, but varying strain in space has been very hard to control.

Their top-down plan patterns sideways strain gradients with helium ion implantation through a patterned mask. In thin films of the antiferromagnetic nodal line semimetal GdAuGe, sideways strain gradients induce near-room-temperature ferromagnetic response, versus kept weak or opposed spin order under uniform strain. Magnetic force microscopy and nanobeam X-ray diffraction tie the spin response to spots of largest strain gradient, confirming the flexomagnetic effect and opening precise control of spin phases in quantum-material thin films.
arxiv-2602-23594:
Guy Tchuente builds one shared framework for how friends shape choices, putting at its core the rule that turns what peers do into a single measure of pressure. Peer influence becomes a norm game: payoffs depend on one's own action and an exposure index, with equilibrium existence and uniqueness broadly.

Using clear economic axioms, the paper sorts common exposure maps into a small taxonomy of linear-in-means, CES peer-preference norms, and smooth attention-to-salient-peers aggregators, plus rank-based quantile norms as a complementary class. Each aggregator induces a rule for how outside variation spreads through the network. Linear-in-means gives constant transport via the adjacency matrix, recovering classic friends-of-friends instruments. For nonlinear norms, the rule becomes state- and preference-dependent, set by the Jacobian of the exposure map at an outside predictor. The paper adds Monte Carlo evidence and a NetHealth application.
arxiv-2602-23694:
Seungyeol Baek and five co-authors present a clear multi-modal gesture reading method for drone and mobile robot remote control via log-odds ratio fusion. Human drivers still face risky places like crisis zones and factory sites, where natural remote control is key. Hands-free remote control lifts motion and scene sense, lifting safety.

Vision-based gesture reading often drops under blocks, lighting shifts, and messy backgrounds. The new method mixes motion data, accel, gyro, and tilt, from Apple Watches on both wrists with touch sensing signals from custom gloves. A late fusion plan based on the log-odds ratio lifts scores and gives a clear read by sizing channel-specific shares. A new data set of 20 distinct signs drawn from ground-crew aircraft signals mixes synced RGB video, IMU, and touch sensor data. Tests show scores close to a state-of-the-art vision-based rival.
arxiv-2602-23994:
Vrushank Ahire and three co-authors present MINT, a framework that transfers knowledge from brain imaging to speech for early Alzheimer's screening. The 2026 paper notes that structural MRI gives useful biomarkers but needs costly infrastructure. Speech is non-invasive, yet speech-only classifiers lack biological grounding for telling cognitively normal people from those with mild cognitive impairment.

MINT works in three stages. An MRI teacher sets a compact embedding space for the normal-versus-impairment task. A residual projection head aligns speech representations to that space with a combined geometric loss. The frozen MRI classifier then enables imaging-free inference from speech alone. On a large Alzheimer's dataset, aligned speech matches speech baselines, while multimodal fusion beats MRI alone. Dropout regularization and self-supervised pretraining emerge as key design choices in ablations.
arxiv-2603-00294: Qiang proposes a small accelerator for a megahertz soft X-ray laser at 1 nanometre, fitting within 100 metres for labs short on space. The design loops electrons through a linear accelerator many times, joining superconducting tech with diffraction-limited storage ring advances. He studies two hard effects, incoherent and coherent synchrotron radiation, across multi-bend magnet layouts and beam currents. At 60 amperes before final squeezing with 11 bending magnets, sideways beam spread after a 90-degree arc stays below 10 percent.
arxiv-2603-01194: Xiang and nine colleagues infer complete 3D shapes from partial 2D views with RnG, a unified net for rebuilding and making. A rebuilding-guided causal focus trick splits the two tasks at the focus level. It treats the key-value cache as a hidden 3D model that any pose can query for novel-view RGBD output. The model rebuilds visible shapes well while making likely unseen shapes and looks, leading the field on both rebuilding and novel-view making at live speed.
arxiv-2603-01294: Tan and thirteen colleagues present the Spherical Latent Motion Prior, a two-stage method for motion priors for physics-based humanoid control. First they train a tracking controller, then distill it into a spherical latent space shaped by a discriminator, distillation, and a discriminator-guided local consistency rule for meaning. Random sampling stays stable without information loss, and on a two-hour combat motion capture dataset the method preserves fine motion detail. In a two-agent physics-based combat task it produces human-like, physically plausible combat behavior.
arxiv-2603-01394: Manfio, Reis, and Vitório obtain a geometric description of surfaces of arbitrary codimension in warped product spaces, with parallel mean curvature vector field in the normal connection. Their result extends an earlier result by Alencar, do Carmo, and Tribuzy. Warped product spaces combine a line with a curved space through a warping factor, and a parallel mean curvature vector stays unchanged when moved along the surface.
arxiv-2603-01494:
Manisha Mukherjee and Vincent Hellendoorn tackle unsafe code from AI coding tools in this 2026 work. Models trained once cannot keep up as new flaws and new safety rules appear over time. As a result, they can write the same risky code again and again in real projects.

Their method fixes code at use time, with no need to retrain the model. It first spots risks in fresh code, then pulls matching expert posts from a curated Stack Overflow base. Those posts guide a rewrite pass before the code ships. On real and test data, the method made code safer than plain prompts and added no new flaws by static checks. The clear, sourced fixes also help users see why each change was made.
arxiv-2603-01694:
Lirui Luo, Guoxi Zhang, Hongming Xu, and colleagues shape rewards for robot learning from video and text. Their 2026 work tackles a weakness in adding vision-language scores straight into task rewards. A plain sum can shift what counts as the best behavior, and single still images miss motion that unfolds over time.

Their frame, MVR, judges each state by video clips shot from several viewpoints at once. A frozen vision-language model scores how well each clip matches the task text. That score becomes a relevance function that avoids bias toward frozen poses. A shaping rule then fades the guidance once the wanted motion is learned, so the true task reward rules at the end. Tests cover hard humanoid walking and robot handling tasks.
arxiv-2603-01794:
K. Pomorski, A. Augustyn, T. Cap, and colleagues test how a modeling choice shifts predicted fission yields. Their 2026 work compares two liquid-drop prescriptions for the bulk energy of atomic nuclei. The drop model treats a nucleus like a charged fluid drop, and small formula changes can move results.

Both prescriptions run on the same yield observables and the same fission reference case. One adds an explicit isospin term, tied to neutron-proton imbalance, in its volume and surface parts. The team tracks peak positions, widths, and tails of isotope yields for each element chain. Light and mid-weight fragments match well under both formulas, with near-identical peaks. Heavy chains diverge most, since their yield ridges feel isospin terms more. One formula fits the evaluated data slightly better on average, and the spread gauges model doubt.
arxiv-2603-02194:
Mateus Karvat Camara, Bram Adams, and Sidney Givigi audit code behind self-driving research in this 2026 study. Contest leaderboards rank car perception models by test scores alone. High scores say nothing about code safety, upkeep, or readiness for real roads. The team checked 178 top models from two major driving benchmarks.

Static tools scanned each code base for errors, security flaws, and upkeep risks. Only a small share met basic readiness bars: no grave errors and no severe flaws. A few flaw types caused most of the security trouble, so fixes can be focused. Teams that used steady build and release pipelines had cleaner, easier code. The authors turn those patterns into clear guidelines for safer research code.
arxiv-2603-02294:
Nikhileswara Rao Sulake tunes chest X-ray classification for rare diseases in this 2026 study. Chest scans carry many labels at once, and rare findings appear in few images. Models can then ignore rare classes while scoring well overall. The work tests loss functions, network designs, and post-training tricks on a large benchmark.

The benchmark holds about one hundred forty thousand images with thirty disease labels. A loss that boosts rare classes late in training beat standard and lopsided rivals. Among network designs, a large modern convolutional model scored best alone. Retraining the classifier head and averaging test views lifted scores further. On the official test board, the entry placed fifth among sixty-eight teams, and the author candidly discusses the drop from local scores.
arxiv-2603-02394:
M Roa, M Siddikov, Y Gentile, and I Zemlyakov constrain a hypothetical particle exchange in this 2026 physics paper. The odderon is a proposed counterpart to the pomeron in high-energy proton collisions. It would mediate part of how protons and antiprotons scatter elastically. The team works inside the Color Glass Condensate framework, treating collisions as dilute hitting dense.

They build an observable that mixes proton and antiproton cross sections. That mix suppresses uncertainty from the better-known part of the amplitude. Two model forms for the odderon are fitted to data from two collaborations. Both fit reasonably after small normalization tweaks. Large data errors leave the odderon loosely pinned, though. Sharper data and new observables are needed to corner it.
arxiv-2603-02594:
He Jia and Aravindan Vijayaraghavan challenge a popular hardness predictor in this 2026 paper. The low-degree method predicts which high-dimensional problems efficient algorithms can solve. Its success bred a conjecture that it captures algorithmic power broadly. Robust subspace recovery is their test case, a basic problem of finding a hidden subspace amid outliers.

For one natural testing version, the pattern of low-degree moments looks hard up to high degree. That suggests no fast algorithm should exist. Yet the authors give a simple, robust polynomial-time algorithm that solves it. Their method exploits anti-concentration, a property the low-degree lens misses. Noise-tolerant variants fall to the same approach. Universality claims for the low-degree framework thus need revision.
arxiv-2603-03194:
Guoxin Chen, Fanzhe Meng, Jiale Zhao, and a large team test whether coding agents can survive real software work. Current benchmarks mostly grade small fixes inside one repository. Their 2026 benchmark, BeyondSWE, stretches evaluation along scope and knowledge, with five hundred real instances across four harder settings.

The settings demand reasoning across repositories, specialized domain knowledge, migration driven by dependencies, and generating a whole repository from scratch. Even frontier models stayed below forty-five percent success, and no single model led across all task types. A companion search-augmented framework, SearchSWE, helped inconsistently and sometimes hurt, showing how hard it is to mimic developers who interleave searching and reasoning. The pair gives the field a tougher yardstick and a flexible testbed.
arxiv-2603-03294:
Farmers need advice that is accurate, specific, and safe, and general language models often fail that test. A 2026 study tackles the problem for smallholder farmers, using crops and questions from Bihar, India. Plain models gave unsupported claims, vague tips, and a tone poorly matched to farmer needs, which matters when bad advice can harm a harvest.

The proposed system splits fact recall from friendly delivery. Fine-tuning on expert-checked facts, stored as small verified units, teaches the model what is true. A separate stitching layer then turns those facts into clear, safety-aware replies. A new test framework checks facts one by one against expert truth. A smaller tuned model matched larger ones at far lower cost, and the team released its prompt library for others.
arxiv-2603-03394:
Muhammad Waseem and ten colleagues report building a shared sandbox where companies and universities can experiment with artificial intelligence under clear rules. Trials need speed, but also controlled access, separation between organizations, and records of who did what. Practical guidance for such governed platforms is scarce. Their 2026 paper designs one, builds it, and distills the lessons.

Requirements came from industrial partners and were validated in rounds. The design separates a multi-tenant front layer from a control plane, with execution and data kept in their own layers. Governed onboarding, project-based teamwork, approval workflows, and audit logging structure every experiment. Because experiment context and governance decisions persist as records, evaluation evidence can be reused and compared across projects and stakeholders. The authors close with deployment lessons for similar platforms.
arxiv-2603-03794:
Sandipan Dutta, Vanlalruatkimi, and Jonathan Ramdikpuia characterize when families of Möbius transformations behave tamely in the Baire-one sense. Möbius maps, the fractional linear transformations of the Riemann sphere, drive much of complex dynamics. Their 2026 paper studies the Equi-Baire one property for two natural families: the iterates of a single expanding-type map, and the one-parameter subgroups of the Möbius group.

For a loxodromic map, its iterates form an orbitally Equi-Baire one family on the basin that the map attracts. For a one-parameter subgroup, the answer is a clean dichotomy: the family is Equi-Baire one on every compact set exactly when the subgroup is relatively compact in the special linear group. Together the results give a dynamical characterization of the condition, tying a descriptive-set-theoretic property to plain compactness.
arxiv-2603-04194: Wilhelm and others propose noise-aware client choice for carbon-efficient federated learning via gradient norm thresholding. Various client choice plans align renewable energy volatility with stable fair federated training, yet federated privacy leaves client data quality unknown, challenging effective training. To address this they propose gradient norm thresholding with probing rounds for better client choice and noise finding, aiding real carbon-efficient federated deployment.
arxiv-2603-04394: Di Luzio and colleagues frame missing energy searches for anomalous light vectors. Such bosons need new chiral fermions, anomalons, to cancel anomalies. Breaking the new symmetry gives anomalons mass, and integrating them out yields Wess-Zumino interactions from anomaly matching. The authors classify minimal spectra, derive effective interactions, and bound the completion scale. Driven by NA62 and Belle II, they survey flavour and electroweak searches in depth where vectors decay to neutrinos and leave invisible states.
arxiv-2603-04894: Ivoline C. Ngong and colleagues present DP-MTV, a framework for many-shot multimodal in-context learning under formal differential privacy. Earlier private methods stayed few-shot and text-only, so the team compresses hundreds of demonstrations into task vectors in activation space. Private data is split into disjoint chunks with per-layer clipping, and one noise addition covers unlimited queries. At a privacy budget of 1.0, it keeps most of the in-context gain on VizWiz: 50% versus 55% non-private and 35% zero-shot.
arxiv-2603-04994: Bastien Berret and Frédéric Jean present a continuous-time method for optimal feedforward-feedback control of partly observable, stochastic, nonlinear, high-dimensional systems. Stretching nearby optimal control, their feedforward plan outright accounts for feedback uncertainties and latencies. Statistical linearization converts the stochastic problem to a nearly equivalent fixed tuning in a tractable augmented state space that keeps key nonlinearities. Applied to human neuromechanics, the method shows muscle co-shrink emerging as an optimal change to task demands.
arxiv-2603-05294: ELita Lobo and team offer STRUCTUREDAGENT, hierarchical planning interleaving planning and execution via AND/OR trees for long-horizon web tasks. Current LLM web agents falter on complex long-horizon tasks through limited memory, weak planning, and greedy premature termination. The method separates shape planning from LLM reasoning, letting error recovery through node repair, exploration via OR nodes, and modular plans for human intervention. On 630 WebArena tasks it reaches roughly 53% success versus 46% for AgentOccam, and gains reach 10% over the strongest older model on multi-constraint Amazon shopping tasks.
arxiv-2603-05394: Benjamin Proudfoot and team present chance mutual event guesses, using non-Keplerian answers from Beyond Point Masses with a Bayesian method propagating orbital and size uncertainties. Trans-Neptunian binary mutual events provide rare chances to measure small outer bodies. Timing, duration, depth, and probability spreads enable test. Five systems are predicted: Huya, Logos-Zoe, Altjira, Kágára, !Hãunu, and 2001 XR254. Long-older model monitoring is vital, as events are difficult to distinguish from regular rotational light curves. Rapid dissemination of detections benefits the community, letting updated guesses.
arxiv-2603-05494: Casademunt and team use censored open-weights language models made in China as a natural testbed for secret knowledge elicitation. Qwen3 models often state false claims about Falun Gong and the Tiananmen protests, yet sometimes answer right, showing knowledge they hold but hide. For honesty elicitation, tuning on generic honesty data, few-shot prompting, and sampling without a chat template best raise truthful answers. On the lie-spotting side, the censored model sorting its answers nears the best an uncensored model can do, and no technique wipes out false answers.
arxiv-2603-05694: Fishell and team prove exact building of Moore machines as state-space models. These Moore-SSMs keep the original machine's symbol structure and input-output action in Euclidean space. Weighing SSM training with passive and active automata learning, SSMs need far more data than symbol methods. SSMs also fail to learn state structure. Symbol structure provides a strong built-in bias, and starting SSMs with symbol-learned guesses learns faster and better. Closing in runs 2-5 times faster than random start, with better scores.
arxiv-2603-05894: Sotnikova and colleagues analyze variability of the blazar Ton 599 across wavelengths from 1983 to 2025. Gamma-ray, optical, and radio emissions correlate with lags around 0 to 360 days, indicating a shared population trigger. Lomb-Scargle and Weighted Wavelet Z-transform reveal components between 1 and 8 years. A binary black hole model with a precessing jet yields orbital periods between 1 and 2 years and precession periods between 5 and 8 years. This implies a system modulating emission through orbiting and jet precession. Differing periods reflect regions along a stratified jet, while flares likely arise from jet shocks.
arxiv-2603-06194: Zhang and colleagues propose MICA for multi turn emotional support dialogue: a critic free RL framework tackling sparse rewards and weak credit assignment. Responses shape user states, so matched state comparison is unavailable and trajectory supervision falls short. MICA draws immediate and delayed credit from one potential function over the user's support state, combining an incremental distance reward with its Monte Carlo return into a mixed advantage. On EMPA, EQ-Bench, and EmoBench, MICA beats GRPO and REINFORCE++, gaining up to 42.5 on EMPA with no added rollout cost.
arxiv-2603-06294: Chen and his team put forward that quasi periodic oscillations in radio flux and linear polarization link to kink instability in relativistic magnetized jets. Simulations fit seen curves of flux and polarization shifts, and the kink model accounts for flux polarization anti link. These oscillations point to kink instability in fast jets, of note for magnetic field shape near black holes and particle speeding in jets.
arxiv-2603-06594: Schwinn and team show LLM-as-a-Judge tools, the standard for natural language processing evaluation including safety testing, fail under red-teaming spread shifts. Victim models show generation styles, attacks distort output patterns, and doubt varies across jailbreak scenarios. An audit with 6642 human-verified labels reveals judge performance falling to near random chance, against human agreement reported. Many attacks inflate success rates through using judge gaps, not by drawing harmful content. The authors propose ReliableBench, a benchmark of rated acts, plus JudgeStressTest, a dataset showing judge failures.
arxiv-2603-06894: Chen and colleagues prompt an LLM to write CAD programs from a reference shape plus modeling steps, adding to scarce training data. CAD programs are scripted parametric models for precise design and making, yet LLM outputs lack the shape complexity of real factory designs. The shortfall traces partly to narrow training data. Varying the reference shape with organic shapes widens the spread of new programs, giving the model richer examples to learn from.
arxiv-2603-07094: Brice and colleagues study team games where players cooperate against an opponent to reach target states, but each player randomizes privately, with no shared random source. They show memoryless strategies suffice for the threshold problem, placing it in the existential theory of the reals and enabling value iteration algorithms. They also prove the threshold problem is NP-hard and almost-sure reachability is NP-complete. A new logic, IRATL, extends standard temporal logic to this private-randomness setting.
arxiv-2603-07194: Budaca and colleagues map shape change across the ruthenium-98 to ruthenium-106 isotope chain. Using covariant density functional theory with a density-dependent point-coupling parametrization, they find very shallow prolate and triaxial ground-state deformation. Feeding that into prolate gamma-stable and gamma-unstable Bohr-Mottelson models with an octic potential reveals a shape phase transition from low to high deformation. It also shows shape coexistence and mixing among spherical vibrator, gamma-unstable, and prolate configurations in ground and excited states.
arxiv-2603-07294: Kryklyvets and colleagues build a bird-focused helper that answers questions from pictures, sounds and text. Broad multimodal models stumble on fine-grained species detail, so the team gathered data covering over 1,000 species with structured question-answer pairs. Their MAviS-Chat model draws on that data for species spotting, question answering and scene description. A companion test set checks those skills across modalities, and the model beats its baseline by a wide margin.
arxiv-2603-08094: Akyar and colleagues introduce non-Abelian patchworking, a new concept arising as the real locus of non-Abelian complex-phase tropical hypersurfaces. Non-Abelian tropical geometry makes sense for any reductive complex group. But full understanding so far covers tropicalizations of surfaces inside three-dimensional groups, namely PGL2 and SL2. Those two groups are linked by a two-fold covering. The note announces the framework rather than completing it, setting out the concept while its theory is developed enough to support this spin-off.
arxiv-2603-08194: Artemev and colleagues study multipoint Virasoro conformal blocks on the sphere in the comb channel. They derive an asymptotic formula for these blocks at large intermediate dimensions. They apply the WKB method to the classical BPZ equation, a tool for studying Virasoro blocks via the monodromy method. The comb channel chains the blocks in a line. Uses include a possible extension of Zamolodchikov's elliptic recursion and amplitudes in minimal string theory. Their formula passes nontrivial checks, matching known exact results for five-point blocks in special cases.
arxiv-2603-08294: Popov and colleagues explain the brightest hypersoft X-ray sources as disc accretion onto a binary black hole inside a hierarchical triple system. With each black hole near 15 solar masses, the inner binary would sit only about 0.01 astronomical units apart. If the donor feeds in at least ten to the power of minus eight solar masses per year, the circumbinary disc around the pair can reproduce the most luminous supersoft sources. That ties their extreme soft X-ray glow to triple-system accretion.
arxiv-2603-08394: Lemos studies bound states in a semi-infinite square potential well, a less studied variant of a staple first-year quantum physics problem. The finite square well has much writing on allowed levels, which require solving a special equation by number, graphing, or rough math methods. For this well, energy values are also set by such a rule, found here by a standard graphing method. A simple rule yields the number of steady states.
arxiv-2603-08494: Changkai Li recasts constrained tuning as geometry, with limits set by operators that mark which moves stay open. In that view, the best first step is a gradient bent by a pseudoinverse, which shows how limits warp the climb. Motion piles up on a few leading spectral modes, and one shared rule tells when several goals still allow a common open move.
arxiv-2603-08694: Talya Eden and Seshadhri give a clean, full account of an average-degree estimator for graphs of bounded arboricity. The earlier algorithm hid its simple core inside a larger result and bled log factors through parameter search. Their note presents the method without those losses, reaching a near-perfect estimate with a query count tied to arboricity, degree, and precision.
arxiv-2603-08794: Alexander Farren and colleagues fix the imaginary side of the de Sitter wave function from its scale dependence under renormalization. Shift-symmetric scalars should give a purely real wave function at tree level, but a renormalization anomaly breaks that rule. Their all-loop result ties the imaginary side to scale dependence alone, yielding endless links among correlators of massless fields and their momenta.
arxiv-2603-08894: Yihang Zhao and colleagues explore GenAI tools for socially shared metacognition in group work. Poorly designed systems push plain orders that groups follow without thinking, eroding self-rule. Group awareness aids instead surface social and mental awareness, spark useful friction over gaps, and trigger self-driven discussion, and the paper offers early design rules for GenAI-aided versions.
arxiv-2603-09094: Zixuan Wang and colleagues tackle video generation that obeys real physics, a weak point for diffusion models fed plain prompts. Their method treats a scene as a chain of linked events that unfold and change over time. One module breaks the prompt into basic event units, using physics formulas as checks that pin down cause and effect. A second module turns those units into time-aligned vision-language prompts and builds keyframes step by step.
arxiv-2603-09494: Edoardo Bellincioni and colleagues study solids that melt while sliding down heated inclines, using butter-like systems of ice and paraffin wax on a controlled ramp. Motion is set by a coupling of heat flow, gravity, viscous loss, and the phase change itself, in ways that lacked quantitative tests. Their experiments reach terminal speeds from 0.01 to 2 meters per second across wide conditions. A model of the feedback among melt-layer thickness, speed, and heat transfer fits all data with no adjustable parameters.
arxiv-2603-09994: Ruchira Dhar, Qiwei Peng and Anders Søgaard test how language models handle adjective noun composition, a core part of language. They probe the skill two ways: by task prompts and by reading the models' internal states. A striking split appears, since models build sound compositional representations inside yet fail to use them reliably in task answers. The gap, they argue, shows why contrastive evaluation gives a fuller picture of model skill.
arxiv-2603-10094: Parisel uses temporal braid groups to spot risk of privilege creep in cloud access graphs. Inside strongly linked groups of the changing graph, he probes with a Burau Lyapunov exponent that marks the edge between two risk regimes. Parisel proves no Abelian stat, such as edge counts or net privilege flow, can fix that exponent. The small edge still sorts spread risk from focused risk well enough to drive fix choices on its own.
arxiv-2603-10194: Pratyay Kumar and coauthors assess security risk across open source Model Context Protocol servers, which now plug language model agents into live tools. No large scale weakness study of these servers existed before. Static code analysis finds Common Weakness Enumeration flaws, which they map to attack patterns and threat classes through MITRE CAPEC. A multi metric scoring frame then combines likelihood and impact, revealing many exploitable weaknesses.
arxiv-2603-10394: Ziqi Pan and co-authors ask whether phones that move expressively can act as facilitators in face-to-face group discussion, without losing their normal functions. A design workshop with twelve people surfaced common group-work problems and shaped attention-efficient movement cues, guided by group-development theory. The team built AnimaStand, a stand that animates each phone in step with the talk. In a Wizard-of-Oz study with stranger groups, the cues re-engaged quiet members and balanced group dynamics, though task performance did not improve.
arxiv-2603-10494: Weixin Liu studies how to keep AI hospital summaries faithful to patient records when the claim checker itself is noisy. A verifier can reward summaries that simply say less, so the proposed VERI-DPO framework controls for coverage. It samples several summaries, splits them into claims, checks each against the evidence, and forms pairs only when one summary is better supported at similar content. Standard preference training then distills those pairs. On MIMIC test data, unsupported claims fell sharply, blinded judges preferred the output, and gains transferred to new patients.
arxiv-2603-10594: Jean-Baptiste Vincent and co-authors describe the Asteroid Framing Cameras aboard ESA's Hera mission to the Didymos system, target of the DART impact test.
