Two identical panchromatic cameras will support navigation and science, imaging both asteroids from varied distances and angles across mission phases. Their mapping will feed hazard detection, dynamics, shape reconstruction, surface mapping, and photometry, with flybys reaching very fine detail at the impact site. The paper gives technical specifications, reports calibration status, and sums up what is planned for cruise and for the asteroid phase.
arxiv-2603-10694: Catarina P Coutinho and co-authors borrow the mathematics of border completion in the visual cortex to build convolutional filters that resist image occlusion. Their network, BorderNet, is designed from that model of how vision fills in missing edges. They tested it under stripe and grid occlusions, on EMNIST, MNIST, and Fashion-MNIST. In all cases BorderNet improved performance over the comparison setup. The gains varied with occlusion severity and dataset, but the design helped throughout.
arxiv-2603-11094: Ben Halstead and coauthors fingerprint the concepts inside data streams. These concepts are the stationary stretches between concept drifts. Systems can then tell whether data matches a known concept or a new one. Earlier representations used only a few meta-information features. They often could not distinguish concepts. This left systems exposed to drift. Their FiCSUM framework builds fingerprints from many supervised and unsupervised features. It uses a dynamic weighting that learns which features signal drift. It beats state-of-the-art methods across eleven datasets.
arxiv-2603-11194: Idel Waisberg and Boaz Katz revisit Alpha Crucis. It is the nearest very high multiplicity massive star system. They use archival interferometer data to untangle its inner architecture. The data resolve a known close companion in the A component. They reveal that the B component is also a close binary. This upgrades the system to seven stars. Combining interferometry with radial velocities yields the full inner orbit and dynamical masses. The two inner binaries' orbital planes sit strongly misaligned. This points to a dynamical formation history.
arxiv-2603-11294: Jérémy Scanvic and Nils Laurent present EquivAnIA, a spectral method for anisotropic images. It keeps its answers consistent when images are rotated. How things point matters across medical imaging. Yet many methods were never checked for whether their main directions and angular profiles rotate as they should. Built from cake wavelets and ridge filters, the method proves robust across synthetic and real images of structures and textures. It also succeeds at angular image registration.
arxiv-2603-11394: Kevin Guo and coauthors show that long conversations quietly erode language model reliability, a risk static benchmarks miss entirely, with direct stakes for medical chatbots. Their stick-or-switch framework splits questions into sequential presentations and scores two behaviors: holding a correct answer against wrong suggestions, and switching when a correct suggestion arrives. Across seventeen models and three clinical benchmarks, a pervasive conversation tax cuts accuracy and sound abstention by up to thirty percent on average. Models also abandon initial abstentions for wrong and right suggestions at nearly identical rates.
arxiv-2603-11594: Shahid and co-authors predict chemotherapy outcomes early by pairing language models with survival analysis. Chemo is costly and harsh, so early warning of failure would help doctors. The team uses language models and ontology tools to pull phenotypes and labels from notes. The test case is breast cancer, drawing on vitals, staging, biomarkers, and drug plans. A Random Survival Forest then predicts time to failure, reaching a C-index of 73 percent. Used as a classifier, it scores above 70 percent on accuracy and F1.
arxiv-2603-11994: Kenyon, Bromley, and Najita open a survey series with the host star data behind the Cold Debris Disk Surveys. Spitzer and Herschel targeted these stars in a search for cold dust around them. The catalog holds data for 3675 stars, from distances and light measures to spin periods and X-ray output. The authors check how often stars have companions and sort stars into the field, clusters, and moving groups. Later papers will use this base to study dust emission and how it changes with age.
arxiv-2603-12594: Jiansong Zhang and co-authors propose a new aim for contrastive learning: grow entropy between augmented views in small steps. Static augmentations and strict invariance rules can hold such learning back. Their IE-CL treats the encoder as an information bottleneck. A learnable transform creates entropy gain, and a regularizer keeps that gain while meaning stays intact. On CIFAR, STL-10, and ImageNet tests, the method helped most in small-batch settings. Its parts also plug into older frameworks.
arxiv-2603-12694: Zhenkun Shi and co-authors predict which reactions an enzyme catalyzes, without going through EC numbers first. Older methods predict an EC number and then look up its reactions. That detour adds ambiguity, since proteins, numbers, and reactions map many-to-many. Their RXNRECer is a transformer ensemble with protein language models and active learning. It beat six EC-based baselines on curated and time-split tests. Uses range from proteome-wide annotation to spotting enzyme promiscuity.
arxiv-2603-13294: Reva Schwartz and Gabriella Waters describe FRAME, a forum for real-world AI measurement and evaluation. Leaders must make high-stakes AI choices without dependable evidence from their own settings. Model-centric metrics are scalable but abstract, and they smooth over how use varies in practice. FRAME combines large-scale trials with structured observation of use, outcomes, and causes. A Testing Sandbox captures AI in real workflows at scale. A Metrics Hub then turns those traces into actionable indicators for decision-makers.
arxiv-2603-13894: Lin, Liu, and Zhou propose a self-training method that fixes wrong labels while a network learns. Their setup pairs a classifier with a neural correction function, tuned by decoupled bilevel optimization. A small clean dataset guides the pair through noisy posterior simulation and mid-level features. The loop feeds corrections back, which stops errors from compounding. Tests on CIFAR and Clothing1M reach top-level accuracy with less training time, and theory supports the method's stability.
arxiv-2603-13994: Adeli and co-authors ask whether vision models group objects the way people do. Their benchmark has people judge if dot pairs sit on the same object across more than 1,000 trials in natural scenes. Model scores come from a simple readout that predicts human reaction times. Newer models align better, with gains from both design and training goals. Transformer models trained with the DINO method align best. A new metric shows that stronger object-based structure in a model tracks human grouping.
arxiv-2603-14094: Abdulsamad and co-authors make Bayesian experimental design robust to wrong model assumptions. They cast design as a max-min game between the experimenter and an adversarial nature under information limits. The robust goal turns out to rest on Sibson's alpha-mutual information, with a tilted posterior as the safe update. Nested Monte Carlo estimates of that quantity are biased and noisy. A PAC-Bayes search over random design policies gives firm lower bounds on the robust gain instead.
arxiv-2603-14494: Yang and co-authors look for gas rotation in galaxy groups with the kinetic Sunyaev-Zeldovich effect. Rotating ionized gas leaves a dipolar mark on the cosmic microwave background. The team picks fast-rotating groups from the SDSS-DR7 sample. Satellite redshifts give each group a spin direction. Stacked Planck maps then show a tentative signal at 2.3 sigma. Mean spin speeds land near 100 to 200 kilometers per second. The peak value is 158.8, with an error of 13.6, they report.
arxiv-2603-14794: Chu and Patel release Face-to-Face, a video dataset of two-person talk-show exchanges with Jimmy Fallon. Most audio-visual sets hold lone speakers in short monologues. Conversation timing stays out of reach there. F2F-JF spans 70 hours in 14,000 clips of guest-host turns. A semi-automatic pipeline tracks speakers, diarizes speech and checks output by hand. Aligned host and guest tracks ship with tight crops and metadata. Cross-person context yields small, steady gains in emotion and video scores.
arxiv-2603-14894: Chugh, Prasad and Shah pick explanation perturbations by expected information gain with EAGLE. Post-hoc explainers fit a local surrogate around one sample of interest. The black box stays closed, so perturbed inputs must carry the lesson. Random perturbations waste queries on low-value points. EAGLE treats perturbation choice as active learning with information rewards. A linear surrogate learns fast under that sampling. Feature ranks ship with uncertainty estimates attached. Theory bounds total information gain as O(d log t), they prove.
arxiv-2603-14994: Qiu and co-authors tackle private Select-Join-Aggregate queries over large databases. Current methods protect each user, but they solve costly optimization problems. The team shows that a prior sampling method can err ten times more than the base mechanism. Their method, DP-S4S, samples aggregation units instead of users. It also builds new math for such queries under Renyi differential privacy. Tests on real data show it scales well while keeping results useful.
arxiv-2603-15694: Raitio builds quark and lepton masses inside a supersymmetric preon model. Quarks and leptons act as three-body composites of smaller preons. A metacolor force binds them near 10^14 GeV. Four numerical methods, checked on the hydrogen atom, reproduce the electron-to-up mass ratio. The Pauli principle predicts the down quark heavier than the up quark. A spectator field gives neutrinos a small seesaw mass near 0.1 eV. Anomaly inflow at the binding scale generates the baryon asymmetry.
arxiv-2603-16394: Wiggins explains out-of-time-ordered correlators for readers from two fields. Classical chaos means tiny changes grow fast, within a rich phase space. Quantum mechanics is linear, so the analogy needs care. The OTOC is often sold as the quantum butterfly effect. Wiggins shows how classical sensitivity maps to operators that fail to commute. He marks what the OTOC can and cannot diagnose. A shared linear view of both worlds closes the tour.
arxiv-2603-16594: Brofas and Diakonos study how finite size reshapes critical correlations in momentum space. Heavy-ion hunts for the QCD critical point rely on baryon fluctuations. Near that point, correlations should grow long-range and scale as power laws. The fireball's small size and short life cap that growth. The team derives the two-point function for a finite system. Its effective scaling exponent matches the endless case only in one window. That window sits inside the range experiments can reach.
arxiv-2603-16694: Tan and co-authors probe how much of supply chain attacks any telemetry can see. Modern attacks run only at runtime and scatter evidence widely. No dataset held multi-source logs with full chain ground truth. Their SynthChain set is built from real malicious packages and campaigns. Seven scenarios span PyPI, npm, and C++ chains. Annotations mark 2,919 verified compromise indicators across 22 log files. No single source recovers even 40% of attack steps. Fusing two sources lifts reconstruction about 1.6-fold.
arxiv-2603-17094: Kamoi and co-authors argue that simulated human conversation should be judged on its flaws as well as its polish. Real conversations include misunderstandings, interruptions, and other inconsistent or uncollaborative moves. Their framework, CoCoEval, detects 10 such behavior types at the turn level. It also provides a benchmark of professional scenarios with collaboration and conflict. They compare human chats with simulations from GPT-4.1, GPT-5.1, and Claude Opus 4. Simulated chats showed far fewer of these behaviors under plain prompting. Prompt tuning and fine tuning did not control the behaviors reliably.
arxiv-2603-17194: Méndez, Chaudhari, and Arias link hydrogen impurities in metal oxides to microwave loss in superconducting devices. Two level systems in disordered solids are a known loss source, but their spread is hard to predict. Their framework uses machine learned potentials, checked against density functional theory, to map impurity patterns. From these, they derive defect densities and dielectric loss. Applied to niobium and tantalum pentoxides, the method implicates interstitial hydrogen as a loss source. It matches the contrast seen between the two materials.
arxiv-2603-17794: Zhang, Lv, and Huang build hydrodynamics for fluids that carry spin and dilation charge. An entropy-current study yields the flow rules, with bulk viscosity and a dilation conductivity. Wave analysis finds a gapped dilation mode and frozen long-wave sound. The slow limit lands on known microstretch fluid theory. Coupling to electromagnetism adds scale-anomaly terms to the currents. Near-conformal fluids that expand or shrink fast are the target setting.
arxiv-2603-17894: Holubec and Cichos review feedback control with delays in active matter. Sensors and responses never act at once, so delay shapes what active systems do. Delay alone can spark activity, chirality, drift, and group patterns, they write. It also works as a dial that flips systems between dynamic states. The review spans single swimmers and many-body crowds, plus lab demos. Delay reads as a hidden axis of morphological intelligence.
arxiv-2603-17994: Huong, Dong, and Hernandez revisit the flipped standard model, which adds a U(1)_N gauge group. A dark charge set by weak isospin shapes the model, much like electric charge. They find neutrino masses arise from a radiative inverse seesaw run by dark fields. The dark matter pick is a light fermion near the keV scale. Late entropy from long-lived particle decay trims its early overproduction to the seen level.
arxiv-2603-18294: Rajkomar and co-authors find a validity gap in health AI benchmark composition. They profiled 18,707 consumer health queries across six public benchmarks with a 16-field taxonomy. Objective data appears in 42% of queries, but mostly as wellness wearable signals. Lab values, imaging, and raw records stay rare, and suicide or self-harm queries sit below 0.7%. They urge standard query profiling like clinical trial reporting to fix the mismatch.
arxiv-2603-18694: Ratliff and co-authors tune soft dendrimer particles so they self-assemble into quasicrystals. Each dendrimer pairs a central polymer core with stiff linkers and flexible coronas. The pair interaction shows two competing length scales that shift with core and corona traits. A simple model captures that potential, backed by fast Monte Carlo runs. Some parameter choices yield stable twelve-fold quasicrystals. Changing the polymer build alone widens or shrinks the stable region. The results point builders toward molecules that could form soft quasicrystals in the lab.
arxiv-2603-18894: Vedanta and Kumaraguru test corruption in multi-agent systems that mimic public governance. Language agents take formal government roles under varied authority setups. An independent rubric judge scores rule-breaking across 28,112 transcript segments. Governance structure drives corruption outcomes more than model choice, among models below saturation. Regime and model pairing swings are large. Light safeguards help in some setups but fail to block severe cases in others. The authors argue for pre-deployment stress tests, enforceable rules, audit logs, and human oversight on high-impact acts.
arxiv-2603-19094: Gipouloux and co-authors build quantum versions of active particles whose motion comes from crafted dissipation. A linked, uneven bath supplies the drive that makes a particle active. One model hops on a lattice with both clean and lossy steps. Others adapt classic active forms like run-and-tumble and active Brownian motion. All show key active traits in the tests. Motion shifts from plain diffusion to active diffusion over time. Edge effects run strong through a skin effect. Circuits or cold gases could host such systems, they suggest.
arxiv-2603-19894: Guardia and co-authors study how asteroid orbits can drift near the 3:1 Kirkwood gap in the asteroid belt. They use the restricted planar elliptic three-body problem, with the Sun and Jupiter acting on the asteroid. Jupiter's own orbit is taken as nearly circular. For a rich set of starting states, the asteroid's eccentricity wanders over time. That wandering looks like a diffusion process, with chance coming from the starting state. The result shows ordered and chaotic motion can coexist in the belt.
arxiv-2603-20094: De Santis and co-authors use language models to unify aerospace component qualification data. Satellite board designers need each part's qualification status fast. Siloed department databases make that status hard to retrieve and often inconsistent. Their pipeline builds a virtual knowledge graph over the varied sources. Language models help clean the data and enrich retrieval, cutting manual work. Queries run through ontology-based access for structured facts. A vector search finds qualifications by similar text. A cost-benefit study favors this pipeline over retrieval setups that rely on models alone.
arxiv-2603-20294: Kulkarni constructs a three-dimensional CSS quantum error-correcting code on the face-centered cubic lattice. Qubits sit on lattice edges, and both stabilizer types have weight 12. Checks confirm the code is valid and holds 130 logical qubits at one size. Its encoding rate reaches about 67%, far above the cubic toric code. The minimum distance is only 3, proven by exhaustive checks. Kulkarni also adapts a matching decoder to the lattice geometry. The code shows a tenfold coding gain at low error rates.
arxiv-2603-20394: Carlson and Shephard set out a framework for asking when time series predictions are causal. Their potential system is a nonparametric model of time series behavior. It measures how moving an assignment at one time affects a later outcome. The setup accounts for observed features along the way. It gives causal content to tools like local projections and impulse responses. It also underlies structural vector autoregressions and time series experiments. The work bridges a gap with cross-sectional causal methods.
arxiv-2603-20494: Tannier and co-authors introduce PARHAF, a French corpus of clinical reports for fictitious patients. Privacy rules block sharing of real medical records for language research. PARHAF instead uses expert-written reports on invented cases. A structured protocol joined clinician skill with national epidemiological guidance. In total, 104 medical residents across 18 specialties wrote the reports. The corpus holds 7,394 reports covering 5,009 patient cases. Special subsets serve oncology, infection, and coding extraction tasks. The reports are openly licensed for free sharing.
arxiv-2603-20594: Yang and Lan study ringdown waves from black bounce spacetimes. One metric can rest on more than one matter source. They use the Simpson-Visser case, which shifts from black hole to wormhole at a set bounce size. They derive master equations for a fluid source and for a field based source. Time domain runs then yield the quasinormal modes. The field source damps faster in the black hole branch. It damps slower in the wormhole branch.
arxiv-2603-20994: Hornig and Mirsky formalize intelligent disobedience, where an assistant breaks a human order to prevent harm. Shared autonomy creates this tension often. Their Intelligent Disobedience Game models a human leader and an assistive follower with unequal information. It uses a Stackelberg game setup over many steps. They characterize best strategies for both sides. They also name safety traps, where the system avoids harm forever but never reaches the human's goal. The game is recast as a multi-agent Markov decision process, giving a compact testbed for training agents.
arxiv-2603-21294: Dorschel and co-authors show that standard cell libraries can hide stealthy hardware Trojans. They revisit a public data set of microscope images of four chips at shrinking technology nodes. Prior work could not tell whether detection gaps came from insertion tricks, image quality, or the libraries themselves. With new metrics, they find clear differences between process nodes. In every case, some cells perform distinct logic yet look identical in backside images. They exploit this to build a privilege escalation backdoor in an Ibex RISC-V core.
arxiv-2603-21694: Barcau and co-authors study bridges, a kind of morphism between encryption schemes. To each bridge they attach an encryption scheme of its own, and they examine that scheme's security. Their construction recipe is inspired by Gentry's bootstrapping, the trick behind fully homomorphic encryption. The main theorem says a bridge's security reduces to the security of the first scheme, plus one technical extra assumption. The work maps how security travels across these connecting structures. It sits in theoretical cryptography, with definitions and reductions rather than experiments.
arxiv-2603-22194: Finski gives analytic formulas for two invariants of graded linear series. The invariants are the Kodaira-Iitaka dimension and the multiplicity. Both are expressed through the intersection theory of a plurisubharmonic envelope. He refines the formulas at two levels, pointwise and metric. At the pointwise level, partial Bergman kernels converge weakly. At the metric level, he computes volume ratios for unit balls under sup norms. He also defines a non-pluripolar version of the dimension. It sits above the classical invariant and below earlier numerical versions.
arxiv-2603-22294: Jayaraman and co-authors improve synthetic training data for hard reasoning tasks. Small models learn well from data made by large models, if the data is good and varied. The team studies the spread of generated examples in embedding space. They find a clear link between local example density and accuracy nearby. Dense areas predict well, and sparse areas predict poorly. Their pipeline samples with embeddings to target the thin spots. Across several benchmarks, the targeted data lifts performance in a steady way.
arxiv-2603-22394: Bae and co-authors define a new kind of early-universe perturbation, kinetic isocurvature. In this pattern, dark matter density stays even against photon density. What varies from place to place is the dark matter's kinetic energy. Such patterns arise when a heavy field decays into fast dark matter at varying rates. As the dark matter cools, the energy gaps leave density nearly untouched. That lets the pattern slip past cosmic microwave background limits. It survives instead as patch-to-patch shifts in the free-streaming scale.
arxiv-2603-22494: Dutta and co-authors ask whether a new pseudoscalar particle could add to Higgs plus Z production at the LHC. Such a particle arises in models with extended scalar sectors, like the two-Higgs-doublet model. Made through gluon fusion, it could rival the standard rate. The authors compute total and detailed cross sections for two mass ranges. A light pseudoscalar near 95 GeV adds too little to constrain the models. Heavier ones can overshoot current data and so rule out parts of the parameter space.
arxiv-2603-22794: Qu and co-authors present Flickerformer, a network that removes flicker from burst photos. Flicker comes from unstable light and row-wise exposure faults. It has two traits the authors exploit: periodicity and directionality. A phase-based module merges burst frames by phase correlation. An autocorrelation network picks up repeating patterns inside each frame. A wavelet-based attention module uses high-frequency cues to restore dark regions. Tests beat prior top methods on both scores and visual quality.
arxiv-2603-22994: Mehrabankar and co-authors track how quantum correlations fade in two coupled oscillators in a thermal bath. They follow quantum discord, entanglement, and purity over time. The system starts in a squeezed vacuum state. Heat speeds the loss of correlations and purity. Stronger dissipation also hurts correlations, yet it raises steady-state purity. More squeezing protects correlations and extends entanglement life. Discord proves hardier than entanglement, which can die suddenly and revive. The authors draw lessons for robust quantum information protocols.
arxiv-2603-23194: Lei and co-authors present PhysSkin, a framework for real-time physics-based animation across shapes. It follows the spirit of linear blend skinning. Continuous skinning fields lift low-dimensional motion handles to full deformations. A neural autoencoder learns those fields with no mesh dependence. Its encoder uses transformers, and a decoder uses cross-attention. A self-supervised physics strategy balances energy, smoothness, and orthogonality goals. On-the-fly normalization and conflict-aware gradient fixes aid training. PhysSkin generalizes across shapes and discretizations, the authors report.
arxiv-2603-23394: Zheng and seven co-authors model DNA-based molecular communication with a microarray receiver. Bound DNA signals suffer inter-symbol interference and colored counting noise. Their Markov model rests on a voxelized reaction-diffusion picture. A block-structured matrix tracks transport plus binding and unbinding. From it they read the channel impulse response, gain, and memory length. They derive a binomial noise model with an exact covariance. Two receivers follow: a differential-threshold detector and a decision-feedback equalizer. Which receiver wins depends on the memory regime.
arxiv-2603-23694: Kats and five co-authors weave contrastive learning straight into medical image registration. Aligning scans across time or modality fights shifting brightness and warped tissue. Their model, CoRe, trains its features and its alignment in one joint pass. The features learn to shrug off tissue warps while staying true to anatomy. Tests cover belly and chest scans, within one patient and across patients. CoRe beats strong rival methods on both fronts.
arxiv-2603-23794: Wesp and co-authors use sparse autoencoders to make medical image features easier to read. Vision foundation models encode scans in dense vectors that clinicians cannot inspect. The team trains autoencoders on embeddings from BiomedParse and DINOv3, using 909,873 CT and MRI slices. The sparse features rebuild the vectors well and keep most task performance with just 10 features. They also match named concepts and support search by plain language. The authors see a path to concept-based medical vision.
arxiv-2603-23894: Kemp studies Latin squares that contain disjoint subsquares whose orders sum to at most the full order. When the sum equals the order, such an arrangement is called a realization, and existence is only partly solved. Kemp proves a general necessary condition for existence. He settles existence fully when there are at most three subsquares, or when all subsquares share one order. He also proves that such a square always exists when the full order is at least the largest subsquare plus the sum of all orders.
arxiv-2603-23994: Nie and co-authors study why iterative generative optimization with language models often fails in practice. Such loops improve code, workflows, or prompts from execution feedback, yet only 9 percent of surveyed agents used automated optimization. The authors blame hidden design choices: the starting artifact, the credit horizon, and how trials are batched as evidence. Case studies in MLAgentBench, Atari, and BigBench Extra Hard show each choice can decide success. They give practical guidance for setting up these learning loops.
arxiv-2603-24294: Lee and co-authors present VERIA, a method that augments rare driving classes for 3D object detection. Rare classes vary widely, and copy-paste augmentation adds little new variety. VERIA builds synchronized image and LiDAR instances with off-the-shelf foundation models. It then checks each instance in stages, on meaning and on geometry, keeping ones that match real LiDAR statistics. Step-by-step yield logs show where the pipeline loses candidates. On nuScenes and Lyft data, rare-class detection improves in both LiDAR-only and multimodal setups.
arxiv-2603-24594: Jacot introduces the Multilevel Euler-Maruyama method for solving stochastic and ordinary differential equations. The method uses a ladder of drift approximations, from cheap and rough to costly and accurate, needing only a few evaluations of the best one. When the drift is harder than Monte Carlo, the method reaches a target accuracy at the cost of one drift evaluation, beating the classic rate. For diffusion models, the levels are UNets of growing size. Experiments on CelebA image generation show up to fourfold speedups, confirming the theory.
arxiv-2603-24894: Deglurkar and co-authors calibrate reachable sets with an active learning method, Approximate Pick-to-Learn. Reachability tools built on learned models need calibration to keep guarantees honest. Random sampling inside the reachable set can demand costly sample counts. Their method adapts the Pick-to-Learn algorithm, which carries generalisation bounds, to active sample choice. Sample selection maximises an approximate error function, and conformal prediction keeps it close to true model error. On a simulated drone racing task, it needs fewer samples and yields more accurate sets than baselines.
arxiv-2603-25494: Wang and co-authors fill in full 3D room scenes from one indoor photo with AdaSFormer. Indoor completion is harder than outdoor work: layouts tangle and objects hide each other. Transformers see the whole room at once but eat memory and blur fine detail. Their serialized design learns shifts that resize its field of view per spot. A center-based position code and a blend layer join map and photo traits cleanly. On NYUv2 and Occ-ScanNet it sets the best scores yet.
arxiv-2603-25594: Ley, Tran, and Zweibel extend the double-adiabatic equations into the relativistic regime. These equations track how pressures evolve in a magnetized plasma without collisions. The authors solve the drift kinetic equation for a uniform plasma. Their solution depends on the magnetic field and density changes. For an ultrarelativistic gas, they derive formulas for the parallel and perpendicular pressures. They test the results with particle-in-cell simulations of shearing and compressing boxes. The results apply to cosmic rays and pair plasmas in jets and accretion flows.
arxiv-2603-25694: Zelakiewicz and co-authors ask what one visit by the Habitable Worlds Observatory could reveal about an Earth-like planet. They model photon-counting noise for a design with a charge-6 vector-vortex coronagraph. They pair that noise model with five modern Earth models seen at quadrature. Spectral retrievals with the POSEIDON code then try to recover surface and air makeup. The authors find strong ties among radius, surface pressure, surface type, and cloud cover. These ties can hide signs of life, such as the red edge from chlorophyll.
arxiv-2603-25894: El-Awady models plastic deformation in metals by listening to the sounds the material makes. The data come from compressing nickel micropillars, which emit acoustic pulses as they deform. A wavelet method with Morlet transforms picks out events across frequency bands. It finds small events that past work missed. The events line up well with stress drops in the loading curve. Machine learning on engineered features beats raw-signal classifiers, El-Awady reports. Clustering reveals four event types tied to distinct deformation mechanisms.
arxiv-2603-25994: Shi and co-authors present NLCE, a method that erases a concept from image generators without harming its neighbors. Removing one concept can weaken related ones nearby in meaning. NLCE works in three stages and needs no retraining. First, a spectral tweak dims the target concept in embedding space while steadying its neighbors. Next, an attention gate finds spots where traces of the concept remain. A final gated step erases only those spots. On flower and dog breed data, close categories survive far better, the authors report.
arxiv-2603-26094: Pattanaik and Mishra hunt for signs of the Type-I seesaw in neutrino data. Their model has three active and three sterile neutrinos. An exact seesaw relation links the heavy sterile sector to what experiments see. They scan the 21-dimensional parameter space with Monte Carlo methods. Only points that fit current oscillation data within three sigma survive. Light sterile states bend spectra strongly at DUNE, NOvA, and JUNO. Heavier ones fade from view. Combined limits squeeze the mass sum to about 0.05 to 0.07 electron volts.
arxiv-2603-26494: Roll asks whether quantum language models truly use quantum effects, or just run classical tricks on quantum hardware. He runs the first mechanistic study of these models, mixing gate ablation, entanglement tracking, and density-matrix swaps. The test task needs long-range links between tokens. One-qubit models prove exactly simulable by classical means and copy the classical plan. Two-qubit models instead store context in entanglement between qubits, backed by three causal tests. On real hardware, noise kills the entanglement plan while the classical one survives.
arxiv-2603-26694: Vilela Mendes explores whether spacetime carries a hidden Kähler or quaternion-Kähler structure. He embeds real Lorentzian spacetime in a manifold built from higher division algebras with Hermitian metrics. Making the symmetry demands of those algebras fit together yields a set of quantum numbers. The numbers recall those of the Standard Model of particle physics, which he takes as a hint. Real spacetime then sits as a submanifold that inherits the symmetry limits of the larger space around it.
arxiv-2603-27094: Panchigar and co-authors introduce the Sovereign Context Protocol, an attribution layer between language models and human content. Models consume vast human work for training and live answers, yet creators stay invisible. The protocol logs, licenses, and attributes every access event by default. Six core methods cover creator profiles, search, retrieval, scoring, verification, and auditing. Access runs over REST and MCP-ready interfaces. A threat model spans five adversary classes, and revenue follows a log-proportional rule. A reference build exists in FastAPI.
arxiv-2603-27394: Andreev studies small spin waves in four-part antiferromagnetic materials. The base state has spins in an up-up-down-down pattern. He works out wave speeds for spins along the magnet axis. He then treats spins set across that axis. In that case up to four waves can appear. At least one wave always has a squared frequency below zero. That means the state is unstable. The math uses a chain of spins and a smooth medium limit.
arxiv-2603-27494: Zhao and co-authors train vision models to crop images with real care. Many models glance at the whole scene and skim the crop. Their two-stage reinforcement method attacks that habit. Stage one blurs the global view to create an information gap. The model must then mine the crop for answers. Stage two adds a grounding loss for exact crop boxes. Only a few box labels are needed. Tests show clear gains in fine visual question answering.
arxiv-2603-27594: Liu and Xie prove stability for fluid-structure interaction schemes. Their methods couple fluid flow and elastic solids in one system. A new Piola-type map handles the moving fluid mesh. Backward Euler steps advance both model forms in time. Hybrid discontinuous Galerkin methods cover flow and solid parts. A Galerkin method moves the fluid mesh itself. Proofs cover time-only and full discretization. Velocity fields stay exactly divergence-free. Tests confirm the schemes behave as promised.
arxiv-2603-27694: Gu and co-authors ask if language models truly mimic human thought. Behavior copies may hide shallow pattern matching. Their benchmark tracks 217 AI researchers over time. Each author's papers stand in for their thinking path. Tests force cross-domain and time-shifted generalization. A new metric scores individual cognitive alignment. Top models and boost tricks face the full suite. Results form a first map of this hard question.
arxiv-2603-27894: Albertini and D'Alessandro design quantum controls that shrug off model errors. Real devices drift from their nominal Hamiltonians. Sensitivity functions capture how paths bend under such drift. The control task trades field energy against sensitivity size. A single qubit with dephasing gets full treatment. State transfer is the test goal there. At huge sensitivity weight, the best control zeroes it out. Elliptic integrals give the exact solution.
arxiv-2603-28394: Güemes-Palau and four co-authors survey how researchers model network performance, from early simulators to deep learning. The field predicts how packet flows will behave in a given network, feeding planning and control tools. Classic methods rest on discrete event simulation and queueing theory. Newer work adds parallel simulation, machine learning, and hybrids. The survey sorts these into a taxonomy and tracks how aims and evaluation habits shifted over decades of wired network research.
arxiv-2603-28894: Yadalam and Mitchison present a tensor network method to compute charge transfer statistics in quantum circuits. The system is an interacting lattice with U(1) symmetry, split at an interface. Their method uses a matrix product state form of the process tensor. That form captures how the bulk affects the interface degrees of freedom. A truncation scheme keeps the normalization and traits of the generating function. Tests on the Heisenberg XXZ circuit model recovered the transport exponents. They cover ballistic, superdiffusive, and diffusive regimes, plus anomalous scaling outside the ballistic case.
arxiv-2603-29194: Tiwari and Fofadiya present a multi-layer memory framework for language-model agents. Long chats suffer semantic drift and unstable recall. Their design splits dialogue history into three layers. Working, episodic, and semantic layers store different kinds of memory. Adaptive gating controls what gets retrieved. Retention rules keep growth bounded across sessions. On LOCOMO and LOCCO tests, success rate reached 46.85 percent. Six-period retention hit 56.90 percent, and false memories fell to 5.1 percent.
arxiv-2603-29294: Kamiya and co-authors test the CITIUS detector with heavy charged particles and neutrons. CITIUS was built as a fast X-ray detector for SPring-8-II. The team fired alpha particles from an americium source at it. Four bias voltages set how far charge spread in the device. A Geant4 model was fitted to the measured cluster shapes. The fit fixed four model values. The team then used the model to predict image sharpness. In gain-selecting mode, sharpness improved a lot for both particle types.
arxiv-2603-29394: Suh and co-authors present AA-Splat, a feed-forward method for 3D Gaussian splatting without aliasing. Fast splatting methods render new views from sparse inputs. Wrong screen-space filters cause artifacts at new sampling rates. Their design adds a 3D band-limiting filter to the pipeline. It uses maximal frequency bounds from many views. An opacity balancing step merges the expanded primitives smoothly. Against a leading baseline, image quality rose by several decibels. Gains held from quarter scale to four times scale.
arxiv-2603-29694: Paxton and co-authors test how skin color affects skin lesion segmentation. Early melanoma detection depends on clean lesion outlines. Fairness work has focused on classification, not this earlier step. They test three strong models on two public dermoscopic datasets. Instead of coarse tone groups, they use continuous pigment measures per image. Distribution distances gauge the contrast between lesion and skin. Global tone showed only weak links to segmentation quality. Low lesion-skin contrast tracked larger errors across models. Fairness fixes should target low-contrast lesions first.
arxiv-2603-29994: Arzel and Lehdili merge stochastic control with deep hedging for options under transaction costs. They first derive the best hedge for a European call under CARA utility. That route yields a no-transaction band from a quasi-variational inequality. They then build two neural variants of a band network. One centers delta explicitly. The other bakes in the Whalley-Wilmott formula as a prior. The second converges faster and tracks control bands closely. Both extend to bull call spreads.
arxiv-2604-00294: Vyacheslav Yukalov and Yukalova offer a way to sum virial expansions, density-power series for equations of state, divergent at finite densities. Padé summation, the usual fix, suffers non-unique approximants and false poles, and can miss poles that physics demands. Their self-similar method is regular, uniquely defined, needs no fitting parameters and can reveal true poles. Its accuracy matches fitted Padé sums and Monte Carlo, and it recovers the function exactly, shown for hard-disk and hard-sphere fluids and power-law systems.
arxiv-2604-00594: Ge and colleagues offer a framework that predicts, task by task, whether an agentic coding benchmark task will succeed or fail. As coding agents shift from single-step generation to multi-step tool use, knowing which tasks will challenge agents, and why, grows harder. Aggregate pass rates hide task diversity within a benchmark. The framework augments item response theory with rich task features, drawing on issue statements, repository contexts, and test cases, plus solutions. It also splits agent ability into language-model and scaffold components.
arxiv-2604-00694: Tham and colleagues argue that internal APIs, not browser-first design, should power the agentic web. Most sites are built for human browsers, not agents. Agents browse pages, inspect document models, and decode routes, a slow, brittle process done over and over. Every modern site exposes internal APIs behind its interface, first-party endpoints powering its functions. Unbrowse, a shared route graph, turns route discovery by browsers into an index of callable first-party interfaces. It learns routes passively from web traffic and serves saved routes by API calls.
arxiv-2604-00794: Pabst and Hassanali challenge the usual reading of water's strange behavior as proof of two distinct liquids. Using machine-learning-accelerated simulations checked against spectroscopic, structural, and dynamical experiments, they show that supposed two-liquid signals match the onset of a glassy, non-ergodic state instead. Their mapping across pressure and temperature points to a simpler reading. Low-density water may simply have a glass-transition temperature of 189 K, plus or minus 8.
arxiv-2604-00894: Kolb and Sikstel present MultiWave, a C++ framework for hyperbolic balance laws, designed as a lab for quickly building and testing math concepts. They show a discontinuous Galerkin method with multiresolution grid tuning, noting a modular design that lets users extend the code while reusing older code. Scaling studies on a spread-out memory machine show speed holds to large rank counts. This tuning cuts cost per time step a lot against uniform-grid runs at full detail.
arxiv-2604-00994: Miehling and Kuebler present a multimodal pipeline for analyzing state-funded news coverage of the Israel-Hamas war on YouTube Shorts. It combines automatic transcription, aspect-based sentiment analysis, and semantic scene classification. Applied to over 2,300 Shorts and more than 94,000 frames, it finds transcript sentiment on specific aspects varies across outlets and over time, while scene types track visual cues matching real-world events. Smaller domain-adapted models beat large transformers and language models on sentiment analysis, showing how useful resource-efficient approaches are for humanities research.
arxiv-2604-01094: Bajaj and colleagues show that several language models display a serial-recall pattern in context, giving peak probability to tokens right after a repeated token. Using the free-recall paradigm from cognitive science, they run ablations and find that induction heads, attention heads that look to the token following a previous occurrence, drive the effect. Removing high-induction heads sharply cuts the +1 lag bias, unlike random-head removal, and hurts few-shot serial recall more. The work ties induction heads mechanistically to ordered retrieval and temporal context handling.
arxiv-2604-01194:
AgentWatcher is a rule-based monitor for prompt injection attacks in 2026. Large language models and their agent applications are highly vulnerable. Prompt injection can steer an agent through text it merely reads.

State-of-the-art detection methods carry two limitations, the authors argue. First, effectiveness degrades significantly as context length increases in long inputs. Second, they lack explicit rules defining what prompt injection is. Detection decisions thus stay implicit, opaque, and hard to reason about. A rule-based watcher aims to fix both problems at once. Explicit rules make each flag explainable to a human reviewer. Security readers get a monitor designed for long, real agent contexts.
arxiv-2604-01294: Chiba and colleagues study the tree-ring structure of Galactic bar resonance in N-body Milky Way simulations, with or without Sagittarius dwarf galaxy perturbations. In an idealized disk model, stars trapped in corotation resonance form tree rings in phase space. As the expanding resonance captures surrounding stars at its surface, earlier-captured inner-disk stars stay near the core. The paper shows this structure emerges in a noisy disk, despite spiral arms, Sagittarius encounters, changing pattern speed, and numerical noise driving stellar diffusion.
arxiv-2604-01394: Yasaveev and colleagues describe a method for measuring B meson production fractions at the Upsilon(4S) resonance in B factories. Counting single- and double-inclusive charmed meson production at the resonance gives tagging of B0 anti-B0 and B+ B- events. A feasibility study says precision close to the current world average can be reached without assumptions, since calculations rely solely on event yields.
arxiv-2604-01494: Delgado Cervantes and colleagues present MOVis, a lightweight tool that visualizes missed patches between source and target software variants. Clone-and-own development produces independent variants, so a fix landing in one repository often never reaches the others. PaReco has shown thousands of missed patches exist across ecosystems, yet its output gives limited support for understanding propagation. MOVis loads PaReco's classifications and shows patched and buggy hunks, highlighting regions and structural differences that hinder reuse. That lets developers locate missed fixes, understand adaptations, and maintain consistency across variants.
arxiv-2604-01594: Harootonian and colleagues test whether large language models decide what to teach by reasoning about a learner's knowledge or by simple rules. In a task used to study human teaching, a teacher model sees a learner's path through a reward-annotated directed graph. It must reveal one edge so the learner picks a better path if they replan. They fit models' trial-by-trial choices with human cognitive models, including a Bayes-Optimal teacher inferring missing transitions via inverse planning. Comparison shows Bayes-Optimal teaching best explains most models' choices.
arxiv-2604-01794: Avesani and colleagues develop a framework for sparse multiscale kernel approximation of scattered data problems using samplets. Samplets analyze localized discrete signed measures, enabling quasi-sparse kernel matrices for smooth kernels and smoothness detection. They select sites using the kernel Hilbert space norm of samplet coefficients, yielding few sites that greatly shrink the problem. On the reduced subspace they solve an l1 least-squares problem with a semismooth Newton method, stabilized by online low-rank SVD against ill-conditioning. Tests in two and three dimensions show sparser reconstructions.
arxiv-2604-01894: Sapoutzoglou, Terzakis and Pateraki offer SHARC, a scheme for rebuilding 3D shapes of any hole count from spherical harmonic pieces. Distance fields anchored at inner reference points capture fine surface detail, with a cost rule balancing sparse placement, central position and visibility. Each point's visible distances, sampled by ray casting, become harmonic coefficients via a fast transform, then pass a low-pass filter and a consistency fix. Tests beat leading rivals on rebuild accuracy and speed without bloating the model, and the code is public.
arxiv-2604-01994: Zhang and colleagues animate 4D scenes from 3D views with Resonance4D, skipping heavy video and optical flow systems costlier than the simulator. Their move, dual domain Motion Supervision, enforces spatial consistency for local shape change and frequency consistency for global patterns. Text grouping plus guided start splits Gaussians into object part regions for joint optimization of parameters. Tests on made and real scenes show strong quality and motion match. Peak GPU memory fell from over 35 GB to around 20 GB, letting 4D simulation run on one home graphics card.
arxiv-2604-02094: González, Elvira and Míguez rethink importance sampling by treating observations as random, not fixed. In their frame a link function joins the fixed observation and random observation views. Monte Carlo error stays finite and converges at the standard rate for any dimension exactly when that link function is Bochner integrable. The result names the quantity that controls error growth with dimension and offers a principled escape from worst case analyses. Worked examples cover linear Gaussian systems and bounded observation models.
arxiv-2604-02394: Muneeb and Ascher benchmark 86 heritability methods across six tool families and ten method groups on 10 UK Biobank traits, yielding 844 estimates. The trait heritability varies widely, with about 16 percent of estimates negative, concentrated in free regimes. Algorithm choice and GRM scaling move estimates most. Yet downstream risk score performance barely tracks the magnitude, with near zero, non significant correlations for both frameworks tested. The measure is best read as a method sensitive modeling parameter, reported with its full recipe, not a stable scalar input.
arxiv-2604-02494: Becerra-Deana and colleagues use a mode selective photonic lantern for multi plane confocal imaging. The fiber device turns single mode light into multiple linearly polarized modes, allowing detection of multiple planes at once. With a four port lantern handling three group modes, they demonstrate high throughput imaging across planes at once. Focus differences across modes enable multi plane detection via a spatial division multiplexer, with some trade off in resolution and field of view.
arxiv-2604-02594: The CMS collaboration reports the first evidence in CMS data for production of two Z bosons plus a photon in proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV. Using data from 2016 to 2018 with 138 inverse femtobarns, the ZZ-photon signal reaches 3.7 standard deviations observed against 3.1 expected. The measured fiducial cross section is 60 attobarns, and the related four-lepton-plus-photon channel reaches the 5.0 standard deviation observation threshold.
arxiv-2604-02794: Zhang and eight colleagues present CharTool, a tool-integrated system for chart reasoning in multimodal language models. Charts demand fine-grained visual grounding and exact numerical computation, yet training data is scarce. Their DuoChart pipeline mixes synthesized and real charts for training data, while CharTool adds image cropping for local perception and code-based computation for arithmetic. CharTool-7B beats its base model by 8.0 percent on CharXiv reasoning.
arxiv-2604-02894: Reiher and Zotova answer Leo Versteegen's question on large sum-free sets in finite vector spaces. For n at least 3, every large sum-free set in F5 to the power n falls into two cases. Large means size at least 28 times the (n minus 3)th power of 5. Such a set either sits inside two parallel hyperplanes combined. Or it is isomorphic to a product of a special sum-free 28-set in F5 cubed with F5 to the power n minus 3.
arxiv-2604-02994: Kougang-Yombi and Hązła connect worst-case code properties with random-noise performance by bounding weight distributions directly. They extend a recent list-decoding result from linear codes to all codes, then improve the minimum-distance bound for linear codes for alphabets of four or more symbols. Their approach leans on erasure behavior and inequalities from Samorodnitsky, yielding a broader method for judging symmetric-channel performance.
arxiv-2604-03194: Rather, Wang, and Li study when the smaller quotient matrix of a split matrix holds every distinct eigenvalue of the full matrix. They correct the distinction between the coarsest equitable partition and the smallest capturing quotient, then give an exact lifting method and an eigenspace test. Twin cells and geometric multiplicity yield further capture results, checked across several graph matrix types.
arxiv-2604-03494: Selco and colleagues show that disorder can stop shielding a driven quantum system from heating once pulse control adds a second drive frequency and the disorder itself shifts. In a carbon-13 nuclear-spin network in diamond, they see sharp heating peaks at double- and triple-spin-flip resonances forecast by two-mode Floquet mixing. A switching-noise model traces the uptake to electron-spin motion that tunes rare nuclear clusters into multi-photon match.
arxiv-2604-03594: Paul and Proistosescu propose a way to test objective tuning methods with the Single Column Atmosphere Model. It keeps key physics of general flow models at far lower compute cost. A perfect-model test with a known true parameter set makes fake readings like those from ARM field campaigns. Point guesses cut model-observation mismatch greatly without finding true values. A Bayesian setup with a Gaussian Process mimic and Markov Chain Monte Carlo gives tighter limits and steadier finds.
arxiv-2604-03694: Leif Azzopardi and Frans van de Sluis examined why shoppers who value ethical, environmental, and social concerns often buy products that clash with those values. A survey of 286 recent buyers found many were simply indifferent or uninformed, while hard-to-find and unreliable information widened the gap further. The authors read part of the gap as a search problem, calling for tools that surface responsible product facts.
arxiv-2604-03794: Takeyuki Iwasaki and Yutaka Hori derived guaranteed upper and lower bounds for transient moments in stochastic chemical reaction networks, where copy numbers jump as a Markov chain. Exact statistics stall because moment equations never close, so the pair turned to Kolmogorov's backward equation, a dual view of the governing equation. Combined with generator monotonicity, the dual view yields a finite linear system whose inner products give bounds across many starting states at once.
arxiv-2604-03894: Amir Babak Aazami analyzed the normal form of a curvature-related operator for gradient Ricci 4-solitons in the work of Cao and Tran. He showed that the curvature operator of the Koiso-Cao soliton inherits that normal form. Work by Johnson then yields a normal form for that operator relative to algebraic Kähler curvature operators. The note is short and technical, pinning down the algebraic shape of a key example.
arxiv-2604-04394: Jeong and Lee study Stackelberg Q-value iteration in two-player general-sum Markov games. Single-agent learning has succeeded in theory and practice, but general-sum games resist extension. The authors introduce a relaxed policy condition fitted to the Stackelberg setting and model learning as a switching system. Building upper and lower comparison systems, they prove finite-time error bounds for Q-functions and characterize convergence. To their knowledge, these are the first finite-time guarantees for Stackelberg Q-value iteration in general-sum Markov games.
arxiv-2604-04694: Kyriazis and four colleagues present Mestra, a system for CGRA tenancy with dynamic scheduling and resource allocation. Modern coarse grain reconfigurable arrays grow in size, making efficient use by one application difficult. Multi-tenant CGRAs promise better hardware use, but attempts fail on fragmentation and migration. Mestra handles fragmentation from out-of-order kernels by supporting stateless and stateful live kernel migration. On an Alveo-U280 FPGA card, sharing improves workload makespan by up to 70.48 percent. Live kernel migration reduces tail latency on fragmented layouts by up to 29.60 percent.
arxiv-2604-04794: Gao and seven colleagues measure luminosity functions for central and satellite galaxies in haloes from redshift one to zero, from DESI and HSC data. Satellite functions shift little over that span. Blue satellites fit a Schechter function with a slope near minus 1.2. Red satellites show a faint end upturn with a slope near minus 1.75 in all bins. The low mass red sequence was in place by redshift one, favouring early formation over quenching. Satellites fade faster than models predict, and quenched fractions bottom out near a billion solar masses.
arxiv-2604-05194: Koch and Nandan widen saddle-nodes to account for center shapes and define their ghost pulls, filling a gap in tools for transient motion. Long waits matter in ecology, brain work, and cells, and ghost pulls draw notice for their traits and seen presence. Concepts and tools for sorting ghost gears lag behind those for final motion. They give methods to spot ghost pulls and forms such as ghost channels and ghost cycles, lighting transient motion, including ghost splits. The methods ship as PyGhostID, an open-source Python package.
arxiv-2604-05794: Li and three colleagues reconstruct strand-level hair from single-camera video with EfficientMonoHair. Fusion-patch multi-view optimization cuts iteration counts while parallel hair growing relaxes voxel limits for stable large-scale tracing. Real hairstyles reconstruct with high fidelity, and synthetic tests match leading quality while running nearly ten times faster.
arxiv-2604-05994: Zhou splits the superfluid weight of magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene into conventional band-velocity and geometric interband-coherence parts. In the flat band, quantum geometry gives 22 to 26 percent of the weight at charge neutrality, rising to about 55 to 58 percent once remote bands join, purely through interband coherence. That share peaks near fillings of plus or minus two, where superconductivity runs strongest.
arxiv-2604-06094: Chirkov and Lobanov fix a mismatch in quantum convolutional networks, where shifting an image pixel should shift its encoded form in step. They prove every layer respecting this pixel cyclic shift takes one specific form: a Fourier-mode multiplexer, then an inverse quantum Fourier transform. From that result they build a deep network with measurement-based pooling, deferred conditioning, and cancelled transforms between layers. They also prove its gradients stay bounded below as depth grows, ruling out a depth-driven barren plateau.
arxiv-2604-06194: Chaimanowong argues that unregulated generative AI can harm content platforms themselves, not just displaced creators. Human creators typically go unpaid for works used in training, while cheap machine output threatens to crowd out human shares and pollute future training data. The paper shows unregulated use distorts the content mix in ways that lower consumer engagement and platform profit. A simple economically driven creator compensation scheme instead rewards high-value human creation without needing an AI detector, cutting data pollution while lifting engagement and profit.
arxiv-2604-06494: Guija-Valiente and Suárez give neural networks design tools for Scalable Vector Graphics, closing the people gap. DesigNet is a hierarchical Transformer-VAE working on SVG strings with continuous command coding. Two modules do the core work. A continuity self-refinement module predicts grades for each curve point and sets them through Bézier control points. An alignment module snaps horizontal or vertical lines. It yields editable outlines with competitive results and notably higher continuity and alignment accuracy, making outputs easier to refine and use professionally.
arxiv-2604-06594: Peng, Min, and Jiang show that the breathing oscillation of a scale-invariant quantum gas directly reveals its energy fluctuations. In gases with SO(2,1) symmetry, the oscillation size links exactly to energy spread. The link's ratio is fixed only by the Bargmann index, which labels the system's symmetry representation, so it ignores microscopic details and driving methods alike. Excited breathing states also follow a single-parameter statistical pattern, opening a symmetry-based way to read nonequilibrium energy statistics from collective motion.
arxiv-2604-06794: Luo and four colleagues free chain-of-thought decoding from fixed answer sets. Prompt-free CoT-decoding builds reasoning paths without hand-built prompts, but only for set-answer problems. Their GCoT-decoding branches in two stages, combining Fibonacci sampling with error backtracking to propose paths. Each path splits into reasoning and answer spans for confidence scoring, and similar paths merge into a consensus answer instead of a plain majority vote. Tests on six datasets covering fixed and free questions keep strong fixed-task scores while lifting free-task results.
arxiv-2604-06994: Altilia and five colleagues design and characterize a homodyne detector for pulsed sources at 100 MHz. Conventional amplifier designs suffer nonlinearities with pulses, but the new approach amplifies the photocurrent at the photodiode node without loops. Theory predicts variance, signal-to-noise ratio, and correlations. Built with two photodiodes and a 1030 nm laser at 100 MHz, the detector shows linearity and shot-noise variance scaling with power. Tuning the integration window gives about 14 dB signal-to-noise ratio, with negligible correlations.
arxiv-2604-07194: He and five colleagues watch magnetostriction, the shape change of a magnetic gas, shift from strongly stretched to nearly round. Their subject is a flat gas of erbium-166 atoms, imaged in place. They track the crossover from an anisotropic superfluid core to isotropic thermal wings and build a mean-field model that reads temperature and chemical potential from a single fit. The low-density wings follow a local equation of state, giving a cleaner path to thermodynamics in two-dimensional dipolar superfluids.
arxiv-2604-07294: Kim and Ryu pack the Galois cohomology of negative Tate twists into one shared cyclotomic complex. The complex lives over the cyclotomic tower of the rationals, the chain of fields built from roots of unity. Descent plus a branch split shows each twist acts only on its own branch. Each twist is then read off by setting the Iwasawa variable at a single point, giving plain formulas for the first and second cohomology groups in the p-adic case.
arxiv-2604-07394: Qiu and seven colleagues present Flux Attention, a layer-wise hybrid attention scheme for long-context inference. Fixed full-sparse splits fail as retrieval needs shift by task, while head-level sparsity unbalances compute and stalls decoding. A light layer router sends each layer to full or sparse attention based on context. Training takes just 12 hours on eight A800 GPUs. Prefill speeds up to 2.8 times and decoding up to 2.0 times, beating baselines on the speed-accuracy trade-off.
arxiv-2604-07694: Jo and Masuda offer temporal hypergraph models in which each node switches between low- and high-activity states, and an edge produces timed events with chance set by high-state counts. Data show timed meetings show event runs and time links. For two making rules, they derive gap spreads and self-links of event runs, for edges and nodes. Despite node-state moves, event flows mix Poisson, short parts, yielding longer-tailed gap spreads and fading self-links. The model shows the link on edge size, seen in data.
arxiv-2604-08094: Roncallo and four colleagues study combining quantum binary models into a multinomial classifier with a hybrid divide-and-conquer approach. Strategies include one-vs-one, one-vs-rest, and a binary decision tree. Each method is benchmarked for compute overhead and impact on quantum advantage. Against a classical binary model copied the same way, the decision tree proves cheap, matching other methods' accuracies with overhead capped at a log function of the total number of classes. The comparison shows when hybrid quantum-classical classification pays and when classical methods suffice.
arxiv-2604-08294: Monte e Freitas and three colleagues evaluate Vision Language Models for Action Quality Assessment across domains, tasks, representations, and prompting strategies. Action Quality Assessment applies to physical therapy, sports coaching, and competitive judging. Vision Language Models hold considerable promise for Action Quality Assessment, but their real performance is largely uncharacterised. Baselines show Gemini 3.1 Pro, Qwen3-VL, and InternVL3.5 barely above random chance. Skeleton data, grounding prompts, reasoning structures, and in-context learning give isolated gains, but none works always.
arxiv-2604-08794: Chandramouli, Sprenger, and Hoefer describe standing forms of the non straight Schrödinger rule with a PT even Wadati field settling toward non straight plane waves. The field mixes an across space varying gain loss profile with a pushing real part. It allows homoclinic forms nearing the same plane wave and heteroclinic forms nearing others in the far field. Far field analysis and number based tests probe whether they exist, their splits, and structure, with use for echoing wave making in spreading media with local gain and loss.
arxiv-2604-09094: Sankaran, Farahbakhsh, and Crespi ask whether abusive speech can be detected from audio in low-resource Indic languages. Transcription is unreliable without strong recognizers, and it throws away tone and emotion that often carry the abuse. Using CLAP, a shared-representation model, direct audio detection comes within one to three points of a fully supervised system. It far outperforms zero-example prompting. Adding a handful of labeled examples per language helps little and varies unpredictably. CLAP audio representations offer a strong, cheap foundation, cutting labeled data needs.
arxiv-2604-09294: Liconti and colleagues introduce POMDAR, a dexterity benchmark for human-like robot hands based on measured task performance. Dexterity is often used in mixed ways, with systems judged under different rules that block fair comparison. POMDAR defines dexterity as performance across hand motions drawn from human motor control groupings, in reality and simulation. Four setups cover upright and flat setups, steady spinning, and pure grasping, with frames to limit motion and block workarounds. A score mixing rightness and speed measures dexterity as throughput.
arxiv-2604-09494: Whitecross and Rahimi propose RecaLLM, tackling lost-in-thought with explicit in-context lookup. RecaLLM is a set of thinking language models post-trained for strong long-context use. In-context lookup and thinking are intertwined: lookup aids thinking, while thinking decides what must be found. In tests, lookup scores fall even after a short thinking span, showing a snag called lost-in-thought. RecaLLM weaves thinking with explicit lookup for middle sub-tasks, with constrained decoding allowing word-for-word copying of evidence spans and RULER and HELMET results.
arxiv-2604-09594: Vira and Harris introduce the Spatial Competence Benchmark. It tests whether large models hold a consistent internal picture of an environment and use it to infer structure and plan under constraints. Tasks span three hierarchical capability buckets and demand executable outputs. Outputs are checked by deterministic verifiers or simulators. Three frontier models score steadily worse up the ladder. Token-budget gains concentrate at low budgets and saturate fast. Failures mostly come from locally plausible geometry that breaks global constraints.
arxiv-2604-10394: Graven studies flat regions ruled by a log weighted quadrature law. A weight that blows up at the origin breaks the tame classical picture. When the region holds the origin, its data stay fixed only up to a point charge there. A broad Schwarz function rule plus a singular inverse problem frame the theory. For simply linked regions, the Riemann map test turns on a rational function exponent.
arxiv-2604-10494: Zhang and six colleagues probe block floating point chips for fault weak spots. Block floating point suits edge neural chips, yet its fault behavior stayed little mapped. Bit and path level fault runs show uneven weak spots and blunt end to end checks. Their fix splits mantissa math from the shared exponent path in a row column blocking plan. The result nears dual backup safety at about 3.6 percent speed cost and under 2 percent hardware cost.
arxiv-2604-10594: Cébron and Personnettaz derive one theory for drag on a conducting sphere oscillating inside a spinning spherical cavity of fluid. The problem matters for planets and liquid-metal tests. Earlier theories handled confinement, spin, viscosity, and magnetism only one at a time. Their framework covers polar and equatorial modes, including Slichter modes of inner cores and deep oceans, with force laws and energy-loss predictions. It accounts for viscous and magnetic pressure, magnetic tension, Alfvén waves, and layers. Computer tests back the predictions across a broad range.
arxiv-2604-10794: Koukoutsis and six colleagues develop a symplectic design for quantum computing on Hamiltonian systems. First, quantum change matches exactly to Hamiltonian flow on a Kahler surface. This enables a shape quantization scheme for systems with vastly packed codes. Second, Liouville-integrable motion induces unitary flow via action-angles and Koopman-von Neumann codes. This allows fast side-by-side flow of large groups, with linked codes. For non-integrable systems, Lie theory builds near-symplectic maps to solvable forms. Derived cost includes exponential memory packing and power-law speedup.
arxiv-2604-10994: Kaleta and five colleagues present LumiMotion, the first Gaussian-based method using scene motion to guide inverse rendering. Inverse rendering recovers lighting and material properties, but existing Gaussian splatting methods target static scenes and assume simple lighting. Motion reveals the same surfaces under changing light, giving stronger cues to separate material from light. LumiMotion learns a dynamic splatting model that lets moving regions deform while static regions stay stable. Tests show gains of 23 percent on albedo and 15 percent on relighting over the next-best baseline.
arxiv-2604-11294: Verbruggen, Sallouha, and Pollin classify cross-technology interference for open radio access networks without one heavy monolithic model. Splitting the work across time, frequency, and channel-state domains taken from the same data stream, their distributed design reaches 400 microseconds of inference latency on standard CPUs. That is nine times faster and eleven times cheaper than a leading frequency-only classifier, at a cost of only 4 percent accuracy, while holding above 90 percent accuracy under heavy interference.
arxiv-2604-11394: Al-Dahmani and three colleagues evaluate TabPFNv2.5, a transformer-based tabular foundation model, for IoT intrusion detection in smart cities. On the TON IoT dataset it runs 40 times faster than Random Forest while holding 97 percent binary classification accuracy. This supports a hybrid pipeline where the foundation model screens threats rapidly and ensembles handle detailed classification. Scanning attacks prove hardest to catch, at 69.8 percent F1. Cross-device generalization hinges on feature similarity.
arxiv-2604-11694: Hada and Okumura study cosmology with halo clustering from galaxy distributions. Small-scale clustering matters for full-shape work, where satellite galaxies feed one-halo terms and Finger-of-God effects. Using DESI-like red galaxy mocks from AbacusSummit at redshift 1.1, they model the reconstructed-halo spectrum with field theory. Reconstruction systematics fit within field theory: a multipole rescaling from large data captures the dominant effect, while counterterms absorb small-scale residuals. The sample yields unbiased constraints, with growth-rate uncertainty falling over 20 percent and stable fits beyond usual limits.
arxiv-2604-12094: Adlam argues wavefunction collapses, or quantum events, in relational quantum mechanics have a simple account. Describing a system against a reference breaks down when the system interacts with it, since the latter cannot be framed relative to itself. That break clarifies recent concerns about quantum events in such views. The solution requires taking quantum theory as incomplete, which she argues is most likely inevitable for any precise account of quantum events.
arxiv-2604-13494: Nengroo, Islam, and Ghosh test a string-inspired gravity theory, called Kalb-Ramond gravity, against black hole images. They work out the shadows cast by charged, spinning black holes in that theory and compare them with Event Horizon Telescope views of M87* and Sagittarius A*. The comparison caps the theory's symmetry-breaking parameter at about 0.19, using the Sagittarius A* image.
arxiv-2604-13694: Sun and four colleagues localize language-model behavior to the weights that truly source it, not just activations that pass signals along. Their Weight Patching method swaps selected module weights from a behavior-specialized model into a base model of the same architecture under a fixed input. A vector-anchor interface judges whether a task-relevant control state has formed. The analysis finds layers of sources: shallow candidate carriers first, then aggregation and routing modules, then downstream execution circuits. Its scores also guide better model merging.
arxiv-2604-13794: Huettner characterizes the unique component-efficient rule for networks with externalities. Existence is the main challenge. The rule must satisfy balanced contributions on every edge. Construction uses only spanning-tree edges. Here, a cycle-sum identity bridges it, reducing non-tree contributions to subnetwork relations. The BCE rule matches the Myerson value for TU games and its Jackson-Wolinsky generalization without externalities. It restores the externality-free value. Unlike FCE, it never collapses to a graph-free formula. In short, the rule shares value fairly across the network.
arxiv-2604-14194: Krishna proves two finite-field versions of the Tarski-Maligranda inequalities for sub-normed linear spaces over fields where two is nonzero. The two bounds control the gap between vector norms using sums, differences, and maxima of their combined norms. The results carry a classical Banach-space inequality into the finite-field setting.
arxiv-2604-14294: Chubukov, Esterlis, Abanov, and Prokof'ev challenge the belief that Migdal-Eliashberg theory holds at strong coupling until a dressed phonon softens near zero. They analyze instead a collapse to a polaron or bipolaron ground state, bounding the Fermi-liquid collapse coupling. At density extremes, the switch precedes phonon softening in two- and three-dimensional systems. In three dimensions the bound shrinks toward zero at edges. Near half-filling, a charge-density wave leads instead, strong-coupling theory stays intact nearby, and the polaron state emerges from the ordered state.
arxiv-2604-14594: Basak, Chakraborty, and Mathur frame quantum field theories with a Daubechies wavelet basis in position space, joined with similarity renormalization group flow equations. The basis recasts free scalar field theory as coupled pinned oscillators, each labeled by a spot and a resolution index. The Hamiltonian then splits into fixed-scale blocks plus blocks coupling other scales, and flow steps decouple the scale modes into a block-diagonal form. With rising resolution, the low-energy spectrum comes from the working lowest-scale block alone, cutting cost sharply.
arxiv-2604-15294: Yang and seven colleagues probe whether language models can grasp viewpoint rotation from text alone, without any images. Asked to track a viewpoint through described rotations and predict what would be seen, both language and vision-language models score poorly where people score perfectly. Layer probes show the models encode viewpoints but fail to bind them to observations, and tuning only the key attention heads improves scores without erasing general skills.
arxiv-2604-15594: Pathak, Biswas, and Roy present DataCenterGym, a physics-based testbed for scheduling jobs across far-flung data centers with several goals at once. It couples compute queues, building heat flows, local HVAC behavior, and heat-linked service slowdowns in a Gymnasium-ready interface. A layered predictive control scheduler that places jobs with heat and power in view beats baseline schedulers on standard and sensitivity tests.
arxiv-2604-15694: Li and seven colleagues split discrete diffusion into jump when and jump where, with one head for exit rate and one for jump spread. The bound splits too, into a Poisson gap for timing and a class gap for aim, with a plain, steady loss to train on. Their pure-uniform Neural CTMC scores 16.36 on TinyStories, far past GIDD at 37.60 and MDLM at 42.66. It also tops OpenWebText perplexity at the same token spend, with 183.6 at 128 steps against MDLM at 210.5 and GIDD at 249.8.
arxiv-2604-15794: Liu, Chen, Zhou, Tu, and Manoharan heal LLM skill loss from tune-forget, squeeze, and snip with self-teaching tune-ups, where the learner sips from its best form. They tie healing to shape match: as the learner's deep-layer shape lines up with the teacher's best shape, scores come back. Centered kernel match gauges that line-up and holds firm under spins and scales. Tests back a link between score healing and shape match, tying hands-on healing to shape theory.
arxiv-2604-15994: Xu and eight colleagues introduce ReactBench, a benchmark testing topological reasoning in multimodal models on chemical reaction diagrams. Such models handle single elements and linear diagrams well, but falter on branching paths, converging flows, and cyclic dependencies, even counting endpoints. Reaction diagrams span linear chains to cyclic graphs and demand local recognition and global reasoning. With 1,618 expert-annotated question-answer pairs across four levels, tests on 24 models show a gap over 30 percent between anchor-based tasks and holistic structural reasoning. That gap marks a reasoning bottleneck, not perception.
arxiv-2604-16694: Tian and colleagues propose RankGuide for small model work through rank routing and steering. Big reasoning models gain power from stepwise chains, but pay latency and cost. Small models write steps for a speed trade-off, yet failure-spotting remains hard. In text and hidden spaces, the authors identify overconfidence, uncertainty and revalidation as modes.
