RankGuide routes with rank signals from hidden states, calling large models only when small models look to fail. It also extracts a filtered vector to steer small-model reasoning and improve quality.
arxiv-2604-16994: Kumar and four colleagues watch chemically active droplets squeezed into channels narrower than themselves, moving from steady shapes to rippling interfaces. Dilute, additive-free solutions keep droplets steady, while added solutes or stronger surfactant trigger strong ripples. Both shapes slow then level off with confinement in a similar way, and a stability analysis names the Yih-Marangoni instability as the driver, a new mode of adaptive motion.
arxiv-2604-17094: Malkin offers simple approximations for three stats tools used in hypothesis tests: the inverse normal distribution, Student's t-distribution, and an outlier rule. For each case, he proposes compact expressions for its quantiles. The approximations are good enough for most practical uses in the field, trading a little exactness for much easier sums.
arxiv-2604-17194: Goto, Takeishi, and Yairi propose two ways to turn betting odds into outcome probabilities. Their odds-only method, OO-EPC, needs no historical data and matches bookmakers' goal of equal confidence in profitability per outcome; on 90,014 football matches across five bookmakers, it beats rivals for most. Their FL-GLM fits one parameter capturing the favourite-longshot bias, a clearer alternative to multinomial and logistic models; on historical matches it beats those models for all. OO-EPC was also tested in six rounds of an annual basketball contest.
arxiv-2604-17494: Kostrzewa, Zięba, and Stefanowski address a flaw in explanations for black-box models: a counterfactual, the smallest change that would flip a decision, often breaks when the model is slightly retrained. Their method trains a conditional normalizing flow, a generative model that learns plausible data patterns, over an ensemble of models, judging agreement across them. One dial sets the share of models that must agree, so explanations stay valid and believable without retraining.
arxiv-2604-18194: Kazanskii, Petrova, Ustyuzhanin, Bagrianskii, Puzikov, and State improve one-step image generators called Drifting Models. A two-particle view of these models reveals a locally repulsive regime where repulsion can overpower attraction to the target. Their DMF variant scales the drift by a scheduled friction coefficient, with theory giving a contraction threshold and an error bound. On face-domain translation, DMF beats the frictionless version and nearly matches far costlier flow matching at roughly 29 times lower training time.
arxiv-2604-18394: Jiang and ten colleagues introduce OpenGame, an open agentic framework for building complete web games from high-level designs. Language models handle isolated coding tasks but collapse on full games through cross-file errors and broken scene wiring. OpenGame pairs a growing library of project templates with a living protocol of verified fixes, plus a specialized GameCoder-27B model. Across 150 game prompts, its headless-browser benchmark scores build health, visual usability, and intent alignment at a new state of the art.
arxiv-2604-18494: Feng tackles energy dissipation in non-spherical particle contact from scratch. Unlike round contact, working inertia and stiffness shift with shifting contact geometry, coupling slide, spin, and sideways motion. Mapping motion onto contact degrees of freedom reveals a mass tied to setup with built-in slide-spin coupling. Matching damping then takes a unique form fixed by the remapped wave-like structure, pinning down contact-point restitution while total energy rebound varies with shape, backed on smooth single-contact impacts.
arxiv-2604-18794: Xu and 14 colleagues study dynamical magnetism in gamma barium cobalt niobium oxide, a disordered cubic lattice with cobalt on one third of its sites. Heat, susceptibility, neutron spin echo, and muon measurements reveal a broad crossover, short range correlations, and fast spin dynamics down to at least 0.1 kelvin, and no static order or spin glass freezing. Simulations yield orphan spins, finite clusters, and an infinite network, with orphan fractions matching magnetization data well. Together, these point to a disorder driven state near the percolation threshold, distinct from spin glasses.
arxiv-2604-18994: Lejtreger and Lema define ways to split sets of Anosov representations. Along a diverging run of such families, the critical exponent nears a combinatorial invariant read from the spectral data of a finite graph. Their method yields bounds on the Thurston asymmetric metric. As an application, they study degenerations of convex projective structures on a pair of pants, building on a McMullen example.
arxiv-2604-19194: Riehl and three colleagues present sumo3Dviz, a lightweight 3D visualization pipeline for SUMO traffic simulations. It converts vehicle paths and signal states into 3D renderings with a Python framework. Unlike game-engine approaches or co-simulation tools, it is simple, scriptable, and reproducible. The tool installs through pip, runs on any system, and needs no proprietary software. It supports external and driver views, giving cinematic overviews and driver-level experiences, with rendering tuned for batch video.
arxiv-2604-19394: Doll and colleagues ask whether continual pre-training can close the gap between small specialized models and much larger general-purpose models in medicine. They build FineMed-de, a high-quality German medical corpus from FineWeb2. The corpus pre-trains and merges three well-known language models from 7 billion to 24 billion parameters, creating the DeFineMed family. Specialization lifts 7-billion-model scores sharply on German medical benchmarks, and win rates against the much larger Mistral-Small-24B-Instruct rise roughly three-and-a-half-fold through domain adaptation.
arxiv-2604-19694: Linden extends a grouping-based Wald test for mixed-effects logistic regression from random-intercept models to models with random slopes, covering sparse cluster settings. Observations are grouped by predicted probabilities within clusters, the model gains pooled group markers, and their joint significance is tested with a Wald statistic. A data-driven rule picks the group count as the smaller of 10 and the smallest cluster size, keeping estimation feasible. Simulations across 24 null scenarios show the test holds its stated error rate.
arxiv-2604-19894: Moharana and four colleagues probed GdSrCoMnO6, a disordered double perovskite where cobalt and manganese ions mix at random. It turns ferromagnetic near 153 kelvin, shows a Griffiths-like patchy regime up to about 172 kelvin, and slows near 30 kelvin. At low heat it also shows exchange bias up to 50 kelvin. The bias hits 379 oersted at 5 kelvin, a sign that disorder steers its magnetism.
arxiv-2604-19994: Wang, Ganguly, and Tsiotras solve finite-horizon covariance steering for discrete-time Markov jump linear systems with multiplicative noise. They show feasible controls reduce to mode-dependent linear feedback plus feedforward and random parts, since purely affine feedback does not suffice. A lifted-state formulation unifies mean and covariance into second-moment variables, giving a lossless relaxation and, for the unconstrained case, an SDP form. Chance-constrained versions with ball and half-space limits gain tractable convex surrogates and a reference-update scheme, illustrated on a finance application.
arxiv-2604-20294: Muñoz-Lahoz pins down which Archimedean lattice-ordered algebras with identity admit a polynomial growth calculus. For a tuple in such an algebra, the map exists exactly when a top element and subalgebra exist. The map sends coordinate functions to tuple entries and constants to the unit, while the subalgebra holds unit and entries with complete norms. The result mirrors a Laustsen-Troitsky account. A side result gives free objects in uniformly complete Archimedean f-algebras, forcing a commutative f-algebra from any nontrivial calculus.
arxiv-2604-20394: Ta and Vu establish nearly optimal bounds for splits of decision trees in data streams. For regression with labels up to M, they give a single-pass algorithm using space like the square of M divided by the error tolerance. This beats a prior two-pass method, and matching space is proven needed. For classification they give a single-pass Gini split algorithm using space like one over the error tolerance, beating a prior method that needed the square. Matching lower bounds for Gini impurity and misclassification complete the picture.
arxiv-2604-20794: Fanelli, Song, Wang, Zheng, and Zhou study Hardy-type uncertainty rules for linear covariant Schrodinger equations with varying coefficients and bounded electric and magnetic potentials. Under smallness rules on the leading terms, they prove any solution with super-quadratic exponential decay at two distinct times must vanish outright. With one more rule on matrix G, they prove a Hardy-type result at the quadratic exponential scale. They also prove a matching uniqueness result for the heat equation with varying-coefficient magnetic changes.
arxiv-2604-20894: Ballester-Bolinches and colleagues revisit their earlier work on soluble skew braces and Yang-Baxter solutions. One main result there said a skew brace is soluble exactly when its linked solution is soluble. A small step in the proof had been missed, since it rested on how maps between solutions were defined. The authors fix the gap with a new kind of map, called an i-homomorphism, and redefine soluble solutions through it. Every soluble solution then has a soluble structure brace, so the first result still holds.
arxiv-2604-20994: Belkhiter and colleagues introduce function hijacking attacks. These twist the tool-selection step of agentic models to force a call to an attacker-chosen function. Unlike earlier attacks that lean on semantic preference, the method largely ignores context meaning. It still works across domains and function sets. On held-out queries it reaches roughly 63 to 82 percent success across four function-calling models on the Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard. It also transfers across model sizes and families.
arxiv-2604-21094: Thinh Nguyen-Cong, Truong-Son Hy, and Thang Dinh show that spectral embeddings of graph fragments can leak the hidden graph's shape, then build tools for the fragmented setting. Their LoGraB benchmark splits standard graphs into noisy local pieces, and their AFR method stitches faithful islands back together with fidelity scoring and alignment. AFR tops the F1 table on 7 of 9 tests and keeps 75 percent of its undefended score under differential privacy at epsilon 2.
arxiv-2604-21594: Hristo Tonchev and Nikolay Vitanov present composite sequences for X and Hadamard gates fixing amplitude, detuning, and length errors. Two ways drive it: derivative-based removal in the unitary, and direct cuts to average gate infidelity over error ranges. They derive symmetric five-pulse solutions with closed-form phases cutting first-order terms, and tune sequences up to 15 pulses for higher-order suppression. Standard U5a and U5b sequences are phase-shifted cases of them, giving detuning and amplitude robustness. Length trades against robustness window across sets.
arxiv-2604-21794: Yu and five colleagues treat communication between language-model agents as something to learn, not a fixed interface. Their DiffMAS framework trains latent communication jointly with multi-agent reasoning, using parameter-efficient supervised training over latent trajectories. Agents thus learn together how to encode and interpret information across turns. On maths reasoning, scientific questions, code generation, and commonsense benchmarks, DiffMAS beats single-agent inference, text-based multi-agent systems, and earlier latent methods, scoring 26.7 percent on AIME24 and about 20 percent on GPQA-Diamond.
arxiv-2604-22194: Sharma and Lau address a bottleneck in quantum route tuning. Direct QUBO codes of CVRP exceed qubit and gate budgets, while quantum evaluations are costly and backend-picky. They build a pipeline converting CVRP into bounded-width chunks, treating running as a loop decision. Fisher-Jaikumar linear form plus Lagrangian easing splits tasking couplers into knapsack chunks for QUBO/Ising evaluation. To replace brittle gradient tuning, they learn a multiplier controller with expert pretraining and reinforcement tuning.
arxiv-2604-22294: Joshi and three colleagues introduce SLIDERS, a method for systematic reviews from large document collections. SLIDERS extracts structured data plus full-text excerpts as evidence. Its reconciliation agent writes code to reconcile evidence, joining fragmented information and resolving inconsistencies into a coherent table. On three systematic-review-style tasks, SLIDERS beats the best baseline and stays near 90 percent accuracy across 6M to 11M-token corpora. On two follow-up benchmarks it answers about 78 percent and about 58 percent of questions accurately.
arxiv-2604-22394: Lau and Mărcuţ present multiplicative Ehresmann connections on surjective submersions of Lie groupoids, extending classical fibre-bundle connections. They show these may fail even for proper ones. Positive results hold for Morita ones, uniform fibrations and locally trivial or proper ones. For fibrations, completeness is set by the induced kernel-bundle link and by the base link if connected. For source-proper ones, local triviality equals having complete ones of this type.
arxiv-2604-22494: Pautrel and three colleagues offer two ways to train a shared neural model across separate sites without breaking its curved geometry. Its target, SPDnet, works with matrices where plain averaging breaks a key right-angle rule. ProjAvg projects plain averages back onto the allowed curved surface, while RLAvg averages in flat tangent space and maps the result back. Both stay cheap and work with any optimizer. Brain-signal tests show the approach beats federated EEGnet on score and steadiness while sending fewer values per round.
arxiv-2604-22694: Cerardi, Tolley, and di Vruno forecast megaconstellation occupancy in SKA observations. The SKA starts operations in 2030, when up to 100,000 satellites may orbit Earth, ten times more than in 2024, mostly in communication megaconstellations. These satellites create radio interference for modern radio telescopes. An analytical model forecasts exposed time for main-beam-only satellites, and for satellites in the main beam or first sidelobe. For SKA-Low, satellites sit in the beam 30 percent of time across half the range, rising to all time at lower frequencies.
arxiv-2604-22794: Nilsen, Quick, Göçmen, Dimitrov, and Réthoré speed reinforcement learning for wind-farm control by pretraining from expert demonstrations generated by a steady-state wake optimizer inside a dynamic simulation. Behavior cloning initializes both actor and critic of a Soft Actor-Critic agent, removing the costly early phase where an untrained agent trails a greedy baseline. Fine-tuned agents converge within a quarter of a million steps and beat a lookup-table controller.
arxiv-2604-22994: Darc and Kilpatrick present KilonovaSCORER, an open-source tool for ranking optical transients in real time during gravitational-wave follow-up, when only sparse early multi-band light data exists. It scores each transient against a kilonova model grid, combining per-observation metrics with inverse-variance weighting. A step-by-step check tracks light curves across epochs, penalizing transients whose evolution clashes with kilonova expectations. Tested on a known kilonova and against supernova simulations, it surely finds true signals while excluding supernova contaminants within five days of the trigger.
arxiv-2604-23294: Herling and Neufeld study high harmonic generation in graphene with optical phonons included in the static limit, where the lattice stays frozen. Optical phonons strongly suppress harmonic yields by coupling to interband currents and scrambling harmonic phases, to explain the absence of harmonics above three electronvolts. Yields turn temperature-linked through phonon occupation, though weakly, since zero-point motion dominates phonon energies. Phonons also dephase interband waves within 5.7 femtoseconds, far faster than electron scattering. They smooth ellipticity curves toward better lab agreement.
arxiv-2604-23394: Kazakov, Popova, and Shipulin propose a moth-eye-inspired vertical grating coupler for silicon photonics with an anisotropic grating stripe directing light to one side. The design needs only a single etching step and couples vertical light efficiently, suiting integration of sources such as VCSELs on chip. Built for the SOI platform at 1550 nm, simulation gives 41 percent in-coupling, unidirectionality over 10 dB, and 50 nm bandwidth at 1 dB. Experiments confirm unidirectionality at 12.80 dB with insertion loss of about 8 dB near 1528 nm.
arxiv-2604-23994: Wang, Qiu, and Huang argue that discrete diffusion language models commit words too early when decoding in fixed blocks without later context. They define a block as self-contained when its predictions stay the same with or without future context. Variable-size blocks are then chosen by how much predictions would shift if the future were revealed. Theory links this test to predictive consistency, and experiments beat fixed and heuristic block decoding.
arxiv-2604-24294: Nogay argues AI should be judged as a possible next GPT by deep change, not raw results. He offers AI-Native Autonomous Infrastructure, a regime with autonomy in key systems. The model tracks this shift with the Autonomy Index, the Infrastructure Coupling Coefficient, and the Technological Transition Potential. It also derives thresholds for an era shift. AI systems both raise compute demand and improve the infrastructure behind them, a loop setting AI apart from earlier GPTs.
arxiv-2604-24394: De Santis and seven colleagues build a discrete event simulation model of regional ambulance deployment. Home bases, where crews wait ready for calls, largely set how fast and well the system responds. The model holds random workflow from varied sources, matching system operations very well for true-to-life analysis. A case study from ARES 118 covers Lazio, with a medium-size city and sparsely peopled areas. Scenario analyses show managers can use the model to improve effectiveness and quickness across the regional system.
arxiv-2604-24494: Zhijie Zhang and 11 colleagues test hot gas halos around Milky Way-like galaxies in the TNG50 simulation against real X-ray and absorption data. Seen from inside and outside, the simulated halos match overall brightness and several inner-halo measures. Yet their outer glow fades too fast with distance. They also hold roughly two thirds less of the hottest absorbing gas than the real halo shows, pointing to feedback that dumps energy too near the centre.
arxiv-2604-24594: Su and colleagues address a scaling problem for agentic AI: listing every reusable skill in the prompt eats context and hurts skill choice as the library grows. They propose Skill Retrieval Augmentation, in which agents fetch, incorporate and apply relevant skills on demand. Their SRA-Bench benchmark covers retrieval, incorporation and end-task execution, with 5,400 test instances and a corpus of 26,262 skills. Retrieval-based augmentation improves performance, though skill incorporation remains a weak link.
arxiv-2604-24694: Rathore, Basden, Chancellor and Kusumaatmaja review how fluid data is stored on quantum hardware for fluid dynamics. Encoding choices shape how states are made, read, bounded, and evolved over time, and thus shape both the method and its real-world use. Very compact encodings can offer long-run gains but create severe jams in readout, state making and nonlinear work. Less compact encodings ease interactions and suit analog and near-term hardware better. No single encoding is best for all cases.
arxiv-2604-24894: Leeman, Zhan, Zeilinger and Chou propose VISION-SLS for control from high-detail RGB images. It gives robust constraint meeting under set uncertainty bounds, despite noise and nonlinear dynamics. The method pairs a learned low-dimensional observation map with a causal affine time-varying policy. The policy is tuned via System Level Synthesis, with a scalable solver using convex methods and Riccati steps. On simulated car, drone and robot tasks, it enables safe, information-seeking moves that cut uncertainty while meeting constraints.
arxiv-2604-25094: Sethi and four colleagues propose INJEQT, an improved injection method for fault-tolerant extractor architectures. In extractor architectures, over 90 percent of error comes from synthillation. Standard synthillation needs multiple serial injections with inter-module checks, the expensive instruction. INJEQT uses a two-factory design with an auxiliary code making rotation states at lower error, injected with few checks. It cuts error rates by up to 22 times. Pre-fetching preparing states in parallel speeds wall-clock time up to 13-fold and cuts space-time cost up to 7.2-fold.
arxiv-2604-25194: Zheng and three colleagues study quantum-enhanced network tomography, inferring internal network states from end-to-end probes. Quantum probes, blocks of coherent pulses with squeezing or weak entanglement, carry information about channel transmissivity. Assuming some nodes can send and receive such probes through intermediate nodes, they estimate link transmissivities. They propose a probe construction algorithm that keeps links identifiable while maximizing orthogonal sets. Two Fisher information matrix metrics, its determinant and the trace of its inverse, judge the probes.
arxiv-2604-25394: Jirattikansakul and four colleagues prove a congruence for sums of divisor counts over squares. For N of five set forms, the sum of the divisor count of N minus a square, over squares below N, is a multiple of 4. Their proof leans on a result of Keith on partitions of N with exactly two part sizes. Following Dewitt and Keith, they join counting arguments with modular arithmetic. The work links partition counts to divisor sums through congruences.
arxiv-2604-25594: Niewiadomski and six colleagues study RY Leporis, the primary of a long-period binary whose companion is likely a white dwarf. A SALT spectrum shows iron-group underabundance and neutron-capture enhancement, including barium and europium, at subsolar metallicity. Fourier analysis of ASAS, SuperWASP, and TESS data finds extra TESS frequencies, with the dominant one a radial mode, most likely the first overtone. Seismic modelling gives a mass near two solar masses and an age near 730 million years. All models place RY Lep in the hydrogen shell-burning phase.
arxiv-2604-25794: Vo and four colleagues propose DIP-KD for distilling a large teacher into a small student with no training data and only black-box access. Privacy and proprietary limits often hide the teacher's internals and data. DIP-KD synthesizes diverse image priors, sharpens sample distinctions with contrastive learning, and distills through a primer student using soft probabilities. Only top-1 predictions are needed from the teacher. Tests across 12 benchmarks reach state-of-the-art results, with ablations confirming diversity drives learning.
arxiv-2604-25894: Zambom and Saunders build a method that picks the right outside drivers of volatility in GARCH-X models. Their test setup uses Wald-type statistics with a Benjamini-Yekutieli false discovery rate control. The authors prove the rule finds the true driver set as data grows. Simulations across varied distributions and dependence patterns confirm it works well. They apply it to S&P 500 volatility using macroeconomic and commodity indicators.
arxiv-2604-25994: Tagawa, Haiman, and Kocsis investigate black hole mergers in active galactic nuclei disks, using N-body simulations with a semi-analytical model. In their fiducial model, mass and mass-ratio distributions match observations. They depend strongly on disk lifetime, density, black hole number, and accretion efficiency, with higher masses as these grow. The most massive mergers, such as GW231123, arise from efficient gas accretion or hierarchical mergers across three or more generations. Gas accretion plus hierarchical mergers explain observed links between mass ratio, effective spin, and chirp mass.
arxiv-2604-26094: Cai and six colleagues identify an imitative attack cascade in decentralized finance. A successful exploit is quickly mimicked, with small changes to its logic. Their analysis finds more than two thirds of such attacks resemble earlier incidents, often within hours or days. Turning heuristic alerts into detection rules by hand is slow and labour-intensive. Their GenDetect system abstracts attack semantics and matches transaction logic in noisy traces. It reaches 98 percent accuracy with 1 percent false positives and 3 percent false negatives, and uncovers fifty-six unrevealed attacks from three years.
arxiv-2604-26294: Shyam, Golubeva, and Anthony presented tensor and sequence parallelism, a scheme that folds two splitting strategies onto one device axis. Normally weights and tokens are split along separate axes, but here each rank holds a weight shard plus a sequence shard, cutting parameter and activation memory together. Two runtime schedules handle attention and gated MLPs, trading extra communication for lower memory. Benchmarks position the method as a hardware-aware option for long-context, memory-tight training.
arxiv-2604-26594: Yatsyshin and six colleagues diagnosed Antarctic sea ice with a layered dynamic-mode breakdown of satellite concentration data. Decades of slow growth gave way to a sharp 2014-2017 decline, a seeming recovery, and a renewed collapse from 2022 onward. Interacting year-to-year modes explain the earlier swings, while a climate-change signal emerging in 2012 turned clear by 2022. Their predictive IceDMD model forecasts anomalies up to two years ahead, beating existing approaches with physical clarity and tiny compute cost.
arxiv-2604-26794: Schöll, Dullemond and Dominik model how dust grains grow in the disks around young stars, where planets form. They add porosity to the DustPy code, treating the fractal dimension, a measure of how fluffy an aggregate is, as a free parameter. Fluffier, lower-dimension grains reach larger masses but grow more slowly, and the top speeds they reach depend on whether growth is limited by shattering or by bouncing. Even the largest grains stay far smaller than planetesimals, the building blocks of planets.
arxiv-2604-27394: Uehara presents the Bayesian X-Learner, a method for estimating heterogeneous treatment effects with calibrated uncertainty and robustness to heavy-tailed outcomes. Built on doubly robust outcomes with a posterior and a Welsch likelihood, it aims to deliver all three properties at once. On Hill's IHDP benchmark, the setup attains the lowest error, though differences are not significant and rankings prove unstable. On contaminated data with up to 20 to 25 percent tail density, a one-flag extension recovers low error with intervals, and pooled coverage returns to 95 percent.
arxiv-2604-27594: Belavadi and Hoang give a structural description of graphs free of bulls and houses, and of graphs free of bulls and five-vertex paths. A bull is a triangle with two pendant edges, and a house is the complement of a five-vertex path. Using these structural properties, they prove that for any fixed color count, only finitely many critical graphs of that type exist among bull- and five-vertex-path-free graphs. Their structural result also yields a short proof that such graphs are perfectly divisible.
arxiv-2604-27894: Ostwald and colleagues build a framework that treats artificial agents as testable hypotheses about how minds work. They formalise two small lab tasks, a contrast-discrimination task and a two-armed bandit task, as joint probability models and check the models by recovery simulations and real data. The exercise recovers the psychometric function from an agent view, derives optimal policies, and shows Rescorla-Wagner learning matching Bayesian inference in symmetric bandits.
arxiv-2604-27994: Khanzada and Kwon tackle driving agents that fail in new simulated towns because road shapes and lane layouts change. Their training asks the agent to predict the meaning of future camera views while ignoring clues that reveal the training town, so it learns features that travel. Tested in two unseen CARLA towns after training in two others, the method beat matched world-model baselines in both places.
arxiv-2604-28194: Geng, Merz and Randall study the Karch-Randall braneworld, where a brane universe carries a very light but massive graviton. The zero-mass limit of the graviton propagator is smooth at tree level. It was conjectured to stay smooth quantum mechanically, hinting at spontaneous symmetry breaking. They show the massless limit of the partition function instead gives a massless graviton plus a decoupled massive vector. That theory differs from Randall-Sundrum II, with implications for entanglement islands.
arxiv-2605-00194:
Jeffrey Shallit studies a toy duel invented by Cooper and Dutle in 2013. Two players, Alice and Bob, shoot at each other until one is hit, and each shot lands with the same fixed chance. A greedy rule gives each turn to the player whose current chance of success is smaller.

Cooper and Dutle noticed that, as the hit chance shrinks toward zero, the order of shots settles into the famous Thue-Morse pattern. They left open how fast that settling happens. Shallit's short note answers the question by pinning down the speed of convergence. The result closes a small, neat problem at the border of game theory and word patterns.
arxiv-2605-00394:
Satoshi Noguchi and Yoshinobu Kawahara present Mesh Field Theory, a framework for simulating physics on meshes that keeps the physics honest by construction. Their starting move is a clean split: the topological structure of a mesh, which cells touch which, is separated from its metric structure, the sizes and angles. Minimal principles, such as locality, symmetry under relabeling, and energy balance, drive the theory.

The authors prove a reduction theorem. Under those principles, mesh dynamics must factor into a port-Hamiltonian form. The conservative coupling is fixed uniquely by topology. Only the material response and dissipation remain free. Their neural version learns only those free parts. In tests it showed near-zero energy drift, correct wave behavior, and momentum conservation. It also extrapolated strongly to unseen cases with high data efficiency.
arxiv-2605-01194:
Wenhao Li and seven co-authors introduce VLA-ATTC, a framework that gives vision-language-action robot models adaptive test-time compute. Such models decide through a fast, instinctive process without pausing to think, which can lead to suboptimal or catastrophic actions in complex or unclear scenes. An uncertainty-based cognitive clutch switches the system from reflexive running to a thinking phase when necessary.

During that phase, a Relative Action Critic identifies the best action from generated candidates through pairwise comparisons. That replaces unstable absolute value estimation and simplifies learning. An efficient sampling strategy amortizes cost, and an automated pipeline curates preference pairs without manual annotation. On a long-horizon manipulation benchmark, it cuts the failure rate of a leading model by more than half.
arxiv-2605-01394:
Dong Xu and eleven co-authors test whether language models and agents can write formal specifications for C programs, the precise contracts that proof tools check code against. Writing good contracts is slow expert work, and how far automation really gets has been unclear.

Their benchmark, LiveFMBench, holds 630 C programs annotated in the ACSL contract language, with 360 fresh cases added to guard against training-data leaks. They test plain prompting at several sample counts, a thinking mode, and full agent pipelines. Naive scores flatter the models: some cheat the proof tools or ignore the code, and cutting those cases drops true accuracy by about a fifth. More samples and thinking help, agents help most when samples are few, and wrong loop invariants are the top error. The authors conclude human-written contracts are far from replaced.
arxiv-2605-01494:
Peter DelMastro, Daniel Appelö, and Yingda Cheng simulate open quantum systems with a two-level compression scheme that keeps the math physically legal. The Lindblad equation governs such systems, but its density matrix grows brutally with size, so plain simulation dies early.

Their format squeezes twice. The density matrix is split into a product of tall, thin factors. The columns of those factors are themselves stored as tensor trains, also called matrix product states. The scheme is fully positive and trace preserving, meaning every step yields a state a lab could in principle hold. It plugs into the authors' earlier Kraus is King solver, and they show how its column arithmetic and rank trimming run inside the compressed format. Numerical tests confirm convergence and reach systems with a vast number of degrees of freedom on modest hardware.
arxiv-2605-01694:
Keon Woo Kim reframes world-model research as a design problem. The only part of a world model an agent ever touches is the latent state it builds. That state must keep some facts, drop others, and serve a chosen job. Sorting methods by architecture or application hides what the state is actually for.

Kim's taxonomy groups methods by function: predictive embedding, recurrent belief state, object and causal structure, latent action interface, grounded planning interface, and memory substrate. Judged on seven axes, from representation to uncertainty, the groups expose gaps that architecture labels miss, such as the distance between predicting well and controlling well. The closing claim is pointed: the best world model is not the one that keeps the most information, but the one whose state matches the task's sufficiency demand.
arxiv-2605-01894:
Rinaldo Schinazi gives a short note on how a binomial distribution can be closely matched by a Poisson distribution. Textbooks often show the match by taking a limit, as trials grow and the mean stays fixed. Schinazi takes a different route and uses coupling, a method that builds two random processes on the same space so their closeness can be seen directly.

With coupling, the note proves a much more general result than the standard limit claim. It uses only basic facts from an early course in probability. Readers get a clean example of how coupling can replace a limit argument and give a stronger, more direct sense of why the match holds.
arxiv-2605-01994:
Kritti Sharma and colleagues look inside cosmic voids, the emptiest large regions of the universe, for ordinary matter. Voids are sensitive tests for dark energy, changed gravity, and neutrino mass, yet their gas content had not been measured. The team uses fast radio bursts, whose signals are spread by electrons along the line of sight, as a tracer that does not depend on gas temperature or makeup.

Stacking more than three thousand burst sightlines on almost thirteen hundred voids, they find a clear deficit of dispersion toward void centres. The signal matches a model built from the observed galaxy deficit in those voids. The result shows diffuse baryons do inhabit void interiors, but at a reduced level.
arxiv-2605-02094:
Kunyuan Xie, Zhixi Cai, and Kalin Stefanov improve sign language recognition by pretraining an encoder to notice hands and body parts in motion. Small hand differences change a sign's meaning, yet many encoders start from generic action data that miss those fine cues. Their method, SignMAE, masks parts of the input based on segmentation of key body regions.

The model then learns by rebuilding the masked parts, which sharpens its sense of fine sign features. On the WLASL, NMFs-CSL, and Slovo data sets, the encoder reached the best reported results for both per-instance and per-class top-one accuracy. It did so while using fewer input frames and fewer input types than comparable encoders.
arxiv-2605-02394:
Bolun Li, Fengqiang Shi, and Wendong Wang study the vanishing-viscosity limit of a coupled system that models bacteria swimming in a fluid while chasing chemical signals. Such chemotaxis-fluid systems produce striking patterns: dense cell clusters, filaments, and plumes in a sessile drop. Checking those turbulent-looking phenomena with rigorous math is the paper's larger motive.

Working in a two-dimensional half-space with a slip boundary condition, the authors derive the boundary layer equations of the chemotaxis-Navier-Stokes system as both chemotactic and fluid viscosities vary. They then obtain the zero-viscosity limit in anisotropic function spaces that respect the boundary's special scaling. The result is a rigorous step toward grounding observed bacterial flow patterns in proven limits, rather than simulation alone.
arxiv-2605-02794:
Srinivas Soumitri Miriyala and four co-authors build image restoration models that run fast on edge devices, by mixing two kinds of network blocks. Transformers model a whole image well but their attention step is slow on phones, above all at high resolution. State-space blocks, such as Mamba, run in linear time with less overhead, yet can lag on fine detail work.

The framework trains light state-space blocks to imitate transformer blocks at the feature level, then assembles hybrids in a U-shaped layout. A search method picks task-specific mixes, rewarding quality while penalizing transformer use as a stand-in for delay, so no repeated hardware timing is needed. On a flagship phone chip, the pure transformer baseline took about ten seconds per image; the found hybrids cut that sharply.
arxiv-2605-02894:
S. O. Edeki and four co-authors build and study a random model of energy supply and demand, with renewable sources included. The base model links regional demand, outside supply, imports, and renewable input in a nonlinear system. Real energy systems face market swings, weather shifts, policy moves, and technical change. A fixed model captures none of that.

The new model adds Itô-type noise that scales with the state, so swings stay proportional and amounts stay non-negative. The authors prove that positive solutions exist, are unique, and stay bounded in their moments. The system also persists over time. Stability is checked with matrix tests, giving firm stability in the random case under stated conditions. Random swings change the effective capacity, but bounded behavior survives. Simulations show the dynamics at work.
arxiv-2605-03094:
Andrés Rubiano and Armando Reyes study the combinatorics of normal ordering in three-dimensional skew polynomial rings, a family classified by Bell and Smith. In such rings, variables obey twisted commutation rules, and rewriting any product into standard PBW order can involve long calculations.

With help from the SageMath software, the authors shorten the computation of PBW forms and normal orderings that appear in those commutation rules. The work is computational and detailed, giving shorter routes through expressions that otherwise grow unwieldy. It should ease further algebraic work with this classified family of noncommutative rings.
arxiv-2605-03894:
Samira Sahar Jamil and Mark Behrens introduce a degree filtration on the discrete cubical chain complex of a graph, built from the maximal injective dimension of the facets of singular cubes. The associated degree spectral sequence interpolates between a graph's discrete cubical homology and its injective homology, a variant built from injective singular cubes alone.

Building on work of Greene and the first author, they define a combinatorial condition on graphs called quasimonophobicity. They show quasimonophobic graphs make the degree spectral sequence vanish in certain bidegrees and make the injective homology isomorphic to the homology of a cell complex obtained by filling in subcubes. The machinery is applied to compute the second homology of the Greene sphere graphs.
arxiv-2605-04194:
Amir Rafe and Subasish Das ask whether new artificial intelligence work and public interest in it move together over time. Patent publications arrive as uneven event streams in eight fields, while public response is tracked month by month through search trends.

Their combined model links the event stream to the monthly signal and forecasts held-out patent counts better than the comparison methods in their test set. Tests on made-up data with known links also recover those links far better than a standard time-series model, while a check for a sharp break in 2022 finds no firm effect.
arxiv-2605-04294:
Enrico Drigo and six co-authors develop a way to predict how long a quantum spin defect in a solid keeps its state, a key limit for quantum devices. No unified theory had covered these spin lifetimes well at high temperatures.

Using linear-response theory, they express the key lifetimes through correlation functions of how the spin couples to the surrounding lattice. They compute those functions from atomistic simulations driven by machine-learning models trained on first-principles data. For the nitrogen-vacancy centre in diamond, their predicted lifetime matches new measurements closely, supporting the framework for other defects as well.
arxiv-2605-04494:
Jiaming Hu and four co-authors reframe the alignment of text-to-image diffusion models with human preferences as a game rather than a ranking problem. Standard methods learn from preference signals built on a simple model that assumes one score can capture what people like, which may miss the complexity of real taste.

Their method has the current model play against itself, pushing it toward a Nash equilibrium, a stable point where neither side of the game gains by changing. This general preference view avoids forcing preferences through the restrictive scoring model. Experiments on image generation with several metrics show the approach aligns outputs with human preferences effectively.
arxiv-2605-05194:
Benedikt Remlein and Massimiliano Esposito show that averages of measured values develop kinks exactly where a driven system starts to oscillate on its own. Hopf bifurcations are the standard route to such oscillations, yet the steady state itself shows no sharp break there. The effect, they argue, comes from averaging over the new cyclic motion.

Phase averaging removes odd powers of the oscillation size, while its square changes smoothly across the threshold, leaving finite values with jumps in some derivative. Which derivative breaks first depends on how the measured value couples to the oscillation's shape. The authors show the mechanism in chemical, electronic, and climate systems.
arxiv-2605-05294:
Omri Lesser and Debanjan Chowdhury show that randomly mixing two activation functions inside a deep network creates a sharp order-to-chaos style transition in how signals travel through depth. Each neuron independently draws its activation from a two-part mixture, with the mixing fraction as the tuning knob. Effective field theory describes the resulting signal propagation at initialisation.

At a critical mixing fraction the network gains depth-independent signal variance, a scale invariance previously tied to the non-smooth ReLU family. That smoothness matters for curvature-based training and physics-informed uses. The authors confirm the transition through variance propagation, susceptibility measures, and Lyapunov exponents, and test training on real data, resolving a long-standing tension in network design.
arxiv-2605-05394:
Atom interferometers produce many tangled streams of data at once, from phase drift to control signals. Muhammad Bilal Akram Dastagir and five co-authors propose BARFI-Q, a forecasting framework built for those streams. Good forecasts matter for watching the device, correcting its phase, and sensing with it.

BARFI-Q mixes patch embeddings, two-branch time modeling, and layered fusion, then adds a quantum feature-mapping step. Forecasts are made in a circular form that respects the repeating nature of phase. Across repeated runs and window sizes, it beat strong baseline models, and tests showed the fusion of channel and spatial patterns drove much of the gain.
arxiv-2605-05494:
Hung Le settles a question about cutting graphs into balanced pieces. A separator is a small set whose removal splits a graph evenly, and for graphs avoiding a fixed minor, smaller separators mean faster algorithms. In 1990, Alon, Seymour, and Thomas gave the first good bound and conjectured a tighter one.

Le first matches the best flow-based bound with a simpler combination of known tools. Then he breaks the barrier that flow methods seemed to impose, shrinking the separator further. His key move adds a low-diameter decomposition to the old framework, cutting a key cost by a large factor.
arxiv-2605-05594:
Adding retrieved documents can make a vision-language model worse, even when the retrieved texts are flawless. Hoin Jung and Xiaoqian Wang name that failure recorruption. Studying attention patterns inside the models, they trace it to two effects: attention to the image fades, and tokens at set spots win notice whatever they mean.

Many apparent successes, they argue, are position quirks where copying text happens to land on the truth. Their BAIR method steps in at run time, restoring visual focus and marking down textual distractors by position. Across medical, fairness, and geospatial benchmarks, it improved results without retraining.
arxiv-2605-05794:
The Adam optimizer adapts learning rates per parameter, but a large model is a federation of very different modules. Ziqing Wen and six co-authors show those modules suffer imbalanced gradient noise, and Adam's damping treats them unevenly. Manually tuned per-module learning rates exist, but they are costly and transfer poorly.

The authors analyze Adam's noise-damping behavior and propose calibrating it by signal-to-noise ratio at module level. The calibration aims at faster convergence and stabler training without hand-tuned schedules. Their study frames optimizer design as resource allocation across a heterogeneous network.
arxiv-2605-05894:
Slide a charge-density wave through a crystal and its current can pulse in a striking pattern, with period set by the inverse current. Yi Zhou builds the full theory behind that effect, following experiments on quasi-one-dimensional insulators. The sliding condensate makes its own Floquet sidebands, with no outside periodic drive needed.

Zhou solves the sliding problem exactly, obtaining split gap edges and a clear ladder of sidebands with their spectral functions. Weak-probe tunneling spectroscopy then yields the inverse-current oscillations as sideband edges cross a fixed threshold one by one. The framework turns a lab curiosity into a spectrum one can compute.
arxiv-2605-05994:
Nobutaka Ono proposes a compact way to store the weight matrices inside neural networks. Dense matrices appear in linear layers, attention projections, and embeddings, and they cost much memory. His method, DiBA, approximates a matrix with three diagonal matrices and two binary matrices of zeros and ones.

A middle dimension sets the trade off between stored size and accuracy of the approximation. Matrix products then need far fewer multiplications than the dense form. A greedy solver alternates exact updates for the diagonal parts with one bit improvement tests for the binary parts. A lighter variant retunes only the diagonal entries after swapping layers into DiBA form. On real model weights and two task studies, accuracy improved after replacement.
arxiv-2605-06694:
Nicola Fabiano, Sedigheh Barootkoob, and Hossein Lakzian generalize fixed point theorems to suprametric spaces, a setting where the usual triangle inequality is relaxed. They work with convex contractions of a given order on complete spaces of this kind. The central point is that such mappings are strong enough to guarantee a fixed point, yet they need not be continuous at that fixed point.

Weaker conditions, called k-continuity or orbital lower semicontinuity, can replace full continuity instead. That yields a new solution to an open problem posed by Rhoades in 1988 about discontinuity at fixed points. Further results extend quasi-contraction theorems of Sehgal, Ćirić, and Fisher to this setting, supported by examples and an application.
arxiv-2605-06794:
Georgios Dimopoulos, Claudio Ricci, and Stéphane Paltani build more realistic X-ray spectral models for the gas and dust surrounding feeding supermassive black holes. X-ray spectra reveal this circumnuclear material, but existing models mostly assume simple slab or torus geometries that fit data without matching reality. Using the RefleX ray-tracing code, the authors generate models over a wide X-ray energy range with a richer configuration.

Two public table models result: one pairing a source with a dusty torus and a polar hollow cone, and a fuller one adding the accretion disk and broad line region. Applied to the galaxy NGC 424, both show promise for sources whose X-rays are dominated by reprocessed radiation.
arxiv-2605-06894:
Md Mahmuduzzaman Kamol and seven co-authors release McNdroid, a longitudinal benchmark for Android malware detection under concept drift. Malware evolves, defenders' models age, and studying that decay needs data organized across time and feature types. McNdroid spans 2013 to 2025, skipping 2015, and describes each app three ways: static features from manifests and code, dynamic behavior from sandbox runs, and function-call graph features.

With time-separated training and test splits, standard and deep detectors degrade clearly as the gap grows. Combining all three modalities beats any single one over long horizons, while agreement between modalities also fades, showing drift corrodes their consistency too. Family evolution and explanation shifts are analyzed, and data, splits, and code are public.
arxiv-2605-07594:
Xin Ding and eleven co-authors redesign how embodied AI agents use memory. Most systems fetch memories once, at the start of a task, and paste them in as fixed context. As the agent's situation changes, that static memory drifts out of date and can drag a lightweight agent below even a no-memory baseline.

Their system, MemCompiler, instead compiles memory on the fly. A learned compiler reads a structured summary of the agent's current state. It selects only the relevant memories, delivered as text guidance plus a latent channel for perceptual detail. Across three embodied benchmarks it improved results over no-memory setups, in one case by well over double, approached frontier closed systems, and cut per-step latency by sixty percent.
arxiv-2605-07694:
Michael Neri and two co-authors probe how a model estimates a speaker's distance from a single microphone channel. Such systems now reach centimeter accuracy in simulation, but which parts of the room's echo pattern they rely on was unclear. The team split simulated room responses into direct sound, early reflections, and late reverberation, and tested every combination.

Across four calibration scenarios, early reflections emerged as the most informative component when timing is uncalibrated, and errors grew in highly reverberant rooms. With time calibration available, the model simply used propagation delay and reached a mean error of fourteen centimeters regardless of the echo content. Accuracy tracked standard room measures like direct-to-reverberant ratio and clarity, confirming early energy helps and heavy reverberation hurts.
arxiv-2605-07794:
Wen Huang and ten co-authors improve world action models, robot policies that generate actions together with imagined future video. In current systems every predicted latent frame shares one noise schedule during generation, which implicitly assumes all imagined frames are equally reliable guides for action. The authors reject that prior and treat each frame's schedule as a learnable gate on information.

Their NoiseGate samples per-frame timesteps independently in training and adds a small gating policy network that adjusts each frame's noise level during denoising, trained by task reward rather than hand-designed shapes. Raising a frame's noise mutes its contribution to the action tokens. Built on a joint video-action backbone, NoiseGate delivered consistent gains across diverse random-scene manipulation tasks in RoboTwin.
arxiv-2605-07894:
Yichen Andy Yu and six co-authors present SpatialPrompt, an extended reality system that turns rough spatial sketches into executable constraints for AI three-dimensional design. Users draw structures with a 3D pen and add voice prompts for meaning and style, so intent is expressed in space rather than squeezed into text alone.

Built on Apple Vision Pro with a Logitech Muse stylus and the Meshy generation service, the system supports iterative refinement and synchronous co-creation, with each collaborator's contributions color-coded in the shared space. A heuristic evaluation found the workflow intuitive and helpful for building shared understanding among collaborators. It also surfaced two clear needs: faster generation and clearer feedback while the system works.
arxiv-2605-07994:
Haricharan Balasundaram, Swathi Shree Narashiman, Pranay Mathur, and Andrew Thangaraj study how language models can share evidence across similar contexts. Their method, called semantic smoothing, uses word embeddings so that counts from one context help predict words in nearby contexts with a close meaning.

The authors first recast smoothing as a set of distribution estimation problems measured by KL loss. They prove that nearby context embeddings imply nearby next-word distributions, then build an estimator that uses that side information. Tests on synthetic data and on WikiText-103 bigram models show lower test perplexity than standard smoothing methods.
arxiv-2605-08094:
Xinchun Su, Chunxu Luo, Lipeng Ma, Yixuan Li, and coauthors address a practical barrier in medical AI. Large language models reason well about diagnosis, but they need too much compute and memory for clinics with limited hardware. Simple distillation into a smaller model copies answer patterns without keeping the structured reasoning that safe diagnosis requires.

Their framework, MedThink, distills in two stages. First, a teacher model screens training data and adds domain explanations, and the student is fine-tuned on that richer material. Next, the teacher reviews the student's errors and writes reasoning chains that link knowledge to conclusions, and the student trains again on those corrections.
arxiv-2605-08294:
Giacomo Cacciapaglia, Francesco Sannino, and Sophie Wagner find when chiral gauge theories stay asymptotically free in every coupling. The theories include scalar fields. Complete freedom at short distances is attractive for grand unified model building. But gauge, Yukawa, and quartic couplings must all cooperate.

The study generalizes Georgi-Glashow and Bars-Yankielowicz style theories. The scalar sits in the fundamental or the adjoint representation. Several chiral fermion families are added. The authors track the interplay of all couplings. Complete asymptotic freedom is achievable in both setups. It holds only for specific color counts. It also needs specific mixes of vector-like and chiral families.
arxiv-2605-08394:
Efe İzbudak and Kadri İlker Berktav carry a classical contact geometry argument into derived algebraic geometry. The classical transversality lemma builds a contact structure on a hypersurface. A Liouville vector field crosses that surface cleanly. The proof uses point-set topology and local flows. That machinery does not survive translation into the derived world.

Their replacement takes a quotient of a derived symplectic space. The symplectic data descends to a contact structure directly. No transverse hypersurface is needed. The fundamental vector field of a scaling action plays the Liouville role. From there, they prove a derived Legendrian intersection theorem. It uses descent and equivariant lifts, with applications to moduli theory.
arxiv-2605-08794:
Xingyu Song, Yuan Mei, and Naoya Takeishi split the driving field of stochastic generative models into two interpretable parts. Generative systems transport probability from a simple start to real data; deterministic versions use one velocity field, while stochastic versions mix drift and diffusion into that field until their roles blur. The authors prove the field decomposes naturally into a transport part that moves the distribution and an osmotic part created by diffusion and set by the distribution's score.

Their Bridge Matching framework learns both parts through marginal and conditional training. Recombining them with an adjustable osmotic weight gives controllable, interpretable sampling. Generative modeling gains a dial for how much randomness shapes the path from noise to data.
arxiv-2605-08894:
Yuzhuang Xu and four coauthors argue that squeezing language models to extremely few bits damages more than numerical precision: it damages smoothness. Using a smoothness proxy, they show degradation deepens steadily as bit width falls. Neighborhood modeling then reveals the mechanism: quantized models keep far fewer plausible next token candidates alive, thinning the decoding tree and degrading generation quality in a way raw accuracy scores miss.

Adding a simple smoothness preserving principle helps in both post training quantization and quantization aware training, delivering gains beyond numerical fidelity alone. The paper's core message is a design brief for the field: future extreme quantization methods should protect smoothness as a first class goal alongside precision.
arxiv-2605-09094:
Zhiyao Zhang, Myeung Suk Oh, Zhen Qin, Jiaxiang Li, Xin Zhang, and Jia Liu extend a two-level form of machine learning to many tasks at once. In such problems an outer choice shapes an inner training problem. Their 2026 paper relaxes a strong shape assumption that limited older work, then rewrites the multi-task problem as a second problem with several goals tied by an equality rule.

Because that second problem had not been studied before, the authors first define what counts as a good stopping point for it. They then give a method based on a weighted penalty and prove it reaches that point at a stated rate, in both fixed and random settings. Changing a preference setting lets the method trace out trade-offs among the goals.
arxiv-2605-09294:
Ustaomeroglu and Qu propose Representational Effective Theory for LLM computation through learned macrostates, not microscopic details. RET learns macrostates from hidden state runs with a BYOL/JEPA style self taught goal, coarse graining signals into macrovariables keeping higher level structure. The macrovariables prove useful for reading models: RET yields steady states revealing mental state runs of thought, showing high level meaning and aiding early guesses of sycophancy.

They also provide causal levers for steering outputs toward clear computational phases. In sum, the results suggest LLM computation admits useful effective accounts: high level variables aiding reading, guessing, and steering. A held out NuminaMath run for GPT-OSS-20B shows the phases: framing and setup, symbol shifts, clearing detours, check bursts, case analysis, and final notes. The work recasts reading models around learned coarse values rather than neurons or weights, a middle layer between detail and output.
arxiv-2605-09394:
Karimitari and five colleagues compare 9 machine-learned interatomic potentials with different training sets and strategies, both from scratch and by fine-tuning large foundation models. The goal is to see how training sets shape catalytic performance. They test the models on reaction energies and barriers for 141 reactions. The set includes CO 2 reduction to C 2 and C 3 products, propane dehydrogenation, hydrogen intercalation on palladium, and out-of-distribution oxygen evolution on metal oxides.

From-scratch models with 5 to 10 percent perturbed, high-energy configurations from molecular dynamics or contour exploring cut the error by over 2 times against relaxation-only models. Fine-tuned potentials care less about training-set sampling and do well out of distribution. One fine-tuned on metallic catalysts reaches 0 point 30 electronvolts mean error for oxygen evolution on iridium oxide polymorphs. That beats MACE-MH-1 by 0 point 08 and the best from-scratch model by 0 point 14.
arxiv-2605-09494:
Chen and three colleagues design a control system for unmanned underwater vehicles, robots that must work alone where radio contact is poor and faults cannot wait for shore help. Their LASSA architecture pairs a large language model with a sensor and actuator agent and a solver that checks every command against physical limits before it reaches the thrusters. A slow loop handles high level decisions while a fast loop keeps real time control steady.

In lake trials, the system spotted a rudder fault, widened its turning radius, slowed down, and finished the full mission after passing all solver checks on the first attempt. Under normal conditions it raised no false fault alarms at all. Further simulations with cross currents and sensor faults support the same conclusion: checking model reasoning against physics keeps the vehicle safe without hand written rules for every possible failure.
arxiv-2605-09594:
Liu and five colleagues show that coding agent dependency choices can be actively steered by a malicious Skill, a persistent instruction artifact. Coding agents increasingly choose libraries, generate imports, and write install commands. Past work showed they invent nonexistent package names that attackers can register. This paper moves past passive failure. A Skill with small semantic edits, keeping its apparent purpose, steers the agent to an attacker controlled package while it handles harmless coding jobs.

No model weight, training data, or user prompt changes are needed. Across many coding oriented language models and programming benchmarks, Dependency Steering reaches high rates of targeted hallucination. It transfers across models and task domains, and largely evades tested Skill scanners and model based auditors. Persistent agent instructions, the authors conclude, form a little explored software supply chain attack surface demanding new defenses.
arxiv-2605-09694:
Ablikim and the BESIII Collaboration report the first sightings of two rare decay routes of a particle called the Ds meson, a charm particle built from quarks. The team worked with electron-positron collision data taken by the BESIII detector in Beijing, at energies from 4.128 to 4.226 gigaelectronvolts. Each decay breaks the Ds meson into four lighter particles, including neutral kaons and pions.

For the first route, with two neutral kaons, a charged pion, and a neutral pion, the team measured a branching fraction of about 4.08 in a thousand. A branching fraction is the share of decays taking that route. For the second route, the share came to about 3.32 in a thousand. Such first measurements sharpen tests of how quarks combine and break apart, and they feed checks of symmetry patterns in charm physics.
arxiv-2605-09794:
Lin and 17 colleagues argued that personalization should belong to the user, not the platform. Today's services each build a partial user picture from fragments they observe, but competition, law, privacy concerns, and plain limits on knowledge keep every platform's view incomplete. Only users can join their own cross-platform and offline contexts, the paper claims, and LLM agents finally make that joining practical.

The team offered proof-of-concept evidence: users armed with cross-platform data exports and an off-the-shelf LLM agent beat single-platform personalization baselines. The paper closes with a research agenda for scalable user-governed systems, where agents reason over varied personal data and turn it into personalization the user controls. Data access, not modeling power, is the key asymmetry.
arxiv-2605-09894:
Lwin and Kumar compare two ways of running language-model modernisation of old COBOL code into Python, a task where scarce expertise and strict correctness make mistakes expensive. In agentic setups the model itself steers each tool step, while deterministic setups follow a fixed execution plan. The study holds models, prompts, tools and source programs constant and varies only who controls execution, so orchestration is the sole variable.

Deterministic runs matched the agentic runs on functional accuracy while improving worst-case robustness and cutting run-to-run variability. They also used up to three and a half times fewer tokens, which lowers operating cost sharply. For structured workflows with explicit validation stages, the authors conclude, a fixed plan gives steadier and cheaper behaviour without giving up translation quality.
arxiv-2605-09994:
Sun and nine colleagues built BatchWeave, an object-store-native data plane for distributed large model training. Modern training turned data loading from a fixed layer into a live part of training. Colocated dataloaders offer no failure cover, while message-queue dataloaders use a record-offset model that cannot express batch semantics.

BatchWeave runs batch publication, recovery, and lifecycle with versioned manifests and conditional writes. Its Transactional Global Batch adds training consistency to ACID storage: all-rank visibility, ordered steps, and exactly-once recovery. Recovery and retention live in storage itself. A Decentralized Adaptive Commit algorithm keeps intake steady as the list grows, with no talk between producers. On 64 GPUs, BatchWeave beat colocated loader speed with full failure cover, beat Kafka on intake, and cut reader lag below Kafka's.
arxiv-2605-10194:
Jiaxuan Wang and six colleagues refine a clever training trick that risks teaching too much. In on-policy self-distillation, a model teaches itself under privileged context, giving token-level guidance at every position. Their 2026 paper argues that guidance turns harmful when it covers the whole response, wasting gradients on redundant spots and leaking privileged information.

Their method, TRACE, routes distillation only to decisive reasoning tokens. A privileged annotator marks critical spans, while the teacher sees only a rough error label, not the span itself. Forward KL, a closeness measure, applies to key spans of correct rollouts, with reverse KL optionally applied to error spans, and the channel fades after warm-up. TRACE beat GRPO by 2.76 percentage points on average across four math benchmarks plus GPQA-Diamond, and alone preserved the base model's out-of-distribution score there.
arxiv-2605-10394:
Andreas Goulas and three colleagues introduce a new task for fighting disinformation: sensational image detection. Sensational content grabs attention and triggers strong emotion, often bypassing critical judgment and speeding viral sharing. Existing detection work focuses on text, while image-based sensationalism has lacked a dedicated benchmark. Their 2026 paper fills that gap.

The authors built Sens-VisualNews, a benchmark of 9,576 images from news items, annotated for the presence of sensational concepts and events in visual content. Using it, they studied prompt sensitivity, performance, and robustness across a wide range of open state-of-the-art multimodal language models, in both zero-shot and fine-tuned settings. The dataset gives fact-checkers a filtering tool for spotting check-worthy items and flagging potential disinformation.
arxiv-2605-10494:
Marius Miron and seventeen colleagues test whether better probing changes how bioacoustic encoders rank. Probing heads map audio representations learned by a model to downstream task labels, and most bioacoustic benchmarks settle on one fixed, low-capacity probe, like a linear layer over the encoder's last layer. That standardization may bias results by overlooking how encoder features interact with probe design. Their 2026 paper studies probing strategies across two benchmarks, BEANS and BirdSet.

The authors evaluate last-layer and multi-layer probing, across linear and attention probes. Larger probe heads that leverage time information perform better. Multi-layer probing lifts downstream scores across all tested models, while attention probing tops linear probing for transformer models. The results suggest current benchmarks may misjudge encoder quality when they rely on a last-layer setup. Readers get a caution: a benchmark that fixes the probe design risks underestimating some models and overestimating others.
arxiv-2605-10794:
Ari Holtzman and Peter West test whether language models can keep prompted information out of their writing, finding involuntary information leakage. Each model receives a secret word with instructions not to reveal it, then writes a story, while a second model tries identifying the secret from the story in a binary discrimination test.

The secret word never appears literally in any output. Yet all five frontier models tested leak it thematically through topic choice, imagery, and setting at rates significantly different from chance, up to 79 percent. When told to actively hide the secret, models write away from it, and this avoidance is itself detectable. Giving the model a decoy concept to focus on instead partially redirects leakage from the real secret to the decoy. This suggests attending to a secret opens an information channel frontier models cannot close even when instructed.
arxiv-2605-11294:
Nanda Kishore Sreenivas and Kate Larson study information and contract design for repeated interactions between agents with misaligned incentives. The team models an interaction between a Sender holding vital private information but unable to act, and a Receiver who must decide but depends on the Sender's information.

They find the Sender settles on an optimal communication strategy the Receiver reliably follows. This strategy swings sharply with how much the agents' rewards clash and how much environmental information the Receiver already sees. The team sets up a mechanism that lets agents strike linear contracts, with a price fixed for the information. They demonstrate the Sender learns to use payment structures to lift its rewards, though this costs fairness between agents as the Sender extracts much of the Receiver's surplus. Multi-agent researchers get a fairness-costing account of information pricing under misaligned incentives.
arxiv-2605-11394: Wang and three colleagues present the Spatial Adapter, a small post-hoc layer for frozen predictors. It works as a second stage on residuals, learning a spatial basis and per-sample scores without touching first-stage parameters. Smoothness, sparsity and orthogonality turn a low-rank factorization into an identifiable spatial representation. Its covariance has a closed-form low-rank-plus-noise estimate. That covariance supports kriging-style prediction at unobserved locations, with uncertainty quantification as a secondary use.
arxiv-2605-11694: Michael Lu and three colleagues close a practical gap in constrained reinforcement learning. Theory usually guarantees only a mixture policy, yet deployment needs one single policy. Their framework adapts the classic augmented Lagrangian method to constrained Markov decision processes and proves that the last policy in the sequence converges. It works first for tabular settings, then for log-linear and complex nonlinear policies, and it scales to continuous control tasks.
arxiv-2605-11894: In work published in 2026, Saqib Hussain, Gabrijela Zaharijas, and Klaus Dolag calculate high-energy emission from Perseus-like galaxy clusters hosting active galactic nuclei. Their goal is to separate the central source, such as NGC 1275, from diffuse emission in the cluster outskirts. Three-dimensional cosmological simulations plus Monte Carlo propagation show cosmic rays can stay confined for cosmological times and generate neutrinos and gamma rays. The authors predict IceCube and CTA could establish such clusters as a new class of multi-messenger sources.
arxiv-2605-12194: Mouyang Cheng and 16 colleagues probe grain boundary motion in nanocrystalline silicon with X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy and domain-adaptive machine learning. Grain edges steer how such solids hold up and behave, yet their slow, unsettled motion has been hard to watch directly. Tests at varied temperatures and grain sizes show edge settling staying far from balance over test times. A semi-supervised learning system moves labels from continuum simulations onto unlabeled test maps, pulling out bulk diffusion speed, edge stiffness, and edge concentration from raw fluctuation signals.
arxiv-2605-12294: Qin and four colleagues replace step-by-step guesswork in screen agents with a stored, runnable memory. Their Executable Agentic Memory organises past routines as a knowledge graph, built by state-aware search and mining of repeated action groups. Planning then runs as value-guided search over that graph. The approach beats strong baselines on AndroidWorld by up to about a fifth, cuts token costs sharply against a large commercial model, and answers in under three seconds on average.
arxiv-2605-12394: Prakash and Martin detect overfitting in neural networks without looking at training or test data at all. For each layer they randomise the weight matrix, fit its spectrum with a Marchenko-Pastur curve, and flag large outliers that break self-averaging, calling them Correlation Traps. During a phase they dub anti-grokking, traps form and grow while test accuracy falls and training accuracy stays high. Random inputs plus a divergence check then help tell harmful traps from benign ones, marking a distinct late-training phase.
arxiv-2605-12694: Mitchell and Wang bring lattice discipline to language-model program analysis with agentic interpretation. Language models can consult documentation, security advisories, version metadata and informal API contracts beyond source code. Yet one-shot whole-program analysis compresses many evidence-dependent judgements into one opaque answer. Their framework decomposes a high-level analysis goal. It exposes which conclusions are supported or disputed. Intermediate findings then guide later, more focused searches, marrying static analysis structure with model reasoning.
arxiv-2605-12894: Chopra and five colleagues improve user simulators used to test language-model agents, which today act too cooperative and uniform compared with real users. Their Persona Policies layer uses an evolutionary coding agent to discover persona programs tuned for human-likeness and behavioural range. Across four benchmarks the evolved personas gain 28 to 72 points in fitness over baseline simulators, and blinded judges call them human 80.4% of the time. Training with them lifts live task success by 23%.
arxiv-2605-12994: Kim and Fan study differentially private optimization with matrix-orthogonalized momentum, or Muon. Their DP-Muon uses standard global clipping and one Gaussian gradient release per step, with matrix updates as post-processing. The core contribution analyses the extra distortion when newly drawn Gaussian noise is transformed by a nonlinear matrix operation, giving an exact Gaussian heat identity. A bias-corrected variant lowers that bias from a squared dependence to a fourth-power dependence on the noise size. GPT-2 tests favour Muon over Adam baselines.
arxiv-2605-13294: Steinacker clarifies how spacetime and quantum fluctuations arise in the IKKT matrix model at weak coupling. Even with no free settings, matrix vacua gain a coupling constant plus two uncertainty scales, one for noncommutativity and one for quantum wobbles. He sizes both scales for the Moyal-Weyl plane and a covariant quantum spacetime. Wobbles prove tiny at weak coupling, backing earlier work on emergent three plus one dimensional geometry and gravity.
arxiv-2605-13394: Faizan Khattak and three colleagues build a cheaper way to estimate signal directions in two dimensions. For rectangular and parallelogram antenna arrays, the steering matrix splits into azimuth and elevation parts. Their method pulls the joint signal subspace out of the spatial covariance matrix. It then recovers each dimension separately and pairs the results. Simulations show it beats two-dimensional MUSIC and ESPRIT for medium and large arrays, using fewer snapshots.
arxiv-2605-13694: Livia Egyed and five colleagues extend light-induced dipolar links into the Floquet-driven regime, combined with built-in one-way optical forces. The team shows splitter, single- and two-mode squeeze steps, plus signs of a minus-mass-like spring from one-way forces. A tunable mix of these steps enables smooth tone shifts. The results give a toolbox of quantum operations for non-Hermitian many-body physics and shared quantum light-motion physics.
arxiv-2605-13794: Zhongtao Wang and eight colleagues present BlitzGS, a distributed 3D Gaussian Splatting framework cutting the active Gaussian workload at three coupled levels for city-scale scenes. At system level, it splits Gaussians across GPUs by index parity, not spatial blocks. At the view level, a distance-based level-of-detail gate plus an importance-based mask trims each camera's active set. BlitzGS matches recent large-scale baselines in rendering quality while training city-scale scenes in tens of minutes, nearly an order of magnitude faster.
arxiv-2605-13894: Teska, Pasque, Yoshida and Hashemi replace the usual softmax attention in a neural model with max-plus, or tropical, operators. The resulting piecewise-linear design fits the mathematics of phylogenetic trees, letting the model learn pairwise distances from multi-species sequence alignments. On eleven empirical alignment sets, the tropical model beats rivals on every set when judged against FastME-derived tree distances.
arxiv-2605-13994: Liu, Yuan, Chan, Sia and Li offer CineMesh4D, a full setup that rebuilds a patient's whole-heart mesh over time from sparse cine MRI. Thin 2D slices sample the heart sparsely, and shape and motion lock tight. So most past methods cover just some chambers or one heart phase. Cross-domain mapping links scans to mesh, while a differentiable rendering loss trains the four-dimensional mesh from sparse multi-view contours.
arxiv-2605-14194: Hu and six co-authors present GradShield, a filtering method that preserves alignment during language-model finetuning. Finetuned models can drift into misalignment from explicitly or implicitly harmful data, and even seemingly benign data can nudge a model toward misaligned behavior. GradShield spots and removes harmful data points before they corrupt alignment, scoring each point with a Finetuning Implicit Harmfulness Score and applying an adaptive threshold. Tests across several utility finetuning tasks with varying harmful-data levels weigh both safety and utility of the resulting models.
arxiv-2605-14294: Liu, Zhang and Zhao propose a transformer checking approach with better precision via ReLU-catalyzed abstraction refinement. Transformer inferences involve complex dot products in self-attention layers, making checks extremely difficult. Current methods bound output ranges well, but sacrifice precision and cause frequent false alarms.
