ReLU gives a precise non-linear bound for dot products, letting the team use convex relaxation work for ReLU to derive precise bounds. Rule-based and optimization-based classics are extended to them, yielding two new frameworks for efficient and precise checks.
arxiv-2605-14994: Ainesh Bakshi and three others prove sharp bounds on the eigenvalues of Kikuchi graphs, confirming four recent conjectures. The largest eigenvalue of the level-k Kikuchi Laplacian, signed or unsigned, is at most the edge count plus k. Applied to quantum optimization, product states reach ratios of five eighths for Quantum Max Cut and five sevenths for the XY model. Combined with existing algorithms, the bounds yield fast methods reaching 0.614 and 0.674 respectively.
arxiv-2605-15094: Mishel Carelli connects termination of integer linear-constraint loops to generalized Collatz sequences, integer sequences linear on every residue class modulo a fixed number. Termination asks whether a loop admits any infinite computation, a question still open for such loops in general. Whether such loops end remains open for loops over integers, rationals, and reals. For one-variable loops, Carelli proves ending is decidable in polynomial time, if a long-standing conjecture holds. In reverse, any choice method for one-variable loops would settle given cases of that conjecture.
arxiv-2605-15194: Rui Wen, Kansei Inamura, and Sakura Schafer-Nameki analyze one-way fusion-category symmetries on tensor-product Hilbert spaces, with mixing from quantum cell machines. Recent cases hinted any buildable symmetry must be weakly integral. Under real rules on defects, the authors prove that QCA and symmetry indices follow from categorical data up to relabeling freedom. They also build a lattice model for every weakly integral fusion-category symmetry, and give a direct realization of Tambara-Yamagami categorical symmetries.
arxiv-2605-15294: Jasper Laumen, Leonne Snel, and Frits Vaandrager propose a simple active-learning algorithm, drawn by L-sharp, for learning minimal separating automata. A deterministic finite machine splits two disjoint tongues by taking every word of one and refusing every word of the other. Such learners serve network-invariant learning, part-based checking rules, log-derived state machines, and bug-pattern notes. Tests show the new method a lot beats old active learners on random and industrial benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-15494: Hirotsugu Fujii, Tetsufumi Hirano, Kazunori Itakura, Yasushi Nara, and Shujun Zhao model forward hadron output in proton-proton crashes at LHC energies. Their event tool rests on the color glass condensate picture. They test three start models for the growth equation. LHCb data back two HERA-tuned variants, with gaps that widen at high sideways momentum. A second test backs one factor form over a rival at mid-rapidity. They also give forecasts for future ALICE runs.
arxiv-2605-15894: Ranjith Chodavarapu builds a probabilistic tool for grading wildfire smoke severity in satellite patches as Light, Moderate or Heavy, with confidence estimates in one pass. The model pairs a pre-trained EfficientNet-B3 backbone with a CBAM module and an evidential head predicting Dirichlet concentration parameters. It separates vacuity from dissonance with no Monte Carlo sampling. On 16,298 real patches it reaches 93.8 percent weighted test accuracy. Keeping only the most certain half of patches lifts the score to 96.7 percent, and the Moderate class shows the highest epistemic uncertainty.
arxiv-2605-15994: Sant'Ana works out how Tan's contact scales for trapped Tonks-Girardeau bosons at finite temperature in the canonical ensemble. The leading term matches the local-density approximation. A new subleading term captures the gap between canonical and grand-canonical descriptions. The result speaks to labs that trap atoms in one dimension and test such gases today, where that correction reaches several percent.
arxiv-2605-16394: Prooth and seven others report glowing nanodiamonds averaging around 60 nm with mean spin T1 times of 800 microseconds and a maximum over 1.8 ms, close to bulk values. Crystal defects limit how well nitrogen-vacancy diamonds sense external fields, by shaping their spin relaxation and coherence times. Their advanced growth method uses heterogeneous nucleation on pre-engineered sites, a nearly ten-fold improvement over commercial diamonds of 50 to 150 nm. Heavy-nitrogen doped shells for sensing near the diamond surface are also made, with scalability addressed for production volumes.
arxiv-2605-16494: Daraban and three colleagues show how a single dark state reshapes the long-run behavior of a dissipative spin chain. Neighboring sites in the chain share correlated loss. The zero-momentum mode stays dark for one particle, yet fades slowly once other modes dress it through a dissipation-driven nonlinearity. The momentum spread takes a universal scaling shape, and the total density decays slowly. Matrix-product-state simulations confirm the pattern, which survives soft-core interactions. The work also clarifies conflicting results in recent studies.
arxiv-2605-16594: Lu, Hao, Moya and Lin develop fPINN-DeepONet, a physics-informed operator-learning method for mixed diffusion-wave equations with fractional time derivatives. Such equations model memory effects in how things spread and how waves evolve. The method pairs a first-order approximation for the fractional derivative with operator learning. Tests on fixed and varying fractional orders, changing in space and time, and on noisy data show it is accurate and robust.
arxiv-2605-16794: Zhang and colleagues develop a game framework for coincident-peak pricing, used in U.S. power markets to split capacity and grid costs. The model couples nonlinear cost sharing with day-ahead and real-time choices, testing best-response and fictitious-play rules. On ERCOT peak-day data, fictitious play surely reduces peaks, while best response varies and can raise peaks when capacity is tight. Finer action detail lifts peak shaving, player count matters little at fixed flex, and smooth or diverse signals beat herding-prone grid signals.
arxiv-2605-16994: Singh and Desai compare dark-matter models for the Milky Way rotation curve using Gaia DR3 data and Bayesian model comparison. They test three baryonic models against seven dark-matter models across four recent rotation-curve compilations. The Einasto profile gives the preferred phenomenological fit over the NFW profile across most dataset and baryonic combinations, and cored dark profiles beat the cuspy NFW profile. Modified Newtonian dynamics, tested with three interpolating functions, fits worse than the preferred dark-matter profiles, while no baryonic model wins decisively.
arxiv-2605-17394: Taha El Bakkali and colleagues study stochastic zeroth-order optimization of smooth nonconvex goals under heavy-tailed gradient noise. These methods see only noisy function values, so they build finite-difference guesses from scalars. Their robust scalar-clipped method clips each scalar directional slope before combining. Given sample-wise smoothness and a weak moment tail condition it finds an approximate stationary point with high probability, matching optimal first-order accuracy dependence. A momentum variant is also analyzed.
arxiv-2605-17594: Kantor gives a simple construction of complete sets of mutually unbiased bases, a concept from quantum information where distinct bases overlap uniformly. Using bent functions, he writes the new basis vectors as explicit linear mixes of the standard basis. The construction is direct and elementary, supplying complete MUB sets without heavy machinery. Its brevity is the point: one clean idea yields the full family.
arxiv-2605-17694: Anvesh Rao Vijjini, Sagar Manjunath, and Snigdha Chaturvedi test whether language models copy human reactions to power gaps in conversation. They give models high- or low-status job personas and stage multi-turn talks between roles like principal and teacher or judge and lawyer. They then track matching language, pronoun choice, persuasion, and compliance with unsafe requests. The models show many classic power effects, with variation, linking simulated status to both helpful and risky behavior.
arxiv-2605-17894: Yifan Shen and six colleagues introduce ChildAgentEval, a benchmark that judges interactive AI agents against child developmental stages. Top agents still fail simple tasks a child handles with ease, exposing a gap between artificial and human intelligence. Inspired by the Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children, the benchmark compares multimodal agent reasoning with age-specific human stages. It reveals where current agents can and cannot mimic age-specific cognition. The work offers a psychometrically grounded yardstick for cognitive age alignment in agents.
arxiv-2605-18294: Jin Higashitani expresses the periods of Ikeda-Yamana lifts in a 2026 paper, in terms of special values of L-functions. Starting from Yamana's lift of Hermitian modular forms to automorphic forms on the unitary group, the paper treats Hecke eigenforms of level 1 and odd n. The result extends Katsurada's earlier work on Ikeda's conjecture to this unitary setting.
arxiv-2605-18894: Guoyue Luo, Yuntao Ma and Qiang Zou treat large multiscale microstructures as an on-demand generative process, not a full build of every tiny detail. As printing resolution and build volumes grow, explicit models blow up in memory while implicit ones stay compact only for simple periodic shapes. Their ExVCC spline representation allows local refinement beyond tensor-product grids, and an isoparametric scheme defines details at all scales over one shared domain. The result encodes huge detail compactly, evaluates it locally, and lets a change spread automatically across scales.
arxiv-2605-19194: Rui Chu offers MMoA, a looped mixture-of-agents build adding LSTM-based gating to agent choice, swapping static routers that miss time and context links across layers. The loop router tunes agent shares from current inputs and past routing calls, aiding aware merging. On instruction tests with MT-Bench, Arena-Hard, and AlpacaEval 2.0, MMoA matches old mixture-of-agents scores while switching on fewer agents. On that test it wins 58.0 percent of match-ups against 59.8 percent for mixture-of-agents, while lifting run speed by up to 4.6 percent.
arxiv-2605-19394: Lenin and team present EmbGen, a pipeline that teaches small tuned models with synthetic examples built from a domain corpus. Teacher-model pipelines often yield samey outputs and miss links across passages and documents. EmbGen splits a corpus into entity-description pairs, reassembles them by embedding similarity, and samples question-answer pairs within and across clusters. Against three rivals on three datasets, it lifts a combined accuracy-and-completeness score by 12.5 percent at five million tokens and 88.9 percent at twenty million on the most varied set.
arxiv-2605-19494: Mondello and team use high-throughput Bayesian optimization to design cement-salt composites for seasonal heat storage. Salt hydrate storage offers much but couples makeup, synthesis feasibility, performance and cost in tricky ways. Searching over salt type, concentration and cement ratios, the campaign found Pareto-optimal mixes based on calcium chloride, zinc nitrate and lithium chloride. The lithium chloride mix reached about 458 kilojoules per kilogram, and new mixes beat earlier cement materials five times, though trailing silica-gel rivals.
arxiv-2605-19794: A reproducible protocol for four-person meeting capture comes from Seikavandi and colleagues in AffectAI-Capture. Eye tracking, wearable body sensors, room and close audio, multi-view video, event logs and self-reports share one timeline with standard outputs. Bench tests check audio quality and video timing, while full sessions with people remain in progress. The work links task design, tools, timing records and packaging for meeting research.
arxiv-2605-19894: Xiaodong Yang, Subhabrata Sen and Yue Lu study multi-view spiked Wigner models, where several noisy matrices share correlated latent spikes. They build a spectral estimator from linearised approximate message passing and derive its exact sharp transition formula. Below a signal-to-noise threshold of one, no informative outlier appears past the bulk edge; above it, an outlier pins at one with clear overlaps to the latent signals. For many spike priors this spectral threshold matches the information-theoretic one, ruling out a statistical-computational gap.
arxiv-2605-20094: Cássius Anderson Miquele de Melo and Ivan Francisco de Souza present higher-order motion through the Pais-Uhlenbeck case and coupled oscillators. Most laws use second-order derivatives, and Ostrogradski first widened Hamilton's equations to Lagrangians with higher orders. That method rarely appears in textbooks. The authors show how to apply it to that oscillator, hoping it can anchor talk in upper-level mechanics classes.
arxiv-2605-20194: Aisvarya Adeseye, Jouni Isoaho and Adeyemi Adeseye propose parallel-chunk work on texts, merged with evidence links. Sequential runs let early or strong concepts hide weaker ones, causing bias and gaps. Their method splits texts into chunks run side by side, cutting earlier influence. Findings are merged with evidence links, curbing sway while lifting traceability. Tests show it cuts omission errors by about eighty-four percent and baseless claims by up to ninety-one percent. Evidence traceability rises by up to one hundred thirty percent, most for smaller models.
arxiv-2605-21094: Donggyu Lee, Taekyung Lee, and Jaewoong Choi address image recovery without paired training data, using only separate noisy measurements and clean signals. Their method learns a transport map that moves the noisy distribution toward the clean one, with a likelihood-based cost and relaxed matching rules for varied noise and uneven classes. A quadratic cost term yields one unique map, and tests top rival unpaired methods.
arxiv-2605-21294: Masafumi Niwano and colleagues study SMC X-1, whose pulsar mass sits near or below the neutron-star lower limit. Its double-peaked optical light curve, from tidal distortion of the donor star, constrains binary parameters. TESS optical and MAXI X-ray data show optical changes synced with X-ray super-orbital modulation, in the conjunction minimum and peak asymmetry. A modified ellipsoidal model, in which a precessing disk alters X-ray irradiation, explains the pattern and revises the pulsar mass.
arxiv-2605-21394: Ahmed Abbas Jaber Al-Furaiji and co-authors study similarity solutions for the flux-limited Keller-Segel system with a time-varying chemical decay rate. Treating decay rate as an arbitrary function, they carry out a Lie symmetry analysis and use equivalence transformations for a complete group classification. They identify the kernel symmetry algebra for arbitrary decay functions and three distinguished cases: constant decay, inverse-time power-law decay, and exponential decay. For each case, they construct an optimal system of subalgebras, derive similarity reductions, and find explicit solutions.
arxiv-2605-21494: Tino Werner studies double descent for least-squares interpolation on tainted data via simulation. Huge models can perform well despite standard theory predicting overfitting. Double descent, where error decreases after a certain size, opened a new research line. Robust statistics considers fitting on tainted data, where failing rules make points appear as odd points, potentially severely skewing standard estimators. He asks whether double descent appears in linear regression with tainted training data, comparing least-squares interpolation with robust rivals.
arxiv-2605-21594: Luca Mantani probes the SMEFT landscape via Bayesian model choice for indirect search. He develops a method for indirect search in the Standard Model Effective Field Theory. It is based on Bayesian model choice over term subsets, understood as a structured space of rival guesses rather than a single large model. Bayesian reasoning works at the level of model space itself. It assigns later odds to term subsets and side inclusion odds to single terms. A genetic method searches the discrete model space.
arxiv-2605-21794: Mandela Quashie and co-authors rework the Scovel-Weinstein framework for cutting the Vlasov-Poisson system while keeping its Hamiltonian form. Particle-in-cell methods use macro-particles with position and speed, while decorated ones add shape degrees of freedom in a finite Hamiltonian model. The first form dates to thirty years ago but its promise stayed untapped. The authors build the model, compare it with the standard method, and show far fewer decorated ones match its accuracy, giving a new model for kinetic plasma simulation.
arxiv-2605-21994: Yoav Kor Sade and co-authors present Ex-GraphRAG, an interpretable evidence router for graph-augmented language models. GraphRAG feeds models subgraphs from knowledge graphs through message-passing graph neural networks, but iterated aggregation entangles node contributions, so no audit shows which entities shaped the output. Ex-GraphRAG replaces that opaque encoding with a traceable one, exposing each entity's influence. Tests reveal: the nodes that dominate output are often disconnected in the retrieved subgraph, joined only by low-attribution intermediaries whose removal cuts multi-hop QA by up to 28 percent.
arxiv-2605-22094: Vasily Pisarev studies a different algorithm for the minimal-weight-matching centrosymmetry parameter. In 2020, Peter Larsen found flaws in such methods in current molecular dynamics packages. Larsen proposed a rigorous formulation in terms of minimal-weight matching on a fully connected neighbor graph, using Edmonds' blossom algorithm. Pisarev instead explores path-finding with A-star search for the same task.
arxiv-2605-22194: Antonio Cossidente and co-authors study intersections of two Desarguesian spreads in projective space. They show the intersection comes from a subgeometry over a suitable extension field, combining an account of point sets closed under q-order subgeometries with a Moore-matrix model. This yields Segre varieties and a geometric account of their maximal subspaces. As a main use, two distinct spreads sharing a pseudo-arc of size k+1 intersect exactly in a specified system of subspaces of the Segre variety. The work links spread intersections to subgeometry structure.
arxiv-2605-22394: Hapka, Tucholska and Pernal review methods that recover dynamic correlation for multireference wave functions from reduced density matrices. Such methods need at most the two-electron matrix of the starting wave function. Two kinds are covered: DFT methods and ab initio adiabatic connection methods. Tests on biradicals, excitation levels and iron spin-state splits rank MC-srPDFT best among DFT methods. Yet all DFT methods fail on spin-state gaps for transition-metal complexes. Linearised AC0 rivals or beats dearer perturbation theory across all test sets.
arxiv-2605-23094: Noriega Cedeño asks whether synthetic brain MRIs truly improve tumor classification, testing StyleGAN2-ADA augmentation on BRISC 2025 sets. Twelve class-plane models were trained, with and without InceptionV3 feature-space filter. Three classifier types were tested: a random forest, a compact two-headed convolutional network, and MobileViTV2, at 1:1 and 1:2 mixed ratios. The random forest gained nothing. The convolutional network's mean gains did not survive checks. Filtered 1:1 mixing lifted MobileViTV2 accuracy by 1.02 percent. Utility proved design- and ratio-tied, not promised by visual looks.
arxiv-2605-23394: Scholes and colleagues test a wearable quantum magnetometer as a fix for spatial aliasing in ground magnetic surveys, where slow old instruments blur fine detail. They carry both a proton magnetometer and an optically pumped magnetometer along a 20-kilometer line across the Highland Boundary Fault in Scotland. They sample every centimeter on foot instead of every 200 meters. The dense, fast readings cut noise and reveal small structures under 200 meters wide, with easier carrying and richer data as a bonus.
arxiv-2605-23494: Mousavi and three colleagues test earthquake forecasting in the Alborz region of northern Iran, using a homogenized catalog of 23961 quakes from 2006 to 2024. The background seismicity rate gives a steady spatial signal, with probability gains of five to six at low alarm rates along major faults. The b-value, a measure of quake-size balance, shows little skill at low magnitudes but turns positive above magnitude 5.3. Combined, the two indicators detect 81 to 83 percent of larger quakes at moderate alarm rates, the best setup tested.
arxiv-2605-23594: Magnani and Tripaldi study Stokes' theorem for differential subparts adapted to the twisted geometry of graded groups, stressing Carnot groups. They present geometric rules for Stokes-type rules to hold for the Rumin complex and a new spectral family tied to the weight layers of the de Rham complex. The spectral complexes recover Stokes' theorem on smooth inner graphs, with rules set by base submanifold degree. Both can be read through the standard de Rham complex via the Leibniz rule and summing over classes, R-manifolds and spectral shapes.
arxiv-2605-23894: Okada and Kasai build regular quantum error-correcting base matrices from a two-branch method over finite fields, turning regularity, orthogonality, and short-cycle rules into coset conditions. An exhaustive search yields bases for several degree pairs, and a cyclic lift randomizes edge links under checks. Their example gives a code with 10240 physical qubits for 4108 logical ones, girth at least eight, and no logical representatives up to weight 16. Joint belief-propagation decoding with repair rules reaches a frame error rate near one in ten million at the noise level.
arxiv-2605-24194: Rocha builds Orlicz-Hardy and Orlicz-Calderon Hardy spaces on the Heisenberg group and studies their link through the Heisenberg sub-Laplacian. Under suitable terms, every distribution in the Orlicz-Hardy space can be written in exactly one way through the sub-Laplacian of a function in a matching Orlicz-Calderon Hardy space. That gives one solution for each distribution.
arxiv-2605-24394: Zuo, Boyang Zhang, and Fumin Zhang present RoboHitch, tying hitch knots from human demos with disordered 3D keypoints and RGB images. Knot tying with bendy linear objects is hard: existing methods track ordered keypoints, but repeated bending and crossings cause drift and mismatch. RoboHitch drops the need for explicit order. A Graph Autoencoder pulls geometric features from untracked keypoints, a Convolutional Autoencoder adds visual context, and cross-attention fuses both to predict pick-and-place affordances under occlusion. Real-world tests complete hitch knots even with self-occlusions.
arxiv-2605-24494: Partha Ghose rebuilds electrodynamics on persistent stochastic processes, treating finite-speed random spread as basic rather than derived. Dirac and Maxwell wave equations then emerge from telegrapher dynamics after analytic continuation. Mass and charge become persistence and coupling scales, while particles and fields appear as stable collective modes. The 2026 framework claims no change to quantum electrodynamics predictions, but gives a new picture of what lies below. Bound states, light emission, and gauge effects get the same treatment, as stable or shifting modes of the random flow.
arxiv-2605-24594: Kaixiang Su and three colleagues tackle crystal structure determination from powder X-ray diffraction, a hard problem when data are noisy or structures complex. Purely data-driven AI models learn direct pattern-to-structure maps and fail on complex or unusual cases. Their hybrid ab-initio method splits the task into discrete selection of space group, unit cell, and Wyckoff sites. Continuous optimization then refines atomic coordinates within those sites. AI peak analysis, density estimation, and energy minimization under physics constraints make the approach robust for challenging cases.
arxiv-2605-24994: Chakir Fikri proves a simple probability rule for ideal delayed-choice quantum eraser setups. Such tests are often cast as defying classical causal intuition by linking detections to later choices. Post-selection is known to shape the observed interference patterns, yet their structural roots lack a unified account. Fikri shows four plain properties cannot hold together: free choice, no losses, fixed routing given the choice, and distinct conditional detection patterns. That clash classifies eraser schemes plainly. It shows how conditional interference arises without exotic mechanisms.
arxiv-2605-25294: Junho Lee, Kwanseok Kim, and Joonseok Lee say image generators ignore the natural geometry of pictures. They find that meaning lives mostly in directional parts of an image, while size-like parts track a global average, in both pixel and latent spaces. That pattern suggests pictures sit naturally on a sphere-like surface rather than in flat space. The team builds two flow methods for that curved geometry: one uses angular distance, the other constrains motion to the surface. Both beat flat-space baselines.
arxiv-2605-25394: Ashwath Vaithinathan Aravindan and Mayank Kejriwal propose a simple prompting trick that helps small language models admit uncertainty instead of answering wrongly with confidence. Their Second Guess method adds an 'I don't know' option and watches answer stability. Models that truly know an answer pick it consistently, while uncertain models waver once abstention is offered. Tested on four small models and four benchmarks, the method achieves the best composite risk improvement, about 11 percent. It keeps an 8 percent improvement on fine-tuned models where entropy methods degrade, helping weak models most.
arxiv-2605-25794: Le, Abel and Laforge study early-warning models from learning system logs, which predict course results in time to help learners. Early scores often look better than they should when temporal leakage lets pipelines use information not yet available. They formalize cutoff-based prediction and introduce LEAP, enforcing cutoff-first truncation and auditing feature provenance. On the Open University dataset, scores rise as the window expands, with a gain around week three. Random Forest leads early on, while Gradient Boosting takes over later.
arxiv-2605-25894: Noseda, Soldati and Paina ask whether news mood, fundamentals and market dynamics predict direction on earnings days. They build a feature space from 15 metrics, 3 indicators and FinBERT news mood scores. Long short-term memory and attention models face a logistic regression baseline, with and without it. Long short-term memory shows higher precision via safe bets. The attention model catches volatile moves better, with higher macro F1. Ablations show mood helps.
arxiv-2605-26094: Singh, Ghosh, Saboo, Halder and Majumder ask whether twisted light can spin up a dipolar Bose-Einstein condensate. STIRAP, a slow light-pulse method, can seed quantised vortices in plain condensates. Whether it works in dipolar condensates was open, since long-range dipole forces compete with short-range contact forces. With Gaussian and Laguerre-Gaussian beams on a thin trapped condensate, the authors reach superfluid, droplet and supersolid phases. Momentum transfer and vortex lifetime hinge on the phase, with the vortex steadied in the supersolid phase.
arxiv-2605-26594: Xiaoli Wang and three others derive analytic coupling terms for spin-adapted time-dependent density functional theory of open-shell molecules. Spin-adapted methods already sharpen excitation energies and gradients, yet their non-adiabatic couplings for spin-preserving excitations were unknown. The team implements ground-to-excited and excited-to-excited couplings for X-TDDFT atop existing code with modest overhead. Benchmarks cut errors by a third to two thirds versus standard TDDFT. Internal-conversion rates shift by up to a hundredfold, and copper porphyrin pathways get revised.
arxiv-2605-26894: Zhang and six colleagues propose SIMPC, an unsupervised method for denoising point clouds by learning exact links between noisy points and the true surface. For each noisy point, it creates a mirror point on the far side of the surface, guided by geometric priors, and enforces consistency between the denoising targets of each pair. The method localizes the surface well, beating leading unsupervised rivals on synthetic and real data and topping several supervised ones.
arxiv-2605-26994: Huang and seven co-authors present ChartAct, a benchmark for dynamic chart understanding, where key facts appear only after hovering, clicking, zooming, or dragging. The set holds 673 dynamic charts from 8 real chart sites and 1,440 question-answer samples across 7 chart types, each in two settings. Tests on 11 advanced multimodal models and GUI agents show clear limits: the best model, Claude-Opus-4.7, averages 84.5 percent success, while most models stay below 60 percent.
arxiv-2605-27294: Vyzantinos Repantis and colleagues ask whether retrieval readers fail from longer context or from rival passages that compete with the right one. Holding passage count and length fixed, they swap hard rivals for weaker real passages and watch scores recover. The matched control isolates a genuine competition effect beyond context length, clearest for answer inclusion and F1.
arxiv-2605-27394: Tatiana Chakravorti and colleagues test a hybrid prediction market for judging whether findings replicate. Algorithmic agents trained on past replication outcomes trade beside human experts, pooling machine patterns with domain knowledge. Except for a few cases, the hybrid market matches or beats machine-only markets, giving more accurate and reliable replication forecasts.
arxiv-2605-27494: Syed Huma Shah asks when reusing a cached answer is safe in retrieval-augmented generation. His GroundedCache router admits a cached answer only when four gates hold together: query similarity, evidence overlap, source-version validity, and lexical support from fresh evidence. The router drives unsafe servings to zero on HotpotQA regimes and under 2 percent on document drift, at near-baseline latency.
arxiv-2605-28294: Asha Ram Gairola and Nidhi Bisht bound joint approximation by a sum-integral hybrid operator. They show the operator's slopes tend to the target slopes, with rates for the miss, for both values and slopes at once. The brief paper gives error bounds for function and slope approximation in one setup.
arxiv-2605-28394: Gaurav Rai and Ojaswa Sharma present Sketch2Motion, turning hand-drawn sketches and text prompts into 3D animation. Motion is built on a skeleton and guided by a text-to-video diffusion model, with no paired motion data needed. Smoothness, shape, and contact constraints steady the result, and a spring-mass simulator adds secondary motion. Tests show coherent, text-matched animation for biped, quadruped, and inanimate characters, beating baselines without such guidance.
arxiv-2605-29194: Jules Berman and colleagues present a method for generating paths of random physical systems. They attach a fresh, high-dimensional random label to each step in the training data and fit a map from the current state plus label to the next state. The labels act as extra coordinates, so the model can offer several plausible next states instead of collapsing to an average. At run time, new labels are drawn at each step and the map is rolled forward, yielding varied paths with one network pass per step.
arxiv-2605-29394: Zhichen Tang presents EvoMD-LLM, which recasts species-level molecular dynamics as a symbol language of time. Reactive paths become chains of events, each token standing for a species plus its stay time. This lets standard next-step models learn piecewise change over time through fast fine-tuning. Time scaffold treats event length as a plain language token, cutting invalid or made-up outputs. On forecast tasks, it scores up to sixty-six percent and beats step-by-step neural networks and language-based rivals.
arxiv-2605-29594: Sung-Soo Byun, Meng Yang, and Eui Yoo work out the free energy expansion for a determinantal Coulomb gas in the plane under an outside pull plus a point charge. For simply or doubly linked droplets, they push the expansion through the constant term with all coefficients spelled out, widening earlier round-case work. They pin the constant term to the Liouville action of the droplet shape. Their proof deforms the charge spot and stretch factor, tying free energy shifts to fine asymptotics of flat orthogonal polynomials.
arxiv-2605-29694: Qian Bin, Ying Wu, Franco Nori, and Xin-You Lü show in theory how a three-way link can yield tied bursts of light and sound quanta. The direct link builds high-order multi-quanta states with no extra middle steps, dodging the weak rates that dog chained steps. That opens a path to efficient even-count bursts, such as two photons with two phonons, despite energy loss. Adding two-photon loss then unlocks odd-count bursts, such as two photons with one phonon, by curbing single-photon loss.
arxiv-2605-29994: Lukas Einhaus, Natalie Maman, Julian Hoever, Andreas Erbslöh, and Gregor Schiele speed tiny nets by precomputing layer outputs into FPGA lookup tables. Lookup-table precomputation gives light nets with ultra-low latency but scales poorly, and depthwise-separable convolutions only partly fix scaling. The team generalizes to wider grouped convolutions, adds a new block, and guides block hyperparameters with an algorithm. On MIT-BIH heart data, the accelerators fit an AMD Spartan 7 S15, hitting up to ninety-five percent F1 with few thousand tables and no DSP or BRAM.
arxiv-2605-30194: Vanessa Zema and Pasquale Pavone trace the low-energy excess in cryogenic calorimeters to thermal-contraction mismatch at interfaces. Sensitive rare-event detectors show a rising low-energy spectrum of unknown origin. They trace it to mismatched contraction between the absorber and the silicon dioxide layer under transition-edge sensors. Contraction during fabrication and cooldown can nucleate surface dislocations, and other mismatched interfaces can do the same. A simple elastic model links the effect to observations. The paper proposes designs to test and mitigate it.
arxiv-2605-30294: Ingo Wald and nine co-authors present RaFI, a CUDA and MPI based framework easing GPU-enabled data-parallel code in which rays or similar jobs move between GPUs. RaFI gives CUDA kernels a simple interface to forward work items to other GPUs, while managing all CUDA and MPI work required. They cover RaFI's motivation and implementation, and demo its potential in several example applications.
arxiv-2605-30594: Abreu and Biscainho present FiPA-SR, a system that restores missing high frequencies to bandlimited audio. Unlike models tied to one input bandwidth, it uses FiLM conditioning layers to adapt reconstruction to each bandwidth within a single model, building on an earlier framework. Tests on the MUSDB music dataset show it beating the AudioSR system at three input sampling rates. It uses roughly a third of the graphics memory and runs far faster than a diffusion-based baseline. The design suits practical bandwidth extension across varied sources.
arxiv-2605-30694: Mahadevan offers a category-theory frame for choice making, joining planning, reinforcement learning, causal action, online learning, and equilibrium. A Universal Decision Learner stretches a partly given choice rule from seen settings to new ones via two universal builds. Left Kan extensions cover rollout, aggregation, and candidate generation; right Kan extensions cover consistency, constraint satisfaction, and fixed-point meaning. The point is not one shared method, but one shared problem: stretch local choice data in the standard way. Bellman equations, planning, causal actions, regret, and equilibria all arise as cases.
arxiv-2605-30794: Kou and colleagues introduce MechVQA, the first dataset for mechanical drawing understanding by multimodal large language models. Drawings stay brittle for these models, as dense annotations and weak domain knowledge make cues easy to miss. MechVQA holds 3.3 thousand pictures with 21 thousand question-answer pairs across ten tasks in Recognition, Reasoning, and Judging. Built through a semi-automated pipeline with quality control, it offers a testbed for real-world drawings. The authors build MechVL through multi-stage training, beating the closed-source baseline by over seven and a half points.
arxiv-2605-30894: Mi and colleagues tackle a skew in synthetic face data for face recognition training. Diffusion methods can make lifelike faces with identity match, yet models trained on them still lag real models. The authors trace the gap to visual tendency: synthetic sets overuse certain looks, because stray visual cues leak into learned identity. Their SteerFace nudges identity vectors toward orthogonal directions on the embedding sphere, curbing reliance on stray cues while keeping identity. An adaptive version tunes strength per sample, and tests show less skew and better recognition.
arxiv-2605-30994: Dong and colleagues improve multimodal sentiment analysis, combining language, visual, and acoustic signals. Old methods fail in two ways: fixed conflict controls cannot adapt across samples, and language bias misguides learning from other signals. Their MCAF first builds a causal model to strip language bias, yielding a clean guide. A dynamic router then judges how the three signals interact at three levels, weights them, and a denoising step filters leftover noise. Tests on two benchmarks set new best scores on key metrics.
arxiv-2605-31194: Blasi and colleagues compute, from first principles on the lattice, how fast bubbles nucleate when topological defects seed a first-order phase transition. In their cubic-anisotropy test case, line-like domain walls seed the bubbles in two space plus one time dimension. Lattice rates agree very well with a semi-classical domain-wall prediction across the parameter space, including fluctuation effects beyond spherical symmetry for the first time.
arxiv-2605-31394: Manente, Alfò and D'Angelo model healthcare mobility in Italy with a dynamic latent space model. Seeking care elsewhere drives inequality and financial imbalance in split health systems. North-south gaps in flows among 109 local health bodies have deepened divides, yet flow structure and timing remain poorly understood. Their Bayesian model for one-way weighted networks handles excess zeros, wide spread and network links, with sender and receiver effects. It reveals the shifting shape of the system, sizes the COVID-19 shock, and uncovers gaps in outward pull and patient attraction.
arxiv-2605-31494: Zhang, Yang, and Kasneci present CoRP, a way to fold rewarded perturbations into a single model for language-model post-training. Recent weight-space methods sample noisy variants around a base model and ensemble the best rewarded ones at test time. That costs many forward passes per example. CoRP instead combines reward-weighted updates with a held-out validation gate, using no gradients through the model. Across five models and five tasks, the average gain over the base model is 8.1 points.
arxiv-2606-00294:
Mahmoud and co-authors map how news tales use time as a frame, not just a clock. Time words do more than place acts in line. They can bend how a tale is read and felt. The team calls this craft temporal framing in news work.

They build a scheme of eight time frames from past work. Pros tag a dual-tongue news set by hand for those frames. The set holds 458 tales in English and German. More than two thousand framed lines sit in a pool of far more lines. The team tracks which frames show most and which pair up. Word cues for each frame are charted too. Trained tools spot frames far past zero-shot tools.
arxiv-2606-00594:
Shi, Shi, and Wang set a far-field form of the p-Laplacian face task with a sharp wall kept. Face tasks join two zones at a wall with set terms. Far-field forms spread each point's pull past its near kin. Most such forms blur the wall they aim to keep.

Their form is built from an energy frame for the task. Wall terms of Neumann type fall out of that frame in a plain way. Wall terms of Dirichlet type are held by a fine term. A kin task with skin terms shows the form's reach. Proof shows that as the far reach shrinks to nil, best fits land on the local task's best fits. Grid tests back that land.
arxiv-2606-00894:
Balestra and co-authors review a family of metal-rich superconductors in this 2026 paper. The family is the eta-carbide-type compounds, lately a lively class in superconductivity research. Odd superconducting traits grow from their complex metallic bonding. Several members are bulk superconductors, with names like Nb4Rh2C and Ti4Ir2O among them.

Transition temperatures reach about 10 kelvin. Upper critical fields climb as high as 30 tesla. The heat values look normal for intermetallic superconductors. The field values do not: many of these high-symmetry crystals break the weak-coupling Pauli limit by a wide mark. The review ties such traits to crystal symmetry, hard synthesis, and the mix of transition metals. Electronic structure gets a full pass as well. Open questions close the survey, with a hunt for new family members. The paper serves as a map of a young field for materials physicists.
arxiv-2606-00994:
Wang describes a pipeline that pulls plant and pet traits from text at vast scale in this 2026 paper. The source is the Tropical Species Encyclopedia. The goal is structured trait records a reader can audit. Language models do the reading, but four guards keep each row honest.

A versioned registry of 39 trait keys fixes the allowed values to a typed schema. Each row carries a verbatim quote from its source as proof. A confidence label marks each row high or medium, and low rows are dropped before storage. Past versions of each record are kept. The run covered near 410 thousand species in over 700 thousand passes. It stored about five and a half million trait records, most at high confidence. In checks, nine of ten quotes match their source word for word. Wang claims auditability, not per record truth: all rows await human curation.
arxiv-2606-01294:
Le and co-authors fix the read step in linear attention. Linear attention cuts the quadratic cost of softmax attention. It keeps a running fast-weight state as it reads. But it lags on in-context recall and long texts. Past fixes change how memory gets written. The read step stays the same in those fixes. Every past key adds to the output alike. Useful targets get diluted by stored bulk.

Their curvature-conditioned query shrinks the query before reading. A Taylor expansion of softmax gives a local quadratic model. Its curvature matches the running key covariance. The step contracts the query along high-variance directions. Gains appear on GLA and Gated DeltaNet tests.
arxiv-2606-02294:
Vivier-Ardisson and co-authors turn large neighborhood search into a sampler for neural layers. Practitioners solve hard combinatorial problems with large neighborhood search. It refines a solution by re-optimizing subsets of variables. Most neural combinatorial layers still assume exact global solutions. Those are computationally intractable for hard problems. Regularized LNS bridges that gap in this work.

Local subproblems are regularized or perturbed in the method. The heuristic becomes an efficient MCMC sampler over feasible solutions. Fenchel-Young losses come with that sampler form. Under entropic regularization, exact block Gibbs sampling is proved. The number of iterations interpolates between regimes smoothly. Users can trade compute for sample quality by that knob. Differentiable optimization layers gain a scalable solver. Operations research and machine learning meet here.
arxiv-2606-02494:
Boston and co-authors argue that young agentic systems fail in structure, not in tasks. Production agents are often partial assemblies. Structural defects dominate the failure landscape. Task-level monitors then lose their signal. The team builds a monitoring and triage method for this stage.

Evaluation splits into three dimensions: quality, suitability, and efficiency. Monitoring runs at three scopes: within-run, cross-run, and structural. Variance serves as the core signal. Severity classes borrowed from FMEA route the findings. A synthetic testbed holds 220 runs over 120 document bundles. Controlled errors are injected. Scope decides what a monitor finds. Within-run monitors surface stage defects. Cross-run monitors surface integration fallout. A structural monitor spots an integration gap with perfect consistency. Injected task errors stay hidden against clean baselines. Triage sends most findings to automated tracking. The authors urge teams to deploy monitoring early.
arxiv-2606-02594:
Basti and co-authors report first results from TRIO, a transportable ring laser gyroscope. The work sits inside the GINGER project. GINGER plans an array of large ring laser gyroscopes at the Gran Sasso underground laboratory in Italy. The goals span fundamental physics tests and geophysics. A new design cuts spurious rotation of instrumental origin. Spacers let the cavity side grow from 1.5 up to 5 meters.

TRIO is the prototype, with a side length of 1.52 meters. It was conceived as a movable instrument. The team measures Earth's angular velocity with it. Results test both the prototype's performance and the design behind GINGER. Data are compared with older gyroscope prototypes. The large GINGERINO gyroscope, already running at Gran Sasso, is one reference. The readings support the path toward the full array.
arxiv-2606-03394:
Alenezi examines how generative and agentic AI are reshaping software engineering work. Coding once centered on humans writing code by hand. It now centers on directing, checking, and governing systems that act on their own. Alenezi draws on recent peer-reviewed studies and large sets of field data. One source tracks coding agents that sent hundreds of thousands of pull requests.

Three paradigms are set side by side: traditional, generative AI enabled, and agentic AI enabled. The synthesis maps which tasks are automated, which are augmented, and which are new. A competency framework sorts the skills future engineers need into five groups. These cover technical, cognitive, social, governance, and workplace skills. Nine testable claims follow, with notes for schools, firms, and leaders. As code grows cheap, lasting value lies in clear intent and sound judgment.
arxiv-2606-03494:
Ivanov and Kharuk study renormalization in four-dimensional Yang-Mills theory with a cutoff. The cutoff is set in the coordinate picture. A background field method frames the generating functional. The cutoff enters through quasi-local averaging of the fields. Two forms of that averaging are put forward.

The strong form averages the fluctuation fields directly. The weak form is a version built to respect gauge changes of the background field. The authors study singular terms in the first two quantum corrections. Those terms are compared in detail with dimensional regularization. The action and the equation of motion are checked after the procedure. New counter-vertices get special attention. Their locality and their link to the cutoff value are analyzed. Field theorists get a careful test of an alternative to the standard scheme.
arxiv-2606-03794:
Garcia Camargo, Wang, and Ribeiro set limits on how graph neural networks transfer across wireless network scales. Such networks allocate radio resources well by using graph structure. Models trained on small graphs should serve large deployments with little loss. Wireless conflict graphs are sparse: each node links to few others. The theory here covers graphs drawn from sparse random geometric graphs.

Conflict graphs model interference among links in those networks. Random geometric graphs sit close to deterministic grid graphs. That closeness bounds the loss when a policy moves across scales. Link scheduling validates the theory in practice. Learned policies beat existing benchmarks at scale, time after time. The authors also probe how their assumptions shape real performance. Network engineers get grounded guidance on when small-graph training is enough. Transfer can be trusted within the proven bounds.
arxiv-2606-03994:
Lee and co-authors build SimuScene, a tool that rebuilds 3D scenes from one image. The scenes must be ready for physical simulation. Robot handling work needs such scenes, and single-image tools often fall short. They may give good shapes object by object. Joined scenes can still sink, hover, or overlap, then collapse in simulation.

SimuScene puts physics inside the shape and layout steps. It runs gravity tests on rebuilt objects as a measuring tool. Failures of support or overlap become numeric correction signals. Those signals drive stretching along the gravity axis and shape resampling. Tests show top scores for stability and geometric fit, they report. Rebuilt scenes were also used for humanoid control and robot-arm tasks.
arxiv-2606-04094:
Erandi Chavez and co-authors describe in 2026 a method for imaging radio sources at many frequencies at once inside a Bayesian framework, sharpening both the picture and the color information it carries. Combining frequencies fills in spatial detail that any single frequency misses.

Their method, CHIBI, builds the image model around the known spectral behavior of synchrotron radiation, the emission that dominates galactic nuclei. Demonstrations on jet sources from a long-running telescope catalog produced higher-fidelity images and maps of spectral slope. Simulated data for the Event Horizon Telescope and its planned successors showed the same gains for imaging the black hole in M87. The authors stress that the gains come inside a statistically grounded framework, not from ad hoc sharpening.
arxiv-2606-04194:
Christian Lysenstøen reports in 2026 a training-free recipe for searching long conversation histories, the memory bottleneck for chatbots that meet the same user over many sessions. Recent work showed that scoring a session by its single best-matching turn beats averaging, and he builds around that effect rather than claiming it.

Fusing that dense similarity score with classic keyword search lifted top-hit accuracy by nine to seventeen points across six encoders on a standard benchmark. A popular web-search reranker, by contrast, hurt accuracy here. One popular way of softening the best-turn score collapsed for half the encoders. The author separates which questions gain from meaning-based search and which from keywords, framing the study as a controlled recipe, not a memory system.
arxiv-2606-04294:
S K Leggett and Pascal Tremblin revisit a puzzling cold companion in 2026. It is a Y dwarf, one of the coldest known brown dwarfs. It orbits the white dwarf WD 0806-661, which pins down the system's distance and age.

Two recent analyses of Webb telescope spectra had clashed with each other. Both also clashed with models of how such objects cool. Leggett and Tremblin confirm the dwarf's brightness. They revise the system age to about one and six tenths billion years. Then they fit the full spectrum with an updated model family. The fit works across nearly the whole range. It gives a temperature near three hundred fifty-seven kelvin and a mass near seven Jupiters. That sits well with cooling models after all.
arxiv-2606-04694:
Payoungkhamdee and colleagues teach small language models to stay multilingual, in a 2026 arXiv paper on distillation. Small models are efficient, but their multilingual ability collapses at sub-billion scales, especially for Southeast Asian languages. Their framework, DuDi, distills a teacher into a student with dual signals: an online sequence-level signal plus off-policy and on-policy token-level signals.

A cross-lingual verbalizer refines the teacher's feedback, improving how well it transfers across languages. On the SEA-HELM benchmark, across multiple model families, scales, and teacher-student pairings, DuDi consistently outperformed competitive distillation baselines. Ablations confirm that sequence-level optimization, token-level supervision, and cross-lingual verbalization contribute complementary and transferable signals. The work targets the practical problem of serving capable multilingual models cheaply in regions whose languages large models serve worst, where a small model that keeps its languages has outsized value.
arxiv-2606-04894:
Bordoloi, Shivkumar, and Iyyani test whether a radiation mechanism can explain how gamma-ray burst spectra evolve within a single pulse. Gamma-ray bursts are the brightest explosions in the universe, yet their mechanism is unsettled. Spectra are described by the Band function, summarized by a peak energy and a low-energy slope, alpha. The authors model thin inverse Compton scattering inside a standard fireball jet and track the spectrum's evolution with two binning schemes.

They find this mechanism produces a positive correlation between peak energy and alpha, with alpha evolving from very hard, Planck-like values above plus 0.5 to softer values below minus 0.67. Such hard slopes are inconsistent with standard synchrotron emission. The tracks reproduce both commonly observed patterns, hard-to-soft evolution and intensity tracking. This evolution within the peak-energy-alpha plane therefore serves as a signature of inverse Compton scattering as the dominant prompt-phase mechanism.
arxiv-2606-05194:
Ian Rios-Sialer and colleagues investigate how a large language model represents temporal preference in this 2026 arXiv paper. Models are asked to make decisions that trade near-term gains against long-term consequences, yet little is known about how they represent or resolve tradeoffs. The team applies mechanistic interpretability tools to a distilled model, Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507.

Combining gradient-based attribution with activation patching, two methods that test which internal components cause a behavior, they localize a subgraph for temporal preference in mid-to-upper-layer nodes. They find the geometry of time horizon encoded in the residual stream at those layers. The unintervened model discounts the future several times less than humans do, but the preference is unstable across contexts. That argues for control rather than reliance on whatever training instilled. The authors report evidence that steering vectors can shift the model's temporal preference in a direction.
arxiv-2606-05294:
Pradip Kattel, Yicheng Tang, and Natan Andrei study two fermion chains with identical spectra but different dynamics in this 2026 arXiv paper. One chain is interacting and the other is quadratic, meaning free, yet a nonlocal nonlinear unitary transformation maps one onto the other while preserving the many-body spectrum. The pair is solvable on both sides, which makes the contrast clean.

Operators that evolve inside a linear subspace in the quadratic model turn into interacting operators in its partner. They generate higher-body terms with Lanczos coefficients growing like the square root of the step index, a signature of strong operator growth. Despite sharing a spectrum, the two models realize distinct phases and different notions of operator complexity, measured through Krylov complexity. The results show that a free many-body spectrum and interacting operator dynamics are fundamentally compatible, so spectra alone cannot settle how a system scrambles information.
arxiv-2606-05394:
Abhinaba Roy, Junyi Liang, and Dorien Herremans present nnAudio 2 in this 2026 arXiv paper, an update of the open-source nnAudio toolbox for audio feature extraction. The original toolbox computes spectrogram transforms as neural network layers inside PyTorch. It had been stranded by TorchScript incompatibilities, inverse-transform edge cases, and dependency drift.

The update resolves TorchScript compilation failures in the short-time Fourier transform and its inverse. Inverse STFT behavior is clarified by limiting inversion to the uniform frequency-bin setting and raising runtime errors for unsupported scales, replacing poor reconstructions. Compatibility with modern SciPy is restored for the combined-frequency-and-periodicity transform, and the variable-Q transform now reduces to the constant-Q transform when its setting is zero. An inverse constant-Q transform based on Landweber iteration is also introduced, rebuilding waveforms above 30 decibels signal-to-noise, and the test suite passes.
arxiv-2606-05494:
Ahmed Alansary and Ali Hamdi present MASF in this 2026 arXiv paper, a framework that improves text summarization by letting several models compete. Relying on a single model gives inconsistent quality: a summarizer that excels on one article's structure or topic may falter on another's. MASF hedges that bet with an adaptive selection strategy.

It integrates multiple fine-tuned transformer summarization models. For each article, every model generates a candidate summary. The candidates are scored with automatic metrics capturing word overlap and meaning, and the highest-scoring one becomes the output. Trained and evaluated on the CNN/DailyMail news dataset, the framework achieved the highest BERTScore among all compared methods, at 88.63 percent, and it also outperformed several large language models used directly as summarizers. Combining models under a selector, the authors conclude, is an effective route to better summaries without a single ever-larger model.
arxiv-2606-05594:
David Mellafe measures a gap in Chile's cyber defenses in a 2026 arXiv paper. Chile named nine hundred fifteen operators of vital services, such as power, water, banks, and hospitals. The question is whether outsiders can report security flaws to them. Mellafe defines a coverage gap: the distance between public exposure and a working channel for flaw reports. The study checks every operator with public sources only.

Only sixteen of the nine hundred fifteen operators publish a verified contact channel for flaw reports. Fewer than ten do so among physical services like energy, health, and transport. All four banks and both big phone firms lack one entirely. About eighty-four percent of operators also have flawed email security settings. Mellafe places Chile about eight years behind the United States and Britain on email rules. A four-stage road map, modeled on United States and British toolkits, closes the paper.
arxiv-2606-06694:
More home hunters now ask chatbots where to live, which raises a fairness worry. Samad and co-authors audit that risk in this 2026 arXiv paper on racial steering, the old practice of guiding buyers toward or away from areas based on race. They tested seven language models in four United States cities, slowly adding lifestyle details to each request.

Steering appeared, but it did not point the same way in every city or test. Adding stated preferences often increased or reshaped the steering, which suggests the models read the same preference differently depending on the user's stated race. The authors argue that steering grows out of how a model interprets a request together with what it has absorbed about each place. One city's results, they warn, cannot be assumed to hold in another, so local checks are needed.
arxiv-2606-06894:
Building a malware detector with machine learning means juggling many design choices at once. Vhito, Suaboot, Werapun, and Rattanavipanon offer a decision framework in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their FDM scores candidate setups against the realities of deployment. Five inputs drive the score: platform limits, budget, latency, update pace, and sensitivity.

The framework ranks options across nine design dimensions. Four experiments checked its advice on three data sets. One held Windows program call traces from eight malware families. Others held malware images and Android app data. In binary detection, XGBoost gave the best accuracy per resource. It hit about ninety seven percent accuracy in under seventy megabytes of memory. In multi class tests, classical models beat deep recurrent ones. Transfer learning cut training time roughly in half. The message: fit the tool to the setting, not the fashion.
arxiv-2606-06994:
Sentence encoders turn text into points in a space where nearby points share meaning. Mohr, Dujany, Souquet, and Freitas ask what makes those spaces represent concepts well in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their lens is compositionality: can the space realize each concept family's combining rule without distortion? Training used millions of synonym and definition pairs.

Four principles emerge from controlled ablations. First, fine tuning reshapes latent geometry rather than expanding it. Second, semantic signal concentrates in the final layer before concept training. Pooling across layers adds nothing. Third, hard negatives sharpen calibration but not ranking. Those two skills can be tuned apart. Fourth, supervision must match the concept's composition type. Set style training helps some families and degrades others. Relational and intensional concepts suffer most, a structural limit of current practice.
arxiv-2606-07294:
Saberi and colleagues use the Hubble Space Telescope to probe the hot outer atmosphere of a dying star in this 2026 arXiv paper. The star is R Leo, a nearby Mira variable on the asymptotic giant branch, the late life stage of Sun-like stars. Its chromosphere, the layer above the visible surface where temperature rises again, shapes the star's chemistry and mass loss. Ultraviolet emission lines from magnesium and carbon serve as diagnostics of that layer.

The carbon line ratios imply an electron density near a billion particles per cubic centimeter in the emitting gas. Modeling shows the carbon emission comes from a compact shock-heated shell at roughly twice the star's photospheric radius, heated to about ten thousand degrees. The magnesium lines form over a much wider region extending many times farther out. An aluminum line's small blueshift supports the picture of pulsation-driven shocks moving through the atmosphere.
arxiv-2606-07394:
Hamdi, Ayar, and Javanmardi diagnose where video instance segmentation systems lose performance, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The task combines detecting objects, outlining them, and tracking their identities across frames, but benchmark scores blend all three error sources. Their diagnostic framework casts identity and class assignment as an integer linear program, creating an oracle that isolates each error source. They applied it to 7 methods, online and offline designs, across benchmarks and an occlusion-heavy diagnostic set.

Tracking instability emerged as the bottleneck for online methods, with gaps exceeding 20 average-precision points under occlusion. The tracking gap grew sharply with video length and instance density. Classification errors mattered on benchmarks but became negligible where tracking failed worst. Stronger image backbones raised scores yet left tracking gaps largely intact, proving the weakness is algorithmic rather than about visual features. A visual tool, TrackLens, exposes the failure modes behind the gaps.
arxiv-2606-07494:
Xuanjun Chen and colleagues harden detectors against synthetic speech generated by neural audio codecs, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Codec-based generators produce realistic fake audio, threatening voice security systems. Training detectors on resynthesized speech helps, but models trained on proxy data generalize poorly to wild fakes. Their method, domain-shift feature augmentation, simulates wild variation during fine-tuning by turning fixed feature stats into random distributions, exposing the detector to plausible shifts before deployment.

They built a test set that extends a codec-fake benchmark with 40 unseen models and long audio. Combining a post-trained self-supervised speech backbone with the method achieved state-of-the-art detection across codec attacks on the benchmarks. The gains held on the extension set designed to break generalization, supporting the claim that the augmentation narrows the proxy-to-wild gap rather than overfitting one generator family. The tougher benchmark is a contribution.
arxiv-2606-07694:
Kyeongjun Lee and Heeyoung Kim tackle vessel traffic forecasting in busy ports in this 2026 arXiv paper. Predicting ship movements matters for port planning and navigation safety. The catch is that traffic counts at many port locations sit at zero most of the time, with sudden bursts of activity. Standard spatio-temporal graph neural networks, which learn from connected locations over time, tend to collapse toward predicting near zero everywhere.

The authors add a learnable Tweedie head, an output module based on a distribution family built for data mixing zeros with positive values. It plugs into existing network backbones unchanged, and it learns how variable each location is. On a traffic graph built from tracking data for the ports of Los Angeles and Long Beach, the head improved forecast error across several backbones. Gains were strongest where models failed before, on the non-zero bursts that matter for traffic control.
arxiv-2606-07794:
Kwan, Chen, and Brehmer study how people would lay out timelines in physical space if software stopped forcing a straight line, in this 2026 arXiv paper for Graphics Interface. Timelines are strong storytelling tools, but most tools prize tidy chronology above all. Fully free layouts capture the irregular feel of lived time better, at the risk of confusing viewers.

In a formative study, twelve participants freely arranged historical and personal events around a room. Their strategies varied widely, reflecting personal and context-dependent mental models of time rather than one natural layout. Participants also considered how a visitor would move through their arrangement, turning layout into something like choreography. From that analysis the team built a proof-of-concept tablet augmented-reality app for drawing and viewing spatial timelines. The work argues timeline tools should treat relative position and situatedness, where events sit in a place, as first-class choices.
arxiv-2606-07894:
Takada and Mori automatically improve the prompts that language models use to untangle group chats, in this 2026 arXiv paper. In multi-party chat, several conversations interleave in one stream. Dialogue disentanglement separates the stream back into coherent threads. Language models are promising for it but still score low with ordinary prompts.

The authors split the prompt into three parts: task instruction, utterance representation, and output instruction. Their method, DD-GEPA, optimises all three with GEPA, an evolutionary prompt optimiser for compound AI systems. Most prompt tuning treats wording as one block; here the structure itself is the search space, so the optimiser can discover, for example, that utterances need speaker markers presented differently. On benchmarks, the optimised prompts improved disentanglement accuracy over the originals. They could even surpass carefully hand-crafted prompts, suggesting prompt engineering for this task is better searched than intuited.
arxiv-2606-08394:
Haoran Zhao, Han, and Hovy probe whether correct answers from multimodal models hide internal instability, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Multimodal language models are usually judged by external behavior: picking the right image-text match or rejecting an unsupported caption. But a correct answer does not show that the model's internal decision state stayed stable when the question was made semantically stressful. Their framework, Structured Semantic Stress Evaluation, tests exactly that gap between behavior and internals.

The setup anchors on a positive example: an image-supported caption is contrasted with semantic stress candidates, plausible but conflicting alternatives, under both original and swapped option orders. Hidden states are extracted at the pre-answer decision state, the moment just before the model commits. The analysis focuses on strict-correct trials, where the model picks the right caption under both orders.
arxiv-2606-08494:
Chevalier and a large team present a new way to find the seeds of stars inside computer simulations, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The processes determining the stellar initial mass function, the distribution of star masses at birth, remain major open questions in star formation. What counts as a core is itself unclear. Yet how cores are extracted from simulations critically shapes the resulting mass function. Today cores are mostly detected by density or brightness alone, which can merge or split structures for purely numerical reasons.

Their tool, called vibes, defines cores through a direct application of the virial theorem, the balance between gravitational binding and internal motion that decides whether a structure holds together. It builds structures around density peaks and applies virial criteria to decide their extent. Membership is earned by dynamics rather than a density threshold, so the cores carry more physical meaning.
arxiv-2606-08594:
Jasmeet Singh Bindra and Panwar ask how big a neural network really needs to be to clean brain signals, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Architectures for electroencephalogram denoising, removing muscle and eye artifacts from brain recordings, have scaled from tens of thousands to tens of millions of parameters. Yet no prior study isolated model capacity as the experimental variable, or tested whether reconstruction metrics predict downstream usefulness of the cleaned signal. The authors address both gaps with a controlled sweep.

Holding architecture, loss, data split, and training recipe fixed, they varied only the channel width of a minimal convolutional network, from roughly one thousand to forty thousand trainable parameters. Evaluation spanned a large denoising benchmark, cross-dataset transfer tests, and downstream motor-imagery classification with five decoder families. The framing reveals benchmark saturation and a metric-utility gap, where prettier reconstructions do not mean more useful signals.
arxiv-2606-08694:
Biroli, Welling, and Vitelli decode what a generative model has secretly learned about a physical system, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Generative models increasingly capture correlations in many-body systems, but what they learn remains largely opaque. The authors establish a criterion quantifying a variational autoencoder's capacity to reconstruct the joint probability distribution of a many-body system. A capacity bound compares the rate of the latent channel against the bipartite mutual information of the data.

Using this bound, they show the decoder of any successful autoencoder is structurally identical to a finite-size mean-field factorization. That is the classic approximation treating each part as feeling only the average of the rest. A successful reconstruction is therefore direct evidence for a latent mean-field theory, and that theory's microscopic parameters can be read off the trained decoder. They validate the conclusions on solvable models.
arxiv-2606-08894:
Sun and colleagues test whether reasoning vision-language models can ignore misleading pictures, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A vision-language model answers questions about images; reasoning versions think step by step before answering. Earlier robustness tests blurred or dirtied images to check whether the model could still see the evidence. This team studies a different failure: the image stays clear, but a meaningful yet irrelevant cue is added.

Their benchmark, Distract-Bench, adds verified distractors that leave the correct answer unchanged. They evaluated eight open-source and two closed-source models. Under blur and noise, reasoning models roughly matched their non-reasoning base versions. Under semantic distraction they did worse. In one comparison a base model kept about ninety-two percent relative robustness while its reasoning-tuned variants fell to between eighty-four and ninety percent. Traces showed the distractors entering the model's reasoning and being treated as evidence.
arxiv-2606-08994:
Ukarapol, Sarapat, and Chukamphaeng stop language models from slipping into the wrong language, without any retraining, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Language confusion is the failure to keep generating the requested language, a common flaw of English-centric models answering in other tongues. Fine-tuning fixes it at a price. Their method, Language-Aware Token Boosting, nudges generation directly: at each step it boosts tokens of the desired language, favoring them among the model's choices.

An adaptive variant adjusts the boost by the model's own confidence that it is on-language. In summarization experiments, both methods reduced language confusion and improved multilingual alignment while preserving summary quality. The gains held without touching the model's weights, so the technique can wrap any deployed system. The authors note limits around out-of-vocabulary tokens and token-level language identification, and release their code publicly.
arxiv-2606-09494:
Dario Sergo and his co-authors build a dynamical theory for when living communities link into one vast web or split into patches in this 2026 arXiv paper. The pattern is called percolation. Field studies see it in drylands, where grazing or rain can tip plant cover from linked clumps to lone scraps. Past work leaned on grids and computer runs, with thin exact theory.

The team uses a discrete form of the Lotka-Volterra model, the classic rules for species that compete and grow. Their version keeps the broad traits of the full model yet can be solved on paper. On random interaction graphs, they map when surviving sites form a giant linked cluster. A key point is reach: not all steady states can be reached by the living dynamics. Which states are within reach sets when clustering and percolation switch on.
arxiv-2606-09594:
Jonathon Cottom and Emilia Olsson show that two alike ways to pose a Bayesian inverse problem can give unlike answers in this 2026 arXiv paper. An inverse problem infers hidden inputs from data and a model equation. One route solves the equation first and samples only the inputs. The other keeps both inputs and state as free values and fines any breach of the equation.

The second route is tempting, since it skips a costly solve at each step. But the authors prove the two forms are not the same as probability measures. As the fine grows harsh, the full-space form drifts to the reduced answer times a determinant factor. The team derives fixes for plain, weighted, and rescaled fines that restore the right limit. The moral is sharp: a zero breach alone does not prove the sampling is sound.
arxiv-2606-09694:
Rui Ding and his co-authors map where steady clouds of scalar field can cling to a spinning black hole in this 2026 arXiv paper. The hole is a BTZ type, a three-dimensional toy, warped by a Kalb-Ramond field. That field breaks Lorentz symmetry, the rule that physics looks the same to all movers. Clouds form at the superradiant edge, where the hole's spin would feed a wave.

The edge depends on three knobs: the Kalb-Ramond strength, the spin, and a Robin condition at the far boundary. For zero or negative field strength, the cloud zones form smooth, single runs. For positive strength, the lines bend, and one fixed boundary rule can allow clouds in split zones. Checks with ringing modes and horizon flow signs backed the cloud readings. The field strength also shifts the boundary value where clouds switch on.
arxiv-2606-09994:
Regis and a co-author examine whether a pseudo-scalar field could be the dark energy driving cosmic acceleration, in a 2026 arXiv paper on cosmology. A pseudo-scalar field carries a single value with a sign-flip twist. If such a field couples to photons, it rotates the polarization plane of the cosmic microwave background, an effect called cosmic birefringence. The authors test several shapes for the field's potential energy.

Combining expansion-history observations with birefringence measurements, they constrain each model's parameters. An axion-like potential works only for large values of its anomaly coefficient, a number setting the photon coupling strength. Potentials shaped as quadratic, linear, or Ratra-Peebles forms can explain both dark energy and the rotation signal together. In those working cases, the symmetry-breaking scale sits close to the grand unification scale, linking dark energy to very high-energy physics.
arxiv-2606-10094:
Battu models how predictive AI can settle a person's thinking before they have explored enough options, in a 2026 arXiv paper on cognition and AI. Predictive systems change the timing: they supply answers and decision paths before the person's own search unfolds. He calls this exogenous exploratory compression and models attention moving over a landscape of strategies.

The model yields three main results. First, steady AI support cuts exploratory response by weakening inner perturbations, even when variety in search remains. Second, curvature builds and relaxes unevenly, producing hysteresis and slow recovery of movement in search after help ends. Third, timing matters as minds develop: early help narrows later exploration before broad variety has formed. The paper derives testable forecasts about exploratory entropy, early convergence, and slow recovery, suggesting such systems reshape cognition itself.
arxiv-2606-10194:
Sheikh and colleagues assemble a large benchmark for testing AI systems on climate science across text, video, and figures, in a 2026 arXiv paper on machine learning evaluation. Their framework, MMClima, contains over one hundred four thousand expert-validated question-answer pairs spanning five core climate science domains, built by automated claim extraction and question synthesis with human validation in the loop.

Using MMClima, they benchmark leading multimodal language models on factual recall, visual interpretation, and cross-modal synthesis. They also fine-tune on the textual split to produce a domain-adapted seventy-billion-parameter baseline that outperforms strong open and closed models on textual question answering. The dataset, evaluation pipeline, fine-tuned weights, and data creation framework are all released publicly. The authors position MMClima as standardized infrastructure for multimodal climate evaluation, comparable in spirit to general benchmarks but grounded in expert-checked scientific content.
arxiv-2606-10694:
Lu and colleagues give language models long-term memory in this 2026 arXiv paper. A model's context window is finite, so assistants must store conversations externally and fetch them back. Flat text systems lose relations between facts, others overwrite facts as they change, and retrieval is often query-blind. REAL stores memory as a temporal, confidence-aware directed graph, each fact carrying entities, a relation, valid times, a confidence score, and an intent label.

Updates are non-destructive, keeping parallel fact versions, so evolution stays visible. Retrieval anchors on query-relevant entities, splits their exploration intents, and runs a guided beam search for a compact evidence subgraph. When expansion stalls, counterfactual inference invents paths to recover missing evidence via implicit logical relations.
