In experiments, REAL improves long-term memory performance by an average of 22.72 percent over flat-text, graph-based, and state-of-the-art memory managers.
arxiv-2606-11094:
Blachar, Pajot, and Salez prove a long-standing conjecture in a 2026 arXiv paper on graph geometry. Discrete Bakry-Émery theory adapts curvature, the bending measure from smooth geometry, to networks through the curvature-dimension condition, CD. The conjecture says bounded-degree graphs with nonnegative curvature must have polynomial growth: balls of vertices expand at most polynomially with radius.

They prove it for all edge-regular graphs, where every edge plays a symmetric role, with a volume doubling estimate whose constant depends only on the degree. The key is a surprising self-improvement phenomenon. Any edge-regular graph satisfying the curvature condition with dimension infinity in fact satisfies it with some finite dimension parameter, explicit and optimal. That hidden finite dimension forces the tame growth. The result may matter beyond this conjecture, since finite dimension unlocks tools the infinite case lacks.
arxiv-2606-11394:
Orozco-Duarte and five co-authors present the first spatially contiguous study of the Helix Nebula in a 2026 arXiv paper. With integral-field spectroscopy from the SDSS-V Local Volume Mapper, they achieve nearly complete coverage. Spaxel-by-spaxel analysis measures extinction, density, temperature, ionization structure, and abundances, from forty-one optical emission lines.

The maps reveal a stratified nebula. Highly ionized gas concentrates toward the central cavity; low-ionization material dominates the bright shell; neutral gas is enhanced outside. The Helix is low-density, with electron densities near one hundred per cubic centimeter, and its temperature varies by thousands of kelvin across ionization zones. Their oxygen abundance is near-solar, consistent with complete sampling. The abundance pattern points to a major contribution from unobserved triply ionized oxygen, so variations are driven by ionization effects, not true inhomogeneity. A sulfur deficit near one dex matches the known sulfur anomaly.
arxiv-2606-11594:
Zenghua Zhou and seven colleagues provide new formulas linking star colours to star temperatures in this 2026 arXiv paper. Effective temperature, the surface temperature that matches a star's total light output, usually needs a spectrum, which most stars in big surveys lack. The team instead calibrates simple colour measures, differences in brightness between filters, against temperatures found by the Infrared Flux Method.

Their sample combines 3,902 stars from the GALAH survey and 2,535 from APOGEE, all with good measurements. They fit low-order polynomial formulas for both dwarf and giant stars, with and without a term for metallicity, the share of elements heavier than helium. Long-baseline colours spanning wide wavelength gaps work best. The widest combinations reach internal precision near thirty to fifty kelvin. Comparisons with older formulas mostly agree, though some older scales run cooler by over one hundred kelvin for certain colours.
arxiv-2606-11694:
Suhyoung Choi studies the stability of certain space-time geometries in this 2026 arXiv paper. A Margulis space-time is a complete flat universe with Lorentzian geometry, the maths of relativity, formed by dividing flat space by a free group of symmetries acting cleanly. The case of interest includes a parabolic element, a borderline symmetry type tied to cusps and horizons.

Choi proves an openness result: small deformations of the group still act properly, as long as their linear parts stay Fuchsian, a known class of surface symmetries. The number of distinct parabolic elements can rise or fall under deformation, so that feature is not rigid. The proof builds on the author's earlier compactification, adding a boundary to control behaviour near the parabolic parts, plus work by Carrière.
arxiv-2606-11894:
Yuto Furutani and three University of Tokyo colleagues rebuild 3D scenes from messy photo collections in this 2026 arXiv paper. Three-dimensional Gaussian splatting represents a scene as clouds of soft blobs and renders new views quickly. Feed-forward versions predict the scene in one pass, avoiding slow per-scene optimisation, but they struggle with real collections full of varying light and passing objects. The bottleneck is training data: collections with many viewpoints, many lighting conditions and transient objects barely exist.

The team built the WildCity dataset: two hundred scenes under one hundred seventy lighting conditions with transients present, totalling over three hundred thirty-seven thousand images. Their model, Wild3R, learns appearance consistency across viewpoints, conditioned on reference views, while removing transient content. Experiments show it beats existing feed-forward approaches, including pose-free ones, and matches optimisation-based methods that need camera calibration or point clouds.
arxiv-2606-12194:
Hametner and Tyrrell show that the standard way to build large solution-free sets can always be beaten, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The setting is additive combinatorics over finite fields, number systems where arithmetic wraps around. A cap set is a set with no three-term arithmetic progression, no evenly spaced triple, inside such a space. The usual construction forms direct products of a good small set, stacking copies into higher dimensions.

The authors prove that for any set avoiding nontrivial solutions to a genus-one linear equation, a mild regularity condition, some higher-dimensional set does better per dimension. Applied to cap sets, no single fixed example can yield the best growth rate through products alone. The gain they prove is real but tiny, far too small to move the current record bound in practice. Its force is structural: products are provably not the end of the story.
arxiv-2606-12394:
Niwa and co-authors clean a noisy quantum operation by running it many times, and prove the cleaning rate cannot be beaten, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A noisy qubit unitary channel applies an unknown rotation followed by depolarizing noise, static-like corruption. Purification combines many uses into a superchannel recovering the original clean operation. For state purification the best strategies are parallel. For channels, the authors first show numerically that sequential strategies, adapting later uses to earlier outcomes, strictly win at finite use counts.

They then give a concrete parallel protocol built on a new entanglement-assisted error-correcting code. It suppresses the leading noise term in proportion to one over the number of channel uses. That scaling is asymptotically optimal in the low-noise regime. Even sequential strategies, despite their finite-size edge, cannot beat the rate asymptotically. The result sets the benchmark for denoising unknown operations.
arxiv-2606-12494:
Wang and Wang build a flight simulator for traffic disasters, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Generative simulators forecast how systems evolve, reducing costly real-world trial and error. The hard version is event evolution: how an accident's impact ripples across a road network over time. Earlier models missed either the events' rich descriptions, mixing structured data with free text, or the network's topology, its web of connections. Their Net-Ev squared framework handles both.

Training runs in two stages: structure-guided masked pre-training, then a topology-aware diffusion process that denoises through graph downsampling and upsampling, U-Net style. At run time, a plain natural-language description of an event suffices to generate the simulation. The pair also release a benchmark of over six and a half million aligned event and traffic pairs spanning four road networks. A metric, JL-MMD, grades how faithfully generated dynamics preserve topology.
arxiv-2606-12594:
Joshua Ong and co-authors build theorem provers that punch far above their weight, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Lean provers check mathematics, but top ones demand huge budgets. Verified proof data are scarce, and proof searches run long. Their family spans autoregressive models at four and thirty-two billion parameters, plus a first diffusion-based prover that refines proofs iteratively.

Training leans on a Lean-verified corpus sorted by difficulty, taught as a curriculum. Filtering keeps proof traces inside an eight-thousand-token budget. Their Augmented Lean Formalisation mutates problems into variants, filled in by self-distillation, multiplying training signal without verifying every mutant. The four-billion model beats a six-hundred-seventy-one-billion rival on the MiniF2F test, scoring eighty-six percent against eighty-two at pass thirty-two. The thirty-two-billion model reaches ninety-three percent, best among open provers.
arxiv-2606-12694:
Kook and Vempala give a nearly tight cost bound for sampling from logconcave distributions, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A logconcave distribution is a probability distribution whose logarithm curves downward. Sampling means generating random points following such a distribution, starting from a warm start, an initial guess already close to the target. Cost is counted in evaluation queries, calls revealing the defining function.

One algorithm, called In-and-Out, combined with a trick named exponential lifting, handles all cases in their analysis. The new ingredient is a sharper bound on the Poincaré constant of the lifted distribution, a quantity controlling how fast sampling settles down. Earlier analyses carried an extra term inflating costs for well-conditioned problems. Removing it lets one bound cover constrained cases, such as a Gaussian restricted to a convex body, and smooth strongly logconcave cases, at nearly best possible rates.
arxiv-2606-12794:
Zhang and colleagues present a computation-assisted method for picking out nonlinear signals in 2-dimensional spectroscopy, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Two-dimensional spectroscopy probes ultrafast quantum dynamics by spreading a response across 2 frequency axes. Phase-cycling picks out 3rd-order signals, but weaker higher-order signals overlap them in the spectrum, and pushing phase cycling to higher orders grows costly.

The strategy takes data in a rotating frame, a shifted frequency reference, and applies a frame-shift algorithm. Signals of different nonlinear orders shift at unequal rates as the frame changes, so each order can be tracked and separated. In a rubidium vapour experiment, the team picks out a 7th-order nonlinear signal from the 3rd-order components present, reaching quantum-coherence dynamics without falling back to weak excitation. The authors offer it as a route to ultrafast dynamics beyond standard 3rd-order spectroscopy.
arxiv-2606-12894:
Selvan and colleagues study longitudinal particle separation, sorting particles along the flow direction rather than across it, in curved microfluidic ducts, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The authors use a duct with an elliptical centreline and a rectangular cross-section, where the radius of curvature varies along the duct's length.

Because the cross-sectional equilibria depend on it, the varying curvature causes bifurcation behaviour along the duct. A duct undergoing a periodically varying saddle-node infinite-period bifurcation, called SNIPER, lifts longitudinal clustering at the expense of cross-sectional grouping. The effects depend on size: for large particles, longitudinal clustering weakens at higher Reynolds numbers and with falling eccentricity, while small particles keep grouping across a wide range of shapes. Smaller eccentricities enable simultaneous sorting both ways, while larger ones strengthen lengthwise sorting but hurt cross-sectional sorting.
arxiv-2606-13494:
Azuma and colleagues present NavWAM in this 2026 arXiv paper, a model that lets a robot navigate toward a pictured goal. Goal-conditioned navigation is hard because the robot sees part of its surroundings and must anticipate how moving changes its view and whether that approaches the goal. Navigation world models predict those views, but they remain forecasting modules: a planner must convert predictions into motion. NavWAM, a diffusion-transformer policy, closes that gap by representing future observations, goal-progress values, and action chunks in one latent sequence.

Learning prediction with the actions and values that drive closed-loop behaviour makes the foresight executable. The model is built through simulation pretraining followed by adaptation on a robot. This combination aims to transfer the breadth of simulated experience into reliable performance. The authors argue unifying world modelling and control in one system is the route to capable navigation.
arxiv-2606-13594:
Chen and colleagues ask whether artificial agents can share internal states directly in this 2026 arXiv paper. Multi-agent systems usually communicate through text, paying a lossy, costly decode and re-encode at every hop. Sharing key-value caches, the memory transformers build while processing, is a promising alternative. Prior work mostly used copies of the same model, dodging the hard problem of aligning different models' internal languages. Existing methods also assume shared input and use transferred caches mainly for steering.

The authors study the stronger question: can heterogeneous agents be aligned well enough for genuine mind reading, transferring both what one agent sees and how it thinks? Their information-structure analysis reveals a duality governing when context-aware transfer works. The work pushes agent communication beyond language toward dense latent exchange. If internal states can cross model boundaries faithfully, agent systems could collaborate at a fidelity text cannot approach.
arxiv-2606-13694:
Liu and colleagues make sleep staging cheap enough for mobile devices in this 2026 arXiv paper. Sleep staging, classifying each short epoch of a recording as wake, light, deep, or REM sleep, underpins home sleep monitoring and closed-loop stimulation therapies. Standard sequence models such as recurrent networks and transformers are too expensive for phones and wearables. The authors propose Random Attention, a lightweight temporal module based on fixed random projections. It replaces learnable sequence modelling with similarity-based pooling, adding almost no parameters beyond the epoch encoder while still smoothing predictions.

They also give the module a theoretical reading through a prior kernel that splits it into a global smoothing term and a feature similarity term. On two sleep datasets, Random Attention improves epoch-wise baselines by 1 to 3 percent in accuracy and F1 score, reaching performance with far heavier models. The work targets the practical frontier of digital health.
arxiv-2606-13794:
Demir, Ahmad, and Fichter combine interpretable learning with nonlinear control allocation for aircraft in this 2026 arXiv paper. Overactuated aircraft have more control effectors, surfaces and thrusters, than needed, so a control allocator must decide how to share the forces among them. Standard allocators assume linearity, but nonlinear dynamics and strong coupling between effectors break that assumption away from gentle flight, degrading accuracy and robustness. High-fidelity onboard models restore accuracy at prohibitive computing cost, while black-box learned models sacrifice the clarity that checking and fault finding require.

The authors learn an explicit, physics-constrained model of the control power mapping from flight data, using a sparse method for nonlinear dynamics. The resulting mapping is compact, readable, and admits analytical slopes for the splitter. An integrated method then performs the nonlinear split on that learned model. The approach targets flight regimes where linear allocators fail, without giving up auditability.
arxiv-2606-13894:
Benedek, Koren, and Fried shrink the memory cost of training neural networks with the AdamW optimizer. AdamW stores two moving averages per weight, adding about twice the model's size in training memory. Their 2026 arXiv paper introduces Gefen, which shares second-moment estimates across blocks of weights and compresses the first moment with a learned codebook. The theory: large mixed curvature entries force squared gradients toward similar values, marking natural sharing blocks.

Gefen infers the blocks from initial squared gradients, needing no architecture details or extra settings. Its codebook is learned exactly by a histogram-based dynamic program. The result uses about eight times less optimizer memory, saving six point five gibibytes per billion parameters, while matching AdamW's performance. Among rival low-memory optimizers it posts the lowest peak footprint. Freed memory allows larger microbatches, lifting throughput by fifty-six percent in one distributed setting.
arxiv-2606-13994:
Kothamasu, Smith, and Yadav expose a safety hole appearing when harmful requests are chopped into harmless-looking pieces. In a decomposition attack, each subtask seems benign alone, yet together they complete a malicious goal. Current safety tests rarely model this pattern realistically. Their 2026 arXiv paper introduces DeCompBench, a benchmark built decomposition-first with a graphical framework and four design criteria.

State-of-the-art agents refused monolithic harmful tasks at high rates. Refusal dropped sharply on decomposed versions of the same tasks. Agents often fulfilled the adversarial objectives without noticing the cumulative intent. The benchmark spans eight harm categories. Audit tampering makes up twenty-four point four percent of tasks and financial crime twenty-two percent. The dataset is public. The authors call for defenses reasoning about intent accumulated across steps.
arxiv-2606-14294:
Belbachir and Zeggada roll dice over tilings to extract exact statistics of the multibonacci numbers. The multibonacci, or s-bonacci, sequence generalizes Fibonacci: each term sums the previous s terms, and its numbers count tilings by tiles of lengths one through s. A known probabilistic model colors board cells randomly and ties a random variable to the tilings; the authors previously extended it to tribonacci. Their 2026 arXiv paper generalizes the model to all s, using colored tilings with k-ominoes up to s.

They establish the variable's distribution in terms of multibonacci numbers and compute its expectation in closed form: two to the power s plus one, minus three. The second moment follows as an explicit formula in s. For Fibonacci, s equals two, the second moment is 853/9 and the variance 628/9; for tribonacci it is 54840/49. The proofs exploit a restart property of the tiling process.
arxiv-2606-14394:
Gandhi and Raicu report a 2026 arXiv study of blockchain design, the shared ledger technology behind digital currencies. Public blockchains process transactions slowly, and simply enlarging blocks or shortening block times creates delays and forks. Sharding splits the work across parallel groups called shards, each handling part of the traffic.

The authors built a configurable simulator using the SimPy toolkit to model mining, checking, shard coordination, and message spread. In a local data-center setup the simulator reached about one point six million transactions per second with two hundred fifty-six shards, and about six hundred thousand per second across a global network. Beyond a certain shard count, coordination traffic began to dominate and gains flattened out.
arxiv-2606-14594:
Manita and Amari compare how open-source projects govern AI contributors in a 2026 arXiv paper. Coding agents now plan changes, edit files, and submit pull requests with little supervision, but open-source workflows assume a legally accountable human behind every contribution. Incidents and nuisance volume during twenty twenty-five and twenty twenty-six showed the gap has real operational costs.

The authors code the contribution policies of six organizations, including SymPy, LLVM, matplotlib, and the Apache Software Foundation, and trace processes in depth for two of them. They derive a six-dimensional taxonomy covering disclosure, responsibility, oversight, licensing, enforcement, and maintainer workload, plus an ordinal policy maturity score. Mapping documented agent incidents onto the dimensions shows where each policy fails, and aligning the dimensions with frameworks like the European AI Act reveals gaps neither side closes.
arxiv-2606-14994:
Kanungo offers an introduction to Sobolev spaces and their role in partial differential equations in a 2026 report. Classical solutions must be smooth enough to satisfy an equation at every point. Many physical problems, such as flows with shock waves, admit no such solutions. Sobolev spaces widen the frame by treating derivatives in an integrated, weak sense.

The report traces the history from Dirichlet's principle to Sobolev's work in the nineteen thirties. It then gives basic definitions, examples, and the function spaces built from weak derivatives. Central results include the Sobolev embedding theorem and Rellich's theorem, which control how these functions behave. The closing application is the elliptic regularity theorem, showing when weak solutions gain smoothness. The author aims the text at students with real analysis and PDE background. Sobolev spaces, the report stresses, now form the backbone of existence and uniqueness theory for weak solutions.
arxiv-2606-15294:
Roy and coauthors locate the mobility edge of a disordered quantum system from its spectral form factor, in a 2026 condensed matter paper. The mobility edge is the critical energy separating trapped states from extended ones. In crowded quantum systems it marks where thermal behavior gives way to frozen dynamics. Finding it requires solving the full Hamiltonian, which caps system size. The spectral form factor measures energy links and is computable without exact solution. The authors track how its correlation hole deepens with temperature.

A critical temperature emerges where the form factor's behavior changes character. Statistical mechanics converts that temperature into an energy density. In a disordered Heisenberg spin chain, that energy matches it. Two checks, perturbation spread and optical conductivity, give the same value. The phase diagram reveals frozen, quenched, and annealed regimes around the transition. The method offers experiments a shortcut route to phase boundaries.
arxiv-2606-15394:
Heim and coauthor locate the dominant zero of the Nekrasov-Okounkov polynomials in a 2026 number theory paper. These polynomials arise from a famous hook-length formula in partition theory. Each polynomial has many complex zeros, and experiments long suggested one real negative zero stands apart as largest in absolute value. No structural explanation for that distinguished zero was known.

The authors derive a determinant formula for a wider family of recursive polynomials, then show the nontrivial zeros are exactly the eigenvalues of an explicit nonnegative staircase matrix. That matrix is primitive, so Perron-Frobenius theory applies: its largest eigenvalue is real and simple, which forces the dominant zero to be real, negative, and simple as well. Spectral radii also grow strictly along the family. Turning a zero problem into a matrix spectrum problem gives the observation a finite-dimensional proof.
arxiv-2606-15594:
Nath and colleagues present a framework for safe robot motion planning from camera pixels in 2026. Planning in learned latent world models is efficient, but imperfect latent predictions can make a safe plan dangerous on the real system. Their system, SLS-squared, wraps the latent planner in robust model predictive control with guarantees stated in probability.

An action-conditioned joint-embedding world model with compact latent states supports gradient-based trajectory optimization. Conformal prediction then calibrates bounds on the latent prediction error, and a GPU-accelerated system-level synthesis scheme turns those bounds into robust constraint sets. A learned, conformalized constraint checker lets the planner impose safety constraints during closed-loop execution. On vision-based control tasks, including guiding a rope over an obstacle, the framework improves goal reaching and safety over latent world-model and safe-planning baselines. The nominal planner collides in cases the robust one threads safely.
arxiv-2606-15894:
Malekolkalami and Haditale analyse the geodesics of regular phantom black holes in 2026, across flat, de Sitter, and anti-de Sitter asymptotics. A phantom field is a scalar field with negative kinetic energy, a candidate driver of cosmic acceleration. Here it is self-gravitating, with scale parameter b setting its coupling strength to gravity. Its effect along a trajectory can mimic repulsion or attraction.

Using the effective potential, they examine circular orbits, stability, and light deflection in the flat case. The verdicts differ by asymptotics: circular orbits are impossible in the flat case and unphysical in de Sitter. But in anti-de Sitter, stable and unstable circular orbits form past a threshold b. Their angular frequency rises with b, peaks, then declines. Massive particles take the shorter falling path in the flat case; massless ones do in anti-de Sitter. One coupling parameter reshapes all motion around these black holes.
arxiv-2606-15994:
Liang and colleagues present an agentic framework for migrating deep learning workloads from PyTorch to JAX in 2026, a translation that is usually manual and error-prone. PyTorch's eager style clashes with JAX's functional, stateless discipline, and models struggle with strict API alignment. The system combines curated in-context learning, an execution oracle, and an autonomous self-debugging loop.

The in-context material anchors idiomatic JAX style and test generation. Crucially, expected outputs are not deduced by the model: the source PyTorch modules are run to capture actual tensor states, an unchangeable oracle. The agent synthesises tests from that oracle data, executes them, and feeds tracebacks back for self-correction. The combination reaches ninety-one percent equivalence on neural modules, against nine percent for a pure baseline and twenty-seven for instructions alone. Validated across models including SAM and T5, at low overhead, it offers a blueprint for cross-framework migration.
arxiv-2606-16494:
Liu and co-authors discover in 2026 that multimodal question-answering systems suffer the opposite context disease from text models: not lost in the middle, but lost at the end. Knowledge-based visual question answering feeds a reader passages retrieved from a Wikipedia-scale base. In text-only models, context use is U-shaped, favoring the start and end. The authors run the first probe of this in this setting, moving only the gold passage's slot.

Across three open-source vision-language readers and two benchmarks, the shape flips to primacy. Gold-at-first beats gold-at-last by 16 to 26 points in every reader-by-benchmark combination, per the report. The effect lives at prompt slot zero of the instruction-tuned reader. A text-only control shows the multimodal setting amplifies a text primacy by 2.2 to 4.5 times. Three training-free retrieval-side fixes leave the gap intact on a frozen reader.
arxiv-2606-16594:
Chyczewski, Xu, and Zhu read the magnetic state of an insulating crystal in 2026 through a sheet of graphene laid on top of it. Their stack pairs monolayer graphene with NiI2, a helical antiferromagnet that is also multiferroic but far too resistive for direct transport measurements. The idea is that magnetotransport in the graphene layer above it reports how the interface state behaves.

The central signature is in the first-harmonic longitudinal magnetoresistance under in-plane fields: large, anisotropic low-field peaks appear that are absent from a graphene control device on hexagonal boron nitride. The peaks vanish above the multiferroic transition temperature of NiI2, tying them to the magnetic order rather than to graphene itself. Measurements across temperatures, including nonlinear signals, give more evidence. The work shows sensitive probing of phase transitions in a helical antiferromagnet.
arxiv-2606-16694:
Raj and Reddy offer a theory of deep transformers in a 2026 paper on how these models reason in context. Transformers learn links among many coupled variables, yet their inner workings stay murky. The authors model a deep transformer as a mean-field interacting system, where many units act together under limits on communication, locality and depth.

Within that picture, internal states called function vectors let the system infer a hidden context variable at finer and finer scales across layers. The theory predicts a specific link between layered, non-Gaussian structure in the hidden variable and the depth a transformer needs. Tests with constrained linear attention models confirm the predicted pattern of adaptive inference. Feedforward blocks and depth together let transformers run a much richer class of in-context learning methods than earlier accounts described. The work gives a physical language for why depth helps a model adjust to each prompt.
arxiv-2606-17294:
Guerrier and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on visual navigation for robots, targeting a hidden flaw in how navigation foundation models output their moves. Such models predict normalised actions to stay general across robot bodies, but rescaling a normalised path changes its physical shape. That mismatch degrades navigation and raises collision risk when the same policy drives a different robot or runs at a different scale in the world.

Their system, VISTA, conditions the model on its normalised action history alongside camera images, giving explicit context linking predictions to real displacement. A DINOv3 vision encoder supplies richer features, helping in repetitive places that lack distinct landmarks for orientation. In zero-shot real-world tests across outdoor, forest, and office settings, VISTA reached perfect goal prediction accuracy. It also crossed nearly all path checkpoints on average in unseen environments.
arxiv-2606-17694:
Shukla, Boby, and Kumar present a 2026 research article in Optica on optical binding between gold nanoparticles when the simple dipole picture breaks down. Light scattered between particles creates binding forces that set their spacing and stiffness, the basis of optical matter. Most earlier work assumed tiny particles, but the interesting range now is hundreds of nanometres wide. There, quadrupole and octupole resonances join the dipole in shaping the force landscape between a pair of gold particles held in a beam.

Using generalised multiparticle Mie theory, the authors compute force maps at the wavelengths where each mode peaks and dominates. Mode symmetry, they find, strongly rearranges the zero-force points and the stiffness of the bound pair. The results are tied to standard experimental setups rather than idealised geometry alone. That gives builders of programmable metafluids and tiny light-driven machines a mechanical design framework.
arxiv-2606-17894:
Sau and colleagues ask whether scrambled classical and quantum information can be unscrambled perfectly at a network junction, in a 2026 quantum information paper. Classical demultiplexers route one input signal to a chosen output port and leak nothing elsewhere. Quantum transmission lines carry systems directly, so both kinds of information can ride in one quantum package, raising the question of perfect joint routing.

The authors answer yes, by introducing a device they call a quantum demultiplexer, which sends classical content to a classical port and quantum content to a quantum port without loss. They characterize exactly which such devices work and give simple circuit realizations for them. A stronger variant handles senders who do not know what kind of data they are sending. The results tie the device's power to how incompatible certain quantum instruments are.
arxiv-2606-17994:
Hou and colleagues test whether cosmology's tight limits on neutrino mass survive a loosened assumption about the early universe, in a 2026 paper. Standard analyses assume the primordial universe started purely adiabatic, with all components sharing one pattern of fluctuations. The team adds a possible neutrino density isocurvature mode, a separate pattern in the neutrinos alone, and refits the newest sky and galaxy data.

Combining Planck, ACT, and South Pole Telescope microwave data with DESI galaxy measurements and supernovae, they find the mass limit barely moves. In the standard model it stays near five hundredths of an electronvolt, and the isocurvature share is consistent with zero. Letting dark energy vary over time loosens the limit far more than the new mode does. The authors flag a tension: the tightest bound sits below the minimum mass the normal neutrino ordering requires.
arxiv-2606-18194:
Steier defines an equilibrium concept for games whose players are still learning, in a 2026 paper. Repeated finite games are usually judged by their end states, but agents following entropic mirror descent arrive somewhere through a particular trajectory, and some equilibria are never selected by that dynamics. His Ergodic Deviation-Robust Equilibrium demands three things at once from the same profile and the same learning run.

The limit profile must be an approximate Nash equilibrium at a product distribution. Along the whole path, no fixed coalition's cumulative gain from deviating may grow faster than the square root of time. And the limit must be a fixed point of the learning map itself, chosen by the dynamics rather than merely certified after the fact. Steier proves the deviation rate is the best possible order, gives existence in potential games, and extends the selection idea to monotone polymatrix games.
arxiv-2606-18394:
Hu and colleagues present JetSpec, a method for speeding up language model generation through speculative decoding, in a 2026 machine learning paper. Speculative decoding drafts several tokens cheaply and verifies them in parallel. Raising the draft budget helps only if acceptance stays high and drafting stays cheap, a trade-off earlier draft heads could not escape.

JetSpec trains a causal parallel draft head on fused hidden states from the frozen target model. It drafts a whole candidate tree in one forward pass while keeping branch-wise causal conditioning that earlier one-pass drafters lacked. Its candidate scores therefore line up with how the target model itself factorizes text. Across math, coding, and chat benchmarks on Qwen3 models, JetSpec beat bidirectional and tree-based rivals, reaching roughly ninefold speedups on a math benchmark on hardware. Tests inside a serving stack showed further latency gains under realistic loads.
arxiv-2606-18594:
Azimi and colleagues at the University of Alberta benchmark a basic choice in robot reinforcement learning: how the policy's actions are represented, in a 2026 robotics paper. The action space shapes motion smoothness, safety, and how well a policy trained in simulation survives transfer to a real robot.

They compared four representations (pose increments, pose velocity, joint position increments, and joint velocity) on picking up and pushing a cuboid with a real robot arm. Training happened in simulation, with zero-shot deployment on hardware. Joint-space actions transferred best, and joint velocity won overall, achieving perfect picking success in their runs, the greatest pushing displacement, and the smoothest trajectories with the lowest jerk. Actions run through a tuned impedance controller behaved more compliantly and softened collisions, at some cost in raw performance. The authors offer the comparison as practical guidance for teams setting up vision-based manipulation.
arxiv-2606-18694:
Nunley rebuilds the attention mechanism out of coupled oscillators that by design fail to agree, in a 2026 machine learning paper. Self-attention pulls token representations toward consensus with the context they attend to. That suits retrieval: it records where a context is. Prediction needs the reverse: moving toward what came next.

The Frustrated Synchronization Network couples each token not to the tokens it attends to, but to their successors. It is a Kuramoto-Sakaguchi coupling, whose frustration angle is set by the data's own transitions. Every coefficient of the coupling is a named quantity from synchronization theory. That makes the trained layer readable. At one million matched parameters on character-level text and code, the network reached lower validation loss than a tuned transformer. Its edge focused on long-range copying. An oscillator-native variant neared transformer quality with no feed-forward network.
arxiv-2606-18794:
Liu, Tao, and Xin settle an open problem on how lattice polytopes behave under joins, in a 2026 combinatorics paper. Ehrhart theory counts the lattice points in dilations of a polytope. What happens to traits such as Ehrhart positivity, and the integer decomposition property, when two polytopes are joined, had been listed as an open problem. The list came from the American Institute of Mathematics.

The authors construct counterexamples showing the join of two Ehrhart positive polytopes need not be Ehrhart positive. They then prove the integer decomposition trait and the spanning trait are inherited by the join, when both factors have them. The very ample property is not passed on, though. Unimodular, regular, and quadratic triangulations are kept under joins. As a side result, they state a necessary and sufficient condition for the Cartesian product of two Gorenstein lattice polytopes to remain Gorenstein.
arxiv-2606-19094:
Ansari studies whether newborn stars move in line with local magnetic fields in 2026. Magnetic fields are thought to shape molecular clouds and star birth. Yet how far young stars keep a dynamic link to the magnetic setting they formed in is poorly known. The study compares proper motions of young stellar objects with local field directions in seven nearby star-forming regions, using Gaia and Planck dust data.

More than two thousand young stars are analyzed across clouds like Taurus, Perseus, and Orion. For each star, the angle between its motion and the local field is computed. Every cloud shows a clear departure from random angles, so a real link exists. The preferred direction varies strongly by region, though. Four regions favor alignment of motion with the field, while three favor perpendicular motion. Median angles span a wide range across clouds.
arxiv-2606-19394:
Hamoud describes epimorphisms of hypergraphic automata and their input symbol semigroups in a 2026 algebra paper. Hypergraphic automata have state sets and output symbol sets that are hypergraphs, preserved by the transition and output functions. Universally attracting objects in this class are called universal hypergraphic automata. Their input semigroups are algebras of mappings whose properties link tightly to their structure.

A central contribution is two notions of epimorphism for hypergraphs, in weak and strong forms. These notions diverge in general. For a key subclass, though, they necessarily coincide. That subclass includes machines whose state and output hypergraphs are projective or affine planes. The main results give exact conditions for a triple of maps to be an epimorphism of universal ones, stated via the maps on state and output hypergraphs. The result turns an abstract question into checkable data.
arxiv-2606-19494:
Apurba Pokharel and Ram Dantu model what happens when language model agents debate and revise answers over several rounds, in a 2026 study. Such multi-agent deliberation is now widely used to lift reasoning scores. Pokharel and Dantu treat the exchange as a closed-loop system, like a control loop that keeps feeding its own output back in.

Each agent carries a hidden inner belief, an anchor, that keeps pulling its stated view toward itself. The pair show the anchor can be recovered from the debate record alone. An anchor also explains how trust in the right answer can climb past every starting view, which classic consensus rules rule out. Tests on three open-weight model families find anchors pull with similar strength but sit in different places. Only far-off anchors let debate escape the range of first opinions, a clue for safer agent teams.
arxiv-2606-19594:
Théo Saulus, Simon Lacoste-Julien, and Dhanya Sridhar learn causal abstractions without a human hypothesis in 2026. A causal abstraction states when a simple high-level model mirrors a detailed low-level system's response to interventions. Past work tests expert-proposed abstractions rather than discovering them.

Saulus and colleagues flip the task: learn the high-level model straight from low-level measurements. Their route leans on low-rank causal discovery assumptions. First, observations from a low-rank graph induce latent variables that form a causal abstraction. Second, identifiability results pin down what those latents can mean. Third, a practical objective learns the high-level structural causal model itself. Discovery replaces guess-and-check for coarse causal models of brains, cells, and other layered systems. Intervention questions can then be asked at the level where answers guide action.
arxiv-2606-19794:
Kwan Soo Shin and In Seok Kang ask in 2026 why vast AI spending yields so little measured productivity growth. Standard production functions treat AI as one more separable input beside capital and labour. That framing, they argue, builds the paradox into the theory itself.

Value from AI flows through human cognition, a mediator the standard frame omits. Their Intellectually Converged Human framework names the missing trait convergence capacity. It spans embodied understanding, metacognition, time integration, and integrative thinking. Effective human capital equals raw human capital scaled by an augmentation factor. That factor depends jointly on AI use intensity and convergence capacity. Firms that deploy AI before building capacity thus buy tools their staff cannot fully convert into output. The frame offers a human-centred mechanism behind Solow's old productivity puzzle.
arxiv-2606-19894:
Xinhe Mu, Zaijiu Shang, and five colleagues prove a universal approximation theorem for the score functions behind diffusion models in 2026. Earlier theory leaned on smooth densities or tidy manifold supports, while real data bring sharp edges, gaps, and disjoint clusters. Their result covers any distribution on any compact set, with only the set's upper Minkowski dimension, a measure of intrinsic size, entering the cost.

A discrete-mixture construction shows a ReLU network can approximate the score with complexity growing exponentially in that intrinsic dimension alone. The ambient dimension, by contrast, no longer forces an exponential blow-up. Paired with known results on solving the backward diffusion equation, the theorem explains why diffusion models cope with irregular, non-smooth data. Generative modelling gains a firmer theoretical footing for the messy structure of real perceptual data.
arxiv-2606-20194:
Maxime Rombach and eleven colleagues present the design and first prototypes of robotic positioners for MOSAIC, the multi-object spectrograph planned for the Extremely Large Telescope. Their 2026 paper describes about 250 robots that will pick off skylight at the telescope's focal surface and feed it to near-infrared and visible spectrographs. The ELT's giant scale creates three headaches: beams cannot focus into a single fiber, each positioner must aim at a pupil center nearly thirty-eight meters away, and a full-field corrector is impossible.

Each robot therefore carries relay mirrors that patrol its patch of sky. The mirrors re-image its sub-field onto fixed fiber bundles behind the focal plane. Each unit also adapts to local telecentricity and carries its own small dispersion corrector. EPFL designed the units and will supervise mass manufacturing.
arxiv-2606-20394:
Amit Jain and Richard Linares let a language model run the research loop for spacecraft control policies, but only under audit. Their 2026 paper presents AutoResearch, a framework where an LLM autonomously develops control policies distilled from expert solvers. At each iteration the agent reads a problem description and the run history, proposes one edit to the training script, executes it, and logs the outcome. The model never flies the spacecraft; it only develops the policy offline.

A credibility layer certifies every reported result against the problem's own measured seed noise, using reseeded verification and leave-one-out pruning of the agent's edits. Applied unchanged to two aerospace problems, a rendezvous and a safety-constrained docking, the audited policies cleared seed noise by many standard deviations against known optimal-control benchmarks. Every claim the agent makes has survived a noise audit.
arxiv-2606-20494:
Levente Bodnár, Jun Gao, Oleg Pikhurko, Mingyuan Rong, and Shumin Sun prove strong non-principality for positive codegree Turán density. Their 2026 note works with k-graphs, where the positive codegree of a graph counts, for each (k-1)-set lying in some edge, the fewest edges containing it. The density asks how large that minimum can stay while a family of forbidden graphs is avoided.

For every k at least three, the authors construct two k-graphs F1 and F2 whose joint density is strictly between zero and the minimum of their separate densities. Forbidding both graphs together is therefore not governed by whichever is worse alone. This strong form of non-principality shows the joint problem has genuinely new behavior. Codegree extremal problems cannot be reduced to one forbidden graph at a time.
arxiv-2606-20794:
Krishna Naidoo and three colleagues introduce a gravity model class in 2026 that lets dark energy cross the phantom divide, where its equation of state passes below minus one. Recent analyses favor such crossing, drawing interest to scalar-tensor theories. Their Asymptotic Cubic Galileon models sit inside Horndeski gravity. They remain minimally coupled to matter while producing the crossing behavior.

The models are tested against cosmic microwave background data, baryon acoustic oscillations, and supernova distances. They can fit the expansion history from all three jointly. Galaxy and void observations add stronger limits. Those perturbative tests confine viable models to a defined region of the wider Horndeski space. Model comparison favors these models and a flexible dark energy model over the standard cosmological constant model. Phantom crossing, if real, would reshape how physicists explain cosmic acceleration.
arxiv-2606-20894:
J Socorro and three colleagues find exact solutions in 2026 for a K-essence cosmology model built from a power-law scalar potential. K-essence models use a scalar field with nonstandard kinetic terms to drive cosmic expansion. Their potential comes from a Sáez-Ballester form with a negative power law. A field redefinition reshapes the equations. The new form matches a previously solved universe model.

That match yields exact classical solutions for the scale factor and scalar field, within a Hamiltonian formalism. The dynamics show late-time accelerated expansion. The deceleration parameter tends toward the de Sitter value. At the quantum level, a Wheeler-DeWitt equation is derived and solved exactly. Few cosmology models allow both classical and quantum exact treatment. A fully solvable case gives a clean test bed for ideas about the early and late universe.
arxiv-2606-20994:
Narges Zare, Divya Ramesh, and Cori Faklaris present a work-in-progress framework in 2026 for mapping AI courses across technical content, societal harms, and workforce skills. AI is now embedded in daily life and work. Students must connect how systems work with what they can harm and what jobs require. Teaching often splits those topics apart. Ethics, design, and job preparation sit in separate courses.

Their mapping links technical systems, societal harms, and workforce competencies in one view. It starts with institutional courses and expands through an external registry of hundreds of courses. Early findings from six courses show a pattern. Technical coverage is often strong. Societal harms appear but are unevenly integrated. Workforce skills are rarely assessed explicitly. Literacy that stops at awareness, they argue, leaves graduates unprepared for responsible action in workplaces where AI decisions carry real consequences.
arxiv-2606-21094:
Tzu-An Sheng and fourteen colleagues present an analysis note in 2026 on long-range near-side correlations in electron-positron collisions with W boson pair events, using archived ALEPH data from LEP. High-multiplicity events test collective behavior in collision systems. A prior study at the same collider found gaps between data and simulation at high multiplicity. Long-range correlations seemed to emerge even in this simplest collision system.

At higher energies, W pair production grows important above certain multiplicities. Complex color-string layouts from W decays could explain part of the excess. Higher final-state multiplicity alone could also explain it. The note dissects those rival accounts in events at 183 to 209 giga-electronvolts. Archived data still have discovery value here, because the question of where collective behavior begins bears on how physicists interpret far larger systems such as heavy ion collisions.
arxiv-2606-21294:
Stefano Franzoni, Christopher Bulte, Leonhard Scheck, Christian Keil, and George Craig ask in 2026 how much weather satellites' solar channels can reveal about clouds for weather models. Visible and near-infrared images carry rich cloud detail, but feeding them into forecast models is hard because the signals are nonlinear, ambiguous, and strongly correlated across channels. The team tests six solar channels from the Flexible Combined Imager on Meteosat Third Generation.

They build a Backward Operator, a regression network that converts reflectances into cloud variables with stated uncertainty. It estimates optical thickness, cloud fraction, ice fraction, and particle sizes as a joint Gaussian distribution, trained on synthetic images from ICON model runs. The retrievals are unbiased and well calibrated, and combining channels helps substantially despite their correlation, offering model-ready variables instead of raw reflectances.
arxiv-2606-21694:
Keenan Avers, Phineas Sobel, and seven colleagues grow and measure a tunable kagome-lattice metal in 2026, the double-alloy series Lu-Y-(Nb-Ta)6Sn6. Kagome lattices, built from corner-sharing triangles, host flat bands, van Hove singularities, and Dirac points prized for correlated-electron physics. A new growth method yields long, high-quality single crystals, letting the team dial two substitutions at once.

Yttrium substitution gradually suppresses the charge density wave order, while quantum oscillations show up in both magnetization and magnetoresistance across the whole series. Tracking Fermi surfaces and effective masses, they find the surfaces shrink with both substitutions. Mass scales with Fermi wavevector in a way that points to Dirac-like dispersion. Because the tuning barely adds disorder, the series offers a clean dial for studying how kagome ground states and band features evolve.
arxiv-2606-21794:
Bang and colleagues present, in 2026, a way to simulate a relativistic particle on a quantum computer inside a finite one-dimensional box. First-quantized simulation stores the particle's position in a register of qubits, but relativity makes kinetic energy a nonlinear function of momentum. The hard part is the box's edges, usually treated with periodic or with fixed Dirichlet boundary rules.

Starting from the positive-energy kinetic operator, the authors build weakly relativistic lattice Hamiltonians whose corrections need only two momentum moments. With periodic edges those moments come from a cyclic shift of the register, while fixed edges use an open-chain difference plus small endpoint terms. Energy estimates then need shift measurements, a few endpoint overlap checks, and position sampling for potentials. Tests on a cosine potential, an infinite square well, and a harmonic well all agreed well with direct matrix results, with each error source kept apart.
arxiv-2606-21894:
Kang, Ray, and Roychoudhury ask, in 2026, what skills software engineers will need now that coding agents write much of the code. Their paper distils two round-table meetings of researchers and industry practitioners held that year in New York and Singapore. Rather than surveying tools, the authors focus on where the profession itself is heading and what that means for training.

One finding stands out: as agents take over implementation, verification and validation grow in importance, because someone must still judge whether the produced software is right. Anecdotes from both meetings backed that shift. From the discussions the authors identify the core skills developers need in the agentic era, spanning critical review, specification, and system-level judgement. They close with implications for how universities and employers should educate the next generation of software engineers.
arxiv-2606-22194:
Seip and colleagues connect, in 2026, an information-theoretic quantity to the training loss of neural network decoders for quantum error correction. Error correction protects logical information up to a noise threshold. Coherent information measures the maximum rate at which that information can pass reliably through a noisy channel.

The authors prove coherent information is a sharp lower bound on the binary cross-entropy loss of decoders that track logical operators. They build a transformer decoder based on maximum likelihood decoding and train it to estimate coherent information directly. On the surface code under code-capacity, phenomenological, and circuit-level noise, the network predicts the quantity accurately. Its threshold estimates closely match known theoretical limits. As a decoder it significantly outperforms minimum-weight perfect matching on logical error rate. A soft post-selection scheme is proved optimal and shown to scale.
arxiv-2606-22494:
Ramesh Nandipalli and Chandranath Adak build a sign language translation system in this 2026 paper. Sign language is the main communication mode for many deaf people, yet tools that turn signing videos into text remain scarce for Indian languages. Their pipeline first recognizes the sign, then translates the result.

The first stage fine-tunes VideoMAE, a video transformer model, on thirteen classes from the AI4Bharat Indian Sign Language corpus. It reached seventy-eight percent validation accuracy on short clips. The second stage uses Meta AI's NLLB-200 model to render each English word in Hindi, Telugu, and Bengali. A per-class breakdown names the main failure modes, such as confusable sign pairs like ugly, deaf, and blind. A Streamlit demo lets users upload a video and receive the translations. Limits are plain: few classes, isolated words rather than full signing, and sensitivity to signer style.
arxiv-2606-22694:
Danial Kamali and five colleagues make spatial reasoning explicit in this 2026 paper. Vision-language models stumble when a spatial relation's meaning depends on the frame of reference, such as left from a viewer's perspective versus the object's own. Existing neuro-symbolic methods lean on brittle geometry and hard decisions over noisy perception.

SATURN reconstructs an approximate three-dimensional scene from the input. It derives soft, perspective-aware predicates, keeping uncertainty alive instead of forcing early yes-or-no calls. A training-free symbolic executor written in Python composes those predicates through multi-hop inference. The team also built 3D FORCE, a diagnostic benchmark varying reasoning depth, view, and perspective composition. Standard models degraded sharply as complexity grew, while SATURN stayed stable and beat strong baselines. On the real-world MindCube benchmark, SATURN reached seventy-eight point six percent overall accuracy, fourteen points clear of the strongest baseline.
arxiv-2606-22794:
Lin Sun and nine colleagues redesign robot control models in this 2026 paper on vision-language-action systems. These models pair a slow vision-language backbone with a fast action expert. Updating the backbone often wastes compute, while updating it rarely leaves the action expert working from stale context. The split also discards useful features from the backbone's middle layers.

Their architecture, UniFS, unifies the two speeds inside one backbone. Layers are grouped so shallow layers refresh quickly for fast-changing dynamics and deeper layers update slowly, caching stable meaning. A latent vector inversion step reroutes features so fast signals guide fine action detail and slow signals guide coarse planning. Multi-level supervision trains the hierarchy from coarse to fine. On the LIBERO robot benchmark, UniFS reached a 98.3 percent average success rate, beating the VLA-Adapter baseline by 2.5 points while also reducing average inference latency.
arxiv-2606-22894:
Di Hou, Thai P.D. Nguyen, Kim-Chuan Toh, and Guanyi Wang relax sparse quadratic programs in this 2026 paper. A quadratic program with a sparsity constraint, limiting how many variables may be nonzero, is generally NP-hard. Solving one globally depends on tight convex relaxations, stand-ins that bound the true optimum.

Their sparsity-cone semidefinite relaxation uses a matrix one dimension smaller than standard liftings, plus a single sparsity-cone constraint handling the sparsity requirement. They prove it is as strong as the standard SDP-RLT relaxation, and that projecting onto the sparsity cone reduces to a one-dimensional subproblem. From the dual problem they derive presolving rules: a way to fix individual variables, a screening cut excluding larger support patterns, and a refinement step improving the certificates. Their solver, a two-phase Riemannian augmented Lagrangian method, matched the standard relaxation's bound quality in experiments while running much faster.
arxiv-2606-22994:
Nils Grandien and colleagues ask whether sparse autoencoders learn sensible concept ladders in a 2026 interpretability paper. A sparse autoencoder rewrites a model's internal activity using a large set of mostly silent features. Researchers hope those features name concepts the model uses. Some methods arrange features into hierarchies, from broad ideas down to narrow ones. Until now, nobody had agreed on what a good hierarchy must satisfy, so claims rested on cherry-picked pictures.

Grandien and colleagues draw requirements from older work on semantic networks and taxonomies. They turn those requirements into a concrete scoring protocol. Applied to current methods trained on images, the protocol finds usable raw material but weak finished ladders. One failure stands out. Features get absorbed into broader neighbors, in both a sharp and a gradual form, and that absorption steadily damages hierarchy quality.
arxiv-2606-23094:
Vamshi Krishna Bonagiri and colleagues examine cognitive digital twins in a 2026 ethics paper. Such a twin is a running computer model of one specific person's mind. It updates from behavior, context, or body data to predict how that person thinks, or to speak and decide in their place. Twins blend personal modeling, simulation, and proxy action in one system. Rules for assistants, recommenders, and automated decisions cover that blend only partly, the authors argue.

Bonagiri and colleagues make four contributions. They define these twins and separate them from neighboring systems. They propose a governance frame built on five ideas, from who holds authority to how long a twin stays available. They catalog twin-specific risks, including false portrayal, shadow twins, and power gaps between proxy and person. Finally, they list safeguards for high-risk twins, covering consent, purpose limits, validity checks, review, and retirement.
arxiv-2606-23394:
Yixuan Zhu and colleagues ask whether language model embedding spaces mirror expert knowledge structure in a 2026 paper. Embeddings turn text into geometry, and categories can look cleanly separated there. Separability alone does not prove the geometry matches how experts organize a field. The team tests this in mental-health language, where symptom relations supply an expert reference map. Online community style and emotion could fake a match, so confounds need care. They compare pretrained and fine-tuned embedding models at two sizes across twenty-eight Reddit communities.

Zhu and colleagues build category prototypes and compare their distance patterns against an expert symptom matrix. Pretrained embeddings already aligned measurably with expert structure inside the mental-health subset. Fine-tuning strengthened alignment the most at the finest category level, and the larger model aligned better both before and after tuning. Alignment survived controls for emotion, word choice, style, and topic mix.
arxiv-2606-23694:
Misra, Sharma, Agarwal, and Aggrawal add global community structure to graph based text classification, in a 2026 paper on natural language processing. Graph methods turn words and documents into nodes linked by lexical and semantic ties, then pass information between neighbors. Documents of the same class tend to cluster tightly in such graphs. Most classifiers exploit only local neighborhoods, ignoring that community pattern, which blurs class boundaries and over smooths the learned representations.

Their model, ModTGCN, trains with two objectives: classification loss plus a modularity term rewarding class coherent communities, scored on a similarity graph built from transformer embeddings. Splitting the classic heterogeneous graph into separate parts, one linking documents to words and one linking words to words, speeds training by two to ten times. Gains appear on five benchmarks, largest on complex datasets where classes mix heavily.
arxiv-2606-23794:
Somigliana and colleagues exploit a lucky geometry, two young stars seen at complementary tilt angles, to view both gas and ice in planet forming disks, in a 2026 paper on star formation. HK Tau is a binary of two similar young stars. One disk faces us at moderate tilt, the other nearly edge on. Using the Webb telescope's mid infrared instrument, the team took spectra of both.

The moderate tilt primary shows a rich spectrum dominated by carbon dioxide lines. The edge on secondary is line poor, as models predict for such tilts. In compensation, its view reveals ice bands: water ice, carbon dioxide ice, and an ammonium feature. Extended hydrogen emission surrounds both stars, with an X shape around the secondary pointing to a wide, slow wind.
arxiv-2606-23894:
Ahmed asks whether dissipation, usually treated as the enemy of quantum prediction, actually makes open quantum systems easier for neural networks to learn, in a 2026 paper on quantum machine learning. Simulating open quantum systems is exponentially expensive by direct methods. Neural ordinary differential equation models offer a shortcut: a network learns the evolution rule, then rolls it forward. Ahmed trains such models on Heisenberg XYZ spin chains, with and without dissipation.

Closed systems quickly become unlearnable: fidelity collapses as the chain grows, failing outright at four qubits. Adding dissipation reverses the trend, opening a broad high fidelity regime at intermediate sizes. Moderate dissipation genuinely helps the model learn nontrivial transient dynamics. Stronger damping merely simplifies trajectories toward the steady state, so high scores flatter the model.
arxiv-2606-24094:
Zhong and colleagues unify image clustering under a single agent driven by written guidelines. Clustering means grouping pictures into sensible categories. Tasks differ wildly. Some want broad categories, others fine distinctions. Some judge the whole image, others a local detail. Class sizes range from balanced to heavily skewed. Their 2026 framework lets a text guideline state the rule, instead of training a separate model per task.

Generative Concept Proxy Modeling turns guidelines into embeddings. It does so by extracting concept proxies, stand-ins for the ideas the text names. When clusters must be found on their own, an LLM Traversal over a minimum spanning tree applies model judgement with care, only where semantic choices are truly hard. Across scenarios from general to fine-grained and global to local, the hybrid agent beats specialised methods again and again. Zhong's team presents guideline text as the missing universal interface for clustering.
arxiv-2606-24894:
Anzhe Xie and five colleagues introduce RWGBench, a benchmark for judging how well language models write related work sections. Fluency is not the hard part of that task. Related work writing is scholarly positioning: choosing citations, organising them, and framing how a paper differs from what came before. Standard evaluations borrow summarisation metrics, scoring text similarity to a reference. RWGBench scores the citation decisions themselves.

The benchmark is built from 40,108 computer science papers, with a retrieval corpus of 1.09 million documents. Its test set holds one hundred papers with their published related work sections. Evaluation is multi dimensional, covering citation selection, contextual fit, organisation, and discourse structure. Experiments on current systems reveal systematic weaknesses that similarity scores had hidden. Xie and colleagues argue that positioning quality, not surface resemblance, is the right target for this writing task. The benchmark is offered as a yardstick for future related work generators.
arxiv-2606-24994:
Wenyang Hu, Junxiang Jia, and four colleagues fix a blind spot in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards for language model reasoning. The method fails at both difficulty extremes. Easy prompts yield all correct rollout groups with little diversity and no gradient signal. Hard prompts yield all incorrect groups, so no positive reward exists to learn from. Their framework, ExTra, extracts exploration signals from the model's rollouts and stays compatible with GRPO training. Two mechanisms do the work.

A novelty reward adds embedding based diversity bonuses after group normalisation, paying extra for varied correct solutions. Entropy guided prefix regeneration resumes exploration from promising intermediate steps. On six mathematical reasoning benchmarks, ExTra lifts the Qwen3-1.7B model over plain GRPO. Gains run about five points on single sample accuracy and about seven points when sampling sixteen attempts. Trajectory level exploration signals improve both one shot accuracy and coverage at inference time.
arxiv-2606-25094:
Andrew Pearce-Crump studies two discrete second moments of Dirichlet L functions, sums taken over the function's nontrivial zeros that involve the derivative at each zero raised to a negative power. Results of this kind were known for the Riemann zeta function; his work carries them to the Dirichlet setting, uniformly in the conductor.

The bounds are proved under the Generalised Riemann Hypothesis. They also assume that the zeros are simple. The bounds capture a definite proportion of the conjectured asymptotic size. That proportion equals one half when the conductor grows slowly, recovering the Dirichlet analogues of theorems of Milinovich and Ng and of Sinha for fixed conductor. It degrades gracefully for large conductor. Pearce-Crump also states the conjectured true leading order, and versions averaged over the family of primitive characters.
arxiv-2606-25194:
Counting holes and loops in data is easy to state but hard to use inside optimisation, because those counts jump in discrete steps. Satoshi Kanno and Yoshi-aki Shimada propose in 2026 a smooth stand-in built from the Hodge Laplacian, an operator whose low modes encode homological information such as Betti numbers. Their framework works both for point clouds, through Vietoris Rips style constructions, and for graphs built from cliques. Heat and resolvent filters turn the spectrum into differentiable losses.

For point clouds, the new losses spread gradient information more evenly across points and behaved more smoothly when persistence pairings changed, compared with losses based directly on persistent homology. For graphs, simple spectral moments tracked a normalised first Betti number and could be combined with ordinary feature objectives. The authors also sketch links to quantum trace estimation.
arxiv-2606-26094:
Babak Rahmani, Sebastian Dziadzio, Joschka Strüber, and Matthias Bethge set a reverse-engineering challenge for AI systems. Scientists often infer hidden mechanisms from outward behaviour. Their benchmark asks a learner to rebuild an agent's hidden decision program as runnable code. Seventy-five policies, generated by language models and calibrated by Elo rating, hide across five game environments.

Probes make the task tractable. The learner designs custom opponent policies to force revealing behaviour from the target. It then submits executable code as its hypothesis. Scoring uses continuous action-distance measures against the true policy. Recovered code also gets tested in head-to-head tournaments. Twelve frontier models attempt the benchmark. Recovery quality spans a wide range, closing between about a third and nearly three quarters of the initial distance. Weaker models gain the most competitive edge from recovered policies, since probing substitutes for missing strategy skill.
arxiv-2606-26194:
Jose Bermudez and colleagues weigh city trees from the air, without ground labels for training. Urban trees store real carbon, yet city biomass maps stay coarse and inconsistent. Their framework covers an 810-square-kilometre urban-rural landscape in southern Ontario. Leaf-off lidar and near-infrared photos from provincial mapping flights supply the inputs. A dual-stream network, trained on rule-based pseudo-labels, marks buildings and two tree types in the imagery.

Crowns come next. Multiscale watershed segmentation outlines individual tree crowns in the marked areas. A power-law proxy from crown area and height, calibrated on nearly twenty-two thousand inventoried trees, converts crowns to biomass. On held-out tiles the marking scores run high across classes. Matched test pairs show solid predictive accuracy, a bit lower under real segmentation than under inventory geometry. Crown outline errors, not the biomass formula, dominate the remaining error.
arxiv-2606-26894:
Minh Duc Do, Tillmann Rheude, Noel Kronenberg, Roland Eils, and Benjamin Wild present MICViT, a transformer model for three-dimensional brain MRI. Brain scans come in several modalities, image types that highlight different tissue properties. Learning from them is hard: the data are huge, and patient numbers are small next to the variety of anatomy and disease. Combining the modalities well is the central challenge.

MICViT models context at three levels. Within each modality it attends locally and globally. Across modalities it again attends locally and globally, letting image types inform each other at every scale. The test task was predicting brain age. Three data sets, from large biobank to small clinic cohorts, were used. The model consistently beat leading convolutional and transformer rivals, and gained more from added modalities than they did.
arxiv-2606-27094:
Palma and colleagues test whether diffusion models, a generative artificial intelligence method, can learn real climate patterns from very few records. Their focus is ENSO, the El Niño and La Niña swings of Pacific Ocean surface heat that steer world weather. Only about seventy years of good monthly maps exist, far fewer than such models usually need. With enough data, the model recovers both plain and skewed pattern families correctly.

Cutting training size exposes the gap starkly. Roughly seven hundred real monthly maps fall about ten times short of the near seven thousand needed for stable learning. Not every diffusion setup recovers the right low-order structure either. Pre-training on climate model archives with a learned model tag, then fine-tuning on real maps, closes the gap. That recipe beats both synthetic benchmark models on observed statistics.
arxiv-2606-27294:
Wang and Achour build generative models that run on analog hardware instead of digital chips. Coupled oscillators and analog Ising machines solve differential equations at a sliver of digital energy cost. A mismatch blocks them: modern generative models want flexible software-defined dynamics, while hardware dynamics are fixed by physics. Their Analog Interaction Systems framework defines what such hardware can express. In the 2026 hardware paper, the expressivity gap against neural baselines is measured directly.

Two hardware-friendly tricks narrow the gap: parameters that switch over time, and hidden physical states. A Wasserstein GAN training method fits the models without forcing them to track one set path. Sparse links and low-bit parameters prove necessary for practical builds. Energy per generated image lands near twenty-three microjoules for their chosen design in the reported estimate, about a hundredfold better than digital baselines. Image quality scores beat prior analog generators severalfold.
arxiv-2606-27394:
Abolfadl leads a team forecasting where wireless networks and mobile computing research will head, using an automated machine learning pipeline. Publication volume has outgrown manual trend watching. Their framework chains clustering, topic modelling, and time-series analysis over a corpus of well over one hundred thousand abstracts from leading venues. Semantic embeddings from a scientific-text model start the process. In 2026, meta-learning then picks the clustering algorithm best matched to the data's own features.

Topic modelling is tuned per cluster by successive halving, with language-model assistance for readable labels. Forecast models, from ARIMA to recurrent networks, project each topic's popularity forward. Topics sort into strong, weak, and noise signals by their forecast trajectories. Reported prediction error stays low on the held-out evaluation. The pipeline adapts to other domains without redesign. Research planners gain an early-warning instrument for emerging and fading themes.
arxiv-2606-27594:
Multiple orthogonal polynomials obey several orthogonality rules at once. Standard orthogonal polynomials obey just one. Roozbeh Gharakhloo, Maksim Kosmakov, and Kenta Miyahara connect the two worlds in 2026. They derive explicit formulas that express the multiple kind through the standard kind. Two settings are treated. One is the real line, and the other is the unit circle.

The formulas also reduce the matching Christoffel–Darboux kernels. These kernels are workhorse sums used across random matrix theory. The reductions recover two known results. One is Zinn-Justin's kernel for the external-source random matrix model. The other is Baik's formula for the spiked source model. Concrete examples follow. On the real line, the multiple Hermite kernel is written with classical Hermite polynomials. On the unit circle, arc-indicator weights show resonance-type zero escape for the multiple kind.
arxiv-2606-27894:
Measuring very low temperatures with a quantum probe is hard, because thermal signals fade fast. Marek Winczewski, Michał Horodecki, and Ricard Ravell Rodríguez study a bosonic probe in 2026. The probe is a quantum harmonic oscillator, strongly coupled to a bosonic bath. Dynamics are treated two ways, by an exact solution and by a renormalised master equation.

Quantum Fisher information is extracted from the time-dependent covariance matrix for Gaussian probe states, including squeezed ones. In the strong-coupling regime it is non-monotonic in time. Bath-memory revivals make a finite interrogation time strictly optimal. The Markovian version rises steadily instead, so its best time is infinite. Squeezed initial states give a large early advantage that thermalisation erases. At equilibrium, strong coupling turns an exponential error blow-up into a milder polynomial one. The model maps onto circuit quantum electrodynamics.
arxiv-2606-27994:
Private set intersection lets parties find shared items without revealing the rest. Zixian Gong and three colleagues present a multi-party quantum version in 2026. Existing quantum schemes are limited in their threat models. Collusion between a third party and some participants is a particular gap. Their protocol stacks two encryption layers. One gives verifiable outsourced quantum evaluation. The other manages the keys with a threshold scheme.

The intersection is computed through a controlled-AND circuit. Simulations run on the IBM Quantum Platform. The team checks correctness and privacy against the third party, outside eavesdroppers, and colluding insiders. Verifiability against a malicious third party is proved. The construction extends to private set union through open-controlled operations. A modular view offers several variants. Compared with prior schemes, the protocol gives more flexible set operations. It also resists third-party collusion better.
arxiv-2606-28094:
Removing an object from a photo means removing its shadows and reflections too. User masks are often inaccurate, which makes the task harder. Qinming Zhou and eight colleagues present OSOR in 2026, a one-step diffusion inpainting framework for effect-aware object removal. An occupancy-guided discriminator gives precise boundary supervision for stable single-step training. An alpha head predicts proper removal regions from pretrained diffusion knowledge, handling imperfect masks. A verification pipeline filters noisy instruction triplets into effect-aware supervision at scale.

The curated dataset, CORNE, holds 280 thousand verified removal pairs. OSOR surpasses strong multi-step diffusion baselines in perceptual quality. It runs four to thirty times faster than they do. A 1024 by 1024 image processes in under one second on a single A100 GPU. Shadows and reflections are treated as part of the object to remove.
arxiv-2606-28194:
David Steinmann, Antonia Wüst, Kristian Kersting, and Wolfgang Stammer built COCOLogic-V2, a test set for checking whether computer vision models truly reason with logic. The images are real-world photos, and each sample follows or breaks rules written in first-order logic, the formal language of statements about objects and their relations.

Steinmann and colleagues sort samples into clear positives, far-from-boundary negatives, and near-boundary negatives that only just break a rule. Models separated positives from far negatives easily but failed on the near-boundary cases that demand careful checking. Visual noise and the huge space of possible rules made few-shot learning, learning from a handful of examples, harder still. Visual logical reasoning, they conclude, remains an open problem.
arxiv-2606-28394:
L. A. Muñoz, writing alone, inverts the problem of anastylosis, the painstaking reassembly of a collapsed monument's fallen stones. Conservators normally match blocks by expert judgment, slowly and subjectively. Muñoz instead trains a system to look at a collapsed assembly and predict the tower that stood before, borrowing the puzzle structure of the game Jenga.
