The framework couples a full rigid-body physics engine, GPU accelerated, with friction thresholds drawn from earlier engineering analysis. Across hundreds of simulated episodes at three friction levels, a dual-stream neural network learns to predict how many blocks were removed, from where, and with what balance and torque risks. A smooth three-dimensional video then plays the reconstruction backward. Muñoz discusses what computer-assisted anastylosis could mean at the Maya site of Uxmal.
arxiv-2606-28494:
Luca Maxia, Hua-Sheng Shao, Lukas Simon, and Guoxing Wang fix a long-standing flaw in quarkonium theory. Quarkonium, a heavy quark bound to its antiquark, should be the cleanest system in strong-force physics. Yet second-order corrections in non-relativistic QCD often turn huge and negative, predicting impossible negative decay rates and ballooning error bars instead of steady improvement.

Maxia and colleagues identify the source of the blowups and propose a simple remedy centered on soft effects, the low-energy gluon effects their analysis singles out. Applied to S-wave color-singlet quarkonium production and decay, the approach restores much better convergence, with successive approximations settling down as they should. Predictions also agree better with measured data, returning a flagship framework to health.
arxiv-2606-28694:
Aaron Scher, writing alone, asks how the world could ever check a promise to pause frontier artificial intelligence research. Proposals for an international halt to superintelligence development depend on verification, and since algorithmic progress comes from research itself, the research may need restricting too, not just computers and data. Scher stays agnostic about which research would be banned and studies only the checking.

Early chapters map the considerations that make research restrictions verifiable or not, including the experimental infrastructure serious work requires. The core is a catalogue of twenty-eight candidate verification mechanisms, from whistleblowers and search warrants to audits of training code and conventional intelligence gathering. Some are not yet implementable and some may prove undesirable. Mapping the option space, Scher argues, is the foundation for developing the promising few into tools.
arxiv-2606-29094:
Chang, Hong, Pham and Venkataraman build DiLaServe, a serving system for diffusion language models, a new class of models that generate many tokens in parallel by repeated denoising. Such models promise higher throughput than conventional word-by-word models at similar quality. Serving them under latency guarantees, called SLOs, is hard: quality depends on a confidence threshold, load fluctuates, and approximate caching makes each step's cost uneven.

DiLaServe schedules with deadlines in mind and adjusts the confidence threshold to control load. It reconfigures the cluster via a quality-aware optimisation problem that models the step-level cost differences from approximate caching. Across benchmarks and real-world traces, SLO attainment improved by up to about fifty-seven percentage points. End-to-end latency fell by up to 46 percent, with accuracy cost under one percent.
arxiv-2606-29194:
Li, Liu and Liu present Agora, a multi-agent AI system that evolves both trading strategies and the scoring function used to judge them. Automated alpha mining usually holds the scorer fixed. A search converging against a fixed scorer, they argue, overfits whatever the scorer cannot penalise. Their framework, Sealed Joint Search, sets structural conditions so joint search cannot collapse into self-confirmation.

Five specialised language-model agent classes communicate through typed channels, jointly evolving eight skill libraries, while independent evaluators keep the judge sealed. Run for one hundred outer rounds on a Chinese stock index universe, Agora reached a holdout Sharpe ratio, a risk-adjusted return measure, clearly above the strongest baseline. Pre-loading the two metrics Agora discovered into a frozen library recovered only a fraction of the gap. Caveats: the full run used one seed, and the signal concentrates on the short side.
arxiv-2606-29294:
Glazunov surveys links between quantum physics and one of mathematics' deepest open questions, the Riemann hypothesis. The Hilbert-Polya conjecture suggests the zeros of the Riemann zeta function are eigenvalues of some quantum system. His overview covers results in that direction, alongside new work on p-adic quantum computing, where numbers are measured by a different notion of size.

He also treats entanglement built on lattice spin models, plus algebraic models of entanglement. Because his quantum computing discussion uses both photons and electrons, he briefly presents their known properties. The article is a compact map of several research threads rather than a single new result: the zeta function connection, p-adic methods, spin-model entanglement and algebraic entanglement models. Glazunov writes from the Glushkov Institute of Cybernetics in Kiev.
arxiv-2606-29494:
Jha, Yuan, and Fang improve 3D Gaussian SLAM, a system that tracks a camera while building a labelled three-dimensional map. SLAM, short for simultaneous localization and mapping, underpins robot navigation. Such systems borrow labels from two-dimensional models, yet those labels are not equally trustworthy. Occlusions, weak boundaries, and vague ray paths can bake lasting errors into the map.

Their system, VCS-SLAM, checks each label for geometric reliability before fusing it. Tests cover visibility consistency, surface-supported boundary evidence, and ray-level conflict uncertainty. A reliability-aware objective then suppresses occluded updates and reduces label bleeding, where a label spills onto the wrong surface. Vague regions receive labels later, once evidence firms up. On the Replica dataset, consistency, boundary preservation, and reconstruction quality all improved. On ScanNet, with real RGB-D input, tracking stayed competitive.
arxiv-2606-29894:
Georgiev and five colleagues introduce SABER-Math, a fully automated benchmark — the first of its kind — for rating information retrieval in maths. AI agents increasingly search problem databases and theorem libraries, but no expert-labelled test existed to compare maths retrievers fairly.

Starting from 283,000 high-school maths problems with solutions, language models extract solution summaries and topics for each problem. The benchmark finds relevant documents through topic and summary similarity. A Swiss-style tournament of model preferences then assigns fine-grained ratings. Testing word-based retrievers, maths-specific systems, and embedding models, the authors find modern embeddings beat classical baselines yet still struggle in symbol-heavy Algebra and Calculus. General benchmarks such as MTEB do not predict maths search performance.
arxiv-2606-29994:
Cesar Diaz-Londono and six colleagues measure flexibility in fast electric vehicle charging. Planners often treat charging as freely shiftable in time. Real cars are constrained by battery management systems and connection times. Protection limits also shape what charging can do. The authors build a framework respecting each session's actual trajectory.

They reconstruct profiles from two hundred fifty-two real charging sessions. One hundred forty-one representative power and charge profiles result. One-way flexibility is bounded by the energy that can shift. Two-way flexibility is bounded by dischargeable energy under feasibility constraints. Charging past eighty percent charge adds time for little gain. Higher charger power saturates against battery limits instead. Time between twenty and eighty percent falls by over sixty percent. Mean power rises by up to forty percent. Extractable energy can more than double, depending on activation timing.
arxiv-2606-30094:
Wen-Yuan Ai reconsiders when domain walls form in the early universe. Domain walls are vast sheets separating regions with different vacuum states. A small bias favoring one vacuum can make such networks decay. The conventional formation rule uses the false-vacuum fraction after the phase transition. Ai argues that this static rule cannot be generally valid.

The old criterion ignores the dynamics of the phase transition itself. Ai evaluates the false-vacuum fraction at a later, physical moment. That moment is the freeze-out temperature of false-vacuum correlation volumes. Judging formation there yields a substantially stricter criterion. The same picture gives a consistency condition for gravitational wave estimates. Those estimates assume a scaling regime for the wall network. Freeze-out must precede the network's annihilation temperature for them to apply. The result tightens predictions for wall-driven gravitational wave signals.
arxiv-2606-30194:
Panchugopal Bikram, Sudipta Kundu, and Hariharan G extend a classic ergodic theorem into noncommutative algebra. The Wiener-Wintner theorem concerns weighted averages along an orbit. Its weights are powers of a complex number on the unit circle. The authors work where the underlying space is a von Neumann algebra. An amenable group acts on it by trace-preserving automorphisms.

First they establish a Jacobs-de Leeuw-Glicksberg decomposition for the action. The algebra splits into almost periodic and weakly mixing parts. That split mirrors the classical structure theory of group actions. The decomposition then powers their main application. They prove a noncommutative Wiener-Wintner theorem for these group actions. Pointwise convergence of weighted ergodic averages is the heart of it. The group need only be locally compact, second countable, and amenable. Finite von Neumann algebras supply the noncommutative stage.
arxiv-2606-30594:
Philip Lynch, Alessandra Buonanno, Aldo Gamboa and Maarten van de Meent speed up simulations of eccentric black-hole binaries. Future detectors will track long, slowly tightening orbits, including oval-shaped eccentric ones. Effective-one-body models capture such systems well. But resolving their rapid orbital wiggles over a long inspiral is costly, especially for light or lopsided pairs.

The team rewrote the nonspinning equations using osculating orbital elements, quantities that track the momentary orbit. They then applied near-identity averaging, which strips out fast wiggles order by order. The averaged system evolves on the slow radiation-reaction timescale, then maps back to full dynamics for the plunge. Inspiral cost fell by up to two orders of magnitude. Overall waveform speed-ups ranged from one and a half to eight times, with mismatches kept tiny across a broad parameter range.
arxiv-2606-31194:
Mishra and two colleagues follow how a filament channel formed and erupted in solar active region 12975. That region produced two coronal mass ejections, huge bursts of solar material, linked to M-class flares on 28 March 2022. New magnetic flux rose from 27 March and then moved in shearing motions.

Their time-dependent magnetofrictional model, driven by electric fields from surface magnetic maps, rebuilds the corona over about fifty hours. It forms a twisted sigmoidal flux rope beside older fields and tracks magnetic energy and helicity, a measure of twist. The helicity ratio hits 0.23 at the observed eruption, below the later model threshold of 0.32, which shows how hard eruption timing is to pin down.
arxiv-2606-31294:
Huang and two colleagues extend the Chen-Ding construction of self-dual cyclic codes to cases it did not cover. A self-dual cyclic code equals its own dual, a trait prized in error correction. Its minimum distance, the smallest gap between codewords, is central to judging how good the code is.

Chen and Ding handled odd order of the field size modulo the code length. Huang handles even order. The new codes keep square-root lower bounds on minimum distance. By reading consecutive zeros in the dual defining set, the team fix exact parameters for Euclidean and Hermitian families. Elsewhere they refine parameter choices to gain larger distances at the same length and dimension, and several families gain tighter bounds.
arxiv-2606-31594:
Alharbi and Ahmed compare five machine learning algorithms for intrusion detection on a realistic Internet of Things network. Connected devices in homes, hospitals, and transport are resource-poor, which makes them soft targets. The Gotham2025 dataset, from a testbed of 78 emulated devices speaking MQTT, CoAP, and RTSP, offers a lifelike ground for the contest.

Random Forest, XGBoost, logistic regression, naive Bayes, and a deep neural network all train on the same traffic. Random Forest wins, reaching an F1-score of 0.99 on attack classification in the reported tests, ahead of the deep network and the simpler models. The comparison gives IoT defenders a grounded ranking for a realistic mix of devices and protocols, rather than results from a toy network.
arxiv-2608-00194:
Pisoni, Tiunov, and Calascibetta compress multiscale turbulence statistics with tensor trains. Capturing those statistics in compressed form is a core challenge for reduced-order modeling. Their target is a highly intermittent passive scalar. A hybrid tensor train approach anchors the method. It blends the compressed form with standard decomposition tools.

The hybrid matches Galerkin, wavelet, and standard tensor train results on structure functions. It improves the handling of intermittent, non-Gaussian fluctuations, they report. Those fluctuations are where compression usually strains most. The results open a route to evolving passive scalar dynamics in compressed form. Quantum algorithms for fluid transport are a named future use.
blake-songs-innocence-experience-1794:
William Blake wrote, illustrated, and hand-printed Songs of Innocence in 1789, then added the darker Songs of Experience five years later. The combined book appeared in 1794. Blake called the two sets the two contrary states of the human soul.

Short lyric poems pair off against each other. The Lamb answers The Tyger, and happy childhood scenes face the grim streets of London. Simple words carry deep questions about God, freedom, and cruelty. Few books of English poetry are quoted more often, and Blake's own pictures for the poems are just as famous as the words.
burton-first-footsteps-east-africa-1894:
Richard Burton traveled in disguise to the forbidden city of Harar in 1854 and 1855. First Footsteps in East Africa tells how he did it; the 1894 edition is the fuller text, printed after his death. Harar, in what is now Ethiopia, barred Christians on pain of death.

Burton posed as a Muslim merchant, relying on his languages and his nerve. He spent ten days in the city, met its ruler, and got out alive, the first European known to do so. The return brought a spear attack that scarred his face for life. The book mixes danger, learning, and dry wit.
chopin-bayou-folk-1894:
Kate Chopin published Bayou Folk in 1894, her first collection of stories, after years of writing about the Louisiana she had married into. Chopin lived in New Orleans and in the Cane River country around Cloutierville. The twenty-three stories draw on Creole and Acadian life she observed at close range.

Désirée's Baby, the most famous piece, turns on a young mother's unknown ancestry and her husband's pride, ending in one of American fiction's great shocks. Other tales follow planters, servants, children, and wanderers through fairs, feuds, and romances. Chopin writes dialect with care and judgment without cruelty. Bayou Folk founded Creole local color and announced a writer far ahead of her time.
cia-0000008694:
Thanh Ha district, in Hai Hung province, is the site named in an October 1972 sighting of two American pilots. Hai Hung covers flat Red River plain country east of Hanoi. Late 1972 was a season of heavy bombing and hard fighting across the north.

Pilot sightings in the war's last months carried double weight: rescue had little time left to run. After the ceasefire, the same reports became evidence in accounting for the missing. Analysts had to sift hope from rumor in a flood of claims. This report preserves one claim with its district and date intact.
cia-0000012294:
The Defense Intelligence Agency was days old when Richard Helms wrote its director in October 1961 about setting up a top-level channel. The DIA had just been created to speak for military intelligence with one voice. Helms's memo opens coordination between the new agency and the CIA's richest source, the Penkovsky operation, then at full flow.

The letter is an institutional handshake: two agencies agreeing how one spy's product would be shared. Its subject, the establishment of that channel, shaped years of joint work. For readers, it shows a new agency tested at birth by the biggest case of the day.
cia-0000012394:
Leeds, England, hosts meeting number four on April 23, 1961, and the record follows the operation north. Moving the sessions out of London spread the risk and varied the cover. The industrial city's mills and moors made an odd backdrop for the Cold War's most sensitive talks, which was much of the point of going there.

The record keeps the northern leg of the debriefings in order. Handlers took the colonel where the watchers were not. For readers, the page shows the roadshow of secrets at work: plain, busy towns hiding the era's most wanted conversations.
cia-0000013294:
Captured Americans were marched north in 1968, and a CIA report from June that year tracks the movement. Its subjects are civilian and military personnel taken in South Vietnam. The road north ran through camps and way stations toward Hanoi's prisons. The journeys were measured in weeks of marching, on short rations, under guard, through country at war from end to end.

The report maps the captives' forced journeys route by route. Families learned from such pages where a man had last been seen alive. For readers, the report is the transit watch of the prison system: the prisoners, moved.
cia-0000014794: The Net That Covers the World, by E. H. Cookridge, fills a CIA file dated April 4, 1974. Cookridge wrote under the name Spiro Edward, per the title. The file notes the book's account of spy services and their work. Such roundups fed the public picture of a world wrapped in secret nets.
cia-0000015394: An interview on unidentified flying objects fills a CIA file dated June 5, 1957. The person interviewed is cut out as deleted in the title. The topic at least survives, which sets this file apart from its blank twins. Someone's views on saucers were worth a talk and a typed record that summer.
cia-0000037894:
Photo comparison results for Lieutenant Commander James E. Dooley fill a CIA record dated January 1, 1971. The case number is deleted in the released copy. Dooley served in the Naval Reserve, as the initials USNR in the title record.

The results set down the analysts' judgment after comparing photographs in Dooley's case. Naval officers lost over Southeast Asia filled many pages of the missing lists. The file shows the identification process serving the Navy's families as it did the other services. It worked one careful comparison at a time. Each answer was entered into the man's own record.
cia-0000048994: An announcement of a killing in El Salvador survives in a CIA item from 1980, kept in the Truth Commission file series. The bare title gives no victim and no place, only the fact that a death was formally declared. In the war's paperwork, even a notice this thin marked a life, and the Truth Commission kept it with its records of the dead.
cia-0000049094: Additional details on a Salvadoran prisoner exchange fill a CIA item from 1984, kept with the Truth Commission records. Exchanges were the war's rare bargains, each name on the lists argued over by both sides. Details like these, numbers, names, and places, were the currency in which such bargains were struck.
cia-0000049194: Supporters of Roberto D'Aubuisson discussed plans in 1990 to assassinate the president, and a CIA item preserves the conversation. Assassination talk on the far right was a constant of the war years, and each report had to be weighed for seriousness. The item survives in the Truth Commission files on the war's right.
cia-0000049294: Reactions to arrests in El Salvador are gathered in a CIA item from 1986, kept with the Truth Commission records. Arrests of the powerful, or of their men, set off tremors that the files were built to catch. The spread of reactions, anger, relief, and warning, mapped where the country's loyalties sat that season.
cia-0000049394: Dated January 2, 1991, declassified CIA document 0000049394 relates to the Jesuit killings and notes the matter proceeding slowly amid charges involving the government. The heading is awkwardly worded in the original record. Readers get a brief agency note whose main point is delay in the Jesuit case, preserved as part of the Truth Commission file.
cia-0000098094: Cuban government policy regarding the Guantanamo Naval Base is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000098094, dated January 2, 1964. The heading names Havana's policy toward the base as its topic. The brief file is a declassified policy item on that single enduring issue, preserved among the agency's cluster of Cuba records from that winter.
cia-0000098694: CIA Agents Receive Death Sentence is the heading of declassified CIA document 0000098694, dated July 6, 1963. The title does not say where, or by whom, the sentence was given. Readers get a short declassified sentence record whose omissions are its central limit, a stark headline preserved without the court or country in its heading.
cia-0000107294: Foreign Ministry's Noteon Photo of Three American Pilots is the heading, with note on run together, on declassified CIA document 0000107294, dated June 6, 1991. The title describes an official note about a photo said to show three American pilots. The ministry and its country are not named in the heading. The brief record preserves the run-together spelling as released.
cia-0000121494: A September 1950 CIA memorandum for the President warns of the threat of full Chinese Communist intervention. The heading does not name Korea, but that war was its subject. Weeks later, Chinese armies poured across the Yalu River, and the paper stands as the warning that reached Truman first. China entered the war in force that October and November, and this September warning became one of the era's most studied cases of a forecast unheeded.
cia-0000124294: A November 1957 CIA report surveys Soviet rockets and earth satellites. A month after Sputnik, the agency was assembling all it knew about Moscow's launchers in one place. The paper serves as a first inventory of the new age that the satellite had opened. Surveys written in the first month after a shock tend to overreach and underreach at once. That makes this one useful evidence of the agency learning in public.
cia-0000132294: A Turkish official stands at the center of Situation Report 603 in the CIA's Iraq-Kuwait series. The report is dated January 1, 1991. It covers political developments, but the official's statement is cut off in the record title. Turkey held the coalition's northern flank, so its words carried unusual weight. Ankara had to balance NATO membership against its own regional fears. The short report notes what the official said.
cia-0000132494:
On April 4, 1960, CIA analysts took stock of where Cuba's new government was heading. The revolution was fifteen months old, and Castro was remaking the island's politics and economy. Washington's sharpest worry was growing Soviet influence so close to Florida.

The briefing captures that early watchfulness: a revolutionary government still defining itself, and an American agency trying to judge its loyalties. Same-day companions in this record cover the political situation and the wider Caribbean. Together they show the questions that drove U.S. policy toward Cuba through 1960 and into the Bay of Pigs year.
cia-0000132594: Peru weighing a break in relations with Cuba fills a CIA document dated August 6, 1960. Lima's decision, when it came, would join a regional freeze-out of Havana. Another Andean government was moving toward the same step that winter. The short document weighs the chances of a Peruvian break as analysts judged them at the time.
cia-0000135694: Filed among the Spanish papers of Brigade 2506, this document is dated 3 January 1961. That was the day the United States broke diplomatic relations with Cuba, though nothing in the catalog record ties this item to that event, and no such tie is claimed. The brigade was in training for the invasion. The record gives no subject. The document survives in Spanish in the CIA's declassified release, dated to a charged week in the brigade's history.
cia-0000135894: From 2 February 1954 comes a CIA meeting record, since declassified, on a meeting with a person whose name is deleted. Behind the paper stands PBSUCCESS, the covert CIA campaign against President Arbenz that closed with the 1954 coup in Guatemala. Records like this one let the operation be studied from the inside, in the terms its own staff used.
cia-0000136294: Dated 3 May 1954 and now declassified, a CIA cable records an analysis of available information, its short form cut off as inf, for two readers. Lincoln handled the field traffic of PBSUCCESS, the agency effort against the Arbenz government in Guatemala in the early 1950s. Records like this one let the operation be studied from the inside, in the terms its own staff used.
cia-0000136394: Regional command for the project is set up in this November 1953 cable signed under Richard Helms's office. From a stated date, all addressees will constitute a regional command with project headquarters at LINCOLN under Jerome C. Dunbar, named special deputy for the project. Addressees will devote top operational priority to it and take guidance directly from LINCOLN; before 1 January cables still go to the Director, after that date to LINCOLN. It is the PBSUCCESS chain of command on paper.
cia-0000136994: ONTRICH is proceeding to ADAM, this June 1954 cable announces. It went to the Guatemala station with pleasure. His plan should stay secret for four or five days. He will retire when directed. As the agency's representative, he must keep his links covert. The ambassador, the embassy, and the station must all stay hidden connections. He should not visit the embassy often. He should not meet American staff openly. His duties are twofold. He will settle remaining business with CALLIGERIS. He will also serve as personal advisor as desired.
cia-0000140394: A professional hypnotist is vetted in this January 1952 interview report. The Contact Branch arranged the meeting through the New York office. The man has an exceptionally good reputation as a hypnotist. He is also a professional engineer and accountant. He stands about six feet tall and wears horn-rim glasses. He appears highly intelligent, courteous, and cooperative. The writer fenced with him for about forty-five minutes. General hypnosis talk filled that time. No security interests were disclosed until competence and secrecy were established.
cia-03164694:
Cambodia opens the Central Intelligence Bulletin dated 8 October 1959, though the brief files it under Asia-Africa with the bloc section blank. Prince Sihanouk calls on Cambodians to choose between his leadership and exiled dissidents Sam Sary and Son Ngoc Thanh. He charges both with SEATO backing. A failed coup plot by Dap Chhuon sits behind the challenge.

Laos follows: rebel harassment continues widely, with skirmishes and concentrations in the south. Resupply aircraft to a surrounded post at Muong Son drew fire on 5 October. The dissidents, probably helped by North Vietnam, aim at a strong bargaining position. Ceylon's prime minister promises the American ambassador a moderate course, and regrets closing British bases. Lebanon's President Shihab forms an expanded cabinet. A late item reports Baghdad quiet under tight security after an assassination attempt on Qasim.
cia-03188694:
Current Intelligence Bulletin dated 11 August 1957, issued by the Office of Current Intelligence, carries three main items listed in its contents. The first reports that Saudi Arabia may be weighing fresh arms support for rebels in Oman. The second follows a reported trend toward the governing parties in Bonn. The third covers an order from Peiping for a new mass campaign to win peasant cooperation.

In the Bonn item, the bulletin reports embassy doubts that the opposition would succeed, and notes plans for a letter from Adenauer to reach every household in the last campaign week. In the Oman item, it recalls rebels housed and trained in eastern Saudi Arabia during 1956 and early 1957 before entering Oman. Claims throughout are presented as reporting and comment.
collectanea-hermetica-vol-4-1894:
W. Wynn Westcott put out the Collectanea Hermetica as a set of brief tracts. Book Four, from 1894, holds Aesch Mezareph, or Purifying Fire. Westcott was a chief of the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn. The set aimed to print rare texts of the hid arts in cheap form.

Aesch Mezareph is a Kabbalistic tract on the fire that cleans the base stuffs. It ties the names of God to the metals and to the soul's purge. The text comes from the school of the Kabbala Denudata in Latin dress. The wee book is a rich source for the alchemy of the Jews.
constitution-argentina-1994:
Argentina's basic law began in 1853, and the hosted text is the version reformed in 1994. It builds a federal state, so each province keeps its own government and its own basic law. The first part gives rights and promises of the state, covering speech, faith, property, and fair trials. A part added in 1994 brought in fresh rights, among them care for shoppers and for nature.

The second part sets up the powers of the nation. A president heads the branch that runs the state day to day. Congress holds two houses, a Senate for the provinces and a Chamber of Deputies for the people. Courts, the provinces, and the city of Buenos Aires each get chapters. The 1994 reform also cut the term of the president and allowed one re-election.
constitution-ethiopia-1994:
Ethiopia's constitution was adopted in 1994 and took force in 1995, founding a federal republic built around ethnic groups. Its opening words place sovereignty not in one people but in the nations, nationalities, and peoples of Ethiopia. Early chapters cover the state, then human rights and democratic rights in detail.

The federation pairs a House of Peoples' Representatives, which makes laws, with a House of the Federation, which speaks for the ethnic groups and settles disputes among them. A prime minister holds real power, while a president serves as head of state. One famous clause gives each nation a right to leave the federation, a promise few charters make. States run their own affairs, schools, and police.
darwin-zoonomia-vol-1-1794:
Erasmus Darwin published Volume 1 of Zoonomia; Or, the Laws of Organic Life in 1794. Darwin, a doctor and poet in Lichfield, was the grandfather of Charles Darwin. In Zoonomia he set out a full system of life, disease, and change in living things.

Darwin sorted diseases by their causes and argued that all life arose from a single living filament. Over long ages, he said, creatures changed as they strove for food, safety, and mates. That was an early form of evolution, decades before his grandson's theory. Volume 1 lays out the system and its laws, and it shows how bold medical and natural thought had become by the 1790s.
dekker-selected-plays-rhys-1894:
Ernest Rhys edited a one-volume selection of Thomas Dekker's plays for the Mermaid series in 1894. The Mermaid volumes brought the old English dramatists back to common readers in cheap, handy form. Dekker, Shakespeare's cheerful contemporary, had long been hard to find in print.

Rhys chose from Dekker's best work, the comedies and city plays that made his name. Dekker's London of apprentices, shoemakers, and rogues comes alive in these pages. His prose pamphlets on plague and coney-catching share the same warm eye. The selection served for years as the standard way to meet Dekker, and its notes and glossary still help new readers.
doe-osti-3383765-closeout-document-usdoe:
Professor Moshe Gai of the University of Connecticut closes grant DE-FG02-94ER40870 with a technical report from the Laboratory for Nuclear Science at Avery Point. The grant ran from June 1, 1994 to August 31, 2023, twenty-nine years of support from the Nuclear Physics program of the Office of Science, totaling about 4.2 million dollars. Few closeout documents span a whole career's program.

The science falls in three lines. Detector research and development produced the O-TPC and the OPAC2. Nuclear astrophysics work treated the standard solar model's boron-8 neutrinos, the beryllium-7 proton capture reaction, and helium burning, including oxygen formation through photodissociation of oxygen-16 as a window on carbon-12 alpha capture. Nuclear structure work covers the structure of carbon-12 and of beryllium isotopes. A full publication list, 1994 to 2026, closes the volume.
dorsey-a-study-of-siouan-cults-1894:
Dorsey followed his Omaha study with this wider 1894 report comparing the cults of the Siouan peoples. Drawing on his knowledge of the Omaha, Ponka, Osage, and Dakota, he set their religions side by side for the Bureau of American Ethnology.

The study covers sacred societies, mystery rites, dances, and the beings each group honored. Dorsey shows how shared ideas about power and spirits took different forms in each tribe. He prints prayers, songs, and ritual terms in the native languages with translation. Though dense, the report is a key early attempt to compare Native American religions as systems.
dubois-pithecanthropus-erectus-1894:
Eugene Dubois, a Dutch army doctor, published his monograph on the Java fossils in 1894, in German. Digging near the Solo River at Trinil, he had found a skullcap and a thigh bone. He named the creature Pithecanthropus erectus, the upright ape-man.

Dubois argued the bones formed a link between apes and humans. Many scholars first doubted or dismissed the claim. The find was the first fossil hominin reported outside Europe. Now classed with Homo erectus, it vindicated the search for human ancestors in Asia. Dubois guarded the fossils jealously for years, which only sharpened the long controversy.
erman-life-ancient-egypt-1894:
Adolf Erman rebuilt the daily life of old Egypt in Life in Ancient Egypt, in English from 1894. Erman led the Berlin school, the most strict crop of sages then at work. H. M. Tirard turned his German text to English. House by house, shop by shop, he shows how folk there dwelt, dressed, ate, wed, and worked.

He draws each scene from texts and finds, not dreams. Kings get brief room; plain folk get the book. Few works on Egypt have been used so much since. It is the lost world at home, at ease.
europmc-pmc10013894:
Douglas, Ewell, and Brauer compare the quality of survey data from five online research platforms in a 2023 study. Online studies now recruit large numbers of people fast and cheaply. Yet researchers worry about careless respondents and automated bots filling in answers.

The team collected data through MTurk, Prolific, CloudResearch, Qualtrics, and SONA, then checked each set for signs of poor attention. Their comparison shows which sources gave cleaner data. It names clear steps that labs can take before they collect data. The paper offers practical guidance for anyone who runs or reads online human research.
europmc-pmc10172194:
Sun and colleagues map cell-level chemical changes in gastric cancer using spatial multi-omics in a 2023 study. Gastric cancer forms in the stomach lining and is often found late. How a tumor rewires its chemistry, cell by cell and place by place, shapes its growth and its talks with nearby healthy cells.

The team combined imaging and molecular profiling to chart that rewiring in place. Their maps show which tumor regions run which fuel programs and how tumor and non-tumor cells interact. The work may help design treatments aimed at the tumor's chemistry.
europmc-pmc10190894:
A. T. MacConkey, bacteriologist in charge of the serum laboratories at the Lister Institute, summed up the prevention of tetanus in a summary drawn from the British Medical Journal of December 1915. His anchor is the official memorandum on wounds in war from July 1915, which calls the preventive use of tetanus antitoxin a step of well established value. Every wounded man was then ordered a preventive dose.

The dose named is 500 United States units, given under the skin away from the wound and as early as possible. Among men dosed within a day, only 36 cases followed in six months. MacConkey checks the claim against reports from 16 writers covering 83,593 war wounds in allied and enemy armies. He also warns that men can carry tetanus for weeks before it shows. Readers get the wartime case for routine antitoxin.
europmc-pmc10225594:
Mitra and co-authors trace CAR T cell therapy from bench to bedside in a 2023 review. In this therapy, a patient's own T cells are engineered in the lab to hunt cancer. The approach won its first approval in 2017 for children and young adults with a form of leukemia that had resisted other care.

The review recounts the decades of work behind that breakthrough. It explains how the engineered cells are made and given, and their striking results in blood cancers. It also covers side effects and the push to make the therapy work in solid tumors.
europmc-pmc10250194:
Punjani and Fleet present 3DFlex, a method that finds the structure and motion of flexible proteins from cryo-electron microscopy, in a 2023 paper. Cryo-EM photographs vast numbers of frozen molecules and averages them into a three-dimensional shape. Flexible molecules break that averaging, since each copy bends in its own way, and modeling them is a top challenge in the field.

3DFlex learns how a molecule bends and sorts the images by pose. It then rebuilds both the shape and the range of motion. The method reveals moving parts of molecular machines that older tools blurred away.
europmc-pmc10301994:
Al Kuwaiti and colleagues review the role of artificial intelligence in healthcare in a 2023 paper. AI tools have spread fast through medicine, from scan reading to virtual nursing. The authors base their review on the published literature and sort the field into key areas of use.

They cover imaging and diagnosis, virtual patient care, drug discovery, and hospital management. For each area they weigh proven gains against risks such as bias and privacy loss. The review gives readers a structured tour of where AI already works in care and where caution is due.
europmc-pmc10468394:
Watson and a large team gave a method in 2023 to design brand-new proteins with AI. Proteins are cell machines whose shape sets their job. Past design tools each fit a narrow task. The team adapted diffusion models, the AI type that builds images from noise, to protein shapes.

Their tool, RFdiffusion, starts from the RoseTTAFold prediction network, tuned to clean noisy shapes. It can build plain chains, binders that grip a target, and symmetric multi-part forms. Watson built and tested hundreds of the designs in the lab. One binder's true shape, read by a cold electron scope, matched the design near exactly. The binder gripped a flu protein as planned.
europmc-pmc12094094:
Lagier and a large team reported growing gut microbes once thought uncultivable in 2016. DNA methods had revealed vast numbers of unknown gut species. Growing them in pure culture had fallen out of fashion. Yet culture stays key to learning what each microbe does. The journal later retracted the article.

Their approach, called culturomics, tries many growth conditions at once. Fresh samples and new protocols widened the catch. The team reported 1,057 species from the human gut. Of those, 531 were new to the gut list. Readers should weigh the findings with the retraction in mind.
europmc-pmc12148494:
Bunne and many co-authors laid out a plan for a virtual cell in 2024. Cells drive health and disease, yet models capture them poorly. New artificial intelligence tools and rich cell data change that outlook. A virtual cell would simulate molecules, cells, and tissues together.

Such a model could predict how cells act in new states. It could guide lab work and speed discovery. Building it demands shared data, open science, and teamwork across fields. Bunne sets priorities and chances for the effort. The vision treats the cell as a system computers can learn.
europmc-pmc1240994:
Greer and colleagues dosed volunteers with perchlorate to find safe levels in 2002. Perchlorate taints groundwater across the Southwest at low levels. It blocks iodide from entering the thyroid gland. That blockade is both its drug use and its toxic risk.

Thirty-seven volunteers drank perchlorate water for 14 days at four dose levels. Thyroid uptake of radioactive iodine was measured before, during, and after dosing. Uptake at 8 and 24 hours tracked each other closely. Greer charts how uptake falls as dose climbs. Those curves anchor health limits for water contamination. Thyroid uptake returned to normal 15 days after the dosing stopped. No sex gap appeared in the response.
europmc-pmc1241394:
Schantz, Widholm, and Rice reviewed PCB exposure and child brain function in 2003. PCBs are industrial chemicals that persist in soil, water, and food. Better chemistry now profiles single PCB types in human tissue. Different types carry different toxic profiles.

Cohorts in Taiwan, Michigan, New York, Holland, Germany, and the Faroe Islands were compared. Each reported negative links between prenatal PCB exposure and child test scores. Memory, attention, and related skills were affected. The pattern held across settings and exposure routes. Schantz weighs how this growing record should shape risk assessment.
europmc-pmc12857194:
Verma and a large team mapped genetic architecture across 2,068 traits in 2024. Human genetics has under-sampled diverse populations. The VA Million Veteran Program is among the largest American biobanks. About 29 percent of its members trace to non-European reference groups.

Over 635,000 participants contributed health record linked data. More than 44.3 million genetic variants were genotyped. The scale supports association studies across many ancestries at once. Missing causal factors and health disparity roots are the targets. Verma shows diversity at scale can fill long-standing gaps. It appeared in Science in 2024. In total, the scan found 26,049 links between gene variants and traits across groups.
europmc-pmc1324794:
Schaffer and co-authors imaged brain surface blood flow after vessel blockage in 2006. A dense arteriole network overlies the mammalian cortex. The team asked whether it reroutes blood after an occlusion. Rodent cortex was imaged with two-photon microscopy at single-vessel scale.

Flow returned quickly past a blocked vessel by reversing direction. The first branch downstream regained perfusion through one reversed vessel. Blocking the main middle cerebral artery flipped flow in about half of distant downstream vessels. Schaffer shows collateral rerouting is fast and widespread. That rerouting may limit stroke damage in surface networks.
europmc-pmc1434494:
A pig germ caused a severe outbreak in China in the summer of 2005. Tang and co-authors investigated cases of toxic shock, a crash marked by fever, low blood pressure, and organ failure. The germ was Streptococcus suis type 2, a microbe of pigs that rarely harms people.

The team studied sick people and pigs, and grew 45 germ strains from samples. Tests in pigs and gene checks showed the strains were strong and closely matched. Tang also linked the outbreak to a like event in 1998. Their report marks the first clear proof that this pig germ can cause toxic shock in people.
europmc-pmc1456994:
Ernst and Bar-Joseph built a tool in 2006 for a common lab bind. Gene activity studies over time are often short, with just three to eight points, due to cost. Generic tools fit such short runs poorly. Their program, STEM, was made for short series from the start.

STEM groups genes by how their activity rises and falls. It can compare two runs and chart the trends. It also links groups to a gene function database for sound biological reads. Ernst notes that most time series studies are short, so a tool shaped for them fills a real gap. STEM is free for academic use.
europmc-pmc2020494:
Rosen, Fox and Gill reviewed in 2007 how well HIV treatment programmes in sub-Saharan Africa keep patients in care. Antiretroviral therapy, drugs that suppress HIV, was expanding fast across the region. Long-term retention is vital for those programmes to succeed. The team searched databases, conference reports and project documents from 2000 to 2007 for non-research programmes.

They found 32 publications covering 33 cohorts and 74,192 patients in 13 countries. Reported retention was 79.1 percent at six months, 75.0 percent at one year, and 61.6 percent at two years, with wide variation between programmes. Loss to follow-up caused 56 percent of attrition, and death caused 40 percent. The authors warn that short reports may overstate retention, and urge better patient tracing.
europmc-pmc2125494:
Charles W. McClure, Beth Vincent, and Joseph H. Pratt of Harvard Medical School measured fat absorption in dogs missing some or all of the pancreas in 1917, a problem open since Claude Bernard's day. Their comparisons separate two things usually confounded: the gland's juice in the gut, and the gland tissue left in the body.

The tissue's condition, then, does not govern absorption. What matters is the juice reaching the intestine: exclude the secretion and absorption is always markedly disturbed. Yet even after complete removal of every scrap of pancreas, considerable fat absorption still takes place. The daily protocols are unglamorous evidence: fatty, rancid stools crowded with muscle fibers and fat drops, weights logged beside them. Readers get the pancreas's fat role narrowed to its juice, and the juice itself shown helpful but not indispensable.
europmc-pmc2125794:
Rufus Cole asked why immune serum sometimes fails against pneumococcus pneumonia, publishing his answer in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1917. He studied the fluids that collect in infected chest cavities and the blood of infected rabbits and patients, testing how fast injected immune bodies vanish and what removes them from action.

Cole found large amounts of a soluble substance in pneumococcus chest fluid that neutralizes pneumococcus antibodies, and similar material in infected rabbit blood. Injected immune serum disappeared quickly in infected rabbits, blocked by this substance, and the same rapid loss showed in badly infected patients. Serum worked only once the blocking substance was itself neutralized. His practical advice followed directly: give serum early in severe cases, and give a large first dose.
europmc-pmc2128394:
William A. Hagan studied the guinea pig disease caused by Bacillus abortus, the cattle abortion germ, dose by dose. His paper appeared in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1922. He computed how few organisms infection takes and followed how animals gain the upper hand over weeks.

The germ's infectivity for guinea pigs is extremely great: somewhat fewer than one hundred organisms infect most animals. A rare animal resisted far larger challenges, though even the toughest was infected by under ten thousand. Dose chiefly changes the timetable, not the outcome: small doses run a slower course, but the end results are practically the same. By the clumping test curves, animals generally begin mastering the disease around the tenth week. Germ counts in the organs start falling near the fourth week, then drop fast after the tenth, matching the blood curves.
europmc-pmc2128494:
S. L. Warren and G. H. Whipple extended their Roentgen ray intoxication work across the animal kingdom, in the fourth paper of the series. It appeared in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1923, from the University of California medical school. Earlier papers had fixed the fatal gut injury in dogs; now rats, guinea pigs, cats, rabbits, birds, frogs, and reptiles took the same abdominal dose.

The common laboratory mammals proved about equally sensitive, with very similar sickness and almost identical gut damage. Rats and guinea pigs were slightly more sensitive than dogs, cats, and rabbits. Birds, frogs, and reptiles stood apart: they tolerated two or three doses lethal for dogs, a resistance the authors cannot convincingly explain. Human case reports point the same way as the mammals. The gut's sensitivity to radiation, they warn, must be weighed carefully wherever belly or pelvic radiation is used in people.
europmc-pmc2128594:
Paul A. Lewis and Dorothy Loomis compared antibody formation in normal guinea pigs and in guinea pigs infected with tubercle bacilli. Their paper, on what they call allergic irritability, appeared in the Journal of Experimental Medicine in 1924, from Princeton. Both groups received like amounts of sheep red blood cells, and the anti-sheep antibody was measured.

The tuberculous animals made much more anti-sheep antibody than the controls did. The guinea pig's antibody curve also departed from curves known in other animals, a peculiarity the authors record. The work belongs to a larger effort: learning how the inborn factors that govern natural resistance to disease actually function. An existing tuberculosis infection, the result suggests, leaves the antibody machinery in a readier state, answering an unrelated challenge harder than a healthy animal does. Lewis and Loomis are careful about how far this one experiment reaches into that large question.
europmc-pmc2131494:
Ralph Muckenfuss, at The Rockefeller Institute for Medical Research, wrote part eleven of the bacteriophage studies of d'Herelle in 1928. Animals immunized with lytic filtrates make serum that can neutralize bacteriophage. He asked how that anti-phage serum works, and whether the neutralization test could serve in the diagnosis of disease, as Sonnenschein had proposed.

Each bacteriophage acts as a specific antigen of its own. The antibodies against the phage are separate from those against the bacteria used to grow it. Neutralization behaves much like toxin meeting antitoxin. Serum from mice infected with mouse typhoid did not gain power against phages of the infecting germ. On that record, Muckenfuss judges the proposed diagnostic use impractical.
europmc-pmc2140394:
Selig Hecht, at Creighton University in Omaha, analyzed the dark adaptation of the human eye in a 1920 paper. In darkness, the eye's threshold for seeing falls to a small fraction of its value in light. Aubert and others had measured that fall since 1865. Hecht asked what chemical course the measured curve follows.

The fall of the threshold follows the course of a bimolecular chemical reaction, in which two substances join. Hecht proposes that dim-light vision rests on a reversible light reaction: a sensitive substance splits into two products in light. Dark adaptation is then the dark reaction, the two products reuniting to rebuild the sensitive substance. The model ties the clam and Ciona work of his earlier papers to the human eye.
europmc-pmc2359994:
O'Connor and colleagues reviewed a scanning method for testing blood vessel drugs in 2007. The method is DCE-MRI, a form of magnetic scan that tracks a contrast dye through tissue. Antiangiogenic drugs block new vessel growth, while vascular disrupting drugs attack vessels that already feed a tumor.

The authors explained that this scan type is now common in early trials of such drugs. For some vessel-blocking drugs, scans showed clear drug effects and stronger effects at higher doses. They set out the choices that shape scan quality, covering how data are collected and analysed in the T1-weighted form of the method. They also flagged weak points where the technique still needed work before results could be compared across trials.
europmc-pmc2373894:
Itoh and co-authors compared sex chromosome gene dosage in birds and mammals in 2007. Dosage compensation means evening out gene output between the sexes, since one sex carries two copies of the sex chromosome and the other carries one. Mammals manage this well, but birds, where males have two Z chromosomes and females one, were a mystery.

Using gene chips, they measured male-to-female activity ratios in zebra finch and chicken, plus mouse and human data. In birds, Z-linked genes ran clearly higher in males than ordinary genes did. In mouse and human, X-linked genes matched ordinary genes closely, showing effective balancing. Even the many human X genes that escape silencing did not break the balance. The authors called birds an unmatched case of living without real dosage compensation.
europmc-pmc2376094:
Galluzzi and co-authors reviewed how viruses control cell suicide at the mitochondria in 2008. Mitochondria are the cell's power stations, and they also hold a trigger for apoptosis, the program that makes infected cells kill themselves. Killing infected cells is an ancient defence, so many viruses must disable it to survive.

The review catalogues viral tricks on both sides of that switch. Some viral proteins mimic the host's own Bcl-2 family, the proteins that guard the suicide trigger, and block death so the virus can finish copying itself. Others push death along, killing immune cells or bursting infected cells to spread the virus. Still others, with no host look-alike, grip key parts of the death machinery directly. The authors focused on the mitochondrial step, where the decision to die is largely made.
europmc-pmc2488194:
Johnson and colleagues hunted hidden drug resistance in newly diagnosed HIV patients in 2008. Standard resistance tests read the dominant virus, missing rare resistant copies that can still wreck a first treatment. The team applied sensitive real-time PCR tests, each tuned to one resistance mutation, to patients in the United States and Canada.

Among 205 people whose virus looked fully drug-sensitive by standard testing, 17% carried one to three hidden resistance mutations, and 2% carried resistance to two drug classes at once. Samples that already showed resistance often hid extra mutations too. The clincher came from 316 patients starting an efavirenz-based regimen: hidden mutations appeared in 7% of those whose treatment failed, but under 1% of successes, a statistically sharp gap. The authors argued baseline testing should use sensitive methods so first regimens are not chosen blind.
europmc-pmc2592694:
van der Schaar and colleagues filmed individual dengue virus particles entering living cells in 2008 to map the virus's entry route step by step. Dengue is the world's most common insect-borne viral infection, yet how it invades cells was unclear. The team tracked single labelled particles alongside glowing markers of the cell's uptake machinery.

The virus moved by diffusion across the cell surface until a ready-made clathrin-coated pit, the cell's standard cargo intake dimple, snagged it. All entry used this clathrin route. Inside, particles rode compartments marked Rab5, which then matured into late endosomes by gaining Rab7 and shedding Rab5. Fusion between the viral membrane and the compartment membrane, the step that releases the virus's contents, happened mainly in those late endosomes. The timeline gives drug designers precise steps to block.
europmc-pmc2600394:
Lanciotti and colleagues characterised in 2008 the Zika virus behind a 2007 epidemic on Yap Island in Micronesia. Physicians there saw an outbreak of rash, conjunctivitis, and joint pain that a rapid test blamed on dengue virus. Samples sent to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention told a different story, and the team set out to identify the virus fully.

Antibody tests confirmed a recent flavivirus infection. Genetic sequencing of amplified fragments showed about 90 percent identity with Zika virus. That virus is mosquito-borne and was first isolated in Uganda in 1947. The team determined the full coding region sequence of the Yap virus and described its serologic properties, including how patient antibodies react. The episode was the first documented Zika outbreak outside Africa and Asia.
europmc-pmc2675494:
Cruz and Wishart reviewed in 2007 how machine learning, software that finds patterns in past data, is used to predict cancer. The field had grown fast on new gene and protein measurements too complex for hand analysis. The reviewers surveyed which methods were used, what data fed them, and how well they worked.

Clear trends stood out. Studies leaned hard on older neural network methods, and on prostate and breast cancers above others. Protein markers and gene chip data were the favorite inputs. Many studies also skipped proper testing on fresh data, a basic safeguard. In the well-tested work, learning methods beat standard prediction by 15 to 25 percent on who gets cancer, whose returns, and who dies of it. The methods, they add, are also teaching basic lessons about how cancers grow.
europmc-pmc2678294:
Rumble and co-authors presented in 2009 SHRiMP, a program for placing millions of very short DNA reads onto a genome. New sequencing machines read genomes in scraps of 25 to 70 letters. Mapping those scraps back to a reference genome is the first step of most studies, and it gets hard when the new individual differs from the reference at many spots.

SHRiMP pairs a fast first pass with careful alignment that handles both ordinary reads and a color-coded kind from one major machine. A statistical model weeds out false matches. The team tested it on a sea squirt, Ciona savignyi, an animal famous for its scrambled variation. The program mapped the second sequenced individual's reads accurately onto the reference despite the heavy differences. The run also confirmed just how variable this species is, a good sign for studies of wilder, less tame genomes.
europmc-pmc2715894:
Vanengelsdorp and co-authors surveyed in 2009 honey bee colonies hit by Colony Collapse Disorder, a sudden loss of adult worker bees in the United States over two winters. Hives were left with brood and food but few adults, and few dead bees nearby. No single cause was known when the study began.

Across sixty-one measured factors, from bee body state to pathogen and pesticide levels, no one measure stood out as the likely cause. Bees from collapsed colonies carried more pathogens at once than bees from healthy colonies. That pattern points to a mix of infection and other stresses, or to shared exposure, rather than to one agent acting alone.
europmc-pmc2791494:
Forristal and colleagues studied how low oxygen shapes human embryonic stem cells, which can become any cell type in the body. Embryos start life in low oxygen, yet labs usually grow these cells in room air. Their 2010 work compared growth at room air with growth at just five percent oxygen, mimicking the womb where embryos begin, and tested oxygen-sensing proteins called hypoxia inducible factors.

Cells in room air grew more slowly and made less of three proteins that keep stem cells flexible. Silencing one sensor, HIF2A, cut growth and lowered those same proteins, while a marker of early change rose. A third sensor, HIF3A, tuned the other two, and low oxygen clearly suited the cells better.
europmc-pmc2828994:
Jewkes and Morrell argued in 2010 that South Africa's HIV epidemic runs through cultural ideals of manhood and womanhood, not just private choices. Research already showed that unequal power in couples and partner violence raise women's HIV risk, and that violent men more often carry the virus themselves.

Drawing on the idea of hegemonic masculinity, the authors describe a dominant ideal of black African manhood prizing toughness, control over women, and many sexual partners. The matching ideal of womanhood prizes compliance and tolerance, even of cheating and violence, often traded for material security. Women with the fewest resources can least afford to break these scripts. The authors urge prevention aimed at changing gender ideals, rather than only coaching single behaviors.
europmc-pmc2837394:
Penny and colleagues argued in 2010 that brain model comparisons should judge whole families of models, not crown a single winner. Researchers compare math models of brain data by their evidence scores, then usually discard all but the best. That habit turns brittle when hundreds of models compete or when each person's best model differs.

Grouping models into families that share one trait, such as serial versus parallel processing, lets the data answer the trait question directly. Averaging parameters across a family then gives estimates that no longer hinge on one exact wiring diagram. The team demonstrates both moves on dynamic causal models of speech brain imaging data, asking which regions receive input and which links a task adjusts.
europmc-pmc2853094:
Northover and colleagues reported in 2010 the thirteen-year follow-up of ACT I, the first British randomized trial of chemoradiation for anal cancer. The trial's 1996 results had already made combined chemotherapy and radiation the standard over radiation alone. This update tracked all five hundred seventy-seven randomized patients for relapses and deaths through 2007.

The benefit endured and grew clearer with time. For every hundred patients given chemoradiation, about twenty-five fewer suffered local relapse and about twelve fewer died of anal cancer by twelve years. An early bump in deaths from other causes faded away by year ten. Only eleven patients relapsed locally after year five, a fact the authors say should shape how future trials choose their endpoints.
europmc-pmc2871794:
Frank and co-authors mapped in 2010 the microbes living in the human nose. They asked how those microbes relate to carriage of Staphylococcus aureus. That germ can cause skin, blood, and heart infections. About half of healthy adults carry it in the nose at least sometimes, and carriage usually comes before infection. The team sampled five healthy adults over time plus hospital patients classed as carriers or non-carriers.

Healthy noses were dominated by skin-like bacteria, mainly two groups that thrive on the face and nostrils. Hospital patients' noses held far more staphylococci and far fewer of those usual residents, most sharply in one group. The pattern suggests the resident community helps keep the dangerous germ in check, and disturbing that community may open the door to carriage.
europmc-pmc2885494:
Harrison and co-authors traced in 2009 how body inflammation drags mood down, with a focus on a small brain area called the subgenual cingulate. This area is strongly linked to depression, and immune signals are known to spark low mood. Sixteen healthy men got a typhoid shot or salt water in a crossover study. They viewed faces with feelings during brain scans.

The shot raised markers of inflammation and made mood worse within hours. The size of the mood drop tracked shifts in the cingulate's activity while the men viewed the faces. Inflammation also changed how the cingulate linked with reward and emotion areas. A clear brain circuit thus carries the effect of body inflammation into mood.
europmc-pmc2912394:
Van der Meijden and colleagues discovered in 2010 a new human polyomavirus hiding in the skin lesions of a heart transplant patient. The patient had trichodysplasia spinulosa, a rare skin disease seen only in people with suppressed immunity, marked by spiny facial growths. Rolling-circle amplification, a technique that copies small circular DNA, recovered the full viral genome from plucked spines.

The genome spans a little over five thousand DNA letters in the family's usual layout, with early genes for replication control and late genes for the shell proteins. Its closest relative infects orangutans, and it sits a step further from the Merkel cell virus that causes a rare skin cancer. Finding the virus exactly in diseased skin makes it the prime suspect for the condition and adds a member to the human virus roster.
europmc-pmc2952094:
Yamagishi and Matsui reviewed how sugar-damaged proteins drive kidney disease in diabetes, in a 2010 article written as worldwide diabetes counts headed toward several hundred million people. Kidney failure from diabetes had become a leading cause of dialysis.

Compounds called advanced glycation end products form faster under high blood sugar and collect in tissues. Acting through their receptor, they spark oxidative stress that injures kidney filters over time. Tight sugar and pressure control help but fall short, so the authors present this product and receptor system as a target for new treatments that might halt progression.
europmc-pmc2957394:
Spurling and a team of colleagues reviewed studies on how drug company promotion affects doctors' prescribing in a 2010 systematic review. Companies spend a large share of revenue courting prescribers while claiming the contact also educates.

Across the gathered evidence, the team found no sign that exposure to company material made prescribing better. Instead, several studies linked greater exposure with prescribing more often. Others linked it with choosing costlier options, or prescribing less well. With industry spending so large, the authors argue the information channel deserves scepticism. It also deserves tighter separation from clinical education and from everyday prescribing habits.
europmc-pmc3003694:
Marim and co-authors established a way to grow macrophages, key immune cells, from frozen mouse bone marrow in a 2010 methods study. Genetically altered mice made such cells a workhorse, yet no one had shown they could come from stored marrow.

Their freezing protocol kept marrow able to yield macrophages for over six years. Cells from frozen stocks matched fresh ones in switching on activation markers after bacterial cues or infection. They also handled two live invaders, a bacterium and a parasite, just as fresh cells did. Early tests suggest dendritic cells can be raised the same way.
europmc-pmc3070694:
Tiemersma and colleagues estimated in 2011 how long untreated tuberculosis lasts and how often it kills, using studies from before effective drugs existed. Many patients worldwide still go undiagnosed, so the natural course of the disease remains a live question, and disease models need honest numbers for it. The team reviewed the old literature for patients without HIV, split by whether their sputum carried visible bacteria.

For the more infectious form, roughly seven in ten patients died within ten years across the old studies. For the less visible form, the estimate was about two in ten. From first illness to cure or death took about three years on average for both forms, a year longer than many models assumed. The authors say model builders should keep the fatality figures but stretch the timeline. The work also frames what treatment programs prevent.
europmc-pmc3078894:
Chablais, Veit, Rainer, and Jaźwińska created in 2011 a heart attack model in zebrafish. Unlike earlier fish models, it starts like a mammal heart attack yet ends in full repair. Freezing a spot on the fish heart killed about a fifth of the wall, mimicking the massive cell death of a human infarct. Simple cutting models used before did not reproduce that death pattern.

Early healing looked mammalian: clotting, scar building cells, and collagen laid down in the wound. Then the paths split. Fish heart muscle cells reentered the growth cycle and invaded the damaged zone, while scar tissue was dismantled cell by cell. Within two months the wall was new muscle and heart tracings showed normal function restored. A distinctive support protein marked the busy border zone. The model lets researchers hunt for what mammals lack.
europmc-pmc3100594:
Sutherland asked in 2011 a pointed question about a much studied cell enzyme: which of its nearly one hundred proposed targets does it truly act on inside living cells? The enzyme, GSK3 in short, is proposed to tag proteins in almost every tissue and process, and it is a tempting drug target in diabetes, brain disease, and cancer. Many proposed targets rest on test tube evidence that may not hold in the cell.

The paper audits the evidence target by target, separating those with strong in vivo support from those with only suggestive data. The confirmed set still spans core processes such as sugar storage, cell division, and gene control, so the enzyme's importance is not in doubt. The dispute is over its exact reach. Sutherland argues that drug developers need this honest map, because blocking the enzyme will touch every genuine target at once, wanted or not.
europmc-pmc3192794:
Marwan Baliki and colleagues found that each chronic pain condition reshapes the brain in its own pattern in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Chronic pain is usually treated as a state of altered activity, but lasting pain may also physically reorganise the brain. Structural scans compared patients with chronic back pain, a regional pain syndrome, and knee arthritis against healthy controls.

Only the back pain group showed changed whole-brain grey matter volume, while each condition carried a distinct regional pattern and its own large-scale network signature. A shared set of regions tracked how long pain had lasted across all groups. Combining the patterns into one index classified individual brains to their condition with high accuracy, and back pain reorganised the brain more slowly but more extensively than the regional syndrome.
europmc-pmc3197594:
Ana Negredo and colleagues discovered a new Ebola-like virus in dead bats in Spain in a 2011 paper in PLoS Pathogens. The virus family includes some of the most lethal primate pathogens known, previously found naturally only in Africa and the Philippines. The bats, from a cave in Asturias, had died in a wider European die-off, and their organs showed signs of viral pneumonia.

Genetic screening of lung and spleen found sequences of a filovirus unlike any known, provisionally named for the cave. Bats carrying African family members stay healthy, so this virus's role in the die-off is suggestive rather than proven. The find extends the family's known range into Europe and raises fresh questions about bat reservoirs on the continent.
europmc-pmc3203094:
Yang Zhang and colleagues described a simpler way to prepare rice protoplasts in this 2011 paper in Plant Methods. Protoplasts are plant cells stripped of their walls, widely used to test gene function quickly. Rice protoplasts usually came from cultured cells or seedlings grown in darkness, which limits studies of light and chloroplasts.

Their method isolates protoplasts directly from normally grown young green rice leaves, without special chemicals or vacuum equipment. The cells took up plasmids of many sizes with strikingly high efficiency, including several plasmids at once. The team verified the system with protein blotting, localization, and interaction assays. Because the protoplasts stayed photosynthetically active, turning on one light-related gene raised the activity of several photosynthesis genes.
europmc-pmc3207894:
Chaokun Li and colleagues presented FastCloning, a simpler way to insert DNA into plasmids, in this 2011 paper in BMC Biotechnology. Molecular cloning is often slow and frustrating, relying on purification steps, kits, or special enzymes. Their method needs only standard PCR and a high-fidelity polymerase.

The vector and the insert are amplified separately in few cycles, with short overlapping ends designed into the primers. After an enzyme step destroys the original template DNA, the mixture goes straight into bacteria, with no gel purification and no ligation kit. Fewer cycles also mean fewer random mutations. The authors showed the method is reproducible and versatile, handling chimera construction, insertions, and multiple mutations across a stretch of DNA.
europmc-pmc3279294:
Preethi Srikanthan, Andrea Hevener, and Arun Karlamangla asked whether low muscle mass worsens the metabolic cost of obesity, in this 2010 analysis in PLoS ONE. Muscle loss, or sarcopenia, often accompanies obesity and could compound insulin resistance. Using a large United States health survey of more than fourteen thousand adults, they measured muscle by electrical impedance and related it to insulin resistance and blood sugar control.

Sarcopenia was tied to insulin resistance in both non-obese and obese people, independent of other factors. Among the obese, it was also tied to poorer blood sugar control, though not among the non-obese. The links ran strongest in people under sixty. Because the data are a snapshot, cause cannot be proven. Still, the authors suggest low muscle may be an early warning sign of diabetes risk. They urge work on preventing the sarcopenic-obese state.
europmc-pmc3302894:
Laroui and co-authors worked out how a chemical used to trigger gut inflammation in mice actually does its damage, in a 2012 study. The chemical, known as DSS, reliably causes colon inflammation resembling human bowel disease, yet it harms living tissue while leaving lab grown cells alone. None of its breakdown parts explained the effect, which deepened the puzzle.

The team found that DSS latches onto medium length fatty acids that are naturally present in the colon. Together they form tiny fat coated particles that can merge with the membranes of colon cells. Once inside, these particles appear to switch on inflammatory signals. Most harm falls on the far end of the colon, and the authors suggest reshaping the chemical to keep its targeting while removing the damage.
europmc-pmc3321794:
Grandadam and colleagues reported the first locally caught cases of chikungunya in mainland France, in a 2011 paper. Chikungunya is a mosquito carried virus that causes fever and severe joint pain, and it had been spreading to new regions worldwide. In September 2010, people in southeastern France who had not traveled caught the infection near home.

The tiger mosquito that carries the virus is established in that part of France, which made local spread possible. The team read the genomes of viruses from travelers who imported the infection and from the locally caught cases. Comparing them revealed fresh features relevant to how the virus might emerge and spread in Europe. The short report stands as an early warning that tropical mosquito diseases can take hold in temperate Europe.
europmc-pmc3365894:
Gronenschild and co-workers tested whether the computing setup itself changes brain measurements from FreeSurfer, the standard software for measuring cortical thickness and anatomical volumes. Using thirty MRI scans, they varied the software version, the workstation type, and the Macintosh operating system version, then compared the outputs.

The newest software version differed significantly from its two predecessors, shifting volume results by around nine percent on average and thickness results by a smaller margin. Changing workstation or operating system produced differences roughly half as large — comparable to effects reported in disease studies. The authors advise against upgrading software or switching machines mid-study without repeating the analysis.
europmc-pmc3383994:
Reijns led a team reporting in 2012 that mice cannot develop without RNase H2, an enzyme that trims stray RNA building blocks out of DNA. Such ribonucleotides slip into DNA easily and weaken it. In simple yeast the enzyme is optional, but in people faulty versions cause a brain inflammation disease.

Mouse embryos lacking the enzyme stalled from an early stage onward. Their cells carried over a million stray ribonucleotides each, and the damage switched on a p53-driven alarm response. The work crowns RNase H2 as a key guardian of the mammalian genome. It also shows these stray blocks are the most common internal DNA flaw in dividing cells.
europmc-pmc3418594:
Pearce and a large team followed British children and young adults in 2012 to measure cancer risk after CT scans. The scans are clinically valuable but expose patients to ionizing radiation, and children are more sensitive than adults. The cohort covered well over one hundred seventy thousand patients first scanned before age twenty-two, tracked through national registries.

Risk of leukemia and brain tumors rose with the radiation dose absorbed. At the higher cumulative doses seen in the study, the risks roughly tripled compared with the lowest-dose group. Because these cancers are rare, the absolute danger stayed small, about one extra case per ten thousand head scans in the first decade. Still, the authors urge keeping doses low and choosing radiation-free tests when suitable.
europmc-pmc3433794:
Peyrot, Barnett, Meneghini, and Schumm-Draeger surveyed insulin users and their doctors across eight countries in 2012 about sticking to insulin therapy. Over fifteen hundred patients and more than twelve hundred physicians answered. The study asked how often doses get skipped and why, and how well doctors think treatment is going.

A third of patients admitted skipping or missing insulin at least one day in the past month, averaging over three days. Doctors estimated worse adherence than patients confessed. The top reasons matched on both sides: being busy, travel, skipped meals, stress, and embarrassment in public. Most doctors said their patients lack adequate control and that fear of low blood sugar stops them pushing doses harder. Less restrictive regimens are needed, the authors conclude.
europmc-pmc3464294:
Xu and colleagues tested whether cell stiffness can reveal how likely ovarian cancer cells are to spread, in a 2012 PLoS ONE study. Knowing which tumors will spread helps doctors plan treatment for each patient. The team pressed on single cells with an atomic force microscope, a tool that measures how much a cell gives under a tiny probe.

Cancer cells from the ovary proved softer than healthy ovarian surface cells, and their stiffness varied less. The most invasive line was softer still than its less invasive parent line. Xu's group linked the softening to changes in the actin skeleton that holds a cell's shape. They propose stiffness as a simple physical marker of spread risk.
europmc-pmc3478794:
Liana and co-authors reviewed the fast-growing field of paper-based sensors in Sensors in 2012. Paper wicks liquid on its own, costs little, and can be burned after use, making it attractive for cheap test devices. Such sensors target clinic diagnosis, food safety checks, and pollution monitoring, above all where labs are scarce.

The review covers how the devices are printed and patterned, how results are read, and where they are already used. Simple strip tests give yes-or-no answers, while newer designs steer fluids through shaped channels for exact readings. Liana's team admits accuracy and sensitivity still lag behind lab gear. They expect better printing and reading methods to close that gap and widen use.
europmc-pmc3610294:
Daphne Vogel and colleagues examined the activation state of macrophages in multiple sclerosis lesions in the Journal of Neuroinflammation in 2013. Macrophages both damage tissue and support repair in MS, and their behavior depends on how they are switched on. Lab models sort them into classic inflammatory M1 cells and healing-style M2 cells.
