The team first calibrated markers on human macrophages grown each way, finding CD40 the clearest M1 badge and the mannose receptor the clearest M2 badge.

In brain tissue, M1 markers covered the microglia of normal-looking white matter and filled active, myelin-stripping lesions. M2 markers sat on fat-laden macrophages inside lesions and around blood vessels. Double staining settled the picture: about seventy percent of CD40-bearing macrophages in lesions also wore the M2 badge. Real lesion cells, the authors conclude, live between the textbook poles, mixing attack and repair programs in one cell.
europmc-pmc3690694:
Wilkinson and colleagues measured how leucine and its breakdown product HMB affect protein metabolism in human skeletal muscle. Leucine, an amino acid from food protein, is the strongest dietary trigger for building new muscle protein. The team asked whether HMB shares or extends that effect. They used tracer methods in volunteers.

Both compounds quickly reached the blood and muscle and both stimulated protein synthesis, leucine more strongly. HMB also cut muscle protein breakdown by more than half, an effect that did not depend on insulin. The authors read this as HMB driving muscle anabolism through partly different routes from leucine, combining a modest synthesis boost with a clear anti-breakdown action.
europmc-pmc3697994:
Xie reviews the TRAF family of signalling proteins, adaptors that connect tumour necrosis factor receptors to the cell's response machinery. Six mammalian TRAFs are known. Beyond linking receptors to downstream partners, most also act as ubiquitin ligases, and their pathways switch on NF-kappaB, MAP kinase, and interferon responses.

Studies of mice lacking individual TRAFs show each member has non-redundant jobs in immunity, development, tissue balance, stress responses, and bone metabolism. Xie also surveys the growing evidence tying TRAF faults to human disease, including cancers and autoimmune conditions. That evidence has renewed interest in the family as drug targets, and in tests that read TRAF pathway activity in patients.
europmc-pmc3709294:
Keniger and colleagues reviewed the evidence on what people gain from interacting with nature. Research claims benefits for body, mind, and social life, and the team asked how solid and how general that evidence is.

They found the literature lopsided. Studies cluster in Western countries at high latitudes, social scientists dominate the field, and physical health, thinking performance, and psychological wellbeing draw far more attention than social or spiritual effects. Most evidence is correlational, and almost nothing is known about which features of a setting, such as biodiversity or closeness, deliver the benefit. The authors map these gaps for a rapidly urbanizing world.
europmc-pmc3798594:
Satomi Kobayashi and eight co-authors reported a validation study in the Journal of Epidemiology in 2012 on two Japanese diet questionnaires. One is comprehensive, with 150 items; the other is brief, with 58 items and fixed portions. Both ask people to recall their usual diet. The team tested how well each ranks nutrient intakes against weighed food records.

Ninety-two women and 92 men in three areas of Japan completed sixteen days of food records and filled each questionnaire four times, once per season. Median correlations with the records, across 42 nutrients, sat near 0.5 to 0.57 for both tools, in both sexes. Mean intake estimates matched the records for only a minority of nutrients. The authors conclude both questionnaires rank people's intakes satisfactorily, even if exact levels are often off.
europmc-pmc3840294:
Sean C. Taylor, Thomas Berkelman, Geetha Yadav, and Matt Hammond set out a lab method in Molecular Biotechnology in 2013. Western blotting finds and sizes proteins in a mix, a daily task in life science labs. Using it to count proteins with trust has long been doubted.

Each step, from gel to glow-based readout, can skew the count. The authors lay out a fixed method with standard checks at each stage, plus newer reagents and readers. Their aim is that labs can show real gaps in protein levels with sound statistics, not just darker bands. The paper serves as a practical guide for anyone who needs blot numbers that hold up under review, rather than rough yes-or-no reads.
europmc-pmc3855694:
Epigenome tools are the offering of Qiang Song and co-authors in PLoS One in 2013. DNA methylation is a chemical mark that helps control gene use. New sequencing reads those marks base by base across whole genomes, and public data sets now pile up fast.

The team built two linked resources. MethPipe is a software path that turns raw reads into mark maps and pulls out key features at low and high levels. MethBase is a store of public mark maps, each with notes, ready for side-by-side checks. Together they let a lab compare its own maps with the public stock in a few steps. The authors aim to speed shared, cross-study work in a fast-growing field.
europmc-pmc3882494:
Venkatraman Chandra-Mouli, Donna R. McCarraher, Sharon J. Phillips, Nancy E. Williamson, and Gwyn Hainsworth review teen contraception in Reproductive Health, with the record dated 2014. In low- and middle-income countries, many teens face early pregnancy, unsafe abortion, and infections from unprotected sex. Access to contraception is a key shield.

Teens, married and single alike, need contraception, yet they hit steep barriers. Laws, clinic rules, cost, shame, and poor information all block use, and correct steady use is harder still. The review gathers study proof and program lessons on what lifts access. School and community education, youth-friendly services, and clear laws all help. The authors frame contraception as one part of a wider teen health strategy.
europmc-pmc3909994:
Robin L. Carhart-Harris, Robert Leech, and six colleagues set out a theory of consciousness in Frontiers in Human Neuroscience in 2014, built around the idea of entropy, a measure of disorder in a system. Brain scans taken under psilocybin, a classic psychedelic drug, anchor the argument. The authors treat the psychedelic state as an early, primary form of consciousness.

In primary states, they argue, brain activity grows richer and less ordered, hovering near a tipping point between order and disorder. Normal waking thought, by contrast, keeps entropy low, which gives it focus, self-awareness, and a firm grip on reality. Entry into a primary state is tied to a breakdown of the usual organized activity in the brain's default-mode network. The theory can be tested in sleep, early psychosis, and anesthesia.
europmc-pmc3981094:
George F. G. Allen and three colleagues report a new trigger for mitophagy in EMBO Reports in 2013. Mitophagy is the cell's way of eating its own worn mitochondria. The team built a screening test for it. Mitochondria carried a tag that changes color in the recycling compartment. Screening compounds with that test surfaced a surprise family. Iron chelators, which lock iron away, triggered strong mitophagy.

The iron-loss route has its own rules. It needs the cell to run on sugar fermentation. It does not need PINK1 or Parkin at all. Those two proteins run the best-known mitophagy route. That route is the one broken in some Parkinson's cases. The new route worked in normal human skin cells. It also worked in cells from a Parkinson's patient with mutant Parkin. The authors suggest switching it on could help diseases where clearing bad mitochondria is the goal.
europmc-pmc4009794:
Johanna Haiko and Benita Westerlund-Wikström review the bacterial flagellum as a tool for sticking and invasion, in Biology in 2013. The flagellum is a whip-like tail built from more than twenty proteins. Its classic job is swimming: the tail spins and drives the cell. The tail's main protein also alerts the host immune system.

Work gathered here shows the tail doubles as a grip tool. Whole tails help bacteria cling to and enter host cells. In germs such as E. coli and Pseudomonas, the tail protein or its cap protein does the gripping. One study showed the tail protein of a harmful E. coli type helping it slip into cells through fat rafts in the cell skin. Grip often needs motion first, since the tail brings the cell to the surface. The authors argue the tail should count as a true disease factor, not just a motor.
europmc-pmc4030994:
Markus J. Tamás, Sandeep K. Sharma, Sebastian Ibstedt, Therese Jacobson, and Philipp Christen review how heavy metals wreck protein folding, in Biomolecules in 2014. Metals such as arsenic, cadmium, mercury, and lead are plainly toxic, but the molecular route was long unclear. Proteins were known targets, yet one mode of attack drew notice only lately.

Loose, still-folding proteins expose many grip points that metals can latch onto in stable complexes. Folded proteins, with set shapes, offer far fewer. Metals thus jam the folding of new proteins, block the refolding of damaged ones, and drive clumping inside living cells. Clumps strain the cell's quality control systems and can kill the cell. The review covers how cells fight back with chaperone helpers and disposal systems. Long exposure tracks with folding diseases of the brain.
europmc-pmc4038494:
Timothy P. Robinson and ten colleagues rebuild the world maps of farm animal density, in PLoS ONE in 2014. Livestock underpins the food and income of close to a billion people. Head counts run to well over a billion cattle, close to two billion sheep and goats, about a billion pigs, and nearly twenty billion chickens.

An earlier global database, from 2007, mapped densities on cells of about five kilometres. The new work gathers fresher, finer local statistics and a richer set of predictor maps. Its model places animals at one-kilometre detail and checks its own accuracy more openly. Full new maps cover cattle, pigs, and chickens, with a partial map for ducks. The layers are released free through the Livestock Geo-Wiki. Uses range from disease studies to waste, emissions, and land-use planning.
europmc-pmc4102394:
Mahmoud Ghandi, Dongwon Lee, Morteza Mohammad-Noori, and Michael A. Beer improved computer prediction of DNA regulatory elements by allowing gaps in short sequence words. Their methods paper appeared in PLoS Computational Biology in 2014. Models often count k-mers, DNA words of fixed length, but longer words become too rare to count reliably.

Gapped k-mers let some positions vary, so longer patterns stay measurable. The team built a classifier, gkm-SVM, plus a robust way to estimate word frequencies and a fast tree structure for large genome-wide jobs. Against their earlier tool and rival approaches, the new method predicted working regulatory elements and tissue-specific enhancers far more accurately, at times doubling precision. It also won consistently on human ENCODE binding data sets.
europmc-pmc4105594:
Concepció Violan, Jose M. Valderas, and colleagues reviewed observational studies of multimorbidity, living with several long-term conditions at once, in primary care. Their systematic review appeared in PLoS ONE in 2014. Multimorbidity is a major concern for family medicine, yet basic evidence on its scale and patterns was scarce.

Thirty-nine publications covering more than seventy million patients in twelve countries met their criteria. Studies counted anywhere from five to over three hundred conditions, so reported prevalence ranged wildly, from about thirteen to ninety-five percent. Every study linked multimorbidity with older age, and lower social position and sex also mattered. The commonest conditions shaped the clusters seen. The authors urge standard definitions and better-designed studies to guide care.
europmc-pmc4120194:
Martin A. Katzman and a Canada-wide group of experts wrote care guides for fear ills, stress after trauma, and fixed thought-and-act ills. The guides came out in BMC Psychiatry in 2014. Fear ills are some of the most common ills of the mind. Up to a third of people meet one in their life, yet many cases are missed and go without care.

The group built the advice by joint views, with a search of past work from 1980 to 2012. Each cure, by talk or by drug, was scored for strength of proof. A care grade then weighed gains against side effects. Ten parts cover how to spot and treat the ills, seven named ones, and care for groups such as young people. The aim is the best care in day-to-day work.
europmc-pmc4120694:
Ricardo Cabezas, George E. Barreto, and colleagues reviewed how astrocytes, star-shaped support cells, modulate the blood-brain barrier, with a focus on Parkinson's disease. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Cellular Neuroscience in 2014. The barrier tightly controls what passes between blood and brain, keeping the brain's chemistry stable.

Astrocytes help build and maintain the barrier by releasing factors that tighten the seals between vessel cells. In disorders from stroke and trauma to Alzheimer's and Parkinson's, the barrier breaks down and astrocytes turn reactive, worsening the leak and endangering neurons. In Parkinson's, a leaky barrier may let harmful proteins and reactive species build up. The authors argue that protecting the barrier and its supporting unit could slow the disease.
europmc-pmc4193194:
Lissette C. Sánchez-Aranguren, Marcos Lopez, and two co-authors reviewed oxidative stress in preeclampsia in Frontiers in Physiology in 2014. Preeclampsia is a dangerous pregnancy disorder marked by high blood pressure and protein in the urine from week 20 on. It affects 5 to 10 percent of pregnancies and can kill mother and baby.

The review ties the disorder to the lining of the blood vessels, which works badly in these patients. Poor placenta growth leaves tissue short of oxygen, and the strain releases reactive oxygen species that injure vessel walls. Obesity, insulin resistance, and high blood fats feed the same fire. Trials giving antioxidant vitamins to prevent the disease have largely disappointed. The authors set out what that failure teaches about timing and targets.
europmc-pmc4243194:
Tanya Abramsky, Charlotte Watts, and ten co-authors reported a violence prevention trial in Kampala in BMC Medicine in 2014. The SASA! program mobilizes whole communities to question violence against women and the norms that excuse it, aiming also to cut HIV risk. Its trial, run from 2007 to 2012, randomized eight communities, four to the program and four as controls.

Surveys of adults aged 18 to 49 before and four years after launch found deep norm shifts. Acceptance of partner violence fell sharply among women and men in program communities, and belief that a woman may refuse sex rose. Women's reported experience of physical partner violence in the past year ran 52 percent lower, though that estimate carried wide uncertainty. The authors present SASA! as proof that community work can move both attitudes and behaviour.
europmc-pmc4270294:
Simone Gupta leads a team that read the gene activity of postmortem brain tissue from people with autism and from matched controls. Their study appeared in Nature Communications in 2014. Gene hunting in autism had found great variety, so the team looked instead for shared patterns in which genes are turned up or down.

Using RNA sequencing, they found two linked patterns. A set of genes tied to microglia, the brain's immune cells, ran in step with a set of genes tied to nerve cell activity, and both ran off course in autism. The work points to an interplay between immune response and nerve signaling as a core feature of the disorder.
europmc-pmc4292994:
Dan Knights and a large group of collaborators examined how a patient's own genes shape gut microbes in inflammatory bowel disease. Their study appeared in Genome Medicine in 2014. Genes and microbes each link to the disease on their own, but risk models that treat them apart leave much unexplained.

The team paired genome data with microbe profiles read from gut samples across large patient groups. Certain gene variants tracked with shifts in specific bacterial groups, and the combined picture fit disease patterns better than either side alone. Transplant work cited in the paper shows microbe shifts born from genes can themselves stir gut inflammation. The study sets up gene-microbe interplay as a core part of bowel disease.
europmc-pmc4304694:
Alan Brown, Fei Long, Robert A Nicholls, Jaan Toots, Paul Emsley, and Garib Murshudov describe new tools for building atomic models into cryo-electron microscopy maps. Their paper appeared in Acta Crystallographica Section D in 2015. Cryo-EM had begun delivering near atomic views of large cell machines, but fitting and refining a model inside those maps lagged behind.

The tools extend the Coot and REFMAC programs long used in crystallography. They handle the quirks of EM maps, including local resolution changes and flexible fitting of model parts, with restraint libraries to keep chemistry sane. The paper is a practical account for structural biologists moving into the cryo-EM era, written by the teams behind the software.
europmc-pmc4305394:
Christopher S Ahn and Christian M Metallo argue that mitochondria, far from being shut down in cancer, act as factories that feed tumor growth. Their review appeared in Cancer and Metabolism in 2015. Many cancer cells favor fast sugar breakdown, which led to an old assumption that their mitochondria were broken or idle.

In fact tumors keep working mitochondria and often push more material through them. The organelles supply the building blocks for fats, amino acids, and nucleotides that dividing cells need in bulk. Blocking these supply lines slows some tumors in tests, which makes mitochondrial metabolism a live drug target. The review gathers the evidence pathway by pathway.
europmc-pmc4382694:
Xunyu Lu and Chuan Zhao built a cheap electrode that splits water efficiently, in Nature Communications in 2015. Making hydrogen by electrolysis needs an oxygen-making electrode that works hard without costly metals. The best known catalysts use iridium or ruthenium oxides, which are rare and pricey. The pair deposited a porous nickel-iron coating, as thin sheets full of tiny holes, directly onto nickel foam, a spongy metal support, using an electric plating method.

In alkaline solution the electrode started making oxygen at a low extra voltage of 200 millivolts. It delivered very high currents, 500 and 1,000 milliamps per square centimeter, at only slightly higher voltages. It also held up through long runs at high current. The authors present it as the most efficient oxygen electrode of its kind reported then, suited to industrial water splitting.
europmc-pmc4392294:
Paul Weimer wrote a solo review on the microbes of the rumen in Frontiers in Microbiology in 2015. The rumen, the first stomach chamber of cattle and sheep, hosts hundreds of bacterial and archaeal species plus fungi and protozoa that ferment plant fiber for the animal. A core set dominated by two bacterial phyla recurs across animals. Weimer uses the rumen to show two ecological traits: redundancy, where many species share jobs, and resilience, the power to recover after disturbance.

Those traits keep digestion steady across diets, but they frustrate attempts to engineer the rumen for better fiber use or lower methane output. Added probiotic strains usually fail to establish against well-adapted residents. Exceptions succeed only when the newcomer fills an empty niche, such as bacteria that detoxify plant poisons. Each animal's community is also partly its own, complicating one-size fixes.
europmc-pmc4396394:
Naoomi Tominaga and co-authors found that breast cancer cells bound for the brain first soften its barrier, in Nature Communications in 2015. Brain metastasis kills many breast cancer patients, and crossing the blood-brain barrier is its key step. Cancer cells release extracellular vesicles, tiny parcels carrying proteins and microRNAs, to signal other cells. The team showed these vesicles from brain-seeking cancer cells break down the barrier in test systems, and they pinned the effect on one microRNA, miR-181c.

That microRNA lowers a target gene, PDPK1, which misplaces actin, the cell's scaffolding protein, loosening the barrier's tight structure. Injected vesicles were preferentially taken up by the brain in mice and promoted brain metastasis of breast cancer cells. The route suggests both a warning signal in blood and a possible point to block spread.
europmc-pmc4421794:
Pierre Barbier de Reuille and a large international team introduced MorphoGraphX in eLife in 2015, a software platform for measuring how living forms take shape. Growth blends gene activity, cell division, and physical force, but shape change is hard to measure. Flat views distort curved organs, while full three-dimensional analysis is slow and costly.

MorphoGraphX works directly on curved surface images drawn from three-dimensional data. It can outline cells, track cell lines over time, and measure glowing gene signals on those surfaces. Its modular build lets users add existing tools or write new ones. Measured cell shapes can also be exported as starting points for computer models of growth, linking form, genes, and mechanics.
europmc-pmc4453294:
Chun-yu Li and seven co-authors compared human mesenchymal stem cells from bone marrow and from fat tissue in Stem Cell Research and Therapy in 2015. These stem cells are candidates for cell therapy. For clinical use they must be grown in large numbers without animal products, and platelet extract is one serum substitute. The two sources had not been compared under those conditions.

Grown side by side in platelet extract medium, both cell types were checked for shape and surface markers. The team also checked colony formation, growth rate, and ability to turn into bone, fat, and cartilage lineages. Proteins they release and effects on immune cells were measured too. The head-to-head design shows which traits the source tissue fixes and which the growth medium controls. Such comparisons help therapy makers choose a source and prove their product stays consistent across batches.
europmc-pmc4476094:
Xiaoying Zhou, Chengqiang Yin, Yini Dang, Feng Ye, and Guoxin Zhang tested a blood marker for stomach cancer in Scientific Reports in 2015. Long non-coding RNAs, RNA molecules that regulate genes without making proteins, have shown promise for early cancer detection. The team reasoned that cancer-linked RNAs might leak into the blood as tumors begin, where a simple blood draw could catch them.

From eight candidate RNAs, one called H19 stood out in paired tissue and blood tests. In a larger set of patients and healthy controls, blood H19 was much higher in gastric cancer patients, and a standard accuracy analysis rated it a good discriminator, including for early-stage disease. Levels fell after surgery to remove the tumor. The authors propose plasma H19 as a potential non-invasive aid for diagnosing gastric cancer, pending wider validation.
europmc-pmc4489294:
Damian Smedley and a very large community of co-authors described the BioMart community portal in Nucleic Acids Research in 2015. Biological databases had multiplied worldwide, each with its own interface, forcing researchers to learn many systems to gather data. BioMart offers one interface over many independent databases, which stay hosted and funded by their own organizations rather than moving into a single center.

The portal gives access to hundreds of data sets spanning genomics, proteomics, model organisms, cancer, and classification systems, contributed by dozens of scientific organizations. New databases had joined since earlier reports, and support for analysis and visualization tools improved. A new enrichment analysis tool, which tests whether a gene list leans toward certain functions, is available both graphically and as a web service. The portal fields over a million requests a day, the authors report.
europmc-pmc4490394:
Anu-Maarit Moilanen and nine co-authors reported a new prostate cancer drug candidate, ODM-201, in Scientific Reports in 2015. Prostate cancer growth is driven by the androgen receptor, a switch turned on by male hormones. Even cancers that resist hormone removal still depend on that switch, because the receptor gene gets copied extra times or mutates to evade current drugs.

ODM-201 binds the receptor tightly and fully blocks it. That includes the mutant forms that arise under treatment with the leading second-generation drugs. One of those drugs no longer works once a specific mutation appears. It stopped testosterone from moving the receptor into the cell nucleus and slowed the growth of receptor-overexpressing cancer cells in dishes and in mouse grafts. Early human trials had already suggested good antitumor activity and a favorable safety profile, the authors report.
europmc-pmc4525294:
Lingshu Wang leads a twelve-author team testing vaccine designs against MERS in Nature Communications in 2015. The MERS coronavirus causes severe lung disease, and no vaccine existed. Earlier efforts focused on one piece of the virus's spike protein, the part that grabs host cells. The team reasoned that a narrow target might miss the strongest antibody responses.

Vaccines built on the full spike DNA, or on its S1 subunit as a protein, raised strong neutralizing antibodies in mice and monkeys against several virus strains. The antibodies hit the grabbing region and other spike parts too, and blocked the virus by more than one route. Vaccinated rhesus macaques were protected from pneumonia on scans after challenge, supporting full-spike designs.
europmc-pmc4575194:
Xue-yan Zheng leads a ten-author team pooling studies on dirty air and asthma attacks, in PLoS ONE in 2015. Air pollution is a known trigger of asthma flare-ups, but the size of the risk from each pollutant had never been fully pinned down. The team searched the literature without language limits for time-series studies of asthma emergency visits and hospital admissions.

Of 246 studies screened, 87 fed the analysis. Short-term rises in ozone, carbon monoxide, nitrogen dioxide, sulfur dioxide, and both coarse and fine particles each went with significantly more asthma emergencies and admissions. Ozone, for one, raised risk by about 0.9% per step in exposure. Sensitivity and subgroup checks tested the stability of the pooled risks.
europmc-pmc4579394:
Jie Huang leads a twelve-author team sharpening genetic guesswork with a British reference panel, in Nature Communications in 2015. Genome studies type only some DNA positions. The rest are imputed, meaning inferred from reference genomes. Rare variants are the hardest to infer, and poor references leave them blurry.

The UK10K project sequenced the genomes of 3,781 British people at shallow depth. It caught variation present in as few as one person in a thousand. Realigning those genomes after the first calls raised accuracy sharply. Merging the panel with the 1000 Genomes panel helped further. The gains covered rare variants in both British and Italian samples. A fast approximation keeps the method quick without losing that accuracy.
europmc-pmc4639894:
A 2015 study by Halu Fei and colleagues deals with a hydrogen-making catalyst built from single cobalt atoms on nitrogen-doped graphene. Splitting water for hydrogen fuel usually needs platinum, which is scarce and costly. Their catalyst spreads tiny amounts of cobalt as individual atoms across a carbon sheet. The work appeared in Nature Communications.

The catalyst worked in water with very low extra voltage, about thirty millivolts, and stayed robust. Measurements pointed to cobalt atoms held by nitrogen as the active sites. Using single atoms wastes almost no metal, since every atom can take part. The authors propose this atomic design as a general route to extremely efficient catalysts from cheap, abundant elements for clean energy devices.
europmc-pmc4653394:
Simon G. Coetzee, Gert A. Coetzee, and Dennis J. Hazelett presented a 2015 tool called motifbreakR for judging how a DNA variant affects transcription factor binding sites. Genome studies find many risk variants in non-coding DNA, where their effect is hard to read. A variant inside a binding motif may strengthen or weaken protein binding. The paper appeared in Bioinformatics.

The R package scores the DNA around any variant against motif libraries from public sources, using a choice of algorithms. It reports how much binding information one gene copy gains or loses versus the other. It works on novel variants and on any genome packaged in Bioconductor. For researchers sorting through genome-wide association hits, motifbreakR offers a fast first test of whether a variant plausibly disrupts gene regulation.
europmc-pmc4702794:
Michael Kuhn, Ivica Letunic, Lars Juhl Jensen, and Peer Bork updated the SIDER database of drug side effects in Nucleic Acids Research in 2016. Side effects burden patients and stall drug development, yet records of them sit scattered in package inserts. SIDER pulls those records into one searchable picture linking drugs, their targets, and their harms. Release four, covered here, grew the collection by forty percent over the previous version.

The database now holds 1,430 drugs, 5,880 side effects, and over 140,000 drug-effect pairs. For many pairs, the team extracted how often the effect occurs, and for some, how that rate compares with placebo. A companion set of drug indications, mined from the same inserts by language software, helps weed out terms that name the treated disease rather than a true side effect. The resource feeds research into why drugs harm as well as heal.
europmc-pmc4737894:
Vale, Burdett, Rydzewska, and their STOpCaP collaborators gather every randomised trial adding docetaxel chemotherapy or bisphosphonates to standard care in hormone-sensitive prostate cancer. They pool survival results as the big trials report. Five docetaxel trials cover metastatic disease.

In metastatic disease, adding docetaxel improves survival, with a hazard ratio of 0.77 that translates to about nine percentage points more men alive at four years, and it delays treatment failure as well. In locally advanced disease without spread, three trials show no survival benefit so far, though failure-free survival improves. The adaptive framework lets the pooled answer update as further trial results arrive.
europmc-pmc4740994:
Onakpoya, Heneghan, and Aronson systematically gather every medicinal product withdrawn from the market over suspected adverse reactions, a removal history never before mapped in full. They find 462 products withdrawn between 1953 and 2013, most often because of liver toxicity.

The evidence behind most withdrawals is thin: anecdotal reports underpin 72 percent of cases. Only 43 products, about nine percent, were withdrawn worldwide, while 39 percent disappeared in a single country, and withdrawals were least likely in Africa. The median gap between the first reported reaction and withdrawal was six years. It did not shrink over time, which the authors read as a case for better coordination between regulators.
europmc-pmc4783894:
Magdalena Działo leads seven authors in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences in 2016 on plant phenolics for skin troubles. Phenolics are plant chemicals that guard the plant itself, and they fight oxidation, swelling, and germs in human tissue too. Because they come from nature and carry low toxicity, they draw interest as gentle skin treatments.

The review gathers reports on single phenolics and on plant extracts for aging skin, wounds, burns, acne, and skin cancer. It sets out how each compound is thought to act, from soaking up damaging oxygen forms to calming immune overreaction. The authors note the gap between lab promise and clinic proof, and call for trials that test dose and delivery through the skin's tough outer layer.
europmc-pmc4815194:
Alexander Peltzer and six co-authors introduce a software pipeline for ancient DNA in Genome Biology in 2016. Rebuilding a genome from an old bone or tooth is a chain of fussy steps. Ancient DNA is scarce. It is broken into short bits. It is also chemically scarred. Standard genome tools misread it unless tuned with care.

Their pipeline, EAGER, strings the whole chain into one package. It cleans reads and places them on a reference genome. It checks the damage pattern that proves age. It scores quality. It calls gene variants with filters fit for ancient damage. The pipeline wraps proven tools for each step. It adds new ones shaped for old samples. The authors offer it as a single, easy entry point for labs.
europmc-pmc4896994:
Christian P. Klingenberg, writing solo, compared concepts of allometry in geometric morphometrics in 2016. Allometry means size-linked shape change, a core idea in evolution and development studies. Two schools frame it unlike each other. The Gould-Mosimann school treats allometry as shape shifting with size, measured by regressing shape measures on a size gauge.

The Huxley-Jolicoeur school treats it as joint change among traits that each carry size, read from the first main axis of variation. Klingenberg's review is the first full side-by-side of methods in this frame, covering the shape spaces each method assumes and how size correction should run. The choice of school shapes results, so the map helps researchers pick with open eyes.
europmc-pmc4915494:
Markus Barth and co-authors reviewed simultaneous multislice imaging in 2016, a method that speeds magnetic resonance scans. The trick excites several slices at once and unmixes them with parallel reconstruction. Speed gain equals the number of slices taken together, with only a small signal cost, unlike in-plane speedups.

Full gain holds at the fixed echo times that many brain scan types require. Some versions also cut the radio energy soaked into tissue. Faster scans mean less motion blur, more subjects per day, and finer time detail in brain activity studies. The review covers design choices, reconstruction routes, and artifacts, a field guide as the method moves into routine scanners.
europmc-pmc4916494:
Hemasri Akkiraju and Anja Nohe reviewed the role of chondrocytes in cartilage in 2015, from joint building to osteoarthritis and repair. Chondrocytes are the cells that build and tend cartilage, the smooth cap that spreads load across joints. They run matrix turnover, the steady rebuild that keeps the tissue sound. When their balance fails, osteoarthritis follows.

In disease, the cells swell into a hypertrophic state and release matrix-chewing enzymes, among them MMPs and ADAMTS types. Limb-building signal paths reawaken and drive the damage, though their control is still being mapped. Stem cell routes for regrowth get a closing survey. Saving the caretaker cell is the shortest path to saving the joint.
europmc-pmc4961794:
Lei Li leads a team showing that SIRT7, a member of the sirtuin enzyme family, removes succinyl tags from histones. Their study appeared in Nature Communications in 2016. Sirtuins are known as deacetylases, enzymes that strip acetyl tags using NAD+. What SIRT7 itself does was unclear. The team found it is drawn to DNA double strand breaks by the damage sensor PARP1. There it strips a succinyl tag from histone H3 at one site, lysine 122.

That edit helps chromatin, the packed form of DNA, condense around the break, which aids repair. Cells lacking SIRT7 packed chromatin poorly after damage and died more easily under genotoxic stress, stress that harms DNA. The authors cast SIRT7 as a histone desuccinylase, a new activity for the family. They argue the finding links epigenetic editing, genome stability, and cell survival into one pathway.
europmc-pmc5069794:
Carl R. May, Mark Johnson, and Tracy Finch tackle the problem of context in implementation science in Implementation Science in 2016. Trials often strip away real-world settings to isolate an intervention, yet those settings are exactly where a new practice must survive. Building on their Normalisation Process Theory, the authors offer an ecological model of how people and contexts shape each other while a practice is put in place and spread.

Implementation, in their account, runs through resource mobilisation, collective action, and constant negotiation with context, and these mechanisms adapt as they go. Outcomes hinge on how flexible the intervention's parts are, how much discretion participants have, and how elastic the context proves. Feedback loops and practical compromise, in this view, are the machinery of self-organisation, not noise. The model also warns that rigid trial designs may misjudge interventions built for dynamic settings, a point they plan to develop.
europmc-pmc5113094:
Chen-Zi Zhang, Xing-Qun Cheng, Ji-Yao Li, Ping Zhang, Ping Yi, Xin Xu, and Xue-Dong Zhou reviewed saliva as a diagnostic fluid in the International Journal of Oral Science in 2016. Saliva cleans and protects the mouth and aids digestion, and because blood components seep into it, it carries many of the same markers as blood.

The review gathers work on saliva tests for mouth diseases such as tooth decay and gum disease, and for wider conditions including cancer and diabetes. Useful signals range from DNA, RNA, and protein shifts to changes in the mouth's microbe mix. Because saliva is painless and safe to collect, the authors argue it could replace blood in early screening and support more personal medical care.
europmc-pmc5256994:
Inas Helwa and eleven colleagues compared methods for isolating exosomes from blood serum in PLoS ONE in 2017. Exosomes are tiny cell-made bubbles that carry signals between cells and may serve as disease biomarkers, but pulling them out cleanly and in good quantity is hard. The team set three commercial kits against the standard lab method, differential ultracentrifugation, a long high-speed spin.

Tests ran across starting volumes from five milliliters down to fifty microliters, mimicking scarce clinical samples. All four methods produced particles in the expected exosome size range. The kits, though, yielded far more material than the spin method at most volumes, by eighty to three hundred fold. Marker proteins CD63 and CD9 were confirmed in every preparation, and the RNA recovered was high quality under all methods, with two test RNAs at similar levels. The kits stand as practical substitutes, the authors conclude.
europmc-pmc5286794:
Tan Boon Toh, Jhin Jieh Lim, and Edward Kai-Hua Chow reviewed epigenetics in cancer stem cells in Molecular Cancer in 2017. Many tumours seem to grow from a small set of cancer stem cells, self-renewing cells that seed the tumour and often survive treatment. Epigenetic controls, the chemical marks and packaging that set gene activity without changing the DNA code, are central to how normal stem cells choose their fate.

When those controls go wrong, they can help turn a normal stem cell cancerous. They strip its ability to mature while keeping its self-renewal, and they help explain why treatment response varies between patients. A resistant minority in cancers of skin, stomach, colon, and lung has been traced to faulty epigenetic modifiers. The review tours the main pathways, then covers the epigenetic drugs now in trials that aim squarely at the stem cell pool.
europmc-pmc5290294:
Sharon Swee-Lin Tan and Nadee Goonawardene reviewed how patients' internet health searching affects their relationship with doctors, in the Journal of Medical Internet Research in 2017. As patients arrive at appointments carrying online findings, clinicians worry about trust and authority. The authors searched PubMed and key journals covering 2000 to 2015 for empirical studies of the question.

Eighteen articles met the review's quality bar. They mapped the barriers, helpers, and personal factors that shape whether patients raise their online findings in consultations, and the different ways patients choose to reveal them. The same searching can strain or strengthen the relationship: outcomes hinge on whether the patient discusses the material openly and on the strength of the prior relationship. Done well, sharing tends to improve the partnership. The authors argue that traditional models of doctor-patient communication must adapt to patients who now expect a say in decisions.
europmc-pmc5355494:
Marek Wieczorek and co-authors reviewed how display proteins bend and shift in Frontiers in Immunology in 2017. Cells show bits of germs on surface platforms called MHC proteins. Killer T cells read those displays and, on a match, grow and attack. Two classes of platform split the work: one shows bits from inside the cell, the other from matter the cell has swallowed.

The groove that holds each bit varies by gene variant, which shapes what can be shown. Helper editors in each class swap weak bits for strong ones, a step called peptide editing. Why some variants take editing more than others was not clear. Fresh work points to fleeting mid-states of the bending protein as the key. That flex may drive which bits win the show, and helps explain dominance of some responses and some autoimmune ills.
europmc-pmc5364694:
Quan Nha Hong, Pierre Pluye, Mathieu Bujold, and Maggy Wassef mapped designs for mixed proof reviews in Systematic Reviews in 2017. Some questions need both number data and story data at once. Reviews that join the two have grown in favor, but no one had charted their designs across a large sample, and terms for the steps clash from paper to paper.

They gathered more than four hundred and fifty such reviews from six databases. Most hid how the two proof types were merged, and names for like steps varied wildly. Two broad designs stood out. In a convergent design, both sets are worked in parallel and joined at the end. In a sequential design, one set feeds and shapes the next. The team splits the first design into three sub-forms and offers a shared tongue and clear steps for reporting such work.
europmc-pmc5423694:
Mordecai and co-authors model how temperature sets the reach of three mosquito-borne viruses. Their research article appeared in PLoS Neglected Tropical Diseases. The viruses are Zika, dengue, and chikungunya. Aedes mosquitoes carry all three. Heat shapes how fast mosquitoes breed, bite, and pass on infection. The team built models from those basic traits. They then checked the models against real human case data.

Both models and case data point to one band. Transmission runs from about 18 to 34 degrees Celsius. It peaks between 26 and 29 degrees. Temperature stayed a strong predictor after the team adjusted for population and wealth factors. Their maps show long seasons in the tropics. Temperate zones get at most three months of risk per year. Such short windows make major outbreaks less likely there. The maps can guide mosquito control and public warnings.
europmc-pmc545594:
Yeo and co-authors map how alternative splicing varies across human tissues. Their computational study appeared in Genome Biology. Alternative splicing lets one gene yield many proteins. Between a third and two-thirds of human genes use it. Open questions framed the work. Which tissues splice the most? Do tissues favor different splicing types? What factors explain the patterns? The team aligned expressed sequence tags to the genome. The tags came from about two dozen tissues.

Three tissues stood out for heavy splicing. Brain, testis, and liver topped the list. Tissues also differed in splicing style. Use of alternative 5-prime versus 3-prime sites varied sharply. Some tissues expressed distinctive isoform spectra. The analysis flagged candidate cis-acting elements. Those DNA-adjacent signals likely guide tissue-specific choices. Candidate trans-acting factors emerged as well. Known families include SR proteins and hnRNP proteins. Tissue specialists like CELF and NOVA also feature.
europmc-pmc5491494:
Afroz and co-authors report a protein study in Nature Communications on TDP-43. TDP-43 is an RNA-binding protein found in nerve cells. Clumps of it mark neurons in ALS and frontotemporal dementia. How the healthy protein avoids clumping was unclear. The team studied its normal form in mouse and human brain tissue.

Healthy TDP-43 joins into loose chains called oligomers, they find. A crystal structure shows how the chain links head to tail. This layout keeps the sticky tail ends of each unit apart. Breaking the chains stopped the protein from regulating RNA splicing. Steadying the chains may offer a treatment route, they suggest.
europmc-pmc5491694:
Omata and co-authors present updated clinical guidelines in Hepatology International on liver cancer care. Hepatocellular carcinoma makes up over 90 percent of liver cancers. Most cases worldwide occur in the Asia-Pacific region. Hepatitis B and C infections cause about 80 percent of cases. The guidelines come from the Asia-Pacific liver association's expert panel.

This update revises the panel's earlier guidance. Advice is graded by the strength of its evidence. Topics run from risk factors and screening to treatment choices. Cirrhosis stands out as the single biggest risk factor. The authors aim for advice that fits the region's varied medical settings.
europmc-pmc5499094:
Williamson and co-authors present a handbook in Trials from the COMET Initiative. Clinical trials often pick outcomes with too little care. Mismatched outcomes block fair comparison between treatments. A core outcome set fixes a shared minimum for one disease area. Every trial then reports at least those outcomes.

The handbook guides each stage of building such a set. A four-step process anchors the advice. It also covers putting sets into practice and keeping them current. Patients and the public count as key voices in the choices. The authors plan updates as fresh research appears.
europmc-pmc5537194:
Li and co-authors report a population cohort study in The Lancet on bleeding risks from long-term antiplatelet treatment. Patients take these drugs for life after strokes and heart attacks. Trial data came mostly from patients under 75. Bleeding danger at older ages was poorly measured. The Oxford Vascular Study followed 3,166 patients for up to ten years.

Major bleeding risk climbed steeply with age, they report. Patients over 75 faced triple the major bleed risk of younger ones. Gut bleeds in that group were usually disabling or fatal. Stomach-protecting PPI drugs cut such bleeds sharply. Only 25 patients over 85 need co-prescription to prevent one bad bleed in five years.
europmc-pmc5681994:
Suryavanshi and Kulkarni present a review in Frontiers in Pharmacology. It frames NF-kappaB as a drug target in diabetes. The protein is a master switch for inflammation genes. Lasting high blood sugar switches it on. That switch drives cytokines, chemokines, and adhesion molecules. Overactive signaling harms blood vessels in several ways. It promotes cell death and vessel wall calcification too. These steps end in endothelial dysfunction.

The review maps the protein family and its two activation routes. It traces roles in kidney, nerve, eye, and heart damage. Natural and synthetic blockers are then surveyed. Recent animal and clinical studies are cited as support. Blocking this pathway is pitched as a fresh treatment route.
europmc-pmc5716994:
Duvallet and co-authors carry out a meta-analysis of gut microbiome studies across ten diseases. Single studies often disagree, and varied methods make them hard to compare. The authors built a shared database so the same tests could be run on all studies.

Their database holds 28 case-control studies with raw data and health details. Reworking each study in one standard way, they find clear patterns. Some diseases link to more than 50 genera, while most link to only 10 to 15. Some show added harmful microbes, while others show loss of helpful ones. About half the linked genera respond to more than one disease. Many reported links may thus be a shared response to poor health, not a sign of one disease.
europmc-pmc5742194:
González-Reyes and co-authors review the role of astrocytes in Alzheimer disease. Astrocytes keep the brain in balance and support nerve cells. In Alzheimer brains, their function shifts early, before other signs. Amyloid beta, the clumping protein, disrupts their signaling and calcium control.

Activated astrocytes release agents that drive inflammation in the brain. They also make reactive oxygen that harms nearby cells. A pathway through NF-κB sits at the center of these changes. The review covers plant based and other compounds tested in astrocytes. Some eased inflammation and improved thinking in models.
europmc-pmc5837994:
Ziani, Chouaib, and Thiery review how cancer-associated fibroblasts blunt the immune attack on tumors. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Immunology. These activated fibroblasts fill the stroma around cancer cells. They already had blame for growth, spread, and drug resistance.

The review adds immune sabotage to the charge sheet. Fibroblasts smother killer T cells and natural killer cells. They lure in suppressor cells that calm the response. Their secretions and stiff matrix work as indirect shields too. Striking the fibroblasts, or their signals, might free immunotherapy to work. Some settings hint they can also restrain tumors, a caution for blunt attacks.
europmc-pmc5877694:
Zou and Kumar review cannabinoid receptors and the endocannabinoid system. Their article appeared in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Cannabinoids from the cannabis plant act on two receptors. CB1 is the main subtype in the central nervous system. It has drawn strong interest as a drug target. The review focuses on CB1 and brain signalling. It sums up recent breakthroughs in the field.

The authors define roles for these receptors in signal pathways. They link the system to brain and nerve disorders. Therapeutic promise is weighed against psychoactive side effects. Those effects have limited clinical use so far. Other strategies to gain benefits safely are discussed. The piece maps an ancient plant's modern science.
europmc-pmc5931794:
Araus and co-authors review how high-throughput phenotyping can lift genetic gain in crops. Their review appeared in Trends in Plant Science. Yield gains in major crops have stalled in many regions. Slow field measurement is a key bottleneck for breeding. Sensors can now score many plants fast in the field. Tools alone do not solve the problem, they argue.

Phenotyping must fit trial design and site conditions. Target environments and their main stresses need defining first. Data handling and crop models must grow with the sensors. Breeders and phenotyping experts often work apart. Bridging that gap is central to real gains. Readers get a wide plan for joined-up breeding.
europmc-pmc5936194:
Tully and Urie study the diets and budgets of labouring-class families in Glasgow. Their study appeared in the Glasgow Medical Journal. It follows earlier Glasgow dietary studies going back to 1911. Trade depression and unemployment had deepened since the prior survey. The authors wanted to see the effect on family food.

They studied twelve typical families in June and early July 1922. The group held 94 people, from small children to grown men. Eight fathers had long been out of work. Two others were dockers with shifting hours. The paper records what these families ate and what they could afford.
europmc-pmc5968394:
Koundouros and Poulogiannis review PI3K/Akt signalling and redox metabolism in cancer. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Oncology. Cancer cells rewire metabolism and produce reactive oxygen species. The PI3K/Akt pathway sits at the hub of these processes. It is among the most often faulty pathways in cancer. The authors examine how it drives oxidant production. Mitochondria and NADPH oxidases both play a part.

Reactive species can switch off phosphatases and spark tumour signals, they note. PI3K/Akt activity also helps cancer cells keep redox balance. That balance gives them a survival edge. The review closes with ways to exploit redox faults. Combination therapies may beat drug resistance in such tumours.
europmc-pmc5991294:
Cabanettes and Klopp present D-GENIES, a tool for plotting large genome alignments as interactive dot plots. Their software paper appeared in PeerJ. Dot plots compare sequence sets at a glance. They expose repeats, breaks, and inversions clearly. Older tools often cap the input sequence size. D-GENIES runs alignments with minimap2 under the hood. It works as both standalone and web software.

Users can sort query sequences along the reference. They can zoom into the plot for detail. Image, alignment, and sequence files can be downloaded. The package is open source under the GPL. A public test server is provided.
europmc-pmc5992594:
Chung and co-authors show that niche-driven BMP/SMAD signalling steers lung alveolar stem cell growth and fate. Their study appeared in Development. Type 2 epithelial cells act as stem cells in the alveoli. Stromal cells beside them form part of their niche. The team used organoids and lung regrowth after pneumonectomy. BMP signalling was active in both cell types at rest. It dipped after surgery, then returned during cell change.

In organoids, BMP4 blocked type 2 cell growth, they report. Blocking BMP instead favoured self-renewal over differentiation. Raising BMP pushed cells toward the type 1 fate. Constant BMP in stromal cells weakened their support role.
europmc-pmc6007394:
Parekh, Ziegenhain, Vieth, Enard, and Hellmann present zUMIs, a pipeline to process RNA sequencing data with unique molecular identifiers. Their paper appeared in GigaScience. Single-cell experiments tag reads with barcodes and molecular labels. Good pipelines must tally reads by both marks efficiently. zUMIs handles known and random barcodes alike. It collapses duplicate molecules from exon or intron reads. Missing cell labels can be recovered from read patterns.

An adaptive downsampling tool handles wildly uneven library sizes, they report. It also shows whether sequencing reached saturation. On single-nucleus data, over 35 percent of reads mapped to introns. Those reads raised gene detection and cluster clarity.
europmc-pmc6020094:
Dong and co-authors introduce a web platform called ADMETlab. Their article appeared in the Journal of Cheminformatics in 2018. ADMET covers how a chemical is absorbed and spread. It also covers breakdown, removal, and toxicity. Poor ADMET traits often sink new drugs late.

The platform rests on a database of 288,967 entries. Four modules offer six drug-likeness checks. Users can predict 31 ADMET endpoints for a chemical. They can also run a full systematic evaluation. A search tool finds similar compounds in the database. The site is free to use. Readers get a guide to screening drug candidates early, before costly lab work.
europmc-pmc6061794:
De Coster and co-authors present NanoPack, tools for long-read sequencing data. Their software note appeared in Bioinformatics. New machines from Oxford Nanopore and Pacific Biosciences read very long DNA stretches. Those reads trade accuracy for length. Older quality tools were built for short reads.

NanoPack fills that gap with Python scripts. NanoStat sums up run statistics. NanoPlot and NanoComp draw quality graphs and comparisons. The tools run as commands, a graphic interface, or a web service. The code is free under an open license. Readers get practical help for checking long-read data quality.
europmc-pmc6061994:
Seth and co-authors present OpenSim, software for simulating body movement. Their article appeared in PLoS Computational Biology. Movement emerges from nerves, muscles, and bones acting together. Many key forces cannot be measured in living subjects. Simulation fills those gaps.

OpenSim computes muscle forces and tendon stretch during motion. It can also predict new movements from control models. Users test surgery effects or device designs on a computer. The package is free under the Apache license. Its source code sits open on GitHub. Tutorials and a user forum support its community. Readers get a tour of a shared platform for biomechanics research.
europmc-pmc6072794:
De Vries and co-authors test how drought shakes soil microbe networks. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Grassland mesocosms supplied the test beds. Bacteria and fungi form web-like co-occurrence networks in soil. Those webs support soil function.

Drought pushed bacterial networks toward instability. Fungal networks stayed comparatively steady. Bacterial shifts also tracked soil function during recovery more closely. Drought effects on bacteria lingered after watering resumed. Changed plant cover and drier soil carried the effect forward. Readers get a warning about hidden drought damage. Soil recovery, the study shows, may lag well behind the rain.
europmc-pmc6106894:
Yang and co-authors report a research article in Molecular Cancer on a long non-coding RNA in gastric cancer. The work asks what LINC01133 does in this disease. Gastric cancer is a common cause of cancer death. The role of this RNA in it was not yet clear.

The team measured LINC01133 in 200 tumor samples and matched healthy tissue. They also raised and lowered it in cells and in mice. They report that low levels track with worse spread. LINC01133 soaks up miR-106a-3p, a small RNA. That frees the APC gene and calms the Wnt pathway. The authors say it may help predict outcomes and guide new treatment.
europmc-pmc6108594:
Napso and co-authors wrote a review in Frontiers in Physiology on the hormones the placenta releases during pregnancy. A mother must reshape her heart, lungs, immune system, and metabolism to feed a growing baby. The placenta sits between mother and fetus and helps drive those changes.

The review explains how placental hormones enter the mother's blood and tune her body systems. They also guide how oxygen and nutrients reach the baby. When this tuning fails, problems such as gestational diabetes and abnormal birth weight can follow. The authors link these hormone signals to care in pregnancy and to milk feeding after birth.
europmc-pmc6138894:
Bai and co-authors present a methods article in Journal of Cardiovascular Magnetic Resonance on automated heart scan analysis. MRI scans measure heart chamber size and pumping power well. Clinicians have long traced those scans by hand. Hand work is slow and can vary between readers.

The team trained a deep neural network on UK Biobank scans. The data held 93,500 labeled images from 4,875 people. The network outlined the heart's chambers on its own. Its scores matched expert tracing closely. Errors in volume measures were small. The authors say such tools could speed routine heart assessment and cut reader bias.
europmc-pmc6152294:
Yuan and co-authors wrote a review in Molecules on how network pharmacology can explain the synergy of traditional medicines. Many traditional prescriptions mix several herbs or other components. Their combined effect can be stronger, or less toxic, than any single part. Single-compound research, such as artemisinin, tells only part of the story.

Network pharmacology maps links among drugs, targets, and diseases in biological networks. That systems view matches the holistic outlook of traditional medicine. The review shows how the method can uncover why mixtures work. It may also guide new drug discovery from old prescriptions. The authors present it as a next paradigm for studying complex remedies.
europmc-pmc6153194:
Greenhalgh and co-authors present a realist synthesis in Journal of Patient-Reported Outcomes on patient reported outcome measures, or PROMs. PROMs are questionnaires patients fill in about their own health. The synthesis asks how and when they improve talks between patients and clinicians, and the care that follows.

The team tested two ideas. First, filling in a PROM prompts reflection, helping patients raise issues. Second, PROM scores alert clinicians to problems and prompt discussion and action. They found the form's design and the care setting shape how well this works. Clinicians were broadly supportive, though some feared forms could flatten patients' feelings. The synthesis guides better use of PROMs in daily care.
europmc-pmc6172294:
Nystoriak and Bhatnagar wrote a review in Frontiers in Cardiovascular Medicine on the cardiovascular effects and benefits of exercise. Regular physical activity is firmly linked to better heart and vessel health. Active people have lower rates of cardiovascular death. They also develop heart disease less often.

The review explains the changes behind those gains. Active individuals show lower blood pressure, better insulin sensitivity, and a healthier blood fat profile. Animal studies show exercise slows plaque build-up and raises nitric oxide, which relaxes vessels. The adapted heart beats slower at rest and grows stronger. The authors note where understanding is still thin, pointing to better exercise prescriptions as a goal.
europmc-pmc6180194:
Pati and co-authors wrote a review in Frontiers in Immunology on vaccines built on tiny particles, called nanoparticles. New forms of germs keep testing how we treat and prevent infection. Some vaccines use parts of a germ or killed germs. Live weakened vaccines can, rarely, turn harmful again in people with weak immune systems.

Vaccines based on tiny carriers offer a safer way to deliver the active parts. They can stir both antibody and cell-based defense. The review covers the main designs and how they are made. It also weighs their record against set diseases so far. The authors present this approach as a safe, flexible path to vaccines that can change as germs change.
europmc-pmc6186394:
Zhang and Weinberg wrote a review in Frontiers of Medicine on the epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition in cancer. This cell program helps embryos develop, but tumors hijack it. Depending on signals and gene circuits, cells slide along a spectrum between epithelial and mesenchymal states. Each state carries different traits.

Cells in these states can gain stem-like qualities, invasiveness, and drug resistance. They can also seed metastases in distant organs and drive relapse. A coherent map of the mechanisms is still missing. The authors stress the program's dynamic, plastic nature, since cells can move back and forth. Better understanding, they argue, could yield new therapies that lock cells in less dangerous states.
europmc-pmc6214094:
Ku and co-authors review plant hormone signals under mixed stress. Wild plants face drought, salt, heat, and germs at once. Each stress triggers its own response path. Those paths interact inside the plant. The review appeared in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences.

Calcium sensors often give the first response signal. Abscisic acid is a key stress hormone. It interacts with jasmonic acid and salicylic acid paths. Those paths help split resources between stress defence and germ defence. GTP-binding proteins carry many of these signals. The authors map where the crosstalk points sit. They argue this knowledge can help breeders. Crops that cope with mixed stress could hold yields as climate worsens.
europmc-pmc6333694:
Newson and Thiagarajan review brain wave patterns across psychiatric disorders. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Human Neuroscience. EEG records rhythms from the scalp in named bands. Bands run from slow delta to fast gamma waves. Many studies compare band power between patients and controls. The authors gathered work done at rest, eyes open or closed.

They pooled 184 studies across many disorders. Depression, ADHD, autism, and schizophrenia all featured. So did addiction, anxiety, bipolar disorder, and others. No disorder owned a unique wave pattern. Changes overlapped heavily between conditions. Variability within each disorder was also large. One pattern did recur often, though. Power rose in the slow delta and theta bands. The authors urge care in reading EEG as a diagnostic sign.
europmc-pmc6379394:
Zhu and co-authors report a research article in Nature Communications on strain in perovskite solar cells. Mixed halide perovskites absorb light very well. Yet their films are uneven, with parts that separate and strain the crystal lattice.

Using X-ray methods that probe films at set depths, the team mapped strain across the film. Strain ran in a gradient, in the plane beside the base layer. That strain bent energy bands and changed how charge carriers moved and lived. The work gives cell makers a new fault to control. Less strain may mean more stable, stronger solar cells.
europmc-pmc6416394:
Cheng and co-authors present a network method in Nature Communications for finding drug pairs. Pairs of drugs can work better and harm less than one drug alone. But the number of possible pairs is far too large to test one by one.

Their method maps drug targets and disease proteins on the human protein network. Six classes of drug-drug-disease patterns emerged from that map. Only one class matched pairs known to work in patients. In that class, both drugs hit the disease area but in separate parts of it. The rule may help screen pairs before costly trials.
europmc-pmc6492194:
Trixl and Lusser review 5-methylcytosine, m5C, the understudy of RNA modification. RNA carries over a hundred known chemical marks, and while m6A hogs the spotlight with proven jobs in processing, translation, and decay, m5C was long confined to transfer and ribosomal RNA. New mapping methods have now found it in messenger RNA too, and the field is consolidating fast.

The writers, readers, and erasers of the mark get systematic treatment. In tRNA, methylation at position C38 by Dnmt2 guards decoding accuracy; mice lacking it show developmental delays and faulty production of aspartate-rich proteins. The authors make the case that cytosine methylation is a general regulatory strategy written onto transcripts.
europmc-pmc6509194:
Carroll and co-authors report a new mobile colistin resistance gene, mcr-9. Their report appeared in mBio. Colistin is a last-resort drug for severe infections. Genes in the mcr family can move between bacteria on plasmids. That spread makes them a public health concern.

The team found mcr-9 by screening a Salmonella Typhimurium genome in silico. The strain came from a patient in Washington State in 2010. It resisted many drugs, yet it stayed susceptible to colistin. Sequence checks showed mcr-9 sits closest to mcr-3 and mcr-7. The authors argue for a full reference set of mcr genes. Such a set would help labs screen for this hidden resistance.
europmc-pmc6530194:
Johnson and co-authors study neurologic harm linked to immune checkpoint inhibitors. Their pharmacovigilance study appeared in the Journal for Immunotherapy of Cancer. These cancer drugs can trigger autoimmune side effects. Neurologic ones are rare but can be severe.

The team mined Vigibase, the WHO safety database. It held 18,518,994 adverse event reports. Of those, 48,653 involved checkpoint inhibitors. Reports rose for myasthenia gravis, encephalitis, peripheral neuropathy and meningitis. Myasthenia gravis stood out. It began early, at a median of 29 days. About 20% of cases were fatal. It often came with myocarditis and myositis. Other events began later and killed less often.
europmc-pmc6542194:
Petersen and co-authors report CDC findings on pregnancy-related deaths in the United States, writing in the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report. About 700 women die each year from causes tied to pregnancy. From 2011 to 2015 the national rate was 17.2 deaths per 100,000 live births.

The burden fell unevenly. Black women died at 42.8 per 100,000, over three times the white rate of 13.0, and American Indian and Alaska Native women at 32.5. Deaths came at every stage: during pregnancy, on the delivery day, and up to a year after birth. Heart conditions, infection and bleeding led the causes. Review panels in 13 states judged about three in five deaths preventable, and listed fixes at community, facility, patient, provider and system levels.
europmc-pmc6567594:
Zhu and Chen survey progress on paclitaxel, the yew-derived cancer drug, writing in Cellular and Molecular Biology Letters. Paclitaxel freezes the cell's internal scaffolding: it locks microtubules together so they cannot disassemble, which halts division mid-mitosis. First approved for ovarian cancer in 1992, it became a mainstay across many tumors.

Supply has always been the pinch, since bark holds so little. The review covers the workarounds in turn — cultivated Taxus plantations, a total synthesis too long for commerce, semi-synthesis from needle precursors, and engineered fungi that ferment the drug in rising yields. It also maps the biosynthetic pathway step by step. A final theme looks beyond cell killing: paclitaxel also stirs tumor immunity, opening combinations with immunotherapy.
europmc-pmc6626094:
Jones and co-authors review Raman spectroscopy from basics to frontiers. Their article appears in Nanoscale Research Letters. The Raman effect reads molecular vibrations from inelastically scattered light. It can probe chemistry without labels or contact. Plain Raman scattering is very weak, though, which limits its reach.

The review explains the physics behind the effect and its edge over infrared methods. It then walks through stronger variants of the technique. Covered methods include stimulated Raman and coherent anti-Stokes scattering. Surface- and tip-enhanced forms get full treatment as well. The authors detail setup choices that shape data quality. They also cover analysis methods for the spectra. Recent advances in sensing and imaging close the survey.
europmc-pmc6705894:
Walker and co-authors report teen vaccination rates in the United States for 2018. Their report appeared in the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report. It draws on a national survey of teens aged 13 to 17. The shots covered include those against HPV, meningococcal disease, and whooping cough.

The survey covered 18,700 teens in all parts of the country. Coverage with at least one HPV dose rose from 65.5 percent in 2017 to 68.1 percent a year later. The share fully up to date on HPV rose from 48.6 percent at the start to 51.1 percent by the end. Tdap coverage held steady at 89 percent that year. Gaps by city type and insurance status stayed in place.
europmc-pmc6727394:
Yu and co-authors review circular RNAs in cancer metabolism. Tumors rewire how they use energy to feed their growth. Proteins drive much of that rewiring, but non-coding RNAs help too. Circular RNAs are a newly noticed class of these RNAs, named for their loop shape.

By binding microRNAs or touching proteins directly, circular RNAs steer sugar, fat, and amino acid use in cancer cells. The review picks out examples tied to glycolysis, fat making and breakdown, and respiration. It also covers roles in exosomes and cancer stem cells. Their stable loop shape could make them good targets for treatments aimed at starving tumors.
europmc-pmc6817894:
Park and Chung report a study in Cell Death and Disease on a form of cell death called ferroptosis. In ferroptosis, iron builds up inside a cell and drives damage to its membranes until it dies. A drug called erastin can trigger this death. Autophagy, the cell's own recycling system, seemed to play a part, but its role was disputed.

The team showed that erastin does switch on autophagy. That recycling broke down ferritin, the cell's iron store, and raised levels of the receptor that imports iron. Cells unable to run autophagy kept less free iron and survived the drug. The authors conclude that autophagy feeds ferroptosis by freeing iron.
europmc-pmc6839794:
Vuik and co-authors report a study in Gut on colorectal cancer in young European adults. Rates of this cancer fall in people over 50, helped by screening. In younger adults the trend points the other way. Data for Europe were missing. The team pulled records from national and regional cancer registries to fill the gap.

They covered 143.7 million people aged 20 to 49 years in 20 countries, from 1990 to 2016. 187,918 young adults in that pool were diagnosed with colorectal cancer. On average, rates rose over the period, though the pattern varied by country and age band. Death rates in the youngest groups changed little. The authors call for work on the causes of the rise.
europmc-pmc6905394:
Deagle and co-authors examine a measurement problem in Molecular Ecology. DNA metabarcoding recovers food DNA from droppings or gut contents, revealing what an animal ate. Samples yield counts of sequences per food type. What those counts mean is disputed. Many researchers trust only presence-or-absence data, calling it the safer, more conservative choice.

Sequence recovery is biased: some foods amplify better than others, so counts can mislead. The authors explore real dietary datasets to see how badly, and when relative counts still track the true diet. Getting the true diet by any method is hard, they stress. Their guidance weighs correction factors against study goals, rather than banning counts outright.
europmc-pmc6990394:
Stokes and co-authors set out three postulates linking bacterial metabolism to how well antibiotics work. Their article appeared in Cell Metabolism. Antibiotics attack processes that burn energy, so they disturb a bacterium's metabolic balance as a side effect. Resistance is spreading worldwide, and new angles are needed.

The first postulate: antibiotics shift bacterial metabolism, and that shift helps kill or stall the cells. Second, the metabolic state a bacterium starts in sets how vulnerable it is. Third, deliberately altering that state can boost antibiotic power. The authors build each claim from current evidence. They then point to open areas where exploiting metabolic networks could yield new drugs. Their aim is to move metabolism from side note to centre stage in antibiotic design.
europmc-pmc6997394:
Xu and co-authors show that iron-driven cell death helps destroy the gut lining in ulcerative colitis. Their study appeared in Cell Death and Disease. Ulcerative colitis is a relapsing inflammation of colon and rectum, marked by pain, bleeding, and diarrhoea. The death of intestinal lining cells drives much of the damage.

Ferroptosis, a regulated death tied to iron, was switched on in lining cells from patients and from mice with colitis. Stress inside the cells' protein-folding compartment drove it. The team used mice lacking a protective factor, NF-κB p65, only in gut lining cells. Those mice suffered worse ferroptosis and worse colitis. The active form of p65 normally binds a stress switch and damps the pathway. Blocking ferroptosis, the authors propose, is a promising treatment target.
europmc-pmc7005094:
Anwyl-Irvine and co-authors introduce Gorilla, an online platform for building behavioural experiments. Their paper appeared in Behavior Research Methods. Running studies on the web reaches large, varied samples that labs cannot. Building them, though, demands programming skill, and browsers time stimuli unevenly, a real problem for reaction-time measures.

Gorilla offers a full authoring and deployment tool that needs little code and tackles browser timing head-on. To prove it, the team ran a simplified flanker task on children and adults, at home, in schools, and at public events, on varied machines and connections. The known conflict effect replicated in every group. Sample details span ages, settings, and mobile connections. The paper also reviews earlier tools, names limits that remain for online work, and sketches fixes and features to come.
europmc-pmc7033994:
Stelzer and co-authors review Toxoplasma gondii in farm animals in Food and Waterborne Parasitology. This parasite spreads from animals to people. Cats shed its eggs in faeces, which can taint food and water. People also catch it from meat that holds dormant stages of the parasite.

The review sums up how common infection is in the main livestock species. It covers harm to the animals themselves, notably in sheep and goat farming. Risk factors centre on cats, dirty feed or water, and access to tainted ground. Cost data are scarce and old, the authors note. Reports from Britain and Uruguay put losses at about 5 to 15 million US dollars per country each year. New cost studies are needed, they say.
europmc-pmc7038594:
Lim and co-authors estimate how common chronic fatigue syndrome is in the Journal of Translational Medicine. The condition, also called myalgic encephalomyelitis, is a growing health concern, but published prevalence figures vary widely. The team searched public databases for studies from 1980 to December 2018 and sorted what they found by case definition, diagnostic method, and population.

From 1,291 initial articles, 45 articles covering 46 studies entered the analysis, with more than a million participants in total. Average prevalence came out at 1.40 percent, while the pooled figure was 0.39 percent and the meta-analysis estimate was 0.68 percent. Rates were higher in women than in men and shifted with the definition used. The spread itself is a finding: without a shared standard, the true frequency of this illness stays hard to pin down.
europmc-pmc7096394:
Manthiram reflects on the cathode chemistry that made lithium-ion batteries possible, in Nature Communications. These batteries powered the portable electronics boom for nearly three decades and now drive electric vehicles and early grid storage. Their high energy density rests on the electrode materials worked out by basic chemistry and physics research.

The review traces how fundamental studies led to three major families of oxide cathodes, and how each was found, improved, and rationally redesigned. It follows the field from its 1970s and 1980s roots to the 2019 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for the battery's development. Manthiram closes with a personal view of where cathode research should go next.
europmc-pmc7099994:
Yang, Wang, and Andersson review HMGB1, a protein that drives inflammation when released from cells, in Frontiers in Immunology. Inside the nucleus, HMGB1 helps organise DNA in every cell type. Outside the cell, it acts as an alarm signal that switches on innate immunity, whether released on purpose or spilled by cell death.

Two receptors, TLR4 and RAGE, carry most of its alarm effects. New inhibitors can block the HMGB1 and TLR4 link without weakening defence against bacterial toxins, the authors explain. Other drugs stop RAGE from pulling HMGB1 into cells. The review sums up the protein's role in inflammatory diseases and the candidate treatments aimed at it.
europmc-pmc7126394:
Dai and co-authors report a phase 1 trial of immune cells engineered to attack two targets at once in relapsed B cell leukaemia, in the Journal of Hematology and Oncology. Standard CAR T cell therapy aims at CD19, but cancers can escape by losing that marker. Their bispecific cells target CD19 and CD22 together.

All 6 enrolled patients reached remission with no measurable remaining disease. The engineered cells multiplied in the body and appeared in blood, bone marrow, and spinal fluid. No neurotoxicity occurred. One patient relapsed about 5 months later with blasts that had lost CD19 and showed weaker CD22, a warning that tumors find escape routes even against two targets.
europmc-pmc7195694:
Cheng and co-authors use contact tracing in Taiwan to measure how COVID-19 spreads around symptom onset. Their study appeared in JAMA Internal Medicine. They followed 100 confirmed cases and 2,761 close contacts. The overall secondary attack rate was 0.7 percent. Timing of exposure proved crucial to the risk.
