Contacts exposed within 5 days of the patient's symptom onset faced higher risk. Exposure later in the illness carried less danger. Transmission before symptoms also occurred. That pattern means finding and isolating sick patients alone may not stop spread. Wider measures such as social distancing may be needed, the authors argue. The study gave early, hard numbers on a question every health agency faced.
europmc-pmc7198094:
Sahu reviews how university closures during COVID-19 affected education and mental health. The article appeared in Cureus. Universities worldwide postponed or cancelled classes, conferences, and sports as the virus spread. Billions of people went into lockdown. Faculty rushed to move teaching onto online platforms.

Sahu weighs the strain placed on students and academic staff. Young students can adapt to online learning, the article notes. Still, lost campus life and uncertainty carry mental health costs. Meetings moved to video calls such as Zoom. The review urges institutions to treat the crisis as a lesson. Better online teaching systems could outlast the emergency. It also calls for support that protects staff and student wellbeing.
europmc-pmc7224694:
Bar-On and co-authors gather the key numbers of SARS-CoV-2 into one curated guide. Their article appeared in eLife. Viral spread, they argue, is a story told in numbers. The guide draws mostly on peer-reviewed studies. It is organized around two themes: the virus itself, and infection inside one human host.

Readers find estimates for virus size, genome, and copying speed. Other numbers cover how many particles a patient carries and sheds. The authors explain how such values are measured, often in cell culture. They also flag where the numbers remain shaky. A one-step growth method anchors several of the estimates. The article became a popular reference for modelers and journalists. It shows how much pandemic policy rests on a handful of measurements.
europmc-pmc7244094:
Tang and co-authors set out the hallmarks of COVID-19 disease, feature by feature. Their article appeared in PLoS Pathogens. Genetic analysis places SARS-CoV-2 in the same betacoronavirus group as the SARS and MERS viruses. It likely came from an animal reservoir, probably bats. Its symptoms, fever, cough, breathlessness, and fatigue, mimic many chest infections.

No specific treatment existed when the article was written. Care combined antiviral attempts with supportive measures. The authors organize the disease's defining traits, from spread to tissue damage. Cell death programs feature in their account of lung injury. Forms such as pyroptosis and ferroptosis help explain the damage pattern. The piece works as a compact orientation to a new disease. It collects what defined COVID-19 in its first months.
europmc-pmc7245994:
Reichard and co-authors report the brain autopsy findings of a patient who died with COVID-19. Their article appeared in Acta Neuropathologica. The man had first been admitted for heart surgery. Chest imaging then suggested COVID-19, and testing confirmed the virus. He died after more than 2 weeks in hospital despite aggressive treatment.

The autopsy found a range of lesions across the brain. Bleeding spots dotted the white matter throughout the cerebrum. Other areas resembled the myelin-stripping damage of ADEM, an inflammatory condition. Scattered dead neurons pointed to oxygen starvation near death. Notably, there were no large strokes and little inflammation around vessels. The case shows the virus's illness can injure the brain in mixed vascular and immune patterns.
europmc-pmc7271494:
Kale and co-authors review how immune cells might clear harmful senescent cells. Their review appeared in Immunity and Ageing. Senescent cells have stopped dividing for good. Early in life, that stop helps block cancer and aids repair. Late in life, lingering cells release signals that can drive aging and disease.

The authors explain how natural killer cells and other immune cells find and kill such cells. They also show how some senescent cells evade that killing. Cancer cell therapies now in use or in trials could be reshaped for this task. Readers learn why timing matters: remove the cells too early and repair may suffer.
europmc-pmc7285594:
Zhang and co-authors review how a chemical tag called m6A controls circular RNAs. Their review appeared in Molecular Cancer. The tag, N6-methyladenosine, is the most abundant modification on RNA in complex cells, and it steers how RNA is processed, broken down, and translated. Circular RNAs are closed loops of RNA known for stability.

Both the tag and circular RNAs take part in many diseases, including cancers, brain disorders, autoimmune disease, and infertility. Recent work shows m6A is enriched on circular RNAs and governs how they form, where they go, and what they do. The authors gather that evidence, then discuss possible medical applications and the directions the young field may take next.
europmc-pmc7334194:
Collins and co-authors build a reference map of large DNA changes in Nature. Structural variants rearrange big segments of DNA and can strongly affect health and evolution. Small single-letter changes already had population references, but large changes did not.

Working through the gnomAD project, the team catalogued 433,371 structural variants from 14,891 genomes drawn from diverse global populations. They estimate these variants cause 25 to 29 percent of rare protein-breaking events in each genome. Genes that cannot tolerate losing one copy also prove sensitive to extra copies. The reference helps labs judge whether a large change found in a patient is likely harmful.
europmc-pmc7352694:
Wolfson and Leung report an early-pandemic survey in Nutrients on food insecurity among low-income adults in the United States. They fielded a national web survey on 19 to 24 March 2020, as distancing began. Respondents all lived below 250 percent of the federal poverty line, and 1,478 took part.

Only 36 percent counted as food secure, while 44 percent were food insecure. Among those with very low food security, under one in five could follow advice to stock two weeks of food. For every basic need measured, food-insecure adults reported more trouble, in a clear step pattern by severity. The authors argue that the crisis magnified old disparities and needs a strong policy response.
europmc-pmc7367094:
Burke and co-authors report the first United States contact-monitoring effort for COVID-19 in the Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report. In January and February 2020, health departments tracked people who had close contact with the first confirmed patients. Daily checks for fever and symptoms ran for 14 days after last exposure.

In all, 445 close contacts were monitored around the first 10 travel-related patients. Of these, 54 developed worrying symptoms and were tested. Two, both household members exposed before diagnosis, tested positive. That gives a symptomatic attack rate of 0.45 percent among all contacts and 10.5 percent among household members. No further spread was found, even among contacts of the two new cases. Contact tracing, the report argues, can help contain early spread.
europmc-pmc7468194:
Yao and co-authors review nanoparticle drug delivery in cancer therapy and its fight against drug resistance. Nanoparticles can carry drugs with better stability and body fit than free drugs. They also gather in tumors and can aim at precise targets.

Hybrid particles join traits of several particle types in one carrier. Resistance in cancer grows from drug pumps, faulty cell death paths, and low-oxygen zones. Particles built against those tricks can restore drug effect. The review covers delivery for chemotherapy, targeted therapy, and immunotherapy. It explains passive and active aiming at tumors. As new resistance tricks surface, particle designs follow them. The authors chart a fast-moving route to stronger cancer care.
europmc-pmc7479594:
Zhang and co-authors tune electrolyte design to let water-based zinc batteries work in deep cold. Such batteries are safe and cheap for large storage. Frozen electrolyte blocks their use at low heat.

The team broke the hydrogen-bond network in a zinc chloride solution. That change dropped the freezing shift point of the electrolyte from 0 to -114 degrees Celsius in their tests. Batteries with polyaniline and zinc then ran from -90 to +60 degrees Celsius. That range covers every temperature recorded on Earth's surface. At -70 degrees the cells stayed robust and held near full capacity over 2000 cycles of use in the study. The work opens a route to batteries for harsh climates.
europmc-pmc7530194:
Johdi and Sukor review immunotherapy options for colorectal cancer. This cancer ranks third most common in the world. Standard care uses surgery, chemotherapy and radiotherapy.

Those treatments can harm healthy dividing cells. Many patients still relapse after treatment ends. Immunotherapy aims to use the patient immune system instead. It can spare cells that lack cancer markers. Responses vary with the state of each patient immune system. Responders often gain better outlook and life quality. The review sets out current options and strategies. It explains where each approach fits and what limits it.
europmc-pmc7563794:
Rahman and co-authors review zoonotic diseases, their causes, impact and control. Zoonoses pass between vertebrate animals and humans. More than 60% of human pathogens are zoonotic in origin.

The review covers bacteria, viruses, fungi and parasites. Climate change and urban growth shape their spread. Animal trade, travel and vector biology also matter. Emerging and returning zoonoses are growing over time. COVID-19 is highlighted as a new zoonotic disease. It likely came from bats and hit millions worldwide. The authors review control steps for major diseases. One Health measures are urged for prevention and control of future outbreaks.
europmc-pmc7566194:
GBD 2019 Risk Factors Collaborators assess the burden of 87 risk factors across 204 countries and territories. The analysis covers 1990 to 2019 at global and national level. It forms part of the Global Burden of Disease Study 2019.

The method pairs risks with health outcomes step by step. A total of 560 risk-outcome pairs met the evidence bar. Exposure levels were modeled by age, sex and place. The team used 30,652 distinct data sources overall. Burden was counted in deaths and disability-adjusted life-years. Years of life lost and lived with disability were included. Combined risks were adjusted for overlap between factors. The work shows where public health is gaining ground.
europmc-pmc7668094:
Miorin and co-authors show how a SARS-CoV-2 protein blocks the cell's alarm system. The protein, Orf6, stops interferon signaling, the cell's early antiviral defense. Past work showed it blocks a key signal protein, STAT1, from entering the nucleus.

The team found Orf6 sits at the nuclear pore, the gate into the nucleus. There it binds direct to the Nup98-Rae1 complex, part of that gate. This binding jams the import path that STAT proteins use. Knowing the exact grip may help design antiviral drugs and vaccines against this and related viruses.
europmc-pmc7721094:
Szymonowicz and Chen review cancers caused by human papillomavirus, or HPV. HPV spreads mainly through sexual contact. It causes nearly all cervical cancers and a growing share of head and neck cancers. It also drives cancers of the genitals and anus in both sexes.

Two viral proteins, E6 and E7, switch off the cell's brake proteins p53 and pRb. This pushes cells to divide without checks and alters DNA repair. The authors compare repair gene patterns in HPV-positive and HPV-negative head and neck tumors. They also review screening, current treatments, and trials that seek better tests and therapies.
europmc-pmc7846794:
Tombor and co-authors follow heart lining cells after a heart attack, one cell at a time. These endothelial cells help tissues adapt to injury. Loss of blood flow can push them toward a fiber-like state. The team sequenced single cells across time after infarction.

Cell growth and inflammation rose and fell in waves. Gene patterns for fuel use shifted with them. Most lining cells entered a short-lived mixed state at days 3 to 7. That state wore mesenchymal genes, then faded by day 14. Tracing cell lines confirmed the shift was brief. Low oxygen and inflammation marks framed the early and late phases. The authors say this brief switch may help cells move and rebuild vessels.
europmc-pmc7877494:
Uyoga and co-authors report a serology study of COVID-19 spread in Kenya. Blood donors gave samples that the team tested for antibodies against SARS-CoV-2. Antibodies show who has already met the virus, even without a recorded test.

By the end of July 2020, Kenya had reported only 341 deaths. The authors found an overall antibody rate of 4.3% among blood donors. Rates peaked in donors aged 35 to 44 years. The low death toll contrasts with many richer countries. The team links part of that gap to Kenya's young population, with less than 4% aged 65 or older. The findings give an early, ground-level picture of how far the virus had spread in the country.
europmc-pmc7966694:
Burton and co-authors present a commission report on global eye health, looking beyond 2020. Vision is the most dominant human sense. The eye, its coverings, and the brain paths behind it must all work together for clear sight. Any break in that chain causes vision impairment. The commission maps the scale of the problem and what can be done about it.

Common causes are shown in turn: trichiasis, corneal scar, cataract, diabetic eye disease, glaucoma, and age-related macular degeneration. Each harms a different part of the visual system. The report weighs the burden these conditions place on people and economies. It argues that eye care belongs inside general health plans, not beside them. Access to care is deeply uneven across the world. The commission sets out steps to close that gap.
europmc-pmc8005494:
Yu and co-authors present a review of pyroptosis, a fiery form of cell death tied to innate immunity. Interest in it has grown fast since the gasdermin family of proteins was found. These proteins punch holes in the cell membrane, and the cell bursts and spills alarm signals. The review gives the basic workings first. It then turns to the link with tumours, where the death can cut both ways.

In some tissues and gene settings, pyroptosis slows tumours. In others it feeds them. The authors weigh that split by cancer type. They set out how the death might be used as a treatment lever. Radiation and chemotherapy can also trigger it as a side effect, which harms healthy tissue. The review aims to help drug designers use the dual effect with care.
europmc-pmc8023694:
Taquet and co-authors chart brain and mental health outcomes after COVID-19. Their retrospective cohort study used the TriNetX electronic health records network. The primary cohort held 236,379 patients diagnosed with COVID-19. Matched control cohorts had influenza or other respiratory infections. The team tracked 14 neurological and psychiatric outcomes over 6 months.

The authors report that 33.62% of survivors received such a diagnosis within 6 months. For 12.84%, it was their first ever diagnosis of that kind. Patients who had been in intensive care fared worse, at 46.42%. Risks exceeded those after influenza and other respiratory infections. Severity of the initial illness tracked the later risk. The study gives planners firm numbers for the care survivors may need.
europmc-pmc8113594:
Dispinseri and co-authors track neutralizing antibodies in 162 symptomatic COVID-19 patients for up to eight months. The cohort gave repeated samples from symptom onset. The team measured virus neutralization and antibodies to spike and nucleoprotein. They also watched replies to seasonal coronaviruses and flu. Early neutralization carried good news for patients. It tracked with a faster turn to a negative swab.

Its absence carried the opposite warning. Patients without neutralizing power faced a higher risk of death. Titers sagged after five to eight weeks in most patients. Yet most patients still had detectable levels at eight months. Age and other illnesses did not erase that persistence. IgG against spike tracked neutralization best of all. Seasonal coronavirus antibodies rose briefly alongside. They neither blunted the new response nor worsened disease. Weak spike replies, the authors argue, mark the critical cases. Care and therapy should reach those patients first.
europmc-pmc8265094:
Duvaud and co-authors describe Expasy, the Swiss bioinformatics portal, as redesigned by its users. The portal gives free access to over 160 resources from the SIB. They serve storage, analysis, and reading of biological data.

In 2020, the site was rebuilt with a user-centred design method. That method shapes screens around the target community's real tasks. Life science and medical researchers worldwide use the portal daily. The paper explains what users asked for and what changed. It offers lessons for other science portals. Ease of use was treated as a research output itself.
europmc-pmc8305394:
Guillamat-Prats reviews mesenchymal stem cells in wound healing, scarring, and regeneration. Tissue repair after damage is still not fully understood. Current therapies to support it remain limited.

Healing runs through cell migration, matrix remodelling, and new vessel growth. Skin then resurfaces the wound. Chronic inflammation and disease can stall closure and leave fibrotic scars. Mesenchymal stem cells are widely used for their repair capacity. Their products, such as exosomes, may carry much of the benefit. The review weighs cell and product routes alike. Safer, cell-free repair is a rising hope.
europmc-pmc8395394:
Nooreldeen and Bach weigh current and future ways to diagnose lung cancer. This cancer is the top cause of cancer death in North America and other rich countries. It is often found late, which is one reason it kills so many.

Care today rests on imaging plus lab checks of biopsy samples. Even so, early disease still slips past these tools. The review sets out the strengths and flaws of each method. It then looks at body fluids as carriers of biomarkers. Such markers could flag cancer earlier and track its course. The authors stress the urgent need for new markers, above all for high-risk groups like smokers.
europmc-pmc8424594:
Snyder and Silva review deubiquitinating enzymes, the proteins that strip ubiquitin tags off other proteins. Ubiquitin marks control a protein's activity, place, and lifespan. These enzymes, called DUBs, counter that signal and keep the system in balance.

Many DUBs guard set pathways with shared cutting methods. Their own activity is tuned by partner proteins, chemical marks, and shifts in location. The largest DUB family uses a cysteine that reactive oxygen can switch off. That makes them sensors of oxidative stress. Faulty DUB action links to cancers and brain disorders. The review argues these enzymes are strong drug targets.
europmc-pmc8433494:
Andreano and co-authors show how SARS-CoV-2 can escape strong antibody defenses. They placed the virus under long pressure from a potent plasma sample taken from a recovered patient. Under that pressure, the virus evolved to dodge the immune attack.

Only three mutations were enough to build the escape variant. The changes sat in both the N-terminal domain and the receptor-binding domain of the spike. The new virus resisted most of the neutralizing antibodies tested. It also showed lower sensitivity to all recovered-patient sera. The authors warn that as population immunity grows, more such variants will emerge. Vaccines and antibody drugs must be built to meet them.
europmc-pmc8516894:
Andersson and co-authors map cell type interactions in HER2-positive breast tumors with spatial methods. Standard tumor sequencing loses where genes are active in the tissue. That loss hides how cells talk to each other. Spatial transcriptomics keeps the map intact.

The team read gene activity across tumor slices and clustered regions by pattern. Shared signatures marked immune and tumor processes. Merging with single-cell data placed each cell type in space. They found tertiary lymphoid-like structures inside tumors. A type I interferon response overlapped zones where T cells and macrophages sat together. A model to predict those structures was built for use in other tissues.
europmc-pmc8744894:
Sagris and co-authors review atrial fibrillation, its causes, risk factors, and genetic roots. This rhythm disorder is the most common one seen in clinical care. It raises the risk of death, stroke, and clots that travel in the blood. Global counts reach about 33.5 million patients.

The review covers how the disorder starts and grows. Electrical and structural changes in atrial tissue form the core. Lifestyle factors, such as inactivity and diet, get a full look. The Mediterranean diet is among the habits discussed. Genetic load also shapes who develops the condition. The authors argue that fixing changeable risks can cut community burden and cost.
europmc-pmc8806194:
COVID-19 National Preparedness Collaborators analyze how pandemic preparedness linked to infection and fatality rates in 177 countries. Rates varied hugely between countries from January 2020 to September 2021. The team sought the conditions behind that spread. Daily infection and death data fed the analysis, adjusted for age, wealth, and other factors.

Standardized rates were tested against twelve preparedness indices. Seven health-care capacity measures and ten social and political factors joined the tests. Trust in people and in government got special focus. So did corruption, movement changes, and vaccine uptake. The aim was to guide investment for future pandemics. Context, the authors argue, shaped outcomes as much as formal readiness.
europmc-pmc8810394:
GBD 2019 Dementia Forecasting Collaborators estimate the global prevalence of dementia in 2019 and forecast it to 2050. Aging and population growth will drive case counts up. The study gives country-level forecasts, not just global ones. It also folds in trends for smoking, high body mass, and high blood sugar.

Cases are projected to rise from 57.4 million in 2019 to 152.8 million in 2050. Age-adjusted prevalence stays near flat over the same span. More women than men live with dementia, at a ratio of 1.69 in 2019. That gap should persist to 2050. Growth varies widely by country, which matters for planning care.
europmc-pmc8960394:
Howes, Thase, and Pillinger review treatment resistance in mental health care and where new help may come from. Many patients gain little from standard drugs. The share runs from 20% to 60% across disorders. Their care costs far more than average. Yet research on the problem stays under 1% of all output. The authors gathered 23 sets of expert rules that define resistance. Four disorders had such rules.

The rules share three core parts but differ in detail. Some disorders have no agreed rules at all. The review gives a checklist to make studies easier to compare. It also treats false resistance with care. Missed doses or a wrong diagnosis can fake the real thing. An assessment plan helps doctors sort true cases. Brain models and new drugs in the works are surveyed. The authors end with advice, led by shared definitions.
europmc-pmc8987494:
Peng and co-authors ask whether drugs against the PI3K/Akt/mTOR pathway are truly making headway in cancer. This growth pathway switches on abnormally in many tumors. It feeds cell division and blood vessel growth. It also helps tumors resist chemotherapy. The review catalogs the pathway's cancer alterations first. Gene changes in its members recur across tumor types. Hallmarks tied to the pathway follow. Cell death, cleanup, and shape change all appear.

Inhibitor research gets the closing focus. Many compounds have entered trials over the years. Results so far are mixed, the authors imply. Understanding the pathway in depth should guide choices. Which patients, which partners, which timing remain open. The authors aim the review at clinical decision makers. The title's question is answered cautiously. Headway exists, but it is hard won.
europmc-pmc9052494:
Yu and co-authors review ways to modify graphene and graphene oxide for new uses. Both materials draw interest for their electronic, optical, and strength traits. The review first covers structure, preparation, and properties, then methods that strip oxygen from graphene oxide. Modification falls into three routes: bonds added on the surface, looser non-bond attachments, and doping with other elements.

Each route tunes the material for uses from electronics to medicine. The authors sum up the gains reported for modified products. They end with open challenges for surface design of these carbon sheets.
europmc-pmc9747694:
Wang and co-authors measure how well antibodies handle the rising BQ and XBB Omicron subvariants. Both families spread fast in late 2022 across many regions. Extra spike changes hinted at stronger antibody evasion. The team tested sera and lab antibodies against them.

Sera from vaccinated and infected people blocked them poorly. Even bivalent boosted sera lost much of their power. Blocking strength fell tens of fold versus older strains. The drop was larger than any seen before this study. Lab antibodies that stopped early Omicron mostly failed here. The team pinned the escape on single spike changes. Grip on the human ACE2 entry point stayed intact. The authors warn the pair threatens current vaccines. They say authorized antibody drugs are inactive against them. Evasion advantage may explain their rapid spread.
fontane-effi-briest-1894:
Theodor Fontane published Effi Briest in 1894, a German novel about a young wife in Prussian society. Effi is seventeen when she marries Baron von Innstetten, a man twice her age. Life in a dull town bores her, and she drifts into a brief affair. Years later her husband finds old letters.

Honor, as his class defines it, forces Innstetten to act. A duel and a divorce destroy Effi's health and standing. Her own parents shut their doors to her for a time. Fontane tells the story with calm sympathy and no easy blame. Critics place the novel among the finest works of German realism.
fox-journal-1694:
Fox's Journal records the rise of the Quaker movement in its founder's own words. George Fox preached the inner light through England, meeting scorn, prison, and crowds who trembled at his message. This text follows the eighth edition of the Journal, first published in 1694 after his death.

The sampled exhortation urges hearers to wait in the light for power. That power, he writes, makes the powers of the earth shake and judges the scorning nature. The lofty and proud who profess the Scriptures are compared to the Pharisees of old. Fox's plain, hammering style fills two volumes with journeys, disputes, and sufferings.
freeman-pembroke-1894:
Mary Wilkins Freeman meant Pembroke as a study of the human will gone diseased, she says in a sketch up front. The Harper printing scanned here dates from 1894. Barnabas Thayer stands as the strongest case of that bent will, drawn from life.

Barnabas can bend at last only through purer, selfless love for Charlotte Barnard. Deborah Thayer, Richard Alger, and Cephas Barnard show the same sickness in other forms. In the tale, a proud father clashes with his son over love, and a family breaks on his hard will. Darker than her famed stories, the novel builds a full tragedy from village flint.
frus-1861-d194:
John Appleton wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 11 May 1861. The dispatch is document 194 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Appleton's May letter reports a Russia that wished the Union well. The czar's court had freed its serfs that spring and felt kinship with Lincoln's stand. His dispatch gave Washington rare good news in a season of European doubt. The serf edict of March 1861 gave Lincoln's cause a warm echo in Russian talk. A warm echo from Russia was one of the few cheers of that grim spring.
frus-1861-d294:
In a letter dated 17 August 1861, William H. Seward gave Mr. Harvey his latest word from Washington. It was printed as Document 294 in the foreign affairs papers sent to the two houses of Congress. The letter comes from the first summer of the Civil War, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1861-d94:
Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Lord Lyons on 4 October 1861. Lyons was the British minister in Washington. The letter is document 94 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Lyons was the man Seward had to face across the table at home. Their letters dealt with the friction of war at sea: searches, seizures, and the rights of British trade. This October note shows that friction handled in formal, careful terms. Lyons and Seward met often in person, and their notes kept the formal record straight. Formal notes gave their talks a spine that mere chat could never supply.
frus-1862-d194:
Document 194 opens the Washington end of the British file: a note dated 3 December 1861 from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington. It is printed in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

December 1861 was the month of the Trent crisis, after a Union warship took two Confederate envoys off a British mail ship. War between Britain and the Union felt close. Notes between Seward and Lyons in those weeks carried the weight of that danger. Both men worked the problem in the same city, face to face. Formal notes left a paper record that both governments could quote back to each other later.
frus-1862-d294:
From Washington, Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed William L. Dayton in Paris on 10 July 1862, in a dispatch printed as Document 294 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It was the first Seward letter in the July run.

Seward wrote with the Richmond campaign lost and Northern morale shaken. His letters abroad in July had a repair job to do: present the retreat as a change of base, not a collapse. Dayton received this guidance as French interest in mediation grew. The letter is part of the administration's effort to manage the story of a bad month. French public opinion ran warmer for the Union after the emancipation news arrived.
frus-1862-d394:
Bayard Taylor, of the American legation in St. Petersburg, wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 25 October 1862. His letter closes the Russian file in this run as Document 394 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Taylor, a well-known travel writer serving as legation secretary, took up the post's pen after Simon Cameron's departure that fall. His October letter reached Washington as the European truce scheme was failing. It ends the file with the Russian channel in careful hands, its friendly tone unbroken through a hard year. St. Petersburg's friendship later sent Russian fleets to American ports in 1863, to great cheers.
frus-1862-d494:
James Shepherd Pike reported to Secretary of State William H. Seward from The Hague on 9 April 1862. The dispatch is Document 494 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the annual message.

Pike wrote in the first shock of the Shiloh news reaching Europe, when casualty lists made the war look endless to foreign eyes. Dutch opinion, commercial to its core, asked how long American trade could bear the strain. His report gave Washington an honest reading of that doubt. Such candor was Pike's habit and his value. Seward could trust the Hague letters. They told him what the Dutch really thought, not what a minister wished they thought.
frus-1862-d594:
In Mexico City, Thomas Corwin received this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward on 14 July 1862. The instruction is Document 594 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the year's official record.

Seward wrote in the aftermath of the Seven Days. The Union's own position had darkened. Its protests over Mexico carried less weight in Paris. His instruction still held the established line: friendship for the republic, disapproval of the French enterprise, and prudence above all. Corwin needed that steadiness from home, since events in Mexico invited bolder gestures than Washington could back. The letter shows two governments' crises interlocked, each limiting what the other could do.
frus-1862-d694: William H. Seward, the Secretary of State, wrote to a Mr. McMath on 1 July 1862. The letter is document 694 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862, the second of his letters to McMath in the file. The evidence names the two men and the date but gives no post for McMath and no topic for the letter.
frus-1862-d94:
In a letter dated 9 July 1862, William H. Seward gave Charles Francis Adams his latest word from Washington. It was printed as Document 94 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. By then, in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1863p1-d194:
A dispatch dated 8 May 1863 carried news from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, to Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington. It is document 194 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. The letter is printed in Foreign Relations of the United States, the official series that publishes American diplomatic papers. It was one of 3 letters between the same men dated that day.

Public meetings across Britain, many of them backing the Union and emancipation, formed part of the picture Adams reported. He tracked opinion as carefully as he tracked ministers. Historians still mine this correspondence for the inside story of Anglo-American relations during the war.
frus-1863p1-d294:
Reporting on 18 September 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, wrote home to Secretary of State William H. Seward. The report is document 294 in the 1863 diplomatic papers. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

For historians, this run is a prime source on Britain's choices. It shows how close London came to stepping into the war, and why it never did. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d394:
On 18 February 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward put the American position in writing to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. This note is document 394 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

Washington believed Confederate agents used British ports, ships, and soil too freely. Seward pressed Lyons to have his government tighten its watch. Historians still mine this correspondence for the inside story of Anglo-American relations during the war. Each side kept copies of the whole exchange, which is why the printed volume can show the argument from both desks.
frus-1863p1-d494:
William H. Seward, the Secretary of State wrote this official letter to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington on 7 May 1863. Such notes moved by hand between the State Department and the British legation, a few streets apart in wartime Washington. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it.

What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. The standing business of this channel was friction at sea. Union warships stopped British merchant ships, and each seizure could spark a formal protest. Readers who work through the file in order will find this letter where the clerks of 1863 left it, in the middle of the stream.
frus-1863p1-d594:
On 23 July 1863, William H. Seward, the Secretary of State wrote to Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy. Britain had not taken sides in the American war, and holding that line was the daily work of this mail.

A reader gets the feel of diplomacy done by hand: formal greetings, careful wording, and hard points pressed without open threats. Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d694:
Lord Lyons sent this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 21 November 1863. It is document 694 in the 1863 Foreign Relations of the United States volume. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington and a key figure in wartime ties between the two nations.

Late November found the exchange still active and still tense in spots. British merchants, ship owners, and officials all had stakes in how the Union ran its war at sea. Lyons put their case to Seward in formal terms. The letter helps a reader hear the British voice in the record. It is not just the American one, near the close of a long year of notes.
frus-1863p1-d94:
On 26 February 1863, Charles Francis Adams wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward for the second time that day. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 94 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The second sheet of a set often took the longer view: not one talk, but the drift of things. Adams wrote that way when the day's news allowed it. This letter is the middle of his 26 February three. With the Seward letter of the same date set nearby in the volume, the day shows both capitals writing hard. They wrote on the same war, an ocean apart.
frus-1894:
The 1894 volume changes the series' shape. Contents now list subjects under each country. Argentina's file turns on copyright, tariffs, and nationality papers. Austria-Hungary's cases ask what naturalization certificates prove. Army service claims shadow several American citizens there. Brazil prints its navy revolt and a broken tie with Portugal. Chile lists claims and an amnesty.

China's file catches a war by indirection. American officers give friendly offices to Japanese in China. Protection of foreigners fills the next heading. Trademark imitation and coolie transport follow. The subject headings make the volume easy to mine. Each case stands labeled on the contents page. A mid-volume Mexican letter haggles over a return under an 1892 act. Case by case, the year accumulates.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d194:
Ambassador Averell Harriman cabled President Roosevelt from Moscow on 6 November 1943 about delivering Roosevelt's message on Turkey to Soviet foreign minister Molotov. Harriman handed it over in person, in the form of a letter, and reports that Molotov was highly pleased with it.

Molotov raised no objection to the safeguard clause in the message. He proposed that the American agreement be attached to the Turkey protocol he and Eden had signed, and that both papers become part of the conference's most secret military record. Harriman explains that Molotov faced gripes from Soviet military men for winning no action on Turkey at the conference, and he asks leave to accept.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d294:
A long secret summary went from Secretary of State Cordell Hull in Washington to President Roosevelt on 23 November 1943, as the Soviet army neared the Polish frontier. Poland's government in exile was growing frantic about its country's future, and Hull passes on the main points of its appeals.

The Polish premier's memorandum of 18 November begs Roosevelt to intervene with Stalin to restore Polish-Soviet relations and protect Polish life and property once Soviet troops enter. Poland refuses even to discuss giving up her eastern lands, which make up half her territory, and calls any vote held under Soviet occupation worthless. East Prussia, Danzig, and Silesia, the Poles argue, are needed for a stable peace and cannot count as fair payment for the east.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d394: The entry under this title is Roosevelt's own sketch of his concept for the United Nations organization, preserved in the Hopkins Papers and undated. The printed entry gives the editors' description of the drawing, since the sketch itself is a diagram of circles. The words inside the circles read: forty United Nations, Executive Committee, and Four Policemen. Below one circle stand the words International Labor Organization, Health, Agriculture, and Food. A later file note marks the sheet as Tehran miscellaneous.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d494:
The Shah of Iran wrote to President Roosevelt on December 6, 1943, a few days after the Tehran Conference ended in his capital. The young Shah, Mohammad Reza Pahlavi, had hosted Roosevelt, Churchill, and Stalin, and the three powers had signed a declaration pledging respect for Iran's independence. His letter appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume.

Iran was occupied by Allied forces guarding the supply route to Russia, so its young ruler had much at stake in the leaders' goodwill. A letter from the Shah to Roosevelt shows a small, occupied country speaking directly to a superpower's president. It adds the host nation's voice to a record usually dominated by the Big Three.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d94: Ambassador Harriman wrote to Roosevelt from Moscow on November 4, 1943, days after the foreign ministers' conference ended in his host capital. The dispatch is Document 94 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Harriman's Moscow letters gave the president a direct reading of Soviet moods before Tehran. The record gives the date and the names and no topic. The dispatch is printed in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1944-quebec-d194:
At 10 a.m. on September 15, 1944, the Combined Chiefs cleaned up their record and closed the conference's business. Amendments to the previous meeting's minutes fixed small errors and one large planning assumption. For production and manpower planning, the date for the end of the war against Japan was set at eighteen months after Germany's defeat, adjustable as the war developed.

The chiefs then approved their final report to Roosevelt and Churchill, as amended in discussion. They also shaped the messages announcing Octagon's results. A paragraph on transferring power to the Pacific after Germany's collapse was added to the letter for Stalin. For Chiang Kai-shek, a sentence promised agreed operations to intensify the offensive, including opening a seaway into China.
frus-1944-quebec-d294: On 17 September 1944 the secretary of state wrote to President Roosevelt, one day after the second Quebec Conference had ended. The message is document 294 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume covering that meeting, issued by the Department of State. It preserves one piece of the follow-up correspondence between Washington and the president in the conference's immediate aftermath.
frus-1944-quebec-d94:
George Elsey prepared a memorandum dated September 8, 1944. Elsey assisted the President's naval aide at the White House. His paper appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume. It belongs to the final week of conference preparation.

Junior staff papers often preserve how decisions were arranged. Elsey worked close to the President's daily military briefings. A memorandum from his desk records staff-level handling of summit business. For readers, it shows the White House machine from inside. Young aides kept papers moving while senior men argued policy. Their notes help historians rebuild the conference's preparation.
frus-1945-50-intel-d194:
A text titled "National Intelligence Authority Directive No. 9" bears the date 18 April 1947. Readers meet it as document 194 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. The National Intelligence Authority, set up in January 1946, oversaw the Director of Central Intelligence and his Central Intelligence Group.

Directives were the rule books of the new system. A short one could fix the duties of a whole office. Directives set who may do what, what must be reported, and which office has the final say. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d294:
Dated 30 June 1948, this memorandum runs from the Director of the Policy Planning Staff (Kennan) to the Under Secretary of State (Lovett). It stands as document 294 in the intelligence volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, covering 1945 to 1950. With the Soviet threat in mind, the Council was deciding what secret work the United States should do abroad.

Memos like this one did the quiet work of the system. They carried facts, advice, and requests from one office to the desk that could act on them. Whole policies can be traced through chains of such notes, each one moving the matter a step. Pages like this one are the bricks of the story: plain, dated, and load-bearing.
frus-1945-50-intel-d394:
Roscoe Hillenkoetter, the first Director of Central Intelligence, wrote to Secretary of State Dean Acheson on 19 August 1949. The letter appears as document 394 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

Hillenkoetter led a young agency that had to prove its worth to older departments. Writing straight to the Secretary of State put the CIA's views before the man who ran American foreign policy. Short as it is, the letter shows the new intelligence chief dealing with the cabinet on equal terms. Papers of this rank were rare enough that each one carried weight beyond its length.
frus-1945-50-intel-d94:
Peurifoy, acting assistant secretary for administration, wrote to both Under Secretary Acheson and Secretary of State George Marshall on 31 January 1947. Marshall had held the secretary's chair for only days. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

A paper addressed to both the under secretary and a brand-new secretary of state catches a department in transition at the top. Byrnes had gone; Marshall, the wartime Army chief, now ran State. The administration's business, intelligence included, had to be laid before the new chief in order. Readers should note the date's place in the larger story: within months, the National Security Act would remake the central system again. Papers like this one readied the ground.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d194:
Should France, Belgium, and Holland be rearmed at once? James Dunn put the British question to Under Secretary Stettinius on 10 November 1944. This excerpt from his “Preparation for Big Three Meeting” paper is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume.

London's embassy had asked the American view. New arms would let those countries' troops share in occupying Germany. They would also fit Britain's idea of a defensive grouping of itself with the states of Western Europe. The Joint Chiefs, asked for a purely military judgment, favor the rearming. Under the British plan, London would arm the Dutch and Belgians. The United States would arm the French, to the tune of eight to twelve divisions, all with fresh equipment.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d294:
When would the German war end? The British chiefs reviewed the planning date on 30 January 1945 in paper C. C. S. 772, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. Their review leans on the latest study by the Joint Intelligence Subcommittee.

One path runs fast. If the Russians overrun Germany's eastern defences before they can be consolidated, the Germans must strip the west to reply. Allied advances on both sides might then force a collapse before mid-April 1945. On balance, though, the paper expects distance and stiffening resistance to halt the Russians near the line of Landsberg and the Giant Mountains. Industrial Silesia would be lost in that case. Its loss would cut finished armaments output, mainly land armaments, by a quarter or more within about six months.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d394:
Complete success, Roosevelt declared, as the plenary opened on February 8, 1945, and Bohlen's minutes follow the report. The President congratulated the foreign secretaries on their work and called on Eden to read their findings. Four subjects frame the session: the world security body, Poland, regular meetings of foreign ministers, and Yugoslavia and Greece.

Eden read the ministers' report on the world organization. It covered seats for two or three Soviet republics among the first members. It also covered which states to invite to the United Nations conference, and when and where to hold it. The bargain that created the United Nations enters the record here.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d494:
No basic quarrel divides us on Italy, Roosevelt assured Churchill in this letter of February 11, 1945. Churchill had voiced concern about their differing views on Italian policy. Roosevelt replied that Matthews, for the State Department, had gone over the ground with Alec Cadogan the day before. Differences in emphasis remained, as was natural.

But both men, Roosevelt wrote, agreed on the important fact. Whatever Italy's past attitude and actions, the allies faced a real problem of the future. Italy was and would remain an important factor in Europe. The letter, sent on the conference's last day, smooths a friction the formal record barely mentions.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d94:
Which choices would the Security Council actually vote on? A briefing book paper dated 15 January 1945 lists them, class by class. It was prepared for the President's trip and is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume of Foreign Relations.

Under the President's formula, every listed decision needs seven yes votes, including the permanent members. The sole break: a permanent member party to a dispute casts no vote on peaceful settlement steps. The classes begin with advice to the General Assembly on admitting, suspending, or expelling members and choosing the Secretary General. They run on through restoring a suspended member's rights, and then to the work of settling disputes without force.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d194:
Acting Secretary Grew gave London a guarded answer on war criminals in a letter dated July 7, 1945. The letter to Ambassador Halifax is document 194 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Halifax had proposed on June 29 that the heads of government discuss war criminals at their meeting.

The question is being given careful consideration by the American government, Grew replies. Much will depend, he says, on the discussions then taking place in London among British, American, French, and Soviet representatives. Those were the talks drafting the charter for trying the top Nazi leaders. The brief letter neither accepts nor refuses the British proposal; it keeps Washington's hands free while Justice Jackson's hard negotiations in London ran their course.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d294:
Washington sent Ambassador Harriman in Moscow a draft plan on June 23, 1945, for running the Allied Control Commission in Hungary in the armistice's second period. The Acting Secretary of State asked for his comments on the points. They were drawn from a draft by General Key, the American military chief in Hungary.

The draft would limit the commission to policing the armistice terms. A Soviet chairman would lead it, with the British and American mission chiefs as vice-chairmen, plus staff and a chief of staff. The cable shows Washington trying to write fair rules for a body the Soviets in practice ran alone.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d394:
Punishment of war criminals is laid out in a briefing book paper that traces the plan's short history. After first talks with the British in London in April 1945, Judge Rosenman, acting as President Truman's personal representative, presented a draft agreement at San Francisco in early May. The British, French, and Soviet representatives received the American plan there.

The draft rested on an earlier report to President Roosevelt by the Secretaries of State and War and the Attorney General. The Moscow Declaration of November 1, 1943, shaped its approach. European Axis criminals proven to have joined in specific atrocities would be returned to the lands where their crimes were committed. There they would be judged.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d494:
Bierut's attitude toward the old government's debts appears in an extract of Harriman's cable from Moscow of June 30, 1945. In their talk of June 25, Harriman reports, Bierut did not raise the constitutional question over the legality of the pre-war government's obligations. He did say he wished to scrutinize the transactions of the government in exile.

His purpose, Bierut explained, was to satisfy himself that those transactions were undertaken in the interests of the Polish state. That seemed a reasonable attitude to Harriman, given the controversies between the two Polish groups. Bierut and all the Poles, he adds, show the keenest desire to obtain, at the earliest moment, the Polish state's assets abroad and American economic help.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d594:
A United States delegation working paper holds a draft proclamation to Japan by the Allied heads of state. Undated but filed July 1, 1945, it is document 594 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. The draft had won approval from the Secretaries of War and the Navy and the Acting Secretary of State.

The draft speaks in the names of the U.S. President, the British prime minister, and China's president. Bracketed lines would add the Soviet leader if his country joined the war. It offers Japan's people a chance to end the war on the terms stated. It points to the vast land, sea, and air forces poised to strike the final blows. It also holds up Germany's futile resistance as an awful example of what Japan faces.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d694:
Ambassador Wilson sent his own reflections on the Soviet-Turkish clash from Ankara on July 2, 1945. The urgent top secret wire is document 694 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. Wilson reads Molotov's demands as an opening move, not a local quarrel.

First, he argues, the campaign runs on a broad front far beyond Turkey. Molotov's hint that Moscow might voice Balkan views points to the whole Balkan question. He cites a Bulgarian bid for an Aegean outlet and radio attacks on Greece's government. Second, the claim to Kars and Ardahan must be taken seriously. It is a matter of prestige to recover what the Czarist regime once held, and the lands guard the approaches to northern Iran. Third, he probes what Black Sea security would truly require of the Straits regime.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d94:
Ambassador Harriman sent Admiral Leahy a two-line answer from Moscow on June 24, 1945. The telegram is document 94 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. Leahy had asked, on behalf of General Marshall and Harry Hopkins, how Stalin would take the American Chiefs of Staff traveling to Berlin with the President.

Molotov had consulted Stalin the night before, Harriman reports, and Stalin had no objection whatsoever to the President bringing his chiefs with him. The short cable closed a question Washington had worried over for days, since some officials feared the military gathering might alarm Stalin or send the wrong signal to Japan. The chiefs could now plan to attend.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1094: Edwin Pauley cabled Washington from Babelsberg on July 17, 1945, asking for material on Italian reparations. A staff officer named Reinstein was preparing a study of possible Italian reparations and restitutions. Pauley wants its outstanding features cabled to him at conference headquarters at once. He asks special stress on what Italy might have available for reparations, and what it could be worth. He also wants official estimates of the imports Italy will need to keep her economy running over the coming year.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1194: Bissell, who ran the ship requirements desk of the War Shipping Administration, wrote inside his own agency on 22 July 1945. His desk counted hulls: how many ships the war effort needed, and where they had to be. Notes from that desk guided where merchant ships were sent. Fleets and armies moved on its sums.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1294:
The Acting Secretary of State set down this memorandum on 23 July 1945. Grew ran the department in Washington while the chief sat at Potsdam. His memoranda fixed the home office's views in the middle of the summit's second week.

A note from the acting chief could settle a desk dispute, record a decision, or frame a question for the team abroad. This one belongs to that daily staff work. It is the Washington end of the department thinking on paper, at a moment when half its mind was in Germany. The record keeps it among the summit's own papers.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1394:
A memorandum by Mikołajczyk dated 1 August 1945 closes his run of papers in the volume. It was written on the day the Potsdam Protocol was signed. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

Ending the run with a formal memorandum, after days of diary pages, returns Mikołajczyk to his public role. The settlement of Poland was now a fact on paper, and his task turned from pleading to recording his position for the future. Readers who have followed the whole run hold a rare thing. Five memoranda and four diary entries give a near-daily account of a great settlement, from the side that lost most by it.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-94:
Benjamin Cohen, a senior State Department lawyer and adviser, took these notes at Potsdam on July 24, 1945. Cohen's notes form one of the parallel American records of the conference. He sat in on talks where exact wording could shape a border or a payment. His pages were printed in the second Potsdam volume of the official Foreign Relations series.

Cohen wrote as a lawyer writes: close to the words used. His notes often catch the sense of a phrase that formal minutes smooth over. For readers, that makes them a sharp check on the official record. They show how much care went into each line agreed at the table.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d794:
Reber wrote to Matthews, the director of European affairs, on July 16, 1945, in document 794. The special assistant reported to his own chief on the eve of the Potsdam Conference. Their office owned the Department's Europe files. The letter entered the second Potsdam volume of the official series.

An eve-of-summit letter inside an office shows final alignment. Reber could flag last facts before the leaders met. Readers see the Department's Europe team closing ranks. The document pairs the home staff with the traveling team: both worked the same files that week. It marks the quiet start of the volume's busiest fortnight.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d894:
The United States delegation put the paper on German reparations before the Potsdam Conference on July 17, 1945. It reports what the Allied Commission on Reparations had settled and what it had not. Seven basic principles stand agreed. One clause of an eighth principle remains in dispute.

The disputed clause says imports approved by the governments should be paid before reparation deliveries from current goods and stocks. America insists such imports must rank as a first charge on German exports. The paper also urges quick agreement on definitions of restitution, war booty, and reparations. It says the definitions and the sharing formula must be settled together.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d994:
Covey Oliver cabled Emilio Collado on July 25, 1945, with news that the Madrid embassy had jumped the gun. It had already joined the British in formally telling Spain that the powers occupying Germany claim title to or control of German-owned assets. Spain was asked to take no step that clashes with that control.

Oliver notes this wording marks the limit of British agreement for now. London will not name the Control Council as the source of authority. France had grudgingly consented to joint warnings before Madrid acted. Washington has now told its missions in Stockholm, Bern, Lisbon, and Ankara to take like steps, though Ankara must await British consent.
frus-1961-63v04-d294:
A telegram from Secretary Rusk to the embassy in Paris, sent November 4, 1963, handles the fall of Diem. Washington means to recognize Saigon's new regime once an interim government forms. The ambassador should tell de Gaulle, but not press France to match the step.

The deaths of Diem and Nhu are called regrettable, and, per Saigon's report, not ordered. The coup is praised as restrained and widely backed. Aid, briefly held, would soon flow again. The new generals, Rusk writes, offer far greater hope than the old regime, in war and civil life alike.
gao-gaoreports-b-296094:
Mathews Associates protested Army awards for BA-5347/U batteries in GAO decision B-296094, dated May 26, 2005. The winners were Ultralife Batteries and Bren-Tronics. The cells use lithium manganese dioxide. The firm attacked its own marks. It also said the winners' cells failed a key test for stored charge.

GAO denied the protest. The Army report showed the marks were sound. The firm did not rebut that case. With no strong reply, the claims fell. Readers can use the ruling as a plain case on proof. A protest needs more than a claim that the marks were wrong.
gao-gaoreports-b-296294:
Kesser International protested the rejection of its bid as late in GAO decision B-296294, dated June 30, 2005. The Army sought grounds care at Fort Benning, Georgia. The bid came in minutes past the close. A guard post hold had cost the courier 20 minutes on the way in.

GAO denied the protest. The hold was not wrong act by the state. It also was not the main cause of the late bid. The hold took place 2 hours before the close. The courier still had time to get there. The late bar thus stood. Bidders bear the risk of last-minute runs.
gao-gaoreports-b-296394:
Vador Ventures protested a General Services Administration award for building care in GAO decision B-296394, dated August 5, 2005. The winner was Odoi Associates. The site was Postal Square. The firm said key staff of the winner lacked a hard test in the call. That test was work on a vast single building.

GAO denied the protest. The test called for work on an 800,000 square foot building. The winner's staff had run two buildings with 971,425 square feet in all. The pair ran as one site with shared systems. GAO said that past work met the test. Close past work can meet a size test when the sites truly ran as one.
gao-gaoreports-b-297294:
Shaw Environmental protested its cut from an Army contest in GAO decision B-297294, dated December 2, 2005. The work was green fix work in California. Sites were Los Alamitos and Camp Roberts. The firm's bid was ruled not fit on tech grounds. It said it was misled and that talks were due. The award went to Clayton Group Services.

GAO denied the protest. The call was clear on its terms. Replies to firm queries matched those terms. The agency had no duty to rewrite the call for one firm's wrong read. Talks were not due. The call had warned award could rest on first bids. A not-fit bid can be cut with no talks in that case.
gao-gaoreports-b-297994:
Client Network Services protested a Transportation award in GAO decision B-297994, dated April 28, 2006. The winner was Computer Sciences Corporation. The site was the Volpe Center in Cambridge, Massachusetts. The work was on-site tech project help. The firm's bid was marked down on staff. Format flaws drove that mark.

GAO denied the protest. The bid broke page caps and font size rules in the call. Firms must write bids in the set form. They bear the risk that extra pages will not be read. A mark down for a form breach is fair. Form rules level the field for all bids. To skip them would tilt the contest.
gao-gaoreports-b-298694:
Kellogg Brown & Root Services, Inc. protested Navy awards of three global contingency construction contracts. The awards went to Atlantic Contingency Constructors, Fluor International, and URS-IAP. The work covers build aid after disasters and in conflict zones. GAO ruled in the B-298694 series on November 16, 2006.

One flaw lay in the cost realism review. The agency cut a cost item from one firm's overhead pool. Rivals had booked the same item as a direct cost. That cut clashed with cost accounting rules and the firm's own practice. GAO also backed the firm's attack on its contingency plan score. The agency left key points unanswered. GAO sustained the protest.
gao-gaoreports-b-305494:
Chemical weapons cleanup funds drew a Senate query answered in this GAO letter, B-305494, dated March 27, 2006. The funds serve the Blue Grass Army Depot in Kentucky. They also serve the Pueblo Depot in Colorado. A senator asked GAO to watch for stalled spending. He feared the Defense Department might be holding back the funds.

GAO checked the books and found the funds put to work. The department had obligated $103 million for the cleanup work at the two sites. GAO found no impoundment of the funds. U.S. treaty duties call for the stockpile to be gone by 2012. The letter shows how GAO tests claims that an agency sits on funds Congress gave it.
gao-gaoreports-b-310794:
S4, Inc. lost its protest. GAO ruled in B-310794 on February 12, 2008. The Air Force sought tech and linked services for its Air Mobility Command. The order went to CLR Group Ltd. at a high price. The call ran as a small-firm set-aside race. It weighed past work, staffing, tech plan, and price. S4 held the low price of the pair.

GAO denied the protest. The pick ran on best value, not low price. The file shows the strengths of each quote were weighed. The winner's tech edge was judged worth the price gap. A slim file claim did not shake that logic.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-194:
Mortgage Financing, GAO-05-194 of February 11, 2005, studies the risk in home loans that ask little or no cash down. The Federal Housing Administration backs billions of dollars in such loans from private banks. Some voices urge it to drop the small cash stake buyers must put in. That step would widen who can buy, and widen the risk of loss.

GAO maps the traits of low and no down payment loans on the market. It weighs past studies on loan size and credit scores. It tracks how such loans have fared. It ends with lessons from other lenders for safe plan design.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-294:
Private Pensions, GAO-05-294 of May 31, 2005, uses the fate of the largest work pension plans to test the rules that fund them. Rules aim to keep plans rich enough to pay each vow they make. Yet big plans have died poor of late. Broad thin funds hint the rules leak. The federal backstop that insures such plans bears the risk.

GAO tracks how the top plans fared on funds and on cash paid in. It zooms in on poor plans and a charge meant to spur them. It weighs what their path means for the backstop's strength. The Comptroller General sent it to each panel with a say.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-394:
Maritime Security, GAO-05-394 of April 15, 2005, grades new port guard teams built to share facts fast. The Coast Guard leads the work to guard U.S. ports from terror. It set port teams that join federal, state, town, and trade hands in one room. Joint watch hubs tie their work in real time. Shared facts are the aim: a threat seen by one is known by all.

GAO asks what mark the teams and hubs leave on that flow. It names the blocks that still slow it. One block stands out in the title: the slow grind of passes that let nonfederal hands see keen facts.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-294:
Whether rural areas get their fair share of development money — and whether anyone can tell — drives GAO-06-294, dated February 24, 2006. Congress asked GAO to update a 1989 study with newer tools. GAO first listed the federal programs that fund economic development. Next it measured how much funding reached rural areas and what share that was. Last, it examined how agencies report the numbers behind such claims.

More assurance is needed that the reported figures are right, GAO concluded. The data flow to a federal aid database that agencies feed unevenly. GAO urged the budget office to press agencies on reporting rules. Agency officials should certify that their data are accurate and complete. Census, which runs the database, needs backing to chase agencies that misreport. The report's caution reaches past rural policy. Any debate built on shaky funding data can mislead the very places it hopes to help.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-494:
Soldiers wounded in battle came home to debts created by pay errors. The report numbered GAO-06-494, issued April 27, 2006, studies military debts of battle-injured soldiers in the Global War on Terrorism. The Army had referred debts of nearly 1,300 battle-injured soldiers for collection. GAO notes the true number may be greater. Most of the debts relate to pay errors, the contents show.

GAO reports the number and dollar amount of debts for separated soldiers. It shows how collection action caused hardship for many soldiers and families. It sees chances for Congress to make the process more soldier-friendly by law. Readers get debt tables, case examples, and the collection process.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-594:
The weather agency is also a big buyer, and its buying arm needed work. Report GAO-06-594, issued June 7, 2006, reviews the acquisition function of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The agency accounts for 45 percent of Commerce Department acquisition dollars. In fiscal year 2005 its acquisition arm contracted for over $851 million in goods and services. It buys ships, satellites, aircraft, and high-performance computers. The contents name three weak areas.

The agency lacks oversight of some field buying, the report says. Policies for complex systems lag day-to-day policies. Action on contracting workforce retirement has been limited. Next steps to strengthen the function are the point. Readers get the findings by area.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-894:
Staffing and foreign language gaps at the Department of State persist, GAO reports in GAO-06-894, dated August 4, 2006. In 2002 State launched the Diplomatic Readiness Initiative to close shortfalls in staff numbers and skills. The gaps had hurt U.S. foreign policy work, above all at posts key to the war on terror.

GAO measured State's progress since that push began. It checked both head counts and language skill among foreign service officers and other staff. GAO urged a planned, results-based path for workforce planning. That path would set direction, size skill gaps, build an action plan, and track its success.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-94:
Cheaper ways to handle low-level radioactive waste are sought in GAO report GAO-06-94, dated October 31, 2005. In 2004 the Department of Energy got rid of more than 378,000 cubic meters of such waste. It ranged from tainted rubble to soil and debris.

In 2002 the department told its sites to weigh full life costs when they pick a waste path. GAO checked if sites used that method to compare choices. It also asked if a department-wide plan for low-cost handling was in place. GAO called for better guidance, watch, and planning to find savings that the sites were missing.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1094:
Rural water projects draw funds from four federal agencies, GAO reports in GAO-07-1094, dated September 7, 2007. Small towns often lack cash to build or upgrade water supply and sewer plants. They lean on federal grants and loans, mainly from the Rural Utilities Service, the Economic Development Administration, the Bureau of Reclamation, and the Army Corps of Engineers.

Doubt arose that the four fund much the same work. For fiscal years 2004 through 2006 GAO counted what each agency pledged for rural water. It set each agency's entry rules beside the next, and the projects they fund. The report rests on agency money data, laws, rules, and policies.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-594:
Job programs for veterans cannot prove their worth, and GAO-07-594, issued May 24, 2007, blames shaky data. The Jobs for Veterans Act of 2002 reshaped two Labor Department programs. One sends outreach staff to find disabled veterans. The other places employment reps in local offices. Both aim to move veterans into civilian work.

GAO found the scorekeeping weak. The two programs serve near-identical groups, yet each is scored apart, which blurs the picture. Constant overhauls of the scoring system added errors and hid trends. How veterans use general one-stop centers is also unclear. Labor has steps under way, and a new reporting system looks promising. States will need time to run it well, GAO warns. Until then, Congress cannot tell what its money buys for veterans seeking work.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-94:
Freight railroads since deregulation are examined in GAO-07-94, dated October 6, 2006. The Staggers Rail Act of 1980 freed most rates. It let railroads charge more to shippers with no options. A federal board guards those captive shippers. They may seek relief above a set threshold. Industry finances have improved since 1980. Traffic and productivity climbed over the decades. GAO reviewed rate and competition data. It also heard experts and shippers. Future freight demand presses on track capacity.

Some shippers pay far more than others for like service, GAO found. Mergers shrank the field of rival carriers. Board remedies draw complaints from both sides. Rate cases are costly and slow for small shippers. Alternatives could ease the captivity problem. Capacity growth may need new public-private approaches. GAO lays out options for Congress and the board. It urges action on competition worries. The report weighs industry health against shipper fairness.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-294:
Weapon quality failures are mined for lessons in GAO report GAO-08-294, issued February 1, 2008. A Senate panel asked GAO to compare defense quality practice with that of leading firms. GAO examined 11 weapon systems with known quality problems. It traced which contractor habits fed those flaws. It spoke with quality chiefs at five top commercial makers of complex goods.

Sound firms lock down requirements early and watch suppliers hard. Defense programs often rush design and accept shaky builds. Recent Pentagon initiatives aim to close that gap. GAO finds the core need plain: sharper focus on requirements and oversight from the start.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-594:
Offshore fish farming rules are mapped in GAO report GAO-08-594, dated May 9, 2008. U.S. aquaculture now sits in nearshore or inland waters under state rules. Interest is growing in raising fish and shellfish in the open ocean, which would fall under federal control. No single law or framework governs that move.

GAO grouped the choices into four areas: program administration, permitting and site choice, environmental care, and research and monitoring. Most stakeholders want the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration as lead agency, with states keeping a strong role. Permit length splits opinion: long terms help investors, short terms ease environmental checks. States now range from 20-year leases to short ones. GAO made no recommendations, urging care on each front.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-94:
When people file for bankruptcy, some agree to keep paying a debt to hold onto property like a car. GAO-08-94, a December 2007 report, checks whether those reaffirmation deals carry the disclosures the 2005 bankruptcy reform law requires. The law's forms must state the amount owed, the interest rate, and income facts used to judge hardship. The reform law ordered this study, and GAO reviewed files in five court districts.

Most deals included the required statements. The interest rate disclosure appeared in an estimated 86 to 97 percent of agreements across the districts, and the amount reaffirmed in 87 to 98 percent. Income and expense facts, needed to spot undue hardship, showed up less often, in 67 to 88 percent of files. The report shows a reform mostly working, with gaps in the hardship data.
godwin-caleb-williams-1794:
William Godwin published Caleb Williams, or Things As They Are, in 1794, and it made him famous. This edition carries an introduction by Ernest A. Baker and a list of the persons of the tale. Ferdinando Falkland is a cultured country squire with a dark secret. Caleb Williams, his young secretary, discovers it. Mr. Tyrrel, a brutal squire, and his cousin Emily Melville, whom he does to death, set the tragedy moving.

Caleb's curiosity turns to flight and pursuit, as Falkland's power reaches into courts, prisons, and roads. Godwin meant the novel as an attack on the laws and ranks of his day, and the plot works like a machine of dread. Few novels of the time match its grip. It shaped tales of crime and conscience for a century after, and its question, who holds power over whom, has not aged.
harnack-history-dogma-vol-1-1894:
Adolf von Harnack's History of Dogma, Volume 1, appears in Neil Buchanan's translation of 1894. Harnack traces how Christian teaching became dogma in the early church. Dogma, in his famous thesis, is the gospel reshaped by the Greek spirit. Creeds and councils of the first centuries receive deep study.

He follows the Apologists, Origen, and the road to Nicaea. The work is a monument of church history in scale and learning. Protestant and Catholic scholars alike must answer its claims. Harnack's liberal reading shapes the narrative throughout. Volume 1 of seven lays the foundation. It remains essential for students of early Christian thought.
hegel-philosophy-mind-wallace-1894:
Part three of Hegel's Encyclopaedia turns from logic and nature to mind, or spirit. William Wallace translated that part into English in 1894. The German text reached its full form in the 1830 edition of the system. Hegel treats mind as the truth toward which nature was heading.

His account climbs three levels, named subjective, objective, and absolute spirit. The first covers soul, awareness, and the free mind of a person. The second covers law, morals, family, and the state. The third reaches art, religion, and philosophy itself. Wallace's version long served as the standard English text. It completes the Encyclopaedia in English dress.
hipparchus-commentary-aratus-manitius-18:
Hipparchus of Nicaea, who worked in the second century BCE, was the greatest astronomer of the ancient world. He found the slow shift called the precession of the equinoxes and built the first star catalogue. His commentary on the Phaenomena of Aratus and Eudoxus is his only work that survives whole. Karl Manitius edited the Greek text in 1894, with a German version.
