Aratus had turned the star lore of Eudoxus into a poem, and Hipparchus checks its claims star by star against his own measures. The tone is dry and exact, a scientist correcting a poet. No English version in the public domain exists. The edition stands here as the record of Greek astronomy at its peak.
history-of-the-decline-and-fall-of-the-r:
Edward Gibbon's fifth volume, in the Reed and Fredrickson transcription of Milman's text, begins with chapter forty-nine and the icon controversy. Gibbon states his maxim at once: the church, in his telling, is treated as subservient to the state. The revolt of Italy, the popes' temporal power, and Charlemagne's coronation complete that chapter.

Arabia and the rise of Islam follow, with the battle by the Guadalete deciding Spain's fate in the middle chapters. Caliph Almamon's astronomers measure the earth on the plains of Mesopotamia under unclouded horizons. This transcription parallels the library's other volume five; the content, Gibbon's sweeping treatment of east and west between icons and crusades, is the same celebrated text.
history-of-the-united-netherlands-1592-9:
Chapters twenty-eight and twenty-nine of John Lothrop Motley's History of the United Netherlands weigh Philip's character and Farnese's death. The influence of the king's rule opens the portion. Heroism among the Dutch answers his system from the other side. Then Farnese dies, and Philip's schemes lose their one great instrument.

Priestly flattery and counsel fill the Spanish court in his place. In France the League's states-general meet at the Louvre while Henry moves toward Rome. Philip orders France's estates to elect the Infanta, with Guise, as their sovereigns. Henry's formal re-admission to the Roman faith defeats the design. His entry into Paris closes the chapters in triumph. Motley delights in the turn: the abjuration Spain demanded became the settlement that ruined Spain's French policy.
history-of-the-united-netherlands-1594:
Chapter thirty of John Lothrop Motley's History of the United Netherlands describes Maurice's siege of Gertruydenberg. The city sits low, almost hidden behind its dykes, where a stream mingles with the Meuse. Nature and engineering together ranked it among the Netherlands' strongholds. Maurice resolved that the operations should constitute a masterpiece.

At Steenwyk he had already taught Europe a lesson in siege method. Now method replaces dash entirely: trenches, batteries, and patience starve the place on schedule. Motley delights in the engineering detail of the young prince's sieges. The chapter marks the republic's military coming of age. Where Farnese once besieged at leisure, Maurice now does the same to Spain. Readers who enjoy war as applied geometry will find this among Motley's most satisfying stretches.
hobson-evolution-modern-capitalism-1894:
Hobson's first major book, The Evolution of Modern Capitalism, came out in 1894. He studies how machine production remade industry and labor. Great factories and joint stock companies crowd out small masters in his account. Workers face displacement as machines take over task after task.

The book founded Hobson's underconsumptionist economics, his lifelong theme. Markets, he argues, fail when wages lag behind what industry produces. That failure drives slumps, empire, and reform alike in his later work. Here the theme appears in fresh, early form. Historians of economics treat the study as a founding text. Its survey of industrial change still reads well.
hunter-blood-inflammation-1794:
John Hunter's Treatise on the Blood, Inflammation, and Gun-shot Wounds appeared in 1794, after his death. Friends published the work he had built over a lifetime of practice. Hunter studied how blood behaves in health and in injury. Inflammation, the body's response to harm, stands at the center of his account.

He applies that physiology directly to surgery, above all to gunshot wounds. When to cut, when to wait, and how wounds heal guide his rules. The book founded scientific surgery on observed fact rather than habit. Its first edition holds his mature system entire. Surgeons read it as a charter. The plain, hard won tone commands respect.
huxley-evolution-ethics-1894:
Late in life, Thomas Henry Huxley turned from defending evolution to asking what it means for how we should live. Evolution and Ethics, from 1894, centers on his Romanes Lecture of 1893. Companion essays round out the volume.

Huxley argues that nature's struggle is not a guide for human conduct. Society, he says, grows by checking selfish instincts, not copying them. The claim split him from friends who read morals straight out of evolution. The lecture remains a key text in debates about nature, ethics, and progress. The other essays return to his long fight for honest, open inquiry.
illuminatus-dirigens-1794:
Illuminatus Dirigens, oder Schottischer Ritter preserves the working of a high grade of the Illuminati. The German text was printed in 1794 as a companion to the latest works of Spartacus and Philo. It passed the Munich censors in February of that year. Few inner rites of the order ever reached print at all.

Inside are the rite's speeches, signs, duties, and lessons for men raised to the Scottish Knight grade. One quoted rule is blunt: a man fit for nothing better stays a Scottish Knight. The print lets readers see how the order trained and tested its senior men. Scholars value it as rare proof of how the higher grades worked.
jacobs-more-celtic-fairy-tales-1894:
Joseph Jacobs made this mate to his Celtic Fairy Tales two years on, in 1894. The first set had won a wide public, and more tales lay to hand. He retold them in the same plain, brisk style as the first. Jacobs held that a folk tale should be told as the folk tell it, with no stiff book words in the way.

Sea maids and water spirits run through this set, as they did through the first. The tales come from Ireland, Scotland, and Wales, the old Celtic lands of the west. With its mate, the set forms the main Victorian hoard of Celtic tales in English.
jay-treaty-1794:
John Jay negotiated the 1794 treaty with Great Britain to settle quarrels left over from the Revolutionary War. Britain still held forts on the northwestern frontier and owed payment for enslaved people carried away at the war's end. Trade disputes and the search of American ships had pushed the two nations close to war again.

Under the terms, British troops would leave the frontier forts, trade would resume, and old debts would go to joint panels for settlement. Many Americans hated the concessions, and the treaty split the young republic's politics for years. President Washington backed it anyway, buying peace while the fragile nation grew stronger.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aaron-solomon-9: Aaron Solomon was a merchant of Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. About 1777 he signed an agreement to take the colonial paper currency sanctioned by King George III, in place of gold and silver. He left Philadelphia for Europe in 1785. The entry is very short, and those two points are the whole of it. The agreement and the departure are the only acts recorded under his name here.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abdeel-or-abrie: Abdeel, also read Abriel, meaning servant of God, was the father of Shelemiah. Shelemiah was one of the men King Jehoiakim sent to seize the prophet Jeremiah and his scribe Baruch. That order is recorded in Jeremiah, chapter 36, verse 26. This brief entry gives no other fact about Abdeel himself. It adds one point about the name as a text matter. The Septuagint, the old Greek version, leaves the name out of the verse altogether.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-of-avil:
Abraham of Avila was a false Messiah and wonder worker at the end of the thirteenth century. Even his name is in some doubt. He could neither read nor write, yet he claimed an angel had helped him write a large book, Wonders of Wisdom, and a commentary on it.

He reached Avila in Spain with a forged letter and a set date: the last day of the fourth month of 1295. Solomon ben Adret urged care and voiced strong doubts. On the day, crowds in white burial garments filled the synagogue, and small crosses were said to appear on the cloth. The tale later helped push Abner of Burgos toward conversion.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abu-l-kheir-fat: Abu-l-Kheir, called Father of the Good, was a Spanish scholar and translator. He was also known as Isaac ben Samuel. He worked in the fifteenth century. Cast out from Spain in 1492, he settled at Padua. There, in 1496, he finished a Hebrew note on Al-Fergani's star book. In part, that note copies Ḥandali. Two years later he turned two Latin star works into Hebrew. None of his works were printed. They sit in script in many libraries in Europe.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-adelkind-794:
Adelkind is a first name and also a family name among Jews. As a first name it shows in a list of martyrs at Nuremberg in 1298. It shows again in a like list for Weissensee in 1303. As a family name it first shows with Baruch Adelkind of Padua. He was of German stock. His son Cornelius became a known printer and book man.

Cornelius worked in Italy in the first half of the sixteenth century. From 1524 to 1544 he served the Venice printer Daniel Bomberg. With his help came Bibles, prayer books, and notes in three rites. He then worked for Giovanni di Gara and for Giustiniani. From 1546 to 1553 he printed and put out books on his own. In 1553 he moved to Sabbionetta to work for T. Foa. Four books bear his name as printer with no other house named.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ahithophel-loos:
The Ahithophel Loosbuch was a book of fate used in popular divination. It took its name from Ahithophel, David's counselor. In medieval Jewish legend, Ahithophel had a role much like that of Mephistopheles. He seemed at once diabolic and all-knowing.

On that fame, a cabalistic work called Sefer Goralot, the Book of Lots, was fathered on him. Its preface claims a great secret: an answer can be had by laying a hand, at random, on a tablet. The tablet holds the numbers one to ninety, or eighty-nine. The book was said to have lain hidden in Alexandria. Later, the tale goes, it was used in Tiberias and elsewhere. The entry treats that tale as the usual legend told of such writings.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alchemy-1094:
Alchemy was the undeveloped chemistry of the Middle Ages. It held that base metals can be changed into gold. It also sought a cure for all disease. The entry finds the Jewish share in it hard to trace in Hebrew writing. No great adept left his knowledge in Hebrew form. Yet almost every major old work on the art is tied, in some way, to the Jews and their lore.

Egypt was the art's home, the entry argues. It grew from the goldsmith's craft of gilding into a hunt for the elixir of life and the philosopher's stone. Its history falls into three ages: Greek and Egyptian, Arabic, and modern, from the sixteenth century on. Old books were fathered on Adam, Abraham, and Moses. A Greek treatise on doubling gold bears Moses' name, and the Leyden papyri hold an "Eighth Book of Moses" full of recipes and spells.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alfasi-masa-ud-: Masaud Raphael Alfasi served as a rabbi in Tunis late in the eighteenth century. He died in 1776. His book of notes on the Shulhan Aruk came out at Leghorn in 1805. The entry also names his two learned sons, who helped him in his work. Solomon died in 1801 and Hayyim died in 1783. Solomon also wrote a book like his father's.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-almosnino-1294:
Almosnino was a noted Jewish family first based in Aragon. The name is said to mean an orator. The entry lists the best known men of the line. One was burned by the Inquisition. One served as rabbi in Tetuan and wrote books. One led the London Spanish and Portuguese group and died in 1784.

Moses ben Baruch gets the longest notice. He was born at Salonica in 1510. He died at Constantinople about 1580. In 1565 he won a plea before the sultan. The plea kept the civil rights of his brethren safe. His books treat the Five Rolls and the Ethics of the Fathers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-amethyst-1394: Amethyst is a kind of quartz with a clear purple hue. Its tint can lean toward a blue violet. It has long been used as a gem stone. Most readers place it ninth on a famed breast-plate. That plate was worn by the high priest of Israel. The stone stood in the third row of gems. Two verses in Exodus are cited for that place. The root of its Hebrew name is not known.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-andalusia-1494:
Andalusia was the largest of the old divisions of southern Spain. It held the Moorish kingdoms of Seville, Cordova, and Granada, plus towns such as Malaga and Lucena. Jews came early to this region, as the Phoenicians had before them.

When Muslim armies took Spain, Jews aided them, and captured Cordova and Seville were left in Jewish care. Under the new rulers Jews won full religious freedom, with a poll tax as their only burden. Under Abd-er-Rahman III, who ruled 912-961, many Jews fleeing Fatimite oppression settled there. The entry traces Jewish life in the region through those shifting reigns.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-antiochus-ix-cy:
Antiochus IX, called Cyzicenus from his city Cyzicus, was a king of Syria who died in 95 B.C. He was half-brother to Antiochus VIII, the king before him. He rose against his brother in 113 and ruled all Syria alone for two years.

After that he had to settle for Coele-Syria while his brother held the rest. Diodorus, as cited here, paints him like Antiochus IV in character and in hatred of the Jews. Yet Judea had grown strong since those days. His bids to aid the Samaritans in 110-107 and to subdue Judea with Egyptian troops both failed, and he gave up further attacks.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aradus-arados-i: Aradus, or Arados, was a Phoenician city on the island now called Ruad, eighty miles north of Sidon. It is the Arvad of Ezekiel, chapter 27, in verses 8 and 11. Tiglath-pileser III called it Armad, and Egyptian monuments name it too. Jews had moved there by Maccabean times, the entry notes, citing First Maccabees, chapter 15, verse 23. For more it sends the reader to the entry Arvad, and it rests on works about Phoenician history and Asia and Europe that it names.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-arnheim-fischel:
Fischel Arnheim, a Bavarian deputy and lawyer, was born at Baireuth on February 23, 1812, and died there on January 31, 1864. His parents planned a business career for him and gave him a strong Jewish education, so that he knew Bible and Talmud early. Love of learning led him instead to the gymnasium and then to law at Munich and Erlangen. In 1848 he became a royal attorney at Naila, and later at Bayreuth.

His skill as a lawyer won him election to the Bavarian legislature for the cities of Hof and Munchberg. He won the freedom of the city of Hof and was reelected four times without opposition. He was the only Jew in his district. In the legislature he used his Bible and Talmud learning to answer anti-Jewish charges from other members.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ascher-benjamin:
Benjamin Henry Ascher, a Hebrew scholar and author, was born in 1812 at Peisern in the grand duchy of Posen. His father, a corn merchant, gave him a careful schooling in both religious and general subjects. In 1840 he went to England and soon mastered English. In 1843 the Great Synagogue elected him its kabranim rabbi, its funeral preacher.

He held that office for over forty years, resigning in 1884, and died in London on February 24, 1893. His books served English Jews directly. In 1847 he issued a new edition of the Sefer Hayyim, The Book of Life, with an English translation. In 1859 he published Solomon ben Gabirol's Choice of Pearls in English with notes. He also won concessions from Sir George Grey so Jewish prisoners could keep their religion.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ashkenazi-zebi-:
Zebi Hirsch Ashkenazi, known as Hakam Zebi, was a rabbi born in Moravia in 1658. He died at Lemberg on May 2, 1718. His father and his grandfather Ephraim ha-Kohen taught him as a boy. At Salonica he attended the school of Elihu Cobo and saw the wreckage left by the Shabbethai Zebi movement, an experience that shaped his whole career.

At Constantinople his learning so impressed the Sephardim that they gave him their title Hakam, which he kept for life. In 1686, when Alt-Ofen was besieged, a cannon shot killed his young wife and daughter, and he fled, cut off from his captured parents. He served as rabbi at Sarajevo until 1689, quarreled with his congregation, and left for Germany. The long entry follows him across Europe's rabbinates.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-attah-hore-ta-d:
Attah Hore'ta is the first of seventeen short verses sung on the Rejoicing of the Law in the Northern rite. The singing comes before the scrolls are taken from the Ark for the processional circuits. The chant is built like a Gregorian psalm-tone and sits in the first church mode, from D to D.

But its opening, middle, and close break the plain-song rules. The entry traces its tune to an old Oriental cadence around the fifth degree of the minor scale. The same cadence turns up in the palm-branch melody of Tabernacles and in the Rain-Prayer.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-azankot-saadia-:
Saadia b. Levi Azanḳoṭ was an Orientalist of Morocco. He lived in Holland in the first half of the seventeenth century. He taught Jewish literature to Hottinger. A poem version of the book of Esther by him survives in print. It came out at Amsterdam in 1647 under the title "Iggeret ha-Purim."

The Bodleian Library holds two manuscripts in his name. One is his copy of Maimonides' guide for the perplexed, written in Arabic characters for the scholar Golius. The other holds his Hebrew rendering of an Arabic poem, bound with a printed copy of the same work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bach-joseph-229:
Joseph Bach was a Hungarian rabbi. He was born in 1784 and died at Budapest on Feb. 3, 1866. After Mannheimer, he was the first German preacher of a Jewish congregation in Austria-Hungary. He taught himself the Talmud at Alt-Ofen, his birthplace. With no teacher he learned several tongues, then spent twelve years at the University of Prague.

Bach married into a wealthy family and settled as a merchant. He soon lost his whole fortune and was left penniless. Need drove him to teaching. From teaching the young he rose to teaching the people at large. In 1827 he became spiritual adviser to a large congregation. Though he had never studied preaching, he was made first preacher of the new synagogue at Pest. He served there over thirty years, and many of his sermons were printed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baku-2394:
Baku is a seaport in Transcaucasia, Russia, on the Apsheron peninsula on the west coast of the Caspian Sea. Its naphtha wells were long known to fire-worshipers. The city is known to have existed in the fourth century, passed to the Arabs in the eighth, and later to the princes of Shirvan. A monk sent to the Tatar khan in 1254 reported the whole country largely inhabited by Jews.

About a dozen Jewish families from Jilan, Persia, settled in Baku in 1794. After Russia annexed the city in 1806, a riot in the Jewish quarter drove them to Kuba. For decades only a few Jewish soldiers and merchants could live there. The petroleum trade changed that: the city grew from 12,333 people in 1867 to 112,000 in 1897, with 2,000 Jews in 1899. A new synagogue rose in 1901.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baraita-on-the-: Baraita on the Mystery of the Calculation of the Calendar is a Baraita cited in the Talmud, at Rosh ha-Shanah 20 b. Special care was taken to keep it secret, so it has not been preserved. The entry judges that the Baraita of Samuel likely took in a large part of it. The one Talmud citation from it has puzzled commentators and modern students of the Jewish calendar alike. Despite many attempts to explain it, the entry says, it remains obscure.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ben-ze-eb-judah:
Judah Löb Ben-Ze'eb, born near Cracow in 1764, died at Vienna on March 12, 1811. After a Polish religious education, he studied Hebrew philology in secret at night. Berlin, then a center of the Haskalah, drew him next, and he later spent about ten years at Breslau.

His Hebrew grammar of 1796 was the first to set out Hebrew grammar in Hebrew itself, with logic, syntax, and prosody. It went through more than fifteen editions. His Hebrew lexicon, based on David Ḳimḥi, ran to six editions and taught German to many readers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-berlin-naphtali:
Naphtali Zebi Judah Berlin, known by his initials, headed the yeshibah of Volozhin, in Russia. Born at Mir in 1817, he died at Warsaw on Aug. 10, 1893. He married into the family of the school's head and took the post himself in 1854.

Under him the student body grew from 100 to more than 400, with funds raised by agents sent across the world. He held to plain logical study and fought bids to bring secular science into the school. An open letter of 1885 states his case, that seminaries had failed to raise true Talmudic rabbis.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-beth-anath-3194: Beth-Anath was a Canaanite city in the territory of Naphtali. Its name contains the name of the god Anath. The entry cites Joshua and Judges for its story. Israel never conquered the city outright. Its Canaanite people became tributary instead. Egyptian inscriptions mention the city several times. Its exact site is not certain. The entry favors the village 'Ainitha in Galilee. It also reports a doubt about that site. A fortress seems unlikely in that fertile valley.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bikkurim-first-:
Bikkurim is the last treatise of Seder Zera'im. It treats the commandment of first-fruits. Deuteronomy chapters twenty-six sets out that command. The duty has two parts. One brings the first-fruit to the Temple. One also makes a declaration of thanks. The treatise runs to three chapters.

Chapter one sorts who may bring and declare. Chapter two compares bikkurim with other offerings. Terumah and the second tithe are its contrasts. Chapter three describes the Temple procession fully. No Babylonian Gemara exists for Bikkurim. The Palestinian Talmud does discuss it at length. Its digressions praise honor for the aged.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bloch-marcus-el:
Marcus Eliezer Bloch was a German ichthyologist and physician. He was born at Ansbach in 1723. He died in Carlsbad on August 6, 1799. Poverty left him almost illiterate at nineteen. Hebrew learning won him a teacher's post in Hamburg. There he mastered German and some Latin. He took his medical degree in 1747.

From 1781 he published his great fish history. Twelve volumes carried 432 fine plates. Princes and patrons funded its later volumes. It remained the century's chief ichthyology work. His prize essay proved intestinal worms hereditary. His fish collection passed to Berlin's museum.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bozrah-lxx-and-: Bozrah raises a puzzle that this entry leaves open. Some scholars hold there was only one Bozrah. On that view, a Moabite Bozrah bore an Edomite king because Edom then lacked fit rulers. Prophets thus aimed words against Edom at Bozrah, Genesis Rabbah adds. Other scholars split the name into two cities. They make the birthplace of King Jobab an Edomite town. Bozrah is also called Job's legendary birthplace or home. The entry reports both views without settling the question.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bresslau-mendel: Mendel ben Hayyim Judah Bresslau, also spelled Bresslauer or Breslauer, was a bookseller at Breslau. He died in 1829. He wrote pieces for the periodical Ha-Meassef. His allegorical ethical dialogue, Childhood and Youth, came out at Breslau in 1786. In 1819 he published a geography of Palestine with two maps. A Hebrew reader and grammar by the phonetic method followed in 1834. That last date falls after the death year the entry gives, a clash it does not explain.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cantori-joshua-: Joshua dei Cantori attacked the Talmud at Cremona in 1559. Steinschneider places him in the Cantarini family. A quarrel with Joseph Ottolenghi, head of Cremona's Talmud school, drove his act. To avenge himself, Cantori joined a converted Jew and charged the Talmud with blasphemy against the Christian faith. The charge brought a public burning of Hebrew books at Cremona that year. Later Cantori was found murdered in a Cremona street. He was buried behind the board in the Jewish cemetery, as a mark of shame. Another source calls him a convert.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-case-casa-or-ka: Joseph b. Abraham Case, also called Casa or Ḳaza, ranked among the leading Polish rabbis of the late sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries. He died at Posen about 1610. Bloch argued that Case also called himself Shapiro, which points away from the Italian origin his surname suggests. Case served as chief rabbi of Lemberg, then as city rabbi of Posen. He left no writings, the entry says. Yet responsa by Solnik and by Meïr of Lublin show his high standing. His son Solomon was also a noted Talmudist.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-chemerovtzy-429: Chemerovtzy is a small town in the government of Podolia, in Russia. In 1898 it held 1,282 people, almost all of them Jews. About 160 Jews followed trades, but most traded for a living. Hair sacks were the chief article of trade, exported to a value of 100,000 rubles a year. Poverty was growing fast. Two charitable groups could barely meet local needs. Schools were a Talmud Torah with 10 pupils and 10 ḥadarim with 178 pupils, split into three levels.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-classical-write:
Classical writers and the Jews surveys how Greek and Roman authors saw the Jews across many centuries. Theophrastus, in the fourth century B.C., seems to name them first, calling them a nation of philosophers who spent days on God and nights on the stars. Aristotle met a Jew in Asia who struck his circle as a Greek at heart.

Early learned Greeks often praised Jewish belief in one God. Hostility grew as Jewish separateness grated on neighbors. Egypt bred the tale that Jews descended from lepers cast out in a plague. Later pages follow Roman-era voices like Philostratus and Dion Cassius. By the third century, the entry notes, pagans treated Jews less as a nation than as a religious body bent on winning converts.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cohen-louis-lou:
Louis Cohen, an English communal worker, was born in London in September, 1799, and died there on March 15, 1882. For two generations he stood near the center of Anglo-Jewish affairs. Elected warden of the Great Synagogue in 1837, he held that post for years. He later sat on the council of the United Synagogue and on its committee of Seven Elders.

On the Board of Deputies his sway was great, and the entry calls him main author of its standing constitution. He backed Sir Moses Montefiore in most ventures. Charity posts ran from the Jews' Free School to the board of shehitah. In business he joined the Stock Exchange in 1819 and founded the firm of Louis Cohen and Co. Botany was his private love.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-compassion-1069:
Compassion, sorrow and pity for one in distress that stir a wish to relieve, is ascribed in the Bible to God and man alike. The Hebrew roots carry the sense of a mother's feeling, drawn from the word for womb. The Rabbis speak of thirteen attributes of compassion in Exodus xxxiv. 6, later sorted under justice, love, and compassion.

The Bible's ruling image is a parent pitying a child, as in Psalm ciii. 13. Pharaoh's daughter shows it toward the weeping babe in Exodus ii. 6. Man owes it to man, and its absence brands a people cruel. Rabbinic teaching makes mercy a mark of Abraham's seed. Philo's line closes one thread: God's pity is older than His judgment.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-confirmation-th:
Confirmation, the rite of, solemnly brings Jewish youth into their ancestral faith. Its first official trace is an 1810 ordinance of the Westphalian consistory at Cassel. Rabbis there had to ready the young and lead the rite themselves. At first only boys were confirmed, at home or in a schoolroom on their Bar Mizwah Sabbath.

Girls entered at Berlin in 1817 and Hamburg in 1818. Orthodox scorn kept the rite out of synagogues at first, then classes began to be confirmed together in them. By custom the rite settled on Shebuot, the feast of the Law's giving at Sinai. Supporters prized its reach for girls, who had no rite of their own. Critics called it a borrowing from the Protestant Church.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-costa-sir-micha: Sir Michael Costa was a musical composer and conductor. He was born at Naples, of a Sephardic family, on Feb. 4, 1810. He died in Brighton on April 29, 1884. He reached England in 1829 and conducted at Her Majesty's Theater in 1831. Naturalized in 1839, he later led the Philharmonic concerts and the Handel festivals. He was knighted at Windsor on April 14, 1868. His works list runs to ten operas and ballets. It also names the oratorios Eli, from 1855, and Naaman, from 1864.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cucumber-4794: Cucumber renders a Hebrew word in Numbers, where Israel longs for Egypt's good things. At least two kinds grow in Palestine, the entry says. One is the common green cucumber known in the West. The other is the Egyptian or hairy cucumber, called by one writer the queen of cucumbers. It runs longer and thinner than the common kind, often over a foot long. The garden of cucumbers in Isaiah means a cucumber plot. Its lodge sheltered the watcher who scared birds and thieves.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-danz-johann-and: Johann Andreas Danz was a German theologian and Hebraist. He was born at Sundhausen, near Gotha, in 1654. He died at Jena on Dec. 22, 1727. He learned Hebrew at Hamburg under Esdras Edzardi. At Jena he became professor of Oriental languages, moving to the theology faculty after 1713. Christian scholars of his day ranked him first in Hebrew. His grammar books stayed standard for near a century. The first, from 1686, treated word forms and sentence building. His Compendium of 1699 went through edition after edition.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-davidson-ellis-:
Ellis A. Davidson was an English author and technologist born at Hull in 1828. Trained at the School of Design and at South Kensington, he became one of the first art teachers sent into the provinces. In 1866 he was made principal art master of the City Middle Class School in London.

Davidson resigned to write a series of school books on technical training, a field where the entry calls him a pioneer. His books teach drawing for carpenters and joiners, house building, and church architecture. He also made drawing models for class teaching. He worked to raise the education of Jewish working people. He died at London on March 9, 1878.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-depping-georges:
Georges Bernard Depping was a German-French historian born in Münster, Germany, on May 11, 1784. He moved to Paris in 1803 and lived there as teacher and writer. Among his works, the one that matters here treats the Jews of the Middle Ages. It appeared in Paris in 1834, with a second edition in 1844.

Depping wrote the book after a Royal Academy prize offer of 1821 asked for the state of the Jews in medieval France. His work won honorable mention, and he widened it to all Europe. The entry praises his diligent use of Christian records. It faults him for rarely using rabbinical sources, which weakens his pages on Jewish literature. He died in Paris on September 5, 1853.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dijon-hebr-5194:
Dijon is the chief town of the French department of Côte-d'Or. Jews settled there from time beyond memory, this entry reports. They lived in two quarters of their own. One street bore the name Rue des Juifs until the French Revolution. The other quarter, the Petite Juiverie, lay in the lower town.

In 1196 Duke Eudes III gave the Jews of the village of Fénay to the town of Dijon, and in 1197 he granted one Jew and his family to a favorite. Dijon Jews appear as creditors of abbots and abbeys in 1216 and 1223. Philip the Bold let twelve Jewish families settle in his duchy in 1374. When Burgundy demanded expulsion in 1382 to 1384, a loan of 3,000 livres to the duke kept the Jews in place.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-earth-5394:
Earth, in Hebrew usage, means first soil as an element. It also means the ground's surface and plowed land. That soil was likely the red earth of Palestine. Josephus links the word for man, Adam, to that red color.

Heaven and earth together make the universe in Hebrew speech. The earth stands on foundations and pillars over the ocean. Yet Job also pictures it hung in empty space. Like other ancient peoples, the Hebrews saw the earth as a disk. Palestine sat at its navel, between Assyria and Egypt. Later writers made Zion the earth's very center.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eisler-moritz-5:
Moritz Eisler was an Austrian educator and philosophical writer. He was born at Prossnitz, Moravia, on Jan. 20, 1823. He died at Troppau on Dec. 21, 1902. He studied philosophy and Oriental languages at Prague. In 1853 Nikolsburg made him religion teacher and school director.

In 1862 Eisler founded a fund for sick teachers and teachers' widows and orphans. It grew into the Moravian-Silesian Hebrew Teachers' Association. He led that body until 1898. His main work lectures on the Jewish philosophers of the Middle Ages. It fills three volumes, printed at Vienna from 1870 to 1883. After forty years of service he retired in June 1893.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eliasberg-bezal: Bezaleel Judah Eliasberg was a Russian Hebraist. He was born at Ivenitz in 1800. He died at Minsk in 1847. The entry gives a single work for him. He turned a medical book by Friedrich Pauliczki into Hebrew. The Polish original became two Hebrew volumes at Wilna in 1834. A short add-on on first knowledge went with it. The work was printed again at Jitomir in 1868. No other facts of his life are given here.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eliezer-of-beau: Eliezer of Beaugency was a French student of the Bible. He lived in the twelfth century. He learned under Samuel ben Meir, the grandson of Rashi. His school sought the plain sense of the text. Eliezer hunted the link from verse to verse above all. That method marks his notes on the prophets. He kept clear of midrash in his work. Only his notes on Isaiah and Hosea are in print. Notes on Ezekiel and other prophets rest in handwriting.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-elkoshite-5694: Elkoshite is the dark tag tied to the prophet Nahum. The Book of Nahum gives him no other name or mark. Jerome took Elkosh as a village in Galilee. Others place a town of that name east of the Jordan. One scholar derives the word from Kosh, a god of Assyria. Kimhi and Ibn Ezra read it as a place or family name. In the family view it matches Kish, the father of Saul. The entry leaves the point open and unsure.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ephraim-mountai:
Mount Ephraim, also called the hill country of Ephraim, is the northern part of the mountain range west of the Jordan. The entry places it from Beer-sheba toward the great plain of Esdraelon. Its southern edge is not fixed in the Old Testament. Benjamites as well as the tribe of Ephraim lived there, and Deborah lived between Ramah and Beth-el.

Shechem sits in a deep gap that splits the range into southern and northern halves. Mount Gerizim rises to 2,604 feet in the south. Mount Ebal begins the northern half, and Carmel ends it at 1,656 feet. The entry calls the land more fertile than Judah's hills, with rich valleys and orchards.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-falk-joshua-ben:
Joshua Falk was a Polish Talmudist born at Lublin who died at Lemberg on March 29, 1614. He studied under his relative Moses Isserles and under Solomon Luria. He rose to head the Lemberg school, where famed rabbis sat under him. At the Council of Four Lands in 1607, many of his proposals were approved.

His Sefer Me'irat Enayim, printed at Prague in 1606, comments on the Hoshen Mishpat with earlier rulings and their sources. Bet Yisrael gives a double commentary on the four Turim, printed in parts from 1635 onward. He also wrote on the ban on interest and left sermons and Talmud notes. A divorce he issued at Vienna in 1611 stirred long debate among leading rabbis.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ferrer-vicente-:
Vicente Ferrer was a Spanish Dominican preacher born at Valencia on January 23, 1350. He died at Vannes, France, on April 5, 1419. He entered the order in 1374 and rose as a cathedral preacher. From 1398 he roamed Spain, France, Italy, and Germany as a wandering preacher. A train of about 300 flagellants followed him, and crowds of thousands left work to hear him.

The entry calls his coming one of the main forces behind the expulsion of Spain's Jews. He forced his way into synagogues with a raised cross and rededicated them as churches. His preaching won over Rabbi Solomon Levi of Burgos in 1390 or 1391. Together they shaped the harsh Castilian edict of January 12, 1412, which fenced Jews into ghettos.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-florence-fioren:
Florence, capital of Tuscany in Italy, had Jews settled there probably before 1400. They were granted many rights at once, though their place changed with the government. Jews were expelled and readmitted at the Senate's pleasure. In 1472, during a plague, all Jews were driven out. They were recalled the next year, when the people wanted them back as money-lenders.

Under Lorenzo the Magnificent, Jews shared in the city's great age of art and learning. Jewish physicians and scholars came to his court. Spanish refugees were later welcomed for their wealth and learning. The entry follows the community through the ghetto years to 1814, when its gates opened for good. Full citizenship came in 1861. Schools, hospitals, and study societies close the account.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-frankel-ludwig-:
Ludwig Fränkel was a German writer born at Leipsic on January 24, 1868. He studied at Leipsic, Berlin, and in England. He took his doctor's degree in philosophy in 1889. He wrote most of the literature articles in a great German encyclopedia of the day. In 1892 he became secretary of the German National Museum at Nuremberg. He left that post in 1893 to teach at Stuttgart. By 1903 he was an instructor in Munich.

Fränkel writes widely on literature, modern languages, German history, bibliography, and folk-lore. One book of his asks why Rome is called the Eternal City. It won a prize in 1886 and was published in 1891. He has edited works of Uhland, Shakespeare, and Schiller for German readers. He also prepared German editions of Manzoni and of Bojardo. Articles by him on Jewish subjects appear in several German journals. Two short source lines close the entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fries-jakob-fri: Jakob Friedrich Fries was born at Barby in Saxony on August 23, 1773. He died at Jena on August 10, 1843. He taught philosophy at Jena and then at Heidelberg, where he also held a post in physics. After he returned to Jena in 1816, he published a harsh review of two pamphlets against the Jews. The entry notes its rude tone. It urged princes to treat Jews as Pharaoh had done.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gamaliel-i-6494:
Gamaliel I, son of Simon and grandson of Hillel, led the great council at Jerusalem in the second third of the first century. He bore the byname Ha-Zaken, the Elder. Like Hillel he made rules aimed at the betterment of the world. Three letters in his name went out on tithes and on an added month in the year.

In Acts he speaks as a Pharisee and doctor of the law held in honor by the people. There he urges care in the case of Jesus followers. Kings and queens are said to bring him rite questions. Paul later boasts of having sat at his feet. A saying marks his death as the end of honor for the Torah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gera-6594: Gera is a name tied to the tribe of Benjamin in three notes. A Gera is called the fourth son of Benjamin in Genesis xlvi. 21. He is missing from the Benjamin list in Numbers. First Chronicles makes him a son of Bela, Benjamin first son. A second Gera was father of Ehud, the judge who served in the days of Eglon of Moab. A third was father of Shimei, who cursed David in flight.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-giza-gizai-6694:
Giza, also written Gizai, was a sabora who headed a Babylonian school in the first half of the sixth century. The old source "Seder Tanna'im wa-Amora'im" names Giza and Simuna as the last of the Saboraim, the pair who kept the tradition right after R. Ashi and Rabina, the last amoraim.

Most of the entry untangles a name problem. Sherira's letter, the key source on the Babylonian schools, never mentions Giza but gives 'Ena in the same role, teaching at Sura after 515. The entry concludes that 'Ena and Giza are one person, the two names being corrupt readings of each other. A third source makes Giza a brother of the gaon Nehilai's ancestor.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-grossmann-ludwi:
Ludwig Grossmann was an Austrian mathematician and political economist. He was born at Leitomischl, Bohemia, on March 14, 1854. As a boy he showed a strong gift for physics and mathematics. Vienna University gave him his philosophy doctorate in 1878. That year he founded a journal of mathematics and physics at Vienna.

He found the curve for the probable length of man's age, the entry says. He wrote much and fought anti-Semitism in print. By 1903 he edited the "Controlle," a journal of political economy. His books put mathematics at the service of national economy.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-habor-6994: Habor was a river that ran through the land of Gozan, known in classical sources as the Chaboras. Its banks became a place of exile for Israelites. Tiglath-pileser sent the Reubenites, Gadites, and half of Manasseh there. Later Shalmaneser placed the people taken from Samaria at Habor by the river of Gozan. The entry rests on I Chronicles v. 26 and II Kings xvii. 6 and xviii. 11. It identifies the river with the modern Khabur.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-halevy-leon-709:
Léon Halévy, born at Paris on Jan. 14, 1802, was a French author and dramatic writer who died at Saint Germain-en-Laye on Sept. 2, 1883. He was a brother of the composer Fromenthal Halévy. After the Lycée Charlemagne he became a follower and helper of Saint Simon. He aided in founding Saint Simon's paper, "Le Producteur." He wrote the preface to his master's work on opinion.

In 1831 he became assistant professor of French literature at the Ecole Polytechnique. He quit after three years. From 1837 to 1853 he ran the bureau of scientific societies at the Ministry of Public Instruction. Then he gave his last thirty years to writing. The entry lists his poems and his Horace in French verse. It lists plays staged at the Théâtre Français and the Odéon. It also names his history of modern Jews of 1828 and his life of his brother.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hanbury-lily-71: Lily Hanbury was an English actress, educated in London and residing there in 1903. Her début came in 1888 in a revival of W. S. Gilbert's "Pygmalion and Galatea" at the Savoy Theater, and she went on to London's leading stages. Her repertory was extensive: Petra in Ibsen's "Enemy of the People," and Julia in "The Rivals," among others. Her chief successes were in Shakespeare under Wilson Barrett and Beerbohm Tree — Ophelia in "Hamlet," Portia in "The Merchant of Venice," Calpurnia in "Julius Caesar," and Chorus in "Henry V."
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hartogh-abraham:
Abraham Frans Karel Hartogh, born in Amsterdam on Dec. 29, 1844, was a Dutch jurist and deputy. He took his law degree at Leyden in 1869 and practiced in Amsterdam. He soon led the Liberal party in the capital. From 1886 until his death he sat in the Second Chamber of Parliament for Amsterdam.

Hartogh carried a bill on civil procedure into law in 1896 after a hard fight. He also won some added rights for women, above all in divorce cases. His books treat state liability for officials' faults and the new procedure law. He died at The Hague on Feb. 13, 1901.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-heilprin-angelo:
Angelo Heilprin, born on March 31, 1853, in Hungary, was an American naturalist, geologist, and traveler. His father Michael brought him to the United States in 1856. He studied mining and geology in London, Vienna, and other European cities. From 1880 he taught at the Academy of Natural Sciences in Philadelphia.

Field trips took him to Florida, Bermuda, and Mexico, where he climbed great volcanoes and measured their heights. In 1892 he led a relief party to Greenland for Peary. After the 1902 eruption that destroyed Saint-Pierre, he climbed to the crater of Mount Pelee while it still worked. His books cover geology, animal spread, and Alaska.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hermann-ludimar: Ludimar Hermann, born in Berlin on Oct. 21, 1838, was a German physiologist who took his medical degree there in 1859. He became a lecturer at Berlin in 1865. He then held physiology chairs at Zurich from 1868 and at Königsberg from 1884. His chief works include a physiology textbook that reached a twelfth edition in 1900, a six-volume handbook, and a work on experimental toxicology. His essays ranged across muscle and nerve physiology, the sense organs, and phonetics.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hildesheimer-sa: Samuel ben Joseph Hildesheimer was rabbi at Frankfort-on-the-Main from 1618 to 1622. He rebuilt the Jewish congregation there after the Fettmilch unrest had broken up its rule, the entry says. On his plan, seven new representatives were added to the old board of ten. They formed a group called the Aussengemeinde. Four of them were to serve two months each year as collectors and synagogue presidents. He also set in order the work of the dayyanim, or judges.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hochmuth-abraha:
Abraham Hochmuth, born at Bán, Hungary, on Dec. 14, 1816, was a Hungarian rabbi. At Prague University he studied Talmud with Rapoport at the same time. In 1846 he became head of a new Jewish school at Miskolcz. He opened a private school there in 1850.

Hochmuth was called to Kula in 1852 and to Veszprim in 1860. He sat in the Hungarian Jewish Congress and later on the board of Budapest's rabbinical seminary. His books treat the Jewish school in Hungary, a study of Leopold Löw, and knowledge and worship of God as a teaching handbook in 1882. He died at Veszprim on June 10, 1889.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hosea-the-proph:
Hosea the prophet lived in the northern kingdom of Israel and stayed there through his career. The book's opening names him as the son of Beeri. His marriage stands at the center of the account. His wife was unfaithful, fled, and had to be bought back by the prophet.

The entry argues that this story is real history, not mere allegory, though the wife's name can be read as a symbol. Other claims get less trust. Ideas that Hosea fled to Judah or served as a priest lack support. Later Jewish and Christian tales about his birthplace, tribe, and burial at Safed are called worthless as history.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ibn-barun-abu-i:
Abu Ibrahim Ishak ibn Barun was a Spanish grammarian of the eleventh and twelfth centuries, probably at Barcelona. He studied under Levi ibn Tabban of Saragossa. Judah ha-Levi and Moses ibn Ezra, his contemporaries, wrote poems for him, and Moses mourned him in an elegy. He knew Arabic letters deeply.

Ibn Barun was the first to see the close kinship between Hebrew and Arabic grammar and word stock. His Kitab al-Muwazanah, the Book of Comparison, treats grammar in one part and the lexicon in the other. Long known only from quotes, parts of it surfaced in St. Petersburg and were printed in 1894. Medieval Hebrew scholars mostly passed him by, a neglect the entry notes with regret.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-isaac-ben-levi-: Isaac ben Levi ben Saul of Lucena was a Spanish grammarian and liturgical poet of the first half of the eleventh century. He was a contemporary of Isaac Gikatilla and Isaac ibn Halfon. Ibn Janah quoted him under the name Isaac b. Saul, and Moses ibn Ezra and Abraham ibn Ezra also cited his verses. Poems survive that carry his name in acrostic, among them a selihah for the seventeenth of Tammuz and a poem for the seventh day of Passover.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-israel-ben-uri-: Israel ben Uri Shraga was a German tosafist of the thirteenth century who died before 1298. Little is known of his life or family, the entry admits. He was a pupil of the tosafist Samuel of Bamberg. About 1250 he was called to succeed his teacher as rabbi of Bamberg. His family perished in the persecution at the century's end, after his own death. His tosafot are often quoted under the heading "Tosafot ha-Rab R. Israel."
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jacob-benno-839: Benno Jacob was a German rabbi and Bible scholar born at Breslau on Sept. 8, 1862. He was educated in his home town at the gymnasium, the university, and the theological seminary, taking his doctorate in 1889. Since 1891 he has been rabbi at Göttingen. His writings include a study of the book of Esther in the Septuagint (1890) and a work on the Bible in scholarship and teaching (1898). He also edited a volume of sermons by Benjamin Rippner and wrote often for Stade's journal.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jaddua-8494:
Jaddua was a high priest at the time of the Second Temple. Nehemiah chapter 12 names his father, though one verse gives Jonathan and another Johanan. The entry weighs whether those names mean one man or two, and whether Jaddua matches the Jaddus named by Josephus for the time of Alexander the Great.

Josephus tells of a high priest who greeted Alexander with respect before the gates of Jerusalem. Talmudic accounts give that same story to Simon the Just. The entry follows Josephus, notes that the Alexander meeting seems to be a legend, and points readers to the hard problem of the priestly lists in Nehemiah and Josephus.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jeremiah-ben-el:
Jeremiah ben Eleazar is the name of two Palestinian scholars treated together in the entry. The first lived in the second century, a fellow of Simeon ben Gamaliel. He is known through one teaching passed on by his pupil Bar Kappara, giving reasons for the death of Aaron's sons Nadab and Abihu. A Syrian church writer later used his reading without naming him.

The second Jeremiah was a story teacher of the later third century with many sayings to his name. He read the Psalms to claim that Adam was first made with two faces, later split apart. He also taught that the builders of the Tower of Babel fell into three groups with three fates, and he treated the crow as a bird of prophecy.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-job-testament-o:
Job, Testament of, is a Greek book outside the canon that retells Job's story as his farewell talk to his children. First printed at Rome in 1833, it drew little notice until scholars took it up in the 1890s and issued new texts and versions. Pope Gelasius had listed it among rejected books around the year 496.

In its telling, Job was once Jobab, a rich ruler of Uz and a descendant of Esau, who turned from idols to the true God. Warned by an angel, he chose a lifelong fight with Satan in hope of lasting fame and a crown in the world to come. His second wife is named as Dinah, daughter of Jacob, a claim the entry notes from tradition.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jose-b-judah-87:
Jose b. Judah was a tanna who lived at the end of the second century. He is known mostly through his debates with R. Judah I. His father was Judah b. Ilai, and he passed on many old traditions learned from him.

The entry gives samples of his teaching. On a verse in Leviticus he taught that a person's yes should mean yes and no should mean no. He read a verse in Deuteronomy to say that troubles sent to a person are dear to God. His picture of two angels coming home with a man on Sabbath eve is also quoted. He held that a convert must accept even the rules taught by the sages.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joseph-ben-tobi:
Joseph ben Tobiah farmed the royal revenues of Egypt from about 220 to 198 before the common era. He was a nephew of the high priest Onias II and founded the Tobiad family. When Onias held back tribute, Joseph went to Alexandria, won over King Ptolemy IV, and gained the post of chief tax farmer for Phenicia and Coele-Syria.

He held that post for twenty-two years and grew very rich. The entry says he used harsh force in gathering taxes, once executing twenty leading men of Ascalon and Scythopolis. His rule helped Judea in wealth but hurt it in morals, the entry argues. Quarrels among his sons split Judea into two hostile camps, the Oniades and the Tobiades.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-judah-ben-ilai-:
Judah ben Ilai was one of the key tannaim of the second century, born at Usha in Galilee. His teachers were his father, Akiba, and Tarfon, whom he served even in small tasks as a boy. Judah b. Baba ordained him while Rome banned the rite. When Hadrian's persecution began, Judah fled Usha and hid.

At the councils of Usha after the ban lifted, he spoke first among the sages, as the best keeper of tradition. He stood close to the patriarch Simon b. Gamaliel II and even won Roman trust by praising their bridges and roads. His own piety was strict: he drank no wine save on days the Law required. His teaching followed Akiba and set law in the form of midrash.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jus-gazaka-or-g: Jus Gazaka, or Gazaga, was the usual Italian term for the right called Hazakah. It bore above all on the renting of houses in the ghetto of Rome. Clement VIII made it part of the law on Jewish tenant rights there. The entry is only a few lines long. It points to printed sets of cases under the law, named in Berliner's history of the Jews in Rome. It also sends readers to a book on Jewish life in the Middle Ages for more.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kahana-jacob-be:
Jacob ben Abraham Kahana was a rabbinical author who died in Wilna in 1826. His father was rabbi at Brestowitz, in the government of Grodno. Jacob married into the family of R. Issachar of Wilna and lived in his father-in-law's house for many years, free to give his time to study of the Law.

In time Kahana stood among the leading Talmud scholars of Wilna, and after Issachar's death he was made trustee of the city's charities. His book "Shiṭṭot" comments on the tractate 'Erubin in three parts, covering the Gemara, the Tosefta, and the matching tractates of the Jerusalem Talmud. It was printed at Lemberg in 1863.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kluger-solomon-:
Solomon ben Judah Aaron Kluger was chief dayyan and preacher of Brody, in Galicia. He was born at Komarow, in Russian Poland, in 1783. He died at Brody on June 9, 1869. He served as rabbi at Rawa, at Kulikow, and at Jozefow. At Brody he held the offices of dayyan and preacher for more than fifty years.

During his long life Kluger wrote a very great number of works. The entry puts them at one hundred and sixty volumes. They cover all branches of rabbinical literature. Only a part of them have been published. His printed works include novellæ on the Shulḥan 'Aruk. He also wrote funeral orations, responsa, and a Haggadah commentary. His rulings on slaughtering were printed in another rabbi's code.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kosteliz-costel: Abigdor ben Simon Kosteliz was an Egyptian rabbi and cabalist who died in 1659. He was born before 1572. He studied under Moses ha-Kohen, head of the yeshibah in Egypt. One of his fellow pupils was David Conforte. That is nearly all the entry states. It gives no writings, no posts, and no life events beyond his teacher, his fellow pupil, and the two date bounds above. Its sources are three short notices in older Hebrew reference works.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kramer-moses-be: Moses ben David Krämer, a Lithuanian Talmudist of the seventeenth century, died at Wilna on Oct. 19, 1683. He served as rabbi in several Lithuanian towns. In 1623 he took the same post at Wilna. Contemporaries cite him often as a leading Talmudist. He left no books of his own. A few glosses survive inside works by his son-in-law and his grandson. Wilna still tells local tales of his piety and learning, the entry says. Elijah of Wilna was among his descendants.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lamego-9594: Lamego, a city in Portugal, had its Jewry on the street now called Rua Nova. Many rich secret Jews lived there and drew deep hatred from Christian neighbors. Jacome da Fonseca of Lamego led the secret Jews' fight against bringing in the Inquisition. A Holy Office court opened in the city in 1542 to public cheers. A mocking program paired the richest secret Jews as musicians and dancers. Panic drove most of them to flee, though many were caught and brought back. The court lasted about six years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-law-civil-13994:
Law, Civil, traces Jewish civil law from tribal custom to the great codes. Old Jewish law drew no line between duty to man and duty to God. The Torah's civil rules fill about fifteen chapters, covering slaves, land, loans, and marriage for a farming people. Land sale was curbed by the Sabbatical year and jubilee.

After the Exile, commerce grew and contract law took the lead. The Mishnah, codified at the end of the second century, joined old custom to five hundred years of growth. Maimonides in the twelfth century and Caro in the sixteenth then codified the whole. Jewish courts still apply this law where parties submit.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-leven-manuel-97:
Manuel Leven, a French physician, was born in 1831. He studied at the Lycée Henri IV in Paris and entered an agronomy institute in 1851. When that school closed a year later, he turned to medicine. His thesis of 1860, on idiocy and cretinism, won a gold medal.

Leven served as a railway company doctor from 1863 and as an ambulance surgeon in the war of 1870-71. From 1873 to 1889 he was head physician of the Hôpital Rothschild. His books treat diseases of the stomach, nerves, and hygiene. With Eugène Manuel he founded a night school for Jewish apprentices in 1848. He also helped found the Alliance Israélite Universelle.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-levy-judah-9894: Judah Levy was a Tunisian rabbinical author who lived and died at Tunis in the mid-nineteenth century. He was a son of Nathan Levy and came first from Gibraltar. Under his own name he printed one Hebrew work, "Mahane Lewiyyah." It has four parts. They treat mourning rules, the duties of Nazirites, Samson's Nazirite vow, and questions of ritual impurity. With David Bonan he also printed two works of responsa on the tractate Sanhedrin, at Leghorn in 1857.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lindo-alexander: Alexander Lindo, an English merchant, died in London in 1818. He dealt in the West India trade. After the Treaty of Amiens he came into dealings with Napoleon. He arranged to ship goods worth £260,000 to the French West Indies for the troops of General Leclerc. The draft drawn on Paris for that sum was dishonored on a slight pretext. Lindo seems never to have got his money. He died in money trouble, and his gift to the Bevis Marks Synagogue was never paid.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lomazy-10094: Lomazy was a town near Brest-Litovsk, Russia. In 1566 no Jew was among its 400 house-owners, yet its customs income was farmed out to Jews. By 1589 Jews held leases on its customs and mills. A cited account says 200 Jews were killed there during the Cossack rising of 1648-49. In 1897 the town had 3,200 people, of whom 1,100 were Jews. The entry relies on archival sources listed at its close.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mahzor-plural-m:
Mahzor, the festival prayer book, is surveyed in a long Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906. The word first meant the yearly cycle itself. Sephardic Jews used it for a prayer collection covering the whole year. Ashkenazic Jews reserved it for the book of festival services alone. Every rite shapes its own Mahzor, so the books differ by country and city.

The article traces the main rites and their spread. The oldest named is the Mahzor Romaniya from the Byzantine empire, printed at Venice and Constantinople. From southern Italy its poetic pieces passed into the Roman rite, first printed at Soncino in 1485. Northern Europe then formed the Ashkenazic rite, with German, Bohemian-Polish, and French branches. The entry follows manuscripts, printings, and commentaries across five centuries. It serves any reader who has wondered why festival prayers differ so much from one community to the next.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-marcello-benede:
Benedetto Marcello, the Venetian composer, is included in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia for his use of Jewish melody. Born at Venice in 1686, he died there in 1739. His fame rests on fifty settings of the Psalms, published between 1724 and 1727. Those noble cantata-style works have been reprinted in many editions.

The article lists the Jewish airs inside eleven of the early Psalms. Six themes come from German Jewish tradition and five from Spanish. A German tune for Ma'oz Zur serves Psalm fifteen. Lekah Dodi, the Sabbath hymn, supplies Psalm nineteen. Other themes come from Hallel, the Kaddish, and hymns of Ibn Gabirol. The writers correct a common error: some historians claimed these were ancient Temple melodies. Marcello's own list of sources shows they were living synagogue tunes. The entry preserves a rare bridge between church music and the synagogue repertoire.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mattithiah-of-p:
Mattithiah of Paris headed that city's Talmudic school in the eleventh century. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and S. Kahn give him a short entry in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The editors identify him, with little doubt, as Mattithiah ben Moses. He was one of the pupils of Rashi, the great commentator, and contemporaries knew him as Mattithiah the Great.

Almost nothing else is recorded here. He corresponded with Samuel ben Meir, the Rashbam, the grandson of Rashi. The Rashbam names him among the “ancients” of Paris, a mark of senior standing in the French schools. For anything more the entry sends readers to “Gallia Judaica” by Gross and to citations in the Mahzor Vitry and other medieval ritual collections. The notice fixes the place of a teacher who stood at the head of Paris learning in the generation of Rashi.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mekilta-plural-:
Mekilta is the halakic midrash on Exodus. Isidore Singer and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach treat it in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its name is a puzzle the article works through. “Mekilta” answers to the Hebrew “middah,” a measure or rule. The legal exposition of Scripture in the work follows fixed rules of interpretation.

Neither Talmud names it as Mekilta; the ancients seem to have called it “She'ar Sifre debe Rab,” the Other Books of the Schoolhouse. The geonim knew it as the Mekilta of the Land of Israel, to set it apart from the Mekilta of Simeon bar Yohai. The entry assigns the book to the school of Rabbi Ishmael, as medieval authorities from R. Nissim to Maimonides did. It admits, though, that its redactor cannot be fixed. It is a model of the source criticism of the encyclopedia: a classic text reached through the history of its names.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-michelson-alber:
Albert A. Michelson, born at Strelno in Prussia on December 19, 1852, became an American physicist of world standing, as Cyrus Adler and Frank H. Vizetelly record in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His father emigrated and settled in San Francisco, where Albert was schooled. He graduated from the United States Naval Academy at Annapolis in 1873.

Michelson resigned from the navy after study at Berlin, Heidelberg, and Paris, and took the physics chair at the Case School in Cleveland. He moved to Clark University in 1889 and, three years later, to the University of Chicago, where he still taught when the article appeared. Honorary degrees from Cambridge and Yale and membership in the Royal Society mark his reputation.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mizrahi-10894:
Mizraḥi — the name simply means an Oriental — belongs to a family of rabbinical authors in the East, with branches at Constantinople and Jerusalem, as the Jewish Encyclopedia records in 1906. Persian Jews settled in Turkey often took it as a surname. The entry strings together the family's scholars across four centuries.

Abraham ben Baruch Mizraḥi was a ritual slaughterer at Jerusalem in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries and wrote a handbook on the slaughtering laws, printed at Amsterdam in 1718. Absalom ben Moses Mizraḥi, three centuries earlier, wrote Imre Shefer, a work on Hebrew poetic form composed in 1391 and quoted by Abraham de Balmes. Carmoly printed it at Paris in 1841 from a manuscript.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mordecai-ben-ja:
Mordecai ben Jacob, known as Mordecai Singer, was a Polish translator who lived at Cracow and died in 1575, as the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and S. J. Levinson note in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His work was rendering Scripture into Judæo-German, the vernacular of Ashkenazic Jewry. Two books of his survive.

He translated the Book of Proverbs, printed at Cracow in 1582, and the Book of Job, printed at Prague in 1597 — both appearing after his death, if the dates hold. To each he supplied a commentary in Hebrew, so the volumes taught two languages at once: the text in the vernacular, the learning in the holy tongue. Steinschneider's catalogue is the entry's chief witness.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-isaac-s-1:
Isaac S. Moses was an American rabbi born on December 8, 1847, at Santomischel in Posen. Cyrus Adler and Gotthard Deutsch wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. Educated at Gleiwitz and Breslau, he came to America and took his first pulpit at Quincy, Illinois, in 1879. He went on to Milwaukee, Chicago, and New York.

Moses wrote books for the school and the synagogue: The Pentateuch, The Historical Books of the Bible, and The Ethics of the Hebrew Scriptures. He edited the weekly Der Zeitgeist with his brother Adolph and Emil Hirsch. He also edited hymnals for Jewish worship. His name is tied most closely to the Union Prayer-Book of 1892, which he likewise edited.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mstislavl-11194:
Mstislavl, a district town in the Russian government of Moghilef, had a Jewish community from the sixteenth century. Herman Rosenthal and S. Janovsky wrote the Jewish Encyclopedia article on it. The community seems to have been poor: in 1639 its synagogue silver was in pawn with a Christian.

By 1897 the Jews of Mstislavl numbered about five thousand six hundred, well over half the town. Among them were nine hundred fifty artisans and over a hundred day laborers. Children learned in the Talmud Torah, and seventy-five attended the city school. The article also notes societies for visiting the sick and for helping the needy.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nahum-of-gimzo-:
Nahum of Gimzo was a tanna of the first century and the teacher of Akiba. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. His nickname, the man of gam zu, came from his motto. At every misfortune he would say: this, too, will be for the best.

Nahum taught Akiba the rules of inclusion and exclusion, and read the whole Torah by them. One verse he refused to stretch: nothing may share the reverence owed to God alone. Paralyzed in old age, he told his pupils he had cursed himself for a delay that cost a starving man his life. He bore his sufferings, the article says, with joy.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nazareth-the-mo:
Nazareth is a town in Galilee, north of Esdraelon's plain. Isidore Singer and George A. Barton wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It sits about 1,200 feet above the Mediterranean Sea. The Old Testament never names the town at all. The New Testament calls it Jesus' boyhood home.

John's Gospel shows Nazareth was an obscure place. Nearby Japhia drew all notice in Bible times. Eusebius placed it fifteen Roman miles east of Legio. Epiphanius says only Jews lived there until Constantine. By the late sixth century, pilgrims came to visit it. Antoninus saw an old synagogue and a church there. Crusaders later rebuilt the town and moved a bishopric there.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-new-moon-blessi:
The blessing of the new moon is said under open sky. Joseph Jacobs and Judah David Eisenstein wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Worshipers face the moon, ideally ten or more together. The rite is old, named in a baraita. Its praise thanks God who renews the moon monthly.

The text calls the moon a crown of beauty. It is a sign that Israel, too, will be renewed. Saturday night, in Sabbath dress, is the favored time. The blessing must not wait past the month's sixteenth day. In Ab it waits until after the fast ends. Dancers once leaped toward the moon in joy. Now worshipers rise on tiptoe three times instead. Greetings of peace close the small ceremony.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-northeim-11594:
Northeim is a town in Prussia's Hanover province. Gotthard Deutsch and Abraham Lewinsky wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It holds 6,695 people, over 100 of them Jews. Jews lived there by the fifteenth century. They paid a small tax twice a year.

The council sheltered single Jews despite ducal expulsions. Abraham won three years' protection from 1556. He paid ten gulden a year for it. The duke used him to supply the mint's silver. In 1571 suspicion of robbers drove him out. Moses the mint man followed with his family. His life protection cost fifty marks in 1589. Duke Heinrich Julius expelled them all in 1591. A diet's act barred Jews again in 1639. Two families returned under Westphalian rule in 1809.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-olschwanger-isa:
Isaac Wolf Olschwanger was a Russian rabbi of wide kin ties. Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Plungian in August 1825. He died at St. Petersburg on August 5, 1896. His line ran back to Mordecai Jaffe, an author. It also ran back to Judah Löw of Prague.

Olschwanger had a full Hebrew schooling as a boy. He read Talmud with Israel Lipkin, a famed sage. He took his rabbi's diploma in the year 1845. Next year he was chosen rabbi at Tauroggen. In time he turned to worldly studies as well. In 1878 he was chosen rabbi at St. Petersburg. He held that post till his death came. He backed groups that spread learning among Russian Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pappenheim-simo:
Simon Pappenheim was a German writer from Dembiohammer. Isidore Singer and Abraham Lewinsky wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born there in the year 1773. He died at Ratibor on August 6, 1840. At first he earned his bread as a home tutor.

Simon then took a post as head of a pottery works. That post was at Ratibor, a town in Silesia. All the while he kept at his books with zeal. He became the house poet of a Ratibor news sheet. That sheet was set up in the year 1802 there. In 1811 its editor gave up the post of chief. Simon took that post in the man's place at once. His verse in the sheet bore a strong love of land. From 1816 he put the sheet out at his own cost.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pekah-11994:
Pekah, son of Remaliah, was a king of Israel. Emil G. Hirsch and Ira Maurice Price wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He seized the throne by murder in about 736 BCE. His reign fell in Israel's last, chaotic decades.

Pekah had served as captain to King Pekahiah. With fifty men of Gilead he killed him in the palace. He then allied with Rezin of Damascus. The two kings marched on Judah to force its king into line. Ahaz instead called Assyria for help. Assyria stripped Pekah's lands, and Hoshea killed him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-philanthropin-t:
The Philanthropin was the high school of Frankfurt's Jewish community. Gotthard Deutsch and I. Kracauer wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Siegmund Geisenheimer founded it with friends in 1804. Its spark came from the movement of Moses Mendelssohn. It still taught Frankfurt's Jewish youth a century later.

At first the school taught poor children free of charge. Paying pupils joined from 1806 and numbers rose fast. A girls' school was added in 1810. The grand duchy took the school into its public system. Hard years followed when state funds were cut. A grand new building opened in 1845.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pius-iv-gian-an:
Pius the Fourth was pope from 1559 to 1565. Gotthard Deutsch and Hermann Vogelstein wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born Gian Angelo Medici, he came from Milan. He stood in sharp contrast to Paul the Fourth. He closed the long Council of Trent at last.

Under Pius the Jews of Rome breathed more freely. He revoked many of Paul's harsh restrictions there. Jews might drop the badge while traveling briefly. They could widen the ghetto and shop outside it. He even let them print the Talmud, renamed. His pressure saved Bohemia's Jews from expulsion.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-prossnitz-12394:
Prossnitz is an Austrian mill town in the province of Moravia. Gotthard Deutsch wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its first Jews likely came late in the fifteenth century. They were exiles from Olmütz who found shelter there in 1454. For long it held Moravia's second largest Jewish group.

That group counted 328 families at its height. Laws once capped how many Jewish families might live in a place. Prossnitz stayed near the top of that count for years. The group rose to note early in the seventeenth century. A scholar named Simhah ben Gershon led it then. The entry names its rabbis and its schools.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rabbi-my-master:
Rabbi, meaning my master, is the title of the learned teachers of Israel. Six writers joined in the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. They are Singer, Broydé, Jacobs, Eisenstein, Kohler, and Landsberg. The title marks a man known for his learning. He is a true teacher of the Law. He is the set head of his community in faith.

The word comes from a Hebrew noun for great. In Bible Hebrew it means great or set apart. In later Hebrew it means master, against slave. It can mean master against pupil as well. In the schools of Palestine the sages bore such names. The article traces the title's rise and its ranks.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ratner-isaac-12: Isaac Ratner was a Russian mathematician born at Shklov in 1857. Herman Rosenthal and Isidor Warsaw wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He wrote math and astronomy pieces for various journals. The article names his book Mishpat Emet, printed in 1884. It criticizes Lichtenfeld's pamphlets against Slonimski's works. Ratner also edited a second edition of a Slonimski book. That book, from 1888, sets out the principles of algebra. Two source lists end the short entry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-responses-to-be:
Responses to benedictions center on the word Amen. Cyrus Adler and Lewis N. Dembitz wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. A benediction begins or ends with Blessed be Thou, O Lord. Hearers answer Amen when a leader reads it aloud.

The article explains that Amen means true or truly. Greek use already treated it as a fixed term. Its roots lie in the double Amen of Psalms. Three books of Psalms end with that response. The Mishnah warns against answering a Samaritan too fast. Hearers must first catch every word he says. A Babylonian teacher warns against shouting Amen too loudly. The response should not outdo the leader's voice. The entry gives rules for a single small word.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-roder-martin-12:
Martin Röder was a German composer and conductor born on April 7, 1851. Isidore Singer and A. Porter wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born in Berlin. He died at Boston on June 7, 1895.

The article says he studied at Berlin's Royal High School for Music. From 1873 to 1880 he was chorus master in Milan. He founded a choral quartet society there in 1875. He conducted opera at Bologna, Turin, and even the Azores. He taught singing in Berlin through the 1880s. Dublin's Royal Academy then employed him for five years. In 1892 he led vocal work at Boston's New England Conservatory. His works include three operas and two symphonic poems. He also wrote books on Italian music life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rome-12294:
Rome was capital of the ancient Roman republic and empire. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Jews have lived in Rome for over two thousand years. That is longer than in any other European city.

The article says they first came from Alexandria for trade. A community may have existed by the second century B.C. In 139 B.C. a decree expelled non citizen Jews. After the Hasmonean wars the community grew very fast. Captives were ransomed or freed by their masters. They settled as traders across the Tiber River. That settlement began the Jewish quarter in Rome. Jews paid the Temple tax to Jerusalem from Rome. Caesar let them hold public worship in gratitude. Grain shares were saved for them past the Sabbath.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosnosky-isaac-:
Isaac Rosnosky was an American merchant and communal worker born at Wollstein, Prussia, on November 6, 1846. Cyrus Adler and Joseph Lebovich wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He came to Boston as a boy and went into business.

Rosnosky won a Boston council seat in 1878 and served in the Massachusetts House. He was the first Jew elected to either branch of that legislature. He returned to the House from 1891 to 1894 for further terms. From 1882 he presided over Temple Ohabei Shalom, Boston's oldest Hebrew congregation. He also helped raise a hospital fund of ten thousand dollars.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sahl-ben-mazlia:
Sahl ben Mazliah ha-Kohen was a Karaite philosopher and writer born at Jerusalem in 910. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He traveled widely as an apostle of Karaism.

Sahl knew the Bible and later Jewish literature deeply, and mastered Arabic. Though Saadia's bitter foe, he aimed most attacks at the gaon's pupil. His polemics fought Rabbinite rules on purity, Sabbath lights, and drawing water. He charged Rabbinite teachers with preaching for gain, unlike the Karaites. His writings also preserve a sharp eye on lax observance then.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-ben-davi:
Samuel ben David Moses ha-Levi was a Polish Talmudist born about 1625. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and A. Peiginsky wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. As a wandering scholar he passed through Meseritz and Halberstadt.

In 1660 Samuel became rabbi of Bamberg, residing at Zeckendorf nearby. His violent temper and self-assertion soon made him many enemies there. He had dared to set his learning against the great Mah RIL himself. About 1665 he resigned, and used the idle years to prepare his Nahalat Shiv'ah. He ended in the small rabbinate of Kleinsteinbach, in Bavaria.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sarah-sarai-131:
Emil G. Hirsch, Wilhelm Bacher, Jacob Zallel Lauterbach, Joseph Jacobs, and Mary W. Montgomery wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906, on Sarah. She was Abraham's wife, first called Sarai. For many years she had no child. She traveled with Abraham from Haran to Canaan. A famine drove them down into Egypt. There Abraham passed her off as his sister.

Pharaoh took Sarah into his house and enriched Abraham. Troubles then revealed the truth, and Pharaoh sent them away. Still childless, Sarah gave Abraham her maid Hagar.
