Two American surveys asked adults whether animals experience emotions, and how often they avoid products or foods that involve animal use; the second survey deliberately recruited many vegetarians and vegans.

Belief in animal emotions predicted avoidance of animal-tested goods, animal events, and animal foods, beyond age, schooling, and gender. Pet contact and personal moral or spiritual outlooks fed those beliefs. Kisley argues consumer ethics toward animals rests partly on how real their inner lives seem.
plos-pone-0354894:
Feng An and Wenyin Tao tackle a hard safety problem: spotting when a large language model reasons in deceptive ways. Older monitors label whole answers as safe or deceptive and lean on heavyweight teacher models. Their 2026 paper instead trains a tiny monitor that reads the model's hidden chain-of-thought states.

The monitor maps those states into a space where honest and deceptive reasoning sit apart. Training pulls similar cases together and pushes unlike ones away, so gradual shifts toward deception become visible. On a sycophancy test set, the contrastive monitor beat a standard classifier at flagging deceptive tendency. An and Tao argue that watching reasoning geometry offers a lighter path to self-supervised safety checks.
plos-pone-0355194:
Hailong Zong and colleagues assess in 2026 genetic variety and yield links in soybean lines from many origins, grown in two settings. Soybean is a key food and oil crop first raised in China, and breeders seek higher yield with good quality. A small set of DNA markers was run across the lines, and a dozen plant traits were measured for variety and grouping.

Plants varied widely in traits such as height, pod count, and seed weight. Marker analysis showed rich variety and split the lines into a few clear groups. Dozens of markers linked to yield traits, with a handful confirmed in both settings. Breeders can use those stable markers to pick parents.
plos-pone-0355294:
Tushna Vandrevala and her team asked Black and South Asian adults in Britain how they decide if health advice can be trusted. Good choices need facts that people can use and trust. Yet groups like these often get leaflets and web pages that ignore their lives, their faith, and their past care. The team held long talks with dozens of people and watched how advice moves in group settings.

Friends, kin, and social media ranked as the most trusted sources of health facts. Dry, stiff advice that felt cold pushed people to search in other places first. Some ways of checking matched those of the wider public. But past events and group norms shaped how checks were made, and why. The team urges health staff to write warm, plain advice with known local voices, or risk being tuned out for good.
plos-pone-0355394:
Mayu Takizawa and co-authors develop in 2026 a fast DNA test that can single out and count the exact bacterium strain used to ferment soybeans into natto. The strain looks almost identical to close relatives, and older markers fail on some odd isolates. Comparing dozens of genomes, the team found one communication gene that stays perfectly intact across the natto line while other markers wobble.

A test built on that gene measured amounts across a very wide range and stayed accurate even when swamped by other bacterial DNA. On shop bought fermented soy foods, test counts matched living cell counts closely. Food quality checks and hospital tracking could both use it.
plos-pone-0355494:
Tingxuan Li, Ziyu Liu, and Deping Zou survey in 2026 Chinese university students who use artificial intelligence tools to write in English as a second language. Their model links confidence with the tools, ease of use, felt usefulness, felt risk, and how actively students engage. Several hundred valid replies were tested with a structural model.

Confidence raised both ease and usefulness ratings. Oddly, students who found the tools most useful also reported stronger risk awareness, rather than less. A positive attitude drove active engagement, which linked more to good than to bad writing outcomes in students' own reports. The authors note self reports cannot prove real gains.
plos-pone-0355694:
Juying Li and five colleagues published a heart attack study in PLOS ONE in 2026. They focused on a cell alarm system that senses stray DNA and triggers inflammation, known as the cGAS-STING pathway. After a heart attack, that alarm may add to the damage in heart tissue.

Li's team searched for markers tied to this pathway that could flag injury, and they traced how the pathway acts after an attack. Their work names candidate markers that doctors might one day measure, and points to steps in the pathway that drugs could target. Both leads matter because limiting early damage is key to how well a patient recovers.
plos-pone-0356294:
Till Kastendieck, Ursula Hess, and Christophe Blaison test how a threat in one place stains feelings attached to places around it, in PLOS ONE in 2026. In two experiments totaling several hundred participants, people faced a threat of electric shock tied to one spot in a screen based environment, the hotspot. Theory predicted the surroundings would split: soured close by, sweetened farther away, a pattern called affective polarization of space.

Self reports confirmed the pattern. Near the hotspot, the area felt negative and highly arousing; farther out, it felt positive with low arousal. Body measures told a narrower story: skin and heart responses showed people felt more threatened near the spot, but did not mirror the polarization. Nor did feelings toward strangers shown at spots shift as predicted. The subjective geography of fear, the authors conclude, is real, but its reach into body and social judgment is limited.
plos-pone-0356394:
Shuang Shi developed a way to align roadside laser scanners and cameras without placing special targets in the street. Matching the two sensors is essential when they are fused to watch traffic across wide areas. The 2026 method reads natural features from real traffic scenes instead of artificial markers.

Shi matches shapes and structures across the two data types, working from rough matches to fine ones. Time consistency across frames steadies the result in busy, changing scenes. On a self-built roadside dataset, average errors stayed very small. The method also held up in dim light, with blocked views, and in dense traffic, which supports its use on real roads.
plos-pone-0356494:
Ronald Kibirige and colleagues studied epilepsy care in two districts of central Uganda, Buikwe and Mukono, in 2026 work based on fieldwork from 2024. People with epilepsy there attend community clinics and depend on daily anti-seizure medicine to stay safe. The team set out to learn how many patients actually take their medicine as directed, and what helps or gets in the way.

About two thirds of the nearly three hundred patients surveyed were taking their medicine well. Better adherence was linked with a modest steady income, while long waits at the clinic and too-low doses were linked with worse adherence. Interviews added human detail: fear of stigma, money worries, family support, and mistaken beliefs about the drugs all shaped whether patients kept up their treatment.
plos-pone-0356694:
Monika Dobrogowska studied young girls and beauty culture in a qualitative PLOS ONE paper from 2026. The trend nicknamed Sephora Kids involves preteens buying skincare and anti-aging products aimed at adults. Dobrogowska examined how concern with appearance and body capital takes hold so early in adolescence.

Through close qualitative work, the study traces how marketing and social media reach ever younger buyers. It also weighs what that early pressure costs the girls it targets. Parents, schools, and regulators debating age limits on such products gain grounded insight here. The work adds a careful voice to a debate often driven by headlines rather than by listening to young people themselves.
plos-pone-0356894:
Khaled A Alrasheed led a team of six authors studying digital tools in green construction, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Building information modeling, or BIM, lets teams design and test a building in software before building it. The team studied how BIM support affects the adoption of green building practice in the construction industry.

Alrasheed's findings show where the digital tool speeds up sustainable construction and where it stalls. Green features often fail on coordination, not intent, and BIM is built for coordination. Knowing its real effect helps firms decide how much to invest in the software and training. As building codes tighten on energy use, evidence on what actually drives adoption is valuable.
plos-pone-0356994:
Samuel J Enumah, Xue Wu, Xueya Cai, and Yue Li examined how reliance on contract labor, such as travel nurses, relates to hospital finances across the United States. Their 2026 study combined national hospital datasets covering nearly three thousand hospitals over multiple years, and tracked operating margins, total margins, and signs of financial distress against spending on temporary staff.

Hospitals spending more on contract labor ran thinner margins and faced more distress. Hospitals with high surgical volume fared better financially overall, but volume did not soften the drag from contract labor costs; the penalty appeared at busy and quiet hospitals alike. With closures threatening access to surgical care, the findings warn that stopgap staffing quietly erodes the hospitals it keeps afloat.
plos-pone-0357094:
Sarah E Stansfield and colleagues modeled a question about HIV prevention pills for women in South Africa. Could women take them only around the time of sex, rather than daily, and still be protected? Their 2026 study built a simulated group from a real Cape Town trial. The trial's records gave sex frequency and pill taking. The team then tested four schedules of the preventive drug combination. Each ran over six months.

Daily use protected best, with effectiveness in the mid-eighties percent range. On-demand schedules landed lower. But women who managed fewer than about three daily pills a week gained slightly from switching. The before-and-after schedule helped them, and they took fewer pills doing it. Offering on-demand options, the authors argue, could rescue protection for women whom daily routines defeat.
plos-pone-0357294:
Stephanie Rupp and Hanna Schwendemann listened to mothers in Germany whose children have speech or developmental concerns, in a PLOS ONE study from 2026. Getting help means moving through referrals, waiting lists, and handovers between services. The authors studied that path as mothers live it, focusing on guidance, transitions, and communication.

Rupp and Schwendemann's qualitative work exposes where the system helps families and where it leaves them stranded. Breaks usually happen at transitions, when one service ends and another has not begun. Naming those weak points gives German health and education services a repair list. The mothers' accounts also remind planners that a pathway is only as good as its worst handover.
plos-pone-0357594:
Shili Yang and colleagues run a fully computational hunt for molecular links between a food toxin and liver cancer. The toxin, made by molds that contaminate stored grain and nuts, is known to harm the liver, but its cancer pathways stay fuzzy. The team merged toxin targets and cancer targets from public databases. They overlapped them with genes changed in a public liver tumor dataset. Then they ranked the survivors. Selection algorithms, docking, and motion simulation did the ranking.

A few hundred shared targets clustered in signaling, cell death, metabolism, and immune pathways. Five candidate genes rose to the top, some raised and some lowered in tumors, each sorting tumor from normal tissue well within the dataset. Docking predicted snug toxin binding, strongest for a major drug-processing enzyme. Yang and colleagues offer the five as leads for lab confirmation.
plos-pone-0357794:
Rili Yu and coauthors published a 2026 anesthesia study in PLOS ONE on why so many shoulder surgery patients wake up nauseated. Surgeons often lower blood pressure deliberately during shoulder arthroscopy to keep the view clear, but pressure dips can provoke nausea. The team reviewed just over three hundred patients and asked whether sustained low pressure, a drop of at least a fifth lasting an hour, independently predicted postoperative nausea and vomiting.

Nearly a third of patients suffered it. In adjusted analysis, four factors stood out: being female, a history of motion sickness or prior nausea, the sustained pressure drop, and, protectively, smoking. Patients with sustained hypotension also endured more severe symptoms when it struck; the association held after adjustment, roughly doubling the odds. Anesthesiologists, they suggest, should weigh the nausea cost when deciding how deep and long to run deliberate hypotension, and flag affected patients for preventive treatment.
plos-pone-0358194:
Xiaoyun Wu, Danting Cao, and Beihe Wu ask whether digital skill buys not just a job, but a better job, in PLOS ONE in 2026. They used a nationally representative Chinese household survey from 2022. From it they built multi part scores for digital literacy and for employment quality, the latter covering pay, security, and conditions. Then they modeled the link between them, with checks for weak spots in the statistics.

Digital literacy came out significantly tied to higher quality employment. The tie strengthened among workers who expected good returns from their skills, and weakened among the already highly educated. It ran strongest in western China and in dense urban clusters, where the authors see either the highest payoff to scarce digital skill or the richest digital economies. Their policy advice targets low skilled workers with tiered training, and urges lagging regions to borrow strength from urban hubs.
plos-pone-0358694:
İsmail Yaşartürk leads a team of four asking whether artificial intelligence can judge children's handwriting as fairly as a human expert, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Sixty-seven fourth graders at a public school produced copying, dictation, and free writing samples, two hundred one pieces. Each was scored on a multidimensional legibility scale twice, once by a researcher and once by ChatGPT, and the two sets of marks were compared dimension by dimension.

Across writing types and scoring dimensions, the artificial intelligence and the human produced no significant differences, with one exception: the slant score in free writing. Their marks correlated strongly and positively. The authors read this as evidence that automated scoring can match expert judgment for handwriting legibility, which could lighten a tedious assessment burden in crowded classrooms. They frame the tool as an assistant to teachers, whose knowledge of each child no scale captures.
plos-pone-0358994:
Michael Kagiri and eight colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It studies Kenya's Electronic Community Health Information System, called eCHIS, used by frontline health workers. The authors examine what enables its use and what blocks it in daily work.

Their lens is the Work System Framework, which looks at people, tasks, technology, and setting together rather than blaming the software alone. Frontline workers' experiences show where a digital system fits community health work and where it fights it. Kenyan health officials and other countries digitizing community care can use these barriers and enablers to plan rollouts.
plos-pone-0359094:
Elif Sertesen Çamöz and five colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on early-onset colorectal cancer, bowel cancer arising in younger adults. It describes a distinct NGS mutational landscape, the pattern of gene mutations read by next-generation sequencing, and its prognostic implications, what the pattern suggests about outcomes.

The analysis is dual-cohort, drawing on two large cancer datasets: the PanCancer Atlas of TCGA and the MSK-IMPACT 50K cohort. Early-onset cases are rising for reasons still debated, so showing their mutations differ from typical cases matters. Oncologists and cancer geneticists treating younger patients are the readers for a two-cohort mutation map.
pmc-10468394:
Watson, Juergens, Bennett, and co-authors present RFdiffusion, a deep learning method for designing brand new proteins. Proteins are the working parts of cells, and making new ones from scratch could yield new drugs and materials. Recent computer methods had made real gains, yet no single method handled many design tasks well.

RFdiffusion aims to be that general method. The authors show it tackling hard jobs such as designing proteins that bind tightly to a chosen target. A broad design tool could shorten the path from an idea for a protein to a real molecule that labs can test.
pmc-10652494:
Yi Li leads a large team in a genome study of a yeast that shrugs off a key drug class in China. The paper is from two thousand twenty-three. Candida glabrata is a top cause of deep yeast infection, and echinocandin drugs are the first line against it. Long watch on drug response was due.

They test over a thousand samples from hospitals across five years. Resistance is rare, under one in a hundred, and one drug of the class works best. Genome reads of the proof strains find shared changed genes, one long known to dull response. Shifts cluster near chromosome ends, and strains that evolve inside a patient swap their grip genes. The drugs stay strong in China, with watch still owed.
pmc-10675194:
Kim and colleagues published in twenty twenty-three a study mapping air pollution across Bucheon, Korea, with a mobile laboratory. Fixed monitoring stations are sparse, especially along roads outside big cities. A vehicle-based lab can fill those gaps by measuring while moving. The team combined the mobile data with geographic information system mapping. They overlaid pollution with traffic, speed, and population patterns. Winter measurements captured the city's pollution in fine spatial detail.

Pollution peaked during commuting hours at intersections and one managed road. Coarse and fine particle levels hit their highs near a concrete plant district. Nitrogen oxide gases also peaked during rush hours in the same areas. The patterns point to traffic and industry as shared drivers. The authors argue hotspot maps should guide tailored local measures. Their method helps cities use mobile data instead of just collecting it.
pmc-10680994:
Amar Ahmad and five colleagues published a population study in two thousand twenty-three on vitamin D and COVID-19 deaths across Europe. Early reports hinted that countries with low average vitamin D lost more people. The team updated that check with data through mid two thousand twenty-three.

They combined COVID-19 records for nineteen countries with published average vitamin D levels. Countries averaging above the midpoint level had lower death rates than those at or below it. A rank correlation also ran negative, linking higher vitamin D with fewer deaths. The authors stress that country-level links cannot prove cause. They call for proper supplement trials while the debate continues.
pmc-10698194:
Edin Muratspahić and co-authors noted in 2023 a built molecule that grips the kappa-opioid receptor in a two-part embrace. The kappa receptor is a prized pain target, but engineering peptide ligands for one receptor remains hard. Their computational method designs conjugates: a lariat-shaped macrocyclic peptide fused to a small molecule opioid ligand. So the hybrid engages the receptor with its peptide and small molecule hands at once.

The lead conjugate joined strong binding with an on purpose mixed profile, activating the kappa receptor while blocking the mu receptor. A pairing to keep analgesia while shedding mu side effects. In male mice it made potent kappa-mediated pain relief. A detailed cryo-electron microscopy form of the conjugate bound to the receptor, supported by molecular motion models. Checked the design model and exposed the residue network, spanning the receptor's outer loops and helices, that controls its signaling bias.
pmc-10700594:
Tatsuji Nishizawa and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-three study of driving on roads covered in volcanic ash. Ashfall can paralyse cities after eruptions. Rescue workers and residents still need vehicles that can move.

Driving tests measured how cars perform as ash depth grows. All-wheel-drive vehicles coped better than two-wheel-drive ones. Two-wheel-drive cars stuck once ash passed a stated depth. Tyres sank and wasted power scraping ash aside. The authors tie safe driving mainly to drive system and ash thickness, which weather and traffic keep changing. Disaster planners get tested limits for evacuation routes.
pmc-10700994:
So Yeong Jeong and eight colleagues test whether adding a CT scan to ultrasound before thyroid cancer surgery changes care or outcomes, in a twenty twenty-three study. Ultrasound is the standard check for this cancer, but it can miss spread to neck lymph nodes. The team reviewed patients operated on in twenty fifteen, comparing those who also had a CT scan with those who had ultrasound alone.

In about sixteen percent of the scanned group, the two methods disagreed on node spread, and the CT was right more often. Only a few patients had their surgery plan changed by the scan. After fair matching of the groups, scanned patients stayed free of recurrence longer. The authors support CT as a useful add-on before surgery.
pmc-10701794:
Osama Alrodiman, Fahad Alwadi, Mohammed Almahdi, and Majed Pharaon report a rare slow-growing nasal cancer in a forty-three-year-old man, in a two thousand twenty-three case report with literature review. Sinonasal non-intestinal-type adenocarcinoma is an uncommon tumor that clinicians must remember when nosebleeds keep recurring.

The patient, regularly exposed to wood and dust particles, had a mass filling the entire right nasal cavity, attached to the septum on imaging. Biopsy confirmed the low-grade diagnosis, although mitotic figures more typical of aggressive subtypes were present. Low-grade tumors carry a better prognosis than high-grade ones. Symptoms such as obstruction and bleeding can drag on for years before diagnosis.
pmc-10704694:
Xiuqin Bao and colleagues reported two previously unknown gene deletions behind a blood condition trait in 2023. Beta thalassemia usually comes from small single-letter changes in the beta-globin gene cluster. Faster sequencing keeps finding new variants, and characterising them helps families understand risk and plan screening before birth.

Each of two unrelated Chinese families carried a different new deletion in the beta-globin gene. On their own, both deletions caused only the mild trait form. Combined with a severe zero-production variant, though, either could lead to intermediate or major disease. The report widens the known variant list for the Chinese population and supports prenatal diagnosis work.
pmc-10707894:
Maria Karelou and eight colleagues synthesized sixteen new quinazoline compounds and tested them against cancer cells. Quinazolinones are a versatile scaffold in medicinal chemistry. The team built the compounds from simple methoxy-bearing starting acids through a straightforward route. Every compound was screened against nine cancer cell lines. A second screen measured activity and selectivity across 109 kinases and four bromodomains.

One compound stood out sharply. Bearing a methoxyphenyl group and a basic side chain, it showed strong activity against most of the tested cell lines. Thermal shift screening helped show which protein targets the series engages. The twenty twenty-three study narrows a broad chemical family to a promising lead. Follow-up work would need to confirm potency and safety in more detailed models.
pmc-10709594:
Kalen Clifton and eight colleagues present STalign, open-source software that lines up spatial transcriptomics data sets so gene activity maps from different tissue slices can be compared. The method measures gene expression in place. But slices warp, tear, and only partly overlap, defeating simple alignment.

STalign uses smooth, invertible deformation mapping to handle partial matches and local distortion. Across methods it achieved a far better match of gene expression and cell types than older landmark methods. Applied to mouse brain data, it lifted region labels from the Allen Brain Atlas onto new samples. It also exposed differences in makeup across structures. The toolkit is released in public, with tutorials for the spatial biology community.
pmc-10726494:
Jonathan Flint leads a team of eight authors reading single-cell methylation maps from mouse hippocampus to learn how to spot which genetic variants actually change gene activity. Connecting variants to behavior is genetics' standing problem. Methylomes from single nuclei across eight inbred mouse strains revealed a density rule: where CpG sites are sparse, cells compensate by methylating new sites to hold levels steady.

Where CpG sites are dense, exact methylation position matters more, and variants there indeed hit transcript levels harder. That gives researchers a prioritization rule for candidate mutations. The authors further argue methylation shapes where mutations are likely to occur at all, making the genome's mutation distribution non-random in a predictable way.
pmc-10730194:
Marcello Abbondio and others mapped gut proteins during stomach infection therapy in 2023. Helicobacter infection is treated with antimicrobials. Drugs reshape gut germs deeply though. Protein-level tracking captures function, not just species. Patients used a set treatment plan. Stool proteins were set side by side across therapy.

Resistance and swelling proteins rose after. Host swelling proteins fell in contrast. Some cancer-linked host proteins also fell. Germ balance was clearly reshaped overall. Protein tracking followed that reshaping well. New treatments could aim to preserve balance. Gut balance becomes a treatment goal. Protein mapping opens that tracking route.
pmc-10733494:
Kazmierczak and co-authors report a rare twin cancer case in a pet dog. The 11-year-old Pomeranian stopped eating and grew lethargic for 18 hours. A belly scan showed a 3 cm mass near the left ovary. Surgery found a second small mass on the right uterine horn. Both organs were removed in the operation.

Lab review named both masses as grade 1 leiomyosarcoma. One sat in the oviduct, a site not yet reported in dogs. The other sat in the uterus, where such tumors are also uncommon. The authors say surgery is a workable cure path. The case adds the oviduct to the map of sites for this tumor.
pmc-10735094:
Li, Jiang, Zhou, and Liao reported a rare rectal growth and reviewed similar cases in twenty twenty-three. A hemolymphangioma mixes blood and lymph vessel tissue. Such growths in the gut are very rare, and only three rectal cases, all widespread, had been reported in English; this one was localized.

Their patient, a fifty-one-year-old woman, had intermittent constipation for three years. Colonoscopy found a bulging lesion on the lower rectum's front-left wall. Ultrasound and MRI mapped a cystic mass with clear borders between rectum and vagina. Surgeons removed it, and pathology confirmed a focal hemolymphangioma. The authors stress that imaging is essential to diagnose these lesions and judge how far they extend before treatment.
pmc-10737394:
Jocelyn Rutledge and Meaghan Barlow wrote this research paper, published in 2023, about what people believe about controlling emotions. It compares younger and older adults, and people with and without a long-term illness.

The study drew on a sample of forty-seven adults. It sorted beliefs into four kinds: whether people think they can control their own feelings, should control them, and the same two views about other people. Adults living with chronic illness reported weaker belief that they could control their own emotions. Younger adults with illness scored lowest of all on that belief. Among healthy adults, the older group showed a different pattern. The paper links these beliefs to emotional well-being across adult life.
pmc-10738494:
Bearden and McAtee reported in twenty twenty-three on a training plan for nursing aides built round a four-part frame for old-age care. The frame asks what matters to the old person, plus drugs, mind state, and moves. A state old-age group paired with a local aide school to build the plan.

Each part was woven into the lessons the aides learn. What-matters talks, safe moves with aids, and signs of low mood or fog were all taught. Drug-free ways to aid sleep and pain were taught in place of more pills. All thirty-four aides in the run met both goals in a live care test.
pmc-10741194:
Shuai Lian and eight co-authors study a cow virus and udder infection in this twenty twenty-three paper. The virus lives in dairy cows around the world and weakens the udder cells' defense against germs. Small bits of virus code, called microRNAs, can switch host genes off and help the virus spread.

One such bit was already known to help a common germ stick to udder cells. The team traced how: the bit targets a mucus gene that normally guards the cell surface. Lab tests confirmed the bit binds that gene and turns it down. With the guard lowered, the germ sticks more easily, a step toward udder infection in herds.
pmc-10741594:
MariaAnna Messina and a team of co-authors work on a flaw in newborn screening, in a study published in twenty twenty-three. Screening spots babies with rare metabolic diseases early, but it also raises false alarms that stress families and cost money. One marker, called C4, rises in two different rare diseases and in healthy babies too.

The team studied the chemical profiles of one hundred twenty-one newborns whose C4 was high. They found seven new ratios between C4 and other markers. Those ratios split the groups well: false alarms from each true disease, and the two diseases from each other. Cut-off values were set and applied to the screening program. The authors say the ratios should cut false alarms and speed the right diagnosis.
pmc-10742194:
Andrea Flores-Espinoza and her team set out traits of gels of gelatin and chitosan for tooth care use. They test life traits, germ-fight traits, and strength traits. Their 2023 study weighs a plant-like polymer in wide use for wound care, for use in tooth care.

Gels were made at three grades of chitosan. They were tested for break-down, swell, and chem build. Stem cells from tips of tooth roots were grown with the gels. That test checked stick and growth through two days. Germ-fight acts were tested on the main germ that drives holes in teeth. Both spread and thin-out ways were used for that test. Pull strength gauged how the gels did as stuff. Break-down and swell spans split by mix. Red-ray checks made the work groups of the gels firm for tooth stuff plans.
pmc-10743494:
Martina Maria Cocco and nine co-authors test whether the Zika virus can kill neuroendocrine pancreatic tumors, in a study from twenty twenty-three. Their group had shown the virus attacks brain tumor cells with unusual specificity and minimal effects in adults. Neuroendocrine tumors of the pancreas were the next candidate.

The virus specifically infected the neuroendocrine tumor cells, halting growth and killing them. Standard pancreatic adenocarcinoma cells, by contrast, were not susceptible, confirming a narrow spectrum. The authors argue the specificity that suits the virus to brain tumors extends to this pancreatic subtype. The findings support exploring Zika-based therapy for neuroendocrine pancreatic tumors.
pmc-10745094:
Hsiang-Lin Tsai and co-authors set two first-line pairs of chemotherapy drugs side by side, for metastatic colorectal cancer that holds a set BRAF mutation. Their 2023 study was done at one centre, based on what was seen in care. It gives early data from the real world.

Twenty-five patients were looked back on. They were treated from 2015 to 2022. All had genetic tests tied to how drugs are dealt with in the body, before care started. One plan raised the dose of irinotecan step by step. The other used three drugs as a set. Both were paired with bevacizumab. In a median follow-up of fifteen months, severe bad events did not split the two arms by a share that counts. Nor did measures of survival at set points in time. These cancers have a poor outlook and split in their results. That is what drives the check.
pmc-10753694:
Ramezani and four co-authors reported a water treatment polymer in twenty twenty-three that responds to carbon dioxide. Forward osmosis pulls water through a membrane using a draw solute, a substance that attracts water strongly. A good draw solute must create high pressure, flow easily, and be cheap to recover afterward.

An earlier version of their polymer grew too thick and sticky at useful strengths. Comparing chain lengths and shapes, they found short chains beat branched ones for low thickness with high pressure. Under carbon dioxide, their solution reached very high osmotic pressure and drew water well from salt water. Under plain air, pressure dropped and the polymer could be recovered with mild heating, easing reuse.
pmc-11532394:
Wang and co-authors reported this plant disease study in twenty twenty-four. A leaf spot disease was killing leaves of a turmeric relative grown in Qinzhou City, China. The leaves showed yellow-brown spots that spread until the leaf died. The team collected the fungus from sick leaves and grew it in pure form in the lab.

By studying its shape and three of its genes, the team showed the fungus was a new species. They named it Curvularia qinzhouensis. It grew best in warm, mildly alkaline conditions. Tests of plant-based chemicals found that honokiol, thymol, and citral all slowed the fungus well. The study gives growers a named cause for the disease and first leads for control.
pmc-11539794:
Chengcheng Li and twelve colleagues found a transcription factor that restores youthful function to aged fat-derived stem cells. Stem cells from fat are used in regenerative therapy, but their power fades with donor age. Comparing gene activity across age groups singled out HES1 as a factor that changes with age. The team raised or lowered HES1 and its target STAT1 in cultured cells. Proliferation, migration, and senescence were then measured.

Boosting HES1 revived the aged cells' growth and movement and reduced senescence markers. HES1 works by binding DNA and suppressing STAT1's production. The rejuvenated cells were finally tested in a skin injury model in male animals. The twenty twenty-four results nominate a single switch for rescuing older stem cell batches, which could widen the donor pool for cell therapies.
pmc-11544794:
Ke Cai leads a twelve-author team analyzing the genetics of the Lvliang black goat, in a study published in two thousand twenty-four. This Chinese local breed is prized for black fur, meat quality, and hardiness. Protecting such breeds requires knowing their genetic health.

Genome-wide SNP data assessed diversity and inbreeding. The population showed high diversity and low inbreeding, good news for conservation. Male goats clustered into thirteen families. Structure analysis placed the breed close to Nanjiang and Qinggoda goats, suggesting shared ancestry. Selection signatures, genomic regions shaped by breeding, were also mapped. The authors provide a baseline for managing the breed's germplasm. Local breeds like this one are genetic insurance for changing farming conditions.
pmc-11583794:
Elliott McDowell and seven co-authors track smokers who used Rogue oral nicotine goods for six months. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. Quit of smokes cuts grave ill risk a lot, and taste is oft named as a help to cut down. Adults chose fruit or mint forms and fills, then took surveys at set months.

Near fourteen hundred adults were in the six-month pool. Fruit users cut smokes a bit more than mint users and quit at a higher rate. Near four in ten in each taste group at least halved their smokes. More fruit use tied to both cut and quit, while more mint use tied to cut alone. The study was watch-only, with no set groups.
pmc-11588394:
Abu-Raya, Langley, and Lavoie wrote a French-language review in twenty twenty-four on nirsevimab, a long-acting antibody drug for infants. Its target is respiratory syncytial virus, a common virus that is the top cause of hospital stays for lung infection in young infants.

The drug is not a vaccine. It blocks a surface protein the virus needs to enter cells, and it works about fifty times more strongly than the older option described. The older drug, palivizumab, was given only to a small group of high-risk infants each winter. The authors say infants should get nirsevimab in their first virus season, with the highest-risk babies first. They report it as safe and effective under age one.
pmc-11592094:
A team including Laura De Plano guides readers through the mouse models used to study Alzheimer's disease. Since the mid-nineteen nineties, labs have built mice that copy parts of the disease, starting with mice that overproduce the protein behind its plaques. Later models added the tangle protein or carried the human risk mutations in their own gene. Each model starts its decline at a different age and pace.

The review describes the most used models and lays out when symptoms and brain changes appear in each. The authors intend the guide as a planning aid, so studies pick the mouse whose timeline fits the question asked.
pmc-11592994:
Lin and co-authors compare outcomes after surgery for two related liver cancers at one center. One is a mixed tumor joining liver cell and bile duct features. It runs a more aggressive course, yet its risks were ill defined. Records covered 82 patients operated from 2011 to 2023. Seventy had the pure bile duct cancer of the liver; 12 had the mixed form. Overall survival for all was 21.6 months, with 11.8 months free of recurrence.

The mixed group showed far higher liver enzyme levels at baseline. Survival and recurrence patterns were set side by side. The small mixed group limits firm claims, but the contrast guides follow-up care.
pmc-11595694:
A team including Qili Liu studies how acidity shapes a fungus that rots muskmelon fruit. The fungus also makes a toxin that can build up in the fruit. The team grew the fungus and infected fruit across a range of acid levels, in dishes and in melons. A mildly acidic setting, near pH 6, suited the fungus best.

At that level it grew fastest, attacked hardest, and made the most toxin. It also released more of the enzymes that chew through plant walls and switched on its toxin-making genes. Strong acid or alkali flipped the results. The paper points to acidity control as one lever against this rot.
pmc-11599594:
Judith Sáinz-Pardo Díaz and Álvaro López García present a free software library that lets researchers scrub identifying details from data before sharing it, in this paper from twenty twenty-four. Open science demands shared data, but privacy law rightly forbids sharing much of it raw. Outsourcing the scrubbing is also risky, so the tool works on the researcher's own machine.

Written in the Python language, the library handles tabular data. The user marks which columns identify people, which could identify them in combination, and which hold the sensitive facts to protect. A range of anonymization methods can then be applied, with controls for generalization levels, suppression, and the anonymity strength required. The code was built with modern practices, including automated tests of coverage. The authors offer it as a practical bridge between open data and data protection.
pmc-11603994:
Chi Sun Yun and ten co-authors profile a skin-disease bacterium from Korean pig farms and its drug resistance, in a study from twenty twenty-four. The germ causes a crusting skin disease in suckling and weaned piglets through skin-shedding toxins. Treatment often fails because the strains resist antibiotics.

Seventeen isolates from piglets with skin lesions, gathered over eight years, were tested for toxin genes and drug response. Just over half carried toxin genes, spread across four toxin types. Genetic fingerprinting split the isolates into eleven groups. All resisted one drug completely, and over four-fifths resisted several drugs at once, including every toxin-carrying strain. The authors offer the profile as a base for smarter treatment and monitoring.
pmc-11604894:
Fei Liu and colleagues published a 2024 study measuring radiation after a targeted cancer therapy in China. The treatment uses a radioactive drug for gut and pancreas tumors. Patients remain radioactive for a while afterward. Families and nurses need safe contact guidance. Thirty patients were measured during treatment.

Dose rates were tracked for hours after injection. Curves predicted exposure at later discharge times. Different waiting times suited different contacts. Adults could resume contact soonest. Young children required the longest caution. Nurses' exposure during hospital care was also measured. The numbers give Chinese clinics their first local reference values.
pmc-11607894:
Nahid Rezaie and six colleagues published a genetics study in two thousand twenty-four on inherited deafness in an Iranian family. The child at the centre was born with hearing loss in both ears and no other symptoms. Faults in the TMPRSS3 gene are a known cause of this pattern.

Whole-exome sequencing found a new single-letter deletion in the gene, never reported before. The change shifts the reading frame and truncates the protein. Both parents carried one copy each, matching the inheritance pattern. Computer checks judged the variant likely harmful. The team also mapped the gene's known mutation spectrum worldwide and screened an Iranian database. Their report widens the known fault list for this gene.
pmc-11618694:
Dacen Waters and colleagues introduced in two thousand twenty-four a new family of twisted graphene stacks with unusually flat energy bands. Layered carbon sheets twisted against each other create patterns where electrons slow down and interact strongly, producing exotic states. Their stacks combine sheets of different thicknesses in a new arrangement.

Calculations showed an electric field can isolate one flat, topologically special band sitting mainly in a single sheet. The resulting states strikingly mirror those in a better-known twisted family, including broken-symmetry phases and superconductivity nearby. Physicists gain fresh building blocks, tunable by layer count, for hunting new quantum phases.
pmc-11621994:
Sebastian Bathiany, Da Nian, Markus Druke, and Niklas Boers test rainforest strength marks. Their study from twenty twenty-four uses a plant growth model. Rainforests like the Amazon may be Earth system tipping points.

A fall in strength may show as slower bounce back in tree mass. Sat records show such a trend, more so in dry woods. The team asked what drives that mark in their model. Dry zones did show the slow bounce mark more than wet zones. Growth pace split by climate seems to drive the pattern. Parts were switched off and on to test it.
pmc-11624594:
Muhammad Zeeshan Akram, Nadia Everaert, and Aleksandra Dunisławska test whether injecting sodium butyrate into eggs helps low hatch-weight broiler chickens catch up, in a two thousand twenty-four animal science paper. Light chicks usually grow worse, and butyrate supports gut health.

Ross 308 eggs received saline or one of three butyrate doses on incubation day twelve. Chicks were then sorted into high and low hatch-weight groups, forming eight treatment combinations. Butyrate influenced performance and gut measures dose-dependently, with stronger effects in light chicks. At the middle dose, light chicks reached the highest day forty-two body weight, beating controls. Gut barrier genes, immunity, and cecal microbes were also tracked.
pmc-11628394:
Troy Kieran, Xiangjie Sun, Taronna Maines, and Jessica Belser mine ferret flu data to find which early measures best predict spread. Their study was published in twenty twenty-four. Ferret tests are central to judging pandemic risk from new flu viruses, but the most telling readouts were unsettled.

The team compiled results from over four hundred and seventy-five donor ferrets infected with ninety-seven recent flu viruses of many types. Spread to cage mates and through air was recorded. Higher virus loads in nose washes tied strongly to contact spread but not to air spread. Viruses that peaked a day after infection, though, predicted spread in both setups. The timing signal could sharpen risk calls for emerging strains.
pmc-11634894:
Sarosh Alam Ghausi and co-authors show that the apparent link between extreme rain and heat was distorted by the clouds themselves. Extreme rain is expected to grow with warming, since warm air holds more moisture. But records often show the rain-heat link flat or negative in warm regions, which clashes with theory. The authors blame a confounder: clouds shade and cool the surface while it rains, so rain days log lower heat for a reason apart from moisture limits.

Using a surface energy balance bound by thermodynamics, they stripped out the cloud cooling effect. The sensitivities turned positive across continents, as theory expects. In the tropics the median swung from minus 4.9% per degree to plus 6.1%. In mid-latitudes it rose from minus 0.5% to plus 2.8%. The scatter between regions shrank by more than 40% in the tropics and about 30% elsewhere.
pmc-11635294:
Radell Echemendía, Carlee Montgomery, Fabio Cuzzucoli, and a wider team wrote this chemistry paper, published in 2024. It reports a direct way to attach fluorine-bearing ethyl groups to sulfoxonium ylides, versatile building blocks in synthesis, using hypervalent iodine reagents.

Adding such groups can tune a molecule's behavior for drugs and materials, but the ylides had not been tailored this way before. The team attached trifluoroethyl and tetrafluoropropyl groups at either of two sites on the ylide. Nineteen examples were made, with yields from fair to high. The study maps where the method works and where it strains. Computer calculations of the reaction path point to a direct displacement mechanism, in which the incoming group swaps in as the leaving group departs. The authors offer the route as a new tool for fluorine chemistry.
pmc-11635694:
Justine Hill and four co-authors studied how two drugs change brain networks. Their paper, from twenty twenty-four, used brain scans of fifty-nine healthy adults. Each person took a dose of methylphenidate, haloperidol, or a placebo pill. The team then watched how time in key brain states shifted. They also tracked links between deep brain areas and the outer brain.

Methylphenidate raised time in two brain states and cut time in a third. Haloperidol raised time in a state that joins sense and rest networks. The size of the brain change from the first drug matched shifts in deep brain links. Readers see how drug action on brain chemistry ties to large scale brain change.
pmc-11640394:
Ryan Durgham and five colleagues review gene expression profiling for the second most common skin cancer, cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma. Most cases are cured by excision, but a small share metastasize, and old staging predicts that risk poorly. A forty-gene test reads tumor biology directly to refine the odds.

Studies suggest joining the molecular result with conventional staging finds high-risk patients better than either alone. That could steer decisions about further treatment and how close the follow-up is. The review weighs practical hurdles: cost, standards, and fit into clinic workflow. The authors present expression profiling as a promising step toward care tailored to each patient, with proof from trials still building up.
pmc-11640894:
Irena Boyce and colleagues price the heart-health gains of a workplace wellness programme. Their cost study from twenty twenty-four extends an earlier risk study. Nearly half of higher-risk employees improved beyond predictions before. Whether that improvement saves the employer money was the next question.

Published cost studies supplied savings per point of risk reduced. The programme's own risk changes anchored the calculation. Reference groups from earlier work structured the estimates. Return on investment was computed from the employer's viewpoint. Comprehensive programmes meet national design criteria that lesser ones miss. Design quality may explain why wellness economics vary so much. Employers gain a worked example of the money case.
pmc-11641094:
Jingya Guo, Seong-Gook Kang, Kunlun Huang, and Tao Tong review smell receptors in fat tissue. Their review from twenty twenty-four deals with odorant receptors past the nose. These receptors are the largest family of their class.

For decades they were thought to sit only in the nose. Evidence now places them in many body tissues. They help control blood pressure, liver sugar, and more. Fat tissue uses their signals in energy balance. Food derived smells can switch these receptors on. That opens a new route toward obesity treatment. Fat cell signals are the focus.
pmc-11642894:
Alakesh Bera and colleagues investigated a membrane protein, annexin A7, as a brake on thyroid cancer and a lever against drug resistance. Thyroid cancer is the commonest endocrine malignancy in the United States and usually curable. The stubborn cases are those that stop responding to standard drugs. Over sixty percent carry the BRAF V600E mutation. Sequencing and protein profiling showed annexin A7 levels reduced in cancer cells, especially BRAF-mutant ones.

Blocking BRAF and its partner MEK raised annexin A7 again. That rise cut a growth signal and switched on cell-death pathways. A second protein, the cell-cycle brake p21, also shaped resistance to BRAF drugs. Raising both proteins together markedly increased cancer cell death. The twenty twenty-four study nominates a two-protein strategy for tumors that have escaped targeted therapy.
pmc-11644894:
Marek Babiuch and Petr Foltynek presented a software framework in 2024 for tiny computers. Microcontrollers run countless connected devices in the Internet of Things. Their software is often written in flat, tangled ways. Big server software long ago adopted cleaner design habits. The team built a modular framework using those habits. It applies classic design patterns and solid design rules. The authors describe common use cases for the approach. Working Internet of Things examples show the framework in action.

The design splits programs into clean, swappable parts. That split helps developers build sturdy and flexible applications. New features deploy more easily in this structure. New sensor types can join without deep rewrites. Upgraded boards and tools also slot in more smoothly. The authors say development runs more efficiently overall. They offer the concepts as guidance for fast-changing device fields. The goal is software ready for future technology shifts.
pmc-11647294:
Andrea Simpson and four co-authors compare childbirth care for doctors and non-doctors in Ontario in this two thousand twenty-four study. Do physicians, as patients, get different maternity care than other women? The team used population records for births over about a decade. They matched physician mothers to non-physician mothers of like age, parity, and pregnancy type. All lived in high-income urban areas.

They compared care before, during, and after birth. The main outcome was whether delivery was by caesarean section or vaginal. Other outcomes covered injuries and complications around birth. Such a study can reveal whether medical knowledge changes the care a person receives. It may also expose gaps that affect all patients. Health system researchers and policy makers are the natural audience.
pmc-11648894:
Doruk Cezan and six colleagues build a soft gel swimmer that steers itself toward light, in a twenty twenty-four study. The swimmer mixes fiber bundles with a light-sensitive network and holds aligned magnetic nanowires along its length. Under a wobbling magnetic field it paddles through water. Light changes the bond between its two networks, bending the body in a way that turns it toward the source.

Tests and a physics model together explain the steering and predict its course. The behavior copies how living things swim toward light. The authors say such hybrid gels could seed smart, self-guided soft robots that sense and answer their surroundings.
pmc-11651894:
Aryel Goes, Pepijn Kooij, Ives Haifig, Odair Bueno, and Andre Rodrigues test whether ant colonies can remember past infections. Leaf-cutting ants farm a fungus for food, and rival fungi attack the garden. The team challenged the garden with two fungi that kill insects and two that compete with the crop. They watched how fast and how hard the ants groomed the garden clean.

Grooming rose most against the killer fungi, and it came faster when the same fungus struck twice. The boost lasted up to thirty days but faded by sixty. A second, different fungus dulled the response. The paper shows a colony-level memory that is real but narrow.
pmc-11654694:
Nicholas Scott, Sowon Kang, and Sapun Parekh show that mechanical forces control how much chemotherapy enters a cell's nucleus, in a study published in two thousand twenty-four. Most first-line drugs must reach the nucleus to work. The nucleus, coupled to the cell's skeleton, is also a mechanical sensor.

Changing the cell's internal filaments, quickly or chronically, altered doxorubicin entry into nuclei. Sudden disruption made nuclei more permeable; long-term strain reduction made them resist. Nuclei extracted from invasive cancer lines each had their own permeability signature. Pre-treating cells with paclitaxel, a mechano-priming trick, markedly improved doxorubicin uptake. The authors call nuclear permeability an unquantified axis of drug resistance. Tuning it might rescue failing drug combinations.
pmc-11656594:
Yuanbi Nie and four co-authors published a medical imaging study in twenty twenty-four on diagnosing Alzheimer's disease from brain scans without paying the full three-dimensional price. Pure 3D analysis overfits; flat slices miss how atrophy patterns relate across views. Their network lets a pretrained 3D model guide a cheaper multi-view 2D one.

Multi-head attention steers slice features toward the atrophy signatures the teacher network knows. A hybrid of convolutional and transformer layers then relates shrinkage across brain structures. On two public datasets the system scored near ninety-eight percent accuracy with specificity above ninety-nine on one benchmark. The authors pitch guided 2D analysis as a pragmatic route to precise, affordable dementia screening.
pmc-11657694:
Nuro, Tolossa, and Giday record wild plants eaten in two districts of southern Ethiopia in twenty twenty-four. Wild foods help rural families, above all when crops run short. Yet these plants get little study and face growing threats. The team spoke with close to three hundred local people and walked fields and woods with guides.

They found sixty-two edible species, most of them shrubs, and fruit was the part eaten most. Most species were picked from grazing land and woods in spring. Two thirds were eaten only in times of shortage. Farm growth was the chief threat, so the authors urge local care and public teaching to save these foods.
pmc-11658294:
Mohamed Saleh, Maryam Ba-Break, and Asma Abahussin interview primary school headteachers in West Yorkshire about what helps and hinders childhood obesity prevention, in a two thousand twenty-four qualitative study. Schools are a front line against childhood obesity, yet programs succeed unevenly.

Thirty-two interviews produced seven themes, spanning staff beliefs, food policies, curriculum, role models, parent partnership, extracurricular activity, and school capacity. Programs varied with leadership commitment, resources, and families' income and culture. Recommendations include raising parent and staff awareness, involving school nurses in training, extending free meals to all primary pupils, and helping schools chase government funding.
pmc-11666494:
Qianyu Liu and colleagues test group computer magnanimous therapy in patients with advanced lung cancer. Their 2024 multicenter randomized trial also uses magnetic resonance spectroscopy to look for related changes in brain metabolism.

Forty-seven patients with stage three or four disease were assigned to therapy plus routine care, or routine care alone. The therapy group received eight sessions over two weeks. After treatment, that group improved on total and enterprising questionnaire scores, while the control group did not. Changes in several brain metabolite ratios were also reported, and some correlated with improvement in the enterprising dimension.
pmc-11671794:
A correction note from two thousand twenty-four fixes a chart in a study by Cheng Zhang and co-authors on a protein signal in prostate illness in mice. The first study looked at how that signal draws in a type of immune cell.

The note says one set of stain images in the chart was used in error, due to a fault while the images were made ready. The right chart is shown. It sets out cell counts, stain work, blood tests, and gene tests for the groups in the study. The authors state that all results and the end claims of the first study stay the same. The note keeps the record clear for later readers.
pmc-11674294:
Schneider and a large team test a heat based scan of saliva and blood for head and neck cancer in twenty twenty-four. The scan warms a fluid sample and reads how its proteins unfold with heat. Each illness can leave its own heat pattern in blood or spit. Spit is easy to collect, but its cancer signals are faint and mixed.

The team found a spin and filter method that gave clean saliva data. Saliva patterns from forty-eight patients differed clearly from those of healthy controls. Blood patterns split the groups much less well. The authors say saliva heat scans could aid early, pain free checks for this cancer, with more polish.
pmc-11675294:
Peizhe Xin, Zihao Fu, Zhiyi Chen, and a wider team wrote this engineering paper, published in 2024. It works out how to run a combined satellite and ground-station wireless network so the total data rate is as high as possible.

In the setup, each user can link to a ground base station or to the satellite, under a scheme that lets users share channels in a stacked way. The team solves the planning problem in two stages. First, users are matched to access points using their own preference lists and the limits of each link back to the core network. Then power levels and receiving beam shapes are tuned in turns, with a neat formula for power at each step. Tests show the scheme works well. When ground links have room, users favor them; the satellite steps in to guarantee service otherwise.
pmc-11676194:
Julio C Osorio and colleagues report a two thousand twenty-four study of a cystine-import gene in lung cancers tied to virus and tobacco. High-risk papillomaviruses cause several cancers and also turn up in lung tumours. Their role in the lung is unsettled.

Over two hundred lung cancer cases were tested for the virus with a multiplex method. A small share carried type sixteen. Gene pattern analysis singled out the importer gene SLC7A11, raised in both virus-linked and smoke-linked cancers. Patients positive for both virus and gene fared worse. Cell tests tied the gene's rise to viral proteins and smoke.
pmc-11676294:
Ismaiel and co-authors recheck the identity of fungi sold and stored under the name Trichoderma harzianum. Fungi in this group serve as the active agent in about 60% of biological fungicides. They used gene sequences for three markers and compared them with current taxonomy.

Across five surveys and 148 strains, the team found 11 distinct species in the group. Many strains filed as T. harzianum proved to be other species. Correct names matter for farm products, since species differ in how well they protect crops.
pmc-11677394:
Vittorio Piloni, Tiziana Manisco, and Marco Fogante propose a standard template for reporting MRI scans of evacuation disorders, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-four. MR defecography images patients straining to empty the rectum. Gastroenterologists and surgeons use it to plan treatment for obstructed defecation and pelvic organ prolapse.

Reports, the authors argue, often omit details that decide management. Their structured template covers nine key descriptors of rectal evacuation. It spans both the static and dynamic phases of the scan. A national interdisciplinary study in Italy is now testing the template's effectiveness and acceptability. Standardized reporting aims to make scans comparable across centers. Better reports should mean fewer controversial, poorly guided treatment decisions.
pmc-11691594:
Borole and six co-authors reviewed add-on treatments for hand and wrist fractures in this paper from twenty twenty-four. Some fractures heal slowly or fail to unite. All four show promise for faster healing and fewer nonunions in the studies surveyed. Costs run high, though, and results swing from study to study. Those two facts have kept routine adoption low. The authors sort the methods into body-based and device-based camps. They close with the open questions and next steps the field needs to answer.
pmc-11693794:
Heakyung Moon and Wonjung Noh present a two thousand twenty-four study of how healthy middle-aged retirees in Korea feel about their own health. Ageing societies face growing numbers of people retiring mid-life. Self-rated health guides what support programs they need.

Data came from a national ageing survey, focusing on a few hundred middle-aged retirees. Higher income standing linked to better self-rated health. More chronic diseases and depression pulled ratings down. Satisfaction with retirement itself was the strongest positive factor. Policymakers get evidence that money, mood, and meaning all shape retiree wellbeing.
pmc-11696394:
Annibaletto and five co-authors worked out the step-by-step mechanism of a gold-driven reaction that builds indene rings, in a study published in twenty twenty-four. Indenes are carbon ring structures found in many useful compounds, and this route makes them from string-like starting materials called ynamides.

The team combined bench experiments with computer modeling. They swapped in labeled versions of the starting material and tried different gold catalysts to watch how each piece moved. The modeling then traced a plausible path. Gold wakes the ynamide into a reactive form, a hydrogen atom jumps across the molecule, the chain curls into a ring, and gold lets go at the end. The hydrogen jump proved to be the slowest step, setting the pace of the whole reaction. The study also explains why some starting materials react faster than others.
pmc-11728294:
Corina-Ioana Anton and co-authors look at tissue signs in infective endocarditis that hits mechanical heart valves. Their 2024 study draws on past cases at a central military hospital in Bucharest. It is a retrospective cohort study.

The team studied samples from ninety-three patients. Their mechanical valves had been taken out by surgery from 2017 to 2024. Forty-one cases were thought to be infective endocarditis, and fifty-two were not. Cases with the disease showed clear traits. Vegetations stood out, as did inflammatory infiltrates that held neutrophils. Cases with no disease showed a unlike profile in the tissue. The team aims to give pathologists more clear rules. Those rules should split true disease from the wear and slow breakdown of prosthetic valves in the normal course of use.
pmc-11732594:
Ardiansyah Pawinru, Nasyrah Hidayati, Eka Erwansyah, and three colleagues test, published in 2024, how much a cavity-linked bacterium sticks to braces hardware. Fixed braces raise mouth bacteria counts, and Lactobacillus acidophilus is one species that thrives. Statistical tests compared the four groups.

pmc-11742094: Cheng and co-authors report a rare case in which HIV treatment triggered a sharp drop in blood platelets. The patient was a 20-year-old man with HIV and coccidioidomycosis, a fungal infection. Strong antiviral therapy can restore immunity, yet the rebound can spark an overactive inflammatory response. That response, called IRIS, usually appears within six months of starting treatment. Here it attacked platelets, which help blood clot. The case adds an unusual form to the known range of IRIS effects.
pmc-11811494:

Wide scans of gene reads and bind sites now make those nets plain. PlantReg starts from their past method to rebuild switch nets. A switch is a gene part that turns target genes on or off. Users give gene lists and the switch lists tied to them.

PlantReg lists the life tasks rich in those genes as its first output. It also shows which switches steer each task and through which genes. The path can run through first, next, and higher targets in the net. Switch cross-talk in a task under study is part of the map. The aim is a clear gene-to-trait path for plant work.
pmc-11864694:
Mingming Xiao, Xianjun Yu, and Si Shi studied drug resistance in pancreatic cancer in 2024. The drug olaparib helps some patients with repair-gene mutations. Many patients resist it from the start or over time. The team searched for what drives that resistance. A protein in the NLR family stood out. Its levels rose in resistant cancer cells. The protein plays roles in DNA damage response and cell recycling. Tests showed it boosts DNA repair capacity. It also raises reactive oxygen output from cell powerhouses.

That oxygen surge switches on recycling after drug treatment. Recycling helps cells survive the drug's damage. Blocking the oxygen surge restored drug sensitivity. Blocking recycling with an old malaria drug did the same. Patients with low protein levels may respond better, the authors suggest. The work names two add-on strategies to test. Both aim to break the resistance circuit at its weak points.
pmc-12668594:
Chari and co-authors propose a new strategy, named heuriskance, for catching pancreatic cancer earlier. Their 2026 paper notes that screening everyone is infeasible for this uncommon but deadly cancer. Instead, the strategy hunts for a heurisk, an early-warning sign meeting three tests. It must mark a high chance of already-present cancer. It must appear with useful lead time. And it must be findable systematically at population scale.

Their worked example is new-onset diabetes defined by blood sugar patterns, already being tested in a dedicated early detection trial. The paper supplies a full playbook: a tiered Define-Enrich-Find risk approach, criteria for choosing a warning sign, success metrics, and five evaluation phases from retrospective to prospective studies. The stated aims are more lead time, fewer advanced-stage diagnoses, and better one, three, and five-year survival after adjustment.
pmc-12691194:
Draghici and a team including Leucuta translate and validate a carpal tunnel questionnaire in Romanian in twenty twenty-five. Carpal tunnel syndrome is the most common nerve entrapment in the wrist. The Boston questionnaire measures symptom severity and hand function. No validated Romanian version existed for local patients.

One hundred ninety people took part, covering three hundred eighty wrists. The group included one hundred thirty suspected or confirmed patients and sixty healthy controls. Translation followed international steps with expert review and pilot testing. The Romanian version showed excellent internal consistency. Scores correlated strongly with nerve conduction measurements. Repeat testing gave near perfect reliability scores. The authors say it is ready for clinical and research use in Romania.
pmc-12701594:
Xu Zhang, Xiang Li, Ming Li, and colleagues report a two thousand twenty-five wireless sensor system that reads maize leaf movement to flag stress early. Drought, heat, and salt quietly cut yields before visible wilting. Leaves move in daily patterns that shift under strain.

A light motion sensor clips to a leaf, its electronics kept separate by flexible cable to avoid weighing the leaf down. Readings streamed wirelessly to a host computer with very small angular error. Daily movement curves were fitted to extract stress signatures. Different stresses produced distinguishable patterns, offering farmers an early-warning channel straight from the plant.
pmc-12706194:
Mairead Skally and colleagues reviewed patient satisfaction with infection control in two thousand twenty-five. Hospitals use many measures to stop infections spreading. Patients rarely help design those measures. Satisfaction with them was seldom studied. The review searched seven databases for hospital studies. Eligible work covered isolation, screening, hand hygiene, and education.

Patient partners helped oversee the review itself. That involvement models the change the authors seek. Methods for measuring satisfaction varied widely across studies. Pooled analysis combined the reported satisfaction outcomes. Results can guide kinder infection control design. Safety steps work best when patients accept them. This review centers the patient experience.
pmc-12709194:
Bope and five co-authors released this software in twenty twenty-five for reading mutation patterns in tumors. Each mutational process leaves a fingerprint in the genome.
