The assignment uses the mutation's three-letter DNA neighborhood and the known signature profiles. The tool shines where mutations are few, a weak spot for older matrix methods. It can refit known signatures or discover new ones from scratch. Balance across both jobs was a design goal. The package runs from the command line and ships with plotting routines.
pmc-12717194:
Mohamed Elmorsy and four co-authors design dyes that push indoor solar cells past twenty-five percent efficiency. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, builds dye-sensitized cells, a cheap solar type. Four new dyes share a naphthalene donor with varied acceptor ends. Light tests, voltage tests, and computer models map each dye's behavior.

Two dyes move charge especially well and absorb toward the red. Paired with a benchmark black dye, they near ten percent in sun tests. A stacked tandem cell then joins the best pair below and black dye above. It tops twelve percent in full sun and near twenty-six percent under room light. Stability held at ninety-five percent in their checks.
pmc-12719394: A correction notice from twenty twenty-five fixes a methods detail in a study of home injuries in older adults. The fix concerns the scale used to rate how well people manage daily living tasks. The notice gives the new wording for that part of the methods. It says the scale was a changed form of one made by Taheri and others. Scores run from zero to sixteen and sort people into three groups by how much help they need.
pmc-12724094:
Paul McCrone led a large team publishing a health economics study in twenty twenty-five on AVATAR therapy, where people who hear distressing voices converse with a digital embodiment of the voice. The parent trial compared brief and extended therapy against usual care. This analysis asks the payer's question: what did the gains cost?

Over twenty-eight weeks, service use and quality-adjusted life years were tallied. Brief therapy cost slightly more than usual care with slightly better outcomes. The extended version actually cost less overall while performing best clinically in the parent trial. Cost-effectiveness planes and uncertainty intervals are reported for both. A therapy that saves money while helping is rare in mental health economics; the extended format makes exactly that claim here.
pmc-12727694:
Xinliang Zhou, Yuta Sakuragi, and Chiaki Katagiri lead a team filming brain cells in the central amygdala as mice face pain, bad smells, and bitter tastes. Their study appeared in two thousand twenty-five. This small brain hub turns aversive signals into avoidance and body stress responses. Whether one cell group integrates all threats or separate lines stay apart was unknown.

Calcium imaging tracked hundreds of neurons during each kind of unpleasant stimulus. Over half the cells answered at least one stimulus. Most of those answered exactly one kind, showing sharp specialization. A minority bridged two kinds, and very few answered all three. So the hub mostly keeps channels separate, with partial merging. The authors read this as graded integration rather than a single alarm bell. The map informs how negative emotion is assembled. It may guide anxiety research toward specific cell groups.
pmc-12727794:
Kao and co-authors weigh steroid add-ons for a severe fungal pneumonia in patients without HIV. Pneumocystis pneumonia burdens many patients whose immunity is lowered by other causes. Whether steroids help in this group has been disputed. The team reviewed cases across several centers in Taiwan. Of 334 patients, 251, or 75%, received steroids on top of standard care. Raw counts showed higher 60-day deaths in the steroid group.

Steroid patients were also sicker at the start, with more shock and worse oxygen levels. After matching and adjustment, steroids no longer tied to higher deaths. The study warns against reading raw gaps at face value in such sick groups.
pmc-12730794:
Song, Zou, and Zou review options when cervical cancer returns in the pelvis after radiation. This relapse has long carried a poor outlook and few choices. The review covers both local and whole-body treatments. Salvage surgery and repeat radiation, with focused beams or implants, each get weighed. Their benefits come with real toxicity risks. Systemic therapy has changed fastest in recent years.

Targeted drugs and immune checkpoint drugs have lifted survival in trials. Named agents include pembrolizumab and cemiplimab. Care is shifting toward personal picks based on tumor traits. The review maps how doctors can combine old and new tools for this hard relapse.
pmc-12733094:
SangYup Lee and colleagues report a two thousand twenty-five study of a battery material that stores calcium ions. Titanium disulfide can host calcium between its layers. Concentrated salt water solutions might make such batteries safer and cheaper.

Electrical tests were paired with structural and surface analysis after cycling. Stronger solutions reduced gas formation and widened the safe voltage range. A narrower working window avoided damaging side products while keeping storage reversible. Layer spacing expanded and contracted as calcium moved in and out. Surface films formed during cycling. Battery researchers get mechanism detail for water-based calcium storage.
pmc-12733394:
Thorne and five co-authors found in twenty twenty-five that conehead termites in Florida oft nest and feed under ground, not just in trees. The kind is a pest from the tropics that plagues New Guinea and Florida too. Past prints called ground parts of their nests rare.

Many finds in one Florida county show full and part ground nests are common there. Their ground runs hide from eye checks of trees and floors. Pest teams must probe soil spots or miss whole nests, they warn. Ways to treat the ground runs are set out as well.
pmc-12733894:
Yu and five co-authors surveyed macrofungi in the Niyang River Basin in twenty twenty-five, pairing two survey methods. Macrofungi are fungi large enough to see, such as mushrooms. Knowing their diversity supports conservation on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, where this basin lies.

One method was traditional field searching, which spots obvious and parasitic fungi well. The other read fungal DNA from soil samples at high throughput. Soil sequencing covered more ground and was not limited by weather or fruiting seasons. It also uncovered rare and previously unrecorded kinds. Field work, meanwhile, caught showy species that sequencing may miss. The authors conclude the two methods complement each other, and both are needed to characterize fungal diversity in complex ecosystems.
pmc-12736494:
Xinyue Hou and nine co-authors read gene spread in farm stands of a prized scent wood tree to speed breed work. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Wild trees of this kind are near lost from home harm, yet farm stock may serve in their place. Three hundred eighty trees from five packs were typed with two dozen marks, and nine traits were taped in a slice.

Farm packs held mid gene spread, a match for wild stock. Heart share tied to stem widths. One mark tied to width traits and four to heart share. The team say farms can stand in for wild seed, with marks to breed by.
pmc-12736794:
Carrie-Louise Thouant leads a team measuring how stroke survivors cheat, usefully, when they move objects, in a study from two thousand twenty-five. After a stroke, patients compensate for weak arms. They bring in the trunk and the shoulder to do the work the arm cannot. Rehabilitation works more well when those strategies are gauged, not guessed at.

Thirty-one sub-acute stroke patients and thirty-one healthy controls did the Box and Block Test. Seven wearable inertial sensors caught the motion of the upper body as they worked. Joint angles and three-dimensional trajectories were rebuilt from the recordings. Clear group differences showed up in mean joint angles across the two sets. Compensation was put in numbers, as percentages relative to healthy movement. The team gives therapists objective numbers to use. With them, they can tailor exercises to each patient's own workaround.
pmc-12740894:
Sofia Thunberg and colleagues published a health study in 2025 on a robot cat in specialist dental care. The patients were children with autism spectrum disorder. Dental visits can bring anxiety and sensory overload for these children. The team tested whether a companion robot could offer support during treatment.

Ten children aged five to ten took part over twelve months. Each child first had a visit without the robot. Later visits, several per child, included it. Video from dozens of sessions was analyzed for themes. The robot sometimes helped training and treatment. Sometimes it hindered progress instead. Overall it seemed useful but not essential, with effects varying by child and moment.
pmc-12744594:
Xingyi Hu, Li Wen, and Caili Zhang published a nursing study in two thousand twenty-five on forward-looking care for lung disease patients. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease narrows the airways and often brings anxiety and low mood. Anticipatory nursing plans care ahead instead of reacting to problems.

The study covered three hundred sixty-nine patients at one hospital, split between routine care and the forward-looking programme. The programme built personal care plans, worked to prevent complications, and supported breathing, circulation, food, and sleep. After six months, the programme group had lower anxiety and depression scores. Their breathing symptoms also cleared faster, quality of life rose on every measure, and complications fell to about a third of the routine group's rate.
pmc-12749394:
Tran and co-authors design a compact antenna with round-polarized MIMO output. Most MIMO arrays feed one element per port, which grows size. Their design feeds dual-polarized elements through hybrid couplers. Two elements thus serve four ports in total. Shared firing of both elements lifts gain as well.

A built prototype matched the design in bench tests. The unit spans about 1 point 41 by 1 point 06 wavelengths in face size. Its working band ran 9 point 5 percent, from 5 point 0 to 5 point 5 GHz. Port isolation beat 10 dB, and gain ran 7 point 8 to 8 point 8 dBi. Targets include Wi-Fi 6, C-band radar, and satellite IoT links.
pmc-12753794:
Aleksandra Wilk and seven colleagues tracked how magnetic nanoparticles change rat blood over a week. They are superparamagnetic iron oxide particles. They are prized for imaging and therapy, but their effects on the body are not fully understood. That gap slows their move into clinic use. The team injected coated particles into male and female rats. The particles had magnetite cores ten nanometers wide. Blood serum was sampled at two hours, one day, and seven days.

Three light based methods profiled the serum. Two read the fingerprints of molecules, and one counted elements with great care. The infrared data showed shifts in the serum that grew over time. The changes hung on time and on sex, and point to sensitive signs of how particles act in the body. Knowing how the body registers these particles is groundwork for safe dosing in future imaging and therapy use.
pmc-12763894:
Fansheng Meng and colleagues published a liver cancer study in 2025. They studied immune cells inside hepatocellular carcinoma tumors. One macrophage type carries a lipid enzyme, SGMS2. Fat-like sphingolipid chemistry shapes tumor immunity strongly. Large public cancer datasets were analyzed first. Single-cell and spatial methods located the enzyme precisely. A hospital cohort validated the cell patterns. Killer NK cells with high NR4A3 were counted. Lab co-cultures tested how macrophages affect tumor cells.

Tumors rich in these macrophages drew more NK cells. Patients with that pattern had better prognosis overall. They also responded better to PD-1 immunotherapy. The macrophage and NK pairing seems functionally linked. Boosting this axis might improve immunotherapy results. Biomarker tests could select likely responders earlier. Further experiments must confirm the causal chain.
pmc-12765894:
Noh and coauthors review diabetes drugs that may restore liver function. The drugs push sugar out through urine each day. That sugar loss drains energy and eases insulin resistance. Proof now shows gains past blood sugar control alone.

Liver fat buildup falls as the drugs work in the body. Cell power units gain guard from stress and harm. Calcium balance in liver cells returns toward normal. Gene paths that burn fat switch on more strongly. Self-cleaning in liver cells also rises with care. The review joins those paths into one liver tale.
pmc-12786594:
Boyu Pan and five co-authors studied how zirconium breaks under load. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, pairs lab tests with computer models. They pulled samples of many shapes in a plain stretch test. Each shape gave a distinct stress state at the break point. The range of stress states was wide, from low to high pull.

The team used those states to tune a known fracture model. With the tuned model, the break of zirconium can be forecast. They also viewed break faces with a strong microscope. Shear ruled the breaks at low pull, while other modes took over at high pull. Readers who design with this metal get a tested way to predict failure.
pmc-12787494:
Nicole Knebusch and eleven co-authors review feeding care for children after liver transplant, in this twenty twenty-five study. The children had a blocked bile duct disease from birth and got a new liver. Good feeding in the first week of intensive care can shape recovery, yet illness before surgery can make feeding hard.

The team read records of well over a hundred children treated at a Texas children's hospital over many years. Most were girls, and the typical age was just over one year. They measured how much of the needed energy and protein each child truly got, by tube or by vein, in week one. The results show where feeding falls short.
pmc-12789694:
Mohan Gupta and Timothy Rickard probed how two kinds of learning interact, in work published in twenty twenty-five. One kind stores facts you can recall on cue. The other builds smooth motor skill, here a finger-tapping task. Past claims say a fact task slipped in mid-training can hurt skill, for one of three reasons the authors name.

When the fact task came late in training, tapping did not suffer. When it came early, skill dipped for a short while. That dip did not track how well each person did on the fact task. The authors weigh what this mixed pattern means for other skill tasks and for when teachers should slot in fact work.
pmc-12805594:
Nicholas Lorenz and others put out a 2025 case report about serious muscle swelling that came after a COVID infection. The patient's illness combined features of two autoimmune conditions, with antibodies linked to both, and also involved swelling of the epiglottis, a flap guarding the airway. Swallowing problems and airway trouble made the case most dangerous.

Autoimmune muscle diseases can surface after viral illness, when an upset immune system turns on the body. The authors stress that doctors should watch for such post-COVID problems early, because prompt treatment that calms the immune system can prevent lasting damage. The case adds to the list of autoimmune after-effects now known.
pmc-12810994:
Maysam Orouskhani and a team including Chengcheng Zhu train a neural network to outline brain aneurysms on vessel scans. Their study was published in twenty twenty-five. Exact outlines help doctors judge these weak artery bulges and plan treatment.

The scans came from two data sets: a public one with one hundred and thirteen cases and a hospital one with two hundred and thirteen. Most bulges were small, with middling sizes of a few millimeters. The team used a self-tuning U-net design, added automatic vessel extraction, and blended loss functions to sharpen the outlines. Training covered both burst and unburst aneurysms. Better automated outlining could speed planning for a condition where a missed detail can be fatal.
pmc-12816694:
Alba Espí-Malillos and colleagues report a two thousand twenty-five food safety study on stand-in bacteria for Listeria testing. Dangerous Listeria strains from raw milk cause outbreaks, but testing them directly is risky. Safer relatives are used as surrogates, with weak evidence.

An outbreak strain was grown in treated and raw milk in cold storage. Three candidate surrogate species failed to copy its growth pattern. Boosting one virulence system did not matter, while boosting another reduced fitness. Raw milk's own microbes stayed largely unaffected. The results warn labs to pick food-test models with care.
pmc-12819494:
T-Y Chen and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-five cohort study of a new wound closure method after polyp removal in the colon. Cutting out large flat polyps can leave tissue prone to a painful burn-related syndrome. Sealing the defect well should prevent it.

The new technique clips the muscle layer directly, not just the surface lining. Hundreds of consecutive patients at one center received either this closure or the standard one. The burn syndrome occurred far less often with the deeper closure. Complete sealing and serious side events were also tracked. Endoscopists get evidence for a safer finish to difficult removals.
pmc-12821294:
Yanlei Dong and Guiyu Zhang present a two thousand twenty-five study of a circular RNA circuit in ovarian cancer. Ovarian cancer is often found late and resists chemotherapy. Small regulatory RNAs help drive its growth.

The pair examined how one circular RNA interacts with a tumour-suppressing microRNA. Data mining split tumours into glucose-related subtypes and built risk models. Lab and animal experiments then tested effects on growth, death, and sugar use. Their circuit links gene control to how ovarian tumours burn glucose. Readers get a possible marker and target in a cancer that badly needs both.
pmc-12830894:
Fatima Zohra Benamara and a large team work on strengthening dune sand for road embankments in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Dune sand is plentiful but weak as a building base. The team mixed in two waste materials: rubber crumb from tires and powder from crushed brick. Their aim was both stronger soil and a use for waste. They tested mixes with rubber at three levels and brick powder at three levels.

Two modeling tools then hunted for the best recipe. One is a classic response surface method; the other pairs a neural network with a genetic search. Both judged the mixes by dry density, friction angle, and cohesion. The best blend used a high rubber share with the top brick dose. The study shows how recycled waste can firm up poor soils.
pmc-12847894:
Zhentao Jiang and seven co-authors build a high-yield way to make bilirubin in the lab, reported in twenty twenty-five. Bilirubin is the yellow pigment left when the body breaks down old blood cells. Making it outside the body had long been held back by low yields and unclear bottlenecks.

The team built the full path from heme, the iron part of blood, to bilirubin in a test tube. They found that loose iron was quietly wrecking mid-step products. Blocking the iron and clearing a gas that stalled the key enzyme lifted the yield sharply. The result is a cleaner, larger supply route for a compound used in research and medicine.
pmc-12852494:
El Orra and colleagues published in twenty twenty-five a case report of a boy's elbow injury with a rare late outcome. At age five, the boy fell from a tree and broke the upper arm bone near the elbow. Surgeons fixed the break with wires and placed his arm in a cast. Five years later he returned with an angled elbow but no pain. Scans showed the rounded joint surface had lost its blood supply and died.

At a check eleven years after surgery, his elbow motion was limited. Scans then showed the forearm bone had slipped out of place toward the middle. The team kept him on long-term watch for joint wear. They stress long follow-up after such childhood breaks.
pmc-13021994:
Ji and co-authors build a rat model of chemical phlebitis, the vein inflammation caused by harsh intravenous drugs. Vesicant and irritant drugs often inflame the vein they enter, causing pain and tissue damage in patients. A lab model lets researchers study the injury and test protective steps safely.

They injected vinorelbine, a chemotherapy drug, into the dorsal foot vein of rats. Six groups of eight rats received set doses or salt solution for comparison. The team recorded general symptoms and examined vein tissue under the microscope. The model maps how this drug injures veins over time.
pmc-13082394: Mohamedelmustafa Yahya Mohamed Eldouma and colleagues report a teenager whose belly pain hid a parasitic cause, in a case report from twenty twenty-six. The seventeen-year-old arrived with an acute abdomen and was diagnosed before surgery with perforated appendicitis. Emergency surgery instead found pus, a cecal mass, and a large cecal perforation. Tissue examination showed living schistosome eggs and granulomas in the cecum. After removal of the right colon, he received anti-parasitic therapy. The authors call it Sudan's third reported large bowel schistosomiasis case.
pmc-13118894:
Ankesh Todi, Hakhamanesh Mansoorzare, and Reza Abdolvand build a micro-accelerometer whose signal could broadcast itself, in a paper from two thousand twenty-six. Resonant accelerometers read motion as a shift in frequency. If that frequency can be pushed into the tens of megahertz, the signal could go out by wireless at once.

The device joins two structures in hybrid form, kept apart in a mechanical sense but linked by wires for charge. A capacitive mass-spring senses acceleration and moves with it. A piezoelectric resonator then changes its stiffness, and with it its frequency, in reply. Model runs and lab tests back the design. A fabrication trick used hardened photoresist as a sacrificial layer, with which the team built the suspended electrodes in place.
pmc-13135594:
Sean Davies and Reza Fadaei review a family of fat-like signal molecules that help set the body's cholesterol and triglyceride levels, in this paper from twenty twenty-six. The molecules, fatty acid ethanolamides, include oleoylethanolamide and palmitoylethanolamide. Body and plant sources both supply them, and supplements of the named two are already sold.

The review gathers new evidence from gene-deletion models and clinical trials. Animals unable to make these molecules handle fats abnormally, while giving the molecules to patients moved lipid levels toward normal. The gut, liver, and fat tissue make them in response to feeding and fasting, and they act through receptors including PPAR-alpha and GPR119. Beyond fats, they help calm inflammation. The authors frame this signaling system as a drug target for fatty liver disease and artery disease.
pmc-13135894:
Marchessaux, Aksu, and Tarkan mapped in twenty twenty-six how climate shifts the heat fit for feeding in water and land species. Warmth moves where species live and how they eat, so tools to see ahead are needed. They used heat curves for each kind to build a fit score map.

Maps split lands and waters into five fit bands for now and mid-century air. Fresh-water kinds tended to gain feeding fit in the small set read. Sea and land kinds moved in mixed ways. Prey maps must join the tool to catch match and mismatch in place, they stress.
pmc-13143194:
Ismail and co-authors compare online and face-to-face practice tests in a merged medical curriculum. Formative tests with prompt feedback help students learn and help teachers spot gaps. In integrated curricula, basic and clinical sciences are taught as one coordinated whole.

Few past studies set online practice tests against in-person ones in such a program. The mixed methods study measured effects on final exam scores and gathered student and teacher views. Comparing both modes on equal terms shows where each format shines. Findings can guide schools that blend digital tools with classroom teaching.
pmc-13151194:
Nicole Lindner and seven co-authors develop Betti, a program to cut inappropriate imaging for musculoskeletal pain in primary care, in a two thousand twenty-six paper. Unneeded scans harm patients and waste money, and past interventions rarely fit real consultations.

Following the Medical Research Council setup, the team built a program theory, reviewed the literature, interviewed patients, and gathered expert feedback. Betti joins a multimedia training module for general practitioners, guideline-based choice support, and patient information materials. A proof-of-concept test found doctors and patients judged it well structured and supportive. One flaw surfaced: patients were not in fact directed to the materials during consultations, prompting a redesign of delivery.
pmc-13154994:
Laura Bracke and her team pick apart how a complement-blocking antibody grips its target. Their study from twenty twenty-six looks at empasiprubart, a trial-stage antibody. The drug stops complement protein C2 from joining its partner. That block shuts down two immune attack paths at once.

The grip of the antibody turns on calcium and on acid levels. Blood and the reuse pockets inside cells differ in both. Those gaps let the antibody drop its load for breakdown. Set mutations stretch how long the antibody stays in the body. Crystal shapes now show the grip in fine detail. Drug makers can copy the reuse trick for other such drugs.
pmc-13158594:
Ryan, Tehan, Gumuskaya, Hutton, and Mitchell test skin care wipes to prevent pressure injuries, in work from twenty twenty-six. Pressure injuries are painful wounds from long pressure on skin, a major risk for frail aged care residents. Prevention is far better than treatment.

The single blind, multicentre randomized trial ran in twenty aged care homes across New South Wales. A wipe soaked with emollient and barrier agents was applied twice daily. Facilities formed strata for fair randomization. The outcome was new pressure injury incidence. A simple wipe routine, if effective, is cheap and easy for staff to sustain.
pmc-13159594:
Luyao Wang and ten colleagues asked whether a past cancer or precancer diagnosis worsens fertility treatment outcomes. Cancer incidence is rising in younger women, and many later seek IVF. The retrospective study ran at a Tongji Hospital reproductive center from twenty fifteen to twenty twenty-two. It enrolled 1,004 patients: 251 with a history of malignancy or precancerous lesions, matched against 753 controls. Cumulative live birth rate across cycles was the main outcome.

The history group showed significantly lower ovarian reserve and poorer embryo outcomes. Both conservative and optimistic cumulative live birth rates ran lower than in controls. Propensity matching balanced the groups' baselines before comparison. The twenty twenty-six findings help counselors give cancer survivors honest odds, and may influence how much time clinicians spend optimizing treatment before starting.
pmc-13166994:
Eden Simonov and colleagues describe a two thousand twenty-six case report of a hidden insulin-producing tumour unmasked by a weight-loss drug. Insulinomas are rare pancreatic tumours and often diagnosed late. Vague, on-and-off low blood sugar symptoms hide them well.

Their patient was a forty-year-old woman without diabetes. Weakness episodes began soon after starting a GLP-1 receptor drug. Tests showed her body made too much insulin during documented low sugar events. Scans found a small pancreatic lesion matching an insulin tumour. Medicine bridged her to surgery, which removed it and ended the episodes completely.
pmc-13171594:
Yihao Zhai and a large team review how a tumor prepares distant soil before its cells arrive and spread. Their review was published in twenty twenty-six. This prepared ground, called the pre-metastatic niche, is now seen as a key step in cancer spread, the main cause of cancer death.

The review sums up what support cells and immune cells do to build the niche. It covers macrophages, cancer-linked fibroblasts, neutrophils, suppressor cells, and T cells. Two processes sit at the center: reshaping the tissue scaffold and muting immune attack. The authors also discuss why certain organs attract spread and how the niche turns into a full secondary tumor. They close with ways these steps might be targeted by future treatment.
pmc-13173394:
Kowalczyk and colleagues apply a liquid laser-based ionisation method to synthetic polymers for the first time. Their 2026 paper tests LAP-MALDI mass spectrometry, a technique previously used on peptides, proteins, and DNA, on four polymer standards: polyethylene glycol, polypropylene glycol, polyacrylic acid, and polystyrene. The goal was a faster, simpler way to characterise plastics and industrial polymers.

The method produced stable ion signals with variation under 10 percent, detecting singly and multiply charged ions in both positive and negative modes. Added salts helped ionise several polymers by attaching metal ions, while polystyrene needed a silver salt and the acid polymer ionised best negatively. Charge states ran lower than with the standard electrospray method but could be steered by setup choices. The authors call the approach rapid and reagent-efficient.
pmc-13178894:
Kyra Mendes de Leon leads a team that tests home HIV viral load checks. Their study from twenty twenty-six deals with self sampled blood. Home sampling could cut clinic visits for folks with HIV.

Folks at an outpatient clinic sampled their own blood at home. A standard device drew the blood for the tests. Results were set against standard lab based HIV tests. Stored low level samples were tested the same way. Only samples with enough plasma volume could be used. Agreement was checked with standard stats methods. Sample quality and ease of use were also rated.
pmc-13179394:
Lindsay Peifer and six co-authors let genetic counseling patients describe the experience in their own words, in twenty twenty-six. Counselors help people live with genetic conditions, but most measures of success are set by providers. Twenty-five patients from three institutions, across prenatal, cancer, heart, and general clinics, were interviewed within two weeks of their session.

Five themes emerged. Patients wanted the counselor to follow their lead and to work with them over time. They valued clear information, and they saw the counselor's expertise and caring manner as unique. Most left with takeaways: new views on their genetic facts, emotional effects, and a sense of power from steps they could act on. Few had entered with a set outcome in mind. The authors say patient-defined outcomes can enrich the models that guide practice.
pmc-13184594:
Brady and co-authors report how older adults handle the setup of digital health tools. Connected devices may improve health outcomes, even for people with many chronic conditions or low health habits. Yet first steps, from unboxing to setup and first use, shape feelings about a device.

A rocky start can end use before any benefit arrives. The report follows older adults through those first steps and records where they stall or lose trust. Lessons point to clearer guides, better support, and design that fits older users. The aim is lasting, meaningful use of health technology.
pmc-13186494:
Ashutosh Aggarwal and six co-authors weigh higher doses of a key TB drug in this twenty twenty-six review. The standard dose of rifampicin sits at the low end of the range where more drug gives more effect. The team asked whether raising the daily dose cures more people or causes more harm.

They searched the literature for trials that compared standard and high daily doses for lung TB. Main checks were whether germ tests turned negative by set points in treatment, and whether severe liver harm rose. Other checks covered death, failure, and return of disease. The pooled answer can guide dosing rules for a disease still treated with old drugs.
pmc-13187394:
Kim, Cho, Jung, Shin, Choe, and Choi refine a claims based algorithm for pregnancy research in Korea in twenty twenty-six. Health insurance claims can identify pregnancies for observational studies. An earlier algorithm was built on pregnancies in women with lupus. Its accuracy for gestational age in the general population was untested.

The team used nationwide claims data from twenty twenty-one and twenty twenty-two. More than five hundred eighty thousand pregnancy episodes were identified. The modified algorithm prioritized early ultrasound codes over later ones. It matched stated gestational age ranges in preterm records far better than the original. Its preterm birth rate also came closer to national statistics. The authors recommend the modified version.
pmc-13193894:
Lingling Meng, Yupeng Di, Lin Ma, and Baolin Qu map trends in research, across the world, in spatially fractionated radiotherapy. They do so with bibliometric analysis. Their 2026 study covers a way that spreads radiation dose in a new pattern in a tumour, to spare normal tissue.

Searches of two large databases, from 2005 through 2025, gave more than four hundred publications that fit. Growth in publications and in citations sped up by a sharp rate in the last five years. That growth formed a pattern in three phases. The United States led in the total count of work put out. France showed the lead in how much its institutions put out, and in citation impact. Work at the base centred on physical dosimetry and on early models from before clinic use. Three tools for analysis tracked networks of joint work and how themes changed over time.
pmc-13194194:
Cankurtaran-Kömürcü and Bilgiçli published in twenty twenty-six a food study adding an edible plant powder to crackers. Polygonum cognatum is an underused plant rich in fiber, minerals, and active compounds. The team mixed its powder into wheat and gluten-free crackers at levels up to fifteen percent. They measured nutrition, antioxidant power, texture, taste, and blood sugar impact. The powder raised protein, fiber, phenols, and several minerals in both cracker types. It also lowered phytic acid, which blocks mineral uptake.

Estimated glycemic index fell sharply as powder levels rose. Wheat crackers dropped from the low nineties to the high fifties. Texture grew harder and spread wider above three percent powder. Tasters liked three to six percent best in sensory tests. Higher levels hurt color, taste, and crispness scores. The authors call the powder a promising functional ingredient.
pmc-13195494:
H Moghaddasi is first author on a 2026 case report series about removing metal foreign bodies from the skull, face, and jaw region with navigation guidance. Deeply embedded fragments from gunshot injuries sit near vital nerves and vessels. Standard imaging locates them poorly during surgery. Three-dimensional image-guided navigation offers real-time positioning from preoperative scans.

Three patients with retained gunshot fragments underwent extraction planned on computed tomography scans. The navigation system guided precise access and dissection with minimal tissue disturbance. In all cases, fragments were accurately localized and removed without significant complications or nerve or vessel injury. Recovery was uncomplicated. The authors present navigation as a safe, effective tool for such complex trauma cases.
pmc-13198594:
Jianan Jie and colleagues link a gene variant to stubborn diarrhea in a child in a 2026 study. Gene sequencing found a new variant in LEF1, a gene that guides cell growth, in a boy with watery diarrhea from age eighteen months. The illness lasted four years and stunted his growth despite standard care.

To test cause, the team built mice carrying the matching variant. Those mice showed weak gut lining, odd gut structure, and worse diarrhea under a gut stress test. Seal proteins that keep the gut barrier tight ran low in both mouse and patient tissue. The variant boosts its own gene's activity and pushes cells toward a state that breaks the barrier. The gene may serve as a diagnostic marker.
pmc-13199694:
Joshua Evan Wijaya and colleagues present a 2026 case report on a mixed lung cancer with two rare gene changes. Combined small-cell lung cancer holds both small-cell and non-small-cell parts in one tumor. Holding two drug-target gene changes at once is extremely uncommon and complicates care.

Their patient was a 63-year-old man with cough and right chest pain. Scans showed a lung mass and swollen chest nodes. A first biopsy read as adenocarcinoma with no targetable changes. After weak response to pre-surgery chemotherapy, surgeons removed the lung lobe. Full study then revealed the mixed cancer plus two gene changes, one in EGFR and one in ALK. Nodes were clear. Targeted therapy followed, with no return on later scans.
pmc-13201094:
Pratyusa Das and eleven colleagues show that the glucocorticoid receptor is needed for the normal growth of growth-hormone cells in the pituitary. Stress hormones are known to help these somatotrope cells mature. Earlier work pointed to the factor FOXO1 in the timing. The team cut the receptor gene Nr3c1 only in the pituitary of mice. They counted cell groups from the embryo stage into adult life.

Without the receptor, somatotropes grew poorly and stayed low at seven weeks in both sexes. Lactotrope cells, which make milk hormone, rose instead, and stayed high only in females. FOXO1 nearly vanished from pituitaries that lacked the receptor, and it stayed low in adults. These twenty twenty-six findings suggest that glucocorticoids set the balance between pituitary cell types, with FOXO1 as the receptor's partner in that choice.
pmc-13202694:
Feelings are learnable, and a 2026 qualitative study authored by H Andersson studies a Swedish school program that taught emotion regulation to teens and parents together. The study explores how participants experienced a preventive skills training of five sessions covering psychoeducation about emotions and regulation plans.

Interviews with seven parents and five teens were analyzed thematically after the training ended. Participants described a real need for emotional awareness that stigma and low knowledge often keep hidden in daily life. Parents helped teens practice the skills at home, and families noted useful insights, though keeping skills alive needed continued practice and better timing.
pmc-13203994:
Both shoulders dislocated backward after a seizure, yet the injury was missed at first, in a 2026 case report authored by César Alejandro Jiménez-Aroche. The article describes a 27-year-old man with no epilepsy history whose tonic-clonic seizure caused bilateral posterior shoulder fracture-dislocations.

Later scans confirmed both dislocations with fractures of the greater tuberosity, while the rotator cuffs remained intact on MRI review. pmc-13206294:
Village health volunteers fight child stunting, but how should they be mentored, and a 2026 systematic review authored by Nintinjri Husnida gathers the models in use. Mentoring formats ranged from structured training and growth monitoring to participatory methods and digital platforms for the cadres. Programs generally lifted volunteer knowledge, skills, and family health behavior, while proof of effects on children's growth stayed mixed. Steady supervision, cultural adaptation, and cross-sector teamwork enabled success.
pmc-13208394:
Vidac and coauthors chart spread patterns in advanced kidney cancer at one center. Kidney cancer spreads in varied and sometimes odd ways. It can reach both common and uncommon body sites. Tissue-confirmed cases give the firmest spread picture.

The team logged spread sites and adverse tissue traits. Rare sites were noted with care in the review. Patterns may help doctors recognize spread sooner.
pmc-13209594:
Qiyue Zhao and colleagues published a taxonomy study in 2026. They describe two new single-celled ciliate species. Samples came from sites in northeastern China. One species was found at a sewage outlet in Harbin. The other came from a puddle near waste disposal. Body shape and hair-like cilia patterns were documented. It sits near another known species genetically. Results suggest one genus is not a natural group. The authors propose revising its family classification. New species records expand knowledge of freshwater microbes.
pmc-13210094: A correction notice from Yaqi Liu and co-authors, published in 2026, repairs wording errors in their 2025 Microorganisms article on gut microbes of the saxaul sparrow under two extreme environments. The notice fixes the legend of a table on bacterial relative abundances. It also corrects descriptions of bacterial composition at family, genus, and species levels, and repairs one species' Latin name. The notice itself is all that survives here, so the study's underlying data and conclusions are not presented.
pmc-13211694:
Zheng Zhang and five co-authors redesign a flu vaccine part to make it sturdier and better aimed. Flu shifts its surface each year, which blunts vaccines. Two spots on the protein head were tested.

Both changed viruses stood up to heat better but entered cells more slowly. In mice, all vaccines fully protected against a lethal dose. One change cut weight loss and raised blocking antibody levels near twofold. The paper backs sugar placement by design as a route to better flu shots.
pmc-13212794:
Jeanne Moor and co-authors examine in 2026 whether girls and boys tolerate the Pfizer COVID-19 vaccine differently over the long term. Sex differences in vaccine side effects are known in adults, but data in children have lagged behind.

Girls showed modestly higher odds of local, general, and muscle symptoms after this vaccine, with age modifying the local effect. After ordinary childhood vaccines, no such sex gap appeared. The authors say approval studies and monitoring should plan for sex differences rather than discover them afterwards.
pmc-13214394:
Yiqian Jiang and colleagues investigate in 2026 how a common cat virus escapes vaccines while barely changing its genetic code. They collected thirteen strains from cats in China's Jilin Province over six years and compared their coat protein genes and immune profiles.

Several lineages circulated together, including some related to strains behind a severe systemic form and others previously seen in dogs. Vaccine-induced antibodies neutralised most isolates, yet two strains from vaccinated cats resisted strongly. Two near-identical strains baffled expectations: serum against one failed against its twin, while the reverse worked. Tiny changes clustered in a variable coat region near antibody targets and the cell-entry docking site explain the escape.
pmc-13216094:
Erika Tapia-Bahena and co-authors present a 2026 laboratory protocol for telling microplastics apart from chitin inside insects. These insects are eaten by people and wildlife, so mistaking body material for plastic would distort exposure estimates.

The team used edible grasshoppers spiked with known plastics and stained them with two fluorescent dyes. Nile red coloured four common plastics green or red at a low dose, while calcofluor white lit chitin blue under ultraviolet light. Using both dyes together separated plastic from tissue clearly, even for particles under fifty micrometres, and infrared spectroscopy confirmed the plastic types. The authors describe the method as cheap, simple, and ready for field studies.
pmc-13216594:
Laura A. Stevens and co-authors present a 2026 field study from the Greenland ice sheet testing a feared shortcut in ice loss. The fear is that draining surface lakes at low elevation could trigger crack-driven drainage of lakes further inland, speeding meltwater delivery to the bed.

A 22-station satellite positioning array watched seven lake basins across a 55-kilometre transect for two melt seasons, catching eleven hydro-fracture events. In four episodes, several lakes cracked close together in time at similar elevations, yet strain rates around higher lakes stayed undisturbed. The authors conclude that surface-to-bed pathways advance inland alongside the melt front itself, not because distant low lakes drain.
pmc-13217194:
Sankar and colleagues report a brain abscess caused by Fusobacterium bacteria in a teenager whose immune system was healthy. Brain abscesses are rare, and Fusobacterium accounts for only a small share of them. Fewer than twenty childhood cases have been reported worldwide, most linked to poor dental health or sinus infection, as here.

The infection grew out of sinusitis, a common illness that very seldom reaches the brain. These bacteria grow without oxygen and often fail to show in standard cultures, so diagnosis can stall. The case warns clinicians to think of anaerobic bacteria when a young patient's sinus disease turns neurological, and to treat fast once imaging points that way.
pmc-13217694:
Xin Zhang and co-authors present a 2026 study of tiny parcels shed by skeletal muscle into the blood, marked by the muscle calcium channel RYR1, as messengers of exercise's metabolic benefits. How muscle talks to the rest of the body during training is a live question in ageing research.

Engineered human muscle tissues in the lab released two vesicle families; the RYR1-carrying ones held twenty-four enriched microRNAs, including classic muscle microRNAs, whose targets map to growth, ageing, and insulin pathways. In two human cohorts, these vesicles rose with chronic exercise training, and people with more of them showed better insulin action, including older adults with prediabetes. The authors propose the vesicles as biomarkers, and possibly mediators, of healthy metabolic ageing.
pmc-13218094:
Babatunde Abdulmujeeb Aremu and colleagues pool published findings on teenage pregnancy in Uganda in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. Pregnancy during the teenage years carries heavy risks for mothers and babies, and cutting maternal deaths by 2030 is a stated global development goal. Country-level estimates are needed to aim prevention efforts where the burden is highest.

Following standard review methods, the team searched PubMed, African Journals Online, and Google Scholar and screened 918 records. Ten studies with 4,143 participants met the entry rules, and quality was checked with established appraisal tools. The pooled prevalence of teenage pregnancy came to 25.5 percent, but individual studies ranged from 3.0 percent to 56.4 percent, showing how strongly place and population shape the figure. The Central-Eastern region recorded the highest estimate, and the authors judge confidence in the pooled result as very low, which tempers how firmly the pooled number can be used.
pmc-13218194:
Eve Bunni and co-authors build a core information set on induction of labour in a 2026 United Kingdom consensus study. Inducing labour is increasingly common, and in England a third of women now have their labour induced. Guidelines say women should receive the information needed for a genuinely informed decision, yet nobody had agreed on what that information must include.

The team first assembled 199 candidate information points from systematic reviews, patient leaflets, interviews, and a stakeholder survey, then distilled them into 46 items for a two-round Delphi vote. Parents made up most of the 368 first-round voters, alongside 58 professionals, and 177 people voted in round two. Forty-four items passed the inclusion bar, and a consensus meeting settled on twelve overarching information points. The final set, populated with evidence aligned to national guidelines, is offered as a standard checklist that women and clinicians can work through together before an induction.
pmc-13218894:
Xu, Zhang, and Zhang hunt fat-mark risk sets for sugar ill in young hosts. Fat mark, BMI, is a cheap screen mark for sugar risk. Its spare risk in young hosts with sound sugar had stayed dim. The pool came from a China health-check bank in the work. Hosts were under age 40, free of sugar ill at the start. Each had full fat facts and one or more check-back meets. Sound sugar meant a fast read past the set line low.

In sum, 103,693 hosts sat in the pool at the start. New sugar ill struck 266 hosts in the track span. Curve fits and bend-line reads weighed fat ties to the ill. Four learn tools met, with a plain fit picked as chief. A bent tool, XGBoost, probed the bent side of risk. Score-share reads told which traits drove the tool picks.
pmc-13219894:
Fakhreddine Alouane and colleagues report an unusually shaped salivary gland tumor of the hard palate in a 2026 case report. Pleomorphic adenoma is the commonest salivary tumor and the palate its favorite site, but it almost always sits as a firm, flat-based lump. This one broke the pattern in both shape and tissue makeup.

A forty-six-year-old woman presented with a stalked, pedunculated mass on her hard palate, its surface ulcerated and X-rays showing pressure erosion of the bone beneath. Surgeons removed the lesion under local anesthesia. Under the microscope it proved to be a pleomorphic adenoma containing fat-cell change, adipocytic metaplasia, an uncommon feature that can be mistaken for malignant transformation. Healing was uneventful and nothing had returned at twelve months. The authors stress correlating clinical, imaging, and pathology findings in atypical variants, and keeping patients under review for late recurrence or malignant change.
pmc-13221694:
Gershon Spitz leads a large team in testing blood marks for mild brain injury in older adults. The paper is from two thousand twenty-six. A mild knock to the head is common in this age group but hard to call, since its signs blend with those of age. Blood tests could help, yet older adults are scarce in past studies.

They enrol adults past sixty at a trauma centre in Melbourne, plus healthy peers with no recent harm. Four blood proteins are read against a strict clinical call of injury. All four run high in the injured group. One, GFAP, sorts injury from no injury with top marks. The set may also sort the grey zone of suspected cases.
pmc-13226694:
K Hoernle and a large geoscience team date a 2026 event in Pacific plate history: the start of subduction beneath the Aleutian arc. When and why one plate began diving there matters for understanding a Pacific-wide reorganisation in the early Eocene. Rock samples from four underwater sequences along the western Aleutians supplied age and chemistry data spanning about 700 kilometres.

Results place the initiation at fifty-six million years ago or earlier. The earliest lavas chemically resemble those from the young Izu-Bonin-Mariana system, a classic subduction birthplace. Plate modelling links the trigger to an arc collision near Kamchatka and the consumption of a mid-ocean ridge, swinging Pacific plate motion from west-northwest to north within a few million years. The authors also raise possible climate connections.
pmc-13227494:
Alicja Bigosińska, Dominika Gondek, Luis Domingo, and Agnieszka Kącka-Zych use computer models to study how certain ring-forming reactions choose their products. Their study was published in twenty twenty-six. The reactions pair electron-hungry allenes, a class of carbon chains, with ring-shaped partners in a classic reaction type called Diels-Alder.

Working within a theory that tracks electron density, the team compared two sulfonyl allenes with two ring partners. Computed reactivity scores cast the allenes as strong electron takers and the rings as strong givers. One pairing needed little energy to start and gave off much heat, picking a single site every time. A second pairing, with an added methoxy group, started even more easily and picked one arrangement fully. The models explain the choices by which carbon forms the new bond first.
pmc-13229394:
Muhamad Reza Utama and a large team publish a 2026 protocol for a realist review of clinical-skills remediation in medical training across lower-income countries. Students and doctors who fall behind in practical skills endanger patients, yet support programmes are understudied where faculty shortages, thin simulation access, and stigma bite hardest. A realist approach asks not just whether remediation works, but how, for whom, and under what conditions.

The review will gather studies, evaluations, and policy documents from the year 2000 onward across medical, nursing, psychology, and education databases, plus grey literature. Following published realist standards, the team aims to name the main challenges and strategies reported, then build an evidence-informed programme theory that training schools in similar settings can adapt.
pmc-13230294:
Busra Nur Koyuncu and colleagues compare in 2026 diet and nutrition in people newly diagnosed with blood cancers against healthy adults. Thirty-four patients with lymphoma, leukemia, or myeloma were matched by age and sex with thirty-four controls. Diet records, food surveys, body measures, and malnutrition criteria captured eating patterns and physical status.

Patients took in far less total antioxidant capacity from food each day than controls did. More than three in five patients met criteria for moderate or severe malnutrition, and low muscle mass was more common among them. Intake of energy, protein, zinc, vitamin E, and folate also lagged behind controls. Variety of foods eaten did not differ between groups. Early diet support at diagnosis is suggested, with outcome trials still needed.
pmc-13232794:
Keita Umejima and colleagues test in 2026 whether starting a manga story on paper changes how the brain handles its second half. Each story was told in two halves from two heroes viewpoints, so finishing well meant joining both views. Readers began on paper or on a tablet, then continued on a screen inside a scanner while rating empathy.

Tablet starters answered joined-plot questions more slowly, and their brains worked harder in core language regions during the second half. Paper starters showed quieter frontal activity, as if the story frame had been built with less effort. Extra supportive activity in tablet readers tracked with correct answers, suggesting strain that still paid off. First-half medium, the work hints, sets up later understanding.
pmc-13234194:
Mohamed H. Mahmoud and colleagues published a 2026 survey study of gold deposits in the Um Balad area of Egypt's Eastern Desert. Precambrian terrain there mixes rock types and fault systems, making hydrothermal gold hard to target. The team combined airborne magnetic surveys, ground gravity measurements, and lab chemistry and mineral tests to map the structures that guided hot, metal-bearing fluids.

Rock samples carried alteration minerals including hematite, goethite, chlorite, and kaolinite, and micro-tests confirmed real enrichment in gold, copper, and silver, with gold reaching a maximum of 5.69 weight percent in the measured material. The integrated maps give drillers a structural shortlist.
pmc-13234294:
Khadija Shakra and co-authors reported in 2026 on improving university learning spaces through creative reuse of waste materials. Their project took place at Beni Suef University in Egypt, in the Faculty of Technology and Education. Work covered classrooms, the lobby and offices, and both the front and back facades. Specialists from architecture, electrical engineering, and art education planned the changes together.

Much of the reused material came from solid waste such as cork, paper, metal, plastic, and wood. Reuse avoided extra carbon emissions linked to buying new materials. Surveys of users found better impressions of the space, a stronger sense of professionalism, and greater awareness of sustainability. The authors propose steady upcycling programs and shared waste rules so other campuses can copy the approach.
pmc-13236094:
A death notices listing published in 2026, in French, records Canadian physicians who died in recent months, with no named author. Entries give each doctor's city, medical school and graduation year, specialty, and date and age at death, plus a link to a fuller obituary. The physicians listed practised across provinces from Ontario and Quebec to British Columbia and New Brunswick. Specialties range from family medicine and emergency care to surgery, anaesthesia, and obstetrics.

Ages at death in the entries span from the mid-fifties to the early nineties, reflecting several generations of practice. Graduation years reach back to the early nineteen sixties for the oldest physicians listed. Several entries note training abroad, including schools in Myanmar, India, Jamaica, and England. The listing serves as a professional record for colleagues and families rather than a research report. Readers can follow each link for service details and fuller life stories.
pmc-13236494:
Qiuyu Zhang, Yu Wu, Dan Luo, and Fengshan Fang summarized in 2026 how two toxins from Staphylococcus aureus damage the human body. The bacterium causes illnesses from skin infections to sepsis and pneumonia, and drug-resistant strains complicate treatment worldwide. No effective vaccine against it exists at present. Alpha and beta hemolysins, which attack red blood cells and other tissues, are the focus toxins.

Alpha hemolysin forms pores in cell membranes, directly injuring host tissue during infection. Beta hemolysin works through a different chemistry, breaking down a key fat in cell membranes. Understanding each toxin's action clarifies how the bacterium invades, spreads, and evades defences in the body. Blocking toxins rather than killing bacteria offers a possible new treatment route as antibiotic resistance grows. The authors offer the summary as a reference for antitoxin therapy development.
pmc-13236794:
Yao, Lee, and Jin propose a faster way to analyse very large studies that follow people over time. Modern health apps gather repeated measures from huge crowds, and standard methods grind through every record again and again. Their method, repeated block perturbation subsampling, works on well-chosen slices of the data instead of the whole mass.

The approach builds on estimating equations, a standard tool for repeated measures that move together within a person. Careful slicing keeps the answers trustworthy while cutting computing time sharply. For app-based health research, where data grow daily, such shortcuts decide whether analysis is a routine step or a bottleneck that stalls whole projects.
pmc-13237494:
Yaroslav I. Molkov and colleagues extended a computer model of four-legged walking in 2026 to study how animals turn at different speeds. Each strategy won at a different speed. Body bending gave the sharpest turns when slow, lateral force worked best at medium speeds, and lateral limb shifting won when fast. Forelimbs consistently led the steering, while hindlimbs handled propulsion and stability in strategy-specific ways. The authors suggest animals pick or blend strategies by speed, a principle that could guide legged robots.
pmc-13237594:
Morishita gauges blood flow imbalance in acute heart failure without invasive tools. Acute failure is seen as a worsened stage of chronic failure. The shift to crisis is still poorly defined in flow terms. A balance view joins venous return and heart output.

The study held 193 patients with chronic failure or related disease. Vein width and body water ratios gave flow estimates. A mismatch index summed the flow imbalance for each patient. The index split into two clusters in the data. That split may mark a pre-crisis flow state. Early flags could guide care before full crisis.
pmc-13237694:
Meng Zhang and colleagues applied failure mode and effects analysis in 2026 to cut infections acquired in the intensive care unit of a cancer hospital. Cleaning quality, checked with fluorescent markers, roughly doubled. The authors credit the structured risk hunt plus bundled action for the gains.
pmc-13237794:
Zhou and colleagues test whether uric acid can protect the brain in Parkinson's disease. Population studies have long hinted that people with higher uric acid develop Parkinson's less often. A signalling route called Nrf2, the cell's master switch for antioxidant defence, carried the effect. The work turns a statistical hint into a mechanism that drug designers can test further.
pmc-13238594:
Al-Nahlawi, Assadian, and Nossrat report a tooth saved by mixing two usually separate treatments, then followed for five years. Their patient, a woman of twenty-three, had deep decay in an upper molar. The tooth's nerve was painfully inflamed beyond recovery. The tissue around the root tip was inflamed as well. That pairing often ends in extraction or full root canal work.

The team combined standard root canal treatment on the dead roots with vital pulp therapy, which keeps living tissue where it survives. Five years on, the tooth still worked. Long follow-up is what case reports owe readers: proof that a clever compromise lasts, not just that it can be done.
pmc-13239094:
Reema Hamasha and colleagues ran a virtual democratic deliberation in 2026 with thirty-three Arab and Middle Eastern North African community members in Michigan, partnered with the ACCESS community organization. They preferred doctors using AI as support, never as substitute, and they questioned whether systems would reflect their community's needs. The authors say community partnerships like this one are the price of responsible AI adoption.
pmc-13239294:
Meiqiong Kuang and seven co-authors compare two first-line regimens for HER2-positive breast cancer that has spread. Their real-world study was published in twenty twenty-six. Both regimens pair a backbone of two drugs with a taxane; they differ in the second HER2 blocker added, and head-to-head proof was thin.

The multicenter review covered four hundred and eleven patients treated between twenty eighteen and twenty twenty-five. One hundred and forty-eight got the antibody pairing; two hundred and sixty-three got the pill pairing. After matching alike patients, one hundred and thirty-nine pairs remained. The pill group went longer before the cancer progressed, both before and after matching. Response rates and safety were also compared. The data give doctors grounded help for a first choice.
pmc-13239994:
Akira Watanabe and colleagues study how bait changes raccoon behaviour in Fukushima's farm landscape in a 2026 paper. Raccoons are an invasive species in Japan, and baiting helps managers trap and observe them, yet free food might also pull animals together and spread disease.

Dry cat food and caramel corn were the top first choices, though individuals differed. During baiting, animals lingered and searched near stations far more, and they ranged closer to trap sites on bait days. Long-term home ranges barely shifted, so the effect was local intensification rather than redistribution.
pmc-13241494:
Zheng and colleagues at Zhejiang University built a heat-and-listen platform for treating dangerously slow heart rhythms. Integrated sensors outresolved thermal cameras while responding faster. Zheng frames the platform as a safer, closed-loop route to rhythm correction.
pmc-13241794:
Santosh Basapur leads a nine-author team testing an intelligent medication system for people living with dementia at home, in a feasibility study published in two thousand twenty-six. Their system automates the chain of custody, verifies actual consumption, and logs adherence automatically. The study assessed feasibility and usability with mixed methods. Removing manual pill counting is the central design move, since counting is where cognitive impairment bites hardest. Caregiver burden was part of the motivation. A device that quietly proves doses were taken could keep people home longer and safer.
pmc-13242494:
Melanie Hawkins, Richard Sawatzky, and Kevin Weinfurt set out the theory behind the argument-based approach to validity in health measurement. Their paper appeared in Quality of Life Research in 2026. The paper pursues two aims: explaining the theory and examining its assumptions about fairness.

The approach starts by stating plainly how scores will be read and used. Assumptions under that statement then direct what evidence to gather and how to judge it. The authors give special weight to equitable consequences, since the same questionnaire can behave differently across groups and settings. A validity argument, in their account, weighs threats and side effects openly. The paper is a reference for anyone defending a measurement choice.
pmc-13242594:
Sokhandan Fadakar Maryem and co-authors present a 2026 cross-sectional study of sexual and reproductive health among teenagers at school in Hulu Langat, a district of Malaysia. Pornography exposure was reported more often than masturbation, and reported sexual activity was very low. The authors question whether teens answer such forms honestly in non-anonymous settings. They recommend clearer, more confidential screening so health programs rest on truer numbers.
pmc-13242694:
Arvin Babaei and co-authors trialed egg white powder as a supplement for diabetic patients on hemodialysis. Their double-blind, placebo-controlled trial appeared in Health Science Reports in 2026. Protein intake rose in the supplement group while phosphorus fell, a rare and welcome combination in kidney care. Blood albumin climbed clearly, cholesterol and LDL dropped, and fasting sugar declined. Antioxidant defenses strengthened while a marker of oxidative damage fell. The placebo group saw no comparable gains. The authors present egg white powder as a safe, practical addition to renal nutrition therapy. Its low phosphorus load is the feature that sets it apart from many protein supplements.
pmc-13243694:
Nasser Shoeibi and colleagues report a diabetic man struck by two aggressive fungal infections of the eye and orbit after COVID-19. Finding one fungus, they argue, should trigger a search for others.
pmc-13245094:
Zhang and co-authors describe a lab tool for making antibody fragments in this 2026 brief report in mAbs. Drug and research work often needs antibody pieces cut free of their Fc tail, but producing them normally takes an enzyme step followed by several purification steps to remove the leftovers.

Packed onto a column, the fusion captures an antibody, cuts it, and lets the clean fragment flow through while the tail and enzyme stay behind. The one-step method suits small-scale and automated workflows.
pmc-13245894:
Seow, Ko, and Low analyzed text messages from a hospital-at-home program in Singapore, in this 2026 Journal of Medical Internet Research study. The messages fell into three groups: clinical checks and advice, practical arrangements such as transport, and the interpersonal tone of the exchanges. The authors say program designers should plan for that relational work, not treat chat as a simple scheduling tool.
pmc-13246394:
Wanxia Jiang explores how park scenery stirs feelings that lead to green behavior in a 2026 survey study. Feeling for nature and bonds with a place may turn pleasant views into care for the environment. The study tests both paths among park users in Chengdu, China.

Surveys from 478 users of three large urban parks fed a structural model. Good views of the landscape raised green behavior both directly and through feelings. Empathy with nature carried the stronger indirect effect, while place attachment also helped. The author suggests park design that deepens emotional ties, not just looks. Such design could support wider city environmental goals.
pmc-13246694:

Two paths carried the link: steadier control of emotions and lower stress from cultural adjustment. Interviews with 22 students added themes of emotional release, social connection, and cultural bridging through music. The authors suggest campus vocal programs as a warm, low-cost support.
pmc-13246794:
Koda and Soejima published this correction in Scientific Reports in 2026. Nothing else changes, but the edit reverses what the paper claimed about a piece of evidence in a real criminal case, which is exactly why the formal correction matters.
pmc-13247794:
Carly Grubb, Jeanine Young, and Levita D'Souza study parents who struggle to follow cot-only sleep advice in a 2026 qualitative analysis. Official guidance has long told parents to never share a sleep surface with a baby. Death rates have not fallen as hoped, and many families still share sleep.

pmc-13248894:
A 2026 correction repairs data errors in a 2013 randomized trial of eucalyptus oil inhalation after knee replacement. The trial had tested whether breathing the oil eased pain and inflammation after surgery. Values in one table were entered wrongly while the manuscript was prepared.

The correction prints the full corrected table of baseline measures for both study groups. It covers pain scores, blood pressure, heart rate, and two blood markers for the 52 patients. A figure unit for white blood cell counts is also fixed, and the corrected figure appears in full. Notes clarify that pain scores were whole numbers only. The record now shows the right starting values for both arms.
pmc-13249194:
Kamil and colleagues mapped a research field rather than a disease, in this 2026 bibliometric study. Their topic was the gut microbiota's role in stunting, the growth failure that still affects millions of young children. The team analyzed one hundred seventy-two publications indexed in Scopus between 2009 and 2025, charting who publishes, where, and on what themes.

Output grew steadily and peaked in 2021. The United States, France, Bangladesh, China, and Indonesia led production, with a 2014 study by Subramanian as the field's foundation. Keywords drifted from plain malnutrition toward gut imbalance, a leaky gut condition, and microbe-based treatments such as probiotics. The authors point readers toward moderate malnutrition and microbiota-directed foods as the next frontiers.
pmc-13249594:
Karsten Dafonte and a German team lay out the ALIVe study, a 2026 protocol for dosing drugs safely in liver cirrhosis. A scarred liver clears many medicines slowly, yet no guideline tells doctors how to adjust doses for it. The project moves in three phases: harvest published dose advice and grade it, settle disagreements through expert Delphi rounds, then test the agreed advice in real patients.

The clinical phase began in January 2025, and one hundred twenty-one patients had enrolled by May 2026. Final results are expected in August 2026. The authors say combining literature, expert consensus, and bedside validation should yield dosing guidance sturdy enough for everyday practice.
pmc-13249694:
Guoyu Ling, Rukayat Akande, and Stewart Albert revisit a blood marker puzzle in this 2026 hospital study. High levels of a hormone-like protein called PTHrP often point to cancer as the cause of high blood calcium, yet harmless conditions can raise it too.

Reviewing records for 236 patients with high calcium and raised PTHrP, the team found 58 with known cancer. The rest had defined non-cancer causes, most often an overactive parathyroid gland. Cancer patients had the highest PTHrP levels, but ranges overlapped. Reading the regular parathyroid hormone level alongside PTHrP sharply improved the odds estimate, and mild PTHrP rises with a normal-range hormone level rarely meant cancer.
pmc-13250194:
Li and co-authors compare drug treatments given before a balloon procedure for a serious form of high blood pressure in the lungs. Their 2026 Open Heart paper uses the United Kingdom's national registry for chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension. Patients received medicines to lower lung artery pressure before balloon pulmonary angioplasty at one national center.

Among one hundred fifty-eight patients, those on two-drug therapy started sicker, with higher pressures and lower heart output. They also improved the most before the procedure, gaining more heart output and dropping resistance further than single-drug groups. Complication rates at the first balloon procedure were similar across the strategies. Lung injury was more common in patients who still had very high pressures at procedure time.
pmc-13250394: Quraish and colleagues report a 2026 Clinical Case Reports case of a twelve-year-old girl who developed gonadoblastoma in both gonads. It appeared four years after her treatment for a Wilms tumor, a childhood kidney cancer. The second tumor arrived silently, found during follow-up rather than through symptoms. The authors use the case to argue for careful, risk-based long-term surveillance after childhood cancer treatment. They also urge doctors to examine incidental gonadal findings closely, even when a young patient feels entirely well.
pmc-13250494:
Zilma Silveira Nogueira Reis leads a large team in a 2026 validation study of drug instructions written by language models. The study tested whether three artificial intelligence systems could turn prescriptions into clear guidance for patients in primary care. Clear instructions matter because confusion about medicines leads people to stop treatment early.

Sixty-two health professionals graded model-written instructions for invented prescription cases while blinded to which system wrote each text. ChatGPT-4.0 earned the highest overall scores, with a median mark of 88.4 points on the grading scale used. A smaller open model scored lower on its own, but its mark rose to 79.9 points when it could draw on patient leaflets. The authors conclude that leaflet support helps smaller models approach the quality of the largest system. They frame the work as a preclinical check, done before any use with real patients.
pmc-13250694:
Abdulqudos Al-Fakih led this 2026 trial of play-based therapy for Syrian refugee children in Jordan. The children, aged five to 13, lived with trauma symptoms after war and flight, and talk therapy can stumble on language and culture gaps.

A total of 102 children were split by chance into sandplay therapy, art therapy, or standard counselling, one session a week for 12 weeks. Trauma scores fell in all groups but most sharply with sandplay, which cut symptom scores far more than art or counselling. The authors back hands-on, word-free therapies as part of wider care for children hit by conflict.
pmc-13251394:
Nidhi Tejan and colleagues present a diagnostic puzzle in this 2026 brief case report. A ten-year-old boy with HIV had suffered two years of heavy watery diarrhoea, a swelling belly, low fevers, and weight loss, leaving him pale and malnourished.

Five stool tests found no parasites, and tissue samples from his small intestine also looked clean. The answer sat in the fluid drawn from that same intestine: under the microscope it held many oval cysts of a parasite called Cystoisospora belli, confirmed by a special stain. The case shows why gut fluid deserves a look when stool tests keep missing the cause in children with weak immunity.
pmc-13251694:
Yilong Zhang and co-authors test a different iron supplement for weaned piglets in a 2026 feeding study. Young pigs need iron, but the usual supplement, ferrous sulfate, is poorly absorbed, and leftover iron in the gut feeds harmful bacteria. The team replaced it with ferrous glycinate, a form the body absorbs more readily, at lower doses.

Thirty piglets were split into three diets: the standard sulfate dose or glycinate at fifty or seventy-five milligrams per kilogram of feed. Growth stayed equal across groups even though the glycinate diets carried up to half the iron dose of the standard. Gut barrier measures improved, and blood tests showed more efficient iron transport. Microbe sequencing found more beneficial Lactobacillus and Akkermansia and fewer Proteobacteria, a group rich in pathogens. The authors explain that less leftover iron in the hindgut starves harmful bacteria of a resource they need.
pmc-13252994:
Raza and co-authors review attempts to heal donor organs while they sit on warm perfusion machines before transplant. Their 2026 Transplantation Direct systematic review follows the shift from simply preserving organs to actively rehabilitating them. Lung perfusion is the most mature field, with kidney, liver, and heart work emerging behind it.

Of thousands of records screened, twenty-one studies qualified, mostly on kidneys and livers in human or pig organs. Treatments ranged from drugs and cell therapies to fat-removal protocols and circuit tweaks. Nearly all studies improved molecular measures, but barely a third improved actual organ function, and few checked results after transplant. The authors want standard reporting and transplant-linked testing to turn rejected organs into usable grafts.
pmc-13253694:
Chun Zhai and colleagues survey what frontline medical staff in China know about Duchenne muscular dystrophy in a 2026 multicenter study. This progressive muscle disease needs lifelong, coordinated care, and new gene-based therapies are raising the stakes for early recognition. The team circulated a structured survey through a national rare disease alliance.

Of 510 surveys distributed, 496 valid responses came back from general, maternal-child, and pediatric hospitals. Overall awareness of the disease scored 54.64 percent, but the profile was uneven: staff knew treatment best, diagnosis less well, and policy worst at 42.74 percent of the possible score. Occupation, education, and years of experience each predicted awareness, with nurses scoring below physicians and technicians. The authors say the sharpest gaps concern genetic diagnosis and orphan drug policy. They call for targeted training for nursing staff to build the mixed teams the genomic therapy era will require.
pmc-13253894:
R Kaufmann and colleagues report stroke treatment results in a 2026 study from a Western European hospital. Some strokes involve two blockages at once, in the neck artery and inside the brain, called tandem lesions. From 2015 to 2023, 64 patients got emergency neck artery stenting during clot-removal treatment, covering 65 procedures.

At 90 days, 41.5 percent of procedures left patients with low disability scores. Complications arose in 10.8 percent during the procedure, and 9.2 percent had symptomatic brain bleeding. Younger age and lower stroke severity predicted good recovery, and the authors say firm safety verdicts await randomized trials.
pmc-13254394:
Yusuf Brima and Marcellin Atemkeng test machine learning on skewed hospital data in a 2026 study. Emergency and intensive care data are imbalanced, meaning rare but critical outcomes are far outnumbered. Six model families were compared on two large data sets, MIMIC-IV-ED and eICU, across seven prediction tasks.

Results split by data set. Newer foundation models ranked best on MIMIC-IV-ED, while XGBoost led on eICU, with other tree methods close behind. TabNet, a deep learning model, degraded most sharply as imbalance grew and cost the most to run. Tree methods scaled best, so the authors call model choice context-based.
pmc-13254694:
Fazle Rabbi and colleagues test whether a mother's diet in pregnancy predicts her child's asthma in a 2026 analysis of Canada's CHILD cohort. Asthma affects over 850,000 Canadian children, and prenatal nutrition is a suspected early influence. Food frequency questionnaires from 2,968 mother-child pairs were distilled into three eating patterns: plant-based, Western, and balanced.

Neither asthma at ages one to three nor recurrent wheeze showed any association with any of the three dietary patterns, in either statistical approach the team used.
