What did predict outcomes was family history and birth timing. A mother's own asthma more than doubled her child's odds, and a father's asthma or wheeze did the same. Each added week of gestation lowered risk, and a mother's prior wheeze strongly predicted her child's recurrent wheeze. Prenatal diet pattern, at least as measured here, does not appear to be a lever for prevention.
pmc-13254894:
Dan Xu and colleagues use dopamine-system brain scans to tell two look-alike movement disorders apart in a 2026 prospective study. Parkinson's disease and the parkinsonian form of multiple system atrophy share slowness, stiffness, and balance trouble, and about a fifth of atrophy cases are misread as Parkinson's even at expert centers. The team imaged patients with 18F-DOPA PET, which measures the integrity of dopamine-producing terminals.

A new adaptive atlas let them align scans precisely without needing an MRI for each patient. Two regional signatures emerged as discriminators. Uptake in the caudate nucleus, a deep brain structure, was reduced specifically in the atrophy group compared with Parkinson's. The cerebellum also showed dopaminergic dysfunction in atrophy patients, despite their having no clinical signs pointing there. The authors present regional pattern analysis, rather than overall dopamine loss, as the way to make this scan decisive.
pmc-13255194:
Shuyuan Zhang, Saeed Shoaie, and Guy Carpenter study taste and mouth microbes in a 2026 paper. During eating, non-volatile flavor molecules mix into saliva and reach tongue receptors, touching the oral microbiome directly. The team gathered taste ratings, saliva microbe data, and saliva chemistry from 53 participants.

Strong taste perception linked to the saliva microbiome through many species acting together, not any single species. Two bacterial products, taurine and ethanolamine, showed the most links, tying to six of eight test solutions each. The authors say group-level microbe pathways capture taste links better than single-species counts.
pmc-13255594:
Junlong Zhu and colleagues report a 2026 study of sialylation, a sugar coating process on cell surfaces, in bladder cancer drug resistance. Standard chemotherapy with gemcitabine and cisplatin helps many patients, yet tumors often recur or stop responding. The team investigated whether abnormal sialylation helps explain who fares worse.

Their analysis linked sialylation-related molecules to patient prognosis, features of the tissue around tumors, and resistance to chemotherapy. The trail led to a central growth pathway, PI3K-AKT-mTOR, which is known to drive cancer cell survival. The work stops short of a clinical test, since the findings need laboratory and patient validation. Still, the authors argue the sugar-coating machinery deserves attention as a source of risk markers and future drug targets for this common urinary cancer.
pmc-13256094:
Nana Sun and a large team report a 2026 food-safety study of cadmium in mantis shrimp sold in Shanghai markets. The animal is a seasonal delicacy, and locals prize its roe and the rich hepatopancreas tissue. The team measured cadmium in five tissues across the shrimp's reproductive development stages using sensitive mass spectrometry.

Cadmium concentrated overwhelmingly in the hepatopancreas and intestine, at levels dozens of times higher than in muscle or gonads. Gonad levels stayed low at every stage and did not track reproductive development, suggesting a barrier in the outer gonad membrane shields the eggs. Risk assessment flagged eating intestine and hepatopancreas as a potential cancer concern. Muscle and roe, the most eaten parts, carried low risk, giving consumers targeted guidance.
pmc-13256294:
Haoze Yang and co-authors report a 2026 study isolating an antioxidant peptide mixture, named PASN, from Argentine squid processing waste. The team separated the smallest peptide fraction, mostly under one kilodalton, and found it had the strongest free-radical scavenging of the fractions tested. Its structure loosened from a rigid helix into flexible turns after enzyme treatment, and it withstood heat past 240 degrees.

In cell tests, PASN proved friendly to both rat neuron-like cells and human astrocytes, boosting their growth. Under stress-hormone challenge it raised survival, cut leakage of a damage marker, and restored a key antioxidant enzyme. It also rescued two brain-related proteins tied to plasticity and sleep regulation. The authors propose the squid peptide as a sustainable nutraceutical candidate, pending animal studies.
pmc-13257294:
Md Fakhrul Islam Khaled leads a 2026 study measuring radiation exposure during heart catheter procedures in Dhaka, Bangladesh. Angiography and stent work save lives yet expose staff to ionizing radiation daily. Two catheter labs at Bangladesh Medical University were monitored over six months.

Seven hundred seventy-six routine procedures were analyzed, most in men aged forty-six to sixty-five and most reached through the leg artery. Each case averaged about fourteen imaging views and eight minutes of screening. Complex cases, wrist access, and stent use each raised views, time, and dose. Operator dose was measured at four working positions and projected to yearly totals. Safety officers gain local numbers where routine monitoring had been limited. The findings support tighter dose tracking and technique choices that protect long-serving lab teams.
pmc-13257494:
Riyadh Alturki and Muhammad Khan examine whether a cement kiln waste can replace much of the cement in mortar. The waste, called alkali bypass dust, is cheap and plentiful but weakens mixes when used plain. Their 2026 experiments test it alongside silica fume and a water-reducing additive.

Replacing up to half the cement hurt workability and strength on its own. The water reducer restored flow and early strength, while silica fume improved later performance. Used together, the blend matched plain mortar strength after twenty-eight days at the highest replacement level. Statistical modeling showed that how the ingredients interact matters more than any single amount.
pmc-13257794:
Atanasi Tashev and colleagues compare wear in three aluminum-silicon piston alloys by experiment and simulation in a 2026 study. The high-silicon alloys differ in copper and chromium content and follow no standard grade. Bench wear tests under boundary lubrication fed a finite element contact model and a classic wear law.

Harder did not mean tougher here: the hardest alloy wore about twice as deep per engine cycle as the softest. Wear coefficients rose in the same wrong direction across the trio. Silicon particle shape and spread, plus intermetallic phases, explained the reversal better than hardness. Engine designers gain a selection warning with numbers attached. Realistic contact simulation joined to measured coefficients offers a reusable framework for screening piston alloys before costly engine endurance runs begin.
pmc-13257994:
Rim Benkabou leads a 2026 study of geopolymer mortar made from broken ceramic sanitaryware. Curing heat, timing, and delay were varied to see how oven strategy shapes strength and fire survival. Direct curing placed samples in heat at once, while delayed curing rested them first, at two temperatures and two durations.

Direct curing won consistently, topping out near thirty-one megapascals when heat started immediately at the higher setting for the longer run. Delayed samples reached only about half that strength in the weakest pairing. After a blast at eight hundred degrees, directly cured pieces kept more of their strength. Microscopy and diffraction backed the mechanical pattern. Waste-valorization builders gain a process rule: cure early and hot for sanitaryware geopolymers destined for demanding, heat-exposed service.
pmc-13258194:
Yi Zuo and colleagues present a 2026 simulation study of patient bias in AI health consultations. A simulated patient agent held three-round talks with six large language models, using 1,273 cases from a United States medical licensing exam dataset. In biased talks, the fake patient pushed a preferred but wrong diagnosis. The team measured diagnostic accuracy, tested prompt-based fixes and temperature settings, and tried splitting chat and final diagnosis between two models.

Biased consultations cut accuracy by about seven to thirty-nine percentage points across models, and smaller models fell close to random guessing. More than a third of errors matched the patient's wrong preference, showing systematic conformity rather than random mistakes. Prompt fixes and lower temperature helped little and inconsistently. The split dual-system design recovered about ten to thirty-nine points, especially in weaker models.
pmc-13258594:
Chufeng Cheng and coauthors build a 2026 material for pulling radioactive strontium out of water. Porous geopolymer beads served as a sturdy support for a crystal compound with strong strontium affinity. Heat based loading anchored the crystals evenly while keeping the pore channels open.

The composite removed about ninety two percent of strontium even in fairly acidic water. Plain beads removed almost none under the same conditions. Uptake capacity was high, and common sodium or potassium ions interfered little. Calcium and magnesium competed more strongly for the binding sites. Nuclear waste treatment gains a bead form that suits later flow through column testing.
pmc-13258694:
Hulya Yilmaz Onal and coauthors profile nutrition and inflammation scores in adults with an autoimmune thyroid disease during 2026 work. Two hundred twenty nine adults with Hashimoto thyroiditis had routine blood based scores calculated. Scores were compared with thyroid function, metabolism, disease length, and vitamin D status.

Vitamin D shortage affected about seven in ten participants. One nutrition score tracked closely with body weight category and insulin resistance. Another score rose with longer disease duration. Inflammation ratios drawn from blood counts added further pattern detail. Clinicians see routine lab scores as a cheap window on the wider health burden of this thyroid condition.
pmc-13259494:
Ming-Xian Zhang and coauthors identify a Penicillium fungus as a new cause of root rot in a medicinal herb in a 2026 report. Diseased rhizomes from Yunnan plantings yielded the suspect fungus. Inoculation tests on healthy material reproduced the rot, satisfying proof requirements.

Genetic markers and form together named the species with confidence. Growth peaked at warm room temperature under mildly alkaline conditions. Darkness favored body growth, while alternating light boosted spore production. Starch fed growth best among carbon sources tested. Growers of this high value herb gain the first warning and biology profile for this pathogen.
pmc-13260194:
Artur Brotons-Rufes leads a 2026 chemistry study of a palladium complex that folds wrongly in standard computer models. Density functional theory, or DFT, is a widely used method for predicting molecular shapes on a computer. For this planar palladium compound, gas-phase calculations produced an artificial folding. The distortion was first blamed on overstated weak pulls between the complex and nearby aromatic molecules, but better fixes for those forces only partly fixed it.

Adding strongly donating ligands made the curvature worse, even with modern dispersion fixes. The authors trace the problem to unrealistic empty space on the side opposite the coordinating ligands in the gas-phase model. Adding a single explicit solvent molecule greatly reduced the folding while keeping the same fixes. They urge modelers to include small but chemically meaningful surroundings for such complexes.
pmc-13260694:
Kenny Hawkins and colleagues present a 2026 report of two exploratory randomized trials of a Ginkgo biloba extract combined with phosphatidylserine, a fat that helps nerve cell signalling. In the first trial, healthy volunteers took 480 milligrams a day of the combination, or a placebo, for four weeks. Mood and cognition were tested at sixty and 180 minutes after a single dose, and again after four weeks. A second trial tested two doses in stressed adults.

After single doses and four weeks at 480 milligrams, participants showed improvements in delayed verbal memory and reaction time against placebo. The second trial, in adults with moderate stress, confirmed benefits on mood states at both 240 and 480 milligrams. Reaction times trended downward across all four cognitive tests, suggesting faster processing. Cognitive effects there were more modest than expected, and the authors call for further research.
pmc-13261594:
Sara Casati and a large team profiled in 2026 cannabis compounds in products seized in northern Italy, watching for semisynthetic variants made to dodge THC rules. Their validated laboratory method separates and measures 31 natural and semisynthetic cannabinoids, including acetylated forms that needed home-made reference standards. The survey covered 151 seized products from 2024 and 2025.

Nearly all products contained semisynthetic cannabinoids above the measurement threshold, including almost every resin sample. One acetylated form of THC appeared most often, in about eighty-five percent of products, followed by a side-chain-extended THC relative. Computer docking against the two cannabinoid receptors suggested the modified compounds may bind more strongly. The authors warn that these fast-spreading products carry poorly known potency and safety. They call for systematic study of their public health effects.
pmc-13261994:
Okechukwu Ugwu and co-authors review the protein-RNA partnerships that fine-tune plant chemistry on the fly. Beyond gene switches, RNA-protein complexes edit, move, and translate messages within minutes, suiting fast environmental responses. Their 2026 synthesis weighs the evidence for their grip on medicinal and aroma compounds.

Some complexes gather into droplet-like granules that stash or destroy messages as conditions change. Others, guided by small RNAs, silence the very factors that build flavonoid and related pathways. The authors sort solid mechanistic proof from mere association, and grade the mapping tools honestly. Non-model medicinal plants remain the biggest blind spot.
pmc-13262594:
Bingqing Zhu and colleagues pin down how much remimazolam sedates children of different ages. Dosing a fast, short-acting sedative safely demands age-specific numbers, so their 2026 trial splits one hundred twenty children into toddler, preschool, and school-age bands. A biased-coin staircase method homes in on the dose that works for nearly all.

Toddlers needed the most drug per kilogram, schoolchildren the least, with preschoolers between. Wake-up took longest in the youngest group, around half an hour. Side effects stayed rare: one case of low blood pressure and a handful of slow heartbeats or oxygen dips. The table of doses is the study's practical gift.
pmc-13262794:
Christina Dyar, Elise Green, and Christine M Lee asked in 2026 whether a person's reason for using cannabis and the setting combine to predict heavier use episode by episode. Phone-based momentary surveys tracked 571 young adult women who used cannabis regularly, with sexual minority and gender diverse participants deliberately oversampled. Each use event recorded motives, company, and intoxication.

Coping motives predicted longer and stronger intoxication only when the person used alone. In company, the coping link vanished entirely. Social and enhancement motives raised intoxication on their own, and social settings added their own lift without any interplay. The pattern means coping research that ignores setting can misread the risk entirely. The authors say solitary coping use deserves targeted attention in prevention work aimed at young women.
pmc-13263394:
Syeda Hani Ammad and co-authors present a 2026 case report of bladder stones in a young man with a spinal injury from a gunshot. Bladder stones are solid masses that form inside the bladder. A 19-year-old had lived with a neurogenic bladder, meaning nerve damage left it unable to empty, since being shot in the lower back eighteen months earlier.

He depended on a permanent catheter and had earlier needed a colostomy, a surgical opening for stool. Doctors found fourteen stones, a strikingly high number at his age. The authors stress that patients with nerve-damaged bladders and long-term catheters need close observation, careful catheter care, and early treatment to prevent recurrence.
pmc-13263494:
Nurlign Zelalem and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on delays in emergency cesarean delivery in public hospitals of northwest Ethiopia. Guidelines call for delivery within thirty minutes once surgery is decided, when mother or baby is in danger. The team studied 523 women who had emergency cesareans in early 2024.

Nearly eighty percent of deliveries missed the thirty-minute standard. Delays were strongly linked to missing operating room materials and to no free operating room being available. Operations led by integrated emergency obstetric surgeons, a mid-level surgical cadre, also took longer to reach delivery. The authors recommend fixing supply and room-availability problems and call for quality improvement studies.
pmc-13264094:
Shayantan Banerjee, Vijay K Tiwari, Karthik Raman and Mohammad Inayatullah derive immune gene signatures for chemotherapy response in triple-negative breast cancer in a 2026 analysis. Immune cells inside a tumor, called tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes, often predict whether early chemotherapy will clear the cancer. Using single-cell data from tumors sampled before treatment, the team built an eighty-gene signature tied to immune activation and cell abundance.

A refined thirty-gene panel predicted complete response versus leftover disease across eleven independent patient groups. Central genes included well-known T cell signals, and shared control factors suggested a stable immune program. Such a test could help doctors sort patients toward standard therapy or trials for likely non-responders before treatment starts.
pmc-13264194:
Evija Skujina and Irina Pilvere analyze live cattle exports across European Union states from 2014 to 2024 in a 2026 study. Farm policy reforms and green strategy goals are reshaping the cattle sector, and trade patterns differ sharply by country. The authors combined export values, cattle population trends and clustering methods to group twenty-three member states by how export intensity and herd change move together over the decade.

Total live cattle export value rose strongly while the overall herd shrank, a split pattern the authors call decoupled. Three country groups emerged, from export-heavy states with falling herds to domestically focused states with low export intensity. Uneven structures raise questions about long-term competition and how common policies land in different national farm systems.
pmc-13264294:
Fan Yong and colleagues model present and future habitat for the leopard cat in China in a 2026 study. This small wild cat holds protected status and signals healthy ecosystems. The team combined several distribution models with niche analysis. Suitable land was mapped for today and for future climates. Temperature seasonality and slope emerged as leading influences on where the species can persist, across the southeast hills and southwestern plateau regions.

Suitable ground currently covers about one sixth of the country. Core areas look stable, with some northern expansion, local losses and a northward drift of the range center. Future niches closely resemble today ones, yet most current habitat faces strongly novel climate conditions. Corridors, anti-fragmentation work and conflict prevention form the proposed adaptive response.
pmc-13264794:
Tae Hwan Park and a large team prospectively study thick dermal matrix sheets for filling breast volume defects in a 2026 single-center report. Twenty patients received the thick material as a deep layer under reshaped gland tissue or flap reconstructions between mid 2022 and mid 2023. Outcomes were compared with a larger reference group treated without the thick sheet, covering complications over six months and satisfaction measured with a modified breast questionnaire.

Small to moderate defects are common after mastectomy among Asian women, whose breasts tend to be smaller, and a major flap may be disproportionate there. A sheet up to five millimeters thick offers structure without extra donor-site surgery. Prospective enrollment strengthens the safety picture over retrospective series. Satisfaction data show how patients judge the trade-off.
pmc-13264894:
Tina Mai and co-authors present a 2026 protocol for a scoping review of peritoneal dialysis outcomes in Southeast Asia. In this kidney treatment, fluid is cycled through the belly to clean the blood, and the region promotes it where machine dialysis capacity is limited. North American results will serve only as an outside point of comparison, not a standard.

The review will run from May to October 2026 and search many databases plus registries and government sources for work since 2000, with no language bar at the search stage. Outcomes include patient survival, how long the method lasts, infections, hospital use, heart outcomes, and tube problems. Findings will be mapped by outcome and by country, with local context noted. The data set and search plans will be shared where journal policy allows.
pmc-13264994:
Yan-Min Xu and Bao-Liang Zhong published a 2026 narrative review of the link between body image and depression, tracing fifty years of research. Unhappiness with one's body is common in depression, and the pair set out to show how the field's ideas shifted and what the proof now says about direction and treatment.

They screened literature from 1972 to 2026 and kept 266 records. Across cultures, ages, and clinics, negative body image, above all body dissatisfaction, tied steadily to depressive symptoms. Long-term and twin studies suggest each can feed the other over time. How people judge their looks mattered more than measured body mass. Proposed drivers include self-objectification, social comparison, rumination, and low self-esteem. Treatments that target body image improved it and may ease depression too. The authors urge adding body image checks to depression care.
pmc-13265194:
Xiaokang Liu and colleagues search for gene markers tied to tumour surroundings in differentiated thyroid cancer, in a 2026 study. Remodelling of the tissue around a tumour helps it grow and spread. Which remodelling genes predict outlook was unclear. The team combined clustering with many machine learning models.

Patients grouped into three molecular clusters. Testing of 101 models highlighted five key genes. The signature forecast one-, two-, and three-year survival with very high accuracy. Laboratory checks on patient samples confirmed the gene patterns. One gene was raised in tumours while the other four were lowered. The signature offers a new prognostic lead.
pmc-13265594:
Xudong Rao and co-authors wrote a 2026 perspective arguing that controlled environment agriculture, high-tech indoor and greenhouse farming, should be treated as public city infrastructure rather than a private tech fix. Venture money has driven its growth, they say, yielding few sites, narrow crop choice, and little thought for fair spread across neighborhoods.

The authors propose judging such farms by public value: food justice, public health, and climate resilience. They highlight geospatial AI and high-performance computing as underused tools that could adapt crop care, guide site choices, and find underserved communities for targeted help. Joined with urban data methods, these tools could embed farms in fair, climate-ready city systems. The paper ends with priorities for a public-interest agenda for this farming sector.
pmc-13265694:
Selina Cannon Homaei and colleagues study what happens in mouse brains when a chemical building block is blocked, in a 2026 investigation. An enzyme called GADL1 makes beta-alanine, needed for protective compounds in brain and muscle. Removing the gene lowers those compounds. Consequences for brain metabolism were unclear.

Seven tissues were screened, with deep analysis of three brain regions. Effects differed by region, age, and sex. Mature females showed oxidative stress signs and possible synapse changes in the cerebrum. Males accumulated large amounts of fat in several tissues. Young smell regions showed fat build-up in both sexes, with inflammation only in males.
pmc-13265894:
Farah Budairy and colleagues report kidney cancer in a teenager with tuberous sclerosis complex, in a 2026 case report. The genetic disorder usually causes benign growths across organs. It also hides a risk of early cancers. The patient was a fifteen-year-old girl with extensive skin signs.

Whole-body checks found brain growths and a lung condition linked to the disorder. Imaging also revealed a silent right kidney mass. Surgery removed the kidney, and tissue tests confirmed papillary renal cell carcinoma. The authors stress that skin specialists often spot the disorder first. Prompt screening of internal organs can be lifesaving.
pmc-13266194:
Xiao-Long Lü and colleagues propose in 2026 a graphene-based transistor design controlled by both light and electric voltage. Their model uses materials where electron spin and valley, meaning which energy pocket electrons occupy, can be separated to carry distinct currents. Antiferromagnetic fields and a modified Haldane model create the gapless states needed for that control.

Shining off-resonant circular light shifted the material into new spin-valley states, and stronger light opened a gap that turned current off. Gate voltage then selected fully spin-polarized current, mixed spin-valley current, or no current. The proposal offers a blueprint for future spintronic and valleytronic devices that switch with light rather than wiring alone.
pmc-13266894:
Yuxin Cheng and colleagues test in 2026 whether detailed CT measurements can reveal lung scarring in people with connective tissue diseases. Early detection is hard because structural and small vessel changes are subtle. They studied 84 patients, about half with lung disease and half without, using paired breathing scans and lung function tests.

Patients with lung involvement breathed out less air, trapped more air in small airways, and showed fewer small lung blood vessels on scans. Dense areas of lung were larger, while vessel counts fell at several depths below the lung surface. A combined model using age, sex, breathing measures, and scan values separated the groups with high accuracy. Quantitative scanning may flag lung involvement earlier than routine reading.
pmc-13268194:
Yifan Wu and co-authors identify in 2026 a worm protein fragment that lingers in the lung and may explain lasting inflammation after roundworm infection clears. Ascaris larvae must pass through the lungs, stirring strong allergic-type inflammation that can leave chronic damage. The team suspected that worm material retained inside lung macrophages keeps T cells activated long after the parasites are gone.

Using a method that reads which peptides immune cells display, they found an Ascaris-derived fragment from a protein called Kalirin held by lung macrophages and shown to T cells. That fragment was tied to specific helper T cell groups that persisted after infection ended. The finding names a concrete molecular suspect for chronic lung inflammation following this very common parasitic infection.
pmc-13269294:
Waheed Idowu and co-authors published a review in 2026 on treating poor dry-season feed for cattle, sheep, and goats in warm dry regions. Treating straw and crop leftovers with ammonia or urea can unlock fiber and add nitrogen. The review pulled together studies mainly from 2015 to 2025.

Treating feed raised intake by 10 to 40 percent and digestion by 5 to 20 points in the studies reviewed. Animals generally performed better, though gains depended on matching nitrogen release with energy in the diet. Better feed use may also cut emissions per unit of product. The authors note uneven results, nitrogen losses, and slow uptake by farmers as limits still to solve.
pmc-13269394:
Chufeng Xu and co-authors ask in 2026 whether having basic medical insurance changes how middle-aged and older Chinese adults rate their primary care. China's tiered system steers patients toward local care, and insurance is meant to make that path attractive. The team merged two waves of a national family panel into 6,114 people and used methods that track changes within the same person over time.

Insurance was linked to better ratings of facility conditions, the buildings and equipment patients see. It showed no firm link to ratings of service level, the quality of care itself. The facility effect varied by health, age, gender, region, and household registration type. Coverage, the authors suggest, improves the visible setting of care more reliably than its felt quality, a split policymakers should notice.
pmc-13271494:
Maryam Farooqui is lead author of a 2026 cross-sectional survey on how Saudi households dispose of unused and expired medicines, and on the regulatory gaps around that disposal. Throwing medicines in household bins can harm people and the environment, so the team surveyed residents of Qassim about awareness and habits.

Among 877 adults who answered an online questionnaire, 70 percent kept unused medicines, most often in the refrigerator. A striking 88 percent threw unused medicines in household dustbins, as did 92 percent for expired ones. Most, 86 percent, had never received formal education on safe disposal, and 60 percent said pharmacies should be responsible for teaching it. The authors call for awareness campaigns and clear rules.
pmc-13271594:
Io Chi-Yan Hui is lead author of a 2026 scoping review, a broad mapping study, on putting digital respiratory technologies into routine care for people with lung conditions. Digital health is a strategic priority for the European Respiratory Society, but lasting rollout into real clinics is complex and guidance for health systems is thin.

Searching ten databases for work from the past decade, plus crowdsourced additions, the team charted which technologies were used, what rollout strategies were tried, and what challenges and supports appeared. They sorted lessons by equity, patient-professional relationships, the patient journey, and environmental impact, using standard implementation frameworks. As a scoping review, it maps the field rather than judging how well the technologies work.
pmc-13271994:
Zhenzhen Hu and coauthors report in 2026 a case where a steroid injection appeared to trigger a dangerous crisis of an adrenal tumor. Pheochromocytoma can flood the body with stress hormones, and steroids are a known trigger. A 38-year-old woman developed chest tightness, breathlessness, and vomiting soon after a methylprednisolone shot for hives.

Her heart stopped on admission, and she was supported with a heart-lung machine while tests found no infection or blocked heart arteries. Repeated dangerous heart rhythms led to a scan that revealed the adrenal mass, and removal surgery brought clear recovery. The authors also weigh other factors that may have contributed.
pmc-13272094:
Jennessa WX Ng and coauthors grow in 2026 immune and connective tissue cells together in three-dimensional scaffolds of differing stiffness to model fibrotic blood vessels. Vessel stiffening drives high blood pressure, and macrophages and fibroblasts regulate the process jointly. Flat dish cultures miss the mechanical setting that shapes their behavior.

Macrophages grown with fibroblasts in stiff scaffolds raised two surface markers tied to inflammation and fibrosis, while fibroblasts did not change the same way. The cells rarely touched directly, so combined mechanical and soluble signals likely drove the shift. The platform offers a more realistic system for studying vessel scarring.
pmc-13272394:
Angie M Rosero and coauthors measure in 2026 cannabinoid receptors on immune cells of patients with lupus, hunting for patterns tied to disease activity. The two receptors, CB1R and CB2R, tune immune behavior, yet their distribution across lupus lymphocyte types was uncharted. Blood cells from thirty-five patients and thirty-five healthy controls were compared by flow cytometry.

Patients showed higher CB2R and lower CB1R than controls across several cell subsets. CB1R levels tracked closely with disease activity, and patients in remission looked much like healthy controls. Certain B-cell CB2R patterns separated active disease from remission well, suggesting both a biomarker and a drug target.
pmc-13272494:
Kaiyu Zhu and co-authors built a new antibody test in 2026 for peste des petits ruminants, a contagious virus disease of goats and sheep. Fast and reliable testing helps farms judge vaccine response and control outbreaks. Their test targets antibodies against the virus nucleocapsid protein.

The team joined key protein fragments from weak and strong virus strains and made the combined protein in bacteria. They then tuned a blocking enzyme test that uses this protein and a labeled antibody. The test detected positive serum diluted tenfold and gave steady results across repeats. It did not react to several other pathogens. On 100 farm samples it agreed with a commercial kit in most cases.
pmc-13272594:
Janhavi Kulkarni and Suraj Kanase test whether adding trunk work to weight-shift drills helps stroke survivors keep their balance. Weak trunks and uneven weight bearing raise fall risk long after a stroke. Thirty chronic stroke patients were split into two groups for six weeks of training, five days a week.

Both groups practiced shifting weight in a guided, narrowed way. One group also did trunk stability and core work. Both groups improved on balance and trunk scores. The added-trunk group gained far more on both measures. The authors say core work is a cheap, clear add-on that boosts what weight-shift training alone can do.
pmc-13273394:
Chuyao Yu leads a 2026 study asking whether gut microbes cause retinal disease and poor vision. The method uses inherited gene variants as tools to test cause, which cuts confounding. Exposures covered 211 gut microbe groups and 28 related chemicals. Outcomes covered six eye diseases, including diabetic eye disease and macular wear.

The work found 35 microbes and three chemicals linked to various outcomes. One microbe group showed robust cause for choroid and retina disorders after strict correction, with an odds ratio of 0.874. Reverse tests found no clear effect of eye disease on gut microbes. The authors present the findings as new leads for care and prevention.
pmc-13273594:
Junhao Xia and co-authors built a microneedle patch for diabetic wounds in a 2026 study. Diabetic wounds stall because inflammation persists, new vessels form poorly, and immune cells stay in attack mode. Their patch aims to reset that environment while delivering a healing compound through the skin.

The patch blends a gelatin based hydrogel with tiny vesicles made from stem cells and loaded with salidroside, a plant compound. In lab tests the system calmed inflammation and supported vessel growth. Deeper analyses showed it suppressed a key inflammatory pathway and nudged macrophages from attack mode toward repair mode. In animals, treated wounds closed much faster and released fewer inflammatory signals. The authors present the patch as a coordinated repair strategy.
pmc-13273794:
Raimondi and colleagues pool patient-level data from four phase II trials in metastatic colorectal cancer. Their 2026 journal article covers left-sided tumors with normal RAS and BRAF genes. It compares two ways of using anti-EGFR antibody drugs.

One strategy gave the drug as steady maintenance. The other used stop-and-go dosing with planned breaks. The analysis included 378 patients. Overall survival did not differ significantly between strategies. Time without disease growth was shorter with stop-and-go. Yet time until the strategy failed was comparable. Anti-EGFR drugs block a growth signal on cancer cells. The authors say breaks may suit some patients. Survival was not harmed in this pooled group.
pmc-13274394:
Elif Bastug Guven and Ozgur Genc Sen present a 2026 journal article testing how root canal rinse changes while it sits open on a dentist's tray. Sodium hypochlorite is the standard rinse that kills germs and dissolves tissue during root canal work. Its strength depends on its chemistry, which open air and light may alter.

The team measured a five percent solution fresh, after one hour, and after two hours in clear open containers at room temperature. Acidity rose steadily, with pH dropping significantly by one hour and further by two. Surface tension did not change. Measured active chlorine was unexpectedly higher at two hours than when fresh. The authors say clinical relevance still needs study.
pmc-13274894:
Nikolas Reisecker and a large team present a 2026 journal article surveying Austrian attitudes toward anthroposophic medicine, a complementary system blending conventional care with spiritual ideas. The online survey drew 429 completed responses, weighted to match recent election results. It probed who uses such medicine, who sees it as scientific, and what mindsets travel with those views.

Women and people over fifty favored complementary medicine more, and women had used anthroposophic medicine more often. Seeing it as scientific was commoner among older, wealthier, and rural people. Low tolerance for vague answers and a strong sense of personal health control tracked with trust in it. So did authoritarian views, which also tracked preferring eminence-based over evidence-based medicine.
pmc-13275194:
Toshie Yonemochi, Kenji Ina, Hiroko Ina, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2026. It reviews a two-week hospital program that assesses frailty in people on long-term dialysis, and asks which factors in that checkup tie to quality of life.

The program, started in 2023, runs a full geriatric assessment plus motor and mouth function checks, and teaches exercise under Japan's renal rehabilitation guidance. Quality of life was scored with a kidney disease questionnaire. More than forty percent of patients scored low on the physical or mental summary. Muscle weakness was common. The physical score tracked closely with leg strength and six other measures in first-pass analysis. The authors argue that planned rehab during such stays may lift life quality for dialysis patients, a group whose daily burden is high.
pmc-13275394:
Esraa Samir Mohamed, Hanan Said Ali, and Fatma Mostafa Mahrous report a 2026 study of restless legs syndrome in dialysis patients. The work was carried out in 2025 at Banha University Hospital in Qalyubia, Egypt. It links symptom severity with quality of life and with what patients know about their conditions.

Seventy-five patients completed questionnaires on background, knowledge, symptom severity, and quality of life. Most had severe or very severe symptoms, and nearly half reported poor overall quality of life. Worse symptoms tracked closely with poorer quality of life across physical, mental, and social domains. Better knowledge was tied to better quality of life, which points to a role for patient education.
pmc-13275494:
Hao Su and colleagues review metal-based nanomaterials for light-based cancer treatment in a 2026 article. Phototherapy uses light to trigger heat or reactive chemicals that kill tumour cells. Older agents often lack stability, targeting, or strong performance inside the body.

Metal particles can be tuned for light absorption and can also support imaging or combined treatments. The review covers precious and non-precious metals, their killing mechanisms, and design choices that improve safety. Targeting, body compatibility, and heat conversion receive special attention as barriers to clinic use. The authors look toward smart, low-toxicity platforms shaped by responsive design and greener synthesis.
pmc-13275594:
Anna Fleischer and a large team present a 2026 mixed-methods study of taste damage from talquetamab, a myeloma drug known for ruining eating pleasure. Twenty-five treated patients who reported new taste changes completed questionnaires with free-text answers, analyzed independently by two coders. The team then turned the findings, with input from clinical focus groups, into a proposed care workflow and a digital companion concept.

Patients described varied problems: sweet flavors fading or turning unpleasant, bitter and sour aversions, spice burning the mouth, and simple loss of enjoyment. Dry mouth made dry or fibrous foods harder to swallow. Coping tricks that helped included mild herbs, savory umami additions, sauces and soups, temperature and plating changes, and saliva-supportive measures. Both proposed tools still await validation.
pmc-13275994:
Fuqun Wei and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on liver cancer and the cells lining its blood vessels. Those endothelial cells can change into a different cell type, a shift that helps tumors grow. The team asked which endothelial genes drive this shift and predict patient outcomes.

They combined single-cell gene data, which profiles one cell at a time, with large tumor datasets. Nineteen key genes stood out, and the team built a risk model from them. The model split patients into groups with different outlooks, immune cell mixes, and likely drug responses. In lab-grown mini tumors grown with vessel tissue, three of the genes sat in the same spots as known markers of the cell shift. The authors name them as possible drug targets.
pmc-13276594:
Linhao Jing and co-authors present a 2026 journal article on a copper-based nanoplatform meant to wake the immune system against liver cancer. Immunotherapy struggles in liver tumors because they suppress immunity and hide their antigens. One alarm pathway, cGAS-STING, can turn tumor stress into immune priming if switched on inside the tumor.

Their particles self-assemble copper ions with an immune stimulant, then wear a cloak of tumor cell membrane for homing. In the tumor's acidity they release copper, which triggers a copper-dependent death program in cancer cells. That death raised the alarm signal and switched on the pathway, while the stimulant matured dendritic cells, the immune system's teachers. In animals the particles shrank tumors and drew in killer T cells. Combined with a standard immune drug, they erased tumors completely and extended survival.
pmc-13276694:
Carmen Barba and a large Italian commission review epilepsy surgery near the brain's language areas in a 2026 article. Removing seizure tissue risks harming speech and comprehension when it sits close to language circuits. Modern views treat language as a spread-out network rather than two classic centres.

Careful testing before surgery sets a baseline and helps locate both seizure and language zones. Brain imaging can now map language dominance without the invasive Wada test in many cases. Implanted electrodes with stimulation remain central for precise mapping in difficult cases. During surgery, awake mapping in cooperative patients protects speech. The authors weigh options from small removals to larger resections and gentler targeted techniques.
pmc-13276794:
Navya Nair and co-authors wrote a 2026 review on vaginal dilator therapy after pelvic cancer treatment. Radiation, chemotherapy, hormone blockers, and surgery can abruptly cut estrogen and scar the vagina, causing narrowing called stenosis. After cervical cancer treatment with chemo plus radiation, major narrowing may exceed thirty percent without prevention.

Dilators are smooth tubes in graded sizes that stretch tissue, prevent adhesions, and keep the vaginal canal open. Water-based lubricants matched to body chemistry are essential for comfort. The few studies done so far suggest starting early and using dilators with steady habits reduces narrowing severity and improves tolerance and sexual function. Sticking with the routine is the main barrier for many patients. The authors recommend better teaching, early access to devices, and supportive follow-up to raise adherence and benefit.
pmc-13277094:
Zaynab Mousavian and a large team combine protein and metabolite data to study tuberculosis in children, in a 2026 paper. Over a million children fall ill with TB each year, and many go untreated because diagnosis is hard. Blood-based signatures could help where standard tests struggle.

Children with suspected TB in four high-burden countries gave plasma for both data types. Combining the layers revealed immune and metabolic pathways that single datasets missed, including arginine and proline metabolism. Protein data alone classified confirmed TB better than metabolite data did. The combined model added only a slight gain. The authors highlight proteomics as the most promising base for a future childhood TB test.
pmc-13277494:
Zishuo Huang leads a 2026 study protocol for a trial to prevent memory and thinking decline in older adults living in the community in China. Combined programs that cover heart risks, brain training, activity, and diet show promise, but scaling them is hard. The protocol, for a trial across thirteen districts of Changxing County, has no results yet.

The planned trial will enroll 1,170 older adults and 273 community health workers in three groups. Support bundles include staff training, teamwork networks, and an AI-enabled phone mini-program. Outcomes on reach, health, and upkeep will be tracked over eighteen months. The design aims to judge both whether the program works and whether it can be delivered well.
pmc-13277594:
Shabbir Ahmed Mallick and colleagues report a 2026 case of lupus vulgaris, a skin form of tuberculosis, in a three-year-old boy. The disease is common among skin TB cases in adults yet rare in young children. Its slow course and varied look often lead doctors toward the wrong diagnosis.

The boy had an ulcerated facial lesion that had persisted for two years despite earlier care. A skin biopsy showed granulomatous inflammation with the giant cells typical of TB. Stains for the bacteria themselves came back negative, so the diagnosis rested on appearance and tissue findings. Standard anti-tuberculosis treatment healed the lesion well, and the authors stress early recognition to prevent facial scarring.
pmc-13279194:
Karlijn Scheepens and colleagues present a 2026 systematic review of bone scans in children with brittle bone disease. The disease, osteogenesis imperfecta, makes bones break often. The scan method is dual energy absorptiometry, a low dose X ray test used as a stand in for bone strength. Yearly scans often guide care, yet the test misses bone shape and fine structure.

The team searched three databases and kept ninety one studies in the review set. Close detail came from thirty eight studies with near three thousand seven hundred patients. Scan sites were not standard across sites or studies. Links between scan scores, disease type and breaks varied by method and result. The authors show a clear need for shared rules on where and how to scan.
pmc-13279394:
Guojian Ding and colleagues published a 2026 study of a new laparoscopic technique for closing the passage that causes hydrocele in children, a fluid swelling around the testicle. Their method threads a guide wire through the skin to tie off the passage from outside the abdomen. The team reviewed 387 children treated between January 2018 and October 2019, recording hidden openings on the other side, operating times, and complications.

About two thirds had a one-sided swelling; the rest had both sides affected. A hidden opening on the opposite side appeared in 30.6 percent of cases, which supports checking both sides during surgery. Median operating time was 18.6 minutes for one side and 27.3 minutes for two. Over a median follow-up of 24 months, the only problems were mild early port pain in five children and scrotal swelling in two. The authors judge the guide-wire method safe, effective, and cheaper for hospitals.
pmc-13279694:
Jingyuan Li and colleagues published a 2026 biomechanical study testing a new internal fixation device for lumbar spondylolysis, a stress fracture in a vertebra's narrow bridge that often affects young athletes. Using CT scans from a healthy 25-year-old volunteer, the team built a computer model of the lower spine. Versions covered the fracture alone, traditional fixation, and the new device at three stages of added compression. Each model was loaded to simulate six spinal movements.

The new device restricted motion and displacement more than the traditional construct during twisting. Stress on the discs fell, while stress across the bone graft and facet cartilage rose toward natural levels. Tightening the device strengthened that transfer across the defect. The authors read this as a friendlier setting for healing and graft fusion. The work is computational only, offered as design evidence ahead of physical and clinical testing.
pmc-13279994:
Morten O. A. Sommer and Christian Munck issue a 2026 author correction to their 2021 Nature Communications study that forecast spread of antibiotic resistance genes across bacterial genomes. The first study built a statistical method to spot mobile elements linked to gene transfer. It tested forecasts on a database of more than four hundred seventy thousand genomes. Thirty four of ninety four forecast transfers seemed confirmed in that check.

A later critique by Godron and colleagues found that thirty of those thirty four events likely came from contaminant DNA, not true gene gains. In one case, a claimed resistance gene sat on a DNA chunk traced to an Acinetobacter contaminant. The authors accept that contaminant DNA likely inflated their raw count of confirmed events. The correction is a clear case of post publication science repair, where a bold forecast meets a hard data check.
pmc-13280094:
Li and six colleagues study how lactate, a byproduct of cell energy use, affects bowel cancer cells in twenty twenty-six. In patient samples, higher lactate went with later stage disease and shorter time free of it. The team fed lactate to two bowel cancer cell lines in the lab. They tracked cell behavior and read which genes switched on or off.

Lactate made the cells grow and move in more malignant ways. The effect was not due to acid in the dish alone. More than a thousand genes shifted after treatment. Two signal paths lit up, and blocking either one blunted the effect. The work hints lactate is a fuel and a signal for this cancer.
pmc-13280394:
Hany S. E. Mansour and colleagues present a 2026 study of high resolution solar power forecasting with machine learning. Accurate short term photovoltaic forecasts, at sub hourly scale, keep grids stable as solar grows. The team benchmarked six machine learning models against a persistence baseline, which just repeats the last value. Data came from the Yulara Solar System, resampled at five, ten and fifteen minute steps. A full preprocessing frame built time, lag and rolling features and filtered outliers.

Models held XGBoost, Decision Tree, Linear Regression, Ridge, Lasso and Elastic Net. Five error metrics scored them across train, validation and test sets, plus seasonal and stress subsets. Stress scenes held night time and wild irradiance swings. Tree based models beat linear regressors by a lot in both accuracy and robustness. The Decision Tree took the best overall performance in their tests. Fine grain forecasts can smooth solar grid work.
pmc-13280694:
Claire Emilie Bertrand and colleagues tested computer tools for rating feelings in a 2026 study on psychosis risk. Psychosis means losing touch with what is real, and flat or low drive can come first. Such signs are hard to score by eye. The team filmed one hundred one young people at high risk and forty-one healthy peers. Software read their faces during interviews, and photos tested how strongly they reacted.

The at-risk group showed more disgust on their faces than the healthy group. Face signs and feeling reactions barely matched each other. Fewer strong face displays went with weaker outward feeling. Smiling more, oddly, went with lower drive and pleasure. The authors say face software adds facts that mood tests alone can miss.
pmc-13281094:
Weishu Liu and colleagues published a 2026 overview introducing ionic thermoelectrics, which convert heat into voltage using ions instead of electrons. Conventional thermoelectrics power deep-space probes but produce tiny voltages per degree. Ionic versions, soft gels or polymers soaked with ions, show thermopowers of tens of millivolts per degree, thousands of times larger. They are flexible, stretchable, and cheap to process. Those traits suit wearable generators on body heat and sensors for health, robotics, and fire alarms.

The authors are candid about what blocks products: huge voltage paired with tiny power, and sharp temperature sensitivity paired with slow response. The effect remains a physics puzzle about how mass, charge, and heat move together in confined soft matter. Framing a journal special topic, they recruit chemists, physicists, and engineers to rebuild the field on thermodynamics and device physics, so a lab curiosity can mature into low-grade heat technology.
pmc-13281494:
Renfei Luo and colleagues reviewed single-cell maps of immune cells in clogged arteries in a 2026 paper. Artery plaque grows over years and can trigger heart attacks and strokes. Immune cells called T cells help steer that growth. New tools can read one cell at a time, which exposes hidden variety. The review draws on studies of mouse and human plaque. It also uses maps that show where each cell type sits in the vessel wall.

The maps reveal T cell kinds never seen before in plaque. Some cells sit between killer and calming roles, as if mid-change. Local signals in the wall seem to push cells toward one role or the other. With age, the mix of bold and calming cells shifts. The authors say joining cell maps with gene and place data could point to precise new drugs.
pmc-13281894:
Zhuochen Yu and colleagues reviewed nano platforms that fight low oxygen in tumors in a 2026 paper. Solid tumors often starve for oxygen deep inside. That starvation helps them grow, spread, and resist care. Blunt oxygen top-ups leak, fade fast, and can harm healthy tissue. Tiny engineered platforms aim to tune oxygen with precision. The review sorts them by three strategies and explains how each is built.

One family ferries oxygen in from outside the body. A second makes oxygen on site from the tumor's own chemistry. A third slows the tumor's oxygen use, stretching what supply exists. The review weighs how each pairs with other care, like radiation or immune drugs. Fitful blood flow and uneven tumor makeup still blunt all three. The authors map design rules for the next wave of trials.
pmc-13282294:
Ling Zhan and co-authors present a 2026 analysis of safety reports for robotic thyroid surgery over ten years. Robotic removal of the thyroid gland, in the neck, draws patient interest, but device problems were poorly mapped. The team searched a United States device incident database from 2016 to 2025 and hand-checked the reports. Thirty-two reports qualified, and all events happened during surgery.

Most reports involved an energy device used for cutting and sealing, and breakage or fragments were the commonest pattern. Teams often swapped the device or retrieved fragments. Most operations still finished robotically as planned, and only one switched to open surgery. No severe patient injury was recorded. Some reports reached regulators late, beyond the thirty-day window. The authors call for better risk awareness, patient counselling, rehearsed troubleshooting, and faster, standard reporting when devices fail.
pmc-13282394:
Xiaojie Wang and co-authors present a 2026 study combining two scores to predict major heart and vessel events in UK Biobank adults. One score, the metabolic vulnerability index, distils six blood markers of metabolic and inflammatory strain. The other, Life's Essential 8, grades overall cardiovascular health from habits and measures. The team followed two hundred thirty-nine thousand adults free of such events at entry.

Over a median of about thirteen and a half years, more than seventeen thousand major events occurred. Higher vulnerability scores meant higher risk, while high health scores halved risk against low scores. People with both low health scores and top vulnerability had nearly triple the risk of the reference group. The two scores interacted, adding risk beyond each alone for heart attacks and overall events. Analyses suggested better health could prevent many events, partly by lowering vulnerability.
pmc-13282594:
Nehaa Khadka led a 2026 cohort study of hemolytic disease of the fetus and newborn, a condition where a mother's antibodies attack the baby's red blood cells. Using Kaiser Permanente Southern California records from 2008 to 2022, the study described outcomes, care use, and how often the disease returns in a later pregnancy.

Among 464,711 pregnancies, 139 carried the diagnosis. Affected babies had higher rates of early birth, low birth weight, and jaundice, and they stayed longer in hospital and intensive care. Mothers also had more hospital stays apart from delivery. Among women with a prior affected pregnancy, most saw the disease return next time, and some returns were severe.
pmc-13282994:
Acute lung injury meets a plant-and-metal nanomaterial in Xuanpeng Wu's 2026 therapy experiments with fellow researchers. Lung injury of this type is severe and often fatal, with few good treatments. The material joins the metal cerium with tannic acid from plants.

The team made the material by a simple, low-cost method and tested its traits. Tiny grains stayed stable and mopped up harmful free radicals in lab tests. Treated lung and vessel cells showed less cell death and less stress damage. In mice with toxin-induced injury, lungs showed less swelling and less tissue harm. Inflammation markers fell as well. Safety tests support more study of this approach.
pmc-13283394:
Four factors form the SEA score for triple therapy outlook in marker-negative liver cancer, Hesheng Lin's multicenter team reports in 2026. Some tumors lack both common blood markers, which hides outlook. Triple therapy mixes vessel blocking, a targeted drug, and immune therapy for these patients.

Records covered 136 patients at many centers who got triple therapy. A training group of 91 patients built the score, and 45 patients tested it. Response rates were high, with most tumors shrinking or holding steady. Four factors formed the SEA score: tumor size, surgery chance, spread, and age. The score split patients into clear risk groups for survival. It may help pick best-fit patients.
pmc-13284094:
Needle stimulation at acupuncture points eased early ovary failure in mice fed rich diets, report Lele Ling and colleagues in 2026. Early ovary failure is a leading cause of infertility in young women. The team traced benefit to a chemical mark placed on a self-cleaning gene message in egg-support cells.

Mice on high-fat, high-sugar feed developed the ovary condition for testing. Stimulation at three body points improved follicle growth and normalized cycles. Support cell death fell, and inflammation signals dropped after treatment. Single-cell sequencing mapped ovary cell groups and self-cleaning signatures in detail. A writer enzyme for the mark fell as cleaning markers recovered.
pmc-13284194:
A pinch of ceramic powder at just the right dose made plastic joint material last longer, find Ahmed Salama and colleagues in 2026. Their plastic base mimics cartilage for joint replacements. Bone-friendly mineral filler was fixed, while titanium dioxide varied across mixes.

Three blends were pressed and checked for wear, fatigue, and germ killing. Imaging and diffraction confirmed fillers spread well through the plastic base. At three percent titanium dioxide, wear resistance peaked with a dense lubricant film. That same blend also gained fatigue life and higher peak stress. Extra filler clumped and weakened fatigue performance in higher blends.
pmc-13284494:
Fengqiang Gao and co-authors report a 2026 study on sorafenib as protection against liver injury when blood flow returns after a cut-off. Such ischemia-reperfusion injury is a common problem in liver surgery and links to poorer survival. Gene and metabolite profiling pointed to a pathway that boosts antioxidant defense.

A middle dose of sorafenib cut liver cell death, swelling, and programmed cell death in the model systems used here. Blocking a key enzyme in the pathway, or raising HSP90 levels, removed the benefit, which supports the proposed chain. In human transplant recipients, high HSP90 linked to poor graft work. A new oral nanoparticle that targets liver raised the drug effect further.
pmc-13284594:
Israa O Kashmoola, Shatha H Mohammad, and Mohammad H Alsaaty reviewed in 2026 how taking many medicines at once affects bone health in type 2 diabetes. People with this diabetes often fracture more easily despite normal or high bone density readings, so bone quality, not just density, is at fault. The review searched four databases for English work through October 2025 on diabetes drugs and other common medicines.

Diabetes drugs split sharply: some families, including thiazolidinediones and sulfonylureas, raised fracture risk, while metformin and newer gut-hormone and sugar-excreting drugs looked neutral or protective. Steroids, certain antidepressants, acid blockers, and water pills harmed bone, while statins, beta-blockers, and some blood pressure drugs protected it. The authors back regular medicine reviews and dropping risky drugs where possible.
pmc-13285194:
Li Chen and co-authors test a ginseng compound against artery plaque in a 2026 mouse and cell study that mimics menopause. Women after menopause face higher plaque risk, and Panax quinquefolium saponin is known to calm swelling and vessel harm. Ovariectomized ApoE-deficient mice were treated and checked at two plaque stages.

Surgery raised plaque growth, blood inflammation markers, and death of vessel lining cells, while the saponin reversed those harms at both stages. Computer and lab work pointed to estrogen receptor alpha as the key target, acting through two signaling paths. Blocking that receptor largely erased the benefit, while activating it boosted gains. The authors propose the pathway for post-menopause plaque care.
pmc-13285294:
Wenjuan Kang and colleagues test two rhizobium bacterial strains on alfalfa to see which partnership fixes more nitrogen from the air. Their 2026 study matters because alfalfa feeds livestock and enriches soil, yet scientists knew little about how strong or weak bacterial partners change the plant's inner chemistry. One strain, LL2, was expected to outperform another, QL5.

Plants given LL2 grew more effective nodules, higher enzyme activity, and heavier shoots than those given QL5 or no bacteria. Chemical profiling of leaves, roots, and nodules showed LL2 raising compounds tied to photosynthesis, breathing, and nitrogen handling. A sugar-related compound and several acids stood out. The findings point to LL2 as a strong match for the alfalfa variety studied.
pmc-13285594:
Hidden RNA helpers in the Lyme disease germ come to light in a 2026 study by Taylor Van Gundy and co-authors. Proteins that grip RNA steer gene use in all life, yet few were known in Borrelia burgdorferi. The team fished for proteins that sink with small RNAs in gradient tubes, then tested their grip and reshaping skill.

Five proteins passed the lab tests, unwinding, pairing, and swapping RNA strands with ease. Three had been mere guesses on the gene map, while two were known from swimming and steering gear. One lead protein also held RNA inside living germ cells. The finds widen the cast of gene control in a germ with a lean toolkit.
pmc-13286194:
Somayeh Taghidoust Chahardeh, Seyyed Hossein Hosseini, and Ali Shamsi Majelan compare three warm-up styles in elite women taekwondo fighters in a 2026 randomized study. Kicks and jumps in the sport ride on a spring-like cycle in the legs, and each warm-up may tune that spring in its own way. Thirty-six athletes drew lots for active stretching, foam rolling, or band work after a set treadmill start.

Body sensors tracked drop jumps before and after each routine, and the groups parted ways on force measures. Active stretching lifted push-off force and power, while foam rolling mostly shifted how fast force built up. Band work simply held fighters near their starting marks on most counts. Plain jump height and air time barely budged in any group, which tells coaches to match the warm-up to the quality they want to sharpen.
pmc-13286994:
Benjamin Schoeps and a large team present a laboratory test that measures whether a patient's own tumor tissue lets a cancer-killing virus multiply. Published in 2026, the assay addresses a gap in oncolytic virus therapy: doctors cannot yet predict whose tumors will support the virus. Fresh tumor pieces from 133 patients, spanning more than twenty cancer types, were infected outside the body.

Engineered viruses carrying light-producing or fluorescent tags let the team watch replication in real time, confirmed by genetic counting. A semi-automated version using the brightest reporter needed little hands-on time and tracked growth robustly. Picking patients whose tumors permit the virus, the authors argue, could raise response rates in future trials.
pmc-13287094:
A de J Basánez-Muñoz and co-authors link mangrove decline to soil change on Mexico's Veracruz coast in a 2026 ecological study. Within a Ramsar-listed wetland, plots along four shore-crossing transects were classed as intact, semi-disturbed, or disturbed, and their soils and tree structure were measured side by side. The question was whether forest thinning follows the soil, pointing to where restoration must start.

Intact plots carried denser, taller, richer forest than semi-disturbed ones, while disturbed plots held no living trees at all. Statistical ordination fingered silt content and soil acidity as the main factors tracking structural change. Semi-disturbed and disturbed plots overlapped in the analysis, suggesting decline spreads as soils shift. Distance from the lagoon mattered only marginally. The authors conclude conservation must restore soils, not merely replant trees.
pmc-13287394:
Nicole Friel and colleagues report a 2026 review of opioid prescribing after children's knee surgery. The records came from ten sites in one pediatric orthopedic health system. The team studied common sports medicine knee operations done from 2021 through 2023. They counted the first opioid prescription for each surgery and any refills within thirty days. Their goal was to see whether prescribing habits matched across sites.

The review covered 1,834 surgeries in 1,523 patients. The number of opioid doses in the first prescription differed in a clear statistical sense across surgery types and sites. Refill rates, however, showed no link to how many doses the first prescription held. The authors argue that shared prescribing rules could cut needless variation. Standard rules may also lower the risk that leftover pills get misused.
pmc-13287494:
Jian Xu and colleagues present an image-cleaning system in 2026 for underwater photographs, which often carry colour casts, haze, and lost detail from light absorption and scattering. Poor images weaken robot navigation, inspection, and habitat monitoring, so the team combined physics-based colour repair with a learning network.

Early steps fix colour balance and stretch contrast, then wave-based merging keeps structure. Texture maps at four angles guide a second branch that guards fine detail, while a main branch handles colour and form. Tests on three public sets showed gains across six quality scores. Downstream tasks such as edge finding also improved, the authors report.
pmc-13288394:
Rui Zhu and colleagues report a gallbladder injury during laser stone treatment in a 2026 case report. A 26-year-old woman had months of right-sided belly pain from multiple gallstones. Tests showed her gallbladder still squeezed well, and she strongly wanted to keep the organ. Doctors therefore planned a mouth-route procedure that removes stones while sparing the gallbladder. A stent bridged from her bowel into the gallbladder for scope access.

One week later, a thin scope passed through the stent and a holmium laser began breaking the stones. The laser beam accidentally pierced the gallbladder wall, causing an acute perforation. The team placed a drainage tube at once and applied steady suction to divert bile. A check one week later showed the hole fully healed. A second laser session then cleared the remaining stones, and she stayed symptom-free through seven months of follow-up.
pmc-13288694:
Ying Zhao and colleagues study a leftover cholesterol type in diabetes in 2026. The study held 26,302 hospital patients. All had type 2 diabetes. Remnant cholesterol rides in fat-rich particles. It was weighed against standard LDL cholesterol. The target was fatty liver disease.

Nearly half the group had the liver disease. That share was 48.3 percent, at median age 62. Remnant levels tracked disease more closely than LDL. Patients high on remnant but low on LDL faced more risk. The reverse mismatch carried less risk. All three check methods agreed. Cutting remnant levels may aid prevention plans.
pmc-13289094:
Suheyla Kaya and colleagues hunt for predictors of gum margin movement after braces, in a 2026 dental study. Fixed orthodontic treatment can shift the gum line on front teeth, sometimes exposing root surface. The team reviewed records for 88 patients treated at one center, all with healthy gums at the start. Three-dimensional mouth scans measured crown length and the width of firm gum tissue. X-ray measures captured tooth angle and jaw shape.

Baseline width of firm gum tissue, crowding, and sex each predicted how much the margin moved. On the tongue side of teeth, tooth angle, chin shape, and age added predictive power. Changes during treatment mattered too, and growth in firm gum width showed the strongest effect of all. Bone ridge width, by contrast, had no clear impact. The authors say checking gum width before treatment helps flag teeth at risk.
pmc-13289194:
Michael Marll and colleagues study lung damage at TB diagnosis in South Africa in 2026. Their study ran in Johannesburg. It held 258 adults with new drug-sensitive TB. Full lung tests were done at diagnosis. HIV status split the group.

Adults with HIV and TB had better lung scores. Their odds of any odd test were lower. Tight and mixed patterns were also less common. Chest images showed less severe disease too. Yet symptom scores were alike in both groups. Breath quality of life did not split. The authors see a distinct injury pattern. HIV may blunt some lung harm at diagnosis.
pmc-13289894:
Allyson E. Shea and colleagues present a 2026 study on sugar transport in Proteus mirabilis, a top cause of complicated urinary infections. The germ uses sugars during infection, yet which import systems matter for fitness was unclear. The team built 47 mutants, each targeting a predicted sugar transporter gene, and screened growth in dishes and fitness inside the urinary tract.

Pooled sequencing flagged three genes as fitness factors in animals, confirmed in head-to-head mouse challenges. One flagged gene, thought to import xanthosine, did not do so, suggesting a wrong label in databases. A triple mutant missing three transporters copied the key single-gene defect. Raising urine sugar with a diabetes drug boosted colonization overall.
pmc-13290394:
Rainfall shapes how a serpentine-tolerant wildflower times its blooms on either side of a soil boundary, Nicole Ibañez and colleagues reported in 2026. The subject is Antirrhinum vexillocalyculatum, an annual herb that grows on and off harsh serpentine soils.

The team combined a greenhouse common garden along a moisture gradient, a water-limitation experiment, and field observation. Precipitation regime strongly shifted flowering time, and dry conditions shrank floral displays, delayed flowering, and for some traits pushed the two soil populations further apart. In the field, more plants flowered in the wetter area, and gene flow ran mainly from ordinary soil into serpentine populations. Because flowering still overlapped widely, the authors see gene flow as the dominant force, one that drought may weaken.
pmc-13291494:
Bone health is steered by talk between distant organs. Donghao Gan, Lei Qin, and Guozhi Xiao review that web in 2026. Bone loss and joint wear rise with age and weight. Other organs feed into each of these diseases.

Gut, brain, hormone, and fat signals all reach bone. Immune links braid through each of those paths. The review maps axes like gut-bone-immune in detail. Blood markers and scans can now read this crosstalk. Care teams can sort patients by axis pattern. Drug choice may then match the driver organ. Gaps in proof and open questions close the review.
pmc-13291794:
Boris Baruch S Bernatskiy's team presents a 2026 case report on rebuilding a badly damaged front upper jaw with the Bone-to-Soft Tissue technique. Their patient was a 17-year-old who lost a maxillary central incisor to trauma and had severe ridge loss. Implants and standard grafting were poor fits at that age and anatomy.

Surgeons transplanted a combined block of tooth, bone, and soft tissue into the gap, then adapted, stabilized, and restored it in stages. The graft integrated well, kept the soft-tissue shape, and restored the ridge contour on imaging. The authors suggest the method as a biology-based option for select esthetic-zone defects. They also stress that controlled studies must confirm long-term results before wider use.
pmc-13291894:
Nathan Laha and co-authors deploy an AI system that drafts urine drug test interpretations in a 2026 study. Urine drug tests guide care in emergency, pain, and addiction settings, yet tricky patterns need scarce toxicology experts. The team built a predictor of substance use patterns from test data at one medical center. It covered 83,553 tests and twenty-six substances. Predictions were then woven into the live clinical sign-out workflow.

Across substances, the predictor's accuracy was extremely high, with discrimination scores above 0.99 on average. After integration, preliminary AI interpretations cut average sign-out time by about twenty-nine seconds per case. That saving equals roughly a twenty-three percent efficiency gain for the service. Accuracy stayed high while the speed improved, the authors report. They suggest such drafting tools can return expert time to the hardest cases. Wider rollout would need checks at other centers with different test mixes.
pmc-13292294:
Lijun Wen and co-authors recount a 2026 diagnostically tricky case of intrathyroidal thymic carcinoma, a tumor making up under 0.15 percent of thyroid cancers. It usually betrays itself through CD5 and CD117 staining, but exceptions unsettle that rule. Their patient, a 32-year-old Chinese woman seen in 2019, arrived with hoarseness, swallowing trouble, and a firm left thyroid mass.

Imaging showed a lesion of about 4.1 cm in the left lobe plus a tiny right-side nodule, and her left vocal cord was paralyzed. After total thyroid removal and neck dissection, pathology showed CD117, p63, and p40 positivity but no CD5, still fitting the thymic carcinoma diagnosis. A separate papillary thyroid cancer coexisted. The tumor later returned in lymph nodes and, strikingly, gained CD5 expression, which the authors read as clonal evolution.
pmc-13292794:
Aroldo de Oliveira Gomes Golineli and co-authors present, in a 2026 letter, an ecological study of leprosy across towns and cities in Brazil. Leprosy has fallen yet stays clustered in poorer areas, and by 2024 new cases had fallen to 22,129, down from 31,064 in 2014, based on figures the authors report.

Town-level data came from national sources, plus the 2022 census and measures of income, schooling, housing, and social progress. The study looks at how these shared conditions line up with where cases appear. Such maps can guide health teams to places where poverty and weak services let the disease persist, even as national counts improve.
pmc-13292994:
Quan Xu and co-authors report, in 2026, a nature-inspired route to build many complex ring-shaped molecules from one starting material. Making dense three-dimensional ring systems is a long-standing hard task in organic chemistry.

Starting from a marine product idea, the team first made ocellatusone C by an acid-triggered chain reaction, then varied that path to make related bicyclic forms. Computer models guided a light-driven reshaping that reached rare ring layouts, and coupling steps grew the set further. Tests showed strong activity against malaria in the new molecules. The method shows how one precursor can seed a whole family of drug leads.
pmc-13293094:
Abdalmajeed M. Alajlouni and Wael Hananeh test, in a 2026 feeding study, whether zeolite in chicken feed changes harmful genes in gut Escherichia coli. Zeolite is a natural mineral added to feed for its soaking and buffering traits.

A total of 150 chicks were split into five groups getting feed with zeolite shares from 0% up to 30% of the mix. Lab screens checked 11 harm-linked genes in gut bacteria. At the 10% level, no sample met the set mark for the pathogenic type, and key predictor genes were least common. The authors present zeolite as a non-drug way to lower risk, pending more tests.
pmc-13293394:
Zahra Dianat Maharlouei and colleagues test, in a 2026 greenhouse study, whether treated biochar plus native bacteria can clean soils laced with heavy metals and oil waste. Such mixed pollution cuts crop yields and lets toxins enter food chains.

Soil came from industrial sites near Kerman, Iran, yielding five native bacterial types from 30 samples. In 90 pots of spiked soil, maize grew for 90 days under four plans, from plain soil to bacteria-loaded biochar. The loaded biochar cut available metals by roughly half and oil compounds by 70%, based on values the authors report. Maize also grew larger with less metal uptake.
pmc-13293794:
Agustín A. Vera and a large team show, in a 2026 study, how vitamin D helps activated helper T cells grow by feeding on glutamine rather than glucose. Vitamin D calms sugar use in these immune cells, yet early growth stays strong, hinting at a backup fuel.

Human helper T cells grown for four days with vitamin D multiplied more while taking up less glucose and making less lactate. Protein scans showed more glutamine-processing enzymes, and tracing showed more glutamine flowing into growth building blocks. Blocking the vitamin D receptor, glutamine entry, or its key enzyme each cut the effect. Glutamine thus powers the vitamin D growth path.
pmc-13293994:
Ellen King leads a 2026 mouse study of the first messenger RNA vaccine aimed at neuroblastoma, a childhood tumor behind 15% of pediatric cancer deaths. The vaccine uses self-assembling RALA peptides to carry RNA coding for glypican 2, a surface protein common on these tumors. Lab checks confirmed particle form, cell uptake, and function before animal dosing.
