Vaccinated mice mounted a GPC2-specific cell response, with higher IFN-γ and IL-2 signals and stronger TNF-α from helper and killer T cells. In a MYCN-amplified tumor model, growth was delayed by 10–11 days and volume cut by 70% versus controls. Glypican 2 also rises in other cancers.
pmc-13294194:
Magdalena Weidner-Glunde, Michael M. Nevels, and Emma Poole introduce a research collection on how viruses persist in the body. Their editorial argues that latency is not a quiet pause. Instead, a lingering virus keeps evolving, reshaping immunity, and sometimes driving disease.

The featured studies range widely. Persistent coronavirus infection in people with weak immunity can speed mutation and breed new variants. Another review covers gene editing aimed at human papillomavirus genomes that have merged into host DNA. Norovirus work shows lasting immune memory, and Nigerian surveillance reveals very high exposure to insect-borne viruses. A final method improves counting of viruses as they reactivate.
pmc-13294294:
Shin Iinuma, Takahiro Kobayashi, and Yasuyuki Fujita systematically review a rare relapsing skin vessel disease in 2026. Recurrent cutaneous eosinophilic vasculitis appears mainly in single case reports, so features were gathered case by case from three sources, last searched February 16, 2026, with structured extraction and quality appraisal.

Twenty reports gave 24 unique cases. Most people had repeated itchy purple spots on the lower legs, frequent blood eosinophil rises, and vessel damage rich in eosinophils on biopsy. Antibody tests tied to wider vasculitis were always negative in reported cases. Steroids often helped, yet relapse during dose cuts or after stopping was common. Follow-up gaps limit firm guidance.
pmc-13294494:
Areeb Mian and coauthors build a scan texture score for survival after liver metastasis surgery in a 2026 multicentre study. Outcomes after removing colorectal spread to the liver vary widely, and routine CT scans hold unused pattern data. Records from two UK centers gave 959 metastases from 399 patients, with features from tumors and background liver fed to selection tools and machine learners.

Six features formed the risk score. Texture alone predicted 3-year death with an area of 0.77, close to clinic models at 0.82 in the reported figures, and combined models nudged slightly higher. Formal tests found no clear gap between texture and clinic models. High versus low score split survival paths cleanly.
pmc-13294694:
Toru Matsui and colleagues report outcomes for a bleeding-control technique in a 2026 single-centre case series. Colonic diverticular bleeding is hard to manage during endoscopy, and their hospital uses coagulation combined with clipping. Real-world results for that combined approach had been little reported.

Among 256 patients with blood in the stool, 83 received the combined treatment for confirmed diverticular bleeding. Seven patients bled again within 30 days, and procedure-related problems arose in 3 patients, all handled without surgery. The authors present the approach as a practical option when the bleeding diverticulum can be clearly seen.
pmc-13294894:
Barbara Laïk and co-authors peel apart the thin oxide skin that guards cobalt-nickel alloys, in a 2026 surface study. These alloys serve in car parts and magnetic memory, and a film only a few nanometers thick gives them their rust defense. The team read the film's chemistry with X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy and stepped down through it with gentle ion sanding, across blends from pure nickel to pure cobalt.

Earlier work on one blend had shown a patchy skin, with cobalt oxide on some spots and nickel oxide on others. Across the blend series, film thickness and makeup shifted with the cobalt share in ways the authors tie to the metal's magnetism below. The results link a bulk trait of the alloy to the chemistry of the skin that guards it.
pmc-13295094:
Jegan Govindaraj and co-authors devise a quick way to measure a radioactive element in drinking water at almost unimaginably low levels, in a 2026 analytical study. Radium-226 seeps into water from rock, settles in bone, and raises cancer risk, so regulators set strict limits. The method gathers the radium first using cloud point extraction, where a soap-like solution clouds on warming and traps the target, with a selective binder called Macropa doing the grabbing.

Tuning acidity, binder dose, and additives pushed capture above ninety-five percent from quarter-liter samples of tap and bottled water. Plasma mass spectrometry then counted the radium down to levels far below national and international guideline values. The authors note theirs is the first report of cloud point extraction applied to radium. For water utilities, the protocol promises faster, cheaper checks on a contaminant that older methods chase slowly.
pmc-13295594:
Mengsong Zheng and co-authors fuse two natural proteins into one that both grips cells and grows bone, in a 2026 regenerative study. Periodontitis rots the bone socketing teeth, and current materials rarely deliver adhesion and bone-building signals together. Amelogenin, a tooth-development protein, encourages mineralized tissue but sticks cells poorly. Fibronectin carries a famous three-letter grip motif, RGD. The team stitched amelogenin's conserved ends to that motif, creating a fusion named rtAmR.

Stem cells from tooth roots clung to the fusion and spread out at roughly double the rate seen with plain amelogenin. Bone-forming performance matched or beat the natural protein on enzyme activity, collagen output, and mineral nodule formation. In rat jaw defects the fusion rebuilt more bone than either parent protein, without drawing extra inflammatory cells. The authors propose rtAmR as a two-in-one scaffold for periodontal repair.
pmc-13295694:
Inês Pereira and a large team search existing drugs for new uses against gonorrhoea in a 2026 study. The germ is a top priority for fresh treatments as resistance grows. Blocking its pump systems, which throw out antibiotics, could restore drug power, especially if energy supply is also hit.

Computer matching across public databases linked 57 approved drugs to 32 predicted bacterial targets. A shortlist went to bench tests on a reference strain, where two drugs stopped growth at the lowest levels. Two others showed signs of jamming the pumps, and one helped partner drugs in combination tests, marking early candidates for resistant strain work.
pmc-13295794:
Jiayi Wang and Duli Shi study what makes teacher coaching land well, in a 2026 survey of 308 school teachers in the United States. Coaching is a common way to grow teaching skill, yet the human side of it is little mapped. The team asked how the coach-teacher bond, faith in one's own skill, and drive for coaching tie to two results: how welcome coaching feels and how much stress it brings.

Strong bonds with a coach went with warmer welcome, stronger self-faith, and keener drive, above all a sense of gain and fewer doubts. The bond's link to welcome ran through self-faith and felt gain. Its link to lower stress ran wholly through self-faith. The authors urge programs to build real bonds with teachers and feed their drive, not just their technique.
pmc-13295994:
Jessica Wilkins and colleagues use health records in 2026 to study GP contact among adults with eating disorders in England. They compare visit rates before diagnosis with matched people without such disorders, and check whether ethnicity shapes referral onward.

Records covered 46,473 patients and far larger matched controls from 2010 to 2023. People with eating disorders saw their GP about twice as often in the two years before diagnosis, across all disorder types. Contact rates were lower in minority ethnic groups, and Asian and Black patients had lower odds of specialist referral. The authors urge better awareness and fairer primary care.
pmc-13296194:
Ana Amić, Žiko Milanović, and Denisa Mastiľák Cagardová compute how urate, a common antioxidant in human blood, fights the carbonate radical, in a 2026 study. That radical may be a bigger source of oxidative harm than the hydroxyl radical long blamed. Using quantum chemistry, the team weighed how water clinging to the players changes the speed and drive of a one-electron handoff from urate to the radical.

The summed rates matched the measured value well, backing the model. Docking tests placed urate snugly in the active pocket of SOD1, an enzyme where it may cut radical making at the source, and it bound more strongly than a known blocker there. Its grip on a DNA repair enzyme was weaker than that enzyme's known blocker. Motion checks showed urate's binding shook neither protein.
pmc-13296294:
Hailing Lin and colleagues investigate koumine, a plant alkaloid from Gelsemium elegans, as a possible treatment for liver cancer in a 2026 study. Earlier work showed anti-tumour effects in other cancers, yet its role against hepatocellular carcinoma was unclear. The team combined computer-based target prediction with cell and animal experiments.

Network analysis pointed to 124 possible targets, with signalling proteins such as P38 and JAK family members among the core set. Docking tests suggested koumine binds these targets strongly. In cell cultures the compound slowed cancer cell growth, movement, and invasion in a dose-related way. Tumours also grew more slowly in treated mice, with no notable toxicity reported. The findings support further study, not clinical use at this stage.
pmc-13296994:
Federico Fernandez and colleagues test whether chopping sorghum silage longer changes how growing beef steers eat and digest it in a 2026 feeding trial. Seventy-two Angus steers in twelve pens received diets built almost entirely on sorghum silage for eighty-four days. Half the pens got silage cut at a longer setting and half at a shorter one.

Steers on the longer cut ate slightly more feed each day. Their starch digestibility was also clearly higher, by several percentage points. Daily weight gain and feed efficiency, however, did not separate the groups. The authors advise producers using conventional processors to favour a moderate chop rather than cutting forage too finely.
pmc-13297294:
Chenxi Miao and co-authors review, in 2026, CAR-macrophage therapy, a cell treatment aiming engineered macrophages at solid tumours where CAR-T cells disappoint. Macrophages naturally burrow into tumours and can flip local immunity from suppressed to attacking.

Beyond eating tumour cells directly, the engineered cells spread the alarm to other tumour targets, bridging quick innate and learned adaptive attack. The review argues macrophage-specific signal parts beat borrowed T-cell designs. Making enough cells is the big bottleneck, with stem-cell factories and in-body programming via fat nanoparticles offered as practical ways forward for the field.
pmc-13297594:
Blood signals of scarring might one day flag heart transplant rejection without a biopsy, suggests a 2026 study led by Marta Delgado-Arija. Working with 40 serum samples from transplant recipients undergoing routine biopsies, the team hunted for fibrosis-related messenger RNAs that shift during acute cellular rejection.

Several signals differed in patients with rejection, including fibroblast activators such as TNS1, FAP, and ACTA2, plus members of the TGF-β and WNT pathways. Two markers, TNS1 and WLS, separated moderate-to-severe rejection from no rejection with area under the curve values above 0.90. The authors see a path toward gentler monitoring of transplant patients and toward treatments aimed at the fibrotic process itself.
pmc-13298094:
The size of the opening at the top of the chest might help predict trouble after esophagus surgery, suggest Iskan Calli and co-authors in a 2026 study. They measured thoracic inlet dimensions on routine CT scans of esophageal cancer patients who received a neck connection after esophagectomy.

Patients with smaller inlet areas tended toward higher postoperative mortality, and leakage at the connection was markedly more frequent among those who died. The authors stop short of claiming cause, framing inlet shape as one anatomical factor among many. Because the measurements come free from standard scans, they propose adding them to future risk assessment, pending confirmation in larger prospective studies.
pmc-13298394:
Jan Dahrendorff and others track blood microRNA changes with depressive symptom change, in a 2026 long-term public study. MicroRNAs regulate gene action after transcription and have been linked to depression in one-time studies, yet repeat readings are scarce. Sequencing covered immune-cell microRNAs at two time points for 185 people.

No microRNA survived strict correction for multiple testing. Dozens showed nominal links to symptom change, and several matched earlier reports tying them to stress response and brain plasticity. Predicted targets clustered in pathways spanning neurotransmission, stress hormones, inflammation, and circadian control. The authors treat the signatures as preliminary and call for larger cohorts.
pmc-13298994:
Arnab Dey Sarkar and Bard Ermentrout model cortical rhythms with two extra inhibitory cell classes beyond the classic circuit, in a 2026 computational neuroscience paper. Standard accounts use excitatory pyramidal cells plus one fast blocking type to generate gamma and beta rhythms. Their spiking network adds somatostatin cells, which inhibit both main groups, and VIP cells that modulate them.

The network reduces to nine differential equations tracking voltage, firing rate, and synaptic conductance per population. Wide ranges gave several coexisting rhythms at once. Nonlinear dynamics tools then mapped how each blocking class and VIP input shape those rhythms, extending the classic picture of cortical oscillation.
pmc-13299094:
An endoscopic operation through the anus spared patients with low rectal tumors the loss of anal function, report Xiaoke Hu and colleagues in a 2026 multicenter case series. Thirty-seven patients who had declined radical surgery, including older people with serious illnesses and cases that returned after earlier treatment, underwent the sphincter-preserving technique.

Most tumors were low-grade rectal cancers, with neuroendocrine and stromal tumors making up the rest. Every tumor came out in one piece with complete removal, and no severe complications occurred. Over an average follow-up near thirty-seven months, only 2.7% of patients saw recurrence. The authors present the approach as a valuable option for difficult cases.
pmc-13299194:
Natural compounds attack skin cancer through a surprisingly shared set of mechanisms, find Natalia Forno-Bell and co-authors in a 2026 systematic review of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma. Sixty studies covering purified molecules, crude extracts, essential oils, and combinations met their criteria.

Despite the chemical variety, activity converged on cell death programs, redox shifts, blocked growth signaling, cell-cycle arrest, and immune or light-activated effects. Purified compounds showed tighter mechanistic focus, while extracts acted more broadly and less predictably. Several agents worked both in dishes and in animals. The authors offer their mechanism-based sorting as a guide for choosing which natural candidates deserve clinical development.
pmc-13299394:
Ghadah H. Alshehri and a large team survey medication safety practice in selected Saudi hospitals against a World Health Organization global challenge programme, in a 2026 study. Medication safety officers at 28 hospitals listed interventions in place during or before 2025, organised by the programme's domains and priority areas.

Hospitals logged 162 interventions, clustered in medication systems and practice, then staff-focused work. High-risk cases drew most priority-area effort, while care handovers and multi-medicine handling lagged. Patient and public engagement formed the smallest domain share. The authors suggest broadening work on polypharmacy and engagement to strengthen safety, and offer the snapshot for policy planning.
pmc-13299494:
Qingteng Wei and others model what drives healthy behaviour among Chinese university students, in a 2026 cross-sectional survey study. Their model extends the theory of planned behaviour with health consciousness, health knowledge, and risk perception. Surveys from 384 students fed structural equation models of the proposed links.

Health knowledge directly predicted intention to act, and perceived control over their actions matched it as the strongest factor. Health consciousness fed attitudes, social norms, and perceived control. Risk perception also tracked with adopting healthy habits. The authors discuss usable lessons for campus health work, with knowledge teaching and confidence building run side by side rather than alone.
pmc-13299594:
Xinwei Zang, Yunqian Guan, Wanting Xing, and Zhiguo Chen present a fast method for making human cortical interneurons from induced neural stem cells, in a 2026 stem cell study. Existing routes from pluripotent cells are slow and inconsistent across lines. Their small-molecule recipe commits the stem cells to interneuron fate within about two weeks.

Brief pathway blocking set the lineage, and prolonged activation of a developmental signal strengthened marker expression and early maturation pathways. Results reproduced across four genetically distinct lines with few off-target cells. The neurons migrated, produced the inhibitory transmitter GABA, and survived transplantation into mouse brain, forming synapse-like structures. Scalable production for future cell therapy is the goal.
pmc-13299694:
Celine-Chantal Elster-Kann and Beate Muschalla compare employees with emotional exhaustion against employees with work overload in nationally sampled German data, in a 2026 study. More than two thousand working adults were grouped by treatment for exhaustion and by perceived overload, then weighed on working conditions and private traits.

Overloaded employees reported heavier work demands, while exhausted employees were more often women and more often outside their preferred occupation. Social and mental factors such as responsibility and support separated the groups more steadily than physical conditions. Overload without exhaustion emerged as its own state. The authors suggest steps should treat overload as a distinct risk beside illness-related exhaustion.
pmc-13300194:
Jared M. Finkel and colleagues describe a 2026 genetics study that replaced a fission yeast gene with its human counterpart. The yeast gene rpb9 encodes one subunit of RNA polymerase II, the enzyme that copies genes into RNA. Its human version, POLR2I, is linked to cancer drug resistance. Most knowledge of it comes from yeast work, so the team edited the yeast genome to make the human protein in place of its own.

The human protein covered many yeast roles: growth, chronological aging, and stress responses. It also handled new roles in silent chromatin assembly and resistance to a chemotherapy drug and a fungicide. One role, resistance to a transcription blocker called 6-azauracil, was not covered at normal expression levels. The authors offer the humanized yeast as a cleaner way to test which gene functions are shared across species.
pmc-13301094:
Achille Saracco and co-authors evaluate a porous hydroxyapatite bone substitute packed beside locking plates in shoulder fractures, in a 2026 retrospective cohort study. The comparison covered forty-five patients whose fractures with bone loss received the scaffold, and forty comparable patients plated without it. All were followed clinically and radiographically for twelve months, with standard shoulder function and pain scores.

Function improved steadily and pain fell significantly over the year in the cohort as a whole. No scaffold migrated and no graft resorption showed on imaging, and no complication was blamed directly on the material. Recovery curves in the two groups, however, ran nearly on top of each other, with no group by time advantage for the scaffold. The authors are careful to claim feasibility and short to mid term safety only, given the small, non-randomized design and patchy follow-up.
pmc-13302494:
Gianni Dall'Ara and co-authors report early results, in a 2026 study, of catheter-based aortic valve replacement performed at hospitals without on-site heart surgery. Waits for treatment at specialist valve centres can harm patients with a narrowed aortic valve. The TAVI AT HOME study tests whether expert teams can deliver the procedure safely at ordinary hospitals.

The run-in phase enrolled twenty patients at three Italian centres and compared them with forty-one similar cases from a local registry. The home-centre group actually carried more prohibitive-risk patients, yet technical success was slightly higher than in the registry group. No deaths occurred within thirty days in either set, and one-year survival matched. The ethics committee approved expanding the study after this interim check.
pmc-13303394:
Yang and four co-authors wrote in twenty twenty-six on law risks in the use of big health data in China. Such data is now classed as a key state asset with wide use in care and rule. World guides urge morals, safety, fair reach, and last-ing gains in digital health.

Risks named are loss of name hiding, bias in smart tools, skewed share of gains, and wrong acts on morals. The team sets out fixes by case type. Those are tiered guards, live name hiding, checks of smart tools, and a share of gains back to the public. The aim is safe data use with rights kept.
pmc-13303494:
Zhao and a team of co-authors relate two blood markers to eczema and its treatment, in a paper dated twenty twenty-six. They studied 106 patients with atopic dermatitis and fifty healthy volunteers. Levels of interleukin-4 and C-reactive protein were measured by disease stage and severity.

Both markers ran highest in the acute stage and lowest in the chronic stage. They also rose step by step from mild to severe disease. The team tracked both markers across sixteen weeks of treatment. They checked how well the pair flags the disease and mirrors response to the antibody drug dupilumab.
pmc-13303694:
Xue Hu and co-authors share a 2026 case report with a literature review on a malignant nerve sheath tumor arising in the liver. Such tumors usually start in arms, legs, or the trunk, and a liver origin is extremely rare.

A 56-year-old woman came in with upper belly pain and swelling, while blood tumor markers stayed normal. Scans showed a liver lesion with low blood flow, and tissue testing after full surgical removal confirmed the diagnosis. No return or spread appeared during about two years of follow-up. Imaging features from this and past cases may help doctors separate this tumor from more common liver cancers.
pmc-13304094:
Paola Romano introduces a 2026 special issue on the physics and uses of superconductivity, the state where materials carry current without resistance below a set temperature. For decades the effect needed extreme cold, until layered copper materials raised the working range in the late 1980s.

Nine papers in the first edition cover low-temperature, high-temperature, and iron-based materials, their structure, electrical and magnetic traits, and theory. Making and processing methods that lift performance toward real devices also feature. The overview frames where the field stands and what practical gains may come next for energy and other technologies.
pmc-13304394:
Danmeng Li, Alexandria Voigt, and Cuong Q. Nguyen explore, in a 2026 study, how chemical edits to self-proteins change what the immune system displays in Sjögren's disease. The illness attacks tear and saliva glands and is strongly tied to one immune presenter molecule, HLA-DR3. Edits called post-translational modifications can create new targets on familiar proteins.

Computer predictions said edits at key anchor points usually weakened binding to the presenter rather than improving it. Scanning three known target proteins found crowded clusters of editable anchors in particular folded regions. Lab tests on selected edited peptides then showed stronger T cell responses paired with tighter binding. Structural models revealed a slightly shifted fit with a larger contact surface, hinting how tolerance breaks.
pmc-13304494:
Reuven Rasooly and Naomi Balaban develop a cell-based test for active staph food toxins in a 2026 study. Existing lab tests find the toxins but cannot tell live, sickness-causing forms from spent ones, so animal testing fills that gap.

A lab T cell line was engineered to answer active toxin by making an immune signal in proportion to dose. The test covered two major toxin types tied to food poisoning and possible misuse. Heating past a set point sharply cut one toxin's activity, while standard pasteurizing heat cut it only slightly. The method offers a humane stand-in for animal checks.
pmc-13306694:
Lashyn Kiyekbayeva and a large Kazakh team develop a skin gel in 2026 from Nanophyton iliense, a salt-loving Central Asian plant whose chemistry was barely studied. Extracts made with water and alcohol were profiled by two chromatography methods. Antioxidant strength and early safety were checked before gel making.

The extract carried oily terpenoid and sterol compounds alongside phenolics such as catechin and naringin. Its total polyphenol level beat other plant extracts tested the same way, and radical scavenging reached about ninety percent at the top dose. Brine shrimp tests showed no toxic effect at the doses used. Five gels were compared, and the fourth spread smoothly without greasy residue. The authors conclude the plant fits semi-solid topical formulation, with antioxidant activity worth further study.
pmc-13306894:
Huaqun Zhang and colleagues reveal in 2026 how the human Argonaute2 protein assembles the silencing complex that turns off target genes. Four frozen-electron microscopy structures captured the protein holding a small RNA duplex at intermediate steps. Which strand survives decides which messages get silenced, so assembly details matter.

Only one lobe grips the duplex end at first, while a helix tests its stability. Later parts of the protein wedge into the duplex and peel the passenger strand away from its tip. Surprisingly, target-like RNAs can replace the passenger and drive its full ejection, even after cleavage. Messenger RNAs therefore play two roles: victims of silencing and helpers in building the silencer. The authors name this route target-assisted passenger ejection.
pmc-13307294:
Christophe Barbanchon tested repeated virtual motion exposure for balance in older adults in a 2026 study. Eighteen healthy participants over sixty stood quietly and faced simulated forward and backward self-motion plus tendon vibration before and after training.

Repeated optic flow in immersive virtual reality dulled the destabilising pull of moving scenes in reported results. Quiet standing with eyes closed also grew steadier, and sense weighting shifted toward more consistent visual use with weaker visual-proprioceptive coupling. The authors present short VR practice as a targeted way to keep balance strategies flexible with age.
pmc-13307794:
Claudia Maria Tucciarone and co-authors survey in 2026 DNA viruses in non native pond sliders, a turtle that has spread through ponds in northeastern Italy. Mouth and vent swabs came from 164 turtles at three sites, and lab tests hunted herpesviruses, ranaviruses, and adenoviruses in each sample.

No herpesvirus or ranavirus turned up in any turtle they sampled during the survey work. Adenoviruses were common, found in 72 of 163 turtles with full results in hand for that check. Most matched a known turtle type, while one matched a type once tied to deaths in other tortoises. What these viruses do to turtles stays unclear, yet wide carriage argues for steady watch where native species share the water.
pmc-13307894:
Dequan Guo and co-authors assemble in 2026 a disease knowledge graph to aid vet care for captive forest musk deer, a protected species farmed for musk in China. Common ills such as abscess, gut swelling, lung swelling, and parasites strike often, start quietly, and suffer from scattered written records.

Their joint extraction model pulls core medical ideas from loose deer disease texts and links them into a web that vets can search. Tests on medical data sets showed the model could carry over well to new material of like kind. A tidy graph base could speed early spotting and care choices, while also cutting the stress that hands on checks cause shy deer.
pmc-13308594:
Ruiyang Liu and co-authors find in 2026 a driver of liver cancer growth in a metabolic enzyme called PMVK, found through a gene screen in tumour cells. PMVK tags the factor SP1 at one site, which helps SP1 grip DNA and team with fat control factors SREBP1 and SREBP2.

That team switches on fresh cholesterol and fatty acid making, which feeds tumour stem traits and spread in their tests. High PMVK in patient tumours tracked with high tagged SP1 and with poor outlook for those patients. Blocking the pair, by genes or by a known SP1 drug, curbed tumour growth in models. The axis offers a fresh drug target for liver cancer.
pmc-13309194:
Marie-Laure Oberweis, Ana C Blanchard, and Esther Vaugon lay out in 2026 five key points on hantavirus. Hantavirus is a rodent borne disease that must be reported in Canada, with four to five confirmed cases a year. Most cases arise on farms in the prairie west and British Columbia, through touch of infected rodents or their waste.

Two syndromes follow a two to four week wait: a heart and lung form in the Americas, and a kidney and bleeding form in Europe and Asia. Death rates run 12 to 45 percent for the lung form, and 1 to 12 percent for the kidney form. No vaccine or set cure exists, so care rests on support and swift transfer. Andes strain cases need strict isolation.
pmc-13309594:
Donghao Zhang and colleagues build an artificial ionic skin that also blocks electromagnetic interference in a 2026 study. Ionic skins copy human skin signal flow and softness for wearable sensors. Most versions sense well but shield poorly, leaving signals open to outside noise.

A soaking and binding strategy set a flat network of MXene sheets inside a gel while also building a charge slope through its depth. That single build gave strong shielding plus self-powered sensing, since the charge slope makes its own voltage. Stretch and self-healing traits from gel design carry over. The authors present the skin as a step toward wearables that sense cleanly in noisy settings.
pmc-13310194:
Joachim Gæde, Jens Juul Holst, Filip K Knop, and colleagues infuse a gut-bacteria peptide in 2026 into seventeen healthy young men to test safety and metabolic effects. The peptide, made by a common gut microbe, had lowered blood sugar in animal studies. Volunteers received the peptide or placebo into the small intestine after a liquid meal, then crossed over.

Everyone completed the trial, and the infusion was well tolerated with no changes in blood, liver, or kidney safety measures. Compared with placebo, the peptide quickly raised gut hormone GLP-1, insulin, and C-peptide while lowering glucose and another gut hormone. A standard index of whole-body insulin sensitivity also improved slightly. Gut microbes clearly signal to host metabolism, and this first human test supports that idea. Larger trials in people with diabetes are the obvious next step.
pmc-13310394:
Cynthia Mmalebna Amisigo and co-authors review parasites that cause neglected tropical diseases in a 2026 article. Trypanosomatids, including Trypanosoma and Leishmania, cause sleeping sickness, Chagas disease, and leishmaniasis across Africa, Latin America, and Asia. Drugs remain toxic, costly, scarce, and more often resisted, and no effective vaccines exist.

Tactics that let these parasites hide inside cells, dodge immunity, and adapt their chemistry also blunt drug action, breeding tougher strains. New lab work on their unusual cell structures and immune tricks opens fresh attack points. Smart software is entering target and drug screening for these diseases. The authors chart control strategies and argue that drug failure and disease strength must be tackled together.
pmc-13310494:
Linna Hao and co-authors report a rare benign eye tumor in a child in a 2026 case article. Choroidal osteoma is bone-like growth inside the eye wall layer, seen in about 1 per 100,000 people, mostly young women and usually in one eye only. A child with tumors in both eyes, covering the central vision zone, breaks that pattern.

The child had no symptoms despite giant tumors involving the macula of both eyes, and full eye examinations were completed for the record. Early lesions can sit silently even over the center of vision, the authors note. Typical patients report blur, warped sight, or light sensitivity once damage advances. The case urges doctors to keep this tumor in mind during childhood eye checks.
pmc-13310794:
Kayo Sugiyama reports a 2026 case where an aorta tear worsened silently during hospital transfer. A man aged 50 years was moved for stent care of a type B tear in the lower aorta. During transfer the tear spread backward into the upper aorta, a grave turn, yet pulse and symptoms showed no change.

On arrival, open surgery replaced the arch of the aorta with a hybrid graft method. Direct ultrasound during surgery found no tear in the rising aorta, which guided the choice. The man recovered well and stayed well at five year follow up. Teams must watch for silent spread during any transfer.
pmc-13310894:
Nayoung Lee and co-authors test a seaweed pigment against Alzheimer linked stress in cells and mice in a 2026 study. Brain amyloid drives disease advance, and a reactive compound called methylglyoxal adds stress that sparks swelling through a sensor pathway. The pigment fucoxanthin may calm that chain.

Nerve cells dosed with the pigment before amyloid exposure made fewer swelling signals and kept the key switch out of the nucleus. Mice given amyloid into the brain and fed the pigment for 15 days showed lower blood stress levels and calmer brain immune cells. Synapse markers were also guarded. Human proof is still absent.
pmc-13311094:
Hina Durrani and colleagues test whether a shared growth medium changes sugar enzyme levels in parasite relatives in a 2026 study. Kinetoplastids store sugar breaking enzymes in a special compartment called a glycosome. One theory holds that storage lets cells swiftly reshuffle enzyme amounts when food or oxygen shifts.

Six species, both single host and two host types, were grown under varied food and oxygen in one medium. Enzyme levels stayed largely steady across conditions. Slow food removal and oxygen shifts caused only minor moves. Only sudden food return nudged levels down slightly. Steady levels argue against the swift reshuffle theory.
pmc-13311194:
Liufeng Mao and co-authors trace how resveratrol lifts a metabolic hormone against obesity in a 2026 study. The grape linked polyphenol fights fat gain in past work, yet its molecular route was murky. A hormone called GDF15 that steadies energy balance emerged as a key suspect.

In mouse and human cells, resveratrol raised GDF15 making and release in a dose linked way. Gene scans named a stress factor that carries the signal, switched on through a kinase path. Treated mice resisted high fat diet obesity and held higher blood GDF15. Liver, kidney, and colon levels also rose, with stronger brain signaling downstream.
pmc-13311294:
Lan Luo and co-authors present their 2026 study on how the channel protein TRPV4 drives a fiery form of cell death in lung macrophages during acute lung injury. The death pathway runs through damaged mitochondria.

The work traces a chain in which TRPV4 upsets mitochondria, raising reactive oxygen from them, which then switches on the NLRP3 inflammasome. That switch pushes macrophages into pyroptosis, a bursting death that spills inflammatory signals. Acute lung injury still lacks drugs that hit its root inflammation. Naming TRPV4 as a driver gives drug makers a fresh target to test for calming the lung.
pmc-13311794:
Kian-Hwee Chong and colleagues examine a 2026 global records study on whether the timing of sleeve gastrectomy shapes later breast cancer risk in women with severe obesity. Weight surgery can lower cancer risk overall.

The network data held over 4.4 million women with body mass index above 35 recorded from 2010 to 2019. Surgery patients were grouped by how soon the operation followed diagnosis. Early surgery tied to lower five-year breast cancer and metastasis rates, while surgery delayed one to three years tied to higher breast cancer risk in this dataset. Timing, the authors argue, belongs in counseling about the operation.
pmc-13311994:
Xiaoyan Xie and co-authors review the IL-33/ST2 signaling pathway as a drug target in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in a 2026 article. The pathway weaves through oxidative stress, immunity, and lung injury.

Levels of IL-33 and its receptor ST2 run high in patients and track with worse disease, more flare-ups, and poorer outcomes, on the reviewed evidence. Blocking antibodies and receptor inhibitors have calmed inflammation and improved lung function in early studies. How the pathway talks with other inflammatory circuits is still murky. The review maps the biology and the drug pipeline aimed at it.
pmc-13312094:
Rapin Polsook and Yupin Aungsuroch report a 2026 randomized trial in Thailand testing whether a phone-based self-management program improves blood lipids in people with coronary artery disease. Drugs often fail to bring cholesterol and related fats to target, so the authors asked whether structured self-care support could close the gap.

Forty-eight patients at a tertiary hospital were split between usual care and a four-week program run through mobile applications and telephone contact. The program group ended with significantly lower cholesterol, triglyceride, and low-density lipoprotein levels than the control group. The authors conclude that app-guided self-management can improve lipid profiles in the short term and point to a practical role for nurses in delivering this kind of support.
pmc-13312194:
Prabuddha Prakash, Francisco Beltran-Silva, and Arjun Teotia examine, in a 2026 study, how often American high school students check social media, and how that habit tracks with substance use. Earlier work mostly measured total screen time, mixing passive viewing with compulsive checking. The authors instead used the 2023 Youth Risk Behavior Survey. It was the first in its series to ask directly about social media frequency, and it covered 10,027 students. The analysis adjusted for demographics, mental health, bullying, sleep, and activity.

A clear gradient appeared. Students checking social media more than once an hour had a probability of drinking 19 percentage points higher than non-users. Vaping ran 16 points higher and cannabis use 13 points higher. Scaled nationally, the authors link the heaviest checking group to roughly a million extra student drinkers. They suggest the findings bear on laws about design that maximizes engagement, and on marketing rules for alcohol and cannabis.
pmc-13312494:
Weiqian Jin and colleagues describe, in a 2026 study, a nature-mimicking nanoplatform for treating bacterial pneumonia without leaning on standard antibiotics. Their particle, called CM, wraps a copper-based metal-organic framework in macrophage membrane, using the membrane's homing ways so the platform gathers at infected sites.

Shone with near-infrared light, the platform loads copper ions into bacteria, sparks reactive oxygen species and inflammatory signals, and kills the microbes. Gene and metabolite tests showed the light-driven copper overload triggers cuproptosis, a cell death route driven by copper. The treatment also pushed macrophages toward their inflammatory M1 state and reshaped immune cell groups in the lung, so direct killing and immune activation worked together. Tests in cells and animals both backed the approach, which the authors offer as a template for other infections.
pmc-13312794:
Chang Ha Park reviews, in a 2026 article, the plant compound picroside III, an iridoid glycoside flagged for possible antileukemic activity. Its relatives picroside I and II have been studied heavily. A search of the literature from 2000 to 2026 turns up only a handful of papers on picroside III itself, a gap the review sets out to close.

The article walks through the molecule's architecture: a fused cyclopentane and pyran ring core carrying sugar units and varied substituents whose type, position, and orientation differ from its cousins. Those differences reshape its electronics and three-dimensional form. Attached sugars aid water solubility and transport but also leave the molecule open to enzymatic reshaping inside the body, while its many hydroxyl groups offer hydrogen-bonding grips on enzymes. Park argues these features make the neglected compound worth direct biological testing against leukemia.
pmc-13313294:
Shimaa El-Garf and fellow authors measure an immune brake in multiple myeloma in a 2026 study. The bone marrow around this blood cancer is full of blocked immune signals, and the PD-1 and PD-L1 pair is one such brake on T cells, though its solo role stays unclear.

The team ran a cross-sectional study of 39 patients newly diagnosed with the disease. Flow cytometry gauged PD-1 on T cells and PD-L1 on marrow plasma cells, and the values were set against clinical and lab data. PD-L1 strength on plasma cells rose with the share of T cells in marrow, with a correlation of 0.350 stated in the report, while PD-1 on T cells tracked with white cell counts. In stage III patients further links appeared. The data help weigh whether drugs that lift this brake merit trials in myeloma.
pmc-13314094:
Eman Moustafa and colleagues fed fenugreek oil to young Nile tilapia in a trial reported in two thousand twenty-five. A common bacterium causes heavy losses on tilapia farms, and plant oils may boost fish defenses. Groups of fingerlings ate diets with different oil levels for eight weeks, then faced a controlled bacterial infection.

Blood, tissue, and survival checks measured growth, immunity, and damage from infection. The oil carries plant compounds known to support immunity and fight oxidation, and the trial tracked whether that protection held under real infection pressure. Fish farmers get a tested feeding option that could cut losses without relying only on antibiotics.
pmc-13314794:
Yunhao Zhai and a large team build a lab model of mRNA vaccination on chips in their 2026 study. Guessing how well a new mRNA vaccine will work, and how toxic it may be, still leans on animal tests that often miss human responses.

Their setup doses human muscle cells and antigen-presenting cells with fat-bubble mRNA vaccines, mimicking a shot into muscle. Plain mRNA vaccines made antigen right in the presenting cells, while self-amplifying ones needed touch between muscle and presenting cells, as the authors report. Moving those cells and fluids to a lymphoid follicle chip, a tiny fluid device, mimicked drainage to lymph nodes. The chip follicles then grew and made fresh antibodies. The human tissue model may speed vaccine screening without animals.
pmc-13314994:
Mohammed Turky and co-workers set out a privacy-safe way to train AI across dental centers, in a 2026 review. The field is endodontics, the root canal specialty, where sharp AI needs wide, well-labeled data that privacy law keeps locked in each clinic.

Their answer is federated learning: each center trains a shared model on its own data, and only model updates travel, never patient files. The review searched the literature to April 2026 in English and compared how the method works and where it has been used. Standard central training clashes with data rules, they note. The paper lays out build paths, hurdles, and research needs for diagnosis and decision support, aiming to let clinics pool smarts without pooling records.
pmc-13315094:
Quoc Phuong Nguyen, Duy Thanh Doan, and Thi Thu Huong Dinh report a brain infection case where all cultures came back empty, in a 2026 study. Subdural empyema, pus under the skull lining, is a surgical emergency that kills a share of 6 to 15 percent of patients by the range cited in the report.

Their patient was a 51-year-old man with chronic alcohol abuse, high fever of 39 degrees, severe headache, neck stiffness, and a dulled mind. Spinal fluid was thick with cells and protein yet grew nothing, like his blood, urine, and pus samples, though inflammation marks soared. A plain CT read the mass as an old blood clot, but surgery found frank pus. Drainage plus two antibiotics brought full recovery in 24 days, as reported. The case backs MRI and early surgery when cultures stay silent.
pmc-13315194:
Lihui Zhou and colleagues test, in a 2026 cohort study, whether opening a blocked heart artery helps heart attack patients when the procedure comes more than six hours after symptoms start. Guidelines inherited their time window from clot-busting drug trials, not from intervention. The team enrolled 3,720 STEMI patients treated between 2009 and 2022 and divided them into intervention within six hours, intervention beyond six hours, and no intervention. Outcomes were compared with matched analyses.

The gradient was stark. In-hospital death ran 2.8 percent for early intervention, 4.1 percent for late, and 5.2 percent without, and over a follow-up of five years, mortality reached 13.1, 16.0, and 24.0 percent across the same groups. Adjusted models credited early intervention with lower death and major events, while late intervention's advantage over none faded to non-significance. The authors conclude late procedures may ease the hospital course, but survival requires acting within six hours.
pmc-13315894:
Haisheng Lan and colleagues built in 2026 a four-gene lactate score for colorectal cancer that forecasts outlook and immune therapy response. Lactate handling reshapes how tumor, epithelial, and immune cells talk to each other and can turn a tumor immunologically cold.

Single-cell and spatial gene data fed the new LMscore. A high score marked cold tumors full of suppressive cells with poor response to immune checkpoint drugs, and signaling through EFNA1 and EPHA3 linked epithelial cells with fibroblasts. Blocking COX15 in tests slowed tumor growth and restored anti-tumor immunity, offering a target tied to the score.
pmc-13316194:
Alexandra Biácsi and colleagues describe eleven cases in 2026 of heartworm disease in Hungarian zoo animals, caused by the mosquito-borne worm Dirofilaria immitis. Affected animals included three Eurasian wolves, two Arctic wolves, a lion, a leopard, a red panda, an Arctic fox, a harbour seal, and an Asian small-clawed otter.

Post-mortem results suggested heartworm played a part in the deaths of three Eurasian wolves, the red panda, the Arctic fox, and the seal, while other infections were incidental finds. The series gives the first Hungarian records in captive felids and the first report in Arctic wolves.
pmc-13316294:
Liv Cathrine Heggebø leads a 2026 quality check for the PRO-GLIO trial, which tests radiation care for certain slow-growing brain tumors with IDH changes. Before treatment starts across centers, the team asked how much expert drawings of target areas and nearby organs differ from place to place.

Five experts first set shared reference outlines for two cases, then experts at 12 centers in two Scandinavian countries drew their own, and a deep learning tool drew its own as well. Target outlines matched closely, with a median overlap score of 0.92 in the reported cases. Nearby organs varied far more, notably the optic chiasm and memory-related hippocampi. Computer outlines fell inside the human range, hinting they may help, while organ drawing needs closer watch.
pmc-13316594:
Youn-Soo Lee, Alex Soo In Park, and Bo-Young Youn studied a 2026 question in Korean health data. Do people with normal weight but high body fat face the same diabetes risk as people with obesity? The group, called normal-weight obesity, can hide risk behind a healthy scale reading.

Using national survey data from 2019 to 2021, the team matched 684 middle-aged adults one to one by sex and background. Among men, diabetes appeared in 20.00 percent of the normal-weight obese group versus 31.03 percent of the obesity group in the matched figures, while women showed no clear gap. Measuring body fat beyond weight and height, they argue, can flag hidden risk, at least in men.
pmc-13316694:
You Jin Lee and colleagues assembled, in a 2026 study, a living bank of 41 colorectal cancer organoids grown from patient tumors, then profiled them with many molecular tools at once. Such mini-tumors let researchers sort cancers by inner state and match drugs to type.

Their reads revealed a tug between two programs, MYC and PRC, marking stem-like versus more mature tumor states. A new maturation index split the organoids into two clear subtypes along that axis. MYC-type samples ran growth programs and answered better to drugs blocking the MEK and EGFR paths. The same split held in larger organoid sets and a public cancer dataset, tying cell maturity to treatment weakness in a usable way.
pmc-13318094:
Ian M Santiago Velazquez and co-authors report, in 2026, body composition findings in sixteen people with primary ciliary dyskinesia, a rare inherited disorder that damages the airways. All carried the same founder gene variant and were being assessed for possible lung transplantation. Lung tests and imaging may miss overall physical reserve, which matters for transplant decisions.

Electrical impedance analysis measured body water, muscle, fat and related indices. Total body water ran consistently below personal target values, while the share of water outside cells ran high, suggesting altered fluid distribution. Muscle and fat measures varied widely between individuals. No measure correlated significantly with lung function, and older patients showed more spread in weight and fat measures. The authors propose body composition as an added window on fitness.
pmc-13318594:
Longkang Guo and colleagues present a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. They study mind-body therapies for sleep in women around pregnancy and after birth. Poor sleep is common in that period. Drug options raise safety worries, so gentle therapies draw interest. Searches covered seven databases up to January 20, 2026.

Thirteen randomised trials with 782 participants qualified. Most tested mindfulness, Pilates, or yoga. Pooled results favoured the therapies over controls. Sleep scores improved by a mean difference of −2.63 points in the pooled analysis. Results varied a lot between studies, though. Country, programme length, and session length helped explain that spread. Formal grading rated the certainty of evidence as low. The authors urge caution and better trials.
pmc-13318694:
Peipei Liu and colleagues offer a 2026 genetic study of early puberty in girls. They test two variants in the estrogen receptor beta gene. The condition is idiopathic central precocious puberty, with no clear cause. One hundred affected girls from a Shenzhen hospital were enrolled.

Another hundred healthy girls of similar age served as controls. Genotyping used a standard restriction fragment method. The RsaI variant differed clearly between groups. Its R allele appeared in 41.50 percent of patients against 30.00 percent of controls, raising risk. The AluI variant showed no clear difference. A combined pattern, the Rraa haplotype, also appeared more often in patients. The authors suggest genotyping could aid early risk checks, pending larger studies.
pmc-13318794:
Mengxuan Zhang and colleagues report a 2026 nine-year field experiment on green manures before wheat in salty soils. The setting is the Hetao Irrigation District. Treatments mixed feed rape, a non-legume, with hairy vetch, a legume. Two nitrogen rates were tested, including none.

Only green manure type clearly changed later wheat yield and stability. The combined planting beat rape alone on average yield by 17.2 percent at the higher nitrogen rate. Yield stability rose by about a fifth under both nitrogen rates. Mixed planting also raised soil carbon, enzyme activity, and overall soil function. Microbes were mainly limited by carbon and nitrogen supply. The authors recommend mixed green manures to cut fertiliser dependence in saline farming.
pmc-13318894:
Arnab Purohit and colleagues present a 2026 study of gut germs in two destructive termite species, Coptotermes formosanus and Reticulitermes flavipes. These underground termites depend on gut germs to digest wood. The team also tested eugenol, a plant compound that kills insects and germs. Gene sequencing mapped what lived in each gut.

The two species carried distinct mixes overall. Still, both shared a core led by Spirochaetota. One held more Bacteroidota, while the other favoured Firmicutes and other groups. Eugenol killed many termites and reshaped their gut germs by kind. Overall variety stayed similar, but key wood-digesting Treponema fell while other groups rose. Forecast microbe roles in carbohydrate use also shifted. The authors propose germ-targeted, greener termite control.
pmc-13319494:
Prabhakar Dorairaj and colleagues compare, in 2026, three calcium channel blocker drugs for high blood pressure in an Indian multicentre study. Amlodipine is the established standard, while cilnidipine and azelnidipine have extra properties that might change daily pressure patterns. Real-world differences between them were uncertain.

Fifty adults with mild to moderate hypertension took one of the three drugs for eight weeks, with clinic checks and 24-hour ambulatory monitoring before and after. All three groups achieved significant pressure reductions, with no significant difference in overall 24-hour change. Awake-period readings differed slightly between two of the drugs. Target achievement, pulse rate and day-night dipping patterns were broadly comparable. The authors conclude the three options perform similarly in the short term.
pmc-13320094: Hongyu Wang and co-authors issued a correction in 2026 to their study on finding shoulder labrum tears on MRI scans with a deep learning method. The notice itself is short and is the whole item here. It fixes the methods text, which had named only one scan type. Two fat suppressed scan types were in fact used, one based on proton density and one on T2 weighting. The restated methods also spell out the scan setup and how surgeons confirmed each tear during keyhole surgery.
pmc-13320694:
Seungjoo Lee and co-authors draw engineering lessons from desert horned lizards in a 2026 study. The lizard Phrynosoma platyrhinos gathers water through tiny channels in its skin, but how that water reaches the mouth was a long standing puzzle. The team studied jaw motion and the flow physics behind it.

Slow jaw opening paired with fast closing acts as a capillary pump that moves skin water toward the mouth. Guided by that motion, the team built a system that pulls water from damp soil and, at the same time, removes harmful heavy metals from it. The design needs little energy and suits dry regions where clean water is scarce.
pmc-13321394:
Jian-kui Du and a large team study blast lung injury and a protective protein switch in a 2026 report. Explosive shock waves can tear the lung's air barrier, a life threatening harm whose molecular drivers stay unclear. Gene data from single cells pointed to a master regulator called TFEB in stressed lining cells.

Raising TFEB in models eased lung swelling, inflammation, and oxidative harm and kept the barrier intact. A new target of TFEB, the receptor IGF2R, helped control release of two tissue cutting enzymes. A hydrogen sulfide releasing nanozyme switched TFEB on by a sulfur tweak at one site, boosting cell cleanup. The chain offers fresh targets for blast injury care.
pmc-13321794:
Naoyuki Miyashita and colleagues compare two antibiotics for drug resistant lung infection in a 2026 short study from Japan. Macrolide resistant Mycoplasma pneumoniae is rising again in Japan, and minocycline is the advised first choice drug. The team tested whether the quinolone garenoxacin works as well for pneumonia caused by resistant strains.

Fever cleared within 48 hours of starting antibiotics in 90.6 percent of garenoxacin patients and 90 percent of minocycline patients in the study. Those near equal results led the authors to propose garenoxacin as a first choice option as well. A further choice matters for clinics facing resistant infections where standard macrolide drugs no longer work.
pmc-13322194:
Inbal Zigdon and co-authors profile how steroid hormone receptors choose their DNA targets in a 2026 study. Such receptors switch genes on by binding short DNA motifs, but those motifs are too common to explain exact binding sites. The team tracked three receptors with long disordered head regions, called N-terminal domains, across genomes.

Receptors lacking those domains clustered near the AP-1 motif, while full receptors also bound their classic motif far from AP-1 sites. Tests in budding yeast showed the domain can steer targeting even without mammal specific partners. The disordered head thus acts as a guide for genome choice, a lever that might one day tune hormone drug action.
pmc-13322494:
Isadora de Oliveira Lemos, Kelly Cristina Alves Silvério, and Mauriceia Cassol compare two hands-on voice therapies in a 2026 randomised trial. Women with muscle tension dysphonia, where strained neck and throat muscles distort the voice, were assigned to electrical nerve stimulation, manual laryngeal therapy, or both together. Voice symptoms, pain, breathing measures, and felt muscle tension were scored before and after.

All groups eased vocal symptoms, including fatigue, and muscle pain, and all lengthened maximum phonation time. Electrical treatment alone cut breathiness, manual therapy alone cut overall voice change, and the combined arm cut both overall change and vocal tension. Felt tension on examination also fell most clearly in the combined group.
pmc-13322594:
Sanjeeb Pradhan and co-authors test whether fasting time predicts low blood pressure after spinal anaesthesia in a 2026 observational study. Long fasting before surgery is feared to drain body fluid, yet natural compensation may offset that loss. The team measured fasting length, an ultrasound index of vein fullness, and pressure drops in 51 adults having surgery below the navel.

The vein collapsibility index rose clearly with longer fasting. Fasting length alone separated later pressure drops poorly, while the ultrasound index did moderately well and stood as the only independent predictor in adjusted models. A one percent rise in the index raised the odds of a pressure drop slightly, which favours scanning over clock watching.
pmc-13322794:
Tim Schubert and Robert Weidner study soldier acceptance of a shoulder exoskeleton in a 2026 field study. The device aids overhead work during chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear defence tasks. Lab tests had shown muscle effort cuts of 29 to 41 percent, but field views were unknown. Twenty-seven German soldiers wore it for about 30 minutes of set tasks.

Soldiers rated ease of use at 5.15 and wearing comfort at 4.64 on a seven point scale in the survey. Fit with work routines and usefulness scored in the middle range, while felt mechanical support scored low, at 2.78 in the study. Intent to use was moderate. Stronger support and wider task coverage should lift acceptance.
pmc-13324294:
Liyan Ni and co-authors hunt for a protein that predicts sinus surgery relapse in children, in a 2026 proteomic study of chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps. Nasal tissue from a discovery cohort with over a year of follow-up was screened for proteins tied to post-surgery recurrence.

Four candidates emerged from the top differing proteins, and two, SPRR3 and RAB29, ran higher in the recurrence group and sat mainly in the nasal lining. SPRR3 also rose in paired tissue taken at revision surgery, and blood levels ran higher in children who relapsed, tracking recurrence risk. Survival and accuracy analyses supported serum SPRR3 as an early warning marker for relapse.
pmc-13324494:
Hai Zeng and Xinrong Ou present a 2026 case report on antibiotic failure after brain surgery caused by unusually fast kidney clearance. A healthy 51-year-old woman had a right cerebellar meningioma removed and then developed meningitis with no germ grown in culture.

Standard vancomycin doses left blood levels far below the target range even at 18.5 mg per kilogram. Her creatinine looked normal, yet measured clearance reached about 135 mL per minute, confirming augmented renal clearance. Usual screening scores wrongly rated her low risk. Drug level checks guided stronger meropenem dosing and a switch to linezolid, and she recovered fully by day 23 with no relapse.
pmc-13325094:
Ali H. Al-Hajooj and co-authors synthesize paired-metal Schiff base complexes and screen them for medical uses in a 2026 chemistry study. The ligand joins two metal centers, manganese, iron, or cobalt, in one binuclear frame.

Spectroscopy, mass checks, X-ray powder data, and modeling mapped how the ligand grips each metal through oxygen and nitrogen atoms. The compounds killed selected human cancer cell lines in lab screens, and the manganese and cobalt versions cut DNA strongly. The manganese complex also broke down protein fully in gel tests. Cobalt gave the strongest antioxidant action, with an IC50 of 0.0231 micromolar in the reported assay. The manganese form led against bacteria and fungi.
pmc-13327394:
Lakshmi Jogi and co-authors explore future care worries in a 2026 interview study from a large hospital in Bengaluru, India. Parents of adults with mild intellectual disability often fear what happens when age or illness stops them from giving care. Most earlier work came from rich countries, so an Indian view was missing.

Sixteen interviews in all, two for each of four men and four women receiving care, were translated and studied for shared themes. Worries centered on finding a trusted guardian, safety, and daily care, shaped by the adult's needs, the parents' health, sibling ties, and local attitudes. Most families had saved money, wanted kin to take over, and planned for housing and work after their own lifetimes.
pmc-13327994:
Yangjun Liu and colleagues test two exercise programs in postmenopausal women with belly obesity in a 2026 quasi-experimental study. One group did high-intensity interval Nordic walking. Its fast bouts ran at 75 to 85 percent of maximum heart rate, with slower recovery between. Another group did strength training, each three times a week for twelve weeks. A control group received lifestyle education only.

Both programs shrank waist size, the walking group by 2.64 cm from its start on the reported change, alongside checks of blood pressure, triglycerides, HDL cholesterol, and fasting glucose. Interval walking with poles offers a joint-friendly way to attack metabolic syndrome markers, and strength work gives a second route for women who prefer it.
pmc-13328194:
Nor Haji Osman and a large team measure use of electronic record data by health managers in Somalia in a 2026 multicenter study. Records systems were rolled out to strengthen routine information, but whether managers actually decide from the data was unknown. Surveys and checklists covered 405 managers across 45 public facilities in late 2025.

Only 145 managers, 35.8 percent of those surveyed, reported adequate use of record data for decisions, most often to check whether clinical guidelines were followed. Organizational, technical, and personal factors were modeled to find what helps or blocks use. Systems alone do not change decisions, the work implies: training, support, and habits must carry the data into the meeting room.
pmc-13330694:
Yangyang Zhang and a large team build a deep learning tool to predict platinum resistance in ovarian cancer in a 2026 study. Abdominal fluid drawn before treatment mirrors the tumour setting, yet its cell shapes were little used for forecasting. The OVCAP system reads whole-slide cell images at many scales.

The study held 438 patients with advanced disease. Accuracy scores stayed strong across one internal and two outside hospital groups, beating a standard clinical score in the reported values. High-risk cell patterns included bubbly cell interiors and crowded malignant clusters with immune cells nearby. Gene data linked those looks to membrane, fat, and stress pathways. Fluid checks could sort risk before first therapy.
pmc-13330994:
Justin C. Cordova, James B. Young, and James S. Huntley present a Poet's Pen piece on very short medical stories in a 2026 article. At its heart sits The Box, a 55-word story by Huntley about the mysteries of the heart. The format began in 1986 and now marks 40 years as a set writing category.

Such stories limit writers to exactly 55 words, mixing prose and poetry freely within that count. The tight frame lends itself to sharp reflections on doctor and patient bonds. Health training programmes and major medical journals have adopted the form. The authors frame it as a compact tool for narrative medicine, helping clinicians notice and act on patient stories.
pmc-13331194:
Maryo Baakliny and colleagues study routine vaccine views among adults in Lebanon after the pandemic in a 2026 case-control study. The survey ran across all regions from July to October 2023. Participants were adults who had caught COVID-19, split into 277 unvaccinated cases and 453 vaccinated controls drawn from national records.

Vaccinated adults were older, more often employed and schooled, and more often health workers in the reported profiles. They scored higher on vaccine knowledge and attitudes and kept up routine and flu shots better after the pandemic, while upkeep fell among unvaccinated adults. Schooling, age, child count, and attitudes each tied to lower odds of non-vaccination in adjusted models.
pmc-13331994:
Hendin and colleagues reported in 2026 how higher versus lower blood pressure targets affect lung circulation after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest. In this substudy of the randomized BOX trial, comatose survivors were assigned to a low or high mean arterial pressure target, the average pressure driving blood flow. Lung artery catheters tracked pressures for 48 hours. Seven hundred thirty patients were included.

The higher target raised lung artery pressures and filling pressures. Calculated lung vessel resistance dipped slightly during the first day before the groups converged, because heart output rose proportionally more than pressures. The right side of the heart pumped more strongly under the higher target throughout, with the gap widest at 48 hours. Filling pressure fell in both groups but stayed lower early on with the lower target. The authors show pressure targets reshape lung and right-heart loads in ways standard readings can miss.
pmc-13332194:
Nihal Eraydin-Tufek, Gonen Ozcan, and Sila Isler trial non surgical cures for implant gum disease. Their trial from twenty twenty-six deals with early peri-implantitis. The ill is tied to germ films on dental implants.

Implants were split among five care groups for the trial. One group got scraping alone, others got added rinses or sprays. One group got powder spray alone sans scraping. Pocket depth, bleeding, and plaque were checked over six months. All care forms brought clear gains in that span. Which added form helps most is still unclear.
pmc-13332494:
Tamar Bigvava and co-authors report a 2026 case of a blood clot forming in the right ventricle after a front-wall heart attack. The pairing is unusual, since such clots usually follow lower-wall attacks or lung embolism. Their patient was a 39-year-old man with chest pain and breathlessness.

Angiography showed a clot-blocked left anterior descending artery in a left-dominant system, treated with a stent. Four days later an ultrasound found the right ventricular clot, and cardiac MRI confirmed it, showing deep damage across the attacked territory including the tips of both ventricles and heavy small-vessel obstruction. Anticoagulation cleared the clot on later imaging, and after episodes of ventricular fibrillation he received a two-chamber defibrillator. The authors credit the wraparound artery anatomy for spreading damage into the right ventricle and stress MRI's value in spotting such complications.
pmc-13332594:
Rachel Mundaden and colleagues test 2026 whether training helps providers offer the full range of emergency birth control in abortion-ban states. After Dobbs, gaps in abortion and contraceptive care widened in states with bans and thin full-scope services. Yet efforts to expand emergency birth control access and provider teaching have stayed limited. The study delivered an evidence-based training to providers at 283 clinics in Texas, Oklahoma, and Indiana between 2022 and 2024.

A total of 507 providers answered online surveys at baseline and three months after training. Surveys covered attitudes, counseling, and stock for levonorgestrel pills, ulipristal acetate, copper devices, and levonorgestrel devices. Changes were assessed with panel models. The work shows whether focused training can widen real access to all emergency birth control methods where abortion care is restricted, not merely knowledge of one pill.
pmc-13332794:
Melina Heine and colleagues examined inflammation-resolving molecules around heart surgery in a 2026 secondary analysis of a prospective study. Atrial fibrillation after surgery is common and tied to inflammation, but whether the body's active clean-up system, the specialized pro-resolving mediators, plays a part was unknown.

The cohort held 319 adults who had cardiac surgery at one center, with resolvin D1 and D2 measured across the operative period and modeled against later fibrillation. Patients who developed the rhythm problem showed higher predicted resolvin D1 levels, with a mean ratio of 1.19, and lower resolvin D2 at 0.80. The D1 link ran stronger in women than men, and women also tended toward a deeper D2 drop, though that pattern missed significance. The authors read the split pattern as a sign the two mediators do different jobs, and that resolution biology differs by sex.
pmc-13333194:
Shunsuke Shiomi and colleagues build a 2026 bio-hybrid micro-swimmer, Chlamylipo, for tiny cargo delivery. Active transport at micro scale is hard because low Reynolds number physics constrains motion. The swimmer pairs the green alga Chlamydomonas reinhardtii, sealed inside a giant liposome, with a way to transmit propulsion force across a closed membrane. Internal encapsulation protects cargo, yet force must cross the membrane for the swimmer to move.

High-speed imaging showed forward swimming with phototactic directional control, driven by periodic membrane deformations and characteristic fluid dynamics. Flow analysis found rapid oscillations at tens of hertz from flagellar beating, overlaid on slower axial migration near four hertz tied to cell rotation. Matching flow signatures appeared in the outside fluid. The work shows a living-cell engine can drive a liposome carrier, a step toward targeted micro-delivery.
pmc-13333294:
Jinwoo Oh and co-authors describe a multimodal dataset in 2026 capturing how beginners teach themselves a basic laparoscopic surgery drill. The peg transfer task, part of the Fundamentals of Laparoscopic Surgery curriculum, asks trainees to move small objects with graspers under camera view, a core test of hand-eye skill.

Nineteen university students practiced on their own in one-hour sessions of 10-minute practice blocks and 2-minute rests. They stopped when they hit the proficiency bar of ten clean trials within 48 s without drops, or after six sessions at most. The final set holds 85 sessions and 1,971 trials. Every trial synchronizes wrist and tool-handle motion sensors, eye tracking, and trainer-box video, with annotations for completion time, dropped objects, and observer comments. The data are freely posted through the Virginia Tech repository for skill analysis research.
pmc-13333394:
Daniela Averaimo and a team worked through a decade of Italian veterinary forensic archives in a 2026 study, trying to give the field the filing system it lacks. Italy's animal health institutes logged forensic cases with ready-made codes only for wild animal deaths and suspected poisonings, leaving everything else as free-text expert opinion.

The team took records from the Abruzzo and Molise institute between 2013 and 2023. They applied a three-step method: analyze the data, have experts label each opinion by forensic topic, then sort diagnoses into categories. Of 1,221 uncoded cases with an expert opinion, 405, or 33.16 percent, qualified as forensic cases and fell into five categories and 19 subcategories. The leading cause of death differed by animal. Pets died mostly of injury, livestock of attack, and wildlife of unlawful killing. Poisonings and road-killed wildlife were left out since they were pre-classified, so the shares describe this leftover group.
pmc-13333594:
Chi-Chieh Lee and Federico Calegari report a 2026 animal study on whether growing more new neurons in the hippocampus can ease Alzheimer's disease. New neuron growth in this brain region supports memory and mood, but it drops sharply as the disease advances.

Working in the dentate gyrus region of 3xTg-AD mice, the team used a lentivirus to raise the cell cycle proteins Cdk4 and CyclinD1, expanding their neural stem cells. Mice with stronger neurogenesis did better on some behavior tests tied to hippocampal function, including the open-field test and the Morris water maze. The results suggest the damaged niche can still respond to stimulation, pointing to neurogenesis as one part of a future combined treatment.
pmc-13335794:
Nan Meng and co-authors quantified a hidden climate bonus from tree planting in China in a 2026 environmental study. New forests stitch isolated patches together, converting former edge forest into interior forest, and that conversion itself stores carbon.

Using several high-resolution remote sensing datasets, the team estimated biomass gains and albedo losses in transformed forests. Planted forests covered 89.6 million hectares by 2015, about 35.5 percent of China's forest area, and had turned 51.8 million hectares of edge into interior. Those transformed forests gained about 1.4 billion tonnes of CO2 equivalent in biomass between roughly 1980 and 2015, though darker canopy warmed the surface enough to offset part of it. Counting both effects clarifies afforestation's true climate ledger.
pmc-13336594:
Zeming Qiu, Xueyan Xia, and Xiancheng Li comment on a study linking heavy metals in urine to overactive bladder. The study used a large United States health survey and tested metals one by one and as mixes. The comment praises the scale of the work. It then raises points that could change how the findings should be read.

First, the bladder outcome rested on just two survey questions. Those questions cover different recall spans, one year and thirty days. Real symptom scales use more items and were not built as yes-or-no tests. Folding the two answers into one score may misclassify people. The comment also says the survey's complex sampling design needs fuller handling. Clearer limits and extra checks, the authors argue, would strengthen the study.
pmc-13336894:
Yajie Shen leads a large 2026 team that sniffs out respiratory infection by odor in mice. Infected breath carries volatile chemicals, but mixtures are faint and vary between animals. Guided by two marker compounds found in infection, they built a sensor array inside ventilated cages that samples once per second.

Over a 7-day infection cycle the system logged 3,628,800 measurements and caught clear odor shifts between infected and healthy groups. Sensor changes appeared at 7–8 hours after infection, and learning models separated the groups firmly by 9 hours in this mouse model. The best internal accuracy reached 99.88% with support from a blinded check group. Continuous smell monitoring could flag outbreaks far earlier.
pmc-13337094:
Yuan Gao and co-authors starve tumors on two fuels at once in a 2026 therapy study. Tumors switch between glucose and fat burning, the Randle cycle, so blocking one path alone rarely works. Their nanogel carries glucose oxidase, an enzyme that drains glucose, and clings inside tumors for long, deep action.

Adding etomoxir, a fat-burning blocker, imposed dual metabolic suppression and raised harmful oxygen species that killed tumor cells in an immune-visible way. The tumor immune setting reprogrammed toward attack. Adding a PD-1 checkpoint drug then achieved complete tumor regression in 60% of animals with 100% of tumor-bearing mice surviving in the reported experiment. Starvation, oxidation, and immunotherapy form one loop.
pmc-13337394:
Siyao Li and co-authors build an ultrasound radiomics model to predict lymph node spread in diabetic thyroid cancer patients in a 2026 study. Knowing spread before surgery shapes the operation, yet standard checks miss cases. The team gathered 203 confirmed patients from three centers and split them into training and two external validation groups.

Features came from contrast ultrasound timing measures around and inside each tumor. A rim of 2 mm around the tumor beat a 1 mm rim for prediction in all cohorts during testing. The combined model reached AUC values of 0.930 in training and 0.907 and 0.865 in the two validation cohorts in the reported analysis, with good calibration. Such preoperative scoring could tailor surgery for a group juggling two diseases.
pmc-13337694:
Johanna Shriver-Halligan reports a 2026 qualitative study with clinicians who counsel people facing infertility. Infertility often brings stress, anxiety, low mood, and trauma symptoms. Expressive therapies are entering counseling, yet music and imagery work had not been studied with this group.

Five clinicians, four women and one man, took part through purposive sampling. Each joined an online session with a guided music and imagery experience plus interviews. Analysis using in vivo coding and photo methods produced clinical and artistic themes. Clinicians described current symptoms and treatments, and reflected on how the arts method deepened their grasp of what clients live through.
pmc-13339494:
Thomas E. Kraft and a large team set a first human dose for a T-cell engager in blood cancer in a 2026 study. Standard minimal-effect dosing can crawl upward for long before benefit appears. Their ex vivo method used fresh patient marrow to judge the starting dose for forimtamig.

Lab dishes used a myeloma cell line and blood cells, while marrow samples came from myeloma donors. Tumor killing was chosen as the guiding signal. The most sensitive marrow sample pointed to a starting dose of 6 micrograms, adopted for the trial as reported. Activity appeared by the second dose level, supporting patient-based dose setting.
pmc-13339694:
