Quanman Hu and a large team study neutrophil self-destruction in viral brain inflammation in a 2026 mouse and patient study. Coxsackievirus A6 can cause neurologic harm in hand, foot, and mouth disease. The caspase and gasdermin pathway that bursts neutrophils and casts DNA nets was the focus.

Ten-day-old normal and gene-deleted mice received a lethal virus dose, with inhibitors and cell removal as added tests. Infection raised neutrophils in brain and blood plus net markers as reported. Blocking the burst pathway or the net enzyme in neutrophils tested cause directly. Blood from patients checked that the same signals appear in human disease.
pmc-13340394:
Fengrui Liu and colleagues tested AI aided surgery planning in 2026 for Oxford partial knee ops, where right implant size shapes results yet planning before surgery is hard. A look back at one centre covered 190 patients and 190 knees treated from February 2022 to January 2024. AI aided planning for 94 knees was weighed against usual sizing during surgery.

Implant size fit and coverage were weighed between groups, and factors linked to coverage were probed. Better planning before surgery could cut op time, improve fit, and reduce repeat ops. The study tests whether AI planning earns a place in routine partial knee replacement.
pmc-13341394:
Joe Hollinghurst and colleagues built heart risk models in 2026 for patients with MASH, a liver condition tied to higher heart disease illness and death. Using UK Clinical Practice Research Datalink data, the team built the first risk models for heart disease in a MASH cohort. Accelerated failure time models were fitted apart for men and women.

Risk factors from the QRisk3 algorithm were used. They were age, deprivation, body mass index, cholesterol ratio, systolic pressure, ethnicity, smoking, family history, diabetes, treated hypertension, rheumatoid arthritis, atrial fibrillation, and kidney disease. The models give doctors a MASH linked tool to gauge heart risk and target prevention.
pmc-13341694:
Vaccine acceptance predicts uptake unevenly across birth regions in Sweden, in a 2026 survey by Mariam Hassan and colleagues. The anonymous cross-sectional questionnaire reached 3,281 people born in Sweden or in Western and non-Western countries, scoring six domains from trust to norms and access.

Acceptance and actual vaccination aligned strongly overall, but the link weakened for non-Western-born respondents. Vaccinated people born in Sweden scored 9.5 points higher on acceptance than unvaccinated peers, versus only 2.8 points among non-Western-born groups. Descriptive norms, what others visibly do, mattered for the Swedish and Western groups. One-size messaging, the data suggest, misses group-specific drivers.
pmc-13342094:
Zhenyu Huang and nine co-authors publish a complete apricot genome in this two thousand twenty-six paper. Apricot is a prized fruit crop, but its genomic tools lagged behind its relatives. The team sequenced the elite cultivar Sungold with four technologies, mixing short, long, and ultra-long reads plus a scaffolding method. The final assembly runs from telomere to telomere with no gaps. Quality scores place it among the best fruit genomes.

All eight centromeres and most telomeres were resolved in full. Such completeness exposes regions that older assemblies missed. Breeders can now hunt trait genes in the full text of the genome. The paper is a resource announcement for the Prunus research community.
pmc-13343894:
Catherine T. Chaton and co-authors study a wall-cutting enzyme of Enterococcus faecalis in 2026, an opportunistic germ behind hard hospital infections. The enzyme, EpaU, sits in the gene cluster that builds the cell's main surface sugar coat, and the team asked what it grips and what changes when it vanishes.

EpaU's binding end latches onto the intact teichoic acid-like decorations of that sugar coat, while the enzyme itself spreads across the cell surface snipping wall mesh during remodeling. Cells missing EpaU resisted ampicillin more and built up the messenger c-di-AMP, which helps govern internal pressure. The findings tie wall sensing to pressure control and hint at new drug angles based on such enzymes.
pmc-13346294:
Li, Peng, and Li pool studies on what predicts full tumor clearance in a harsh breast cancer type in twenty twenty-six. The type lacks three common drug targets, so chemo before surgery is a main plan. Full clearance in the removed tissue bodes well for the patient. The team searched four databases for studies through mid twenty twenty-five.

Thirteen studies were kept, and seven candidate traits were pooled. Early tumor stage, a high growth marker, and a faulty repair gene each raised the odds of full clearance. A blood ratio tied to inflammation raised them most. Age, tumor grade, and node spread did not predict the outcome. The traits can help tailor care before chemo starts.
pmc-13347394:
Emma Dyhr and co-authors build new antibacterial peptides from the TisB toxin and test them alone and with a standard drug, in a study from 2026. Forty-four variants were trimmed, charged, linked, and scanned to map which parts drive killing, with blood cell harm checked alongside strength against six problem bacteria.

Several hits killed Gram-negative species at levels from 2 to 16 micromolar in the reported tests. While red cell bursting stayed near 20 to 30 percent at a far higher test dose. Gram-positive species needed higher doses, yet the striking gain was pairing, where gentle peptide doses cut the azithromycin needed against three Gram-negative species to useful levels. Toxin systems thus offer fresh antibiotic leads.
pmc-13347794:
Yanti Herawati and colleagues test whether massage aids early baby growth. Their study was issued in 2026. It covers babies aged one to three months. Work ran at a midwife practice. The months were February and March 2023. A total of 75 babies took part. Set rules governed who could join. A standard screening questionnaire scored each baby. Scores came before and after massage. Paired tests compared the two rounds.

Babies classed as developing well rose after massage. The share went from 41.3 percent to 61.3 percent. Mean scores rose too. They moved from 7.65 to 8.75 across the span. The shift cleared the set statistical bar. The authors back gentle massage as an early aid. Parents can learn the method at home. The first year of life is the window.
pmc-13348594:
Min-Gi Kwon and co-authors build a two-target antibody that both wakes a vessel receptor and blocks a growth signal, in a 2026 study. Eye diseases with leaky, overgrown vessels need Tie2 activation plus VEGF blocking, and indirect Tie2 help looked too weak. So a matured activating antibody was fused to five blocker modules and the fusions were ranked in vessel cells.

The lead fusion, MT-103, pairs the activator with receptor domains and was tested in two mouse eye models against a standard blocker and a rival two-target drug. Early cell work showed the activator firing Tie2 paths and matching standard care in one model, supporting direct waking plus blocking as a stronger pair.
pmc-13349394:
Jinchen Pan and colleagues build a theory of referee stress. Their interview study was published in 2026. It covers male student basketball referees in China. Twenty-eight referees gave deep interviews. Coding ran in three passes with software help. No new ideas appeared after the 26th talk. Coding yielded 979 points in total. Those points sorted into 53 first groups. Five main pressure families held them all.

Pressures spanned several sources at once. Personal traits formed one source. Crowd and coach relations formed another. Split-second calls added match pressure. Event mishaps added still more strain. Pressures fed each other in a rising loop. Moderate pressure aided learning, though. Coping leaned on self-calming and peer support. Skill growth helped as well. Stronger backing from organisers is urged.
pmc-13349894:
Kiralina Brito-Arancibia and co-authors examined how heavier job demands affect worker satisfaction in a 2026 occupational study. Modern work keeps speeding up, asking staff to do more tasks faster, with more multitasking and less downtime.

Demand growth has both quantity and quality sides, covering workload, time pressure, decisions, and learning. The authors test whether engagement sits between rising demands and satisfaction, carrying part of the effect. Within the job demands-resources model, heavier demands can either drain workers or, with enough support, spur them. Sorting out that pathway helps employers raise performance without quietly burning out their staff.
pmc-13350194:
Pengcheng Zhu and co-authors reviewed in 2026 how tiny drug carriers might rescue immunotherapy for colorectal cancer. Advanced disease responds poorly to surgery, chemotherapy, and radiation, and checkpoint immunotherapy often fails because the tumour surroundings suppress immune attack.

Nanocarriers such as fat bubbles, polymer particles, and metal particles can ferry drugs into tumours, reshape that suppressive setting, and combine with checkpoint drugs, cell therapies, and vaccines. The review pulls together how each carrier type works, where synergy arises, and what blocks clinical use. Smart delivery that wakes the immune system inside the tumour could widen who benefits from immunotherapy.
pmc-13350494:
Devina Ramesh and co-authors summarised the third annual Transplant AI Symposium, held in Toronto in 2026 by the Ajmera Transplant Center and Mayo Clinic. Clinicians, scientists, and trainees met to take stock of artificial intelligence across organ transplantation.

Talks ranged over organ matching, human and AI teamwork, and predicting survival and risk, including digital twin ideas. Speakers agreed AI helps most when tied to a concrete clinical problem, especially with mixed or time-based data. Worries persisted about data quality, fairness, fitting tools into daily workflow, and keeping clinician oversight. The meeting's message was careful testing before trust.
pmc-13350894:
Yuxuan Lin and colleagues engineered a textured implant material in 2026 that both builds bone and fights gum bacteria. The base is a carbon fibre reinforced plastic used for implants, treated in mixed acids to carve a surface of pores dotted with tiny clusters, best at one acid ratio.

On that surface, bone-forming genes switched on through the Hippo pathway, vessel cells migrated and formed tubes better, bone-eating cells were suppressed, and the gum pathogen P. gingivalis colonised poorly. Rat skull defects confirmed faster bone filling. One surface doing three jobs could cut implant failures from both looseness and infection.
pmc-13351094:
Liancheng Zheng and co-authors reviewed exoskeleton robots in a 2026 mini review, tracing their move from rigid frames toward systems integrated with the body. Wearable robots now serve rehabilitation, mobility help, workplace support, and performance boosting.

The review organises the field by drive systems, control strategies, and human-robot interaction, then by how designs have evolved, what blocks deployment, and where research should head. Papers were picked from major databases for relevance and influence. As devices leave the lab for clinics, factories, and homes, the authors argue design must centre the human wearer rather than machine performance alone.
pmc-13351594:
Evgeny B Topolnitskiy and co-authors wrote in 2026 about CT checks of breathing muscle thickness. The focus was myasthenia gravis. In this illness, lung muscle weakness drives risk of crisis and lung failure. Objective structural checks of the breathing muscle remain incompletely standardised. This curbs its clinical use.

Serena Malloggi and colleagues test whether a brief re-read before sleep strengthens memory for prose in 2026. Thirty-four university students studied a short text and recalled it at once, then were split into sleep and wake groups.

pmc-13352394:
Ying Li and Ö Ece Demir-Lira study how parent speech and gesture shape brain synchrony with their child in 2026. pmc-13352494:
Chelsea R. Moore and others studied how single adverse childhood events relate to teenage substance use, in 2026. The team wanted to know which given events still counted once the others were taken into account.

pmc-13354794:
Asma Belbelazi and others showed a new role for PKMYT1 in the timing and truth of chromosome segregation, in 2026. pmc-13355194:
Anni Wu and co-authors followed 3,503 older adults in urban China in a 2026 study of how social frailty, mood, thinking, and body frailty move together over time. pmc-13355394:

pmc-13355694:
Man Luo and colleagues combined deep learning with radiomics to spot glaucoma in highly myopic eyes from fundus photos, in a 2026 study. pmc-13356694:
Qi-Shun Wu and co-authors systematically reviewed in 2026 kidney involvement in antisynthetase syndrome, a rare immune disease marked by antibodies against protein-building enzymes. pmc-13356794:

pmc-13358494:
Michael Mosebetsi Moleka and co-authors report a 2026 study on recovery after keyhole lung surgery. pmc-13358794:

pmc-13358994:
Derya Yenibertiz and Güzide Tomas grade AI chatbots on a lung disease in a 2026 study. Hypersensitivity pneumonitis is a lung disease caused by breathing in substances the immune system reacts to. pmc-13360094:

It may help surgeons plan care without extra invasive tests.
pmc-13360694:
Yilin Jiang and co-authors carried out a 2026 genome-wide study of MYB gene switches in maize. These switches control many plant jobs, from flower and pollen growth to seed sprouting and stress defense. They also read which switches turn on in growing anthers, the pollen-making parts, across several maize lines. That mix pointed to strong candidates for male fertility. Breeders could use the list to improve seed production, since pollen success drives the corn harvest.
pmc-13362394:
Seung Beom Jin and co-authors present a 2026 study on a tool that predicts where a chemical tag called lactylation lands on proteins. Strict checks with no overlap between training and test data held up, so the tool looks fit for real lab use.
pmc-13364394:
Nikolaos Mouziouras and co-workers warn in 2026 that help from a relay station can hurt a multi antenna radio link when the channel facts are off. A relay that reads a weak signal wrong can pass its error on and add noise at the far end. Clean theory hides this flaw.

Their math maps a zone where direct links beat relay help, set by channel doubt and relay slips. A smart switch that mutes weak relays cut error rates in the mid to high signal range. More antennas also made links tougher. The work guides when to trust a relay.
pmc-13364694:

Methavee Poochanasri and co-authors tested a quick body measure for weak muscles in a 2026 study. They worked with 390 older adults who live with type 2 sugar disease. pmc-13372394:
Levin Stolz and colleagues model how light travels through human dentin in a 2026 study. Older models that assumed uniform travel missed that angular effect and misjudged optical properties.

The team built a combined isotropic and anisotropic Monte Carlo model, fitting it to angle-resolved measurements from three human teeth across visible wavelengths. Tubule diameter near 2.25 micrometres and densities from 19,000 to 60,000 per square millimetre were characterised. Ignoring direction-dependent travel caused absorption errors above 40 percent. pmc-13376094:
Abdullah Alghamdi and colleagues identify silenced immune hubs in lung adenocarcinoma in a 2026 study. pmc-13376794:
Rajiv K Bharti and co-authors scored hand use after wrist nerve surgery in a 2026 study. The nerve pinch in view is the most common of its kind, with numb hands, night pain, and weak grip. A short 11-ask form gives a sound score of arm and hand use.

pmc-13378694:
Sion Kim and others review anode-free all-solid-state these units in a 2026 paper. pmc-13379594:

pmc-13383894:

pmc-13385994:

pmc-13386894:

pmc-13388694:

pmc-13389894:

pmc-13390094:

pmc-13390294:

pmc-13390394:

pmc-13392394:

pmc-13395194:

pmc-13396394:

pmc-13396494:

pmc-13397394:

pmc-13398094:

pmc-13400694:

pmc-13401294:

pmc-13401494:

pmc-13401594:

Correcting radar-based rainfall estimates, among other research and operational uses.

pmc-13402594:

pmc-13430194:
Sidsel Armand Larsen and colleagues test, in a 2026 study, a portable brain-wave kit that brings epilepsy testing to people who cannot travel to it. The device itself and its data transfer never failed during the study. Roughly half the referrals gaining a full answer may sound modest, yet the alternative for many residents was no test at all. Equity in diagnostics is the authors' stated goal.
pmc-13430794:

By the access scale, 82.8 percent of households counted as food insecure, a stark share for a conflict-hit district. Aid planners get a measured baseline for targeting food help, and a reminder that conflict, not just harvests, drives hunger here.
pmc-13430894:
Yue Gong and colleagues trace the genes that let a rising Pseudomonas germ shrug off carbapenem drugs, the last-line drugs for tough hospital infections. This germ, clone ST1976, turned up in China with very high drug-proof levels, yet its gene basis was not clear.

ST1976 ranked near the top of drug-proof clones in Henan Province, and its share grew over time. It also carried more drug-proof and harm genes than other top local clones, a red flag for ward teams.
pmc-13431894:
Bouzar and co-authors audit the quality of evidence synthesis itself in this 2026 meta-research study, named FALCON-1. Their subject is systematic reviews and meta-analyses. All were produced by nursing-affiliated institutions in North African countries between 2015 and 2025. This fast-growing literature had never been checked for methodological rigor or research integrity.

pmc-13433394:
Dale Dannefer, Jessica Kelley, and Olugbenga Okunade opened a two-part work in 2026 on what makes human aging stand apart from aging in all other life. Aging marks near every species, from seed change to tooth wear. Human aging adds gears of hold and shift found in no kin kind, the authors argue.

One gear set sits in the body plan: a built-in bend toward open worlds and flex. The twin set sits in how humans meet their world, soaking it in as habit while also building it fresh through craft and dreams. pmc-13433694:
Zoë Wilson and colleagues improve motion correction for FDG PET/CT scans, where breathing movement now limits image quality as scanners sharpen. A sequential cohort of 145 whole-body scans, previously studied for data-driven gating, supplied the comparison. Imaging teams get a data-driven fix for breathing blur in cancer scans.
pmc-13433794:
Aaron J May and a large team charted in 2026 how far the shell proteins of a deadly virus clan can stretch in shape and immune face before kinship breaks. Pure stocks went through trait reads, while mouse shots raised antibodies that hit many clan fusion proteins at once. Cold-scope frames showed what steadies the pre-fusion shape and where shells touch. One branch member's grip head bore a whole extra part on the stock fold. Shared weak spots span both branches.
pmc-13433894:
Vera van der Nulft and co-authors sifted proof in 2026 on talk tools that ready people with dementia and their kin for talks on future care picks. Mind fade shrinks choice power, so talks must start while voice lasts, yet low readiness stalls them. Five data banks faced a search, with a fresh sweep two years on.

Packs that join guided talk with lessons and tools lifted readiness most, though gains wobbled by group and time. Two studies weighed talk craft: guide warmth, timing, steady threads, and ways to draw people in.
pmc-13434594:
Naemeh Yasrebi's team tested in 2026 how heat and catalyst amount shape the cracking of gasoil over a zeolite catalyst called HZSM-5. pmc-13435494:
Martyna E. Lagoda's team interviewed pork producers and vets in 2026 on animal welfare and sustainable production in North America. Welfare upgrades face cost and operational pressure in a volatile pork market, even though good welfare is tied to productivity and long-term viability. Ten people, four managers and six vets from Canada and the United States, described in open interviews how they define welfare, measure it, and weigh it against output.

The pilot maps definitions, on-farm measures, motives, and barriers, aiming to clarify where welfare and business goals align or clash. Industry readers get firsthand stakeholder language rather than survey tallies, useful for shaping workable standards. The small sample limits generalization, so the value lies in themes for larger studies to test.
pmc-13435594:
Mohammad Naim Azimi's team modeled water, sanitation, and hygiene access in 2026 across eight South Asian countries from 2000 to 2024. Safe WASH access still lags for large populations, held back by inequality, weak institutions, and uneven growth. A Bayesian hierarchical model, plus a governance index built from six dimensions by a neural network, weighed structural, demographic, environmental, and institutional drivers.

Urban growth lifted sanitation but strained water, health spending helped across outcomes, schooling improved water access and cut open defecation, and digital tools emerged as a notable driver. pmc-13435994:
Ermias Wabeto Wana and coauthors compare full maternity care chains in two Ethiopian zones in 2026. A survey of 632 women who gave birth in the prior six months ran from March to May 2024. Pastoral and farming districts in Ari and South Omo were set side by side.

Just 7.3 percent of women finished the full chain of care. Pastoral areas scored 7.5 percent, while farming areas scored 7.0 percent, a gap too small to trust. Urban living raised the odds of full care nearly three fold. Say over household resources also raised the odds. Remote services need stronger outreach, the authors conclude.
pmc-13436194:
Sutterer-Verrelli and colleagues surveyed in 2026 the parents of babies who suffered perinatal asphyxia, oxygen loss around birth, and found heavy stress and trauma even where the children developed on track. The study spanned two German university centers and covered children aged one to five and a half. Groups included babies cooled as treatment, babies not cooled, and healthy controls.

Most children scored age-appropriate on development screening in every group. Parents told a different story: both asphyxia groups reported high stress, highest in the cooled group. Birth-related trauma affected nearly nine in ten cooled-group parents and about three quarters of the non-cooled group, against a small share of controls. Only a fifth of non-cooled families felt support was sufficient, and trauma strongly predicted stress. The authors urge structured support for all such families.
pmc-13436494:
Moritz Göbel's team traced in 2026 how a sugar signal called trehalose 6-phosphate, made in plant veins, steers root growth. The signal mirrors carbon status and helps decide growth, branching, and flowering, but its vein-level control of roots was unclear. By raising or lowering the signal only in veins, and by grafting shoots onto roots, the team separated shoot-driven effects from local root effects.

High vein signal shrank roots, cut root sugars and metabolites, and raised shoot-to-root metabolite ratios, while lowering it did the reverse, with shoot veins as the main driver. Root-made signal also tuned local root growth. Plant scientists get a two-level control story: veins balance carbon between shoot and root, shaping the whole root system.
pmc-13437094:
Dalle and colleagues chart fat-like signaling molecules in the muscles of ALS model mice in this 2026 study. Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis wastes muscle, and the endocannabinoid system, which helps regulate muscle maintenance, had never been studied inside ALS muscle. The team compared a fast-twitch leg muscle and a slow-twitch one in female mice before and after symptoms, and checked human ALS muscle data as well.

The fast muscle lost about three-quarters of its mass. The slow muscle shrank only modestly. The lipid upheaval matched that divide. Far more mediators changed in the fast muscle. Anandamide, an endocannabinoid, rose by over a third there, and its receptor nearly doubled, with changes visible before symptoms and mirrored in human samples. Yet a drug blocking the system's breakdown enzyme improved neither movement nor survival.
pmc-13437794:
Hongyun Cai and colleagues pooled Chinese trials of airway clearance techniques, hands-on and device methods helping pneumonia patients cough out the mucus clogging their lungs. The trials covered ordinary, stroke-linked, and severe viral pneumonia, plus patients on breathing machines. Their 2026 review searched five databases through early 2026 and kept eleven randomized trials testing added clearance work against standard care alone.

Patients getting the techniques were judged successfully treated far more often, at odds near four times the control level. Complications dropped sharply too, to a small fraction of the usual rate. Blood oxygen readings improved widely, though results varied a lot between trials. Methods were shaky, follow-up short, and all trials came from one country. They call for large, international trials tracking outcomes patients feel, such as days out of hospital, before the techniques earn a firm place in care.
pmc-13438194:
Kutnár and colleagues test fully automated deep learning planning for lymphoma radiotherapy in this 2026 study. Intensity-modulated treatment shapes radiation around irregular tumors, but planning is slow and hard to standardize, and lymphoma is an especially varied test case across the body. The team replanned a single-institution cohort of 571 patients. The plans became a consistent fifteen-field reference. They then trained a two-stage pipeline. It predicts dose first, then the beam fluence that delivers it.

Variants trained to copy existing plans predicted dose less accurately than the references, while variants trained with a clinically shaped loss produced better target dose distributions. After the final conversion step, every configuration produced machine-deliverable plans, but all had lower target coverage and hotter spots than human-made plans. The authors conclude the approach is feasible and fast, yet currently inferior for this difficult setting.
pmc-13438594:
Denisa Hathazi and a large team grew human brain organoids carrying a famous mitochondrial mutation to watch how the defect injures the cortex. The m.3243A>G change causes most cases of MELAS, a syndrome of brain disease, acid build-up, and stroke-like episodes. Since each cell holds a mix of healthy and mutated mitochondrial DNA, called heteroplasmy, the team could sort effects by how heavy the mix ran.

Their fibers wasted and the cells died, as in a dead patient's tissue. The model copies the architecture of the human cortex and its mitochondrial pathology, which mice could not offer. The authors offer it as a testbed where the vulnerability of projection neurons can be probed and candidate treatments tried before patients.
pmc-13439194:
Jiaqi Wang and colleagues reveal the lopsided build of the corkscrew motor that drives a gum disease bacterium, in structural work published in 2026. Spirochete bacteria swim by spinning hidden flagella wrapped around the cell body, a trick that works well in thick fluids. The team studied Treponema denticola, a mouth bacterium tied to periodontitis. Electron microscopy, tomography, genetics, and protein tests were combined to map the filament in near-atomic detail.

A sugar-coated core protein forms the filament centre, wrapped by an uneven outer sheath. The main sheath protein locks to the core at set contact points, passing force along the filament. Four smaller sheath proteins line the inner curve, letting the filament keep its bend. Breaking that layout weakened force transfer and slowed swimming, showing why the asymmetry matters.
pmc-13439494:
Bengt Gustafsson recounts, in first person, how he and Holger Wigström worked out the device behind Hebbian long-term potentiation in 1985. Their plan dealt with two puzzles of this memory related change at synapses: why change stays with the inputs that fired, and why paired firing is needed. They proposed that calcium entering through NMDA receptor channels, sitting beside plain glutamate receptors, triggers the change. The channels open with voltage, which would explain why paired activity is required.

The account traces the experiments behind the idea. Blocking inhibition unleashed potentiation, and a branch event in the cell matched success. Pairing single synaptic responses with charge pulses shot into the cell later proved the plan. The 2026 essay is a first hand history of a core idea in brain science, told by a participant who calls himself accidental.
pmc-13440094:
Shi Huang's team studied early life and genes in 2026 in the condition, using UK Biobank and West China Hospital data. Cesarean risk was confined to girls developing rhinitis before sixteen, and antibiotic effects persisted for later onset. One gene-drug link reached genome mark, and a multi-gene score tracked risk slightly. Allergy teams get early-life targets for prevention research, not proven causes.
pmc-13440694:

Forum windows burned hotter than baseline periods, with nationalist voices dominating first screens. Exposed teens adapted by limiting expression, shrinking their circles, or going publicly silent. Silence carried the heaviest long-term identity tension, while limited expression carried the least. Peer support softened tension overall, yet managing visibility raised it, and the two forces interacted. Yang frames support as real relief that still cannot cancel harm while participation demands constant self-monitoring.
pmc-13443194:
N. Venkata Lakshmi and colleagues offer a hybrid formula for mean guesses when survey replies go missing in a 2026 paper. Their log-exponential estimator blends side facts and sample size into one frame. Math work derives bias and error marks through a first-order series, with best terms found by error cuts.

Tests assume gaps strike at random, with near-neighbor fills for lost values. Monte Carlo runs and real sets span radiation data, farm labor data, and tool wear with torque reads from upkeep systems. The new formula beat rival estimators on error in those runs, with relative gains shown across sets. Built-in sample size terms steady the guess in small samples. The authors aim the tool at plants that track wear to time repairs.
pmc-13444694:
Xia Yongning and colleagues report a rare giant nerve tumor in a 30-year-old man with neurofibromatosis type 1, a gene disorder that raises tumor risk, published in 2026. The growth sat in his neck and upper chest, wrapped around key blood vessels, and pressed on the nerves of his right arm. His hand had grown weak, with clear muscle loss.

Care mixed three-dimensional imaging, a step to block one artery before surgery, and full removal of the tumor with vessel repair, all while sparing nerve function. He then had radiation treatment and stayed free of regrowth at checks six and twelve months later. The authors offer the case as a guide for like cases, while warning that these tumors often return.
pmc-13446294:
Shohei Okusa and colleagues report a Japanese woman with Parkinson's disease from a PINK1 gene fault, whose pump infusion care was steered by blood drug measures, published in 2026. Her stiffness began at forty, and standard levodopa helped at first, yet wearing-off came by forty-six and jerky movements by forty-nine. She also faced a known tilt toward psychosis with this gene form.

Ten months in, early-morning anxiety and low mood, plus evening visions with a hostile cast, brought her to hospital. pmc-13448494:

A lattice-driven sharpening effect then beat the usual diffraction limit under an ordinary microscope laser at microwatt power. Resolution reached about a tenth of the light's wavelength, five times finer than comparable reported resists under the same light. Both flat and three-dimensional carving modes were demonstrated.
pmc-13448894:

In that newly formed species, the second subgenome's genes lead expression, against what the standard two-step model of related crops predicts. pmc-13449494:

pmc-13449994:

pmc-13450494:

Higher schooling showed the strongest inverse link, with women with higher education averaging far fewer births than women with none. Demographic, economic, reproductive, and geographic factors were tested together in count models. Policy makers gain evidence that schooling and related supports may matter most for fertility change.
pmc-13450594:

Too much heat brought burnt notes back, so the team names a clear best window and a scent panel to judge it.
pmc-13451894:

pmc-13452194:

Trials spanned three crops, four flight heights, and skies from dawn to bright sun. The model's color error fell below a set low mark and beat four rival fix methods. Cutting either input stream hurt the fix, which shows both carry weight. The authors say farm drones can hold true color without a ground target in each frame.
pmc-13452294:

The authors describe this expectation gap as the central result. They call for research on how such mismatched expectations affect care, and on ways to support clearer conversations about functioning.
pmc-13452394:

pmc-13453094:

pmc-13453294:

Ties to anxiety and depression ran weak and in the reverse direction, with heavier gesture attachment in less distressed smokers. In the final model, cigarettes per day was the sole clear predictor of strong gesture attachment. pmc-13453494:

Solvent-to-leaf ratio was the dominant factor, ahead of water content, ultrasound power, and time. The best settings the model picked predicted a yield near forty-six in a hundred. Chemistry calculations showed the solvent grips sugar units more strongly than plain solvents do.
pmc-13453694:

Three vertebrae showed a widened nerve opening, the mark such a tumor leaves in bone.

That count works out near 353 per 100,000 cats, far above the human rate of 0.22 to 0.38 per 100,000 people. pmc-13453994:

pmc-13454294:

Each person performed five set moves, from sit-to-stand to rolling over. The algorithm matched each signal against stored reference patterns and picked the closest match. It named all 118 healthy signals correctly and 136 of 147 signals from the Parkinson group. Most errors involved standing up or sitting down. The authors call the approach workable but say larger checks are still needed.
pmc-13454494:

Their brain waves showed larger later response peaks, a smaller early dip, and stronger theta rhythms. Links between brain areas in the theta band also ran stronger. A stacked learning model fused these measures and separated the two groups well. The authors say temperament leaves a readable signature in brain dynamics, which may refine early risk checks for decline.
pmc-13455194:

pmc-13456594:

The authors call the short course durable and gentle.
pmc-13457194:

pmc-13457394:

pmc-13458094:

pmc-13458294:

pmc-13459094:
Frontiers Editorial Office issued a 2026 retraction of a 2020 article on chitosan and xanthan gum hydrogels proposed as carriers for an antiviral drug. Concerns had been raised about the trustworthiness of the article's figures, including duplicated images in the original paper. A later correction meant to fix those figures drew further questions of its own.

pmc-13459294:

pmc-13459594:

Samples were drawn before surgery, in the weeks after it, and during later surveillance.

The authors argue such monitoring could sharpen risk estimates and catch recurrence sooner.
pmc-13460194:
Yanhui Li and a large team investigated in 2026 the role of LTB4R, a receptor for a fat molecule that drives swelling, in how esophageal squamous cell carcinoma answers radiation. Earlier work showed this receptor is more common in tumor tissue and drives growth and spread, yet its effect on radiation response was untested. Sequencing pointed to a survival pathway, PI3K and AKT, plus cell-death signaling as the route involved. The authors propose LTB4R both as a marker predicting radiation benefit and as a target for overcoming resistance.
pmc-13461394:
Peng Xue and colleagues searched for signs that flag heart muscle injury in patients with bleeding around the brain from a burst aneurysm. Such bleeding can injure the heart through stress hormones and body-wide inflammation, beyond the brain damage itself.

The study reviewed 208 patients admitted between 2022 and 2024, testing clinical, scan, and lab factors in adjusted models. Three factors stood out independently: wider optic nerve sheath on scans, higher procalcitonin, and fluid flooding the lungs from brain injury. The lung complication carried the largest link, with odds about 18.9 times higher when it was present. pmc-13461494:
Ruixue Song and colleagues graded in 2026 the dietary advice for cardiovascular disease circulating in short videos on Douyin, the Chinese counterpart of TikTok. The team also recorded who uploaded each video and how audiences engaged with it.

Professionals made most of the content, and fruits and vegetables appeared in nearly every video, while advice to cut oil and salt showed up in under half. pmc-13461894:
Li and colleagues argued in 2026 that research on elite athlete mental health should widen its lens to diversity and the chance to thrive. For years the field focused on what compromises athletes, stressing personal factors such as athletic identity, while early work dwelt on retirement crises. Mental skills training and motivation theory filled the textbooks, with culture and context treated as extras.

Thriving matters too, yet it is more than positive language or winning. Proactive education should run through the whole career, and culture should sit at the centre from the start, not be added after general models are fixed. The authors say this wider frame fits athletes' lived realities better.
pmc-13462094:

Within one year, hospital-treated fibrillation was most common with ibrutinib, at a little over two percent, and far lower with the newer and comparison drugs. The authors advise closer heart monitoring for patients on ibrutinib.
pmc-13462194:
Anna Immerz and Franka Zebe-Sheng analysed how singers and pianists in classical song duos breathe together during performance. In a Lied duo, voice and piano interweave as equal partners, so timing and phrasing must be closely coordinated.

Across 282 breaths, partners synced most tightly at the start of musical phrases, less so mid-phrase. Pianists began inhaling earlier than singers, anticipating the vocal line rather than following it. Breathing adjusted to both the partner and the song's structure, not to the singer's needs alone. pmc-13463094:

pmc-13463494:

pmc-13463694:

pmc-13463994:
Zhang and colleagues tested in 2026 whether low-temperature plasma can kill Alternaria, a fungus that rots stored European plums. Plasma is a stream of energized gas that stays near room temperature. Chemical fungicides leave residues and breed resistance, so a clean physical option is in demand. The team exposed the fungus to plasma at rising doses and probed how it died.

Growth and spore sprouting fell as dose rose, and at the strongest setting tested, growth stopped fully and nearly all spores failed to sprout. pmc-13464194:

pmc-13464394:

pmc-13464794:

pmc-13464994:

pmc-13465394:

pmc-13465494:

pmc-13465894:

pmc-13466194:

pmc-13466294:

pmc-13466494:

pmc-13466594:

The review graded how well programs located tumors and separated cancer from non-cancer, and judged bias risk and study design. pmc-13466894:

pmc-13466994:

pmc-13468594:

pmc-13468794:

pmc-13468894:

pmc-13469394:

Its average error fell by roughly thirteen percent on one common measure.
pmc-13469494:

pmc-13469694:

pmc-13470894:
Junhao Zhang and colleagues present a review, published in 2026. It covers how plants adapt to low soil phosphorus. Phosphorus is a nutrient essential for growth. pmc-13471294:

pmc-13471794:

pmc-13472794:

pmc-13472894:

pmc-13473094:

pmc-13473494:
