pmc-13473594:
Song Xiaoyu proposed in 2026 a game-theoretic model for governing disinformation on social media, built on how people actually weigh gains and losses. Viral falsehoods threaten public opinion and social stability, yet traditional models assume fully rational actors and miss loss aversion, the fear of losses more than equal gains. They also miss diminishing sensitivity to larger stakes. The model pits three boundedly rational players against each other: regulators, platforms, and self-media operators who create content.

By adding a prospect-theoretic value function, the author derives the conditions under which the system settles into its ideal cooperative state. Regulators would disclose truthfully, platforms would moderate proactively, and creators would verify before publishing. Simulations show that initial willingness to cooperate, reward and penalty strength, and loss aversion all steer whether the system converges to cooperation or drifts away. The findings translate into policy guidance for curbing disinformation without goodwill alone.
pmc-13474694:
Zhang and co-authors followed 30,847 occupational health records from two Fujian petrochemical plants across 2013 to 2021, testing whether working in heat distorts blood lipids. Their 2026 longitudinal study modeled dyslipidemia against heat exposure alone and alongside co-exposures such as gasoline vapor and hydrogen sulfide.

Single-exposure models paradoxically linked heat to lower lipid risk, which the authors attribute to the healthy worker effect, the fittest workers tolerating hot jobs longest. Once gasoline entered the model, heat flipped to harm: an incidence rate ratio of 1.267 for high total cholesterol, rising to 1.324 alongside hydrogen sulfide exposure. The signal concentrated in women, whose ratios hit 2.240 and 2.347 in the two adjusted models, and in workers aged 35 and over. The authors label the interaction exploratory, not proven.
pmc-13474894:
Stephen Ream, Laura Schoeneberg, and Wilson King describe in 2026 a newborn heart case where one scan set guided a hard surgery choice. The baby had an unbalanced shared valve canal favoring the right side, plus a narrowed aorta. Echo scans could not size the left heart well enough to pick between a two-pump or one-pump repair path. A short magnetic scan with flow mapping filled the gap.

The single data set gave firm chamber volumes and valve sizes for the team. Those numbers supported a one-pump staged path, which succeeded. Flow mapping can answer several planning questions from one session, sparing long scans in fragile newborns. The case adds weight to flow-first planning for complex heart births.
pmc-13476994:
Hironobu Sakurai and co-authors compare surgery results in 2026 for severe versus massive or torrential tricuspid valve leakage. A total of 164 patients with symptoms had valve surgery from 2010 to 2024, alone or with other procedures. Repair was used more often in the severe group than in the extreme group. Follow-up ran a mean of just over four and a half years.

Hospital death stayed low in both groups, and leak grades improved alike after surgery. Five-year survival also matched closely between groups. Better heart pump scores and kidney function each guarded against death or heart failure return. Starting leak grade alone did not drive outcomes.
pmc-13477094:
Sadia Tasnim and co-authors build and validate a low-cost trainer in 2026 for Dor fundoplication, a wrap surgery for reflux. Felt layers mimic the lower food pipe, upper stomach, and diaphragm opening at true scale. Ten expert surgeons scored realism across six domains. Fifty-six trainees then performed the wrap before and after a teaching video.

Expert medians hit the validity bar on every domain, led by relevance and task fidelity. Senior trainees beat juniors on both attempts, which supports skill validity. Confidence rose on the second try across all trainees. A cheap felt model can credibly teach a complex wrap.
pmc-13477294:
In Tae Jin and colleagues present a 2026 UK Biobank study on how much blood pressure changes between two readings taken minutes apart at one visit. Participants had no history of high blood pressure at the start. The size of the change between the two seated readings placed each person into one of four groups.

Larger within-visit changes went together with higher average pressure and more new cases of high blood pressure over time. Death and major heart events also rose step by step across the groups, even after other risk factors were considered. The highest group faced modestly higher risks of death, heart attack, stroke, and heart failure than the lowest. The authors suggest this simple measure could help flag adults who need closer follow-up.
pmc-13478594:
Villaseñor and co-authors scanned rat brains in 2026 to test whether advanced diffusion MRI can reveal the fine disorganization of cortical dysplasia, a malformation where cortex layers form wrongly. They imaged 32 animals, 16 with the malformation and 16 controls, at four ages from 30 to 150 days after birth. Diffusion signals were split by fiber direction relative to the cortical surface, separating fibers running across layers from those running along them.

Affected animals showed diffusion abnormalities in both the radial and tangential fiber components, concentrated in the deeper cortical layers of the brain. Those imaging changes matched what tissue examination shows in this model, namely jumbled neurons and fibers in the same deep zones. Because the method is non-invasive, the authors argue it could track cortical development and disease in living subjects where biopsy is impossible, extending toward clinical study of such malformations.
pmc-13482094:
Gentile and colleagues tackle a data quality problem in 2026 for chest-worn light loggers, the sensors that record how much light a person actually gets each day. Light steers the body clock, but readings are worthless whenever the device sits in a drawer. The team taught a model to tell wearing from non-wearing using movement, orientation, light, and time of day. Four testers generated training data under set wear and non-wear conditions.

The best model separated wear, non-wear, and nighttime placement with 0.95 accuracy in training and kept 0.76 accuracy on fresh data from the same testers. Applied to 20 young migraine patients wearing the logger for a week, it found 92.1 percent of days and 77.9 percent of nights met an 80 percent proper-use bar. The team also set the indoor-outdoor brightness split at 442 lux, far below the traditional 1,000 lux bright-light cutoff.
pmc-13482994:
Yu Chen and co-authors describe a 2026 nano-delivery study for a gardenia compound with antidepressant promise. Geniposide protects brain cells yet reaches the hippocampus poorly on its own. The team loaded it into bubbles shed by star-shaped brain support cells and tagged the bubbles with a nucleic acid guide that homes to the hippocampus, then dosed mice under chronic stress.

Treated mice moved more and gave up less in swim-style tests that gauge despair-like behaviour. Gene scans pointed to one switch: the treatment silenced a stress-raised repressor, which freed a hormone receiver gene, and its downstream signal chain lit back up. Brain checks showed less inflammation, fewer dying neurons, and healthier contact points between cells. The work names a fresh target pair for depression drugs, pending proof beyond mice.
pmc-13483194:
Yuan and co-authors built a scoring chart to predict which dialysis patients will develop headaches during treatment. Such headaches can force sessions to stop early and make patients dread returning. Their 2026 study reviewed 289 kidney-failure patients on regular hemodialysis at one Chinese hospital, splitting them into a group for building the model and a smaller group for checking it. Two selection methods narrowed dozens of candidate clues down to six.

The final predictors were sex, age, weight, pulse pressure change, and blood sodium and phosphorus levels. The chart discriminated well, scoring high on accuracy tests in both the building group and the check group of patients. Its risk estimates also matched observed headache rates closely. Yuan says the tool can flag vulnerable patients early, though hospitals elsewhere should validate it before relying on it.
pmc-13483494:
Dong Zhao and co-authors describe a 2026 test of a safer saliva collection kit that never asks users to blow into a tube. Spit samples give easy, painless DNA, yet open blowing raises infection risk for staff and users. Their closed-chamber kit gathers saliva without blowing, and the team benchmarked it against commercial blowing kits.

Collection speed matched the commercial gear. DNA yield after six months on the shelf also matched, and samples held a full year still gave clean genetic reads in melt-curve tests. A stress test with tiny DNA amounts still typed samples correctly. Spit and blood pairs from the same people passed chip-based quality checks side by side. The sealed design offers clinics a safer route to the same genetic answers.
pmc-13483594:
Chenjun Zheng leads a 2026 multicenter review of children who develop a jerky movement disorder alongside the nerve tumor neuroblastoma. Nine Chinese centers contributed 39 cases seen between January 2015 and January 2025. The syndrome, marked by rapid eye movements and muscle jerks, can leave lasting developmental problems even when the tumor itself is low risk.

Median age at onset was 22 months, and most tumors sat in the retroperitoneum, the space behind the abdomen. Every followed child improved and survived, yet 43.2 percent kept neurological after-effects at follow-up. Starting treatment more than 30 days after onset and later relapse each raised the odds of lasting problems sharply. Early combined immune therapy is highlighted as a factor worth urgent attention.
pmc-13486094:
İlkan Özkan prints plastic loaded with bismuth oxide particles and grades the result as a combined germ-fighting, radiation-blocking surface. Published in 2026, the stereolithography work cures a commercial resin layer by layer at 50-micrometer steps with particle loadings of 1, 3, and 5 percent by weight. Microscopy checks spread, while standard tests cover bacteria, electrical resistance, and shielding.

Particles spread well at low loadings yet clumped at higher loadings as settling took hold during printing. Every loaded surface cut both test bacteria by over 99 percent within a day. Electrical resistance stayed very high, confirming strong insulation, while electromagnetic shielding in the tested band stayed weak. Calculated radiation shielding improved steadily with loading. Dual-use panels for hospitals and laboratories are the natural application.
pmc-13486494:
Hashiramoto and colleagues tested whether an ultrasound check before forceps delivery makes the procedure safer for mothers and babies. Forceps can rescue a stalled labor, but poorly judged attempts cause tears and newborn injury. Their 2026 study at a Japanese center compared deliveries with and without a transperineal ultrasound exam, which pictures the baby's head position through the perineum. It then matched 216 similar cases for fair comparison.

The combined rate of bad maternal outcomes was about half in the ultrasound group, with a relative risk figure near one half of the comparison group's rate. Newborn outcomes improved by a similar margin in the matched analysis. The gain came mainly from fewer difficult deliveries needing three or more pulls. Roughly nine mothers needed the scan to prevent one bad maternal outcome. Hashiramoto urges wider trials on major complications.
pmc-13486794:
Tayeh and colleagues reported two patients whose repaired abdominal aortic aneurysms sprang a hidden leak years later through a tear in the graft fabric itself. The repair, called EVAR, lines the weakened aorta with a fabric stent, and this leak type, IIIb, is rare but can be fatal. Their 2026 case report describes leaks surfacing 60 and 48 months after implantation of two different commercial grafts.

Both leaks resisted easy diagnosis because routine imaging has limited sensitivity for tiny fabric defects. Warning signs included a dense area on scans and a slowly enlarging aneurysm sac, even without a visible leak channel. Open surgical repair remained the definitive fix once the problem was recognized. Tayeh urges lifelong surveillance after EVAR, since no device is immune to late fabric failure and early action prevents rupture.
pmc-13490494:
Huang and co-authors simulated how heavy ions in space radiation shred DNA, building a database for mission planners who cannot run enough experiments. Astronauts beyond Earth's magnetic shield face high-charge, high-energy particles from hydrogen to iron. Their 2026 study ran track-structure model runs with the PARTRAC code across ions and energies up to the giga-electron-volt range, benchmarking against stopping power data and lab readings on human cells.

The model runs matched experimental double-strand break yields where readings exist and extended them to untested ion-energy combinations. Apparent disagreements between experiments were traced to detection limits and analysis choices in the lab methods themselves. Denser ionization tracks produced more clustered, hard-to-repair lesions and streak-like damage foci along each particle's path. Huang presents the database as reference material for estimating astronaut cancer risk.
pmc-13490594:
He and colleagues rebuilt the map of China's underground heat by predicting surface heat flow with machine learning and modeling how rock radioactivity adds heat layer by layer. Deep temperatures guide geothermal energy prospecting, but boreholes are sparse across much of China. Their 2026 study computed temperature profiles from three to ten kilometers deep on a one-dimensional conduction model fed by the improved heat-flow map.

Modeled temperatures matched borehole observations well and revealed broad zones hotter than one hundred fifty degrees in three major geological regions named by the authors. A derived gradient map highlighted eight favorable geothermal belts combining steep gradients with deep heat suitable for engineered geothermal systems. The layered radioactivity treatment beat the older habit of using one average value for the whole crust. He offers the framework for prospecting in data-sparse regions worldwide.
pmc-13491094:
Kalra and a dozen heart specialists reviewed in 2026 why South Asians face heart artery disease early and in high numbers, and how scans can catch it sooner. Standard risk scores often rate these patients too low. South Asians grow artery plaque sooner, carry more of it, and show more risky plaque traits, even when a calcium scan still reads zero or low.

Calcium scoring, a quick scan for hardened plaque, sorts risk in South Asians about as well as in other groups. For younger patients with no hard plaque yet, the authors back a fuller scan called coronary CTA for select high risk cases. That scan can show soft plaque and, with new computer tools, gauge plaque volume and the fat around the vessel. Such detail can trigger strong preventive therapy years before symptoms would.
pmc-13491694:
Abdul-Ganiu Zakaria, Shamsu-Deen Ziblim, and Yakubu Amadu model in 2026 how weather patterns relate to malaria illness in Tamale, a metropolitan area of northern Ghana. Seasonal outbreaks strain clinics there, but the separate roles of temperature, rainfall, and humidity over different time horizons were unclear. Monthly records from January 2014 through December 2020 supplied eighty-four observations for a time series analysis.

The model confirmed a stable long-run link between each weather variable and malaria rates. In the short run, rises in humidity, temperature, and rainfall each came with more malaria. Over the long run the temperature effect flipped, with each added degree tied to about a third of a case fewer per thousand residents. The authors back climate-informed early warning systems built for northern Ghana.
pmc-13491794:
Ashley Lacombe-Duncan and five colleagues survey in 2026 the training primary care providers have for sexually transmitted infection testing with transgender and gender diverse patients. These patients face high infection rates and stigma in clinics, so knowledgeable front-line care matters. Fifty doctors, nurse practitioners, and physician assistants completed questionnaires, and eight sat for interviews during 2024 and 2025.

Nearly half reported five hours or less of training on transgender health topics in total. Fewer than half knew the national testing guidance, and the most requested future topics were taking a respectful sexual history, basic transgender care, and screening rules. More training hours and larger transgender patient panels each predicted stronger self-rated competence. Interviewees described guessing when guidelines ignored their patients, which the authors say education must fix.
pmc-13493794:
Hyeong-Geol Shin and others separate iron-related magnetic signals from other sources in Parkinson disease brains using deep learning. In 2026, the imaging study scans twenty-five patients and twenty-six matched controls at three tesla, applying an AI-assisted susceptibility separation method. Standard iron tests mix paramagnetic iron with diamagnetic tissue such as myelin, blurring interpretation.

The separated iron component rose in the dorsal premotor cortex and in the substantia nigra pars compacta, changes missed by established methods, and premotor iron tracked disease duration. AI preprocessing performed no worse than optimization-based separation for distinguishing patients from controls. The method sharpens iron as a marker for advance and treatment studies.
pmc-13493894:
Tianyuan Zhang and others develop a nanopore reading workflow that captures full-length long non-coding RNAs, including forms without poly(A) tails. In 2026, the method depletes ribosomal RNA and sequences complete transcripts from yeast under glucose and ethanol states, comparing nanopore results with Illumina short reads. Short reads and poly(A) selection routinely miss many such isoforms.

Nanopore reading reached high rightness and recovered far more long non-coding RNAs than Illumina, 260 versus 51, including many more intergenic forms, likely because low-abundance transcripts resist reconstruction from fragments. Levels profiles agreed well within each platform and moderately across platforms. Team studying gene control gain a workflow for isoform-resolved discovery.
pmc-13494094:
Aleix Sala-Vila and colleagues examine, in a 2026 cohort report, whether a fat made in the body tracks with how the brain uses sugar. The fat, palmitoleic acid, rises when people eat more energy than they need, and high levels have been tied to heart risk and lower brain fuel use. The team worked with the PESA study of middle-aged adults who show early artery disease but no symptoms.

Among 461 people, higher levels of the fat in red blood cells went with lower sugar uptake across much of the brain on PET scans, even after heart risk factors were counted. People whose levels stayed high lost more brain sugar uptake over about five years than those whose levels stayed low. Levels were also higher in people who drank more alcohol, and the fat partly explained a link between drinking and later fuel loss in one brain area.
pmc-13494294:
Juan Carlos Jimeno Sandoval and colleagues describe, in a 2026 case series, surgery for cats whose gut ulcers broke through the wall after recent pain-drug or steroid use. Such perforations are rare in cats and carry high risk. The team reviewed records from five UK referral hospitals between 2009 and 2024 and found ten cats that had surgery within two weeks of taking these drugs.

The break sat most often in the first part of the small bowel, with the stomach next. Surgeons used varied repairs, from simple closure to removing a gut segment or part of the stomach. All ten cats lived through surgery, and nine left the hospital; one later died of sepsis and one of renewed ulcer disease. Half the cats were still alive at the close of follow-up. The authors read the outcome as favorable for a grave condition, given prompt surgical repair.
pmc-13495294:
Wangwang Liu and colleagues assess, in a 2026 study, digital slides in residency training for clinical pathology at a Chinese teaching hospital. Digital slides, scanned images of tissue, are spreading into teaching and testing, and the team asked whether they change scores or how trainees learn. They compared exam results from glass slide years with digital slide years for 64 residents.

Scores matched closely between the two formats, and the format itself showed no tie to scores once training year and schooling were counted. Those two factors did matter. A wider survey found two thirds of residents used digital slides, mostly for teaching and exams. Junior residents leaned on the tools most for speed in diagnosis, a pattern the authors tentatively name novice tool dependence. They read digital slides as a sound swap for glass, with a watch kept on how beginners use them.
pmc-13495394:
Ahmed Adel Mohamed leads a large team pooling, in a 2026 review and meta-analysis, trials of imaging-guided versus angiography-guided stent placement in patients with disease in several heart arteries. Standard angiography shows the artery outline but little of wall or plaque. Ultrasound or light imaging from inside the vessel can guide the work more finely, yet its worth in this complex group was unsettled.

Five randomized trials with 3,023 patients qualified. Imaging guidance cut major adverse heart events by over forty percent against angiography alone. Each imaging type helped on its own, and a side comparison found no clear gap between ultrasound and light guidance. A sequential analysis judged the pooled result firm rather than flimsy. The authors back imaging guidance for multi-vessel stent work, while noting the trial count is small.
pmc-13499294:
Majid Reza Farrokhi, Gholamreza Vadiee, and Roghayeh Nematollahi map in 2026 new technologies entering interventional pain care, where procedures target nerves and joints to relieve chronic pain. Digital and bioelectronic tools are arriving fast, yet their proven roles remain unclear. Following standard scoping methods, the team searched five databases up to the start of 2026 and sorted the literature by technology type, clinical use, and reported outcomes.

Four themes organised the field. Computer models that blend many data types aim to pick patients better and support decisions, while closed-loop nerve stimulation adjusts dose from recorded nerve signals. Computer guidance also assists ultrasound-led procedures, and wearables with remote monitoring support long-term follow-up. Early results look promising, though most studies were small, used varied outcome measures, and lacked outside validation, so the authors call for larger multi-centre work.
pmc-13499494:
B Vais and colleagues report in 2026 a case of Sweet syndrome, a rare inflammatory skin disorder, arising after cosmetic face surgery. The syndrome brings fever, raised white cell counts, and painful red-violet plaques packed with a type of white blood cell in the skin. Cases after surgery exist for other operations, yet none had been described after aesthetic procedures, according to the authors.

Their patient was a 60-year-old woman who developed the syndrome after a face and neck lift combined with eyelid surgery and fat transfer to the lower eyelids. Treatment with systemic corticosteroid drugs, which calm inflammation, led to a favourable outcome. The authors stress early recognition, since mistaking the plaques for infection or surgical complications could push patients toward needless further surgery.
pmc-13499594:
Pravendra Singh and colleagues present in 2026 a rare bone tumour case where a growth in the smaller forearm bone spread into its neighbour. Giant cell tumour is benign yet aggressive, usually arising near the knee or wrist end of the larger forearm bone. Involvement of the distal ulna, the wrist end of the smaller bone, is uncommon, and direct spread to the radius is rarer still.

Their patient, a right-handed 23-year-old, had four months of worsening wrist pain and swelling. Imaging showed an expanding hollow lesion with thinned bone walls, and a needle biopsy confirmed the tumour at an advanced local grade. Surgeons removed the bone segment in one block and, finding a small matching lesion on the facing radius surface, cut it out with wide margins; lab tests confirmed the same tumour. At twelve months he had full wrist movement, good grip, and no return of disease.
pmc-13500694:
Luca Quattrocchi and colleagues uncover in 2026 a two-part code that decides which small RNA messages liver cancer cells pack into the tiny vesicles they ship to neighbours. Vesicle cargo can reprogram healthy cells toward cancer-like behaviour, yet the sorting rules were murky. Their work centres on a binding protein, SYNCRIP, and a chemical tag placed on RNA by an enzyme called METTL3. The team tested whether the tag must be present for the protein to grab specific messages in hepatocellular carcinoma cells.

The methylation tag proved necessary for efficient binding and loading in the reported experiments. Silencing the binding protein reshaped vesicle cargo and blunted the vesicles' power to push healthy liver cells toward a mobile, invasive state. Removing the tagging enzyme hit even harder, placing methylation upstream as the master switch. Interrupting this partnership emerges as a candidate way to jam tumour communication and slow spread.
pmc-13500994:
Nadia Siddiq and a team of co-authors report a stress heart condition after surgery, in a case report dated twenty twenty-six. The patient was a young woman who developed Takotsubo cardiomyopathy after an operation. In this state, hard physical stress stuns the heart's main pumping chamber.

The case shows a split in how the heart heals. Muscle recovery can come first, while the heart's electrical tracing stays abnormal. That gap can mislead doctors who judge progress by one sign alone. The authors urge early spotting and close watch to avoid wrong labels and guide care.
pmc-13501294:
Choi and colleagues created RECoDe, the first dataset for extracting diet-disease relationships from research text, in a 2026 study from the CoDiet consortium. Reviews of diet and non-communicable disease evidence are slow because the knowledge sits in plain prose. The dataset contains more than five thousand human-annotated examples spanning many link types, with negative findings too, each checked by up to five people.

Choi benchmarked several language models on the dataset and found a locally run open-weight language model performed best. It reached accuracy on the simpler two-way task and moderate scores on the full multi-class task, using a layered prompting approach with a built-in reflection step. their paired framework combined sentence-level extracts into whole-paper and cross-study summaries. Their combined effect numbers matched diet facts, making the resource a foundation for automated synthesis in nutrition science.
pmc-13501794:
Shiyuan Yin leads a five-author team reporting a 2026 sixteen-year cohort study of mesothelioma at a major provincial referral centre in China. Records ran from 2009 to 2025: 128 cases were identified, and 93 met strict tissue-diagnosis criteria for analysis. The team compared sex balance, tumour site, diagnosis age, and survival against published cohorts from the United States, Europe, and Japan.

The Chinese cohort broke the Western pattern. Men and women appeared in nearly equal numbers, unlike the strong male predominance abroad, and women were well represented in both chest and abdominal forms. Peritoneal disease made up 33.3 percent of cases, higher than global norms, and patients were diagnosed younger than American counterparts. Median progression-free survival was 10 months and overall survival 16 months, with women who had peritoneal disease faring notably better. Only 7.5 percent had documented asbestos exposure, hinting at other environmental or genetic drivers.
pmc-13502594:
Zhiqiang Xie leads a fifteen-author team reporting a 2026 study of prodrugs designed to switch on STING. That innate immune alarm detects DNA and can be harnessed against tumours. Their carriers are deoxyribose cyclic dinucleotides fitted with esterase masks. Such masks create chiral phosphorus centres, and chirality had never been compared. The team separated three diastereoisomers of an alkyne-tagged prodrug and measured stability, cell entry, and activity head to head.

One shape won everywhere. The (Rp,Rp) form activated STING in THP1 cells at an EC50 of 1.7 nanomolar on the reported assay, with a longer pulse than its siblings. In mice it beat the unmasked compound and the benchmark agonist ADU-S100. Given intravenously against CT26 colon tumours it produced a 90 percent response rate, extended survival, and left immune memory against the tumour. Chirality, the authors conclude, is a design variable STING drug makers ignore at their cost.
pmc-13502894:
McKay and colleagues studied what drives suicidal thinking and self-harm in young people judged at high risk of psychosis, using data from an Australian early-intervention trial. Their 2026 study covers 342 young people around eighteen years old. They were assessed for psychosis risk symptoms, suicidal ideation and self-harm, daily functioning, depression severity, and psychiatric diagnoses through structured interviews.

McKay found more than three quarters of the young people reported suicidal thoughts or self-harm, a high burden. Suicidal thinking rose with the severity of milder psychotic symptoms in checks. When all measured factors competed in adjusted models, only depression survived as the linked factor, mainly moderate to severe and ongoing depression. The authors conclude that depression severity should anchor suicide care inside high-risk services, rather than risk features alone. They call for research on how depression and suicidal thinking drive each other in this group.
pmc-13503494:
Xavier Hernández-Yagüe and co-authors report a 2026 study of liver harm after surgery for colorectal cancer that has spread to the liver. They looked for signs that predict sinus injury in the liver and early high pressure in the portal vein. Both problems can follow drug treatment given before the operation.

The team reviewed 108 patients who had at least four rounds of pre-surgery drugs plus targeted therapy. Moderate to severe sinus injury showed up in about one in four patients. Drugs that block blood vessel growth lowered the risk, while a prior step to block portal flow raised it. A large liver removal was the main driver of early portal pressure. Neither problem changed death rates or later survival.
pmc-13503694:
Recep Selcuk Eyceyurt and six colleagues compare two wire types for fixing a broken elbow bone, in a 2026 lab study. The break sits at the tip of the ulna, where the arm muscle pulls hard. A standard repair threads pins and a figure-of-eight band across the break to hold it shut.

Sixty fake ulna bones were cut to mimic the break and fixed in six ways, pairing cable or steel wire with three pin styles. A machine pulled each repair as the arm muscle would, and the force at two and three millimeters of gap was logged. All six repairs held about the same force. The authors note the test used one steady pull, so it says little about wear over time or real healing.
pmc-13505694:
Muhammad Imran Rameel and co-authors report a fast way to make Ti3C2Tx MXene, a flaky two-dimensional material prized for conductivity and surface chemistry. Standard routes can take up to two days and often give low yields. Their method etches and separates the layers inside one sealed heated vessel, finishing in six hours at ninety degrees.

A mild mix of hydrochloric acid and lithium fluoride does the etching, while lithium chloride slips between layers during the same step and loosens them. The yield of separated nanosheets reached about seventy-four percent, with single flakes roughly a nanometre thick. Checks by diffraction and spectroscopy confirmed clean aluminium removal and a surface carrying chlorine, fluorine, and oxygen groups. The product conducted electricity very well. The authors present the single-step route as a practical path toward making MXenes at commercial scale.
pmc-13507094:
Fenghou Yuan and colleagues take, in 2026 work, design cues from the skin of the Asian corn borer caterpillar for flexible impact-proof materials. The skin must absorb hits while the insect tunnels, yet stay soft. Protein tests found two abundant skin proteins that form a sheet-rich layer on chitin scaffolds, the fibrous base of insect skin.

That layer soaks up energy as hydrogen bonds break and protein shapes shift under stress, then recover. Lab tools confirmed the bond patterns behind the effect. A chitin and protein gel built on this plan reached high energy uptake, and its stiffness could be tuned by a chemical step. Fragile goods and soft devices could gain light protection.
pmc-13507194:
Jamie Kweon leads a 2026 pilot study of how magnetic brain stimulation reshapes brain circuits, testing two rival explanations in six healthy adults. The treatment, approved for depression, uses ten pulses per second over the motor cortex. Each volunteer completed four drug visits a week apart, with brain responses and a timed button task measured before and after.

A drug that boosts NMDA receptors, key gates for learning-like change, strengthened stimulation effects versus placebo. Adding a blocker erased that boost, which points to NMDA-driven change as the main route. A calming GABA drug instead lowered responses after stimulation. GABA reduction alone does not explain the effect. Larger trials can now build on a clear mechanism.
pmc-13507294:
Zihao Tian leads a 2026 team that models the daily rhythm of staying home across more than 200,000 United States census block groups. Mobility research usually tracks movement, while the timing of dwelling, the other half of daily life, stays unmeasured. Their STASIS model sums up each area's daily presence pulse with three numbers: swing size, peak timing, and baseline level.

Majority-Black block groups showed smaller daily swings, later activity peaks, and lower home-presence baselines than majority-White and majority-Hispanic areas. A stability index tied timing irregularity to local economic precarity. Pandemic years acted as a stress test confirming uneven rhythm stability. Time itself emerges as a dimension of structural inequality.
pmc-13507794:
Melissa Rowe and six co-authors test whether telomere length, the size of the caps on chromosome ends, limits blood stem cell recovery in mice, in 2026 work. Lab mice normally carry much longer telomeres than people do. The team used a strain with one small change in a telomere gene that gives mice human-length caps. At rest, these mice made blood normally. Problems appeared only when their marrow was pushed hard.

Repeated drug treatment and marrow transplants drained the pool of early blood cells far more in these mice than in normal mice. Their stressed cells also showed more very short telomeres, more DNA damage marks, and more signs of cell death. The results imply that even normal human telomere length sets a ceiling on marrow reserve. That insight may help explain why some people's marrow fails under strain.
pmc-13508194:
Haichen Chen and seven co-authors report an improved operation for penoscrotal transposition, a birth defect where the scrotum sits in an abnormal position, in 2026 work. Older methods could cause heavy trauma, poor blood flow, or weak cosmetic results. Their method, used at their center since 2018, lifts the penis upward through a small cut circle inside a larger marked one. The team reviewed 35 patients treated between 2018 and 2023, most with partial and a few with complete forms.

Full correction was achieved in 33 of the 35 cases. Operations for the defect alone took about 70 minutes on average, and follow-up ran just over a year. Problems were few: one case of partial skin loss at the base and two cases of thick scars, all later resolved. Caregivers reported high satisfaction with appearance after surgery. The authors present the method as a safer, cleaner option for this repair.
pmc-13508394:
Peng Wang and seven co-authors trace why thin air saps endurance, pinning much of the effect on a metabolic switch in muscle, in 2026 mouse work. Mice breathed low-oxygen air matching about 4,500 meters of altitude for up to three days. Endurance and strength tests ran at set times, while gene and chemistry readings tracked muscle change. Endurance crashed hardest at twelve hours, then partly recovered by three days. Gene readings showed a sharp rise in a switch called PDK4 at the twelve-hour mark.

That switch blocks a step that feeds sugar fuel into the cell's power pathway. Blocking the switch two ways, with a drug and with a gene-silencing virus, restored endurance under low oxygen. The authors argue the body overshoots a fuel shift early in altitude exposure. Their mechanism could guide diet or drug strategies for people working and competing at height.
pmc-13509394:
Elizabeth Biggs, Erin Turner, and Shana Lee report a 2026 study of training for educators who support young children with autism who speak very little. Three children aged four to eight took part, each paired with one educator from their own setting. The training taught a play-based approach where adults follow the child's lead and support communication with a speech device or similar aid during play.

Training and coaching raised how faithfully educators used the approach during play sessions. The children's communication showed hopeful gains in those sessions after training began. Those gains did not carry over to play with classmates, which the authors note as the key gap for future work. They argue the training package is ready for wider testing at a larger scale.
pmc-13509994:
Guo and Gao surveyed a 2026 study of generative artificial intelligence in Chinese preschool classrooms and its link to children's creative learning. Such tools entered kindergartens quickly after 2022, yet preschool evidence is scarce. The pair asked whether AI assisted teaching lifts or dulls young children's drive to learn creatively.

Responses came from 486 teachers in fifty-two kindergartens across three provinces, analysed with structural equation modelling. Guo found AI enhanced interactive teaching linked to stronger autonomous motivation in children, while passive instruction that leaned on AI linked to weaker motivation. Motivation fully carried the benefit of interactive teaching into creative engagement. Warm teacher and child interaction blunted the harm of passive AI use. Because data were teacher reports at one time point, cause cannot be claimed.
pmc-13510094:
Yokota and colleagues tested a 2026 piglet study of hydrogen gas inhalation after oxygen deprivation injury at birth. Hydrogen had protected the brain in earlier newborn models, but its effect on lung lining and breathing in the first hours was unclear. The team checked whether the gas stirred lung inflammation or harmed gas exchange.

Sixteen newborn piglets received the injury, with eight breathing hydrogen at low concentration for six hours and eight untreated. Yokota found no rise in two activation markers on the lung lining in the treated group. White blood cells called neutrophils were more numerous in treated lungs, yet blood gases and oxygen measures stayed equally good. The extra cells tracked stronger heart output, suggesting blood flow redistribution rather than harmful inflammation.
pmc-13510194:
Misawa and co-authors look for chemical fingerprints of each risk factor inside fatty liver disease. Their 2026 paper applies untargeted metabolomics, a broad scan of small molecules, to blood from 31 patients with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease and 21 without it. The disease is diagnosed through cardiometabolic factors such as obesity, diabetes, and hypertension, but each factor's separate metabolic imprint was unclear.

Thirty-five metabolites differed between the groups, and 22 could be identified, spanning membrane lipids, amino acids, one bile acid, and a phenol-type compound. Factor-specific links stood out: obesity tracked with higher glutamic acid, diabetes with two particular sphingomyelins, and hypertension with lower levels of two lysophosphatidylcholines. Several altered metabolites connect to oxidative stress pathways, though stress itself was not measured, leaving that link hypothetical. The authors offer the signatures as leads for biomarker discovery.
pmc-13510494:
Guijun Shu, Fangning Zhang, Chuang Yang, Hongyu Jia, Xiao Wang, and Ming Yin present a tiny wireless transmitter that sends brain signals from freely moving animals, in 2026 work. Recording many brain channels at once needs a fast link that stays light on power and small in size. The chip drops a power-hungry timing circuit used in most designs and instead pairs a free-running oscillator with a simple on-off signal scheme.

Built with a standard chip process, the device drew modest power and reached raw input speeds well above the stream needed for live work. Error rates stayed workable at the speeds tested. Linked to a 128-channel recording chip in adult mice, it sent hippocampus spike and rhythm signals wirelessly that matched wired readings. The authors say the design suits untethered brain recording rigs that must stay small.
pmc-13513594:
Takashi Kuwayama and Kazuhiko Kotani present this 2026 scoping review on how rural healthcare struggles with non-communicable diseases, such as heart disease, cancer, and diabetes, changed around the COVID-19 pandemic. Rural areas face worse outcomes for these long-term conditions than cities do.

From a medical database the pair gathered twenty-three articles, split into twelve before the pandemic and eleven after. Earlier reports centered on practical healthcare gaps: poor control of blood pressure and diabetes, unstable drug supply, and thin staff training. Later reports kept those themes but added mental and nutritional health, multiple conditions at once, and money-related inequality. The authors suggest rural disease strategy should widen from clinics toward community and digital approaches.
pmc-13515494:
Sara Sofia Pinheiro, Maria João Cabrita, and Marco Gomes da Silva compare bottle closures for sparkling wine in a 2026 study. In the traditional method, a second fermentation inside the bottle creates the bubbles, and yeast chemistry reshapes flavour during those weeks. Wines were sealed either with a crown cap or with a cork closure used for this stage, then followed for ninety days with measures of basic chemistry, amino acids, and aroma compounds.

Time ruled the results: the sharpest metabolic change came between thirty and forty-five days after bottling. Yeast consumed and released amino acids in a marked reshuffle, while higher alcohols and other aroma compounds built up. Cork-sealed wines tended to ferment a touch faster and developed somewhat different amino acid and aroma patterns. The authors urge caution, given limited replication.
pmc-13517994:
Mesmin and colleagues reported a 2026 case of a dangerous heart rhythm problem linked to berberine, a herbal supplement sold freely, used for blood sugar and heart health. A 92-year-old man came to the emergency department with tremors, incontinence, and brief fainting spells that began about two weeks after he started berberine for his diabetes.

Mesmin describes repeated episodes of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia, a chaotic fast rhythm, with loss of pulse that needed immediate electric shocks. Testing confirmed the pattern as torsades de pointes, a rhythm tied to a prolonged heart-repolarization interval, which was far beyond normal on his tracing. Standard rhythm drugs did not stop the attacks, but lidocaine plus isoproterenol infusions in the ICU did. With berberine withheld, his interval shortened close to normal by hospital day three and he went home without attacks. The authors call for more research and talks with patients about supplement risks.
pmc-13518394:
Ernani Lacerda and three colleagues upgrade a classic iron-removing drug in a 2026 chemistry study. Desferrioxamine grabs iron superbly but slips poorly into cells, limiting it against the iron overload tied to brain diseases. The team welded it to two small amino acids known for crossing barriers: 5-aminolevulinic acid and GABA. Both welded versions were purified and fully characterised by spectrometry and magnetic resonance methods.

Both kept the parent drug's iron grip and antioxidant strength, barely stuck to blood proteins, and could not strip iron from its carrier protein. In human gut-barrier cells both proved harmless, yet only the GABA version reached inside and bound the cell's own iron. Computer modelling matched the bench results closely enough to predict new candidates. Lacerda's team names GABA-DFO a promising intracellular chelator for overload therapy.
pmc-13518494:
Jens Krösche leads a twelve-author consensus building Germany's first structured fellowship in children's anaesthesia in a 2026 paper. Anaesthetising children demands special skills, yet German specialist training sets only a bare minimum of infant cases and no dedicated pathway beyond it. The group designed a competency-based curriculum that builds on the finished specialist qualification.

Graduation skills split into two tiers. Basic skills are taught at every fellowship site, while advanced skills depend on each centre's equipment and case mix. Beyond the bedside, fellows must complete a quality-improvement project, further training courses, certified children's emergency courses, and webinars. Regular standardised review talks track and document each fellow's progress. Krösche's team presents the fellowship as a durable lift for patient safety and care quality in German children's anaesthesia, filling a gap the standard route leaves open.
pmc-13518894:
Zheyuan Zhang and nine colleagues introduce FlyTomo in 2026, software that processes cryo-electron tomography data while it is still being collected. Tomography can reveal molecular machines inside cells, yet the workflow is slow, expert-heavy, and usually checked only after sessions end, when fixing problems is too late.

FlyTomo handles everything from frame alignment to subtomogram averaging at high throughput. During acquisition it diagnoses sample quality, microscope performance, and visible structures in real time, then bundles the metrics into an overview for review. It also files raw and processed data into tidy directories. Tests on viruses and shaved cell samples across microscopes reached resolutions between 3.4 and 7.3 angstroms.
pmc-13518994:
Hua Zhang and colleagues build a scan-based score to separate two look-alike brain tumours. Their study from twenty twenty-six combines several MRI feature types. Solitary fibrous tumours and atypical meningiomas need different management. Telling them apart before surgery is genuinely hard.

Just over one hundred fifty patients supplied the study scans. Models tested clinical signs, texture features, and subregion patterns separately. A combined score using all feature types performed best. Certain scan signs, like dead tissue pockets, helped most. Missing membrane tails also pointed toward one tumour type. Better pre-surgery sorting guides the operation plan. The fused model approach suits other rare tumour pairs too.
pmc-13520294:
Shunta Jinno and colleagues report in 2026 on emergency care in Japan after self-harm or a suicide attempt. Their registry study asks a simple question. Does the day and hour of arrival change the chance of seeing a mental health doctor within one day?

The registry held 1,721 patients seen from December 2022 to December 2023. The median age was 33 years. About seven in ten saw a mental health doctor within a day. Arrivals on Saturdays had lower odds of a prompt visit. Arrivals in the late afternoon and early evening also had lower odds. The results point to staffing gaps outside normal hours that hospitals could plan around.
pmc-13520494:
Sung Min Lim and colleagues build in 2026 expert agreement on how to judge whether hospital antibiotic stewardship programmes in Korea actually work. A national pilot began in late 2024, yet shared success measures were lacking.

Eighteen specialists from societies and agencies rated candidate measures gathered from literature, starting with 59 options in seven groups. Three survey rounds plus a panel meeting narrowed the list using a strict agreement rule. Antibiotic use measures lead the final set, covering therapy days and standard doses per patient-days, plus cuts in broad-spectrum use. Hospitals gain a common scorecard for fair comparison.
pmc-13521894:
Xiong and co-authors tune a molecular switch driven by light, in this 2026 chemistry paper. The switch is built from photofluorochromic crystals. Such crystals change color and glow under light. Uses include optical memory and artificial vision. Switching them inside solid clumps has been the hard part. The team uses Schiff base crystals, where light first moves a proton inside the molecule and then flips its shape.

The key insight is an electronic handshake. During the flip, electrons near the nitrogen atom couple through space with nearby donor groups. The team captured this through space coupling with ultrafast spectroscopy. High pressure tests and calculations backed it. The coupling lowers the switching barrier and steadies the flipped state, raising efficiency. The authors frame this as a design rule. Tune the coupling, and switches, sensors, and logic devices driven by light can be set on purpose, with no trial and error.
pmc-13522294:
Haixiao Liu and colleagues map in 2026 two opposed states of tumour macrophages in lung adenocarcinoma. States split by which signal rules, CXCL9 or SPP1. Single-cell gene reads resolved five macrophage subsets. Survival study and cell talk maps were layered on top.

Cells rich in the CXCL9 signal sat in immune-waking paths. Those cells tracked with better outlook in early results. Lab models then steered the balance in a human cell line. Tests tracked cancer cell growth, move skill and colony growth in shared wells. Grafts in mice stretched the checks. A gene switch link to a metabolic gene start site was proved with reporter tests.
pmc-13522494:
Zhao and co-authors revisit a bedrock climate relationship: El Niño's tendency to starve the Indian monsoon. Their 2026 paper notes the link appeared to weaken after the early 1980s, raising hopes of gentler drought risk. Re-examining records from 1902 to 2023, the team shows the apparent weakening was an artefact of two unusual events, in 1983 and 1997, sitting in the data.

Greenhouse warming, they find, has actually strengthened the El Niño to monsoon connection and is projected to keep doing so. The team constrained models with observations of the Walker circulation, the great tropical air loop El Niño displaces. They estimate monsoon sensitivity to El Niño will grow almost 40 percent by century's end. The mechanism is a stronger rainfall response to the same sea warming, pushing dry sinking air further over India. The authors warn of sharper droughts and food security risks.
pmc-13522694:
Purnima Sahoo, Niyati Das, and Santosh K Panda report a 2026 quality improvement project on kangaroo mother care for very small newborns in an Indian intensive care unit. Kangaroo care means prolonged skin-to-skin contact, which lowers death, cold stress, and infection in babies under one point five kilograms. Staff training, mother counseling with demonstrations and videos, and repeated improvement cycles were introduced over four months in late 2024.

Median time to start kangaroo care fell from eighteen days at baseline to seven days by the second improvement cycle. Daily duration rose from just over three hours to just over six hours. The authors note that patient mix shifted across phases, yet they conclude that structured team interventions can move intensive care practice toward earlier and longer skin-to-skin care.
pmc-13523194:
Bruno Pastene and colleagues study surgical wound infections in intensive care patients across five French units in a 2026 multicenter study. Three hundred thirty-eight adults who had surgery during an intensive care stay of at least two days between 2022 and 2023 were followed for wound infection. Preventive antibiotics given before incision were classified by how broad their coverage was.

One patient in five developed a wound infection, rising to more than one in three when infection was already suspected at surgery. After adjustment, both broad-spectrum preventive antibiotics and no preventive antibiotics were linked to higher infection odds than narrow-spectrum cover. The authors caution that the broad-spectrum link likely reflects sicker patients rather than harm from the drugs. Infections lengthened hospital stays and worsened outcomes.
pmc-13523294:
Zhongqi Kang and co-authors compare advanced MRI diffusion models for grading a growth marker in breast cancer in a 2026 diagnostic study. One hundred twenty-one patients with a common hormone-sensitive breast cancer type were grouped by low, medium, or high Ki67 expression, a marker of how fast tumor cells divide. Sixty-three features were computed from four diffusion imaging approaches and tested for separating the groups.

Twenty-three features differed significantly across the groups. A model from the most advanced diffusion approach, built on three features, identified the low-expression group with the best accuracy, clearly beating the conventional diffusion model. Internal validation confirmed the performance. Because low Ki67 can spare patients unnecessary chemotherapy, the authors present the model as a noninvasive aid to treatment planning.
pmc-13523494:
Yamin Qiu and others develop, in a 2026 study, a grouping method to split very ill ovarian cancer patients into clear subtypes. Patients with this cancer in intensive care vary widely, which clouds outlook and care. The team applied several grouping methods together to medical data of many kinds.

Two intensive care data banks supplied 448 patients. Analysis of the first group gave two phenotypes. One, labeled Critical, showed shaky blood flow and was far sicker, while the other, labeled Stable, kept organ function. The split held up in the external cohort. Critical patients died at higher rates from 28 days through one year. Treatment patterns differed by subtype, although the authors stress those links are early hints rather than causal. They propose the binary system for sorting risk in the ICU.
pmc-13523594:
Sroubek and a large team lay out a pilot trial of pulsed field ablation for a fast heart rhythm flaw in twenty twenty-six. The flaw strikes hearts scarred by prior heart attacks. Standard care burns the bad circuit with radio waves. Pulsed fields may do the job faster with less fluid load, but the pair had never met in a trial.

Forty patients will be randomized evenly between the two catheter types. The main gauge is time needed to silence late abnormal signals. Safety and outcome checks run for six months. The pilot is the first of its kind, the team notes. Its data will shape a larger trial.
pmc-13524994:
Joji Kitayama, writing alone in 2026, reviews chemotherapy given by catheter into the abdomen for stomach cancer that has spread across the peritoneal lining. This spread pattern is the most common and most harmful in gastric cancer. Sparse blood supply and a barrier between abdomen and bloodstream limit systemic drugs, while surgical heated chemotherapy methods are harsh and narrow.

The other route uses a fitted port to give dose after dose of chemotherapy at body temperature into the abdomen, mainly in East Asia. Lasting local exposure comes with modest procedural burden and combines readily with whole-body treatment. Taxane drugs suit the route because they linger in the abdomen and enter blood slowly. The review covers drug reasoning, medical evidence, and coming new ideas in mixing and delivery.
pmc-13525094:
Ramachandra Reddy Gowda Venkatesha and colleagues report a case of recurrent bullous pemphigoid, a rare blistering disease caused by the immune system attacking the skin. Their patient was a 68-year-old man who came in with a burning feeling inside his mouth.

The diagnosis rested on the man's history and a clinical exam alone, without tissue or immune-stain tests. Broken blisters had left raw, red areas, a pattern the team links to antibodies against two skin anchor proteins. The authors stress that dentists should know this disease's signs and refer such patients promptly to a skin specialist. Careful skin protection matters in care, they add, since the disease returns in flares with an uncertain course.
pmc-13526394:
Olivia R. Mitchel and others analyze, in a 2026 registry study, survival among older breast cancer survivors who used vaginal estrogen, a treatment for genitourinary menopause symptoms that hormone therapy often worsens. Whether local estrogen is safe after breast cancer has been debated, and guidance varies, holding back a helpful therapy.

The retrospective cohort used a linked cancer registry and survey program with 25,874 women aged 65 or older diagnosed between 2007 and 2017. About one thousand had used vaginal estrogen after their cancer was found. Simple models linked use with lower overall and cancer-specific death. When use was modeled as changing over time, those links faded to nonsignificance, a sign that immortal time or selection bias explained them. The authors conclude local estrogen showed no survival harm.
pmc-13527094:
Babak Mehdipour, Abbas Niknejad, and Hadi Zare-Zardini test, in a 2026 study, composites built with fibers from sunflower seed hulls, a farm residue, in two plastics. Fibers were pulled out with alkaline treatment and mechanical splitting, then molded into polyester and polyethylene composites at varying fiber shares and tested under standard protocols.

Polyester composites did sharply better. At forty percent fiber, tensile strength rose by half, bending strength rose by nearly two thirds, impact strength more than tripled, and crushing strength reached a high value. Polyethylene composites gained less, with tensile strength up twelve percent and bending strength up thirty-five percent at the top fiber loading, while impact strength fell as fiber rose. The authors urge hull fibers notably for polyester systems needing sustainable reinforcement.
pmc-13527994:
Jing-lan Zhang and four colleagues review dental treatment under general anesthesia for small children with severe tooth decay in China. The 2026 retrospective study followed 269 preschool children treated between 2020 and 2023. Their mean age was just under four years. Success, decay recurrence, complications, and quality of life were tracked for a year.

Treatment success was about ninety-two percent at six months. It eased to about eighty-six percent at twelve months. No child had new decay at one month, but relapse reached about nineteen percent by one year. Pain was the most common problem in the first day. Chewing trouble and weariness were also frequent early on, then faded. Family and child quality-of-life scores improved steadily. Most parents, over ninety-one percent, were satisfied overall.
pmc-13528094:
Omar Z. Harhash and eleven colleagues survey young adults in Palestine about beta-thalassemia in a 2026 study. The inherited blood disorder cuts production of a hemoglobin chain. Prevention rests on awareness and screening before marriage and pregnancy. An Arabic online survey ran from late 2025 to January 2026. It gathered 424 replies through social media sharing.

Eighty-seven percent had heard of the disease. Among those aware, under half showed adequate knowledge. About seventy-four percent held a positive attitude. About eighty-three percent reported prevention-minded practice. Women outscored men on knowledge and practice. Knowledge gaps clustered on treatability, subtypes, and policy. Past screening was rare, yet support for premarital testing and prenatal diagnosis ran high. Knowledge predicted good practice. The authors want education drives that close the specific gaps found.
pmc-13529794:
Fleischer C. N. Kotey and three colleagues track germs on hospital surfaces at a children's hospital in Accra, Ghana, in a 2026 study. The twelve-week watch ran in late 2023 across four departments. Six hundred swabs were taken from high-touch items. Bed rails, incubators, cuffs, and thermometers were among them. Cultures grew 1,120 bacterial isolates from thirty-three genera.

Skin staphylococci led the Gram-positive finds. Acinetobacter baumannii led the Gram-negative side, with Klebsiella and E. coli behind. Thermometers and their trays were among the dirtiest items. One cot topped the single-item list. Drug resistance ran moderate to high in key germs. Some strains resisted nearly every drug tested. The authors urge stricter cleaning rotas for shared small items. Children's wards cannot treat surfaces as background, they argue.
pmc-13530294:
Asghari and eight co-authors wrote a review in twenty twenty-six on a fungal infection in people with HIV or AIDS. The fungi are tiny parasites that often strike weak immune systems. The team pooled studies from twenty seventeen to twenty twenty-five. They found thirty-nine studies from eighteen countries that fit their rules. They merged the rates to get a world estimate of how common the infection is.

About twelve in one hundred patients had the infection, far above healthy controls. Rates ran highest where immune cell counts were lowest. One species caused most cases, with many strains in that species. The authors call for better tests and routine screening in HIV care. They say such steps would improve outcomes and slow spread.
pmc-13530794:
Oladeji and colleagues present in 2026, as conference poster 62, data from the multicenter JUPITER cohort comparing graft sources for medial patellofemoral ligament reconstruction. That surgery stabilizes a repeatedly dislocating kneecap. Surgeons can use the patient's own tendon or donor tendon, with no consensus on which serves better.

The prospective cohort held 671 patients, 285 with autografts and 386 with allografts. The autograft group was slightly older and carried more cartilage damage at entry. Rates of renewed subluxation or dislocation and of reoperation did not differ between the graft types, and neither did complication rates when split by graft source. Where the groups separated was in patient-reported scores: the autograft patients reported significantly better outcomes at two years on two knee scales and again at five years.
pmc-13531194:
Ko and Chui wrote a 2026 editorial on a practical trick for choosing valve size during transcatheter aortic valve replacement in patients born with a two-leaflet aortic valve. Such anatomy is often tapered and heavily calcified. standard scan-based sizing can leave operators torn between two consecutive valve sizes, risking vessel rupture with the larger or leakage with the smaller.

Ko describes a two-patient series in which operators first inflated a slightly undersized balloon at the valve while injecting contrast dye. In the first case, despite a reassuring balloon test, the larger valve was implanted and expanded poorly at its middle even after further inflation. In the second, the same test pointed the team to the smaller valve, which expanded fully with no rupture or leak. The editorial endorses the balloon observation as a simple tie-breaker algorithm when scans leave sizing genuinely ambiguous.
pmc-13531794:
Haniyeh Khalafinejad and colleagues ask in 2026 whether eating quality tracks with sleep in older Iranians. Baseline data from a Neyshabur aging cohort covered 2,026 adults aged 60 and over. A food questionnaire fed a healthy eating score, while a standard index graded sleep quality and length.

Women reported worse and shorter sleep than men. Across all participants, eating score showed no firm link with either sleep quality or sleep length after adjustment. Among women alone, the highest eating group hinted at less short sleep, just short of statistical confidence. The authors suggest other health factors may dominate the diet-sleep tie.
pmc-13531894:
Albert Roberts, Solon Fountzopoulos, and Terun Desai review in 2026 trial evidence on oral cannabidiol for blood pressure in adults. Four databases were searched in September 2024 for randomized trials in people with normal or high pressure. Wide differences in dose and reporting blocked pooled math, so results were summarized in words.

Only four trials with 120 people qualified. Every trial found lower systolic pressure than placebo, strongest at the highest daily dose and under stress or during sleep. Two trials also found lower diastolic pressure. Side effects stayed mild to moderate, yet tiny samples and short runs demand larger trials.
pmc-13534194:
Urszula Nowacka and colleagues run in 2026 a pilot trial of home heart tracing for pregnancies with late-onset fetal growth restriction. Babies growing too slowly late in pregnancy need close checks, which often means frequent hospital visits. In Warsaw, 120 women were split between home tracing with safety scans and standard hospital checks.

Newborn condition at birth was alike in both groups, with no rise in poor outcomes. The home group had fewer emergency caesarean births, lower anxiety at delivery, and fewer clinic visits. The authors call the results early signals, not proof of full clinical benefit.
pmc-13534494:
Dajane Kana Darkushe develops in 2026 strategies for sustainable stormwater control in Dambi Dollo Town in Ethiopia. Flooding grows when runoff overwhelms drains, a common problem in fast-growing towns. Field checks, surveys, interviews with officials and residents, and policy review mapped current practice.

Current practice proved largely reactive, with weak drains, few green spaces, no stormwater-specific policy, and low public awareness. Proposed plans stress green infrastructure, actions at plot to catchment scales, and strong stakeholder roles. Readers in resource-limited towns gain a practical frame for safer, greener water control.
pmc-13536594:
Rong Sun and colleagues weigh in 2026 how much weather factors and air pollution each add to childhood allergic disease in Chongqing, China. Their relative roles were poorly known in subtropical climate settings. Records held over 1.5 million child hospital visits from 2014 to 2019 and 2023 to 2024.

Heat showed the strongest links, raising nose allergy and asthma visits while cutting eczema visits. Single air pollutants mattered far less than heat in the models used. Seasonal peaks differed by disease, so the authors urge season-aware prevention that pairs climate adaptation with clean-air work.
pmc-13537194:
Mingyang Wang, Xiaoyu Yang, and Li Yang question how a pain study grouped its patients over time. The study used repeated sensory tests to track change after lower-limb amputation. Its key measure, the wind-up ratio, shows how pain builds with repeated touches. The letter writers say the findings hinge on how phantom limb pain status was assigned.

Phantom pain status was set after the fact at each visit, using a pain score cutoff. The letter shows that the study's tables seem to use different grouping rules. One table implies five paired records per group, while a figure shows changing group sizes. The writers also flag one participant whose records do not line up between files. They ask the authors to clarify the rules so readers can judge the claims.
pmc-13538394:
Wei Shi, Qiang Zhou, and Yan Song examine social connectedness and climate doubt in China in a 2026 survey study using national social survey data. Doubt weakens public action on climate change, yet Chinese patterns differ from Western accounts. Learning models ranked correlates of doubt, while mediation models traced middle pathways through worldview, risk awareness, and policy views. Regional differences were also mapped.

Stronger social ties tracked with lower climate doubt overall, though the link varied by tie type. Human-centered beliefs, risk awareness, and policy views each carried part of the association, with pathways differing by doubt type. Regional variation ran large, warning against one-size advice. The authors present connectedness as a subtle lever for resilience that must be tuned to local context.
pmc-13538694:
Zhengyi Yu and colleagues track asphalt damage under combined sunlight aging and freeze-thaw cycling in a 2026 materials study. Half-round bending tests measured air voids, bending strength, stiffness, failure movement, and fracture energy in aged and unaged specimens across rising cycle counts. A damage index and correlation analysis ranked which measures best capture the coupled harm.

More cycles raised air voids while strength and fracture energy slid steadily. Sunlight-aged specimens fared worse than freeze-thaw-only peers at equal cycles, though aging also stiffened the mix somewhat. Bending strength proved the most sensitive damage signal, followed by fracture energy and air voids. The authors recommend strength and early fracture energy as key gauges for pavement in harsh climates.
pmc-13539894:
Achmad Syawqie and three colleagues present a 2026 scoping review of sensor devices that might catch oral cancer early from saliva, without cutting tissue. Early detection matters because mouth cancers are often found late, when treatment works less well.

Searching five databases for work published between 2019 and 2025 left nine original studies to chart. Most devices read electrical or light signals, or used tiny transistors, aiming at markers such as interleukin-8 and a cytokeratin fragment. Several reached extremely low detection limits in the laboratory. Reporting of testing time, sample size, and accuracy against real diagnoses varied widely, so the authors ask for standard validation and larger clinical studies.
pmc-13540294:
Sarah Abdel-Gawad leads a 2026 dental materials study asking whether newer all-in-one bonding glues for fillings actually beat the versions they replaced. Manufacturers update universal adhesives often, and claims of progress deserve checking after the bond has aged.

One hundred eighty human molars were bonded with three updated adhesives, their predecessors, or a multistep reference glue, then stored in water for six months. Two updated products merely matched their older versions, and one performed worse than its predecessor. Microscope images showed interface patterns and film thickness varying by application method. The authors conclude that commercial updates do not reliably improve dentine bonding.
pmc-13541194:
Nathan Seegert and colleagues exploit a natural experiment from the COVID-19 pandemic: some American mask mandates came from states, others from counties. If mandates mainly signal how risky public life is, bigger jurisdictions might broadcast differently. Using cell phone mobility and card spending around mandate dates in 2020, they compared the two levels.

State mandates were followed by increased economic activity and about one hundred forty-three dollars more spending per person. County mandates showed no significant effect. The authors read the asymmetry as information revelation: a statewide mandate resolved uncertainty in a way that reassured people, while county signals were too local or noisy to move behavior.
pmc-13541894:
M Bosch-Ramírez and seven colleagues follow, in a 2026 prospective study, older adults treated for faecal incontinence with gentle electrical stimulation of a nerve at the ankle. The condition affects up to half of institutionalised older people, yet treatment evidence in this age group is thin.

Sixty-one community-dwelling patients, median age seventy-one and mostly women, received stimulation in phases over twelve months with checks out to three years. About two thirds were strong responders by the end, and most kept their gains at thirty-six months. Severity scores fell sharply, while quality of life improved only in the depression domain. Older age itself predicted response.
pmc-13542194:
Xiangyu Gao and four colleagues explore, in a 2026 cross-sectional study, whether blood phosphorus levels track with muscle mass in people with type 2 diabetes, a group prone to early muscle loss. Just over a thousand inpatients had muscle measured by dual-energy X-ray scans.

Low muscle mass affected about a fifth of men and a smaller share of women. Higher phosphorus was linked with lower odds of low muscle mass in both sexes after extensive adjustment. The relationship with the muscle index rose only up to a threshold near one millimole per litre, then flattened, with slightly different cut points for men and women. Longitudinal validation is requested by the authors.
pmc-13542494:
Huang and colleagues report a new disease-causing variant in acrogeria, an extremely rare premature-ageing skin disorder first described in 1940, and review how LMNA gene variants map onto its family of diseases. Acrogeria thins the skin and fat of the hands and feet and ages patients far beyond their years. Their 2026 case concerns a 32-year-old man whose mottled pigmentation had spread since childhood. Genetic testing found a previously unreported change in LMNA, the gene that builds the nuclear scaffolding proteins lamin A and C.

The variant, a single letter swap altering amino acid 591, joins the catalogue of acrogeria mutations, and the authors note possible accompanying heart abnormalities worth watching in this patient. Their literature review sorts genotype-phenotype patterns across the laminopathies, the family including Hutchinson-Gilford progeria and muscular dystrophies, where the same gene produces wildly different diseases depending on where the change lands.
pmc-13543494:
Qianting Deng, Chongyun Wu, and Luodan Yang reviewed classroom physical activity breaks in 2026 for university students. Long sitting through lectures dulls thinking, and breaks are well studied in schoolchildren but barely in adults at university. pmc-13543694:
Danielle Amaral e Silva's team compared cocoa in 2026 from two Brazilian Amazon ecosystems: seasonally flooded floodplains, a long-used growing setting, and plain uplands. pmc-13544094:
Combes and colleagues ask what shapes the gut microbes of young broiler chicks: the place where they hatch, or early contact with an adult hen. pmc-13544994:

pmc-13546594:
Lingran Zhao and co-authors reviewed in 2026 the two-way relationship between long-term psychological stress and stomach cancer. The authors judge the link clinically meaningful but not yet proven causal. They call for prospective studies and trials that build stress care into cancer treatment.
pmc-13547094:
Ismail Yigitdol and eight co-authors count hormone disorders in adults with a faulty immune system, in a study published in twenty twenty-six. The condition, common variable immunodeficiency, leaves people short of protective antibodies and prone to infections. Hormone glands can also suffer, both from immune attack and from long steroid treatment.

A dozen of those cases were caused by steroid drugs. Patients with hormone problems were older and heavier, with more autoimmune disease and higher past steroid use. The study also records gene findings. The authors urge routine hormone checks in this group.
pmc-13547194:
Lijeong Hong and Min-Shik Kim tested in 2026 whether people unconsciously learn social patterns the way they learn repeated layouts when searching a scene. In three experiments, volunteers searched for a target face among other faces while the spatial layout was shuffled every trial, removing the usual cue. What stayed consistent instead were social features: which faces appeared together, the overall mood of the crowd, or which way pairs of faces turned.

Search ran faster when the social pattern stayed consistent than when it changed, even though participants barely knew the patterns existed. The crowd mood cue worked strongest of the three. The authors conclude that the mind quietly picks up social structure and uses it to guide attention, much as it uses physical layout.
pmc-13547394:
Sujata Singh and co-authors simulated in 2026 a two-layer solar cell that stacks a lead-free perovskite on top of silicon to catch more of the spectrum than either material manages alone. The top layer uses a cesium germanium iodide perovskite, avoiding toxic lead, sandwiched between charge-selective layers of zinc oxide and copper oxide. The team swept thickness, doping, defect levels, and band gap in software to hunt for the best combination.

Because the work is entirely computational, the numbers describe what the design could deliver if fabrication matches the model. The authors frame it as a route to higher output with a smaller carbon footprint.
pmc-13547894:
Ta and colleagues review in 2026 a side effect of intravenous iron that doctors increasingly recognize: hypophosphataemia, a drop in blood phosphate that can weaken muscles and soften bone. Iron infusions transformed iron deficiency care, and some formulations trigger this drop often.

Reported rates reach above nine in ten patients for the highest-risk formulations, though most cases are mild and pass quickly. Rarely it brings heart rhythm problems or bone disease, sometimes needing hospital care and phosphate replacement. The review illustrates the range with five cases and offers a management pathway. pmc-13548494:

Every one of the top fifty features was already a known movement-related gene or domain, and most of the top hundred had experimental support. The authors argue that tighter taxonomic limits can backfire by shrinking the training set. Readers get a faster route to short, testable gene lists for other complex bacterial traits.
pmc-13548594:
Junyuan Feng and colleagues present a deep learning system that reads brainwave recordings to detect infantile epileptic spasms syndrome, in a 2026 methods paper. This severe infant epilepsy shows chaotic brainwave patterns, and reading the traces by eye is slow and error-prone, delaying treatment. Their system, SinTransNet, splits each recording into five frequency bands, extracts features with wave-shaped convolutional filters, and lets a transformer weigh relationships across bands.

Testing used 129 recordings containing close to two thousand spasm events from the team's own collection. The system reached average accuracy near eighty-six percent, catching about four fifths of true cases while keeping false alarms low. The authors argue that automated reading of this kind could speed diagnosis in pediatric neurology wards, giving infants a better chance at early treatment before developmental harm accumulates.
pmc-13548694:
Youyou Xie and colleagues create radiation-resistant cervical cancer cells in the laboratory to learn how a nuclear protein helps tumors shrug off radiotherapy, in a 2026 study. Resistant disease is a major reason treatment fails.
