A growth pathway downstream, mTOR, linked the two effects. Patient tissue echoed the pattern: tumors from people whose cancers resisted radiation showed high HMGB1 and low activated AMPK. The authors nominate the HMGB1 to AMPK axis as a drug target, while noting patient validation is still thin.
pmc-13551694:

Responses vary, so the team ran a genome-wide CRISPR screen in two cancer cell lines under the PARP inhibitor olaparib, watching which gene losses made cells die. Combining a newer PARP inhibitor, AZD5305, with an autophagy inhibitor, GNS561, acted synergistically in cell lines and worked in mouse tumors grown from those lines. The authors propose the pairing for further development.
pmc-13551794:

They explore nerve-targeted treatments such as sacral neuromodulation and vagus nerve stimulation, borrowed from pain and autoimmune fields, as ways to restore balance. Direct clinical evidence in sexual dysfunction remains limited, so the review charts a research agenda.
pmc-13555994:
Erica De Vita and eleven colleagues published a 2026 scoping review of how risk communication works during public health emergencies. Working within an Italian project on communicating risk, they compared published evidence with the pandemic plans of Italian regions. Their search covered three major databases for studies from 2019 to May 2024, and they examined 18 regional plans with a structured checklist.

Most came from wealthy countries and dealt with COVID-19, with mass messaging through social media far more common than targeted or participatory work. Timeliness, openness, and trust appeared often, while fairness, public involvement, and handling false information were put into practice less often. The comparison shows where regional plans match what studies show and where they still fall short.
pmc-13557794:
Sena Ishikawa and six colleagues looked in 2026 for early metabolic signs of hidden iron deficiency in young Japanese women. Iron shortage is common in this group and can precede anaemia while standard markers still read normal. The team studied 33 healthy women aged about twenty. They split the women by total iron binding capacity, a blood measure of free iron transport space. Bile acid profiles and blood sugar were compared across the two groups.

Specific bile acids correlated with iron transport measures across the group. The authors suggest that this capacity measure may flag a preclinical disturbance that links iron handling, bile acid metabolism, and low blood sugar before anaemia appears. Larger studies would be needed to confirm the pattern.
pmc-13558294:
Yu Chen Lin and a large team survey who takes up anal and cervical cancer screening, with and without HIV. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-six. People with HIV face a higher risk of cancers tied to a common virus. The survey runs through a clinic network that gives HIV care, most of it in Florida.

Women with HIV, in a flip, take cervical screening that meets the guide less than women without it. Worry about HIV status being shared tracks with that gap. The authors call for work aimed at each sub-group's blocks.
pmc-13558594:
S. Sajini, V. Jananee, and E. A. Mary Anita designed in 2026 a blockchain-based authentication framework for networks of connected vehicles. Vehicle-to-everything radio links are open and fast changing, which invites impersonation, fake identity floods, replayed messages, and tampering. Simulations reported authentication accuracy above ninety-five percent and packet delivery near ninety-seven percent, with lower delay and longer network life than rival blockchain schemes. Attack tests covered active and passive threats.
pmc-13558694:

The enzyme, SCD-1, converts saturated fats into the supple kind that cell membranes need, and tumours overusing it grow faster, spread more, and resist a form of cell death called ferroptosis. Four finalists bound stably and tightly, with low drift across the simulations and strong computed affinity. All results are computational, with no cell or animal testing yet. The authors offer the four leads and the AI workflow as a starting kit for tumour-specific SCD-1 drug development.
pmc-13559594:

pmc-13560294:

pmc-13560394:

Questionable practices, including unfair authorship, cherry-picked reporting, and bent readings of data, came across as normal shortcuts. The authors stress they show perceptions, not causal links, and they aim the findings at training reform.
pmc-13560994:
Nicholas Nassikas and a team of co-authors link short heat spells to weaker lung function in older adults. Models that allow lagged and curved effects were used. A hot week, thirty degrees against twenty, came with a small but clear drop in the air blown out in one second.
pmc-13562194:

pmc-13562494:

pmc-13563794:

pmc-13566194:

pmc-13566294:

pmc-13569094:

pmc-13569194:

pmc-13570894:

pmc-13571394:

pmc-13571594:

pmc-13572394:

pmc-13572494:

pmc-13572994:

pmc-13573494:

pmc-13574894:

pmc-13575094:

pmc-13576094:

pmc-13576594:

pmc-13577794:

pmc-13577894:

pmc-13578294:

pmc-13578594:
Dimitri Martel and colleagues check whether MRI maps of fat makeup around the human knee give the same answer a week later, in a 2026 study. Fat chemistry near joints may shift with joint disease, so a steady measure is needed before it can track change. Ten healthy adults, half of them women, were scanned twice, one week apart, on a strong research scanner.

Eight fat depots around the knee were traced, from bone marrow to the fat pads behind and beside the kneecap. Total fat share repeated best, with tight spread across all sites. Saturated fat held nearly as steady. One class of unsaturated fat swung widely, above all in the small fat pads. The authors back the steady measures for future studies and flag the shaky one.
pmc-13578694:
Nicole Klemann and Stefan Endepols published a pest control study in two thousand twenty-six comparing traps and poison bait for house mice. Both methods are common, but head-to-head field data were scarce. Three field trials measured success by feeding and tracking censuses before and after.

Trapping alone cut mouse numbers by about forty to sixty-nine percent across sites. It worked best where infestations were small and food scarce. Peanut butter beat synthetic lures clearly. Follow-up poisoning with brodifacoum then cleared ninety to one hundred percent of the rest. Nearly all trapped mice died quickly, and bycatch of other animals was negligible. The authors recommend traps first, poison to finish.
pmc-13579294:
Tustumi and nine co-authors asked in twenty twenty-six whether Brazil's social health groups speed the spread of keyhole surgery in public wards. Those groups are state-firm teams that run a growing share of public sites. The test case was keyhole gall-bladder removal across the land.

Of more than two thousand sites, eighty-three were group-run. Group sites used keyhole care more, for both planned and urgent cases. They hit a thirty percent use mark about a year sooner than the rest. Blend rule care may lift care spread in mid-wealth lands, they find, with care for bias.
pmc-13580994:
Anne Backes and nine co-workers tested a smart shoe insole that sorts day to day acts while people move in real life. The WalkinSense insole joins foot force sensors with motion sensors. It has no wires. In the 2026 study, 99 people wore it for indoor and outdoor tasks in a near free life setup. Staff watched the tasks to give a true record. pmc-13581594:
Patience A. Afulani and colleagues built and validated a scale for person-centred pregnancy care in low- and middle-income countries. pmc-13583394:
Ana Paula de Andrade Silva and colleagues review capsaicin for burning mouth syndrome in this 2026 paper. The syndrome causes a daily burning feeling inside the mouth with no visible cause, and it mostly affects women over 50. Capsaicin, the hot compound in chili peppers, can be applied in the mouth or swallowed, yet doctors disagree on whether it truly helps.

Searching seven databases, the reviewers found 782 papers and kept only four that fit their rules. Doses and study lengths varied widely, but every kept study reported lower pain scores after capsaicin use. Three trials carried a moderate risk of bias and one a critical risk, so the proof behind the benefit rates as low. The authors urge caution until stronger trials are done.
pmc-13584394:
Zhu, Guo, and Zhang published a 2026 study on a scoring tool for artery hardening risk. Calcium buildup in the belly aorta warns of heart events and early death. No simple tool existed to flag who should get closer checks. The team built a paper scoring chart from a national health survey.

Predicted chances matched real outcomes closely across the risk range. Decision checks showed the chart helps across many cutoff choices. Clinics could run it with facts already in most charts. Early flagging could steer scans toward those at highest risk.
pmc-13584494:
Xuefan Yang and colleagues present a rare cancer case alongside a review of past reports in this 2026 paper. The cancer grew inside a urethral diverticulum, a small pouch off the urine channel in a woman. Such cancers are so rare that no standard treatment path exists, and their vague symptoms often pass for a simple urine infection.

Their patient was a 46-year-old woman with two years of frequent, urgent, and painful urination. Scans found a growth about five centimeters wide around the urethra, and a biopsy showed papillary carcinoma. Surgeons removed the front pelvic organs, rerouted urine through a piece of bowel, and rebuilt the vagina. Final tests showed a high-grade cancer that had reached the bladder wall muscle. The authors press for careful exams and wider sharing of cases.
pmc-13585394:
Ribeiro-Silva and colleagues examine in 2026 whether the weather around a young infant affects how long mothers breastfeed exclusively, using a nationwide Brazilian cohort. Climate change makes both heat and cold exposures a growing concern for infant feeding.

The study linked records for 397,239 children under six months from the national food and nutrition surveillance system, covering 2015 to 2019. It matched them with daily gridded temperature data. Statistical models that account for delayed effects found no national link between cold and stopping exclusive breastfeeding. Heat, by contrast, was associated with about a ten percent higher risk of interruption, and that increase looked similar across infant ages, sexes, and levels of local deprivation. Cold effects may still vary by age and deprivation, the authors note, even though the national picture showed none.
pmc-13587094:
Doi Van Mai, Phu Diep Thien Duong, Tuan Van Nguyen, and Kiet Gia Le Nguyen report removing a large retroperitoneal leiomyosarcoma entirely by laparoscopy, in a two thousand twenty-six case report. Open surgery is the standard for these rare tumors, and keyhole removal of big ones is seldom attempted.

The sixty-year-old patient had six months of dull abdominal pain and a ten-centimeter mass that first looked like a duodenal stromal tumor. The team achieved a complete en bloc resection with clear margins and an uneventful recovery. Pathology confirmed leiomyosarcoma, and genetic testing found a rare TP53 mutation. The authors argue experienced teams can safely offer the laparoscopic route.
pmc-13587294:
Rehab Abd Elhafeez Zaytoun and five co-authors set first norm values for mouth skills in Egyptian children. Their study, from twenty twenty-six, deals with oral motor skills, which drive feeding and speech growth. Weak skills can harm growth, talk, and life quality. Yet many tools in use lack set rules and fair objectivity. The team used a placement therapy tool set with stepped levels. Two hundred seventy-five children of age two to six, all on a typical path, were tested.

Their scores set a first local norm base for clinic use. Early spots of weak skills then have a home yardstick. Readers in child speech care in Egypt get norms drawn from their own children, not imports.
pmc-13587794:
Wang and six co-authors report a heart support case in pregnancy related heart failure, in work from twenty twenty-six. Peripartum cardiomyopathy weakens the heart around childbirth. When paired with severe preeclampsia, high blood pressure of pregnancy, the two are hard to tell apart.

Their patient was a first time mother aged twenty-eight near term with fast worsening breathlessness. Tests showed very high blood pressure, protein in urine, and a sharply weakened heart pump. She was rescued with a heart lung support machine that takes blood from a vein and returns it to an artery. Five year follow up is rare in such reports and shows the long arc of recovery.
pmc-13588194:
Henrique Nogueira Pinto and colleagues link a lab-grown blood-brain barrier to a human brain organoid on a single chip. The barrier guards the brain but also blocks most medicines, and animal models mimic it poorly. Their platform grows a flow-through, vessel-like barrier from human stem cells beside an open chamber holding a mini brain organoid, joined by a gel interface with no artificial membrane in between.

The two parts coexisted stably on the chip. Star-shaped support cells from the organoid reached out, crossed toward the barrier, and touched its vessel cells directly, copying the real neurovascular unit's layout. Because both sides stay open to testing, a candidate drug's crossing and its effect on brain tissue can be read in one run. The authors offer the chip as a human-first stand-in for animal barrier studies.
pmc-13590594:
Meiru Zhou and colleagues review the two-way talk between body clocks and dopamine in Parkinson's disease. Clock upset is a common non-motor feature of Parkinson's, linked both ways to disease, yet its causal role is unclear. This 2026 review looks at how clock glitches relate to early and full Parkinson's, the workings at play, and clock-based treatments.

Broken rhythms may mix with cell stress, swelling, energy failure, and protein-balance breakdown. Clock readings could aid early spotting, tracking, and timed treatments, such as light therapy or timed treatment, to improve quality of life. The authors frame the clock-dopamine talk as a hopeful frontier for Parkinson's care beyond dopamine pills alone.
pmc-13590694:
Chang Liu and eight co-authors build bedside charts that predict death and clot spread in patients with heart valve infection. Their study was published in twenty twenty-six. Infective endocarditis still kills many in hospital and often throws clots to other organs, yet simple risk tools are lacking.

The team reviewed adults with definite infection at one Guangzhou hospital from twenty twenty to twenty twenty-five, judged by current criteria. Six routine measures fed the models: age, growth size on the valve, white cell count, two blood indices, and a nutrition score. Nomograms turned each patient's numbers into a personal risk. Accuracy curves tested the charts inside the same data. The tool aims to flag high-risk patients early.
pmc-13591194:
Victor Ezeugwu and colleagues piloted BIG STEPS, a habit program plus guided stepping training early after stroke. Stroke patients often stay still, slowing healing, yet few programs target sitting time soon after stroke. Their waitlist pilot split 28 stroke patients to early or delayed training: 12 weeks of coaching to cut sitting and raise daily steps, plus usual care for both groups.

Signing up ran at about two people per month, stay-on rates topped 80 percent, and no serious program-linked harms happened. At week 12, the early group hit 6,534 steps per day versus 4,031 in the waiting group, and cut sitting by about eighty minutes versus forty minutes daily. By week 24, groups evened out after the delayed group got training. The authors call the program feasible, safe, and hopeful.
pmc-13591694:
Essa M Rafique and three colleagues review, in 2026, how Tamil Nadu, an Indian state once heavy with HIV, reversed its epidemic early and kept it down. They weigh state data from 2000 to 2024 against peer states and strong global performers. The review credits nimble administration: quick program shifts, joined up TB and HIV care, and services folded into normal clinics rather than kept in stand alone silos.

New infections fell by 94 percent across the period, and adult prevalence dropped to a small fraction of its 2000 level. The state also first in India met the world mark for ending mother to child spread. Rafique and the team offer the model as a transferable plan for other low resource settings.
pmc-13592594:
Lia Brigante and seven colleagues argue that the European Union's first update of midwife qualification rules in 21 years must match world standards. The directive sets minimum training rules for midwives across EU and EEA states, and its reach echoes worldwide because other nations copy EU norms. Midwives, when trained and licensed to global standards, can deliver about ninety percent of essential care for women and newborns, the authors note.

Training and practice standards have moved on over two decades while the law stood still, they say. Aligning the update with current science, global professional standards, and World Health Organization guidance would protect care quality, let midwives work to their full scope, and ease movement across borders. Brigante and the team frame the revision as a global policy moment.
pmc-13592794:
Alexander Muacevic leads a team tracing where stroke deaths happen across the United States from 2020 to 2024. Hospital stroke care has leapt ahead, yet deaths outside hospitals form a blind spot. National mortality records for adults over forty five were sorted by urbanization level and place of death. Smoothed state ratios and inequality indices measured how concentrated deaths were in space.

Deaths shifted outward: medium and fringe suburbs posted the largest relative gains, big city cores stalled, and rural areas dipped slightly. Home deaths spiked in 2021, and hospice deaths kept climbing. Both home and hospital deaths clustered heavily in space, with inequality scores near one half. Muacevic and the team urge folding such maps into stroke surveillance to target emergency care.
pmc-13593694:
Philipp Friedrich Georg Ried and Roland Seifert surveyed German dentists about gum overgrowth caused by medication, a side effect in which the gums swell over the teeth. Their 2026 online survey reached dentists through regional associations, though only 118 usable replies came back from a very large invited pool.

The blood pressure drugs amlodipine and nifedipine, plus the immune suppressant ciclosporin, were named most often as triggers, and affected patients showed no pattern by sex. About seven in ten respondents had treated the condition successfully, most often by teaching better oral hygiene, switching the causative drug, or trimming the gum surgically. Published figures for how often each drug causes the problem vary widely. The authors therefore advise quoting only a narrow range. Readers should check the source data closely before trusting any single number.
pmc-13593794:
Catherine Paterson heads a fifteen-author review of programs that support the minds and daily lives of children and teenagers with cancer, from diagnosis through survivorship. Searching five databases without date limits, the team gathered thirty-four studies from seventeen countries covering nearly two thousand young patients, and combined their results statistically.

Programs that trained thinking skills gave the clearest gains, improving memory and related abilities by a moderate margin. Play and creative therapies, animal-assisted sessions, self-management teaching, and physical activity together improved psychological outcomes such as anxiety and pain. Several of the same approaches lifted quality of life scores as well. Benefits for depression, coping, and fatigue were less consistent. The authors conclude that psychosocial care earns its place across the whole cancer journey, not only during treatment.
pmc-13593894:
Huang and coauthors hunt drugs linked to cachexia in a United States event database. Cachexia is a wasting syndrome that cuts survival and life quality. Systematic proof on drug-induced cachexia has been scarce. The team ran the first large-scale vigilance analysis.

Reports from 2004 to early 2025 were pulled for the study. All reports listed cachexia as an adverse event. The top 50 most reported drugs got deep signal checks. Four methods had to agree for a drug to count as a signal. Risk features were charted for each flagged drug. Results may warn prescribers about wasting risks.
pmc-13594394:
Xiaoqian Duan and co-authors report a 64-year-old man with high-risk Philadelphia chromosome-positive acute lymphoblastic leukemia. He could not undergo a stem cell transplant. Yet he stayed in remission for over three and a half years on an unusual maintenance plan. His leukemia carried a gene deletion linked to relapse and had already returned once during targeted drug treatment.

One intensive cycle of the immune engager blinatumomab combined with dasatinib drove the disease to a deep molecular remission. He then switched to brief monthly outpatient infusions of the same antibody at reduced intensity. Daily dasatinib and regular interferon injections completed the plan. Leukemia transcripts stayed undetectable for nearly three years, with only one brief low-level blip that settled without escalation. He had no unplanned hospital stays and no severe nerve side effects, suggesting gentler intermittent dosing can hold this disease while sparing the patient.
pmc-13594494:
Muhammad Usman Ghani and co-authors review how artificial intelligence might predict atrial fibrillation after coronary artery bypass surgery. The complication strikes fifteen to thirty percent of patients. It also lengthens hospital stays. Their 2026 narrative review gathered nine studies from 2020 onward that combined machine learning with clinical, blood, genetic, and metabolic information.

Across those studies, modern algorithms scored well at separating patients who would develop the rhythm problem from those who would not, beating traditional clinical risk scores. The catch, the authors note, is unfinished homework: few models have been tested outside the hospitals that built them, calibration is rarely checked, and bias remains possible. They argue that pairing explainable algorithms with biomarker data could eventually let teams target preventive care at the patients most likely to benefit.
pmc-13594894:
Xuan Cui and eight co-authors feed hens a five-herb mix with mugwort at its head to guard the egg tube. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-six. One hundred sixty hens past peak lay were split to plain feed or herb feed for eight weeks. Flare signs in tube parts fell in the herb pack.

A slice then met a germ part dare through the vent. Herb hens showed low flare gene marks at two days, low harm scores at four weeks, and held a high lay rate and low feed cost past the dare. Yolk weight and spot scores rose too.
pmc-13595494:
Simon Clay and Wayne Hall wrote a 2026 debate piece about harm reduction. Harm reduction means helping people use drugs more safely. It also fights stigma around drug use. The authors say the field overlooks two large harms.

One harm is environmental damage from illegal drug production. The other is violence faced by people who carry drugs across borders. Many carriers act out of poverty or gang threats. These harms happen before drugs reach any user. The authors argue policy should count them too. A fuller picture could change international drug strategy.
pmc-13595794:
Mia C Somenzi leads an eleven-author team modeling the human blood-brain barrier in a dish to watch how the parasite Toxoplasma gondii, carried by roughly a third of humanity, attacks it. Their 2026 study used brain-like vessel cells grown from human stem cells, a system that mimics the barrier's tight seals.

Infection drove the cells to pour out CCL2, a signal that summons immune cells, and the signal itself turned out to damage the barrier, a previously unrecognized role. The immune messenger interferon-gamma pushed back on both fronts, limiting CCL2 release and protecting the barrier from parasite-driven breakdown. The authors describe this as a defense built into the barrier cells themselves, not merely help arriving from immune cells. The work lays groundwork for understanding how the parasite threatens the brain and where protection might be reinforced.
pmc-13600394:
Mach and colleagues use aged mice to study frailty, many drugs at once, and drug cuts. Older people often take five or more drugs. Stopping some may help, but effects are hard to trace. Mice got one drug, a mix of drugs, or plain food from mid life. At late age, half of each group had drugs slowly stopped. A smart cage then tracked each mouse for close to a full day. It logged rest, moves, and grooming.

Drug mixes changed daily acts in ways single drugs did not predict. Some changes reversed when drugs stopped. Others stayed, and new ones showed. Frailty paths split into four clear groups.
pmc-13600994:
Fabien Squara and his team test a sound probe in the lab at the time. They use it to push the food pipe to one side in care for a fast, off-beat heart. Their 2026 study looks at future cases as they come. It takes up harm to the food pipe, a known side ill of burn of heart flesh near that pipe.

Sixty sick folk were split twixt probe shift care and plain care in steps to seal off lung veins. Barium pics found the food pipe, and the probe moved it from mark spots. A good split was won in near seventy-eight in each hundred of vein pairs. That stood next to thirty in each hundred at the start. Lap twixt vein and food pipe fell from near half to near none in the wake of the shift. Heat checks ran in both groups all through.
pmc-13602094:
Eun Jeong Kim and four colleagues map body shape variation in the stone flounder from Korean coastal waters in 2026. The stone flounder is a commercially valued flatfish of nearshore seabeds. The team measured 81 body indices and applied geometric shape analysis to wild fish from two coastal regions. They weighed the influence of size, sex, and capture site together rather than one at a time.

Classical measurements pointed to body size and sex as the main shape drivers, while site effects were smaller and context-dependent. Geometric analysis agreed, and still detected clear separation between sites. Size and sex each bent the growth trajectory, while site did not. Mitochondrial DNA showed moderate genetic difference between the regions, weakly but significantly tied to shape distance. The authors present a baseline for managing this fishery species and future breeding work.
pmc-13606894:
Caiqin Xu, Tao Zhou, Ying Huang, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2026. It catalogs the MAG2 gene family in alfalfa, genes that help run the cell's internal shipping system for proteins.

The MAG2 complex acts as a tether, catching vesicles that ferry cargo between two of the cell's sorting stations. Using pattern searches against the alfalfa genome, the team found seven family members. Four fell into one branch of the family and three into another. Maps of the chromosomes suggest that copied segments of DNA helped the family grow. The genes share tidy, conserved structures, and their control regions carry many switches tied to hormones, light, and stress. The authors say the genes likely join in growth and stress responses, a claim later lab work can test.
pmc-13608494:
Hajira Karim and colleagues report a two thousand twenty-six multinational survey on gender differences among urologists in kidney stone care. The treatment in focus uses shock waves from outside the body to break stones. Practice patterns may differ between male and female specialists.

Thousands of urologists and trainees from over one hundred countries answered in seven languages. Women were a small minority of respondents. Matching balanced experience, region, and career stage between groups. Matched comparisons then examined diagnosis, treatment choices, and follow-up habits. The study gives stone care a rare, large-scale look at how clinician gender relates to practice.
pmc-13609194:
Peiqi Yan and four colleagues follow the gut microbiome across the stages of coronary artery disease. The microbial community changed most sharply at the heart attack stage. Network connections thinned from mild disease through unstable angina, then flipped to an antagonism-dominated web during heart attack. Stage-specific stool markers could aid staging, the authors propose.
pmc-13609494:
Angélica Ríos-Gallardo and three co-workers review andrographolide, a plant agent, as hope for care of Alzheimer's and Parkinson's ills. Both ills kill nerve cell groups and take in clumps of protein. Cures on hand stay scant, which pushes eyes toward goods from nature with more than one act. It tunes many switch points and paths in brain cells. In ill models it turned back loss of thought and loss of motion. The 2026 review draws the steps behind those guard acts as one. Much proof stays at lab stage. The team maps what is firm and what tests in men must prove before use in care.
pmc-13611494:
Bu and five co-authors evaluated a wireless strain sensor system in this paper from twenty twenty-six. Rock bolts in mines need monitoring that survives processing and radio transfer intact. On a lab fixture, ten loading runs tracked the input almost perfectly. Temperature compensation cut false thermal drift by roughly ninety percent or more. All forty-five alarm trials behaved as pre-recorded expectations said. Fifty of sixty data transfers arrived clean, including one full thousand-record history. The authors call it a one-asset lab proof before underground trials.
pmc-13612194:
Muhammad Ibrar Ahmad leads a seven-author team pooling trials of mixed exercise in women with breast cancer. Glucose, insulin, triglycerides, LDL cholesterol, and systolic pressure did not change significantly. Studies varied a lot underneath the averages, which the authors flag. Secondary analysis hinted that bigger exercise doses bought bigger gains. They call for dose-finding trials to pin down how much combined training is enough.
pmc-13612394:
Ciara Loughrey and a large team tracked how a parasite spreads inside mice, in work reported in two thousand twenty-six. The parasite causes a grave disease that hits the spleen, liver, and bone marrow. Yet it can also sit in other tissues with no clear signs of harm.

The team marked the parasites with tags, so each group could be traced from tissue to tissue. They found the parasites move both ways between the inner organs and the skin, again and again. Some sites sent out far more parasites than the rest, acting as hubs. When immune pressure changed, the main routes changed too. These finds may help explain relapse and failed treatment.
pmc-13612994:
Nikolaos D. Tantaroudas leads a team describing a low-cost platform for watching the health of rural bridges, built under the Horizon Europe FUTURAL project. Their answer combines passing vehicles, cheap internet-linked sensors, and a phone app called FUTURAPP that pairs with small motion sensors plugged into smartphones.

Readings flow to cloud computers for safe storage and handling. A neural network trained on shaking patterns in the 2 to 15 hertz range learns each bridge's normal behaviour and flags changes that may signal damage. Computer models of the bridges, built with ANSYS software, help the team judge what the sensor data mean. The goal is bridge checks that rural towns can actually afford to run.
pmc-13613794:
Adebiyi Adesina, Meltem Odabaş, Heidi Quinn, Moazzam Ali, and Elizabeth A. They priced six methods, from condoms and pills to implants and intrauterine devices, under two futures: current rules on who may provide each method, and wider sharing under the global guidance. Comparing the direct costs shows where savings are largest and which methods gain most. For health planners short of both staff and cash, the numbers show a concrete route to reaching more people with the same budget.
pmc-13614194:
Reem Nsouli leads a team building a tunable light reactor that lets chemists screen 24 reactions at once while setting the light for each well on its own. Being able to vary light itself, like any other ingredient, turns a hidden factor into a measured one. Labs can now learn which light recipe a reaction truly wants instead of settling for whatever lamp hangs over the bench.
pmc-13614294:
Bar Chen leads a large team reporting in 2026 on a transistor-based sensor that can tell living bacteria from dead ones, a skill current low-cost sensors lack. Tests ran in droplets of just half a microlitre of rich bacterial broth, with no washing or sample prep before measuring. The sensor picked up even a single bacterium, gave readings in real time without labels, and rose in a clean straight line with bacterial counts. It also separated live from dead cells. Food plants and water testers could gain a fast on-site check that answers the question that matters most: is this contamination still alive?
pmc-13614994:
Henrique Fernando Lopes-Araujo and colleagues examine a puzzle in Brazil's HIV record from 2015 to 2024 in a 2026 study: new HIV infections rose while AIDS cases and deaths from AIDS fell. Brazil is praised worldwide for its public response to the epidemic. Starting treatment within 30 days rose from 28 percent of patients to 63 percent, while starting more than six months late fell from 35 percent to 10 percent. Faster, stronger treatment explains much of the fall in illness and death. The rising count of new infections points the other way, toward gaps in prevention. The study shows policy makers exactly where the next effort belongs.
pmc-13615594:
Ang and colleagues compare two trifocal lens implants for cataract patients with mild corneal astigmatism, an uneven curve of the eye front. Trifocal lenses split light for near, mid, and far sight. One type also corrects astigmatism, while the other does not.

Records covered one hundred sixty-seven eyes seen six to twelve months after surgery. Sight scores without glasses were much the same across lens groups. The astigmatism-correcting lenses left less leftover focusing error after surgery. Gains stood out most in eyes with against-the-rule astigmatism, where the steep curve runs sideways. No extra glare or halos were reported with the correcting lenses.
pmc-13616094:
Laura Falceto Font led a 2026 methods paper on editing blood-forming stem and progenitor cells with CRISPR/Cas9. The aim was to speed cell therapies and immune therapies toward the clinic. These stem cells can rebuild the whole blood and immune system. Editing them has been slow, costly, and hard to scale, especially for mouse cells. Editing reached up to 80 percent gene knockdown while cells stayed viable. Edited mouse cells rebuilt bone marrow in lethally irradiated mice. pmc-13617094:
Luis Martínez-Heredia and thirteen colleagues examine immune cell patterns in hypophosphatasia, a rare inherited disorder where a missing enzyme, tissue-nonspecific alkaline phosphatase, weakens bones and teeth. Blood tests, inflammation markers, stool markers, and detailed immune cell profiling were combined.

Patients showed lower levels of the enzyme on T cells, B cells, neutrophils, and monocytes, along with shifts in several cell ratios. Immune-mediated inflammatory diseases were common in this clinic group and came with lower enzyme activity and higher gut inflammation markers. Certain cell patterns tracked with having such a disease. Because the study is a single snapshot, the authors stress it cannot prove the enzyme shortage causes inflammation, only that the two travel together.
pmc-13618394:
Shouyu Wu and nine colleagues demonstrate a way to sculpt with light at the nanoscale in three dimensions, using a single femtosecond laser pulse split into thousands of focal points.
